title: How I built Folio: 41 free PDF tools and an editor that changes existing text
description:
Folio is a free online PDF studio: 41 tools to merge, split, compress, convert to and from Word, Excel, PowerPoint and images, OCR, sign, protect and redact, plus a full page editor that can change the text already in a PDF. There is no account and no sign-up. Files are processed on Folio's own server and deleted after 6 hours (24 hours for documents open in the editor).

Open Folio

The problem

Everyday PDF jobs are small: join two files, shrink one to fit an upload limit, turn a scan into searchable text, sign a form. I wanted one place that does all of them without an account or a payment step, and an editor that changes the words already on the page instead of only drawing new ones on top.

Decisions that shaped it

  1. One tool is one Python function. Every tool is run(inputs, options, out_dir) that returns the output files, registered with its title, category, accepted file types and an option schema. The React front end draws each tool's options from that schema, so adding a tool means one function and one registry entry, with no new page to build. Workflows reuse the same registry: the files one step produces are the inputs of the next, so "make searchable, then compress" is just two entries in a list.

  2. Use proven engines, and write the glue. PyMuPDF does parsing, rendering, editing and redaction. pikepdf (qpdf underneath) handles encryption and repair, pdf2docx keeps tables and layout when going to Word, pymupdf4llm keeps headings, lists and links when going to Markdown, and Tesseract does OCR with English, Hindi and Tamil installed. On the server, LibreOffice converts Office files and a headless Chromium prints web pages to PDF.

  3. Edit the real text, not a layer over it. The server renders each page as an image and sends back every text span with its box, font, size and colour. When you click a span and type, the old text is removed with a redaction that leaves images alone, and the new text is written into the same box. Fonts embedded in PDFs are usually subsets that lack the letters you are adding, so Folio looks up the same family among the installed fonts, with metric-compatible free stand-ins on the server (Liberation Sans for Arial, Carlito for Calibri). Every save is a new version of the document, so undo just goes back one.

  4. Text inside pictures gets the same treatment. Scans and screenshots have no text layer, so OCR reads each line, then Folio works out the font, weight and size by rendering installed fonts against the image and comparing. An edit redraws only from the first changed letter onward, with matching anti-aliasing, so the change blends in.

  5. Redaction removes, it does not cover. Matching text is taken out of the file itself, with presets for email addresses, phone numbers and card numbers, and the metadata can be wiped too. A black box drawn over text that is still underneath is not a redaction.

  6. The website says only what the server can do. The same code also runs as a local app on a PC. The website leaves out what its server can't serve: Translate PDF needs a translation model the server doesn't have, so the site lists 41 tools instead of 42, and the pages that manage a computer's own folders, AI models and saved details are switched off there and kept out of search. The privacy line, the tool count and the hours files are kept all come from one file, and the build checks the tool count against the real tool list.

  7. Test every tool. The backend has 161 test functions covering conversions, page organising and security, editor operations, OCR quality, screenshot text editing and batch speed.

Built with

Python, FastAPI, PyMuPDF, pikepdf, Tesseract, LibreOffice, React, TypeScript, Vite, Docker

Originally published at folio.niranjand.in.

title: Building a Resume Editor That Exports Real Text: A4 Layout, Vector PDFs and DOCX
description:
On paper, building a resume editor sounds like a weekend project.

You throw together a two-column layout: form inputs on the left, a live preview on the right, and a shiny "Download PDF" button up top. Simple, right?

Except it almost never is.

The moment a user actually relies on your tool to apply for a job, expectations skyrocket. They expect the exported file to mirror the on-screen preview pixel for pixel. They expect it to fit neatly onto standard A4 paper without awkward blank gaps. They want the typography intact. And most importantly: they expect the output to be a living, breathing document—one with selectable, copyable text that applicant tracking systems (ATS) can actually parse, and maybe even a Word (.docx) file they can tweak later.

While building Pagewise, I quickly realized a fundamental truth that reshaped how I approached the entire architecture:

A document that looks great in a web browser isn’t guaranteed to survive printing, PDF parsing, or external word processors.

Most web tools take the easy way out and treat resumes like glorified screenshots. We wanted Pagewise to treat a resume as a real document.

Here is how we tackled the engineering headaches behind making that happen.

1. The A4 Problem: A Browser Is Not a Sheet of Paper

Web browsers are built for fluid, responsive layouts. Documents are the exact opposite they are strictly bound by physical dimensions.

An A4 page is strictly:

  • Width: 210 mm
  • Height: 297 mm

When you design a document editor purely using pixels or viewport percentages, you set yourself up for heartbreak. A layout might look gorgeous on a 1440p monitor, but the second the user tries to print or export it, things fall apart:

  • Browser print drivers apply arbitrary scaling.
  • Default margins eat away at your layout.
  • Sections awkwardly break right across the middle of a job title.
  • Content spills over onto a practically empty second page.

To solve this, we had to stop treating the canvas like a responsive webpage and start treating it as a physical medium.

Our CSS establishes a rigid document boundary matching real-world paper dimensions:

.resume-page {
  width: 210mm;
  min-height: 297mm;
  box-sizing: border-box;
  position: relative;
  background: #ffffff;
}

@media print {
  @page {
    size: A4;
    margin: 0;
  }
  .resume-page {
    width: 210mm;
    min-height: 297mm;
    margin: 0;
    box-shadow: none;
  }
}

Note: This is a simplified snippet, but it highlights the core mindset shift.

Of course, CSS dimensions alone don’t magically solve pagination. When a user writes a lengthy work history, handling dynamic overflow without severing bullet points mid-sentence requires active content measurement and calculated page breaks.

2. Typography Is Document Geometry, Not Just Decoration

One of the sneakiest bugs we ran into had nothing to do with margins or flexbox it was fonts.

In web design, a font change is mostly cosmetic. In fixed-geometry document design, fonts dictate layout math.

A subtle change in font weight, letter spacing, or line height can:

  • Alter exact line-wrapping points.
  • Expand a 2-line bullet point into 3 lines.
  • Increase section height by just 4 pixels... pushing an entire section onto an unwanted second page.

This becomes a nightmare when your frontend preview uses local system fonts or Google Fonts, while your backend PDF engine runs on a Linux server that has neither. When the server falls back to standard Helvetica or DejaVu Sans, your carefully calibrated single-page resume suddenly bleeds into page two.

Our Font Normalization Matrix

To combat this, we set up a controlled normalization strategy. Whenever a user picks a common font, our pipeline pairs it with verified, metrically close open-source equivalents across environments:

Requested Font Normalized / Open-Source Equivalent
Georgia Lora / Liberation Serif
Arial Arimo
Calibri Carlito

Are they 100% identical down to the sub-pixel kerning pair in every environment? No. But this controlled mapping drastically reduces surprise layout shifts.

The takeaway: If typography shifts between preview and export, your document geometry breaks. Font consistency must be treated as an infrastructure problem.

3. The "Canvas Trap": Why We Refused to Flatten to Images

If you look at how many modern web apps generate PDFs, you'll see a very common shortcut:

  1. Run html2canvas to take a screenshot of the DOM.
  2. Slap that raster image inside a jsPDF wrapper.
  3. Call it a day.

It looks identical to the preview! It’s fast to build!

And it produces a terrible resume.

When you turn a document into a flat picture, you destroy its utility:

Screenshot / Canvas PDF True Vector & Text PDF
Text is baked into flat pixels Text remains sharp, selectable, and highlightable
Copy-pasting text is impossible Recruiters can easily copy contact info or bullet points
ATS parsers fail or require messy OCR ATS software reads native text streams directly
Blurry when zoomed in or printed Crisp vector rendering at any scale
Zero screen-reader accessibility Screen-reader friendly

Imagine a recruiter trying to copy your email or phone number from a resume, only to find they're clicking on a JPEG. Or worse, an automated ATS pipeline rejecting your application because it couldn't extract a single keyword from an image.

At Pagewise, we committed to true vector text. When you download a PDF, the text remains real, selectable text. While no format can guarantee 100% compatibility across every single outdated ATS parser in existence, outputting real text gives candidates the best possible shot.

4. One Data Model, Two Completely Different Export Paths

People don’t just want PDFs. A huge chunk of users still need an editable Microsoft Word (.docx) file—whether to submit through job portals that require it or to make custom adjustments for a specific application.

The naive solution would be trying to convert the rendered HTML into Word, or exporting an image into a DOCX file. Both create a mess.

Instead, we decoupled our document state from our rendering targets. A single JSON resume model feeds into an export dispatcher with two dedicated pipelines:
┌────────────────────────┐
│ Resume Document Model │
└───────────┬────────────┘
│
Export Dispatcher
/ \
/ \
v v
┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐
│ Visual Pipeline │ │ python-docx │
│ (Vector PDF) │ │ (XML-level) │
└────────┬────────┘ └────────┬────────┘
│ │
v v
┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐
│ Sharp, ATS-ready│ │ Native Editable │
│ PDF Document │ │ Word Styles │
└─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘

  • Path A (Visual PDF): Renders the document model through a headless browser environment configured with strict print stylesheets, generating real text, vector borders, and predictable page breaks.
  • Path B (Native DOCX): Feeds the raw structured data into python-docx. Instead of hacking HTML tags into Word, it builds real Word paragraphs, native headings, real bullet lists, and genuine XML table structures.

This means when a user opens the .docx file in Microsoft Word, they aren’t fighting broken floating textboxes or glued-together layouts—they get a clean, standard Word document styled with native typography.

5. The Hard Reality: Document Fidelity Is an Ongoing Battle

Does having a single data model magically solve every cross-format inconsistency?

Honestly? No.

Word and web browsers use fundamentally different layout engines. Word calculates line wraps, margin collapse, and paragraph spacing under its own rules.

A layout that comfortably leaves 15mm of breathing room at the bottom of an A4 PDF might push the last bullet point onto page two in Microsoft Word. A header accent bar that looks sleek in CSS requires a careful table border hack in DOCX XML.

Maintaining parity between on-screen previews, generated PDFs, and native Word documents isn’t a one-and-done feature. It’s an ongoing process of calibrating margins, tuning line heights, and testing edge cases.

6. What Building This Taught Us

Building Pagewise forced us to look past the surface of web UI and think deeply about document architecture.

A resilient document editor has to separate three distinct layers:

  1. Content: The raw data (your jobs, dates, skills, metrics).
  2. Presentation: How that data looks right now on the screen.
  3. Target Output: How that data must behave inside an external ecosystem (A4 paper, Adobe Acrobat, Word, ATS scanners).

When you keep those concerns clean and distinct, the system stops being a fragile hack and starts behaving like a real document engine.

What's Next?

We're continuing to refine Pagewise’s rendering engine to make multi-page handling and layout customization even smoother. Alongside the document pipeline, we've also introduced Wiser AI a companion tool that helps analyze job descriptions, flag missing skills, and suggest targeted resume improvements without taking away user control.

If you want to see how the editor works in practice (or test the exports yourself), check it out here:
👉 Pagewise

Let's Chat

If you’ve built document editors, invoice generators, or report exporters:

  • How do you bridge the gap between browser DOM previews and print/export parity?
  • Do you use headless browser rendering, native PDF libraries, or something else entirely?

I'd love to hear how other teams handle this in the comments!

title: What Makes a Cloud a Cloud? The Five Stamps That Decide
description:
TL;DR: What makes a cloud a cloud is a test in one NIST sentence from September 2011: computing capabilities drawn from a shared pool, reached over a network on demand, released with minimal management effort, and metered, and a service earns the word only when all five stamps that follow from it hold.

  • NIST SP 800-145 (September 2011, authors Peter Mell and Tim Grance) holds the reference definition, and its load-bearing phrases are “shared pool” and “minimal management effort”; a paraphrase that drops either is describing rented servers.
  • The five stamps: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service. A candidate service passes only with all five.
  • Security, automation, resilience, budget-friendliness, and flexibility are badges: outcomes the stamps produce, never parts of the definition.
  • Scalability is designed headroom; elasticity adds automatic shrinking, so a fixed monthly server can scale and still fail stamp four.
  • Amazon S3’s SLA pays a 10 percent credit below 99.9 percent monthly uptime, and egress past the first free 100 GB a month runs about $0.09 per GB.

The label “cloud” costs a vendor nothing to print, so the lesson embedded above replaces it with a test that costs something to pass. This article is the companion to that Whiteboard Architect episode: watch the full episode on YouTube to see the boards drawn, or read on: same claims, sources named, plus the tables and fine print a whiteboard cannot hold.

The cold-open board: the label anyone can print, and the five stamp test that decides.

The sentence that decides, and its two load-bearing phrases

Peter Mell and Tim Grance at NIST published Special Publication 800-145 in September 2011, three pages that still arbitrate the word. The model it describes: capabilities over a network whenever wanted, from a pool shared among tenants, handed back with barely any management effort, metered throughout.

Two phrases in that sentence do the discriminating, and both are checkable. A “shared pool” means no machine carries your name plate: the provider reassigns resources as demand moves, and the strongest location promise is a country or a datacenter, never a rack. “Minimal management effort” means provisioning happens without a human on the provider’s side: you click a console or call an API, and the capacity exists minutes later.

Paraphrase carelessly and the test disappears. A common summary compresses it into delivering IT resources over the Internet: the convenience survives, both phrases go missing, and a rented dedicated server starts calling itself a cloud. The sentence also travels: a later ISO standard carries a compatible definition, and contracts and textbooks worldwide follow it.

What does the NIST sentence say, word for word?

The spine of SP 800-145’s definition, quoted in fragments: computing capabilities are available as “a shared pool of configurable computing resources” that can be “rapidly provisioned and released” with “minimal management effort or service provider interaction.” The full sentence opens with “ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access” to that pool, adds the parenthetical resource list, “e.g., networks, servers, storage, applications, and services,” and sits on page 2 of the paper’s three-page body.

The clause paraphrases drop first is the interaction one. It limits the humans on the provider’s side of each request, so a portal whose every action waits on a sales engineer fails the sentence before a single stamp is checked. Quoting the paper is also the cheapest defense against drift: both phrases live in one sentence a reader can hold against any brochure.

How many deployment models does the standard count?

Four: private, community, public, and hybrid. Summaries that stop at three have usually dropped community, the pool shared by several organizations with requirements in common, for example agencies under one regulatory regime. Hybrid keeps dedicated and rented capacity joined, so a privacy-bound workload stays on the dedicated side while a seasonal surge rents.

Model Who the pool serves
Private One organization, on infrastructure set aside for it
Community Several organizations with requirements in common
Public Any tenant, on published terms
Hybrid A mixture of dedicated and rented, operated as one

The five stamps that decide what makes a cloud a cloud

SP 800-145 lists exactly five essential characteristics; the episode treats them as stamps, and the count has to reach five.

Stamp The demand it makes A service shape that fails it
On-demand self-service You provision compute, storage, or network capacity yourself, by console or API An order form that emails a human account team
Broad network access Capabilities travel by ordinary protocols to a phone as readily as a workstation A cluster reachable only from machines inside one office
Resource pooling Physical and virtual capacity in one multi-tenant pool, rebalanced as demand moves, with location promises stopping at datacenter or country A host that pins you to one named physical box
Rapid elasticity Capacity expands with a spike and contracts after it, sometimes with no operator involved Fixed monthly capacity, even rented and online in minutes
Measured service Usage monitored, controlled, and reported in units that fit the service, visible to both sides A flat monthly price with no meter behind it

Stamp four is the one advertisements lean on hardest. A team that doubles its instance count for a launch and leaves the extras running afterward has scaled; it turns elastic only when the extra instances terminate themselves once traffic falls. Rented capacity faces the same test, and the discriminating half is the shrink.

Stamp five makes the arrangement a utility: infrastructure bills by allocation and consumption, software by subscription or by use, and a capital budget becomes an operating line that tracks usage. Compute meters in instance-hours and storage in GB-months; both parties read the same numbers, which is what makes an invoice arguable line by line.

What the stamps decide, and what the brochure sells

Everything marketed around cloud computing beyond the five stamps is an outcome. The board splits the vocabulary into two boxes: stamps settle whether a service is a cloud at all, badges score how good a cloud it is. Security, automation, resilience, budget-friendliness, and flexibility sit in the second box; none appears in the paper’s characteristics.

Each badge traces to a stamp or to engineering on top of the definition.

Brochure badge Where it actually comes from
Security Configuration plus shared responsibility; the definition is silent on it
Automation The shape minimal management effort takes at fleet scale
Resilience Redundancy engineering, passive or active, on pooled capacity
Budget-friendliness The meter, plus a workload shaped to suit it
Flexibility Elasticity plus self-service: change allocation yourself, any hour

Board 6 of 15: the stamps settle what the thing is; the badges score how good it is.

Where the two usual impostors fail

Two impostors wear the word most often. An on-premises data center is hardware bought and staffed for the busiest hour of the year; the meter fails first, since no per-use bill exists, and self-service usually goes with it, since provisioning runs through a ticket queue. A dedicated server rented online in minutes sits closer: network reachable, quick to order, but fixed. Nothing shrinks the allocation once traffic drops, and the monthly fee is flat.

The claim Stamps it fails Why
A “cloud” private data center 1 and 5, commonly No self-service path, no per-use meter; capacity is bought for the peak
A “cloud” rented dedicated server 4 and 5 Fixed allocation, flat invoice; capacity never follows load
A cloud by the definition None Self-service, network reach, pooled, elastic, metered: five for five

The logo’s sincerity never enters the test: excellent hardware can still stop one stamp short.

Can a private deployment pass the stamps?

Yes, and the definition never asks who owns the plant. The five characteristics and the four deployment models are separate axes in SP 800-145, so a private cloud built on an organization’s own virtualized hardware qualifies whenever it offers the same pattern: a self-service portal, a pooled substrate, allocation that follows demand, and an internal meter. The checklist from this episode applies to it with no edits, which is also why “we bought our own machines” settles nothing by itself.

Two words the brochure merges: scalable and elastic

Scalability is a system’s ability to absorb a growing workload when resources are added; it is headroom an architect designs in, and the adding can stay manual. Elasticity is stricter: the platform provisions and releases capacity on its own, tracking demand closely in both directions, and the difference matters once a bill is attached. A rented server scales, since a second one is one order away; hours after the spike has passed, the invoice still lists two servers. Elasticity removes the second line.

A later episode gives the pair its own treatment. The question to put to any claimed cloud: when demand falls, do the capacity or the bill fall with it, absent a human in the loop?

Automation, resilience, and the energy bill

Automation never appears as a sixth stamp: it is a consequence. Minimal management effort, applied across a provider’s fleet, turns into software doing the installing, configuring, and maintaining. Orchestration, the wider layer, aligns entire workflows, joining configuration, coordination, and deployment in service of larger goals; automation on its own runs one repetitive task, such as provisioning a volume or applying an update. The board draws the relationship as nested boxes: the single task inside, the whole workflow around it.

Board 9 of 15: one repetitive task in the inner box, the workflow around it in the outer.

Where exactly is the line between automation and orchestration?

The size of the job. Automation removes people from one repetitive task: creating an account, provisioning a volume, patching an operating system. Orchestration runs the sequence: it invokes those automations in order, carries state between the steps, and unwinds the work when a step fails. The board’s inner box holds the first kind of job, the outer box the second, and a green arrow connects the small one to the phrase larger goals. Neither box is a stamp; both are what the fifth and first stamps look like from inside the provider’s building.

Resilience, also a badge, reduces to redundancy engineering. Providers keep copies of data and of components across many servers and sites, so the loss of one machine, or of a whole site, removes capacity while the service keeps running. Passive redundancy is capacity held before anything breaks, the way a cluster at half load can lose a node and keep answering, slower; active redundancy is machinery that notices a failure and reroutes the work on its own.

Where do the cloud energy numbers come from?

An IEA estimate put global data center electricity use at roughly 1.5 percent in 2024. Hyperscale operators raise utilization through consolidation and virtualization, site buildings near renewable supply, cool with outside air, reuse waste heat, and shift flexible work into the cleaner hours of the grid. A Microsoft, Accenture, and WSP study cited by the Cloud for Global Good briefing puts the energy saving from moving on-premises software to the cloud at 30 to 90 percent. The top of the range is the best case, and where a given migration lands depends on its shape.

Uptime is sold as nines, paid back as credits

No provider sells constant uptime; the product is a monthly uptime percentage with service credits attached. The Amazon S3 service level agreement shows the standard shape: a credit worth 10 percent of the bill when monthly uptime lands under 99.9 percent, 25 percent under 99.0, and 100 percent under 95.0. The credit is the agreement’s “sole and exclusive remedy”: this refund is the whole remedy. S3’s own exclusions cover factors outside AWS’s reasonable control, from force majeure to internet trouble beyond the network’s demarcation point, the customer’s own actions and equipment, and account suspension or termination. Planned maintenance, the item cloud-SLA summaries usually list, does not appear in that agreement at all.

What do the nines add up to in downtime per year?
Commitment Approximate downtime per year
99 percent 3.7 days
99.9 percent 8.8 hours
99.99 percent 53 minutes
99.999 percent 5.3 minutes

Reading the nines as hours makes the ladder concrete: 99.9 percent tolerates roughly nine hours of downtime in a year, and 99.99 percent about fifty-three minutes. The arithmetic assumes a year of 8,760 hours. The agreement measures monthly windows rather than annual ones, so a single bad month can owe a credit inside an otherwise unremarkable year, and the percentages govern availability, a narrower thing than data durability, which S3 documents separately.


The invoice, item by item

Advertisements say no additional fees or hidden costs; the pricing page answers in a friendly font, and its component list runs storage, requests and data retrieval, data transfer, management and insights, replication, then transform and query. Requests are metered per thousand, a thousand GETs at $0.0004, and reads from the colder tiers, Standard-Infrequent-Access and Glacier, carry a retrieval charge on top of storage. Internet egress is free for the first 100 GB each month, an allowance aggregated across all AWS services and regions, China and GovCloud excepted, rather than an S3-only quota; beyond it S3 charges about $0.09 per GB in the Ireland example. S3 Intelligent-Tiering adds a monthly monitoring and automation charge per object kept there, and the management features meter by the million objects they cover. Storage itself bills the GB-month for whatever remains: the bucket a migration left behind accrues charges exactly like production data, until somebody empties it.

Which S3 line items surprise teams on a normal bill?
Line item What triggers it
Storage GB-months of data at rest; the row everyone expects
Egress Bytes leaving to the Internet; the first 100 GB a month is free account-wide (all AWS services combined, China and GovCloud excepted), then about $0.09 per GB in the Ireland example
Requests Billed per thousand; GET requests run $0.0004 per 1,000
Retrieval Reads from the Infrequent-Access and Glacier tiers, charged on top of storage
Monitoring and automation A monthly charge per object kept in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering class, for watching access patterns and moving objects between tiers
Idle allocations Resources nobody deleted; they bill until someone does

The table reads as a trap only when the shape of the workload is unknown. A static site with a CDN in front sees one row; a nightly full restore from cold storage meets several at once. The meter does not hide these lines; the brochure just declines to enumerate them.

Is encryption at rest automatic on S3?

The blanket claim that providers store your data encrypted flattens several distinct arrangements. Since January 5, 2023, Amazon S3 has applied default SSE-S3 encryption to every newly uploaded object, free of charge. The key-based alternatives, SSE-KMS and DSSE-KMS, wait for the customer to configure them. And responsibility for the data itself is shared across the provider line rather than transferred over it. Encryption is a badge earned by configuration, on both sides of that line.

What makes a cloud a cloud is the sentence NIST published in September 2011 plus the five characteristics attached to it, run as a checklist: the private data center stops at self-service and the meter, the dedicated server rented online in minutes at elasticity and the meter, and a service that meets all five earns the word regardless of who owns the hardware. The rest of the brochure, security and resilience included, scores how good a cloud is; the stamps alone settle membership.

Board 15 of 15: the recap checklist, with the sticky note carrying the operating rule.

Continue learning

  • What Cloud Computing Actually Is: The Honest First Lesson: the series opener: the definition, service models, and history.
  • You Already Use the Cloud Every Day (Without Noticing): the everyday services that were cloud computing before any checklist.
  • Containers vs Virtual Machines: The Problem Docker Solves: the lesson next door, on the machinery that lets one box serve many tenants.

The next lesson in this series, Cloud Trade-Offs, gives a full episode to what a pitch deck leaves unpriced, from the meter that never stops between traffic spikes to the cost of walking away.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI from the script of my video lesson, then checked against its sources before publishing.

title: Amazon WorkSpaces provides a new Windows client experience
description:
Amazon WorkSpaces provides a new Windows client experience for Amazon WorkSpaces Personal. The new client experience includes an updated interface, a simplified connection flow, easier-to-find settings, and the new WorkSpaces Advisor proactive troubleshooting (Public Preview) that suggests actions you can take to resolve common issue

WorkSpaces Advisor proactive troubleshooting (Public Preview) is an intelligent new capability that monitors key metrics from your device, network, and the WorkSpace itself, and provides you with actionable recommendations if there are issues with registration, sign-in, or the connection in general. The new client experience also includes an improved full screen experience, a welcome tour to help orient you, and for WorkSpaces that are admin-enabled, a self-service option to enable nested virtualization.

The new client experience is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Personal is available.

To learn more, visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Windows client documentation or download the Amazon WorkSpaces client.

title: Fluent Interface in C - Look ma, no this!
description:
by Daniel Miller, AI4SQL Team

Can C be Object Oriented? Yes!

Object-oriented languages like Python, Java, Rust, or C++ offer native object methods and automatic object lifetime cleanup, enabling chain operations on data structures, so you can call obj->a()->b()->c() and each method knows what it's working on. These fluent interfaces are common to many libraries that streamline configuration and reduce boilerplate. Let's take a look at an example:

ChSlice *mid = ch_new_String("One_Two_Three_Four")
    ->append("_Five_Six")
    ->split("_")
    ->sub_slice(1, 4);

puts(mid->generic.to_chars()); /* ["Two","Three","Four","Five"] */
ch_release(mid);

This chain of functions takes a string, appends it to another string, splits it into an array, and slices the array in one chain of function calls. It's a pretty basic demonstration of using fluent interfaces for building a data structure with method chaining. But if I told you this was plain ANSI-C, you would think I committed a preprocessor felony and leaked three heap allocations along the way. And there are two big reasons why:

  • There are no objects in C. No member variables or methods. No this or self to reference your object's data. The function append("_Five_Six") has no attached state, seeing only a single string literal and whatever is global.
  • There is no garbage collector. In standard C, chaining heap allocations together without saving each intermediate pointer to a variable and freeing it by hand inevitably results in a memory leak.

Manipulating strings and collections in C usually means threading state through standalone functions (str_append(s, ...)), holding onto every intermediate pointer, and freeing each temporary buffer by hand. We built iso-c-chaining to explore how far we could push fluent method chaining and automatic temporary cleanup using only standard ISO C. Here is how the library appends to a string, splits it on a delimiter, and takes a sub-slice of the resulting array in a single expression.

This code does exactly like you would expect in a modern language. It allocates a string and some kind of array, manipulates them both without a byte leaked, and cc -E shows the preprocessor never touched it. In fact, every C feature powering that chain has been part of the language since 1989 ANSI C (C89).

Party like it's 1989

Let's kick this up a notch. Take a kind of map, put another map inside it, and see what happens. That would surely break this no-leaking-or-preprocessor-tricks little C89 exercise. Well, it's time to party:

ChHash *user = ch_new_Hash(3)
    ->put("name", ch_new_String("Ada"))
    ->put("role", ch_new_Hash(2)
        ->put("title", ch_new_String("Engineer"))
        ->put("level", ch_new_Number(5)))
    ->put("active", ch_new_Boolean(1));

puts(user->generic.to_chars());
/* {"name":"Ada","role":{"title":"Engineer","level":5},"active":true} */
ch_release(user);

These put() calls are being asked to unravel the chain inside the chain of a map inside a map. Where is it going to find the right container? And now there are Strings and Numbers and Booleans, oh my!

How? You might remember: functions in C only see their arguments and whatever is global.

1. Scoping with static

C's static keyword does two different jobs depending on where you put it, and self() uses both at once:

static String* self(String *s) {
  static String *slf = NULL;
  if (s != NULL) {
    slf = s;
  }
  return slf;
}

The outer static scopes self() to the file (the type's .c implementation), but the inner static keeps slf around in every call. We cleverly use NULL to just retrieve the existing value, since we should never be setting our self pointer to NULL.

2. Casting generics

Since struct pointers in C can be cast as their first field, we take advantage of that to give us a baseline of functionality for our types:

struct ch_generic_el {
  int refs;
  void* (*bind)(ChGenericEl *);
  void* (*save)(void);
  void (*del)(void *);
  char* (*to_chars)(void);
};

Putting ChGenericEl first in every struct lets put(char *key, void *val) accept a String*, Number*, Boolean*, or Hash*, cast it to ChGenericEl*, and call to_chars() or del() without caring which type it is.

3. Stacking chains

A single slf pointer works until you build a Hash inside another Hash, where the inner Hash would overwrite the outer one. Adding prev_self and next_self pointers to ChGenericEl turns each type's self() into an intrusive stack:

if (s == (ChGenericEl*)-1) {
  *top_ptr = top->prev_self;
} else if (s != NULL && s != top) {
  s->prev_self = top;
  *top_ptr = s;
}
return *top_ptr;

Constructing the inner Hash pushes it on top of the outer Hash so .put("title", ...) and .put("level", ...) target the inner map, while passing -1 pops it back off. (And in C11, adding _Thread_local to top gives every thread its own independent stack.)

4. Counting garbage

And what about all those potential memory leaks? We're making elements mid-chain that get consumed before the chain is finished. Here we turn to the old classic: reference counting, but with a twist: Every new object starts with refs = 0, meaning nothing owns it yet. If a method like split() or sub_slice() consumes an object whose refs is still 0, it frees that temporary on the spot before returning the next link in the chain.

And when a container method like put() receives an element, it claims ownership:

if (elem == container_slf || el->refs == 0) {
  el->bind((ChGenericEl*)-1);
}
el->refs++;

Note that this means ephemeral objects are automatically released, so the caller needs to bind them manually if the ephemeral object is needed after the chain is complete.

Because the inline Hash enters put() with refs == 0:

  • el->bind((ChGenericEl*)-1) pops the finished inner Hash off the Hash self stack, restoring the outer Hash to the top so .put("active", ...) targets the outer map.
  • el->refs++ transitions the element from an unowned temporary (refs == 0) to a container-owned value (refs == 1). That keeps consuming methods from freeing it mid-chain if you later retrieve it with get(), and lets an element be shared across multiple containers or variables—each owner increments refs, and ch_release() decrements refs on every child in the tree, freeing each object only when its last reference drops to 0.

Now what can we do with this?

You might be thinking, "Wow, we could use this for all kinds of wonderful projects!" We chose a webserver instead:

ch_new_Server(8080)
    ->get("/users", list_users)
    ->get("/users/:id", get_user)
    ->post("/users", create_user)
    ->put("/users/:id", update_user)
    ->delete_route("/users/:id", delete_user)
    ->listen();

Each callback receives the parsed HTTP request: URL :id parameters, query string, and parsed JSON body. This is packaged as a Hash*, and whatever object the callback returns gets serialized to JSON (to_chars()) and freed automatically after the response is sent.

Here is what list_users looks like when wired up to a SQLite Db object:

static GenericEl* list_users(Hash *req) {
  return (GenericEl*)$(db)
      ->params($(req)->get("query"))
      ->query("SELECT id, name, role, score FROM users "
              "WHERE (:role IS NULL OR role = :role) "
              "  AND (:min_score IS NULL OR score >= :min_score) "
              "ORDER BY score DESC");
}

What comes back from ->query(...) is the rare combination of everything we built above: a Slice of Hashes holding Numbers and Strings as database result rows. Because every one of those types shares ChGenericEl, the server just calls to_chars() on the returned Slice to stream out [{"id":1,"name":"Alice","role":"admin","score":98.25}, ...] and releases the entire result tree in a single call once the response is sent.

Wait, what's with the $?

In our earlier examples, every chain started with a ch_new_* constructor. Inside list_users, however, db and req are already-existing objects, so before calling ->params(...) or ->get("query"), we need to reference our previously created elements by calling their bind() function pointer: db->bind((GenericEl*)db).

Nobody wants to type db->bind((GenericEl*)db) at the start of every statement, so the library provides four tiny one-line convenience macros:

  • $(obj) expands to ((obj)->bind((ChGenericEl*)(obj))) which binds a previously created variable so you can start chaining on it.
  • ->$$ expands to ->generic.save() which bumps refs (refs++) at the end of a chain when you want to keep an object in a variable (db = create(Db, ":memory:")->...->$$;) instead of letting the chain consume it as a temporary.
  • create(Type, ...) expands to ch_new_Type(...).
  • ->chars() expands to ->generic.to_chars().

Pulling back a little performance

You might look at this and think, "Wow, this is wrapping every single int in an object like it's a horrible java.lang.Integer." And you would be right, but we can take a page from JavaScript's TypedArrays and not have a bunch of function pointers attached to every element, giving us back the performance we expect from C:

TypedIntArray *scores = create(TypedIntArray, 0)
    ->push_n(6, 42, 15, 88, 23, 16, 4)
    ->sort()
    ->$$; /* [4, 15, 16, 23, 42, 88] */

Now a single TypedIntArray object wraps a raw contiguous int* buffer, so a massive array of integers isn't attached to an even more massive number of function pointers. TypedIntArray, TypedCharArray, and TypedFloatArray are included by default (and can be sorted, mapped, filtered, sliced, and dropped straight into a Hash for JSON serialization), or you can declare one for any fixed-width type with CH_DECLARE_TYPED_ARRAY.

In examples/chain_vector_db.c, TypedFloatArray stores 256-dimensional embedding vectors for over 4,000 Linux whatis man pages in SQLite—computing each vector's norm in a single map + reduce chain:

double norm = sqrt($(vec)
    ->subarray(0, vec->length)
    ->map(square_double)
    ->reduce(add_doubles, 0.0));

Try it out

We've released iso-c-chaining as an open source demonstration library under the Apache 2.0 license for C developers to explore, tinker with, or drop into side projects via its single-header build (chain_single.h). The full source, including TypedArrays, the JSON parser/serializer, and the SQLite/HTTP server examples, is available on GitHub at google/iso-c-chaining. Contributions and feedback may be given on the GitHub project directly.

title: SQL Server Isolation Levels Explained (with NOLOCK and RCSI)
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Isolation levels decide what a transaction is allowed to see while other transactions are changing the same data. They are the reason a report can block an order screen, or why NOLOCK sometimes returns rows twice. Understanding them helps you fix blocking without trading it for wrong results.

The three problems isolation levels prevent

  • Dirty read: you read a change another transaction has not committed yet, and it may later be rolled back.
  • Non-repeatable read: you read the same row twice in one transaction and get different values, because someone updated it in between.
  • Phantom read: you run the same query twice and new rows appear, because someone inserted rows that match your filter.

The isolation levels

READ UNCOMMITTED (and NOLOCK)

Readers take no shared locks, so they are never blocked by writers. The WITH (NOLOCK) table hint does the same thing for one table. The cost is more than "slightly stale data": you can read uncommitted changes that are later rolled back, and because pages can move during a scan, a query can skip rows or read the same row twice. Use it only where approximate answers are acceptable, never for money or anything you write back.

READ COMMITTED (the default)

You only see committed data. In its classic, locking form, a reader takes a short shared lock on each row it reads. If a writer holds an exclusive lock on that row, the reader waits. This is the most common source of readers and writers blocking each other.

READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI)

RCSI is a database option that changes how READ COMMITTED works. Instead of waiting on locks, readers see the last committed version of each row, kept in a version store in tempdb. Readers no longer block writers, and writers no longer block readers. It is enabled by default in Azure SQL Database.

ALTER DATABASE [YourDb]
SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON
WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;   -- needs a moment with no other active sessions

Test before enabling on SQL Server: it adds tempdb load, and code that relied on readers waiting for writers (for example, a "read the latest value then update" pattern without proper locking) can behave differently.

REPEATABLE READ

Shared locks on rows you read are held until the transaction ends, so no one can change those rows under you. New rows can still appear (phantoms). Blocking increases because locks are held longer.

SNAPSHOT

The whole transaction sees the database as it was when the transaction started, using row versions, without taking shared locks. It must be allowed at database level first:

ALTER DATABASE [YourDb] SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON;

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT;
BEGIN TRAN;
    -- every read here sees the same consistent point in time
COMMIT;

If two snapshot transactions update the same row, the second one fails with an update conflict (error 3960) and must be retried. That makes it ideal for consistent reports and less suited to busy update workloads.

SERIALIZABLE

The strictest level: it also locks the ranges you read, so no matching rows can be inserted until you finish. Results are fully consistent, but it causes the most blocking and is a common source of deadlocks. Use it only for short, specific operations that truly need it.

Quick comparison

Level Dirty reads Non-repeatable reads Phantoms Readers block writers?
Read Uncommitted Possible Possible Possible No
Read Committed (locking) No Possible Possible Briefly
Read Committed Snapshot No Possible Possible No
Repeatable Read No No Possible Yes
Snapshot No No No No
Serializable No No No Yes

Check what you are using 

-- Database-level row versioning settings
SELECT name, is_read_committed_snapshot_on, snapshot_isolation_state_desc
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = DB_NAME();

-- Isolation level of current sessions
SELECT session_id, transaction_isolation_level
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE is_user_process = 1;

In transaction_isolation_level, 1 = Read Uncommitted, 2 = Read Committed, 3 = Repeatable Read, 4 = Serializable and 5 = Snapshot.

Practical advice

  • Replace blanket NOLOCK hints with RCSI; you get non-blocking reads without dirty or duplicated rows.
  • Use Snapshot for long reports that need one consistent point in time.
  • Keep Repeatable Read and Serializable for short, specific transactions.
  • Watch out for libraries that silently raise isolation. For example, System.Transactions.TransactionScope in .NET defaults to Serializable unless you set the isolation level explicitly.

Related reading:

  • How to Fix SQL Server Deadlocks
  • How to Delete or Update Millions of Rows Safely
  • How to Find Slow Queries in SQL Server

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: Autopsy #06: Anatomy of a Hydration Mismatch & Full Subtree Bailout
description:
Painted at 320 ms, Wiped Clean at 1.4 Seconds

A product PR added a "Last updated" local timestamp badge inside the catalog header right above the <input name="q"> search bar. Local development ran in UTC on a fast workstation and showed zero visual glitches.

Thirty minutes after deploy, RUM telemetry recorded a CLS spike to 0.28 and a 9% jump in mobile search abandonment across non-UTC timezones. Users could see and tap the search bar at 320 ms, type two or three characters, and watch their input vanish at 1.4 seconds.

  • T+00:00: Streaming SSR release ships to edge workers.
  • T+10:00: FCP holds at 320 ms, allowing mobile users to tap and type into <input name="q"> immediately.
  • T+18:00: At t = 1.4 s when JS finishes hydrating, CLS spikes to 0.28, the filter sidebar jumps, and typed search characters vanish.
  • T+35:00: Mobile search abandonment rises 9% across non-UTC timezones.

Why suppressHydrationWarning Only Hid the Console Error

The first Slack reflex was to add suppressHydrationWarning on the timestamp <span> and wrap the search bar in a useEffect(() => setMounted(true), []) guard. Local console warnings vanished immediately.

In production, the flicker and wiped inputs got worse. suppressHydrationWarning only silences a single text node warning; it does not stop sibling mismatch bailouts when client URL parsing diverges from server defaults, and useEffect mount gating intentionally delays rendering the search input until after hydration, causing a second layout jump.

Five Steps From Early Paint to Destroyed Input

Streaming SSR gives the user interactive-looking HTML before JavaScript arrives. When traditional hydration wakes up and disagrees with the server's text or URL-derived state, the framework bails out of the SSR subtree, discards the live <input> DOM node, and mounts a fresh tree from scratch.

Step Through the Hydration Bailout Timeline

Tracing the Bailout in DevTools

01 → 02: The 1,080 ms Window Where HTML Exists Without JS

In the Network waterfall, the document response arrived as Transfer-Encoding: chunked at 320 ms, painting the header and search box immediately while the 180 KB client bundle was still downloading. Under Streaming SSR & Flushing, early HTML chunks let users interact with native <input> elements long before JavaScript executes.

At t = 1,400 ms, the client bundle finished parsing and called hydrateRoot. Unlike Resumability vs Hydration, which serializes listener closures into HTML, traditional hydration must re-execute the entire component tree on the client to attach event handlers and verify DOM parity.

02 → 03: One Mismatch, One Discarded Subtree

Opening the console on a UTC+2 browser profile logged: Warning: Text content did not match. Server: "14:00" Client: "16:00". That single string divergence inside <CatalogHeader> triggered Hydration Mismatch Mechanics: React marked the nearest Suspense/root boundary dirty, threw away the server-rendered DOM nodes (including the <input name="q"> element), and replaced them with newly created client nodes.

03 → 04: The Query Param the Server Never Saw

Even after fixing the timestamp, mobile users landing on /catalog?sort=price still hit a bailout. The server handler read req.url without forwarding normalized search params into the initial React props, while the client component read window.location.search directly during render. When URL as State Store is parsed differently on server and client, the first client render produces a mismatched filter tree.

04 → 05: Focus Lost in Router Reconciliation

When the root boundary bailed out, Client-Side Router Internals swapped the DOM subtree containing <input name="q">. Because focus and uncommitted input.value live on the physical DOM element instance rather than in virtual DOM props, replacing the node wiped every character the user typed during that 1.08-second window.

Locking Server and Client Inputs to One Snapshot 

export function CatalogHeader({ serverUrl, serverIso }: Props) {
  const [clientTime, setClientTime] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const params = new URLSearchParams(serverUrl.split('?')[1] ?? '');

  useEffect(() => {
    setClientTime(new Date(serverIso).toLocaleTimeString());
  }, [serverIso]);

  return (
    <header>
      <time dateTime={serverIso}>{clientTime ?? 'UTC'}</time>
      <input name="q" defaultValue={params.get('q') ?? ''} />
    </header>
  );
}

Architectural Invariants:

  • Zero non-deterministic render values: Never call new Date().toLocaleTimeString(), Math.random(), or window.* during initial render; defer locale formatting to useEffect with reserved layout space.
  • Single URL source of truth: Pass the serialized request URL/params from the server into the root props so server and client hydrate identical trees.
  • Preserve physical <input> nodes: Keep form controls outside mismatch-prone subtrees so user keystrokes typed before JS boot survive hydration.

Golden Rule: Hydration must be a pure function of serialized server props; any client-only clock or URL read during initial render destroys the DOM node the user is already typing into.

title: October 21, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

Apigee Emulator

Apigee Emulator v2.0.2

On October 21, 2026, we released Apigee Emulator version 2.0.2.

This release upgrades the Apigee Emulator runtime to Java 21 (Eclipse Temurin JRE 21) to align local proxy development and policy execution with the production Apigee runtime, while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra datastore pinned to Java 8. It also addresses 46 security vulnerabilities across Netty, Jackson, Apache Log4j, BouncyCastle, Apache CXF, Eclipse Jetty, and the embedded Cassandra Go standard library health-check binary.

The emulator image is available at Artifact Registry.

To upgrade, update the emulator version in your Cloud Code for VS Code settings to 2.0.2. See Manage the Apigee Emulator for details.

Feature

Apigee Emulator

Changed in this release

  • Upgraded the Apigee Emulator runtime JVM to Eclipse Temurin JRE 21 (21.0.12.1.0+1-0, from JRE 11 11.0.31+11), adding JVM 21 compatibility flags (-Djava.security.manager=allow and --add-opens module flags) for JavaCallout, JavaScript (Rhino), and Python (Jython) policies while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra 4.0.19 datastore pinned to Eclipse Temurin JRE 8.
  • Upgraded Netty to 4.1.137.Final (from 4.1.135.Final) and updated netty-tcnative-boringssl-static and netty-tcnative-classes to 2.0.81.Final (from 2.0.77.Final).
  • Upgraded Jackson (jackson-core, jackson-databind, and jackson-dataformat-yaml) to 2.21.7 (from 2.18.6 and 2.19.2) and jackson-annotations to 2.21.
  • Upgraded shaded Apache Log4j (log4j-api and log4j-core) in ConfigUtil.jar to 2.25.5 (from 2.17.1 and 2.25.4).
  • Upgraded BouncyCastle (bcprov-jdk18on, bcpkix-jdk18on, and bcutil-jdk18on) to 1.85 (from 1.84).
  • Upgraded Apache CXF (cxf-*) to 3.6.12 (from 3.5.11).
  • Upgraded gRPC to 1.82.3 (from 1.62.2), Protobuf (protobuf-java and protobuf-java-util) to 4.33.6 (from 3.25.5), and Guava to 33.5.0-jre (from 33.4.8-jre).
  • Removed unused org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-* (9.4.58.v20250814) and commons-collections:commons-collections (3.2.2) JARs from the emulator distribution.
  • Refreshed the Cassandra base image to pick up Go standard library 1.27.0 (from 1.25.11) in the embedded /opt/apigee/ready health-check binary.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: Which Cloud Should You Choose? Help Me Build the Ultimate Cloud Selection Tool! ☁️
description:
Choosing the right cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP) can be an overwhelming task. With hundreds of services, complex pricing models, and constantly evolving features, developers and architects often spend hours comparing options before writing a single line of code.
To solve this, I’ve been building Which Cloud — a lightweight, intuitive web app designed to simplify the cloud decision-making process!

🛠️ What is "Which Cloud"?
Which Cloud is built to help developers, students, and teams quickly compare cloud services and find the platform that best fits their project's technical and budgetary needs.
Whether you're looking for the best serverless environment, managed databases, or identity access management (IAM) solutions, the goal is to make the choice clear and straightforward.

🔮 What’s Next? (Future Implementations)
The project is in its early stages, and there is so much potential to grow. Here are a few features and implementations I'm planning to work on next:

Interactive Cloud Recommendation Wizard: A step-by-step questionnaire (e.g., "Do you need serverless?", "What is your budget limit?", "Are you looking for strong IAM integrations?") that dynamically recommends the best provider.

Deep-Dive Service Mapping: A comprehensive directory that maps equivalent services across AWS, Azure, and GCP (e.g., comparing AWS Cognito with Azure AD / Google Identity Platform).

Real-time Cost Estimator: A simple calculator to estimate and compare monthly costs for basic workloads (compute, storage, and database) across all three major clouds.

Multi-Cloud Architecture Guides: Visual recommendations for hybrid or multi-cloud setups.

title: Catalog-bound Decide+Act: why free tool-calling felt wrong for SysOps writes
description:
This is a submission for the MLH x DEV Writing Challenge

I spent MLH Global Hack Week: Builders Week (Nov 6–12, 2026) fighting a pattern that still shows up in “AI Ops” demos: an LLM that talks about fixing a host, then invents the shell command that would do it.

This is a builder story — process and trust boundaries, not a preprint.

What I Built

Escalane is a catalog-bound Decide+Act harness for SysOps. The model chooses what kind of fix fits; the harness is the only thing that runs. Code + CLI: escalane-lab/escalane.

System One is the decision backend — it answers typed questions (which playbook, safe to mutate, how wide the blast radius is) over a scrubbed state blob. It does not get a free tool belt.

Why not “Agent = LLM + tools”? In SysOps, a “tool” is often a shell-shaped surface. Free tool-calling collapses three jobs that should not share a brain:

  • Judgment — which remediation class fits?
  • Authority — is it safe to mutate this host now?
  • Execution — exact shell args, locks, dry-run, verify

When the model authors commands, prompt-injected telemetry becomes a remote-code path. I wanted a closed action space: pick a playbook id (or escalate), answer safety questions, and let harness-owned catalog templates fill in the shell args from state-bound params — never from model free text.

One simple loop:

  • Ingest — symptoms only; reject command-like fields
  • Decide — System One returns typed answers (choice / confidence / score)
  • Gates — ordered safety checks; fail closed on low confidence
  • Catalog act — template shell args only, or escalate / ask a human

Research default is dry-run (no host mutation). Writes need dual consent: CLI --allow-writes and ALLOW_WRITE_OPERATIONS=true. Fail-closed --require-live refuses silent mock fallback when you asked for a live backend.

Lesson that stuck: harness > model swap. Changing the decision model does not fix unsafe shell-arg authorship. Grammar ≠ semantic safety.

Demo

Docs site: escalane-lab.github.io/escalane-docs. The usable path is a local CLI walkthrough (screenshot below). Dry-run is the default: nothing mutates a host unless you intentionally unlock writes. The model never writes shell args — only catalog templates do.

--gate-config picks how strict the ordered safety checks are. Gates A0–A3 run in order; each can veto before anything runs:

  • A0 — is the chosen playbook in the catalog? (membership)
  • A1 — is confidence high enough? (noul / confidence)
  • A2 — is the blast radius acceptable?
  • A3 — is fitted per-label precision good enough? If not → human review (HITL)

A3 is the strictest research posture. On this live Ollama run with System One d3:4b, it still asked for a human, because fitted label precision was conservative — even though the model picked a valid catalog playbook.

Live decide (no host mutation; fail-closed if the backend is down):

uv sync
uv run escalane decide \
  --backend ollama \
  --model d3:4b \
  --require-live \
  --state src/escalane/examples/incidents/php_502.json \
  --catalog datasets/sysops_decide/catalog.yaml \
  --gate-config A3

Trimmed output from that exact live command on the seed PHP 502 incident:


{
  "model": "d3:4b",
  "backend": "ollama",
  "playbook": "restart_php_fpm",
  "noul": 0.9878,
  "blast_score": 0.9822,
  "gate_decision": "hitl",
  "gate_reason": "label_precision",
  "dry_run_only": true
}

Read that as: live System One answers, catalog playbook selected, dry-run only, no shell args invented by the model, and A3 routed to human review instead of execute.

Public links:

  • Repo: github.com/escalane-lab/escalane
  • Docs / site: escalane-lab.github.io/escalane-docs
  • Harness map: docs/harness-architecture.md
  • System One wire format: Decisions (System One)

Partner Technologies

I did not build on an MLH partner stack for this project — honesty over checkbox.

What I actually used:

  • Python + uv for the escalane CLI and harness
  • httpx for HTTP to local decision backends
  • Ollama / LM Studio for local System One–style decision models (when the eGPU / APU cooperated)
  • A custom Decide→Gates→Act harness with a seed SysOps catalog and mock backend for offline plumbing

Challenges that felt real during the week: model pulls and DNS hiccups, an eGPU busy with chat models so decision models lived on a second box, and the constant trap of “CI green on mock” teaching wiring instead of decision quality. The claim fence and --require-live exist so I stop lying to myself.

We measured gate postures against ungated / free tool-calling baselines on a seed suite — enough to see that catalog membership alone is not enough under injection-shaped prompts. Full metrics stay out of this post; they belong in a later paper draft.

This is a research harness, not a production-certified remediator. Conservative gates will ask for a human more often than a demo agent that always “just runs the fix.”

Hackathon Experience

Builders Week felt like permission to ship the shape of the idea without pretending it was finished science.

What I’ll remember: sticky-note clarity. The model chooses; the harness is the only thing that runs. Locking the CLI path (decide / run / replay), a seed catalog, and the Decide→Gates→Act skeleton mattered more than chasing a flashy demo that shells out from a prompt.

What matured after the week was still builder work: params-from-state as a hard rule, gate postures that are usable (deny-all is a failed product, not a safety win), and fail-closed live backends.

If you are also fighting “LLM with bash privileges,” I would love to hear how you drew the trust boundary.

title: Dynamic Routing Gateway (DRG) no OCI
description:
Para um hackathon do qual ando participando, tive que criar um Dynamic Routing Gateway com túnel IPSec para a infraestrutura da aplicação da minha equipe. Isso foi a inspiração deste artigo. Para quem quiser estiver estudando para o OCI Architect Associate, chega mais.

O que é o Dynamic Routing Gateway (DRG)?

O Dynamic Routing Gateway (DRG) é o roteador virtual do OCI. Ele é onde todo o tráfego entre a rede on-premises e as VCNs acaba passando e também de uma VCN para outra, tanto na mesma região quanto em em regiões diferentes. Na prática, o DRG é o ponto central de uma topologia hub-and-spoke; múltiplos pontos (spokes) se conectam a um único ponto central (hub).


(Imagem criada por IA)

Ele se conecta a quatro tipos de rede:

  • VCNs, as redes virtuais da própria região;
  • Remote Peering Connections (RPC), para falar com DRGs e VCNs de outras regiões;
  • túneis IPSec (Site-to-Site VPN), para o data center on-premises via internet com conexão criptografada;
  • Virtual Circuits do FastConnect, para o on-premises por conexão dedicada e rápida.

Na configuração padrão, as VCNs usam uma route table e os links externos usam outra.

Neste artigo, vamos ver como o DRG funciona, como ele decide onde mandar cada pacote. Por fim, vamos aprender a provisionar um. DRGs são Always Free; nada impede você de ter seu próprio túnel IPSec.

Apenas lembre-se que o tráfego de saída e os anexos (FastConnect e túneis VPN) possuem modelos de cobrança próprios ou limites que não pertencem ao Always Free Tier.

Attachments

Cada rede se liga ao DRG por um attachment. É o attachment que diz ao DRG de onde vem uma rota e para onde mandar um pacote.

Attachment O que é Comportamento de Roteamento
VCN Conecta o DRG a uma VCN regional da mesma tenancy. Importa os blocos CIDR da VCN ou sub-redes específicas.
Virtual Circuit (FastConnect) Integração dedicada via FastConnect. Recebe e propaga rotas via protocolo BGP privado.
Túnel IPSec Túnel criptografado de Site-to-Site VPN. Provisionado em pares de túneis ativos/redundantes com BGP ou rotas estáticas
Remote Peering Connection Conexão entre regiões ou entre diferentes tenancies do OCI. Estabelece trânsito seguro entre DRGs em regiões geográficas distintas.
Loopback Interface bidirecional interna. Permite trocar rotas entre circuitos que normalmente seriam bloqueados por prevenção de loop.

DRG Route Tables

Quando um pacote entra no DRG por um attachment, o DRG consulta a route table daquele attachment para escolher o próximo salto. O próximo salto é sempre outro attachment.

A relação é de 1 para N: cada attachment usa uma route table, mas uma mesma route table pode servir a vários attachments. É isso que permite separar o tráfego. Por exemplo, as VCNs de produção podem usar uma tabela e as de desenvolvimento, outra.

Rotas estáticas e dinâmicas

Uma DRG route table guarda dois tipos de rota:

  • Rotas estáticas: você cria à mão, pelo Console, API, CLI ou Terraform. Cada uma tem um CIDR de destino e um attachment como próximo salto.
  • Rotas dinâmicas: o DRG aprende sozinho com os attachments e as insere na tabela por meio de uma import route distribution (próxima seção).

As tabelas autogeradas

Todo DRG nasce com duas route tables padrão:

Route table Usada por padrão por Importa rotas de
Autogenerated Drg Route Table for VCN attachments Attachments de VCN Todos os attachments (All Routes)
Autogenerated Drg Route Table for RPC, VC, and IPSec attachments Attachments de RPC, Virtual Circuit e IPSec Apenas VCN Routes

Uma VCN enxerga tudo (outras VCNs, on-premises e outras regiões), enquanto o on-premises e as outras regiões só enxergam as VCNs.

Uma tabela definida como padrão para um tipo de attachment é atribuída a todo attachment novo desse tipo, a menos que você escolha outra na criação. Ela também não pode ser apagada enquanto for padrão.

Route Distributions: as routing policies do DRG

Se a route table responde “para onde vai o pacote?”, a route distribution responde “quais rotas entram nessa tabela?”. É por ela que você escreve as políticas de roteamento do DRG.

Uma route distribution é uma lista de regras (statements). Cada regra tem um critério de correspondência e uma ação:

  • Critério: o OCID de um attachment específico, um tipo de attachment (VCN, IPSec, Virtual Circuit ou RPC) ou “Match All”. Na API, o “Match All” é uma lista de critérios vazia.
  • Ação: ACCEPT, que importa ou exporta a rota como ela é.
  • Prioridade: um número de 0 a 65535, único dentro da distribuição. O menor número é avaliado primeiro, e a primeira regra que bate decide.

Remover uma regra também remove das route tables as rotas que ela tinha importado. A ordem das regras só define a avaliação, não a preferência entre rotas importadas (isso é assunto da seção de conflitos).

Import e export

Existem dois sentidos:

  • Import route distribution: fica ligada a uma route table e define quais rotas, vindas de quais attachments, entram nela. Todo DRG nasce com duas: “All Routes” (Match All) e “VCN Routes” (só attachments do tipo VCN). Você pode criar quantas precisar.
  • Export route distribution: fica ligada a um attachment e define quais rotas da route table desse attachment são anunciadas para ele. Existe só a padrão (default export), que anuncia todo o conteúdo da route table do attachment. Não é possível criar novas.

Loopback Attachment

Rotas cuja origem sejam de Túnel IPSec ou Virtual Circuit nunca são exportadas para attachments de IPSec ou Virtual Circuit, seja qual for a distribuição. Isso vale até para rotas que passaram por uma RPC: a origem continua sendo a primeira. Essa regra de prevenção de loops é a razão para a existência do Loopback Attachment.


(Imagem criada por mim)

Como tudo se encaixa

Juntando as peças, o caminho de uma rota até o seu destino fica assim:

  1. Um attachment anuncia rotas ao DRG (BGP, CIDRs da VCN ou RPC).
  2. A import route distribution ligada à route table decide quais dessas rotas entram nela.
  3. A route table passa a ter rotas dinâmicas, ao lado das estáticas que você criou.
  4. Os attachments que usam essa tabela encaminham pacotes com base nela.
  5. A export route distribution anuncia o conteúdo da tabela de volta para o attachment.

Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP)

O ECMP reparte o tráfego entre vários caminhos para o mesmo destino. No DRG, ele vale para Virtual Circuits e túneis IPSec que anunciam o mesmo CIDR on-premises. Ele vem desativado por padrão e é ligado na route table que recebe as rotas, não no attachment. Com ele desligado, o DRG escolhe um único caminho entre os iguais. Com ele ligado, todos entram na tabela e o tráfego é distribuído entre eles, até o limite de 8 caminhos.

Conflitos de Rotas

Quando duas rotas com o mesmo CIDR chegam à mesma route table, o DRG desempata nesta ordem:

  1. Estática vence dinâmica. Sempre. (Não dá para criar duas rotas estáticas com o mesmo CIDR na mesma tabela, mas duas dinâmicas iguais podem ser importadas.)
  2. AS Path. Entre rotas dinâmicas, o DRG analisa o AS Path. Rotas de VCN e estáticas têm AS Path vazio; rotas de IPSec e Virtual Circuit trazem AS Path do BGP.
  3. Tipo de attachment que importou a rota, nesta prioridade: VCN, Virtual Circuit, IPSec e, por último, RPC.

Quando o empate é entre attachments do mesmo tipo:

Tipo Como o DRG escolhe
VCN Uma das rotas, de forma arbitrária mas estável
Virtual Circuit e IPSec O menor AS Path; se empatar, escolha arbitrária mas estável. Com ECMP ligado, todas entram (até 8)
RPC A menor distância geográfica de rede; se empatar, a origem de maior prioridade (STATIC, VCN, VIRTUAL_CIRCUIT, IPSEC_TUNNEL, RPC)

Para ver o resultado, liste o conteúdo da route table. As rotas que perderam aparecem com o status "conflict". Se algo não está roteando como você esperava, é o primeiro lugar para olhar.

Quando usar o DRG

O DRG é a peça certa sempre que o tráfego precisa sair de uma VCN para algo que não é a internet nem um serviço da Oracle:

  • Nuvem híbrida: ligar o data center ao OCI por Site-to-Site VPN, FastConnect ou os dois (VPN como reserva do FastConnect).
  • Hub-and-spoke na mesma região: várias VCNs ligadas a um DRG, conversando entre si sem precisar de um Local Peering Gateway para cada par.
  • Multirregião: VCNs em regiões diferentes conversando por RPC, por exemplo para disaster recovery.
  • Segmentação e inspeção: route tables e distribuições separadas para isolar ambientes ou forçar o tráfego a passar por uma VCN com firewall.

Para internet, use o Internet Gateway (para tráfego iniciado de forma bidirecional) ou o NAT Gateway (para tráfego iniciado apenas pela sua rede). Para serviços da Oracle, como Object Storage, OCIR, , use o Service Gateway.

Criando um DRG

Pelo Console

O caminho é Networking → Dynamic Routing Gateways → Create Dynamic Routing Gateway. Basta escolher o nome e o compartment. Na criação, o OCI já provisiona as duas route tables e as duas import route distributions autogeradas.

Depois, dentro do DRG, crie os attachments e ajuste as route tables e distribuições se o padrão não servir. Por fim, lembre de adicionar a rota para o DRG na route table das subnets.

Com Terraform

O exemplo abaixo cria um DRG, uma import route distribution que aceita só rotas de VCN, uma route table que usa essa distribuição e o attachment de uma VCN:

resource "oci_core_drg" "drg" {
  compartment_id = var.compartment_id
  display_name   = "drg-hub"
}

resource "oci_core_drg_route_distribution" "import_vcns" {
  drg_id            = oci_core_drg.drg.id
  distribution_type = "IMPORT"
  display_name      = "import-somente-vcns"
}

resource "oci_core_drg_route_distribution_statement" "vcns" {
  drg_route_distribution_id = oci_core_drg_route_distribution.import_vcns.id
  action                    = "ACCEPT"
  priority                  = 10

  match_criteria {
    match_type      = "DRG_ATTACHMENT_TYPE"
    attachment_type = "VCN"
  }
}

resource "oci_core_drg_route_table" "rt" {
  drg_id                           = oci_core_drg.drg.id
  display_name                     = "rt-vcns"
  import_drg_route_distribution_id = oci_core_drg_route_distribution.import_vcns.id
  is_ecmp_enabled                  = false
}

resource "oci_core_drg_attachment" "vcn" {
  drg_id             = oci_core_drg.drg.id
  drg_route_table_id = oci_core_drg_route_table.rt.id

  network_details {
    id   = oci_core_vcn.vcn.id
    type = "VCN"
  }
}

resource "oci_core_drg_route_table_route_rule" "static" {
  drg_route_table_id         = oci_core_drg_route_table.rt.id
  destination                = "10.0.0.0/16"
  destination_type           = "CIDR_BLOCK"
  next_hop_drg_attachment_id = oci_core_drg_attachment.vcn.id
}

Dois cuidados com o provider:

  • No oci_core_drg_attachment, o campo route_table_id no nível do recurso está obsoleto. A route table da VCN usada pelo attachment agora vai dentro de network_details.
  • Para attachments de RPC, Virtual Circuit e IPSec, o recurso é o oci_core_drg_attachment_management. Para uma RPC, por exemplo, use attachment_type = "REMOTE_PEERING_CONNECTION".

Para mexer nas tabelas autogeradas sem recriá-las, use o oci_core_default_drg_route_table, apontando para oci_core_drg.drg.default_drg_route_tables[0].vcn (ou ipsec_tunnel, virtual_circuit, remote_peering_connection).

Conclusão

O DRG parece complicado porque junta muitas peças, mas a lógica é simples. O DRG é como um grande hub e o attachment de um recurso liga-o à rede. A route table diz para onde vai o pacote. A import route distribution decide quais rotas entram na tabela, e a export anuncia essa tabela de volta. ECMP e as regras de conflito resolvem o que acontece quando há mais de um caminho disponível.

As tabelas e distribuições autogeradas atendem a maioria dos cenários. Crie as suas quando precisar isolar ambientes ou controlar quem enxerga quem.

FAQ

Qual a diferença entre Local Peering Gateway (LPG) e Dynamic Routing Gateway (DRG)?

O LPG conecta apenas duas VCNs na mesma região de forma não transitiva (ponto a ponto). O DRG funciona como um roteador de trânsito hub-and-spoke, permitindo interligar múltiplas VCNs, conexões on-premises e regiões remotas com políticas centrais de roteamento.

Como funciona o Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) no DRG?

O ECMP distribui o tráfego de rede balanceando pacotes entre até 8 caminhos redundantes que anunciem exatamente o mesmo prefixo CIDR. Ele é habilitado na DRG Route Table e opera com túneis IPSec VPN e circuitos FastConnect.

Por que o tráfego entre VCN e on-premises falha após criar o DRG e o attachment?

Quase sempre a falha decorre da ausência de regras na tabela de rotas da própria sub-rede da VCN. O gateway da subnet precisa conter uma rota apontando o CIDR on-premises tendo o DRG como target (Next Hop).

O que acontece quando duas rotas dinâmicas possuem o mesmo prefixo e mesmo AS Path?

O DRG aplica a prioridade pelo tipo de attachment: VCN tem a maior precedência, seguida por FastConnect (Virtual Circuit), IPSec Tunnel e Remote Peering Connection (RPC). Se ambas forem do mesmo tipo de attachment, o DRG adota uma escolha estável entre elas.

Referências

  • Creating a DRG
  • Changing Route Table Assignment Defaults for DRG Attachments

  • Terraform: oci_core_default_drg_route_table
