title: Autopsy #05: The z-index 9999 Modal Trap (and Its Native Exit)
description:
Trapped Behind a Header With z-index: 2147483647

A minor UI polish PR added opacity: 0.99 and transform: translateZ(0) to the data-grid wrapper to smooth out horizontal scroll jitter. Storybook visual snapshots passed cleanly.

Two hours after release, customer support reported row-action menus clipped beneath the position: sticky; z-index: 10 page header. The menu itself had z-index: 9999, yet it slid cleanly underneath a header with z-index: 10.

  • T+00:00: Grid wrapper GPU promotion ships to production.
  • T+22:00: Users report row action menus (z-index: 9999) rendering behind the z-index: 10 sticky header.
  • T+55:00: Team ships a JS document.body portal with scroll listeners to escape clipping; Android p75 INP jumps from 140 ms to 480 ms.
  • T+90:00: Performance traces show synchronous getBoundingClientRect() reflows on every scroll tick.

Why Higher z-index Numbers Lost the Arms Race

The first Slack reflex was to bump the menu's stylesheet from z-index: 9999 to z-index: 2147483647 and add will-change: transform to the table wrapper. Both changes passed local visual checks on an un-scrolled viewport.

In production, 2147483647 remained trapped behind z-index: 10. The team then portaled the menu to document.body, which fixed the clipping but introduced a scroll listener calling getBoundingClientRect() on every frame, pushing Android INP to 480 ms.

Five Spec Layers From Local Clipping to Top-Layer Exit

This failure sits on a well-documented CSS specification trap: a parent transform or opacity < 1 creates a sealed stacking context and a GPU compositor layer, trapping all descendant z-index values. Escaping via a JS portal trades clipping for layout-thrashing scroll listeners, whereas the native browser Top Layer and CSS Anchor Positioning solve both in the engine.

Watch z-index Escalate Until Top Layer Breaks the Ceiling

Dissecting the Stacking Context Trap

01 → 02: The Computed Style That Sealed the Grid

In Chrome DevTools Elements → Computed, the row menu showed z-index: 2147483647, yet the Layers panel showed it painted inside the .grid-wrapper layer, strictly below .sticky-header. Inspecting .grid-wrapper revealed opacity: 0.99, which per the CSS Positioned Layout specification establishes an atomic CSS Stacking Context. Inside a local stacking context, child z-index values only compete against siblings in that same context; the parent's z-index: auto (or 0) loses to the header's z-index: 10.

Removing opacity: 0.99 still left the menu clipped because transform: translateZ(0) remained on .grid-wrapper. Promoting an element to its own GPU Compositor Layer via transform or will-change: transform also seals a stacking context in CSS, guaranteeing the same clipping bug.

02 → 03: Escaping Clipping by Thrashing the Main Thread

To escape .grid-wrapper, the hotfix mounted the menu inside document.body via createPortal and attached window.addEventListener('scroll', repositionMenu). Opening the Performance panel during a scroll showed 18 ms purple Layout bars firing on every wheel tick.

Reading trigger.getBoundingClientRect() inside a scroll callback forces synchronous layout calculation, the core cost of React Portal & z-index Legacy. Even with a z-index registry, every new overlay forces another number escalation.

03 → 04: Leaving the Document Tree Entirely

Instead of competing inside document z-index strata, native <dialog> (.showModal()) and [popover] attributes promote the element into the Browser Top Layer. Top-layer elements render in a separate viewport plane above every stacking context in the document, regardless of any ancestor transform, opacity, or overflow: hidden.

04 → 05: Letting the Layout Engine Flip the Menu

Once [popover] freed the menu from clipping, the remaining JS code was the getBoundingClientRect() flip logic that kept menus inside the viewport. Replacing that JS loop with CSS Anchor Positioning (anchor-name, position-anchor, and position-try-fallbacks) delegates viewport collision and flipping directly to Blink's layout pass with zero scroll listeners.

Replacing Portals With Popover and Anchor Positioning 

.row-trigger {
  anchor-name: --row-menu-anchor;
}

.row-menu[popover] {
  position: fixed;
  position-anchor: --row-menu-anchor;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline;
}

Architectural Invariants:

  • Never fight stacking contexts with larger integers: Any ancestor transform, opacity < 1, filter, or will-change seals z-index locally.
  • Promote overlays to the Top Layer: Use native <dialog> or popover so overlays sit above all document contexts without DOM reparenting.
  • Offload collision flipping to CSS: Use anchor() and position-try-fallbacks instead of scroll + getBoundingClientRect() listeners.

Golden Rule: You cannot out-integer a sealed stacking context; promote overlays to the browser Top Layer and let CSS Anchor Positioning place them.

title: Amazon VPC, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN now offer a 99.999% availability SLA for cross-Region traffic
description:
AWS now offers a 99.999% availability service level agreement (SLA) for cross-Region traffic over Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) cross-Region peering, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN, with a new capability called Multipath Resilience. Multipath Resilience makes it easier to improve the resilience of mission-critical applications that send traffic across Regions, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming.

The AWS backbone is highly resilient and connects Regions over physically diverse fiber paths. When a path fails, such as during a fiber cut, the network's automatic sub-second rerouting moves traffic to a healthy path. In the rare event that such mechanisms do not resolve the issue in a timely manner, such as when there's a partial degradation, it might take minutes for connectivity to be reestablished. Some applications, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming, can't tolerate single-digit seconds interruptions, let alone minutes of unavailability. Until now, customers running these applications relied on workarounds, including modifying their applications and operating systems to split a single connection into multiple connections, or replicating data into every Region to avoid cross-Region calls. These workarounds add complexity and don't always work, because applications can't control which network paths their traffic takes.

Now, when you turn on Multipath Resilience for a cross-Region VPC peering connection, cross-Region Transit Gateway peering attachment, or cross-Region traffic on Cloud WAN, the network sends copies of each packet across physically diverse paths. It delivers whichever copy reaches your resources in the destination Region first and discards the duplicates. If one path drops packets, a copy is already in flight on another path, so your applications stay connected without waiting for the network protocols to reroute. Multipath Resilience moves this work out of your applications and into the network. Your applications keep using a single connection, with no changes to application code or operating systems, and no need to duplicate data to keep calls within a single Region.

Multipath Resilience is now generally available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the Multipath Resilience documentation. For SLA details, visit the Multipath Resilience SLA. For pricing, visit the Amazon VPC pricing page.

title: TypeError: ‘int’ Object Is Not Callable (Fix)
description:
You run your script. Python stops and prints this:

TypeError: 'int' object is not callable

It's a strange message. You probably never tried to "call" a number. Below you'll see what it means, the six situations that trigger it in real programs, and the fix for each one. I ran every example on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14. All three print the same error.

What the Error Means

Calling something means putting parentheses after it, like print(x), len(items) or score(3, 4). You can call functions, methods and classes. You can't call a number. So when Python hits something(...) and something holds an integer right now, it raises TypeError: 'int' object is not callable. The word in quotes is the type of the thing you tried to call. That's why you may also see 'str' object is not callable, 'list' object is not callable, 'float' object is not callable or 'NoneType' object is not callable. The causes below apply to all of them.

The causes fall into two families. Most of the time, a name that used to be a function got overwritten by a number (causes 1, 2, 4 and 6). The rest happen when you typed parentheses where none belong (causes 3 and 5).

How to Find the Cause Fast

Start with the traceback. It points at the line with the call. Look at the name right before the parentheses and ask what it holds right now. Print it, or ask Python:

print(type(sum), sum)        # <class 'int'> 0  means sum was overwritten
print(callable(sum))        # False means it cannot be called

callable() is a built-in. It gives True for functions and classes, and False for numbers, strings and lists. If the name holds a number, search your file for the earlier line that assigned it. Can't find one? And the parentheses sit after a number or a closing bracket? Then you're looking at cause 3 or 5.

The Six Causes

1. A Variable Has the Name of a Built-in 

sum = 0                               # this hides Python's built-in sum()
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    sum += n

print(sum([4, 5, 6]))                  # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable

Python ships with dozens of built-in names: sum, max, min, len, list, str, input, id and type are a few. If you assign to one, you create your own variable with that name, and yours wins from then on. The built-in isn't gone. It's just hidden. Pick a descriptive name like total instead:

total = 0                              # pick a name that is not a built-in
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total += n

print(total)
print(sum([4, 5, 6]))                  # the built-in still works

Already overwrote a built-in in an interactive session? Run del sum and your variable goes away, so the built-in shows up again (I tested this). In a script, just rename the variable.

2. A Function Was Replaced by Its Own Result 

def score(a, b):
    return a * b


score = score(3, 4)                    # score is now the number 12, not the function
print(score(5, 6))                     # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable

score = score(3, 4) looks innocent. It runs the function and keeps the answer. But the answer goes into the same name as the function, so the function disappears. The second call fails because score is now 12. In a long file it's easy to miss. It often happens when you paste code twice or run a notebook cell twice. Keep the result under a new name:

def score(a, b):
    return a * b


first = score(3, 4)                    # store the result under a different name
print(first)
print(score(5, 6))

3. A Missing Operator Before Parentheses 

a = 5
b = 3
result = 2 (a + b)                     # the * is missing: Python tries to call 2
print(result)                          # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable

In maths, 2(a + b) means two times the sum. Python reads it as "call the number 2 with the argument a + b". The same thing happens with )( between two brackets, like (a + b)(c + d). On the Python versions I tested (3.11 to 3.14), you get a hint before the error: SyntaxWarning: 'int' object is not callable; perhaps you missed a comma?. Spell the operator out:

a = 5
b = 3
result = 2 * (a + b)
print(result)

4. An Attribute and a Method With the Same Name 

class Cart:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0                 # an attribute...

    def count(self):                   # ...and a method with the same name: the attribute wins
        return self.count


cart = Cart()
print(cart.count())                    # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable

Look at self.count = 0. It stores a number on the object. That instance attribute beats the method count you defined with def, so cart.count() ends up calling the number. This is the classic form of the error in object-oriented code. The fix is to give data and behaviour different names. Many people use nouns for attributes (items) and verbs or get_ names for methods (count_items):

class Cart:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = 0                 # data gets one name

    def count(self):                   # the method gets another
        return self.items


cart = Cart()
print(cart.count())

5. Calling the Result of a Call 

def total():
    return 10


print(total()())                       # total() is 10; the second () tries to call 10

total() runs the function and hands back 10. A second () then tries to call 10. Usually it's a double paste. Or you wrapped a call in a function that you thought returned another function. Delete the extra pair:

def total():
    return 10


print(total())                         # one pair of parentheses is enough

6. A Loop Variable That Hides a Function 

for len in range(3):               # len now means 0, 1, 2
    pass

print(len("hello"))                    # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable

This is cause 1 in disguise. It's the hardest one to spot, because the overwrite happens in the loop header. A for loop assigns to its variable, so for len in range(3) turns len into a number. The same goes for for str in ..., for input in ... and with open(...) as list. Use plain names like i, item or row:

for i in range(3):                 # use a normal loop variable
    pass

print(len("hello"))

How to Stop It From Happening Again

Never use a built-in as a variable name. The usual suspects are list, dict, str, sum, max, min, len, input, id, type, file, next and format. If the obvious name is taken, add a word. Try total, items, text or maximum.

Let a linter catch it. Pylint reports redefined-builtin, and flake8 plugins flag the same thing. You usually get a yellow underline in your editor before you run anything. Many editors can run one for you.

Restart after renaming in a notebook. In Jupyter or the Python shell, an overwritten name stays overwritten. Fixing the code doesn't change that. You have to restart the kernel or delete the variable. So if a fixed program still fails there, restart and run it again from the top.

Quick Reference

What you see Likely cause Fix
Error on a built-in such as sum(...) or len(...) A variable has the same name Rename the variable
Error on your own function after using it once f = f(...) replaced the function Store the result under a new name
Error on 2 (a + b) or )( A missing operator Add * or +
Error on obj.name() An attribute and a method share a name Rename one of them
Error on f()() A second pair of parentheses Remove it
Error after a for loop The loop variable has a built-in name Use i or item

The Rule, Stated Once

'int' object is not callable means a name you're using like a function holds a number. Print the name's type. Find the line that assigned it. Rename the variable. No assignment anywhere? Then hunt for a missing operator or an extra pair of parentheses. And keep built-in names out of your own variables. A linter will warn you before the error ever shows up.

Want more Python errors with a clear cause? Try RecursionError, FileNotFoundError, TypeError: NoneType Is Not Subscriptable and UnboundLocalError. New to Python? Start with Python for Beginners.

Download the code: the broken and fixed versions of all six causes are on GitHub in Python-projects/Troubleshooting/typeerror-not-callable. Run any file with python bug.py from inside its folder.

title: SQL Challenge : How to Find the Top 2 Highest-Paid Employees in Each Department Using ROW_NUMBER()
description:
SQL Challenge #103: Find the Top 2 Highest-Paid Employees in Every Department Using ROW_NUMBER()

Window functions are very useful in SQL interviews and real-world data analysis. They help us rank records, compare values and solve problems that are difficult to handle with basic aggregate functions.

In this SQL challenge, let's solve a common business requirement: finding the two highest-paid employees in every department.

The Problem

Suppose you have an "employees" table containing employee IDs, employee names, department IDs and salaries.

You need to prepare a report that returns the top two highest-paid employees separately for each department.

For example, if the IT department has five employees, your query should return only the two employees with the highest salaries in IT. The same logic should apply to every other department.

Your Challenge

Write a SQL query to:

  1. Display employee ID, employee name, department ID and salary.
  2. Use "ROW_NUMBER()" to assign a unique number to each employee within their department.
  3. Use "PARTITION BY" to restart the numbering for every department.
  4. Sort employees by salary from highest to lowest.
  5. Retrieve only the top two highest-paid employees from each department.
  6. Retrieve the results without modifying the original employees table.

Sample Data: employees

emp_id| emp_name| department_id| salary
101| Rahul| 10| 80000
102| Amit| 10| 65000
103| Priya| 10| 90000
104| Sneha| 20| 75000
105| Karan| 20| 60000
106| Neha| 20| 85000
107| Raj| 30| 55000
108| Pooja| 30| 70000
109| Anil| 30| 50000

Think about how "ROW_NUMBER()" and "PARTITION BY" work before looking at the solution.

The SQL Solution (Oracle)

SELECT
emp_id,
emp_name,
department_id,
salary
FROM (
SELECT
emp_id,
emp_name,
department_id,
salary,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
PARTITION BY department_id
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id
) AS rn
FROM employees
)
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY department_id, salary DESC;

Expected Output

emp_id| emp_name| department_id| salary
103| Priya| 10| 90000
101| Rahul| 10| 80000
106| Neha| 20| 85000
104| Sneha| 20| 75000
108| Pooja| 30| 70000
107| Raj| 30| 55000

Why Does This SQL Query Work?

Let's understand the important parts of the query.

  1. ROW_NUMBER()

"ROW_NUMBER()" assigns a unique sequential number to every employee within their department.

  1. PARTITION BY department_id

This is the most important part.

"PARTITION BY" divides employees into separate department groups and restarts the numbering from 1 for each department.

  1. ORDER BY salary DESC

This sorts employees from the highest salary to the lowest within each department.

  1. emp_id

The additional "emp_id" column provides consistent ordering when two employees have the same salary.

  1. WHERE rn <= 2

The outer query filters the calculated row numbers and returns only the first two employees from each department.

  1. Original Table Remains Unchanged

The query only retrieves and ranks records. It does not modify the original employees table.

One Thing to Remember

The main purpose of "PARTITION BY" is to perform calculations separately for different groups of records.

Consider the difference:

  • Without "PARTITION BY": Employees are ranked across the entire company.
  • With "PARTITION BY department_id": Ranking starts again from 1 for every department.
  • "ROW_NUMBER()": Always assigns a unique number, even when multiple employees have the same salary.

Also, remember that "ROW_NUMBER()" returns exactly two employees per department when at least two employees exist, even if multiple employees have the same salary.

Your Turn: Try This SQL Problem

What if the requirement changes?

Instead of finding the top two employees, the business wants to find the top three salary levels in every department, including all employees who share the same salary.

Would you use "ROW_NUMBER()", "RANK()" or "DENSE_RANK()"?

Share your SQL query in the comments. Let's discuss your approach!

SQL #OracleSQL #DataAnalytics #SQLChallenge

title: Fast Disks, Slow WAL Sync: Finding Linux Writeback Throttling
description:
As described in the previous post, the primary now uses a high-I/O Ultra disk. Reads and writes took fractions of a millisecond, yet PostgreSQL WAL synchronization averaged 25-30 ms. Removing synchronous-standby waits didn't help: synchronous_commit=local still requires local WAL durability. With device-read constraints reduced and remote acknowledgments excluded, I traced the primary's synchronization call across the guest-OS boundary.

To investigate those durable-commit timings, I returned to synchronous_commit=on with normal HA for a full repeat, then used a separate pilot prepared for controller tracing.

Measure the synchronization, not only the disk

The relevant cumulative PostgreSQL counters are:

SELECT wal_write, wal_sync, wal_write_time, wal_sync_time, stats_reset
FROM pg_stat_wal;

With track_wal_io_timing=on, the interval mean is:

mean WAL sync ms = delta(wal_sync_time) / delta(wal_sync)

The full runs showed:

Run NOPM Mean WAL sync ms WALWrite observation share
Ultra, normal synchronous commit 55,784 25.443 83.18%
Ultra, local commit 54,556 29.550 87.29%
Full normal-HA repeat 54,163 24.995 83.17%

For example, the repeat's in-window counter endpoints contained 45,266 additional syncs and 1,131,416.247 additional milliseconds of synchronization time. Their ratio is 24.995 ms.

The repeat was measured on November 8, 2026, 10:26:56-11:11:58 UTC with the same 512-worker, 15+45-minute protocol. These durable-regime traces and the later pilot were collected after the asynchronous-commit experiment described in part 4.

Why request completion and fdatasync disagree

fdatasync must synchronize a file's data. With buffered I/O, that can involve preparing dirty pages, submitting writeback, waiting for previously submitted work, and completing the necessary persistence operations. The entire call can therefore include:

PostgreSQL calls fdatasync
    dirty-page writeback and submission
    admission waits before block dispatch
    issued requests and their completion
    remaining file-synchronization work
fdatasync returns

The application call includes work before device dispatch. PostgreSQL can queue other backends behind its WAL write lock while the holder is delayed in that earlier work. I traced the caller to locate the delay.

The captured delay was before dispatch

A 30-second capture during the full normal-on repeat, 10:48:02-10:48:33 UTC, observed 536 completed fdatasync calls, averaging 24.504 ms, in PostgreSQL processes other than the separately classified WAL writer and checkpointer.

Captured sleep/rescheduling time inside those calls was classified as:

Captured stack location Share
Pre-dispatch WBT admission 96.43%
File-writeback completion 3.36%
Block-flush completion 0.20%

An abbreviated stack, from the sleeping function towards its callers, was:

io_schedule
rq_qos_wait
wbt_wait
__rq_qos_throttle
blk_mq_submit_bio
...
ext4_do_writepages

WBT is Linux block-layer writeback throttling. Its admission rules can make a submitting process sleep before work reaches the device. Fast completion of admitted requests does not measure that earlier wait.

These percentages describe captured sleep/rescheduling inside PostgreSQL fdatasync calls, including the delay until a process runs again. The syscall trace covers PostgreSQL synchronization calls broadly, while pg_stat_wal measures WAL synchronization specifically.

A healthy latency controller can still have admission waits

WBT controls write admission using read-latency feedback and write-depth limits. A separate normal-on pilot prepared the instrumentation before launch. Its five short measured captures showed:

Observation Value
PostgreSQL fdatasync calls 867
Mean syscall elapsed time 26.123 ms
WBT share of captured sleep/rescheduling 96.404%
Controller timer decisions 482, all LAT_OK
Observed read minima / target 0.100-0.213 ms / 2 ms
Maximum / normal / background admission limits 191 / 96 / 48

Read latency was healthy in the captured windows while callers still slept in the admission machinery. The captures recorded controller limits and aggregate wait paths. Slow synchronization was also observed before and after the probes ran.

The running kernel was 7.0.0-1017-azure. The upstream WBT implementation and request-QoS implementation explain the policy.

What this establishes

In the captured durable regime, much of the synchronization delay was in Linux's write-admission path, before device dispatch.

Provisioning more disk IOPS leaves the guest-OS admission rule unchanged. The relevant question has changed from the disk's advertised capacity to the caller's progress through writeback. All captures used the original WBT policy.

HorizonDB delegates durable WAL handling and data-page persistence to dedicated storage services. This replaces the compute-local data/WAL writeback arrangement, where we observed Linux throttling, while retaining durable commits. This explains why the workload achieves higher throughput than this PostgreSQL configuration can support.

The lab also tested asynchronous commit, where background persistence continues while commits can return before WAL is durable. Part 4 returns to that result and follows BufferContent into page identification.

title: A silent data-loss bug in a paid product: the draft was in memory the whole time
description:
The bug had been live for weeks and no one had reported it, because it only fired for people who had just paid us money.

What the product does

It's a small tool that generates wedding speeches. Nine questions, three drafts, one payment. The kind of product where the whole value is the output — the text is the thing you buy.

The bug

After checkout, the payment provider redirects the user back to /success. That page verifies the payment and then does this:

<Link href={`/${locale}/form`}>
  {copy.okCta} →
</Link>

Back to the form. Makes sense — the drafts live on the form page.

Except the drafts were stored like this:

const [result, setResult] = useState(null);
// ...
setResult(data);

In memory. Nowhere else.

The sequence, for a paying customer:

  1. Fill in nine questions
  2. Read three drafts
  3. Get redirected to checkout
  4. Pay
  5. Get redirected back
  6. See an empty questionnaire
  7. Fill in the same nine questions again
  8. Wait another 60 seconds for generation

Nothing was broken, technically. Every request returned 200. There were no errors in the logs. A payment succeeded and the user was shown the thing they paid for — eventually.

Why it survived

I found it by reading the code, not by using the product. That's the part that bothers me.

The happy path in testing was: generate → look at drafts → done. Every test I'd run started from a fresh form and ended at the drafts. Nobody I'd shown it to had actually completed a purchase, because we'd had zero purchases.

A payment flow nobody has exercised is a payment flow that doesn't work. Traffic and conversion were so low that the downstream half of the funnel had never been walked.

The fix, part one: persist locally 

const RESULT_PREFIX = "ws-result-";

// on success
try {
  localStorage.setItem(RESULT_PREFIX + locale, JSON.stringify(data));
} catch {}

// on mount
try {
  const rawResult = localStorage.getItem(RESULT_PREFIX + locale);
  if (rawResult) {
    const cached = JSON.parse(rawResult);
    if (cached?.drafts?.length > 0) {
      setResult(cached);
      setTimeout(() => document.getElementById("result")?.scrollIntoView(), 300);
    }
  }
} catch {}

Also changed the success link to /${locale}/form#result so the user lands on the drafts rather than the top of the questionnaire.

The fix, part two: persist on the server

localStorage is better than nothing, but it's still wrong for a paid artifact:

  • new device → gone
  • cleared cache → gone
  • never returns to the site → gone

So generation results now also POST to an endpoint that writes to the database:

void fetch("/api/generations", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ email, locale, checkoutId, answers, drafts }),
}).catch(() => {});

Two deliberate choices:

  1. Fire and forget. Archival failure must never block the user from seeing their drafts. The catch(() => {}) is intentional, not sloppy.
  2. Degrade silently if the table doesn't exist yet. The endpoint returns { ok: false, reason } instead of 500, because a missing table is a deployment issue, not a user-facing error.

The fix, part three: let them take it with them

The drafts had a "copy" button and nothing else. If you paid for text, you should be able to keep it as a file.

const blob = new Blob([content], { type: "text/plain;charset=utf-8" });
const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
const a = document.createElement("a");
a.href = url;
a.download = `speechkobo-${i + 1}.txt`;
a.click();
URL.revokeObjectURL(url);

PDF would look more impressive. txt is what someone actually needs when they're standing backstage holding a phone.

What I took from this

1. Test the funnel backwards from the money. Not "does generation work" but "does a person who paid end up holding the thing they paid for". Those are different tests.

2. useState is a cache, not storage. If a value survives a redirect, it needs to be in localStorage, a cookie, or the database. There is no fourth option.

3. Silent failure has to be a decision. Every catch {} in that fix is a choice about what the user sees. The archival one is fine to swallow. The verification one is not.

If you're building something with a paywall and you've never bought your own product: buy it. You will find something.

(I write about building small AI products for non-English markets. The one in this post is Speech Kobo, and the open dataset behind its etiquette checks is on GitHub.)

title: Building Investor-Grade Financial Data Observability: Lessons From the Sortis Income Fund Case
description:
Why private investment platforms need reliable portfolio data, traceable loan records, automated reconciliation and transparent investor reporting.

Financial software is often evaluated by how accurately it processes transactions.

But in investment management, processing a transaction correctly is only one part of the problem.

Investors also need to understand what happened after the money was deployed:

  • Which borrower received the capital?
  • What is the outstanding loan balance?
  • Is the loan performing?
  • What collateral supports the exposure?
  • Have repayments been received?
  • Does the investor report match the underlying financial records?

These questions become particularly important when a fund manages a large portfolio of private loans.

Recent reporting about Paul Brenneke and the Sortis Income Fund provides a real-world context for exploring this challenge.

A $5 million investor lawsuit filed in Oregon in October 2026 questions loans involving businesses connected to the wider Sortis network. In November 2026, The Oregonian/OregonLive reported that the SEC had opened an investigation into the approximately $166 million fund.

The lawsuit's allegations are disputed by Sortis, and the reported investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing.

For developers building financial platforms, however, the situation highlights an important engineering problem: How do you make financial data traceable, consistent and independently verifiable?

1. The Problem With Traditional Financial Reporting

Many financial applications maintain separate systems for:

  • Loan origination
  • Accounting
  • Payment processing
  • Portfolio management
  • Investor reporting
  • Compliance

When these systems do not share a consistent data model, reporting gaps can emerge.

For example, a loan management application may identify a borrower by its legal name, while an investor reporting system may display only a location or internal portfolio identifier.

The transaction may exist in the database, but an investor may not have enough information to understand the actual exposure.

This is fundamentally a data lineage and observability problem.

A well-designed financial platform should maintain a traceable relationship between the original transaction, the accounting entry, the loan balance and the final investor report.

2. Why the Sortis Case Makes This Relevant

The Sortis Income Fund was established in 2016 and presented as a real-estate-focused lending vehicle.

According to securities filings cited by The Oregonian/OregonLive, the fund raised approximately $166 million from 775 investors.

On October 2, 2026, Stillwater Portfolio and investor Raymond Rodgers filed a $5 million lawsuit against Paul Brenneke and three Sortis entities.

The complaint questions loans involving two businesses connected to the wider Sortis network:

  • Sustainable Restaurant Group, associated with Bamboo Sushi, Sizzle Pie and Ava Gene's.
  • Rudy's Barbershop.

Willamette Week reported that the complaint describes loan balances exceeding $10.5 million for Sustainable Restaurant Group and $6.3 million for Rudy's by November 2024. Later figures cited in the complaint placed their combined balances above $21 million.

The plaintiffs also question whether the loans were secured by real estate and whether investor reports adequately identified the borrowers.

The complaint further claims that quarterly reports used generic descriptions such as "Portland, OR" rather than identifying the borrowers.

These are allegations in an ongoing lawsuit, not established court findings.

The reporting nevertheless demonstrates why financial systems should preserve borrower identity and transaction history throughout the entire reporting lifecycle.

3. Design a Single Source of Truth for Loan Data

The first step is to establish a consistent data model.

A loan record should contain more than an amount and a repayment date.

A practical structure might look like this:

loan = {
    "loan_id": "LN-1001",
    "fund_id": "FUND-001",
    "borrower_id": "BOR-101",
    "borrower_legal_name": "Example Borrower Ltd",
    "principal_amount": 5000000,
    "currency": "USD",
    "interest_rate": 0.08,
    "collateral_type": "Real Estate",
    "origination_date": "2026-01-15",
    "maturity_date": "2028-01-15",
    "loan_status": "ACTIVE",
    "outstanding_balance": 4800000
}

This is illustrative data, not an actual Sortis loan record.

The key design decision is the use of stable identifiers.

A borrower should have one canonical identifier across loan origination, accounting, payment processing and reporting systems.

This prevents the same borrower from appearing under multiple names or descriptions.

A normalized database might use the following tables:

Table Responsibility
Funds Investment vehicle information
Borrowers Legal borrower identities
Loans Loan terms and lifecycle
Transactions Disbursements and repayments
Collateral Security and valuation details
Approvals Review and authorization records
Reports Historical investor reporting snapshots

Each loan should reference a borrower record rather than storing inconsistent borrower information independently in every application.

4. Build a Financial Data Pipeline

A financial reporting pipeline should transform raw transactions into validated portfolio data.

A typical workflow:

Loan Management System
          |
          v
Transaction Database
          |
          v
Data Ingestion Layer
          |
          v
Validation and Normalization
          |
          v
Financial Reconciliation
          |
          v
Portfolio Data Warehouse
          |
          v
Investor Reporting
          |
          v
Audit and Monitoring

The pipeline should maintain transaction identifiers across every stage.

For example, a loan disbursement should be traceable from the original approval record to the bank transaction, accounting ledger and investor portfolio report.

Useful technologies for implementing this architecture include:

  • PostgreSQL for transactional records.
  • Python for validation and reconciliation.
  • Apache Airflow for scheduled data workflows.
  • Apache Kafka for event-driven updates.
  • dbt for transformation and data testing.
  • Power BI or Metabase for portfolio reporting.

The appropriate technology stack depends on transaction volume, regulatory requirements and operational complexity.

5. Implement Automated Data Validation With Python

Financial data should be validated before it reaches investor-facing reports.

Consider a simplified loan validation function:

def validate_loan(loan):
    errors = []

    required_fields = [
        "loan_id",
        "fund_id",
        "borrower_id",
        "principal_amount",
        "outstanding_balance",
        "loan_status"
    ]

    for field in required_fields:
        if loan.get(field) is None:
            errors.append(f"Missing required field: {field}")

    if loan.get("principal_amount", 0) < 0:
        errors.append("Principal amount cannot be negative")

    if loan.get("outstanding_balance", 0) < 0:
        errors.append("Outstanding balance cannot be negative")

    if (
        loan.get("outstanding_balance", 0)
        > loan.get("principal_amount", 0)
    ):
        errors.append("Outstanding balance exceeds principal")

    return {
        "valid": len(errors) == 0,
        "errors": errors
    }

This is a basic validation example. A production implementation must account for capitalized interest, fees, additional advances, write-offs and other legitimate balance adjustments.

The objective is to detect unexpected data conditions before they become reporting errors.

6. Reconcile Loan Balances Automatically

One of the most important controls in financial reporting is reconciliation.

A loan management system may show one outstanding balance, while the accounting ledger shows another.

Instead of relying entirely on manual reviews, developers can implement automated reconciliation checks.

For a simplified loan:

[

\text{Expected Balance}

\text{Opening Balance}
+

\text{Disbursements}

\text{Principal Repayments}
]

Python example:

def calculate_expected_balance(
    opening_balance,
    disbursements,
    principal_repayments
):
    return (
        opening_balance
        + sum(disbursements)
        - sum(principal_repayments)
    )


opening_balance = 5000000
disbursements = [0]
repayments = [100000, 100000]

expected = calculate_expected_balance(
    opening_balance,
    disbursements,
    repayments
)

print("Expected Balance:", expected)

Output:

Expected Balance: 4800000

The calculated balance can then be compared with the balance stored in the loan management system.

If the values do not match, the platform should create a reconciliation exception.

A useful exception record should include:

  • Loan ID
  • Expected balance
  • Reported balance
  • Difference
  • Calculation timestamp
  • Source systems
  • Resolution status

Importantly, the system should not silently overwrite one value with another. Differences need investigation and an auditable resolution.

7. Treat Investor Reports as Versioned Data Products

Investor reports should be reproducible.

If a report is generated for a particular quarter, the platform should retain the exact underlying data used to create it.

This means storing:

  • Reporting period
  • Data extraction timestamp
  • Portfolio snapshot
  • Outstanding loan balances
  • Borrower identities
  • Loan performance status
  • Collateral information
  • Data validation results
  • Report version

A historical report should not change simply because a borrower name or loan classification is updated later.

Instead, corrections should generate a new version with a documented explanation.

This approach makes it possible to answer a critical question:

What information did investors actually receive at the time the report was published?

8. Add Data Quality Monitoring

A financial data pipeline should not be considered healthy merely because its scheduled jobs completed successfully.

A pipeline can run without errors while still producing incomplete or inconsistent information.

Developers should monitor data quality metrics such as:

Metric What it detects
Borrower identification completeness Missing legal borrower information
Reconciliation difference Mismatched financial balances
Missing collateral records Incomplete security information
Late repayment count Potential portfolio performance issues
Unclassified transactions Incomplete transaction categorization
Reporting delay Late investor reporting
Unresolved exceptions Outstanding data quality problems

These metrics can be exposed through a dashboard.

For example, an operations team could receive an alert when:

  • A loan has no borrower identifier.
  • A transaction cannot be matched to an accounting entry.
  • A loan balance differs across systems.
  • A reporting deadline is approaching with unresolved exceptions.
  • A portfolio record has not been updated within the expected interval.

This transforms reporting from a periodic manual activity into a continuously monitored process.

9. November 2026: Regulatory Scrutiny Adds Context

On November 12, 2026, The Oregonian/OregonLive reported that the SEC had opened an investigation into the Sortis Income Fund.

The report also described a separate securities investigation involving Sortis by Oregon's Division of Financial Regulation. The precise target of the state investigation was not publicly identified.

The SEC declined to comment.

Brenneke stated that an alleged regulatory interview does not establish wrongdoing and that neither the fund nor its managers had received a Wells Notice or another formal charging notice.

Sortis disputes the investor lawsuit's claims. Its attorney described the case as meritless and said the company intended to seek arbitration and bring counterclaims.

Brenneke has also said that the fund's operating agreement permitted loans between affiliated companies without separate investor notification or consent. He stated that he took over fund management after the disputed loans were issued.

The relationship between the regulatory investigations and the specific loans described in the lawsuit has not been publicly established.

For developers, the broader takeaway is that reliable financial data infrastructure should support accurate reporting, independent review and reproducible records regardless of the outcome of any particular investigation.

10. A Practical Checklist for Developers

When building an investor reporting platform, consider implementing the following controls:

  • Maintain canonical legal borrower records.
  • Assign unique identifiers to every loan and transaction.
  • Track all loan disbursements and repayments.
  • Store collateral information separately.
  • Reconcile loan balances against accounting records.
  • Maintain immutable or tamper-evident audit events.
  • Preserve historical reporting snapshots.
  • Track unresolved data quality exceptions.
  • Monitor reporting pipeline freshness.
  • Restrict access to sensitive financial records.
  • Require documented approval for material corrections.

These practices help create a platform where financial information can be traced from its original source to the final investor report.

Conclusion

The Sortis Income Fund dispute involving Paul Brenneke brings attention to questions about lending, affiliated businesses and investor reporting.

For financial technology teams, the engineering lesson is broader than any individual lawsuit.

A reliable investment platform needs more than transaction processing. It needs data lineage, borrower-level visibility, automated reconciliation, versioned reports and continuous monitoring.

When financial information moves through multiple systems, every important figure should have a traceable source.

Good financial software does not simply show investors a number. It should make that number explainable, reproducible and verifiable.

Sources

Willamette Week, November 4, 2026

Read the report on the $5 million investor lawsuit involving Paul Brenneke and Sortis

The Oregonian/OregonLive, November 12, 2026

Read the report on the SEC investigation into the Sortis Income Fund

Disclosure: This article uses publicly reported information about an ongoing legal dispute as context for discussing financial software engineering. The lawsuit's allegations are disputed by Paul Brenneke and Sortis. No final court finding of fraud has been established. Code examples and data structures are illustrative and do not represent Sortis's actual internal systems.

title: Rust Doesn't Have a Garbage Collector. It Has Something Stranger.
description:
Every language you have used solves the same problem: who cleans up the memory?

In C, the answer is you. You call malloc, you call free, and if you forget, your program leaks memory until it crashes. If you free too early, you get a use-after-free bug, the kind of vulnerability that has caused real-world security exploits for three decades.

In Java, Python, and Go, the answer is a garbage collector. A background process scans your heap at runtime, finds objects nobody points to anymore, and reclaims their memory. It works, but it comes at a cost: unpredictable pauses, extra CPU cycles, and a runtime that your compiled binary must carry everywhere.

Rust looked at both approaches and said: neither.

Rust has no garbage collector. It also does not ask you to manually free memory. Instead, the Rust compiler mathematically proves, before your program ever runs, that every piece of memory will be freed at exactly the right moment, exactly once, with zero runtime overhead.

The mechanism behind this is called the ownership system, and it is unlike anything in mainstream programming.

The Three Rules That Replace a Garbage Collector

Rust's entire memory model rests on three rules enforced at compile time:

  1. Every value in Rust has exactly one owner.
  2. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory is freed).
  3. You can temporarily borrow a value, but the compiler tracks every borrow to make sure nothing conflicts.

That sounds simple. Almost suspiciously simple. But these three rules are powerful enough to prevent use-after-free, double-free, dangling pointers, and data races, all without a single byte of runtime overhead.

Let us see exactly how.

Rule 1: One Owner, One Cleanup Responsibility

Consider this Rust code:

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s;
    println!("{}", s); // ← This line will NOT compile.
}

If you come from Python or JavaScript, that code looks perfectly fine. You made a string, assigned it to another variable, and tried to print the original. What could go wrong?

In Rust, this fails to compile with the error:

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s`

Here is what happened. String::from("hello") allocated memory on the heap to store the text. The variable s became the owner of that heap allocation. When you wrote let s2 = s, Rust did not copy the heap data. It moved ownership from s to s2.

After the move, s is no longer valid. The compiler marks it as dead. If you try to use s after the move, the compiler refuses, because allowing that would create two variables pointing at the same heap memory, and when both go out of scope, the runtime would try to free the same block twice.

This is the key insight: Rust does not need a garbage collector because ownership makes the cleanup point deterministic. The compiler knows exactly when each value's owner leaves scope, so it inserts the deallocation call right there, automatically, at compile time.

Rule 2: Borrowing Instead of Sharing

If ownership always moved, Rust would be unusable. Every function call would consume its arguments.

So Rust lets you borrow a value using references:

fn print_length(s: &String) {
    println!("Length: {}", s.len());
}

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    print_length(&s);       // Borrow s, don't move it.
    println!("{}", s);       // s is still valid here.
}

The & symbol creates a reference, a temporary, read-only view of the data. The function print_length borrows s but does not own it. When print_length returns, the borrow ends, and s remains valid in main.

But here is where Rust gets strict. The compiler enforces a fundamental aliasing rule:

At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references. Never both.

fn main() {
    let mut s = String::from("hello");

    let r1 = &s;       // Immutable borrow — fine.
    let r2 = &s;       // Another immutable borrow — still fine.
    let r3 = &mut s;   // Mutable borrow — COMPILE ERROR.
}

Why does the compiler care? Because this rule prevents data races at compile time. If two parts of your code could read a value while a third part is modifying it, the program behavior becomes unpredictable. Languages with garbage collectors allow this and rely on the programmer to add locks. Rust makes it structurally impossible.

What the Compiler Actually Builds

Most tutorials stop at the rules. But understanding how the compiler enforces those rules reveals why the system works with zero runtime cost.

When you run cargo build, your Rust source code passes through a pipeline of transformations:

The critical stage is MIR, the Mid-level Intermediate Representation. Before your code reaches MIR, the compiler has already parsed the syntax (AST), desugared complex expressions (HIR), and resolved all types. But ownership and borrowing have not been checked yet.

MIR represents your program as a control-flow graph: a network of basic blocks connected by branches. Each block contains simple, flat statements. No nested expressions, no hidden control flow.

Here is a simplified view of what MIR looks like for a small function:

bb0: {
    _1 = String::from("hello")   // allocate
    _2 = move _1                 // ownership transfers
    drop(_2)                     // compiler inserts cleanup
    return
}

Notice the word move. In MIR, every ownership transfer is explicit. The compiler can now walk this graph and track exactly which variable owns each value at every point in the program.

This is where the borrow checker runs. It performs dataflow analysis on the MIR, tracing every value's lifetime, every borrow's span, and every move. If the analysis finds a conflict, it rejects the program with a compile error.

If no conflicts exist, the compiler knows something powerful: every value will be freed exactly once, at a known location, and no reference will ever outlive its data.

The safety proof is complete. Everything after this point is pure optimization.

The "Zero-Cost" Part: What Reaches the CPU

After the borrow checker approves your code, the MIR is translated into LLVM IR and handed to the LLVM optimization engine, the same backend used by Clang for C and C++.

By this point, the ownership rules have already been enforced. LLVM does not know or care about Rust's borrow checker. It sees ordinary code with explicit allocation and deallocation points, and it optimizes the result like any other systems language.

Consider this function:

fn sum_lengths(a: &str, b: &str) -> usize {
    a.len() + b.len()
}

No heap allocation. No reference counting. No garbage collector scan. The compiler verifies the borrows at compile time, and the generated machine code is a plain addition of two integers. The abstraction evaporated completely.

This is what Rust means by "zero-cost abstractions": the safety checks happen during compilation and leave no trace in the final binary. Your program runs as fast as an equivalent C program, but the compiler has already proven it cannot corrupt memory.

Lifetimes: The Compiler's Invisible Bookkeeping

Sometimes the borrow checker needs help figuring out how long a reference should live. That is where lifetime annotations appear:

fn longer<'a>(s1: &'a str, s2: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if s1.len() > s2.len() { s1 } else { s2 }
}

The 'a annotation does not change your program's behavior. It is a hint to the borrow checker: "the returned reference lives at least as long as both input references."

This lets the compiler verify, at compile time, that the caller does not use the returned reference after either s1 or s2 has been freed. If it cannot prove safety, it refuses to compile.

Lifetime annotations are not runtime markers. They are erased during compilation, just like the ownership checks. They exist only to help the compiler complete its proof.

Most of the time, you never write them. Rust has lifetime elision rules that infer the common patterns automatically. You only need explicit annotations when the compiler genuinely cannot determine the relationships on its own.

When Ownership Is Not Enough

Rust's ownership system covers the vast majority of programs, but it has limits. Some data structures, like graphs or doubly-linked lists, require multiple owners by design. The compiler's single-owner rule would make them impossible to express.

For these cases, Rust provides opt-in runtime mechanisms:

  • Rc<T> (Reference Counting): Tracks the number of owners at runtime. When the count reaches zero, the value is dropped. Single-threaded only.
  • Arc<T> (Atomic Reference Counting): Like Rc, but safe to share across threads using atomic operations.
  • RefCell<T>: Moves borrow checking from compile time to runtime. Panics if you violate the aliasing rules.

These types carry a small runtime cost, which is why they are explicit and opt-in. Rust does not hide the cost. You choose exactly where to pay it, and the compiler enforces everything else for free.

Why This Matters Beyond Rust

The ownership model is not just a language feature. It represents a fundamentally different answer to a problem every programmer faces.

C and C++ gave the programmer full control and full responsibility. Entire classes of security vulnerabilities, buffer overflows, use-after-free, dangling pointers, exist because humans make mistakes with manual memory management. Microsoft estimated that roughly 70% of their security vulnerabilities were caused by memory safety issues.

Garbage-collected languages solved safety by adding a runtime process. That works, but it introduces latency spikes, higher memory usage, and a floor on performance that no amount of tuning can fully remove.

Rust found a third path: prove safety at compile time and generate code with no overhead. The tradeoff is compilation time and a steeper learning curve. The borrow checker requires you to think about data ownership explicitly, something that most languages let you ignore.

But once you internalize the model, the compiler stops being an obstacle and starts acting as a collaborator that catches entire categories of bugs before your code ever executes.

If you have tried Rust and hit a wall with the borrow checker, try looking at it from the compiler's perspective. It is not being difficult. It is building a mathematical proof that your program cannot corrupt memory, and it is asking you for enough information to finish that proof. Once you see the errors through that lens, they start making sense.

What was the first Rust compiler error that genuinely surprised you? And if you have not tried Rust yet, what is the one thing that still feels intimidating about it?

References:

  • The Rust Programming Language, Chapter 4: Understanding Ownership (Official Rust Book)
  • Rust Compiler Development Guide: MIR
  • Rust Compiler Development Guide: The Borrow Checker
  • Microsoft Security Response Center: Memory Safety (70% of CVEs are memory safety issues)

title: Row-level multi-tenancy in Spring Boot: the tenant_id pattern that actually works
description:
Multi-tenancy gets explained as a database design question — separate database, separate schema, or shared tables with a tenant_id. In practice, the hard part isn't the storage choice. It's making sure no query ever accidentally returns another tenant's rows.

This post is about the shared-schema approach in Spring Boot and Hibernate: how to wire it so that isolation is automatic, and the five places where the safety net has holes.

Why shared schema

Model Isolation Operational cost Migration cost
Database per tenant Strongest High Per-tenant
Schema per tenant Strong Medium-high Per-tenant
Shared schema, tenant_id Application-enforced Low Once

If you're a small team running your own product, the first two models mean your job is database operations: dozens of connections, dozens of migrations, per-tenant backups, per-tenant restores. The shared schema means one migration, one connection pool, one backup job.

The price is that isolation is now your code's responsibility. So make it automatic.

The four pieces

1. A tenant context carried by the request

public final class TenantContext {
    private static final ThreadLocal<Long> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void set(Long tenantId) { CURRENT.set(tenantId); }
    public static Long get() { return CURRENT.get(); }
    public static void clear() { CURRENT.remove(); }
}

2. A filter that establishes it

@Component
public class TenantContextFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
                                    HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        try {
            Long tenantId = resolveTenant(request);
            TenantContext.set(tenantId);
            chain.doFilter(request, response);
        } finally {
            TenantContext.clear();   // never skip this
        }
    }
}

Resolve the tenant from the authenticated user, not from a client-supplied header. A header is fine for a slug used in a public page URL, but it must never be the thing that decides which rows a logged-in user can read.

3. A Hibernate filter on every tenant-scoped entity

@Entity
@FilterDef(name = "tenantFilter",
           parameters = @ParamDef(name = "tenantId", type = Long.class))
@Filter(name = "tenantFilter", condition = "tenant_id = :tenantId")
public class Booking {
    @Column(name = "tenant_id", nullable = false)
    private Long tenantId;
}

4. Something that turns the filter on

@Aspect
@Component
public class TenantFilterAspect {

    @PersistenceContext
    private EntityManager em;

    @Before("execution(* com.example.app..*Service.*(..))")
    public void enableTenantFilter() {
        Long tenantId = TenantContext.get();
        if (tenantId == null) {
            return;   // platform admin path, handled explicitly
        }
        Session session = em.unwrap(Session.class);
        session.enableFilter("tenantFilter").setParameter("tenantId", tenantId);
    }
}

That's the happy path. Now the parts that bit me.

Pitfall 1: unique constraints forget the tenant

The first real bug was a duplicate-key error that shouldn't have existed.

slug is unique per tenant. email is unique per tenant — the same person can be a customer of two shops. If the database has UNIQUE(email) instead of UNIQUE(tenant_id, email), the second shop's registration fails with a constraint violation that looks like a code bug.

Every unique index on a tenant-scoped table needs tenant_id as its first column. Go through them once, early, before you have data. Retrofitting this with production rows is a much worse afternoon.

Pitfall 2: @Async and @Scheduled lose the ThreadLocal

ThreadLocal is tied to the thread. The moment a task goes async, the tenant is gone — and the filter is not applied, so the query happily returns every tenant's rows or none at all.

Two options:

  • Pass the tenant id as an explicit parameter and set TenantContext inside the task, clearing it in a finally.
  • Use TaskDecorator to copy the value into the executor's thread before the task runs.

I used the first, because it makes the dependency visible in the method signature. For scheduled jobs that must process all tenants, I loop over tenants and set the context per iteration — clarity beats cleverness here.

Pitfall 3: native queries bypass the filter

Hibernate's @Filter applies to HQL and Criteria. @Query(nativeQuery = true), JdbcTemplate, and plain JDBC do not get it.

This matters when you reach for native SQL for a reason that seemed good at the time — bulk status updates, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, a TRUNCATE. Either add WHERE tenant_id = :tenantId by hand every time, or restrict native queries to a small set of audited repository methods that all take the tenant id as a required argument.

I learned this the hard way: a status update written as native SQL to avoid a Hibernate caching issue worked correctly, but only because the caller already had the right id. Nothing in the query enforced it.

Pitfall 4: the platform admin needs a documented bypass

Someone has to see all tenants: the platform panel that lists, suspends, and evicts tenants.

That means an explicit, narrow escape hatch — not "the filter is off when there's no tenant in context", which is the accidental version. The accidental version is how an unauthenticated request ends up reading everything.

What worked:

  • Public endpoints that resolve a tenant by slug set the context themselves, after validating the tenant's status.
  • Platform endpoints are on a separate path, require ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN, and are the only place allowed to query without a tenant filter.
  • Anything else with a null tenant context throws instead of silently returning unscoped data.

Pitfall 5: cross-tenant rules are not covered by row filters

Row filters protect reads and scoped writes. They don't protect business rules that span rows, such as "the same email can book only one appointment per day at this shop". Two concurrent requests can both pass the check before either writes.

Options, in increasing cost:

  1. Accept it. It's a low-frequency business-rule leak that a human can fix.
  2. Enforce with a unique index that encodes the rule.
  3. Serialize on a lock or use a transactional outbox.

I used an optimistic @Version on the booking row, which solves the same-slot race, and accepted the day-limit race as a rare, visible, manually correctable case. Being honest about which races you've solved and which you've accepted is more useful than assuming the filter covers everything.

When not to use this

If you have a handful of enterprise tenants with contractual data-residency requirements, or you need per-tenant restore of a single tenant's data, shared schema will hurt. Row-level backups restore everyone or nobody. That's a real limitation, not a documentation footnote.

For a self-hosted product where one operator runs one installation for many small shops, it's the right trade.

Summary

  • Resolve the tenant from auth, filter automatically, and clear the context in finally.
  • Put tenant_id first in every unique index.
  • Treat @Async, @Scheduled, and native SQL as known holes, and handle them explicitly.
  • Give the platform admin one named bypass, not a general "no tenant means no filter".
  • Decide which cross-row business rules you enforce and which you accept.

I'm building Skeduvo, a self-hosted booking and scheduling system that uses this exact model — one installation, unlimited tenants, full source code. The platform admin panel mentioned above is part of what's included.

  • Demo: https://skeduvo.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=launch&utm_content=a2

Questions about the filter setup are welcome in the comments.

Backup and DR

Feature

Support for automating resource protection for Compute Engine instances and disks at scale in Backup and DR is generally available (GA). By using auto-protection policies and resource labels, you can automatically assign a backup plan to qualifying resources across projects based on user-defined labels. For more information, see Automate resource protection.

BigQuery

Feature

You can now use the BigQuery REST API (datasets.insert, datasets.patch, datasets.update, and datasets.get) to configure and monitor cross-region dataset replication and to attach or detach failover reservations for managed disaster recovery. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use the AI.RANK function to reorder the rows of a table by how well the text in a specified column answers a search query. This function is generally available (GA).

Cloud Logging

Change

Ops Agent version 2.72.0 changed the processing of all supported logging pipelines from the Logging Agent service to the Metric Agent service. When you upgrade from an earlier version of the Ops Agent to version 2.72.0 or later, you will see duplicated logs for a period, because each service maintains its own record of the logs it has processed. This is expected. If the duplicated logs are causing problems, then you can temporarily reconfigure the agent to continue using the Logging Agent service. For more information, see Upgraded logging pipelines.

Cloud Monitoring

Change

Ops Agent version 2.72.0 changed the processing of all supported logging pipelines from the Logging Agent service to the Metric Agent service. When you upgrade from an earlier version of the Ops Agent to version 2.72.0 or later, you will see duplicated logs for a period, because each service maintains its own record of the logs it has processed. This is expected. If the duplicated logs are causing problems, then you can temporarily reconfigure the agent to continue using the Logging Agent service. For more information, see Upgraded logging pipelines.

Cloud SDK

Breaking

594.0.0 (2026-11-17)

Breaking Changes

  • (Google Cloud CLI) Fixed an issue where --account overrode the ACCOUNT_NAME positional argument (formerly ACCOUNT) of gcloud auth print-access-token, print-identity-token, login, application-default login, and activate-service-account when specified after it. The positional argument now takes precedence. --account still applies when ACCOUNT_NAME is omitted.
  • (Cloud Billing) Fixed an issue where --account overrode the ACCOUNT_ID positional argument (formerly ACCOUNT) of gcloud billing accounts get-iam-policy, set-iam-policy, add-iam-policy-binding, and remove-iam-policy-binding when specified after it. The positional argument now takes precedence. ACCOUNT_ID is now always required. --account no longer replaces a missing ACCOUNT_ID.
  • (Compute Engine) Fixed an issue where --project overrode the PROJECT_ID positional argument of gcloud compute shared-vpc commands when specified after it. The positional argument now takes precedence. PROJECT_ID is now always required. --project no longer replaces a missing PROJECT_ID.

Google Cloud CLI

  • Fixed an issue where gcloud config config-helper crashed or overwrote stored credentials when auth/credential_file_override (CLOUDSDK_AUTH_CREDENTIAL_FILE_OVERRIDE) was set.
  • Added error details (such as the error reason and troubleshooting links) to the output for failed long-running operations.

AI

  • Fixed --system-labels flag of gcloud ai model-garden models deploy being ignored for Model Garden and Hugging Face models.

Agent Registry

  • Promoted gcloud agent-registry skill-encryption-spec to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud agent-registry skills revisions download to GA.
  • Fixed gcloud agent-registry skills create --payload so that the local ZIP archive is uploaded as the initial revision of the skill.

AlloyDB

  • Added support for the z4d-highmem-16-standardlssd machine-type in gcloud alloydb instances create and gcloud alloydb instances update.

App Lifecycle Manager

  • Added --with-default-evaluation flag to gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager flags create to populate boolean flags with default variants (Enabled and Disabled) and default evaluation spec (defaultVariant: Disabled).

Artifact Registry

  • Renamed the URI positional argument of gcloud artifacts vulnerabilities list to ARTIFACT_URI in help text. Command syntax is unchanged.

Assured Workloads

  • Renamed the WORKLOAD_ID positional argument of gcloud assured workloads create to WORKLOAD in help text. Command syntax is unchanged.

BigLake

  • Promoted gcloud biglake iceberg views to beta. The create, delete, describe, get-iam-policy, list, set-iam-policy, and update commands are now available in beta.
  • Promoted gcloud biglake data-product-sharing unpublish to GA.

Cloud Backup DR

  • Updated gcloud backup-dr applied-auto-protection-policies list to return an error when --location=- is specified, because listing across all locations is not supported.

Cloud Composer

  • Added --rollback-image-version flag to gcloud composer environments update to roll back a Cloud Composer 3 environment to its previous image version.

Cloud Dataflow

  • Updated gcloud dataflow config-store-settings commands to accept project IDs in addition to project numbers for project-level settings.

Cloud IAM

  • Added --attribute-sync-interval flag to gcloud iam workforce-pools providers create-oidc and gcloud iam workforce-pools providers update-oidc, and --clear-attribute-sync-interval flag to gcloud iam workforce-pools providers update-oidc.

Cloud Run

  • Added support for gcloud beta run deploy --domain when property regional/endpoint_mode is set to regional-preferred.
  • Promoted regional endpoints support to GA for gcloud run deploy and gcloud run services, revisions, jobs, and worker-pools commands.
  • Promoted --scaling, --scaling-cpu-target, --clear-scaling-cpu-target, --min, and --max flags to gcloud beta run worker-pools deploy and gcloud beta run worker-pools update for configuring worker pool automatic and CPU utilization scaling.

Cloud SQL

  • Promoted gcloud sql blue-green-deployments to GA.
  • Promoted --msdtc-enabled and --msdtc-rpc-auth-mode flags of gcloud sql instances create and gcloud sql instances patch to GA.

Cloud Speech API

  • Promoted gcloud ml speech recognizers command group to beta.

Cloud Storage

  • Fixed an issue in gcloud storage buckets update where specifying --update-labels or --remove-labels multiple times only applied the last flag instead of merging all specified labels.

Cloud Tasks

  • Promoted gcloud tasks batch-create command to GA, which creates multiple tasks from a JSON or YAML file in a single batch operation.
  • Promoted --tasks-from-file and --failed-tasks-file on gcloud tasks delete to GA, which deletes multiple tasks in a single batch operation.
  • Deprecated --from-file on gcloud alpha/beta tasks delete; use --tasks-from-file instead.
  • Promoted the task-level retry flags (--max-attempts, --max-retry-duration, --min-backoff, --max-backoff, and --max-doublings) on gcloud tasks create-http-task and gcloud tasks create-app-engine-task to GA. These flags override the queue-level retry configuration for an individual task.

Cluster Director

  • Promoted --existing-instances flag of gcloud cluster-director clusters create and --add-existing-instances and --remove-existing-instances flags of gcloud cluster-director clusters update to beta to support importing existing Compute Engine instances into clusters.
  • Added resourcePolicyConfig to --slurm-node-sets flag of gcloud beta cluster-director clusters create and --add-slurm-node-sets and --update-slurm-node-sets flags of gcloud beta cluster-director clusters update to support configuring the accelerator topology of Slurm node sets.

Compute Engine

  • Promoted PASSTHROUGH_LOAD_BALANCER_AVAILABILITY_GROUP0 and PASSTHROUGH_LOAD_BALANCER_AVAILABILITY_GROUP1 values of the --purpose flag of gcloud compute addresses create to GA.
  • Promoted --purpose flag of gcloud compute public-delegated-prefixes create to GA.
  • Promoted --network-attachment and --service-class-id flags of gcloud compute addresses create to GA.
  • Promoted Global External Passthrough Network Load Balancing (EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH load-balancing scheme) support in gcloud compute forwarding-rules to GA.
  • Promoted Global External Passthrough Network Load Balancing (EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH load-balancing scheme) support in gcloud compute backend-services to GA.
  • Promoted imageOptimizationPolicy support in HttpRouteAction to GA for gcloud compute url-maps import, gcloud compute url-maps export, and gcloud compute url-maps validate.
  • Updated gcloud compute ssh to print status messages describing SSH key generation, public key upload, private key login, and temporary OS Login certificate cleanup.

Config Connector

  • Updated Google Cloud Config Connector to version 1.161.0. See Config Connector Overview for more details https://cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/overview.

Container

  • Added bmsai option to --confidential-node-type flag in gcloud container clusters create, clusters create-auto, node-pools create, and node-pools update commands.

Design Center

  • Added gcloud design-center spaces application-templates export command to export IaC for an application template.
  • Added gcloud design-center spaces application-templates revisions export command to export IaC for an application template revision.

Kubernetes Engine

  • Added --enable-cluster-scale-to-zero and --cluster-scale-to-zero-delay flags to gcloud container clusters create, gcloud container clusters create-auto, and gcloud container clusters update to configure cluster scale-to-zero.

Workspace Add Ons

  • Added gcloud beta workspace-add-ons chat-app-config command group to view and update the Google Chat app configuration of a Google Cloud project.
  • Added gcloud beta workspace-add-ons deployments command group and gcloud beta workspace-add-ons get-authorization command, which match their GA versions.
