title: I ran the most hyped AI agent catalog on GitHub through three subagents and installed exactly zero agents from it. This post is
description:
The setup

The catalog: 273 agent files across 22 divisions, 169k stars, MIT license. Each file is a role with rules, deliverable templates and success metrics. Solid work, and mostly noise for any specific business: divisions for Douyin, WeChat, Unity, carousel generators for platforms you may not even be able to reach. The useful fraction is maybe 10 percent, but that fraction contains methodologies it'd take you months to polish yourself.
Our side: a CRM where an Obsidian vault is the single database and agents run the operations layer. Five scheduled roles (commercial director, finance director, CEO, marketer, on-call SRE), an hourly inbound cycle over email and messengers, and a company charter with hard gates. An agent physically cannot send an invoice below the price floor or promise a client a deadline without owner confirmation.
That context matters. A prompt is a personality without memory. What turns it into an employee's the bundle: skill plus schedule plus gates plus access to live company data.

The extraction run

Three subagents in parallel, each with a zone: marketing, sales and paid media (53 files), finance, PM, support, product and strategy (40 files), testing, engineering and specialized roles (about 70).
My instruction to each subagent: read everything, return a verdict per file in the context of our system. Steal, skip, or reference. Not a summary, a decision: what exactly to take and where exactly to put it.
By midday I had verdict tables for 160+ files, deep breakdowns of the top five per zone, and an implementation plan. Then the surgery: edits went into concrete role skills, and since our automation prompts reference those skills, every scheduled ritual picked up the new rules on its next run. Nothing was redeployed. Nothing restarted.
If you want to replicate this, the load-bearing detail we found is the verdict format. 'Interesting' is not a verdict. 'Steal the dunning ladder into the commercial director skill, replace our D+7 single reminder with a five step sequence' is.

What came out of it

The dunning ladder. Receivables now walk a fixed sequence: D-3 heads-up, D+1 reminder with the PDF, D+7 serious reminder with the acceptance act, D+14 formal demand plus a pause-work question, D+30 pre-legal. The first three steps send themselves.
Decisions with defaults. The behavioral design principle that tied it all together: every question to the owner arrives with a drafted answer. Not 'what do we do about this debtor' but 'letter drafted, send or edit'. One click beats an hour of deliberation, and default consent beats both.
The evidence protocol. This one targets the real disease of agent-run companies, fantasy reports. The rules we adopted:

  • Every 'it works' claim requires proof: screenshot, curl output, log, green run. Otherwise the status is NOT TESTED.
  • Four statuses: PASS, FAIL, NOT TESTED, NOT DETERMINED. NOT TESTED means the hole is in the testing, not a hidden all-clear.
  • Automatic fail for 'no issues found' without a documented scope.
  • Default verdict for fresh work: NEEDS WORK. First implementations take two or three revision cycles, that's normal.
  • Perfect scores from a previous agent are a red flag. Reproduce two or three claims at random. The citation audit loop. Once a month, 20 to 40 live buyer prompts run through ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Yandex Neuro. The table records who gets cited. Lost prompts, the ones where a competitor wins, get a root cause check (comparison page, FAQ schema, freshness), a fix pack, and a re-check with the same prompt set 14 days later. Benchmark before fixes, always. Sales qualification. Six questions we now ask on every lead, no exceptions: what is broken, why, what does it cost, who else cares, why now, what happens if nothing is done. Plus the value equation as an offer auditor: value = (dream outcome x perceived likelihood) / (time delay x effort). Cut the price only after squeezing the other three levers. ## Why zero agents got installed Three reasons worth stating plainly:
  • A personality without memory is not an employee. Those 273 prompts do not know our clients or our price floor.
  • Idle agents burn attention and budget. Our roles wake in their slot, do the work, write the journal, sleep.
  • Of the file format itself, only three sections survived contact with reality: hard rules (numbered Never/Always), a ready deliverable template, and verifiable metrics. Identity and vibe are cosmetics. ## Takeaways The competitive edge of 2026 isn't access to AI. Everyone has that. The edge is the speed of absorbing methodologies, because the world produces them faster than any human reads. A company with reading and adoption on a conveyor upgrades weekly. A company without one reads about upgrades on LinkedIn. Second: agents don't replace the owner, they prepare decisions. Approval mode instead of decision production. Third: honest systems beat pompous ones. We rejected dozens of prompts with '+300% leads' claims, numbers out of thin air. Verifiable rules went to production the same day. Apply the same filter to everything sold to you as a miracle. Originally published at https://automata.sale/en/blog/ai-automation/273-agenta-v-odin-den/

title: The problem was real before the architecture became complicated
description:
Odecio Souza · Software Developer | Backend Systems, APIs & Automation · ABC Solutions

Build. Secure. Automate. Share.

The problem was real before the architecture became complicated
I started Agenda de Contas to organise household bills, track payments and plan recurring financial commitments. My household and I use it regularly, and it meets our main organisational needs. The application organises financial obligations; it does not process payments or provide regulated financial services.

The first version was an ASP.NET Core application with a browser interface and JSON-based persistence. Alongside the account and payment workflows, I developed reminders and a routine for operating the application on my own Linux infrastructure.

Later, I wanted to support individual logins and multiple families, each with its own accounts, payments, settings and permissions. That raised a more difficult question:

How could I add a multi-family architecture without putting an application I already relied on at unnecessary risk?

Keep a working baseline working
The most tempting migration plan was to replace JSON with PostgreSQL and move on. I resisted that all-at-once approach because the existing application was not a disposable prototype. It was being used in real life.

I chose to evolve the system incrementally. The documented baseline retained the original JSON store while PostgreSQL, EF Core and individual identity support were developed separately. A feature boundary kept the new multi-family path from automatically replacing the working one.

The distinction matters: code can be implemented, reviewed and merged without becoming the documented production baseline.

Here is a simplified view of the two execution paths described in the architecture documentation:

                 ASP.NET Core application
                            |
                     Multi-family gate
                       /          \
                      /            \
              Disabled              Enabled
          (documented baseline)    (controlled testing)
                  |                  |
             ContaStore          Identity + family context
                  |                  |
                JSON             Scoped repositories
                                     |
                                 PostgreSQL

The diagram omits private hosting details. It represents the documented production baseline on the left and a controlled development and test path on the right; it does not prove a PostgreSQL production cutover.

One database per family or a shared database?
One design decision involved a genuine discussion about how to isolate families.

I considered two approaches:

Give each family its own database.
Use a shared PostgreSQL database with strict logical isolation between families.
A separate database for every family can provide physical separation. But for my requirements, it would also increase the work involved in provisioning, schema migrations, maintenance and backups. I considered that complexity disproportionate for the stage of the project.

I therefore chose a shared-database design with family-scoped access.

The selected design avoids managing a database for every family, but it makes application and data isolation essential. Those boundaries were implemented and tested as part of the new architecture, not activated as a verified production cutover.

Tenant isolation needs more than FamilyId
I designed for defence in depth: membership rules, a selected-family context, repository-level scoping, relational constraints and tests that attempt to cross family boundaries.

The multi-family model contains users, families and memberships. A user's Owner, Admin or Member role belongs to their membership in a particular family, not to their identity globally. Accounts, payments, reminders and settings are family-owned. Scoped repositories and authorisation protect read access, while relational constraints help prevent invalid cross-family relationships.

Make the migration explicit and repeatable
Another challenge was the transition of existing records.

I wanted a controlled process rather than an automatic migration silently triggered on application startup. The developed importer was designed around a few principles:

Explicit execution: importing data is a deliberate operation, not a hidden side effect.
Dry-run support: the operator can inspect an intended import without writing records.
Deterministic mapping: the same source records should map consistently.
Idempotency: repeating a successful operation should not create duplicates.
Transactions: a failed operation should not leave partially migrated data.
Strict input validation: missing required JSON collections should not be mistaken for deliberately empty ones.
A concrete validation case illustrates the risk: a JSON object containing only {} should not be accepted as a successful empty import when the required collections are absent. An intentionally empty array is different from a missing or null collection. The documented importer tests this distinction rather than treating incomplete input as a reassuring zero-record result.

I learned to value clear failure behaviour more than a superficially smooth migration.

Test what must not happen
Supporting multiple families changes the security model.

It is not enough for one user to see their own records when everything is configured correctly. I also need evidence that the application rejects access to records belonging to another family.

The documented tests check tenant isolation, invalid roles and memberships, duplicate constraints and cross-family account/payment relationships.

For example, consider an attempt to associate a Family A payment with a Family B account. Repository scoping should prevent cross-family reads, and relational constraints should reject an invalid relationship. This illustrates a tested boundary using fictional families; it is not a real data-exposure incident.

Individual authentication introduced further concerns. Invitation and password-recovery flows need careful token handling and must avoid unnecessarily revealing whether an account exists. Delivery was separated from token generation so that the flows could be tested without relying on a real notification provider or embedding credentials in source code.

For relational tests, the project used disposable PostgreSQL environments. That made it possible to validate database behaviour without touching the data in my household's existing application.

Operations require separate evidence
Developing software and operating it are different kinds of responsibility.

I researched and configured Linux and Docker infrastructure, deployment routines, secure access and automated backups. This work was challenging. It involved documentation, experiments, repeated troubleshooting and learning how to verify that an operation had genuinely succeeded.

Backup hardening is a good example. The reviewed implementation added integrity checks before marking transfers complete, stronger handling of unexpected paths, and compatibility checks for legacy manifest formats.

However, a passing synthetic test is not proof of deployment or recovery on a real machine. Restores and operational activation require separate evidence.

What I would compare differently in retrospect
The separate-database versus shared-database discussion was a real architectural choice during development. Other possibilities are useful retrospective comparisons, not decisions I claim to have explicitly considered at that time.

For example, replacing JSON immediately might have shortened the transition on paper, but it would have combined data conversion with identity and tenancy changes. Relying exclusively on application query filters would reduce some schema work, but it would provide less protection against invalid relationships or missed filters. Treating roles as global would simplify early code but misrepresent permissions for users belonging to several families.

Reflecting on those alternatives has helped me explain why I prefer staged change, explicit tenant boundaries and independent validation.

What runs today and what comes next
As of 17 November 2026, repository documentation identifies JSON persistence as the documented production baseline. PostgreSQL multi-family features have been developed and tested; a live cutover has not been verified.

My household's ongoing use is real, but I am not claiming external customer adoption, commercial revenue or measured time savings. An external-user pilot remains a future milestone.

Before that pilot, I want controlled deployment evidence, an isolated database, checked backup and recovery procedures, a rehearsed import and a rollback plan.

I have learned that engineering means researching alternatives, protecting what works and separating technical progress from operational proof.

The safest migration was not the one that replaced JSON fastest. It was the one that made each consequential step explicit, testable and reversible wherever possible.

Public engineering references
The development history can be explored through public GitHub pull requests:

Agenda de Contas project
Identity and tenant isolation — PR #2
Controlled JSON import — PR #4
Family management — PR #10
Off-host backup hardening — PR #14
Transport manifest compatibility — PR #15
Verification manifest compatibility — PR #16
These references support the implementation history. They do not independently verify my household's experience or current server state.

About the author and AI assistance
I conceived and directed the project, researched technical choices, evaluated alternatives, supervised development, carried out operational work and reviewed and validated results. ChatGPT and Codex assisted materially with research, implementation, troubleshooting, tests and technical documentation. I remain responsible for the direction of the project and the accuracy of this account; I do not claim that all code was written manually without assistance.

Odecio Souza
Software Developer | Backend Systems, APIs & Automation
ABC Solutions · Build. Secure. Automate. Share.

title: AI Image Generation: Saving PNG Buffers to Compatible Object Storage
description:
Short answer: decode the generated image exactly once into a Node.js Buffer, verify that it is a PNG, then save that binary buffer with Content-Type: image/png to compatible object storage; reject malformed base64 before an upload is attempted.

An image worker should treat its decoded PNG as a separate artifact before it writes to compatible object storage. The operational constraint is simple: a successful object write proves that bytes arrived, not that the bytes were a valid generated PNG. Make decoding and PNG validation a local, deterministic step; upload the resulting Node.js Buffer only after it passes.

That choice prevents malformed base64 errors from being misdiagnosed as storage failures, and it keeps retry budgets attached to the network operation that can actually benefit from a retry.

What should a Node.js AI image upload validate before object storage?

Start by naming the representation at the API boundary. An image generator can return ordinary base64 text, a data URL such as data:image/png;base64,..., or a remote URL. Those are three different contracts. Only the decoded bytes are suitable as the body of an object write. Passing a full data URL into a base64 decoder, or passing base64 text directly as the upload body, creates an object that can look healthy in a storage console while failing in an image decoder later.

For a base64 response, select the documented image field, remove the data:image/png;base64, prefix only when the producer explicitly supplies a data URL, and decode exactly once with Buffer.from(value, "base64"). Node's conversion is permissive enough that application code should not use it as the sole validation step. Check that the encoded value is nonempty, has the expected alphabet and padding rules for its declared variant, and stays under a configured size limit before allocating a large buffer.

Then inspect the result. A PNG begins with the eight bytes 89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a; the buffer must be at least eight bytes long and match that signature. The upload body is that validated Buffer, with Content-Type: image/png, not a UTF-8 string derived from it. This is the byte contract: generator output becomes validated binary, and validated binary becomes an object.

Keep the boundary boring.

One representation. One decode. One binary write.

An example contract test can be written without binding the application to a storage SDK. The same test shape works for a Node.js adapter: a valid image reaches put_object, while malformed text and non-PNG bytes stop before any write. This Python fixture is intentionally small; it demonstrates the checks an adapter should enforce rather than a commercial upload recipe.

import base64

PNG_SIGNATURE = bytes.fromhex("89504e470d0a1a0a")


def decode_png(payload: str) -> bytes:
    if payload.startswith("data:"):
        header, separator, payload = payload.partition(",")
        if separator != "," or header != "data:image/png;base64":
            raise ValueError("expected a PNG data URL")

    if not payload:
        raise ValueError("empty image payload")

    try:
        image = base64.b64decode(payload, validate=True)
    except Exception as error:
        raise ValueError("invalid base64 image payload") from error

    if not image.startswith(PNG_SIGNATURE):
        raise ValueError("decoded payload is not a PNG")
    return image

The exact maximum size is a product decision. It should come from expected dimensions, compression, and worker concurrency, not from an arbitrary internet snippet. I'm not sure one ceiling fits both tiny previews and high-resolution exports; per-class limits are usually easier to reason about.

Why malformed base64 decode errors belong outside the retry loop

Malformed base64 is usually a representation error: the wrong JSON property was selected, a data-URL header remained attached, a response was truncated before it reached the worker, or a non-image value entered the queue. Repeating the same parse against the same payload cannot correct any of those conditions. Record a stable rejection category, the encoded character count, decoded byte count when available, declared media type, and a correlation ID. Avoid logging the image content or prompt text. In practice, the important diagnostic question is not “did the upload fail?” but “which representation crossed the worker boundary?” A queue message that carries a string may be valid JSON, have a plausible length, and even produce a nonempty Buffer, while still being a JSON error payload, a data URL with its header intact, or base64 whose final characters were lost during serialization. If the system collapses all of those cases into one upload retry, the queue grows, storage metrics become noisy, and the producer contract remains broken. Put the response-field selection and validation beside each other in the same module, retain only metadata that is safe to inspect later, and make the rejected representation explicit in the event schema. That gives a release owner enough evidence to compare a response shape against its contract without exposing generated content. It also keeps a malformed input from consuming the retry budget reserved for operations that might succeed on a later network attempt.

This separation changes how an AI image pipeline is operated. Decode rejections are contract signals and should be grouped by producing release, model response shape, and queue consumer. Upload failures are transport or authorization signals and can use bounded retries with an idempotent key. When both are reported as a generic “image failed” counter, an on-call engineer loses the one distinction that identifies the owner of the next action.

A good idempotency key is derived from a request identifier rather than from the prompt. Prompts can contain sensitive user material, and keys travel through logs, traces, and support tools. Stable keys also make an uncertain upload outcome safer: a retry addresses the same object rather than scattering duplicate PNGs across a bucket.

The storage decision is an ownership decision

S3 compatibility describes a request and object model. It does not guarantee identical lifecycle behavior, authorization semantics, metadata handling, replication, or recovery operations across every implementation. Before relying on a compatible endpoint, write an integration test that uploads a tiny fixture through the production authorization path, reads it back, compares a digest, and verifies Content-Type: image/png.

The catch is that self-operated object storage is not suitable when nobody owns capacity, upgrades, replication, and recovery drills. A managed service is also a poor fit when policy requires direct infrastructure control and the organization has the staff to operate it. The right choice follows ownership and recovery requirements, not the fact that both endpoints accept similar object calls.

Question What to decide before launch
Write volume Peak generated images, variants per image, retry rate, and worker concurrency
Retention Which originals, previews, and failed artifacts expire; which must be preserved
Recovery Who restores data, how long it may take, and how recovery is tested
Access Which service identity writes, which delivery path reads, and how access is revoked

Capacity estimates should include preview variants, abandoned jobs, retry traffic, and queue catch-up after a burst. Final PNG count alone is a fragile planning metric. Small omissions multiply when a generation feature creates several derivatives per request and workers keep draining after foreground traffic has dropped.

How do you prove that a generated PNG is usable after upload?

Use a fixture set before deployment: valid plain base64, a valid PNG data URL, allowed whitespace if the producer contract permits it, invalid characters, truncated data, an encoded non-PNG payload, an empty value, and an oversized value. Unit tests should assert that only a valid PNG buffer reaches the object-writer interface. The integration test should retrieve the stored object through the same path used in production and compare its digest to the buffer accepted by the decoder.

Measure each boundary independently: generation responses, decode rejections, upload attempts, upload outcomes, digest mismatches, decoded-byte size, queue age, and upload latency. An alert should have a traffic floor and connect to the user-visible image objective. One malformed fixture should not wake anyone; a sustained increase after a release should stop that release because retries are irrelevant to a deterministic decoding failure.

For browser uploads, progress events describe transfer progress, not durable or readable storage. MDN documents upload progress events on XMLHttpRequest.upload; the application still needs its own completed-write record and a verification result. The distinction matters in support tooling, where a nearly complete progress bar otherwise looks like evidence that a generated image is available.

Lifecycle policy deserves a test as well. Amazon S3 documents lifecycle rules that transition or expire objects, but expiration, user-facing undo, and disaster recovery are different promises. Verify the lifecycle behavior required by the chosen compatible implementation with representative test objects, especially where version retention or legal controls are part of the product contract.

The practical sequence is short: identify the response representation, decode once, validate PNG bytes, persist the binary buffer with its media type, and read back a digest in an integration test. Everything else, including retries and lifecycle rules, becomes easier to place once that byte boundary is explicit.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest

title: How we built an image compressor that keeps files in the browser
description:
An image compressor doesn't need a server to receive the original file. On Wezual Tools, we use browser APIs to decode the image, resize it when requested, and encode a new file. The original image stays on the device during compression.

Decode, draw, and encode

The input is a browser File. After decoding the image, we draw it onto a canvas sized for the output. If the user sets a maximum width, we scale down while preserving the aspect ratio. This can reduce the output size before we adjust quality.

Canvas encoding is asynchronous. We check the returned MIME type because a browser can fall back to another format when it can't encode the requested one.

function encode(canvas, type, quality) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    canvas.toBlob((blob) => {
      if (blob?.type !== type) {
        reject(new Error("This browser cannot encode the selected format."));
        return;
      }
      resolve(blob);
    }, type, quality);
  });
}

Treat a size limit as a measurement

A quality setting is an input to the encoder. It doesn't predict a file size. For size targets, we encode at candidate quality settings and inspect each resulting Blob's byte length. If a file can't meet the chosen limit at those settings, reducing its pixel dimensions or switching to a lossy format can help. PNG doesn't respond to the quality slider like JPEG or WebP does.

Test more than the happy path

Try a large photo, a transparent PNG, and a batch of files. Compare the output type, dimensions, and byte size. Be explicit about transparency when exporting to JPEG, which has no alpha channel. Large images also deserve attention because decoding consumes memory based on pixel dimensions even when the input file is small.

You can try this workflow in the Wezual Image Compressor. I'm sharing it as part of the team behind Wezual Tools.

title: oviev: Building a Compiler in Ovie The Self-Hosting Journey
description:
One of the milestones of any programming language is when it can compile itself. Ovie Lang 1.0 ships oviev the Ovie compiler written entirely in Ovie (.ov files).

Two Compilers, One Language
Compiler Language Status
oviec Rust Stable use for everything today
oviev Ovie (.ov) Stage 1 self-hosted, help test it
Both run the same .ov programs:

oviec run hello.ov # stable Rust compiler
oviev run hello.ov # Ovie self-hosted compiler
The File Map
Every file in oviec/src/*.rs has a mirror .ov file in oviev/src/:

Rust (oviec/src/) Ovie (oviev/src/) Purpose
lexer.rs lexer.ov Tokenizer
parser.rs parser.ov Token -> AST
ast.rs ast.ov AST node definitions
hir.rs hir.ov High-level IR
mir.rs mir.ov Mid-level IR
ir.rs ir.ov IR shared types
interpreter.rs interpreter.ov Runtime
semantic.rs semantic.ov Type checking
error.rs error.ov Error types
main.rs main.ov Entry point + CLI
codegen/llvm.rs backend/llvm.ov LLVM backend
codegen/wasm.rs backend/wasm.ov WASM backend
Run oviev
oviev --version
Output:

== Aproko =============================================

OK: no issues found in oviev/src/main.ov

oviev 1.0 Stage 1 Ovie self-hosted (bootstrapped via oviec)
Usage: oviev [file.ov]
Commands:
run Compile and run
check Check for errors
--version Show version
Run a program with oviev
oviev run calculator.ov
oviev routes this to oviec. Both produce identical output. Stage 1: oviev delegates to oviec (Rust bootstrap). Stage 2: oviev compiles its own .ov files without help from Rust.

Look at lexer.ov
The lexer tokenizes source code. In lexer.ov, written in Ovie:

// Token types every keyword the lexer can produce
enum TokenKind {
Oya, Mut, Fn, If, Else, For, While, Return, Break, Continue,
Struct, Enum, Match, Const, Use, Import, Export,
SeeAm, True, False, Unsafe,
Identifier, NumberLiteral, StringLiteral,
Plus, Minus, Star, Slash, Percent,
Equal, EqualEqual, NotEqual, Arrow,
LeftBrace, RightBrace, LeftParen, RightParen,
Comma, Colon, Semicolon, Dot, Eof
}

fn keyword_kind(word: String) -> TokenKind {
if word == "oya" { return TokenKind.Oya }
if word == "mut" { return TokenKind.Mut }
if word == "fn" { return TokenKind.Fn }
if word == "seeAm" { return TokenKind.SeeAm }
return TokenKind.Identifier
}
The Ovie keywords are wired right into the tokenizer in Ovie itself.

The Stage Plan
Stage Status What it means
Stage 1 Now .ov files written. Bootstrap via oviec
Stage 2 Planned oviev compiles its own .ov files
Stage 3 Future oviec (Rust) retired. oviev is primary
Why it matters
Self-hosting is the proof that a language works. When Ovie can describe its own compiler in Ovie, the language is complete enough to build real things. Every .ov file in oviev/src/ is a test that Ovie's syntax is powerful enough to express compiler logic.

Try it yourself
oviec run oviev/src/lexer.ov # run the Ovie lexer written in Ovie
oviec check oviev/src/parser.ov # check the Ovie parser written in Ovie
oviec run oviev/src/main.ov # run the oviev entry point
All pass Aproko with: OK: no issues found

title: Beyond Disk and WAL: What Limits PostgreSQL Scaling?
description:
The earlier tests improved read I/O and removed standby acknowledgment waiting, but the primary still waited for local WAL synchronization. Separate, later durable-regime traces located substantial delay in guest-OS write admission. This post returns to the diagnostic where I stopped waiting for commit durability to see what remained.

I used session-level synchronous_commit=off for the same 512-worker, 15+45-minute workload. This allows a successful commit response before WAL is durable: a crash can lose recently acknowledged transactions. Keep in mind that I do this in a lab to investigate PostgreSQL bottlenecks. It deviates from the initial comparison with HorizonDB's built-in high-availability and from the original durable-HA configuration. Still, let's see how far we can increase the throughput in this lab.

WAL, fsync and full_page_writes remained enabled. Both streaming replicas were retained. Automatic Patroni failover was separately paused for the diagnostic.

Verify the mode, then measure

The override was supplied through the workload's PGOPTIONS. Before launch, a test Pgtcl connection using that environment executed:

SHOW synchronous_commit;

Its recorded check was:

2026-11-08T08:08:47.692827+00:00 BENCH_COMMIT_MODE_CHECK adapter=Pgtcl effective=off

This records the adapter test connection's setting. The workload was launched with the same connection environment, while the server default remained on.

The result was:

2026-11-08T09:08:53.198898+00:00 Vuser 1:TEST RESULT : System achieved 66096 NOPM from 152007 PostgreSQL TPM

93.92% of sampled active-client observations were at LWLock:BufferContent. The question had moved from when WAL becomes durable to which backends needed conflicting access to an in-memory page. I wanted to identify that page before changing shared_buffers.

The page identification below comes from a later synchronous_commit=on follow-up.

What BufferContent protects

BufferContent is a wait for a lightweight lock protecting the contents of a cached relation page, normally 8 KiB. Shared holders can coexist. Exclusive access conflicts with other holders, even when the page is already in memory.

BufferMapping instead concerns associating a block with a buffer slot. BufferIO concerns buffer I/O completion.

For Oracle readers, LWLocks are closer to latches and mutexes than transactional enqueues: they protect shared-memory structures, not business rows until commit. PostgreSQL's heavyweight lock manager is the closer comparison for transaction and object locks. pg_locks and pg_blocking_pids() do not expose a content-LWLock holder.

A buffer pin is different again: it prevents recycling the slot, but does not grant exclusive access to its contents.

Oracle's buffer busy waits includes P1/P2/P3 parameters identifying file, block, and block class. PostgreSQL's pg_stat_activity exposes neither that page identity nor per-wait elapsed time for BufferContent. query_start times the statement, not its current wait. Oracle active-session history is sampled too. Samples and timed waits are different measurements.

Observe active backends

The collector grouped pg_stat_activity by backend type, state, and wait event. This query shows the active-client part:

SELECT wait_event_type,
       wait_event,
       count(*) AS sessions
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
  AND state = 'active'
GROUP BY wait_event_type, wait_event
ORDER BY sessions DESC;

active describes statement execution status and includes statements currently waiting.

These are retained samples from the synchronous_commit=off measured window, November 8, 2026, 08:23:51-09:08:53 UTC:

Observer timestamp, UTC Phase Active clients At BufferContent Percentage
08:24:43.424849 measurement 513 476 92.79
08:34:43.913026 measurement 512 483 94.34
08:44:44.413830 measurement 512 491 95.90
08:54:44.923233 measurement 513 484 94.35
09:08:45.608882 measurement 513 470 91.62

The collector included all active client backends, including its own connection, without database/user filtering. These counts therefore differ from the 512 workload workers.

Across all 45 samples taken one minute apart inside the measured interval, there were 23,063 active-client observations:

Wait Observations Share
LWLock:BufferContent 21,660 93.92%
IO:DataFileRead 981 4.25%
No reported wait 376 1.63%
Client:ClientRead 25 0.11%
IO:DataFileFlush 10 0.04%
IO:DataFileWrite 7 0.03%
IO:DataFileExtend 2 0.01%
IPC:BufferIo 2 0.01%

None of the 45 snapshots contained LWLock:WALWrite or IPC:SyncRep. The 93.92% is 21660 / 23063, the share of sampled active-client observations.

Background persistence continued. In-window WAL counters showed approximately 194.46 MiB/s generated and 220.76 syncs/s. WAL must still precede durable data-page writes.

A buffer is not necessarily a table's data page

Shared buffers can hold more than application table rows:

Page contents Examples
Table heap Row versions, headers and item identifiers
Index B-tree, GIN, GiST, SP-GiST, hash or BRIN pages, including metadata
TOAST relation Out-of-line values and their index
System catalogue Catalogue heap and index pages
Materialized view Stored rows and indexes
Sequence The sequence relation's state page
Relation metadata Free-space-map and visibility-map pages
Unlogged relation Working pages and initialization-fork pages

Partitions store their own pages. The partitioned parent does not store heap rows. Temporary relations use backend-local buffers. WAL buffers and SLRU caches, such as transaction-status caches, are separate structures with different synchronization.

Relation forks and page identity

A fork is a physical part of a relation with a specific purpose:

Number Fork File suffix Contents
0 main none Heap, index or other primary relation storage
1 fsm _fsm Free-space map
2 vm _vm All-visible and all-frozen information for heap pages
3 init _init Unlogged relation's initialization state after an unclean shutdown

Not every relation has every fork. Indexes have no visibility map. See the file-layout documentation.

PostgreSQL's BufferTag identifies a page by tablespace, database, filenode, fork, and block number. All five matter: main-fork block 0 and VM-fork block 0 are different pages. Catalog OIDs and physical filenodes are distinct identifiers. A rewrite can change the filenode while preserving the OID.

Separate follow-up: identifying pages with synchronous_commit=on

For page-level diagnosis, I used a separate 512-worker pilot with synchronous_commit=on and normal HA. BufferContent was still visible in the capture-trigger samples at 5.47-18.75%, enough to trace page contention under ordinary durable commits.

1️⃣ Capture the page tag at the lock event. I traced selected PostgreSQL processes by PID with Linux perf. Uprobes are tracing points in userspace machine code. I checked their instruction locations and registers against the installed PostgreSQL executable.

At acquisition, semaphore-wait and release points, the probes recorded the lock address and the full page tag from its buffer descriptor. Pairing required the same page identity at the beginning and end of an interval.

Eight nominal three-second recordings sampled selected backends and background processes. This is a selected-field excerpt of the decoded, aggregated wait output:

{
  "tag": [1663, 57465, 57491, 2, 10215],
  "waited_loop_count": 78,
  "loop_wait_ns": 2357679631
}

In order, that tag means tablespace 1663, database 57465 (tpcc), filenode 57491, fork 2, block 10215. Fork 2 was recorded by the probe.

2️⃣ Resolve the filenode through the catalogs. Connected to tpcc, the collector mapped captured filenodes through pg_class. This reduced lookup resolves the same identity:

SELECT n.nspname AS schema,
       c.relname AS relation,
       c.relkind,
       am.amname,
       pg_relation_filenode(c.oid) AS filenode
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
LEFT JOIN pg_am am ON am.oid = c.relam
WHERE c.oid = pg_filenode_relation(1663::oid, 57491::oid);

The retained catalog row, reformatted from the collector's JSON:

 schema | relation | relkind | amname | filenode
--------+----------+---------+--------+---------
 public | stock    | r       | heap   |    57491

The relation is public.stock. Fork 2 identifies its visibility map, so this is stock VM block 10215, not stock heap block 10215.

3️⃣ Keep the block identity in the results. These were the leading measured pages by cumulative completed semaphore-loop elapsed time. All have the same tablespace/database/filenode and VM fork:

Stock VM block Completed loops Cumulative loop ms
10215 78 2,357.680
10031 66 2,206.913
10032 63 2,076.327
10033 55 1,984.848

Stock's VM fork was 94,912,512 bytes, or 11,586 8-KiB pages, consistent with those block numbers.

Selected processes contributed these completed loops. The elapsed intervals include semaphore work, rescheduling, and probe overhead. Several loops can belong to one acquisition.

Captured holder operations on these pages included heap_update. The longer waiter intervals remain only partially attributed.

The identification chain in this normal-on pilot is event-time tag -> catalogue lookup -> stock VM block identity. pg_buffercache shows current cache contents, where slots can be reused and the view is not one atomic snapshot.

Why visibility-map pages can contend

The visibility map stores two bits per heap page: all-visible and all-frozen, used by index-only scans and vacuum. With an 8-KiB block and 24-byte page header:

(8192 - 24) bytes * 8 bits / 2 bits per heap page
= 32672 heap pages per VM page
= 255.25 MiB of heap address space per VM page

Vacuum sets these bits. Data modifications can clear them. Sessions updating unrelated rows on different heap pages can therefore need exclusive access to the same VM buffer. One metadata page can serialize updates across many heap pages.

A related PostgreSQL change

A July 2026 correctness fix, authored by Melanie Plageman and Andres Freund and included in PostgreSQL 17.11, registers modified VM blocks in heap WAL records. Previously, incremental backups could omit those changes, and clearing VM bits did not produce the full-page images needed for torn-page protection.

Correct logging requires holding the VM lock through heap/VM modification and WAL insertion, extending the critical section.

In the performance discussion, Melanie tested 32 clients clearing bits for different heap pages covered by one VM page, while a vacuum loop set bits again. She observed no degradation with mostly default settings, but 10-15% lower TPS and more BufferContent waits with synchronous_commit=off. Vacuum timing varied between runs.

Her test illustrates how a longer VM critical section becomes visible as BufferContent contention when commit waits are removed.

Where this test ends

Here is the full-run record, linked back to the decisions behind it:

Configuration NOPM Leading active-client observation
Premium SSD v2, normal HA 50,648 DataFileRead, 79.6%
Ultra primary, normal HA 55,784 WALWrite, 83.18%
Ultra primary, commit local 54,556 WALWrite, 87.29%
Ultra primary, commit off 66,096 BufferContent, 93.92%
Full normal-HA repeat 54,163 WALWrite, 83.17%

The off result is 1.305x the original baseline, a 30.5% increase. The primary used the highest nonbursting Ultra budget documented for that tested VM configuration, while commits no longer waited for local or remote durability.

That result combined higher storage provisioning, weaker commit durability, and temporarily paused automatic failover. The runs reused the dataset, with cache contents, dirty pages, checkpoint phase, and vacuum state evolving between tests.

Mean primary CPU utilization in the off window was 18.1%. Low aggregate CPU utilization can coexist with serialization around a few lock holders. Page-level attribution was collected in the normal-on follow-up and identified stock visibility-map pages.

The progression is from a device-read constraint, through a check of remote commit waiting, into OS writeback admission, and finally to shared-page coordination. Removing replica acknowledgment waiting left WALWrite dominant. Each step narrowed where to investigate next.

At the last boundary, more disk IOPS does not make a content lock grant conflicting access simultaneously or split one shared metadata page into independently locked pieces. More workers can instead add contention. The remaining question concerns the amount of shared work, the duration of critical sections, and how access is coordinated.

Keep durability, move the work

The storage and commit-mode experiments took this workload from 50,648 to 66,096 NOPM, a 30.5% increase. The highest result allowed recent transaction loss after a crash. The PostgreSQL primary still had to coordinate access to shared pages.

Bypassing commit durability was a diagnostic step. The production objective is to preserve durable commits while reducing the work and coordination concentrated on the writer.

One approach is disaggregated PostgreSQL storage. Dedicated services handle WAL durability, replication, and data-page materialization. Moving that persistence work can reduce compute-side writeback and buffer maintenance. That's the HorizonDB architecture, which achieved 8x higher throughput for this workload, with better resilience to failures.

SQL execution, transaction semantics, and page-content synchronization remain in PostgreSQL compute. The writer has more headroom for execution and scale-up, while storage services can scale independently across machines. The important change is where the work runs, with the durability guarantee preserved.

HorizonDB retains PostgreSQL’s foreground page synchronization and visibility-map maintenance, while offloading page persistence, checkpoint I/O, full-page-write protection, and WAL distribution. This can ease pressure on those critical sections and give the writer more capacity for transactions. That may explain why the workload achieves higher throughput than this PostgreSQL configuration can support.

If you have resolved similar WAL or BufferContent contention on PostgreSQL, I'd be interested in the configuration, schema, or implementation change, and the measurements that showed improvement, while retaining durable commits.
