title: Agentic Desktop Testing with tamesu: Test Native Apps the Way a Person Uses Them
description:
Introduction

Desktop apps are the hardest apps to test from the outside. A web page has a DOM and a dozen good test tools. A desktop app has a window.

So desktop UI tests usually go one of two ways. A script clicks at screen coordinates and compares pictures. Or you learn a different test framework for every operating system.

A person does neither. A person reads the window, finds the button that says "Unlock", and clicks it.

tamesu (試す, Japanese for to try, to test) is an open-source CLI written in Go that tests software that way. Version 1.22 adds a desktop target for macOS, Windows and Linux. You write a step in plain language. An agent reads the app through the accessibility tree, the same tree a screen reader uses, and acts on the elements it finds there. There are no screenshots to interpret and no coordinates.

This is the fourth article about tamesu. The first three cover web apps, AI agents and A2A agents. This one covers desktop apps.

Why Desktop UI Tests Break

Coordinate and picture scripts tamesu
A step A click at x, y, or a match on a picture A sentence that says what the user wants
What the test reads Pixels The accessibility tree, as text
A renamed or moved button The test fails The agent finds the element by its role and name
The mouse pointer Moves across the screen Stays where it is: a click is an accessibility press
Cost of AI steps Every run pays for every step Plans are cached, so a stable window replays with no model calls for its goals
Passwords In the script Typed at the last moment, never sent to the model
macOS, Windows, Linux One tool per system One YAML format for the three

A tamesu test mixes three kinds of steps:

  • goal: a sentence. The agent acts until it is met.
  • expect: a sentence. The model says if the window satisfies it.
  • action: an exact, deterministic step, such as a click on a named button or a check on a text. No model is involved.

Use a goal where a person would say what they want. Use an action where the test must be exact.

How tamesu Reaches a Desktop App

tamesu does not talk to the app itself. It runs agent-desktop, a CLI from Vercel Labs that speaks the accessibility API of each system:

  • the AX API on macOS,
  • UI Automation on Windows,
  • AT-SPI on Linux.

tamesu pins one version of that CLI (1.2.0 in tamesu 1.22.0). On first use it downloads the binary into ~/.cache/tamesu/agent-desktop. It checks the file against a SHA-256 that ships inside tamesu before it runs it. To use your own binary, set TAMESU_AGENT_DESKTOP.

A goal step runs in a loop of three stages:

  1. Observe. The window becomes one line per element. A line with a number is something the agent can act on. A line without a number is text it can read.
  2. Plan. The agent gets the goal and those lines. It calls one tool: click, type, select, press, wait or done.
  3. Act. The tool runs on the app. The agent gets the new window and plans again.

The loop ends when the agent calls done. It also ends after max_goal_steps actions (15 by default), and then the step fails.

This is what the agent reads when the demo app of this guide starts:

    window "Mochi Stock"
      text "Mochi Stock"
      text "Enter the staff PIN to open the stock room"
[1]   textfield "PIN" (focused, secure)
[2]   button "Unlock"
[3]  button "Close"
[4]  button "Full Screen"
[5]  button "Minimize"
     text "Mochi Stock"

That is the whole window: nine short lines of text. A small, fast model can drive a desktop app from that.

What You Will Build

You will test Mochi Stock, a small native Mac app for the stock room of Mochi Shoes, the demo shop of the earlier articles. It has a PIN screen, a product list with a search box and a form to receive stock. A command in the menu bar exports a CSV file.

The suite has four tests:

  1. Unlock the app and receive stock, written as goals.
  2. A wrong PIN keeps the app locked.
  3. The search box narrows the list.
  4. The export command in the menu bar shows a confirmation.

Then you will change the app twice. First you rename a button, and the test still passes. Then you add a real bug, and the test fails with the reason.

What You Need

  • A Mac with macOS 13 or newer, for the demo app of this guide. The desktop target also runs on Windows 10 (1809) or newer and on Linux (Ubuntu 24.04 or newer).
  • tamesu 1.22.0 or newer.
  • The Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install), only to build the demo app.
  • A Gemini API key in GEMINI_API_KEY. tamesu calls models through Genkit, so OpenAI, Anthropic and local models work too.

Step 1: Install tamesu and Give It Access

Install the CLI 

brew install xavidop/tap/tamesu      # macOS
go install github.com/xavidop/tamesu/cmd/tamesu@latest   # any platform

Linux packages and a Scoop bucket for Windows are on the install page.

Give the terminal access

A desktop test needs a desktop: the session of a signed-in user, where the app can open a window. Each system asks for something more:

System What it takes
macOS The Accessibility permission for the app that runs tamesu (your terminal, your editor or your CI agent). It is in System Settings, Privacy & Security. Add Screen Recording to get screenshots.
Windows The interactive session of the signed-in user: not a service, not a locked screen.
Linux A graphical session with a window manager and the accessibility bus (at-spi2-core), on X11 or Wayland.

On macOS, grant the two permissions now. You will check them with tamesu doctor in Step 3.

Step 2: Build the App Under Test

Mochi Stock is one Swift file. Create a folder named mochi-stock and save this as MochiStock.swift:

import SwiftUI

struct Product: Identifiable {
    let id: Int
    let name: String
    var units: Int
}

final class Store: ObservableObject {
    @Published var unlocked = false
    @Published var wrongPIN = false
    @Published var exported = false
    @Published var pin = ""
    @Published var query = ""
    @Published var selected = 0
    @Published var units = ""
    @Published var products = [
        Product(id: 0, name: "Trail runner", units: 12),
        Product(id: 1, name: "City sneaker", units: 30),
        Product(id: 2, name: "Canvas slip-on", units: 3),
        Product(id: 3, name: "Leather boot", units: 8),
    ]

    var total: Int { products.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.units } }

    func unlock() {
        unlocked = pin == "2468"
        wrongPIN = !unlocked
    }

    func receive() {
        products[selected].units += Int(units) ?? 0
        units = ""
    }
}

@main
struct MochiStockApp: App {
    @StateObject private var store = Store()

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup("Mochi Stock") {
            Group {
                if store.unlocked { StockView() } else { LockView() }
            }
            .environmentObject(store)
            .frame(width: 560, height: 440)
        }
        .commands {
            CommandMenu("Stock") {
                Button("Export CSV") { store.exported = true }
                    .disabled(!store.unlocked)
            }
        }
    }
}

struct LockView: View {
    @EnvironmentObject var store: Store

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 12) {
            Text("Mochi Stock").font(.largeTitle)
            Text("Enter the staff PIN to open the stock room")
            SecureField("PIN", text: $store.pin).frame(width: 160)
            Button("Unlock") { store.unlock() }
            if store.wrongPIN {
                Text("Wrong PIN. Try again.").foregroundColor(.red)
            }
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

struct StockView: View {
    @EnvironmentObject var store: Store

    var shown: [Product] {
        store.query.isEmpty ? store.products : store.products.filter {
            $0.name.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains(store.query)
        }
    }

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
            TextField("Search products", text: $store.query)
            List(shown) { product in
                HStack {
                    Text(product.name)
                    Spacer()
                    if product.units < 5 { Text("Low stock").foregroundColor(.orange) }
                    Text("\(product.units) in stock")
                }
            }
            HStack {
                Picker("Product", selection: $store.selected) {
                    ForEach(store.products) { Text($0.name).tag($0.id) }
                }
                TextField("Units", text: $store.units).frame(width: 80)
                Button("Receive") { store.receive() }
            }
            Text("Total: \(store.total) units")
        }
        .padding()
        .alert("Exported 4 products to stock.csv", isPresented: $store.exported) {
            Button("OK") {}
        }
    }
}

Three details matter for the tests:

  • The PIN is 2468, and the PIN field is a secure field. It never shows its value.
  • "Canvas slip-on" starts with 3 units, so it shows a Low stock label. The label goes away at 5 units or more.
  • All the state lives in memory. Every launch starts locked, with 53 units in total.

Build and install it

Save this next to the Swift file as build.sh:

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
APP="Mochi Stock.app"

rm -rf "$APP"
mkdir -p "$APP/Contents/MacOS"
swiftc -O -parse-as-library MochiStock.swift -o "$APP/Contents/MacOS/MochiStock"

cat > "$APP/Contents/Info.plist" <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>CFBundleName</key><string>Mochi Stock</string>
  <key>CFBundleIdentifier</key><string>dev.mochi.stock</string>
  <key>CFBundleExecutable</key><string>MochiStock</string>
  <key>CFBundlePackageType</key><string>APPL</string>
  <key>LSMinimumSystemVersion</key><string>13.0</string>
</dict>
</plist>
EOF

mkdir -p "$HOME/Applications"
rm -rf "$HOME/Applications/$APP"
cp -R "$APP" "$HOME/Applications/"
echo "installed $HOME/Applications/$APP"

chmod +x build.sh
./build.sh

installed ~/Applications/Mochi Stock.app

The script copies the app to ~/Applications for a reason. tamesu starts an app by its name or its bundle id, not by a path. So the app must live where macOS looks for apps.

Step 3: Configure the Project

Create a second folder for the tests. Add a file named tamesu.yaml:

version: 1
suites: ["suites/*.yaml"]

genkit:
  plugins: [googlegenai]
models:
  default: googleai/gemini-3.8-flash
  judge: googleai/gemini-3.8-flash
  browser_agent: googleai/gemini-3.8-flash

defaults: { timeout: 3m, max_goal_steps: 10 }
budgets: { max_cost_usd: 2 }
reporters: [console, junit, html]

secrets:
  GEMINI_API_KEY: env:GEMINI_API_KEY
  • models.browser_agent is the model that drives the app in a goal step. The name comes from the browser target; the desktop target uses the same setting.
  • models.judge grades the whole session at the end.
  • budgets stops the run when the model spend passes the limit.
  • secrets are references, never values. env:GEMINI_API_KEY tells tamesu where the key lives.

Step 4: Write the First Test with Goals

Create suites/stock.yaml:

suite: stock
tags: [desktop]

secrets:
  STOCK_PIN: env:STOCK_PIN

targets:
  stock:
    type: desktop
    app: Mochi Stock

tests:
  - name: unlock and receive stock
    target: stock
    steps:
      - goal: "Unlock the app with the PIN {{secrets.STOCK_PIN}}"
      - expect: "The stock list is visible and the Canvas slip-on is marked as low stock"
      - goal: "Receive 5 units of the Canvas slip-on"
      - expect: "The Canvas slip-on has 8 units in stock and no low stock warning"
      - action: { assert_text: "Total: 58 units" }
    assert:
      - judge: "The steps show the app being unlocked and 5 units of the Canvas slip-on being received"
      - metric: { name: goal_steps, lte: 8 }

The target is two lines: the type and the name of the app. The test reads like a note to a colleague. Two goals do the work, two expect steps check the meaning, and one action pins the exact total.

The assert block runs after the steps:

  • judge asks a model to grade the whole session against one sentence.
  • metric checks numbers that tamesu measured. Here the agent may use 8 actions at most.

Check the setup 

export STOCK_PIN=2468
tamesu validate
tamesu doctor

1 suite, 1 test, 0 errors, 0 warnings
ok   config: tamesu.yaml (version 1)
ok   suites: 1 file, 1 test
ok   secret GEMINI_API_KEY: env (link 1 of 1)
ok   secret STOCK_PIN: env (link 1 of 1)
ok   models: default=googleai/gemini-3.8-flash (GEMINI_API_KEY resolved), judge=googleai/gemini-3.8-flash (GEMINI_API_KEY resolved), browser_agent=googleai/gemini-3.8-flash (GEMINI_API_KEY resolved)
skip speech: no speech models configured (speech.tts / speech.stt); audio mode and sip need them
ok   chromium: Google Chrome 157.0.8103.79 (/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome); no browser target configured
ok   agent-desktop: 1.2.0 (~/.cache/tamesu/agent-desktop/1.2.0/agent-desktop)
ok   desktop permissions: the desktop can be read and captured
skip livekit: no livekit target configured
skip sip: no sip target configured

The last two ok lines are the desktop checks. agent-desktop shows the binary a run will use. desktop permissions confirms that macOS lets tamesu read and capture the desktop.

Before the first run, the agent-desktop line says that version 1.2.0 "is not in the cache yet". The first tamesu run downloads it.

Run it 

tamesu run

tamesu run: 1 test, output in .tamesu/runs/2026-11-17T14-43-00
PASS   stock / unlock and receive stock  1m13s

1 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors in 1m13s · 5 model calls, 6801 tokens, $0.0000 · llm cache: 0 hits, 1 misses

Mochi Stock opens, unlocks, receives the stock and closes. Nobody touched the mouse.

What the agent did

Every step is in steps.json, in the run directory. This command lists the actions of the two goals:

jq -c '.[] | select(.kind == "goal") | .actions[] | [.name, .args.element, .args.text]' \
  .tamesu/runs/*/tests/unlock-and-receive-stock/run-1/steps.json

["type","textfield \"PIN\"","{{secrets.STOCK_PIN}}"]
["click","button \"Unlock\"",null]
["click","combobox \"Product\"",null]
["click","menuitem \"Canvas slip-on\"",null]
["type","textfield \"Units\"","5"]
["click","button \"Receive\"",null]

Two things to notice:

  • The agent found everything by role and name. Nobody told it that the product is picked in a dropdown named "Product".
  • The PIN is still a placeholder. The model planned with {{secrets.STOCK_PIN}} and never saw 2468. tamesu puts the value in at the moment of typing, and passes it to agent-desktop on standard input, never as a command-line argument.

After the unlock, the window is richer. This is what the agent reads before the second goal:

    window "Mochi Stock" (focused)
[6]   textfield "Search products"
[7]   scrollarea
[8]    outline
[9]     treeitem "Trail runner 12 in stock"
[10]      cell "Trail runner 12 in stock" (focused)
          text "Trail runner"
          text "12 in stock"
[11]     treeitem "City sneaker 30 in stock"
[12]      cell "City sneaker 30 in stock" (focused)
          text "City sneaker"
          text "30 in stock"
[13]     treeitem "Canvas slip-on Low stock 3 in stock"
[14]      cell "Canvas slip-on Low stock 3 in stock" (focused)
          text "Canvas slip-on"
          text "Low stock"
          text "3 in stock"
[15]     treeitem "Leather boot 8 in stock"
[16]      cell "Leather boot 8 in stock" (focused)
          text "Leather boot"
          text "8 in stock"
      text "Product"
[17]   combobox "Product" value="Trail runner" (readonly)
[18]   textfield "Units"
[19]   button "Receive"
      text "Total: 53 units"
[3]  button "Close"
[4]  button "Full Screen"
[5]  button "Minimize"
     text "Mochi Stock"

A row of the list is a treeitem. The dropdown is a combobox with its current value. The total is plain text.

Good to know:

  • A click presses the element through the accessibility API. The pointer does not move.
  • Text is normally set the same way, with no key pressed. Some fields take text from the keyboard only. tamesu then focuses the field and types with the real keyboard, and the run records a keyboard event in result.json. The three text fields of Mochi Stock are of that kind.
  • The real keyboard types into whatever has the focus. Leave the keyboard and the mouse alone while a suite runs.
  • An expect step sees what the window shows. The secure field shows no value: textfield "PIN" (focused, secure).

Step 5: Run It Again: the Plan Cache

Run the same command a second time:

tamesu run

tamesu run: 1 test, output in .tamesu/runs/2026-11-17T14-44-13
PASS   stock / unlock and receive stock  31.3s

1 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors in 31.3s · 3 model calls, 1660 tokens, $0.0000 · llm cache: 0 hits, 1 misses

The first run took 1m13s, 5 model calls and 6,801 tokens. This one took 31 seconds, 3 model calls and 1,660 tokens.

When a goal succeeds, tamesu saves its actions as a plan in .tamesu/cache/actions. This is the heart of the plan of the first goal:

{
  "goal": "Unlock the app with the PIN {{secrets.STOCK_PIN}}",
  "url_path": "desktop://Mochi Stock",
  "key": "1487a403320f0602b9600cc0",
  "actions": [
    {
      "name": "type",
      "args": {
        "element": "textfield \"PIN\"",
        "ref": 1,
        "text": "{{secrets.STOCK_PIN}}"
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "click",
      "args": {
        "element": "button \"Unlock\"",
        "ref": 2
      }
    }
  ]
}

The next run replays the plan and does not call the agent. The three calls that remain are the two expect steps and the judge, the steps that need judgment. The metrics of the second run say the same:

{
  "cache_hits": 2,
  "cache_misses": 0,
  "desktop_actions": 6,
  "goal_steps": 6,
  "llm_cost_usd": 0,
  "llm_tokens": 1660,
  "observations": 10,
  "turns": 0
}

The key of a plan is the goal, the app and the set of elements in the window (their roles and names). When the window changes, the key changes, and the agent plans again. You will see that in Step 9.

Two flags control the cache:

  • tamesu run --update-cache ignores the saved plans and plans every goal again.
  • tamesu run --replay uses only saved plans. A goal with no plan fails. This is the mode for CI.

Commit the .tamesu/cache folder with the suite.

Step 6: Pin Exact Behavior with Actions

A goal is flexible. Some checks must not be. Add two tests to suites/stock.yaml:

  - name: wrong PIN keeps the stock room closed
    target: stock
    steps:
      - action: { fill: { name: PIN, text: "0000" } }
      - action: { click: { role: button, name: Unlock } }
      - action: { assert_text: "Wrong PIN. Try again." }
      - expect: "The app is still locked and shows no products"

  - name: search narrows the list
    target: stock
    steps:
      - action: { fill: { name: PIN, text: "{{secrets.STOCK_PIN}}" } }
      - action: { click: Unlock }
      - action: { wait: { text: "Total: 53 units" } }
      - action: { fill: { name: "Search products", text: "boot" } }
      - action: { assert_text: "Leather boot" }
      - expect: "The list shows the Leather boot and no other product"

No goal here, so no agent drives the app. Each action names its element the way a person would: by the text on it. The expect at the end of each test still asks the model one question.

The desktop target has six actions:

Action Argument
click An accessible name (click: Unlock), or { role, name }
fill { name, text }: empties the field, then types
press A key or a combination: Enter, Escape, Tab, cmd+s
wait Milliseconds, or { text } to wait until the window holds a text
screenshot A name: the window, saved under screenshots/
assert_text A text the window must hold, or { contains }, { equals }, { matches }

Good to know:

  • Names are matched exactly, but upper and lower case do not matter.
  • Add the role when two elements share a name.
  • A fill takes secrets too. {{secrets.STOCK_PIN}} is replaced at the moment of typing.
  • wait: { text: ... } is the safe way to wait for a screen change. The search test uses it before it types.
  • A desktop app has no URL, no page script and no network of its own to control. navigate, assert_url, eval_js, mock, a11y and visual belong to the browser target only.

Step 7: Drive the Menu Bar and a Native Alert

Mochi Stock has a Stock menu in the menu bar with one command, Export CSV. It answers with a native alert. Add the fourth test:

  - name: export from the menu bar
    target: stock
    steps:
      - action: { fill: { name: PIN, text: "{{secrets.STOCK_PIN}}" } }
      - action: { click: Unlock }
      - action: { click: Stock }
      - action: { click: "Export CSV" }
      - action: { assert_text: "Exported 4 products to stock.csv" }
      - action: { screenshot: export-alert }
      - action: { wait: 700 }
      - action: { press: Enter }
      - expect: "No alert is open and the stock list is visible"

A menu item only answers when it is showing. So the test opens the menu first, then clicks the item. A name alone is the portable way to name a menu, because its role differs between systems.

The alert is not part of the window. tamesu lists what is open on top of the window after it, and searches it first. This is the end of the observation while the alert is open:

      text "Total: 53 units"
[3]  button "Close"
[4]  button "Full Screen"
[5]  button "Minimize"
     text "Mochi Stock"
    sheet "alert" (focused)
     text "Exported 4 products to stock.csv"
[20]  button "OK"

The screenshot action saves what the test saw:

Good to know:

  • Use actions for the menu bar. With tamesu 1.22.0 on macOS 27, the agent does not get the titles of the menu bar in a goal step. A goal such as "export from the Stock menu" fails there. Two click actions work.
  • Close an alert with a key. press: Enter answers the default button. A click on the alert's own button ends in an error: agent-desktop reports that it could not verify the press.
  • Wait a moment before the key. Without the short wait, the key press can fail with a STALE_REF error.

Step 8: Run the Whole Suite 

tamesu run

tamesu run: 4 tests, output in .tamesu/runs/2026-11-17T14-44-45
PASS   stock / export from the menu bar  22.2s
PASS   stock / wrong PIN keeps the stock room closed  16.1s
PASS   stock / unlock and receive stock  30.7s
PASS   stock / search narrows the list  18.2s

4 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors in 1m27s · 6 model calls, 2685 tokens, $0.0000 · llm cache: 0 hits, 1 misses

Four tests, 1m27s and six model calls. Desktop tests take turns. A machine has one desktop, so tamesu runs them one at a time, whatever --parallel says.

Tags and filters select a part of the suite:

tamesu run --filter "wrong PIN"
tamesu run --tags desktop

The app starts clean every time

Each test launches the app, and tamesu quits it at the end of the test. That is why every test of this suite starts at the lock screen with 53 units.

  • An app that was already running is yours. tamesu joins it and leaves it open at the end.
  • An app that refuses to quit, because it asks to save, is terminated.
  • State that an app keeps on disk is yours to reset. Use desktop.args on the target, or before_each and after_each hooks.

What a run leaves behind

File What it holds
screenshots/step-NN.png One screenshot of the window per step
steps.json Each step, its result, its reason and the agent's actions
agent-desktop.jsonl agent-desktop's own trace of what it read and did
transcript.json The steps as a conversation, for judge, contains and regex assertions
result.json Assertions, metrics and events
report.html The whole run as one page, next to junit.xml

The screenshots and the trace cover the app under test only, never the rest of your desktop.

Step 9: Rename a Button

Now change the app the way a designer would. Rename the Receive button:

-                Button("Receive") { store.receive() }
+                Button("Add units") { store.receive() }

Build the app again and run the first test:

./build.sh
tamesu run --filter "unlock and receive"

tamesu run: 1 test, output in .tamesu/runs/2026-11-17T14-47-51
PASS   stock / unlock and receive stock  56.5s

1 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors in 56.5s · 4 model calls, 5300 tokens, $0.0000 · llm cache: 0 hits, 1 misses

The test passes, and nobody edited the suite. Look at the model calls: four, not three.

The lock screen did not change, so the first goal replayed its plan. The stock screen has a new button name, so the key of the second goal changed. The agent planned that goal again, clicked "Add units", and tamesu saved the new plan. The metrics show it:

{
  "cache_hits": 1,
  "cache_misses": 1,
  "desktop_actions": 6,
  "goal_steps": 6,
  "llm_cost_usd": 0,
  "llm_tokens": 5300,
  "observations": 11,
  "turns": 0
}

The next run replays both plans again.

Step 10: Catch a Real Bug

A rename is not a bug. This is one. In Store.receive(), a += becomes a =:

-        products[selected].units += Int(units) ?? 0
+        products[selected].units = Int(units) ?? 0

The app now replaces the stock with the units you receive. Build and run:

./build.sh
tamesu run --filter "unlock and receive"
echo "exit code: $?"

tamesu run: 1 test, output in .tamesu/runs/2026-11-17T14-48-52
FAIL   stock / unlock and receive stock  32.5s
    x step[4] expect: The Canvas slip-on currently has 5 units in stock according to treeitem "Canvas slip-on 5 in stock", not 8.
    x judge "The steps show the app being unlocked and 5 units of the Canvas slip-on being received": Although the app was unlocked, 5 units were not properly received; starting from 3 units in stock, receiving 5 units should have resulted in 8 units, but only 5 units in stock were recorded.
    last turns:
      agent: replayed 4 cached actions (plan 60274b032ed3361120575328)
      user:  The Canvas slip-on has 8 units in stock and no low stock warning
      agent: The Canvas slip-on currently has 5 units in stock according to treeitem "Canvas slip-on 5 in stock", not 8.

0 passed, 1 failed, 0 errors in 32.5s · 3 model calls, 1578 tokens, $0.0000 · llm cache: 0 hits, 1 misses
exit code: 1

Both goals replayed without a problem. The buttons are all there, and every click works. A test that only clicks would pass.

The expect step reads the window and fails: the Canvas slip-on has 5 units, not 8. The judge says the same about the whole session. The exit code is 1, so a pipeline stops here.

Put the += back and build again before you go on.

Step 11: Run It in CI

Replay in the pipeline 

tamesu run --replay --out out

tamesu run: 4 tests, output in out
PASS   stock / export from the menu bar  22.2s
PASS   stock / wrong PIN keeps the stock room closed  12.1s
PASS   stock / unlock and receive stock  32.5s
PASS   stock / search narrows the list  16.3s

4 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors in 1m23s · 6 model calls, 2724 tokens, $0.0000 · llm cache: 0 hits, 1 misses

With --replay, every goal comes from the saved plans. The six model calls are the five expect steps and the judge, so the job still needs the API key. The exit codes are the same as for browser tests: 0 passed, 1 a test failed, 2 config error, 3 infrastructure error, 4 over budget.

Give the runner a desktop

The runner needs what your laptop needed in Step 1:

  • macOS runner: grant Accessibility to the process that starts tamesu.
  • Windows runner: run the job in the interactive session of the signed-in user.
  • Linux runner: most have no screen, so start a session first.

This is the Linux recipe from the tamesu documentation:

sudo apt-get install -y xvfb openbox dbus x11-utils at-spi2-core libatk-bridge2.0-0
export DISPLAY=:99
Xvfb :99 -screen 0 1280x800x24 -nolisten tcp &
openbox &
dbus-run-session -- tamesu run

tamesu's own pipeline tests the desktop target this way on every pull request: against a GTK text editor in a headless Linux container, and against Notepad on a hosted Windows runner of GitHub Actions.

Split a large suite

Desktop tests run one at a time on one machine. To go faster, give each job its own machine and split the suite:

tamesu run --replay --shard 1/2    # job 1
tamesu run --replay --shard 2/2    # job 2

Also New in 1.22: agent-browser for Web Tests

The same release adds a second engine to the browser target. Set browser.engine: agent-browser, and the agent-browser CLI reads the page and acts for the agent. The browser stays tamesu's own Chromium. Mocks, the accessibility audit, visual baselines and recordings work the same under both engines, and chromium stays the default.

Conclusion

A desktop test should say what the user wants, and fail only when the user would fail. The accessibility tree makes that possible. It turns a window into a few lines of text that a model can read and a test can assert on.

The rename and the bug show the difference. A renamed button costs one extra model call, once. A wrong number in the stock list fails the test with a sentence that says what is wrong.

Start small. Take the one flow of your app that someone still checks by hand before every release. Write it as two goals and two expect steps, and run it on your own machine first.

Further reading

  • tamesu on GitHub and the documentation
  • The desktop target: what each system needs, every action, artifacts and metrics
  • The desktop example in the tamesu repository: a note in TextEdit, or in the editor you name
  • agent-desktop, the CLI that reads the accessibility tree
  • The browser target, with the new agent-browser engine
  • Agentic Browser Testing with tamesu, the first article of this set
  • Testing AI Agents with tamesu, the second article of this set
  • Testing A2A Agents with tamesu, the third article of this set

title: Device Status Freshness via Channel Push and Snapshot Queries (Across Trust Boundaries)
description:
A device dashboard needs permission to say "online." A connected browser isn't that permission. Short answer: push metrics over a channel for multiple viewers, keep a metrics API query for first paint, and expire device presence independently of the dashboard's connection. Choose the transport only after checking where identifiers travel, how long copies remain, who can delete them, and which processors receive them.

Pushing requires one publish per change; querying requires one request per client per interval. That favors push as the audience grows, but a green tile without recent device evidence is still misleading. What page fired when that evidence expired?

What would make this dashboard lie about presence?

Consider a hypothetical developer-tools fleet dashboard: a build agent reports its status, an operator opens a wall display, and a second viewer reconnects after missing a change. This is a design exercise, not a report of a production incident. In a review, I'd start with the stale green tile and work backward through the evidence, rather than accepting the dashboard's connection indicator as proof that the build agent is reachable.

The hypothetical postmortem finding is narrow. A viewer's subscription and a device's presence represent different relationships. A channel can carry status, but its existence doesn't establish when the device last supplied trustworthy evidence. Even a correctly delivered event can describe an observation that's already too old to support an "online" label when a viewer uses it.

Unknown is useful.

The invariant is that the display may assert presence only while its device evidence remains fresh under an explicit application policy. A query supplies initial state; pushed changes update it; expiry removes permission to keep claiming "online." That policy belongs in application logic, with a stated observation source and an incident owner. No transport choice eliminates it.

For teams building this workflow alongside other backend services, I recommend trying Infrai for server-side status publishing and initial metrics queries when consolidating those integrations under one key and one bill matters. That means fewer separate service credentials and invoices to administer for that integration, while leaving device evidence and browser authorization as explicit responsibilities. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API, with no SDK required for plain HTTP calls. For a status adapter that also needs other backend services, that breadth and shared interface reduce separate integration dependencies. Neither the credential consolidation nor this integration benefit establishes residency or retention guarantees.

Should a client query metrics or receive channel push updates?

Take an illustrative minute with 12 viewers, a five-second polling interval, and three device-status changes. Polling produces 144 scheduled query requests; pushing produces three publish operations, plus initial queries and the work of delivering events to subscribers. These are arithmetic assumptions, not measurements or a billing comparison. Delivery volume still depends on subscribers, and additional devices or reconnects change the workload.

For a wall display, push makes changes visible without repeatedly querying the metrics API. For a single occasional viewer, polling can be simpler because there is no subscription connection to manage. The query path stays either way.

Delivery isn't presence.

The harder choice concerns the payload. A device identifier can reveal fleet structure; a status timestamp can reveal working patterns. Before forwarding either, draw the path from the device to ingestion, through any metrics store and channel processor, and into the operator's browser. Write down which party receives each field. "We use one API" isn't an answer.

A useful review has four separate entries: processing region, retention period, deletion behavior, and processor identity. Record the evidence for each entry, including whether it covers channel delivery, stored metrics, operational logs, and backups. Deleting an application record shouldn't be assumed to remove every downstream copy. Require the relevant documentation or contractual terms before making that promise.

For this design, send an opaque device identifier and the minimum status evidence the viewer needs; keep credentials and diagnostic payloads outside the broadcast event. That is a proposed application policy, not a claim about automatic platform redaction. Browser access needs its own scoped authorization decision. A consolidated backend credential should stay on the server.

That boundary matters.

Infrai can cover the documented publish and metrics-query operations in this workflow. A specialist provider remains responsible for the transport or storage it operates, and its own terms must establish the applicable processing region, retention, deletion, and processor commitments. The application's evidence policy remains with its owner. An API wrapper, including an AI runtime used elsewhere in the system, supplies no independent contractual guarantee for that data path.

Compare the alternatives at the boundary you actually need

Product category helps narrow the candidates. It doesn't prove that any particular plan meets a data-handling requirement.

Option Concrete fit for this dashboard Trade-off to investigate before choosing
Direct metrics API queries First paint and periodic refresh without a subscription connection Requests grow with viewers and intervals; changes appear at the next successful refresh
Ably A managed realtime messaging candidate when channel delivery is the main specialist responsibility Compare documented connection behavior and data-handling terms with the evidence policy; messaging alone doesn't define device freshness
Pusher Channels A channel-event candidate for distributing status changes to multiple viewers Verify authorization and presence semantics against the entity displayed; an operator connection must not stand in for a device heartbeat
Supabase Realtime A candidate when status updates are organized around database changes Decide whether the stored row reflects fresh evidence, and review database and realtime processing boundaries together
Infrai A common REST integration for publishing status and querying metrics alongside other backend services Verify capability schemas and applicable processor terms; one credential and invoice do not establish data location

Ably and Pusher Channels deserve a direct evaluation when the central problem is operating realtime transport, particularly if the team needs to assess specialist connection behavior in detail. Supabase Realtime deserves evaluation when database changes already define the event source. Neither preference implies that a database row or channel member automatically establishes accurate device presence.

Choose a specialist directly if its documented regional deployment, deletion commitments, or contractual processor boundary decides the project. Choose polling if refresh delay is acceptable and subscriptions aren't justified. Choose a consolidated integration when reducing credential administration matters and data-handling requirements can be established for the actual path. There is no evidence here for ranking these providers by measured latency or availability.

Prevent the stale green tile before selecting a transport

Start by keeping the snapshot query on the backend. This standalone Go program uses the documented metrics query without inventing filter parameters or decoding an undocumented response shape. It reads the credential from the environment, sets the method explicitly, checks status, bounds request time, and retries rate limits with exponential backoff while honoring a valid Retry-After value. Because this is a read, retries cannot duplicate a publish.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 32); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(deadline); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return fallback
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 1<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"),
                time.Second*time.Duration(1<<attempt))
            if delay > 30*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("rate limited: retry after %s", delay)
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("metrics query: HTTP %d: %s",
                res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("query attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the server environment, and run it with Go. The response is printed for inspection; don't treat successful HTTP delivery as evidence that a device is online. Inspect the documented response schema before mapping it into an application-owned projection. Raw responses also need an appropriate logging and retention policy before this inspection program becomes a service.

The preventative projection rule is separate: accept a snapshot, apply only newer authoritative revisions for the same device, and display unknown once the observation's age reaches the freshness deadline. For example, a hypothetical observation for build-agent-17 at revision 41 should not be replaced by revision 40 arriving later. A 20-second expiry might suit an illustrative exercise; production thresholds need justification from the device reporting cadence and tolerated uncertainty. These identifiers, revisions, and thresholds are application examples, not vendor API fields.

There's a startup race to resolve. Obtaining a snapshot and then subscribing can miss a change between those actions. Use a documented replay or cursor mechanism where available, or buffer updates while obtaining a snapshot and reconcile against authoritative revisions. Neither mechanism is asserted here as an Infrai capability. If transport and snapshot cannot establish a reliable handoff, keep a reconciliation query and expire uncertain state.

Clock and ordering assumptions matter too. Define who issues observation timestamps, how device restarts affect revisions, and what the application does with observations from the future. If independent producers cannot establish an authoritative order, a largest-number-wins rule would hide uncertainty rather than resolve it.

Finally, a running UI must reevaluate expiry on a timer, even when no event arrives. Otherwise the policy exists on paper while a quiet dashboard keeps displaying yesterday's confidence. Page on expired evidence according to the device's operational importance; a channel connection metric can help diagnose the path, but it cannot substitute for that page.

Where this advice stops applying

This design fits a status dashboard whose viewers can tolerate an explicit unknown state. It doesn't establish a safety interlock, an audit ledger, or a complete history of every transition. Those requirements need their own delivery, persistence, and recovery design.

Push changes for a shared live display, query for initial state, and make presence a time-bounded claim. Approve the data path separately. If region, retention, deletion, or processor commitments remain unresolved, a visually convincing dashboard is premature.

References

  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Supabase Realtime documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0, a protocol reference rather than evidence of device freshness or contractual processor commitments.

Sources

If this integration boundary fits your dashboard, start with the public schemas in the Infrai documentation.

title: We Stopped a Cloud Server to Resize It and Nine Months of Supplier Messages on Its D Drive Were Gone
description:
Our larger suppliers send us order confirmations, delivery notices and invoices electronically, and we send them our purchase orders the same way. A translation package on a Windows server turns their formats into ours. In 2023 we moved that server from our own building into Azure, and the supplier of the package reinstalled it there.

On the old server, drive D was a data disk. On the new one, the package's engineer found a drive D with plenty of free space and pointed the outgoing queue and the message archive at it.

In Azure, drive D on most virtual machines is not a data disk. It is temporary storage on the physical host, meant for things like the page file. Its contents can disappear whenever the machine is moved to another host, including when it is stopped and deallocated. It even contains a file called DATALOSS_WARNING_README.txt. Nobody had opened it.

In August we stopped the server one Sunday to give it more memory for month end. When it started again, drive D held that readme and nothing else. Two hundred and sixty purchase orders waiting to be sent had gone, and so had nine months of archived messages.

The orders were easy, because our trading system could export them again, and they went out by Monday lunchtime. The archive was not. Our backup of the server had run every night and had never included drive D, because Azure's virtual machine backup does not protect temporary storage. Two weeks later a timber supplier disputed a price we had confirmed electronically in June, and we could not produce the message.

The package now writes only to a managed data disk, which is backed up with the rest of the server, and our build checklist for every cloud server includes listing which folders live on temporary storage. We found two more servers using drive D for something that mattered: a print spool and a folder of scanned delivery notes. Both have moved.

A migration copies the habits of the old building into the new one. Find out what each disk letter means on the platform you have moved to, before something important is written to it.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Quartz job not firing? Causes and how to check
description:
A Quartz job that does not fire is usually waiting for a free worker thread, skipped by its misfire instruction, running on an old schedule kept in the database, or attached to a trigger in the ERROR state; sometimes the scheduler never started. Quartz knows which: the trigger’s state and its next fire time tell you. Here is how to read them, fix each cause, and be alerted the next time a job goes quiet.

Why is my Quartz job not firing?

Quartz does not run a job; it fires a trigger, and the trigger runs the job. When a job goes quiet, the trigger is where the answer is. Five causes cover most cases.

1. The scheduler never started

In Spring Boot, the scheduler starts with the application unless spring.quartz.auto-startup is false. Outside Spring, nothing fires until something calls scheduler.start().

To confirm, look for Quartz’s own line at startup, Scheduler quartzScheduler_$_NON_CLUSTERED started. with Spring Boot’s default name. If it is not in the log, no trigger will fire.

2. Every worker thread is busy

Quartz runs jobs on a fixed pool of worker threads. Spring’s SchedulerFactoryBean, which Spring Boot uses, gives it 10 threads by default. If long jobs hold all of them, the next trigger waits. Once it has waited longer than the misfire threshold (org.quartz.jobStore.misfireThreshold: 60 seconds by default with a JDBC job store, 5 seconds with the in-memory one under Spring), Quartz stops waiting and applies the trigger’s misfire instruction instead.

To confirm, take a thread dump (jstack <pid>): the worker threads (named after the scheduler, …_Worker-1 to …_Worker-10) are all inside your jobs. With a JDBC job store, Quartz also logs Handling 1 trigger(s) that missed their scheduled fire-time.

3. The misfire instruction skips the run

What happens to a missed run depends on the trigger. A CronTrigger uses the smart policy by default, which for a cron means fire once now: several missed runs collapse into one late run. A trigger built with withMisfireHandlingInstructionDoNothing() does the opposite: the missed run is dropped, and the trigger waits for its next scheduled time. No log line names the job.

To confirm, read the trigger’s definition in your code, or the MISFIRE_INSTR column of QRTZ_TRIGGERS with a JDBC job store.

4. The schedule in the database is not the one in your code

With spring.quartz.job-store-type: jdbc, jobs and triggers live in the database and survive restarts. Spring Boot’s spring.quartz.overwrite-existing-jobs is false by default, so a trigger that already exists in the database is not updated at startup. You change the cron in the code, deploy, and Quartz keeps firing on the old one.

To confirm, compare the code with the database:

SELECT trigger_group, trigger_name, trigger_state, next_fire_time
FROM qrtz_triggers;

SELECT trigger_name, cron_expression
FROM qrtz_cron_triggers;

next_fire_time is in milliseconds since the epoch. A date far in the past, or a cron that is not the one you wrote, is the answer.

5. The trigger is paused, blocked or in ERROR

A trigger has a state: NORMAL, PAUSED, BLOCKED, ERROR or COMPLETE. Only NORMAL fires on time.

  • ERROR: with a JDBC job store, Quartz sets it when it cannot load the job, because the stored job names a class this application cannot load: a job scheduled at runtime whose class was later renamed or moved, or a job of another application that shares the same Quartz tables and scheduler name. It logs Error retrieving job, setting trigger state to ERROR. once, and the trigger never fires again on its own.
  • PAUSED: someone, or some code, called pauseTrigger or pauseJob.
  • BLOCKED: the job is annotated @DisallowConcurrentExecution and its previous run has not finished. If that run is stuck, the trigger stays blocked.

To confirm, ask Quartz. With Spring Boot Actuator, /actuator/quartz/triggers/<group>/<name> returns the trigger’s state, previousFireTime and nextFireTime (expose it with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,quartz). Without Actuator, scheduler.getTriggerState(triggerKey) gives the same answer; the trigger_state column above holds Quartz’s internal state instead: WAITING or ACQUIRED for a trigger that will fire, then PAUSED, BLOCKED or ERROR.

Why logs and health checks miss it

None of these causes raises an alarm by itself. Most write nothing, because the job does not run. The misfire line is logged at INFO, and the ERROR line is logged once, when the trigger breaks, then never again. The health endpoint says UP, because the application is fine; Spring Boot has no health indicator for Quartz.

The only reliable signal is the missing run itself.

How to be alerted when a Quartz job stops firing

Have each job report its runs to a service that knows the schedule and alerts when a run does not arrive: a dead man’s switch. It catches every cause that stops the runs (1, 3 and 5), and a delay (cause 2) longer than its grace period, without needing to know which one happened. Cause 4 is different: the job still runs, on the old schedule. To catch it, compare the stored cron with your code after any deploy that changes it (the query above).

How to fix a Quartz job that does not fire

  • Not started: remove spring.quartz.auto-startup: false, or call scheduler.start().
  • Busy threads: put a timeout on every outgoing call a job makes, and raise the pool if the jobs really need to overlap: spring.quartz.properties.org.quartz.threadPool.threadCount: 20.
  • Skipped misfires: choose the misfire instruction on purpose. Keep the default when one late run is better than none; use withMisfireHandlingInstructionDoNothing() only when a late run would do harm.
  • Old schedule in the database: set spring.quartz.overwrite-existing-jobs: true, so the triggers declared in your code replace the stored ones at startup, or reschedule the trigger yourself with scheduler.rescheduleJob(...).
  • Trigger in ERROR: make the stored job loadable first: put the class back under its old name, or replace the stored job with scheduler.addJob(jobDetail, true, true) (the last true lets Quartz store a non-durable job; for jobs declared as beans, one start with spring.quartz.overwrite-existing-jobs: true does it). Then call scheduler.resetTriggerFromErrorState(triggerKey), available since Quartz 2.3.0, or reschedule the trigger. A reset alone sends the trigger back to ERROR at its next fire time.
  • Blocked by a stuck run: find the stuck run with a thread dump and give its outgoing calls a timeout; until it returns, a @DisallowConcurrentExecution job will not run again.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my Quartz job not executing?

Most often its trigger is waiting for a free worker thread, its missed run was dropped by the misfire instruction, the trigger stored in the database still has an old schedule, the trigger is paused, blocked or in the ERROR state, or the scheduler never started. The trigger’s state and next fire time tell you which.

What is a misfire in Quartz?

A misfire is a run that could not start on time, because no worker thread was free or the scheduler was down, and has waited longer than the misfire threshold. Quartz then applies the trigger’s misfire instruction: run once now, or skip to the next scheduled time.

Why did changing the cron expression not change my Quartz job?

With a JDBC job store, Spring Boot does not overwrite triggers that already exist in the database unless spring.quartz.overwrite-existing-jobs is true. The old trigger keeps its old schedule.

How do I fix a Quartz trigger in the ERROR state?

Make the stored job loadable again, usually by restoring a renamed or moved class or replacing the stored job with scheduler.addJob(jobDetail, true, true), then call scheduler.resetTriggerFromErrorState with the trigger key. A reset alone puts it back in ERROR at its next fire time.

How can I be alerted when a Quartz job stops running?

Have each run report to a service that expects it on the job’s schedule and alerts when it is missing, a dead man’s switch.

See also

  • Spring @Scheduled job stopped

Originally published on the SilenceWatch blog. This article was written with the help of AI and checked against the sources before publishing.

title: Deploying a Distributed Object Storage Cluster on Azure
description:
In this project, I built and tore down a small, distributed S3-compatible object storage cluster on Microsoft Azure using Terraform and Silo (a MinIO fork).

Before going any further: this wasn't a massive, fault-tolerant, enterprise production cluster. It was a deliberately small, private 2-node deployment built under a strict 6-vCPU subscription cap and a tight budget. The goal was straightforward—provision the infrastructure with Infrastructure as Code (IaC), keep the storage nodes completely off the public internet, stripe data across four managed disks using erasure coding, and access the admin console securely through a Bastion host.

Getting it working taught me way more from the things that broke than the things that worked on the first try. Here is how the setup works, what went wrong along the way, and what I would do differently next time.

The Setup (Keep It Simple)

Because I only had 6 vCPUs to work with in the spaincentral region, every VM had to earn its place:

  • 1 Bastion Host (vm-acumen-bastion): The only machine with a public IP, locked down with a Network Security Group (NSG) to accept SSH only.
  • 2 Storage Nodes (vm-acumen-node-1 & vm-acumen-node-2): Running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on Standard_E2ds_v4 instances inside a private subnet with zero public internet exposure.
  • 4 Managed Disks: Two 10GB disks attached to each node (LUN 10 and 11), formatted with XFS and mounted persistently via UUID in /etc/fstab to /data/disk1 and /data/disk2.
  • Silo in Docker: Running with --network host across both nodes so they could talk to each other over port 9000 and serve the web console on port 9001.

The Difficulties (What Actually Went Wrong)

1. Hitting the 6-vCPU Wall and "Ghost" Disks

Earlier iterations of this build started with more nodes, which immediately ran into Azure's 6-vCPU quota limit. Scaling back down to 2 storage nodes + 1 Bastion solved the CPU quota, but left behind a hidden FinOps trap.

When I scaled down, Azure didn't automatically delete the unattached OS disk from the old node-4. It just sat there in the resource group quietly draining credits in the background until I ran an Azure CLI check for unattached disks (managedBy==null) and wiped it manually.

  • Lesson: Scaling down compute doesn't always clean up storage. Always audit for orphaned disks after changing node counts.

2. Dynamic IPs Breaking Storage Quorum (and a Terraform NicInUse Error)

Originally, I left the storage nodes' private IPs set to Dynamic in Terraform. The problem with distributed storage is that nodes rely on predictable peer addresses to maintain quorum. If Azure reboots or deallocates a VM and hands it a new internal IP, the cluster breaks.

I updated cluster.tf to enforce static private IPs (10.0.2.5 and 10.0.2.4), but accidentally changed the NIC's name attribute in the same edit (nic-cluster-node-1 → nic-acumen-node-1). Terraform tried to destroy the existing network cards to recreate them with the new name, and Azure immediately threw a 400 Bad Request: NicInUse error because those NICs were still attached to running VMs.

  • Lesson: Renaming a resource in Terraform forces a replacement. Reverting the name string let Terraform update the IP allocation in-place (0 to add, 2 to change, 0 to destroy) in 15 seconds without touching the VMs.

3. Disk Formatting and Quorum Collisions

Terraform provisioned the blank 10GB managed disks cleanly, but formatting them with XFS, grabbing their UUIDs, writing them to /etc/fstab, and getting Silo's startup script (start-cluster.sh) aligned across both nodes took a few rough tries. Early mismatches in disk paths and metadata caused Silo to refuse startup until the drives were wiped cleanly and brought up together—finally reporting a healthy state (healed: 4, skipped: 0).

4. Reaching a Private Dashboard Without Exposing Ports

Since node-1 and node-2 had no public IPs and their NSGs blocked external access to ports 9000 and 9001, opening the Silo web dashboard in my browser required chaining an SSH tunnel through the Bastion host:

ssh -o ServerAliveInterval=60 -J acumenadmin@<BASTION_IP> -L 8081:127.0.0.1:9001 acumenadmin@10.0.2.5

Typing that out every time was so tiring, so I learnt a trick which was to move it into my local ~/.ssh/config using ProxyJump and LocalForward. After that, running ssh silo-dashboard opened the tunnel cleanly and let me manage the cluster at http://127.0.0.1:8081.

5. Real-World Downtime and Ephemeral Cloud Shell

To save credits while not actively testing, my plan was to deallocate the VMs using az vm deallocate. Then real life happened—my area got hit with a week of power outages, and I couldn't get back online to shut the VMs down. Three running VMs plus four managed disks ticking away 24/7 ate about $8 of my credits before I could get back to a terminal.

When I finally logged into Azure Cloud Shell to tear everything down, I got one final reminder: Cloud Shell sessions are ephemeral. My local ~/acumen-azure-terraform folder had reset, so running terraform destroy directly wasn't an option without re-cloning and re-initializing the backend. Since every resource lived inside dedicated resource groups (rg-acumen-infra and rg-acumen-tfstate), I used the Azure CLI to nuke the resource groups directly and stop billing immediately:

az group delete --name rg-acumen-infra --yes --no-wait

Finally, what I'd Improve Next Time

If I spin this architecture back up, there are three clear gaps I want to close:

  1. Automate disk formatting: Right now, Terraform creates the disks, but XFS formatting and /etc/fstab mounting are manual post-deploy steps. That belongs in bootstrap.sh (custom_data) or an Ansible playbook.
  2. Stop passing credentials in scripts: The Silo root password was passed via environment variables in start-cluster.sh. Moving that to a locked-down .env file (chmod 600) or Azure Key Vault is a must.
  3. Actually test node failure: Seeing healed: 4, skipped: 0 confirmed the drives synced properly, but I didn't get to run a destructive failover test (killing node-2 mid-upload) before tearing the lab down to save credits.

Overall, building inside a strict 6-vCPU limit forced me to be deliberate about every resource I spun up—and tearing it all down cleanly was just as important as getting the quorum healthy. If you want to inspect the Terraform files or try deploying it yourself, the full code and documentation are up on GitHub: wandile-lab/azure-silo-cluster.

title: MongoDB Acquires Firebolt to Bring Lightning-Fast Real-Time Analytics Into Its Intelligent Data Platform
description:
Real-time analytics on live operational data, built so applications and AI agents can act on what’s happening now.

The most valuable analytics no longer live in a dashboard. They live inside the application. A logistics app reroutes a shipment around a delay. A retail system reorders inventory before the shelf goes empty. A payments platform flags unusual behavior before the transaction clears.

Each of these decisions requires comparing live operational data against historical patterns. Which routes are backing up, and is that normal? What’s selling faster than usual, and should we restock? Is this login typical for this account at this time of day? Enterprises that can answer these questions in the moment adapt as conditions change. Those that can’t are reacting to yesterday.

Data infrastructure has long been split into two worlds: operational databases that run applications, and data warehouses that analyze what already happened. That paradigm was built for humans looking at morning dashboards, where data a few hours or days old was fine. As analytics moved into applications, real-time analytics emerged as a category of its own, combining complex queries over massive datasets with the speed, freshness, and concurrency that live applications demand. Agents raise the bar on all three. They act continuously, can drive thousands of concurrent queries, and need sub-second answers on fresh data. As businesses rely more on agents, real-time analytics becomes a core part of their data infrastructure.

Eliminate the data-movement tax

Running analytics on operational data often means copying it into a separate system, forcing organizations to build and maintain data pipelines, keep systems in sync, and run yet another platform. Even once the data is flowing, the added complexity, operational overhead, infrastructure cost, and risk of stale answers remain. This is the data-movement tax, and it compounds as agents drive more decisions.

Systems that require customers to move and synchronize data across separate platforms often struggle to deliver fresh answers at the speed and scale that live applications need. For MongoDB customers, the operational data their applications and agents rely on is already in MongoDB, so analytics should be able to run there too, at the source. That's why MongoDB acquired Firebolt.

One platform for operational data and real-time analytics

By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB’s Intelligent Data Platform, we’re bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt’s engine will run right alongside your database, and we’ll keep it in sync automatically, so there’s no pipeline to build or manage. You’ll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure.

Our Intelligent Data Platform already brings together operational data, search and vector search, Voyage AI models, stream processing, and the ability to build and run agents in production. Real-time analytics will extend that foundation, enabling applications and agents to analyze live data and act on it in the moment. Over time, customers will also be able to analyze data from other sources and formats alongside their MongoDB data.

When analytics powers a live application, an outage no longer just delays a report. It breaks the customer experience or stalls an agent mid-decision. MongoDB operates in this mission-critical world: today, approximately 75% of the Fortune 100 trust MongoDB with applications that require the highest levels of security, durability, and availability. We’re bringing that same level of reliability and operational excellence to real-time analytics.

Why Firebolt, and what’s next

Firebolt’s analytics engine is proven in production. It was built from the start for the high concurrency required by live applications and agents, not just internal dashboards and reports. Similarweb, for example, uses Firebolt to power complex, customer-facing analytics over more than a trillion rows at petabyte scale, with dynamic queries delivering sub-second performance without extensive pre-aggregation.

Firebolt’s team has tackled some of the hardest problems in analytical engines. CEO Benjamin Wagner’s background is in analytical database research at the Technical University of Munich. He built the Munich engineering team behind Firebolt’s engine and led engineering before becoming CEO. CTO Mosha Pasumansky was an architect of Microsoft Analysis Services, co-invented the MDX query language, and led the technical development of Dremel and BigQuery at Google.

“Firebolt was designed for the cloud to do what many people believed was impossible: low-latency, high-QPS analytics with fast-changing data on object storage,” says Mosha Pasumansky, Firebolt’s CTO. “We also knew that today’s applications deal with complex and flexible schemas, the kind MongoDB’s document model supports natively. So we made sure to keep the benefits of columnar storage and vectorized processing on those schemas through smart automatic column shredding.”

“Firebolt and MongoDB share the same DNA,” says Benjamin Wagner, Firebolt’s CEO. “We both build mission-critical data infrastructure for engineers. We spent the last several years building an analytics engine for what live applications and agents demand: high-concurrency, sub-second answers on fresh data. Joining MongoDB puts our engine where millions of developers already build. We can’t wait to bring real-time analytics to MongoDB customers.”

We’re thrilled to welcome the Firebolt team to MongoDB, and our teams are already working together to bring Firebolt’s engine into MongoDB. In the coming months, customers will be able to turn on real-time analytics for their MongoDB data, so their applications and agents can act on what’s happening now.

More to come soon. Join the waitlist to be among the first to try real-time analytics on MongoDB.

FAQ

What is Firebolt?

Firebolt is a high-performance analytical database designed for low-latency queries and high-concurrency applications.

Do Firebolt and real-time analytics replace a data warehouse?

No. Traditional data warehouses and data lakes remain the right fit for internal BI, reporting, and data science. Real-time analytics is for application-facing analytics, which has a different set of requirements: complex queries over massive datasets, sub-second responses, high concurrency, and fresh data for live applications and AI agents.

What happens to existing Firebolt customers?

Nothing changes for existing Firebolt customers. They can continue using the product with the same support and service. Firebolt’s customers are a big reason we wanted to bring this team and engine into MongoDB. They’ve shown what the technology can do under real production load.

title: When an Upgrade Crashes on Startup: A Merged Keycloak Fix
description:
How a reviewed pull request fixed a LazyInitializationException that stopped Keycloak upgrades to 26.7.x, and what the review process changed.

Short answer

Upgrading Keycloak to 26.7.x could crash during startup when an instance had more than one realm. The cause was in the realm cache. Model adapters it had already handed out still pointed at JPA entities after the migration cleared the persistence context between realms.

The fix clears those cached adapters at the same point the persistence context is cleared. Keycloak maintainers reviewed it, and it was merged into keycloak/keycloak as PR #51945, closing issue #51304.

The problem: an upgrade that would not finish

Keycloak is the open-source identity and access management server. When it starts on an older database it runs model migrations, and one of them goes through every realm.

Issue #51304 reported that upgrades from 26.1.x to 26.7.0 failed at the last migration step with:

org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException: Cannot lazily initialize collection of role
   org.keycloak.models.jpa.entities.RealmEntity.components ...

Keycloak would not start. According to the report, the crash depended on realm iteration order. If a custom realm was processed before master, which could happen after a database dump and restore, the upgrade failed.

The thread grew to 35 comments. Users reported the crash on 26.7.0, 26.7.1, 26.7.2 and 26.7.3, on PostgreSQL and H2. In the meantime they shared workarounds:

  • Upgrade in two steps, first to 26.6.4 and then to 26.7.x.
  • Start once with the realm cache disabled (--spi-realm-cache--default--enabled=false).
  • Physically reorder the realm table so master is migrated first.

One commenter summed it up: "Workarounds: 4 / Pull Requests: 1 / Fixes: 0." That came from an operator who couldn't use any of the workarounds and needed a real fix.

Root cause

RealmMigration.migrate() already empties the JPA persistence context before each realm with EntityManagers.flush(session, true). That keeps memory bounded. However, the Infinispan-backed RealmCacheSession keeps its own per-session maps of managed adapters for realms, clients, client scopes, roles and groups.

Once the persistence context was cleared, those adapters still delegated to entities that were now detached. When a later realm touched one of them (for example master's components collection), Hibernate could no longer lazy-load it, and the upgrade crashed.

The fix

The pull request adds one method to the cache provider contract and calls it right after the persistence context is cleared:

// RealmMigration.migrate()
CacheRealmProvider realmCache = session.getProvider(CacheRealmProvider.class);
session.realms().getRealmsStream().forEach(realm -> {
    // empty out the persistence context for each realm
    EntityManagers.flush(session, true);
    if (realmCache != null) {
        realmCache.clearManagedModels();
    }
    ...

// RealmCacheSession
@Override
public void clearManagedModels() {
    managedRealms.clear();
    managedApplications.clear();
    managedClientScopes.clear();
    managedRoles.clear();
    managedGroups.clear();
}

No cached adapter outlives the persistence context it was built on. The change doesn't touch realm ordering, the database or the migration steps themselves.

By the numbers

  • Repository: keycloak/keycloak, 37,676 stars (Nov 3, 2026), Java, Apache-2.0
  • Files changed: 4 (3 production files, 1 new test file)
  • Lines: +135 / -0, of which 118 are the new integration test
  • Commits: 2
  • Opened: Aug 21, 2026. Merged: Sep 9, 2026. Time to merge: 18 days, 21 hours
  • Review: approved by one Keycloak maintainer, merged by another

How the review went

The first version changed three files and had no test. An automated reviewer on the repository flagged that gap: a fix for a nondeterministic startup failure should come with regression coverage.

The follow-up commit added RealmMigrationCacheTest, an integration test that runs on the Keycloak server. It primes cached realm, client and role adapters, runs a RealmMigration, and asserts that the migration receives fresh model instances rather than the ones that were cached earlier.

Before maintainers picked it up, people affected by the bug built and tested the PR themselves. One posted in the issue that they had "Tested on PostgreSQL (docker) and H2 (raw binaries). No crash. Looks like it is safe to merge." Another wrote that they "built and tested the PR to run on Windows/Postgres and it solved the migration issue we were seeing."

A maintainer asked for DCO sign-off and arranged a CI run. Another approved the change ("This changes looks good") and raised a broader point. Any caller of flush(session, true) could, in principle, leave managed references with lazy collections behind, so this cleanup might belong inside the EntityManager helper itself. The PR was merged the same day, and the maintainers opened issue #52594 to consider generalizing the approach.

That is the review outcome you want. The narrow fix shipped, and the bigger design question went to the backlog where the project's owners can weigh it.

What this shows about the remediation loop

  • The signal was a real production failure. It came with a stack trace and many independent reproductions.
  • The patch was small and reversible. One new interface method, its implementation, and a single call site.
  • Review made it better. The regression test was added because a reviewer asked for it.
  • Humans stayed in control. Maintainers chose when to run CI, approved the change and merged it.

The Nov 3, 2026 review notes record that the commits lacked DCO sign-off despite the maintainer's request, and that the required AI-assistance disclosure was absent. This case study does not establish who drafted the patch.

FAQ

Did the fix change how Keycloak migrates data?

No. The migration steps and realm ordering are the same. The change only drops cached, session-scoped model adapters after the persistence context is cleared, so later lookups build fresh ones.

Was the change accepted as submitted?

The production change was the same three files from the first commit. The second commit added the regression test after review feedback. Maintainers approved and merged it, and opened a separate issue for a possible broader follow-up.

Where can I read the original discussion?

Everything is public: the pull request, the original issue, and the follow-up issue.

The goal

The issue thread had a reproduction, a root-cause theory and four workarounds, but no fix. What was missing was a reviewable change in the code. When a pull request arrives with its evidence, a narrow patch and a test, maintainers can spend their time on what they care about, including whether the idea should go further.

This fix was developed with Prilog. Read the original case study on the Prilog blog.
