title: I built a free API for 75 frontier AI models. No keys. No bill.
description:
ChatGPT is free in your browser. But if your code wants the same model, you pay for every word.

Same brain. Two doors. One is free. One has a cash register.

That never sat right with me. So I built something. It is called Mirage.

A small app that runs on your computer. Your code gets one simple API. Behind that API: 75 models from 6 big AI companies.

ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Meta AI.

No API keys. No card. No bill. No cloud in the middle.

The trick is almost silly

When you chat on those sites, your browser talks to a hidden API. It is free. You use it every day. You just can not reach it from your code.

Mirage can.

  1. You log into the chat sites in your browser, like normal.
  2. Mirage reads that login from your browser.
  3. It talks to the sites the same way your browser does. It even looks like a real browser, not a bot.
  4. Your code gets one clean API in the exact shape OpenAI uses.

So any app that works with OpenAI works with Mirage. LangChain, OpenWebUI, your own bot. You change one line:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1:3000/v1",
    api_key="obscura-local",
)

reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-chat",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)

print(reply.choices[0].message.content)

That is it. Your app now talks to DeepSeek for free. Change the model name, it is Gemini. Change it again, it is ChatGPT. ChatGPT alone gives you more than 20 models here. All free on Mirage.

What works today

This is not a demo.

Streaming answers. Tool calls. Web search with sources. File upload. Thinking mode. Long chats that remember what you said.

It is written in Rust. It ships as one file. No Docker. No Python. No Node. It runs only on your machine, and your logins stay on your machine.

It keeps 10 browser sessions warm so answers come fast. If a site goes down, it notices, backs off, and heals itself.

"But won't it break when they change something?"

You are already typing this in the comments. I know. Let me answer it right here.

Every tool like this died the same death. The site changes one small thing. The tool breaks. The maker goes quiet. Project dead.

I refused to let that happen. So I built a second tool. It is called Whelmer.

Whelmer records every single message between your browser and the chat site. Every request. Every reply. Nothing hidden. Nothing skipped.

So when a site changes something, here is what happens:

  1. We record the site before the change.
  2. We record it again after.
  3. Whelmer compares the two and points at the exact change.
  4. We fix that one thing. Done.

Minutes. Not days. Not weeks of silence.

They change a thing, we see it, we fix it. That loop is the whole game. The fear that kills tools like this? It does not live here anymore. That is the difference between a toy and a tool.

Whelmer is open source too. One file. Rust. Runs only on your machine. It works with Chrome, Firefox, Edge and more.

One honest note

This uses your own login, on your own computer. Nothing stolen. Nothing shared. It is still a gray zone with these sites, and I will not lie to you about that. Your account, your choice. Use your head.

But "it will break and die"? No. That part is solved.

What is next

Claude. Grok. And 3 more sites. They fight harder. But Whelmer shows us every message they send, so we can learn them fast. If you like taking things apart, I need you.

Mirage: https://github.com/Sumama-Jameel/Mirage
Whelmer: https://github.com/Sumama-Jameel/Whelmer

Star them. Run them. Try to break them. Then tell me what sucks. And one question for the comments:

Is using the free door smart, or is it wrong? Pick a side. I will be down there.

title: Tenant-Safe Customer Support Backups with Go and Presigned Browser Uploads
description:
Short answer: use a private bucket and a short-lived presigned URL for the browser upload; choose Infrai for lower integration friction, and choose S3, R2, or Azure Blob when specialist retention and governance controls decide the purchase.

The practical answer is a private bucket, a tenant-derived object key, and a short-lived presigned URL. The browser uploads the backup directly to storage; the application server authorizes the tenant and never puts a storage credential in JavaScript. For a customer-support system that keeps per-tenant backups and restores a selected snapshot, Infrai is a reasonable fit when reducing integration surface matters more than storage-specialist controls. S3, R2, or Azure Blob is the better choice when immutable retention, replication, or provider-native governance is the real requirement.

This boundary is easy to describe and easy to get wrong. A successful presign request is not proof that the browser uploaded anything.

The URL is temporary.

The object key is an authorization decision.

The restore page fires before the upload failure

The page that matters is the restore page. An operator sees a tenant, a selected snapshot, and a restore operation waiting for an object that never arrived. The first signal was earlier: the browser reported an upload error, but the service counted the presign response as success.

Work backward from that alert. The control plane should count presign successes and failures, while a separate completion signal records the object becoming available. Put the tenant identifier and a normalized operation label in metrics, but do not put the URL, bearer token, or customer filename in logs. A presigned URL is a credential with a short lifetime.

The alert threshold needs a deliberate trade-off. A threshold that is too low pages on ordinary browser and network noise. One that is too high turns a failed support restore into a waiting operator and a late incident. I would page on repeated completion failures for the same tenant or operation, then keep a lower-severity signal for the broader upload error rate. The exact window belongs to the application's normal upload duration, not to an arbitrary global default.

The instrumentation change is small but consequential: measure authorization, transfer, and completion as three separate stages. That gives the on-call a path from the symptom to the missing stage instead of a single green counter.

Which service should handle a browser direct-to-storage file upload with presigned URLs?

The backend should derive the bucket and object key from the authenticated tenant and the server-side backup operation. A browser-supplied tenant prefix is input, not authorization. A user filename can be retained as metadata in the application database, but it should not decide which tenant's object namespace receives the upload.

The browser then sends the file to the returned URL. It must not send the platform's Authorization header to that URL. For browser uploads, CORS is part of the deployment contract: the configured origin, method, and request headers must match what the browser actually sends. MDN's CORS guidance is a useful reference for that half of the path.

Infrai is relevant in the control plane because its storage surface exposes a presign operation while the wider platform presents 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That breadth matters here only when the same support workflow also needs adjacent backend capabilities. It can keep a backup worker, notification worker, and storage integration on one REST contract instead of making each new capability introduce another SDK and credential setup. A team might begin with one upload endpoint, then add restore status, notifications, and a scheduled cleanup path; the practical win is that those additions share discovery, authentication conventions, and examples. The storage decision still belongs to the tenant boundary and retention policy.

The second advantage is more concrete for operations: the API is self-describing, and its discovery surface is public without a key. Each documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. During a handoff or incident review, a worker owner can inspect the request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and example before adding another runtime. That removes integration guesswork; it does not remove the need to validate tenant authorization.

This is a developer-experience recommendation, not a claim that a general platform has the deepest storage feature set. The live capability snapshot is dated 2026-10-23. Record that date in review notes when a decision depends on the discovery catalog, because a catalog is allowed to change.

How do S3, R2, Azure Blob, and a REST platform differ?

Amazon S3 is the specialist baseline. Its presigned URL model fits direct browser uploads, and teams already operating AWS can use its IAM, lifecycle, versioning, object lock, and replication ecosystem. The cost is a larger account and policy surface, especially when the application has to connect tenant authorization to AWS identity rules.

Cloudflare R2 is a credible option for an application already centered on Cloudflare. Its S3-compatible API makes the storage leg familiar to many teams, but the application still owns the presign service, tenant checks, and browser CORS behavior. Existing Cloudflare operations are the deciding context, not a generic promise that all storage APIs are interchangeable.

Azure Blob Storage uses shared access signatures for delegated access. It is a sensible choice for a Microsoft-oriented estate with established Entra and Blob policy operations. Its identity and signing vocabulary differs from S3's, so standardizing on Azure is most useful when the surrounding platform already speaks that language.

Infrai storage keeps the presign operation inside a broader REST surface. There is no SDK installation step for a worker that can issue ordinary HTTP requests, and a single credential boundary can cover more of the support workflow. The trade-off is that storage-specific requirements still decide the outcome.

Option Integration fit Strong reason to choose it Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 AWS SDKs, IAM, and presigned URLs Deep storage governance Account and policy integration is substantial
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible storage in a Cloudflare estate Existing Cloudflare network and operations Tenant and CORS control remain application work
Azure Blob Storage Blob APIs and shared access signatures Microsoft identity and policy alignment Signing and identity semantics differ from S3
Infrai storage One REST presign integration Broader capabilities behind one credential and contract Storage-specialist controls may be insufficient

The explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the control-plane portion of a customer-support upload workflow when one plain REST integration and a broader backend surface reduce the team's integration friction. It is a good fit for the service that authorizes the upload and records its completion; it is not automatically the best place to put a regulated retention policy.

A minimal Go presign client with operational guardrails

The sample below keeps the platform credential on the server. PRESIGN_BODY_JSON is supplied by the deployment from the request schema discovered for the capability; the sample does not invent fields that are not verified here. The request uses the verified route, an explicit method, and an idempotency key so a retry of the control-plane call can be reconciled with the same upload operation.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func presign(bucket, objectKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := os.Getenv("PRESIGN_BODY_JSON")
    operationID := os.Getenv("UPLOAD_OPERATION_ID")
    if apiKey == "" || body == "" || operationID == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY, PRESIGN_BODY_JSON, and UPLOAD_OPERATION_ID are required")
    }

    endpoint := strings.Join([]string{
        "https://api.infrai.cc", "v1", "storage", "object", "presign",
        url.PathEscape(bucket), url.PathEscape(objectKey),
    }, "/")
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewBufferString(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", operationID)

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        response, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second << attempt
            if retryAfter := res.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign failed with HTTP %d: %s", res.StatusCode, response)
        }
        return response, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign rate limit did not clear after retries")
}

func main() {
    response, err := presign(os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET"), os.Getenv("STORAGE_OBJECT_KEY"))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if !strings.Contains(string(response), "http") {
        panic("presign response did not contain a delegated URL")
    }
    fmt.Println(string(response))
}

The returned URL is the browser's upload destination. Do not attach INFRAI_API_KEY to that request. The server should also persist the operation identifier and reconcile completion by tenant plus object key, because standard upload retries and browser refreshes are normal sources of duplicate delivery.

The code deliberately treats 429 and every non-2xx response as an operational result. It honors Retry-After when it is an integer number of seconds, applies exponential backoff otherwise, and caps the loop at four attempts. The 30-second client timeout is a local operating choice, not a service guarantee.

Where a storage specialist wins

The storage caveats are decision boundaries, not footnotes. There is no public or public-read ACL, so static website hosting, permanent public links, and an image-hosting workflow do not fit. Use private or signed-only access for tenant backups.

There is no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite is therefore not a recoverable WORM history through this surface. Strict compare-and-swap writes also need queue or database coordination because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable.

Browser teams should verify CORS early: there is no independent self-service CORS route, even though the bucket model includes a cors_rules field. Lifecycle expiration is no shorter than one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering. Cross-region replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are also outside the verified storage surface; the vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, not GCS or B2.

Those limits make S3 the better choice for regulated retention, object-lock requirements, mature replication, or a storage-heavy platform that already has its governance controls. R2 or Azure Blob may be the better choice when their surrounding identity and network operations are already the team's standard. A single REST contract does not replace a retention policy.

The decision rule for the on-call runbook

Use presigned URLs for the browser leg. Keep tenant authorization in the backend, keep the bucket private, and alert on completion rather than presign issuance alone.

Choose Infrai when the hard part is reducing integration friction across the wider support workflow: one REST surface, one credential boundary, public discovery, and runnable examples across 10 languages. Choose a storage specialist when immutable history, advanced replication, CORS self-service, or provider-native governance is the deciding requirement.

If that boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai storage documentation.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Azure Blob shared access signatures

title: Create a valid XRechnung from PHP or Node.js without Java
description:
From 1 January 2027, German companies with more than €800,000 total turnover in the previous year must issue e-invoices to German business customers (§ 27 (38) UStG). If you maintain a PHP shop plugin, a Node.js SaaS or any app that makes invoices, "a PDF by email" stops being enough for those customers, and an XRechnung file takes its place.

Writing the XML is not the hard part. Knowing it is right is. XRechnung is EN 16931 plus German rules, and the official check is a set of Schematron rules that the KoSIT validator runs on Java. A file can pass the XML schema and still be rejected by a public buyer's portal, for example because the buyer reference (BT-10, "Leitweg-ID") is missing or one amount is off by a cent.

So the question for a PHP or Node.js team is where the checking happens. These are the ways I see:

  • An open-source library in your language. PHP has good ones for ZUGFeRD and XRechnung. Node.js has fewer. A library builds the XML; you still need to check the result against the current official rules yourself.
  • The KoSIT validator in CI. It is the reference, but it needs a Java runtime and a pinned set of rules that you update after each release.
  • An HTTP API that builds and checks in one call. No Java in your stack, rule updates on the service side. The price: invoice data leaves your system, so you need a data processing agreement, and you depend on the service being up.

I build Valinvo, which is the third kind, so I'll show that one with working code and be upfront about the trade-off.

The invoice

The API takes one JSON invoice. Amounts, quantities and VAT rates are strings ("19.99"), never numbers, so nothing is rounded by floating point on the way. A shortened example:

{
  "format": "xrechnung-ubl",
  "invoice": {
    "number": "RE-2026-0042",
    "type": "invoice",
    "issueDate": "2026-10-19",
    "dueDate": "2026-11-18",
    "currency": "EUR",
    "buyerReference": "04011000-12345-34",
    "seller": { "name": "Example Software GmbH", "vatId": "DE123456789",
      "electronicAddress": { "scheme": "EM", "value": "invoices@example-software.de" },
      "address": { "line1": "Musterstraße 1", "city": "Berlin", "postalCode": "10115", "countryCode": "DE" },
      "contact": { "name": "Erika Mustermann", "phone": "+49 30 1234567", "email": "billing@example-software.de" } },
    "buyer": { "name": "Beispiel Behörde",
      "electronicAddress": { "scheme": "EM", "value": "rechnung@beispiel-behoerde.de" },
      "address": { "line1": "Amtsweg 5", "city": "Hamburg", "postalCode": "20095", "countryCode": "DE" } },
    "payment": { "meansCode": "58", "iban": "DE02120300000000202051", "accountName": "Example Software GmbH" },
    "lines": [
      { "id": "1", "name": "Software subscription, October 2026", "quantity": "1", "unitCode": "C62",
        "unitPrice": "99.00", "vat": { "category": "S", "rate": "19" } }
    ]
  }
}

The field names follow the EN 16931 model; GET /v1/formats lists the formats, and an error names any field you leave out.

PHP

Plain curl extension, nothing to install:

<?php
$ch = curl_init('https://valinvo.bmk-hub.com/v1/invoices');
curl_setopt_array($ch, [
    CURLOPT_POST           => true,
    CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS     => file_get_contents('invoice.json'),
    CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER     => ['Content-Type: application/json', 'X-Accept-Terms: 1.0'],
    CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER => true,
]);
$body   = curl_exec($ch);
$status = curl_getinfo($ch, CURLINFO_RESPONSE_CODE);

if ($status === 200) {
    file_put_contents('invoice.xml', $body);
    echo "Saved invoice.xml\n";
    exit(0);
}

$error = json_decode($body, true);
echo "$status {$error['code']}: {$error['message']}\n";
foreach ($error['problems'] ?? [] as $problem) {
    echo "  {$problem['path']}: {$problem['message']}\n";
}
exit(1);

Node.js

Node 18 or newer has fetch. Save as create-invoice.mjs:

import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const res = await fetch('https://valinvo.bmk-hub.com/v1/invoices', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'X-Accept-Terms': '1.0' },
  body: await readFile('invoice.json'),
});

if (res.ok) {
  await writeFile('invoice.xml', Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer()));
  console.log(`Saved invoice.xml: ${res.headers.get('x-validation-status')} (${res.headers.get('x-rule-set')})`);
} else {
  const error = await res.json();
  console.error(`${res.status} ${error.code}: ${error.message}`);
  for (const p of error.problems ?? []) console.error(`  ${p.path}: ${p.message}`);
  process.exit(1);
}

What comes back

With the example above the answer is the XRechnung file and two headers: X-Validation-Status: valid and X-Rule-Set: xrechnung-3.0.2-ubl-invoice. An invoice that fails the official rules is never returned; you get an error instead.

If the invoice is broken, you get JSON that points at the field. I removed the buyer's country code to see what happens:

{"code":"invalid_invoice","message":"The invoice has 1 problem. Fix it and try again.",
 "problems":[{"path":"invoice.buyer.address.countryCode","message":"Required field 'countryCode' is missing."}]}

That is the part I find most useful for a plugin: the path is the one in your JSON, so you can show the user which field to fix instead of a Schematron rule number.

Things to know before you use it

  • No account for a trial. X-Accept-Terms: 1.0 accepts the terms. Without an API key you get 2 created invoices per day per IP address, so test with sample data, not real customers' invoices. Beta keys are free on request.
  • It is a beta, run by a small company, there is a data processing agreement and a subprocessor list.
  • It does not send the invoice. Delivery (email, a portal, the Peppol network) stays with you or your access point.
  • Also checks files you already make. POST /v1/validate takes any XRechnung, Peppol BIS or ZUGFeRD/Factur-X file, so you can keep your own generator and let the API be the check in CI. There is a GitHub Action for that.

Disclosure: I build Valinvo, so I'm not neutral on the API route. Checked against the live API on 16 November 2026 with the example invoice (the curl equivalent of the code above). I wrote this with the help of an AI assistant.

title: Why Date.now() can return values that go backwards
description:
Here's a JavaScript snippet that, on rare occasions in production, will fail:

const start = Date.now();
doSomeWork();
const end = Date.now();
const elapsed = end - start;
console.log(`Took ${elapsed}ms`);
// → Sometimes: "Took -1832ms"

How can end be smaller than start? The work happened in real time, and the calls were sequential. What's going on?

Date.now() reads the wall clock

Date.now() returns the system wall clock, the same clock shown in your operating system's status bar. That clock can be changed underneath your program:

  • Clock step corrections. Time-sync daemons normally slew the clock (speed it up or slow it down a little), which never goes backwards. But when the offset is large, they step it. For example, ntpd steps the clock by default if the offset is above 128 ms (Red Hat NTP docs). A step can go backwards.
  • Manual adjustment. Someone changes the time in the system settings.
  • Virtual machine resume. When a VM is suspended and resumed, its clock may snap forward or backward to match the host.
  • Daylight saving time does not cause this. DST changes the displayed local time, but Date.now() returns milliseconds since the Unix epoch, which has no time zone.

Any of the first three can make two consecutive Date.now() calls return non-monotonic values. It's rare, but it happens often enough in production to be a real source of bugs.

The fix: performance.now() for durations

performance.now() reads a different clock. MDN describes the time origin it counts from as "a monotonic clock: its current time never decreases and isn't subject to adjustments". It returns a high-resolution value in milliseconds, with fractions.

const start = performance.now();
doSomeWork();
const end = performance.now();
const elapsed = end - start;
// elapsed is never negative

Use performance.now() for anything that measures a duration. Use Date.now() when you need to record an absolute moment (a log entry, a database row, a scheduled event). Don't use Date.now() for timing.

The other failure mode: ID generation

A common pattern:

// Generate a "unique" ID using the current time
function makeId() {
  return Date.now().toString(36);
}

This works until two events happen in the same millisecond, and then you get a duplicate. People usually add a random suffix:

function makeId() {
  return Date.now().toString(36) + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 6);
}

Better, but it still has the non-monotonic problem. If your IDs are supposed to sort by creation time (an assumption that often goes unstated), a backward clock jump can produce new IDs that sort before older ones. If you use IDs as cursors in a paginated API, that's a real bug.

UUIDv7 puts a timestamp at the front, so IDs sort by time. RFC 9562 describes optional methods for keeping UUIDv7 values increasing: an implementation remembers the last timestamp it used and counts up from it if the wall clock moves backwards. Many libraries do this, but a plain generator doesn't have to. Node's built-in crypto.randomUUID() only makes random v4 UUIDs, so use a library for v7 and check that it keeps IDs monotonic.

The sneakier failure: cache expiration

This TTL cache looks correct but has the same bug:

class TtlCache {
  constructor(ttlMs) {
    this.ttl = ttlMs;
    this.store = new Map();
  }
  set(key, value) {
    this.store.set(key, {
      value: value,
      expiresAt: Date.now() + this.ttl
    });
  }
  get(key) {
    const entry = this.store.get(key);
    if (!entry) return undefined;
    if (Date.now() > entry.expiresAt) {
      this.store.delete(key);
      return undefined;
    }
    return entry.value;
  }
}

It works until the clock jumps. If the clock jumps forward an hour (a manual change or a VM resume, say), every entry expires at once, because Date.now() is now an hour ahead of when they were set. Your cache hit rate drops to near zero and your downstream service gets hammered. A jump backwards does the opposite: entries live longer than their TTL.

The fix is to base the deadline on a monotonic clock: store performance.now() + ttl, and compare against performance.now(). Or use a cache library that already does this.

What you can do

  • Use performance.now() for durations. Never Date.now() - Date.now().
  • Use UUIDv7 for time-ordered IDs, from a library that keeps them monotonic. Don't build them from Date.now() yourself.
  • Use a monotonic clock for cache TTLs, or a library that does.
  • For absolute timestamps in logs, Date.now() is fine. Just don't rely on it only moving forward.
  • Test the bad case: mock Date.now() and check that your code survives a clock that suddenly moves back an hour.

Precision of performance.now()

Browsers deliberately limit the precision of performance.now() to make timing attacks harder. The High Resolution Time spec sets a default resolution of 100 microseconds, or 5 microseconds when the page is cross-origin isolated, and says implementations may use a coarser value (W3C spec, section 4). MDN gives the same two numbers.

That is fine for almost every use. If you need sharper timing for benchmarks, look into cross-origin isolation (see MDN's reduced time precision section).

For everyday work: performance.now() for elapsed time, Date.now() for wall-clock moments, and don't assume wall-clock time only moves forward.

title: I built a project just to learn Rust: a 3D animated trading floor.
description:
I built a project just to learn Rust: a 3D animated trading floor. Thanks to help from AI it went further than I expected.

PitCrowd is an open-source trading floor where the crowd in each pit moves with the price. Here’s how a Rust newcomer got it built and why it’s now yours to take further.


PitCrowd animated trading floor

Before screens took over, markets were rooms. Traders wearing colourful jackets stood in octagonal pits, shouting and signalling with their hands, and you could see a market: when a price broke, the crowd surged; when it stalled, people drifted off. It was called open outcry. My initial idea was to see if visualising the market like this could provide some kind of advantage over traditional charts.

I also wanted to learn Rust, and to find out what Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe that reads market conditions, could do. So I gave myself a project far bigger than my experience level should have allowed for: rebuild that room, and wire it to live prices.

The project grew and grew and after starting to understand some key Rust fundamentals I asked Claude to step in and help me take it to the next level.

The result is PitCrowd. I think it is a good base to build on and I’ve taken it as far as I can on my own so I am open sourcing and writing this article. I’d love to see how others expand on it.

What it is

The floor has nine pits, one per market: gold, silver, the Nasdaq, the S&P 500, the Dow, the FTSE, the euro, sterling and Bitcoin.

  • The crowd follows the price. A sharp move pulls traders into the pit and it gets loud. A quiet market empties.
  • Paper traders walk the floor. Each strategy is a figure that walks to the pit it’s trading, with its record on a leaderboard.
  • You can trade too. A trade ticket lets you place paper trades alongside them.
  • Bitcoin’s order book stands in the pit. The buy and sell orders waiting in the market appear as walls of liquidity, and as a heatmap panel.

How a newcomer built it

I’ll be upfront: I’m not an experienced Rust engineer. I built PitCrowd with an AI coding assistant as my pair. I set the direction and made the decisions; it wrote a lot of the code; and I had to understand, question and test everything it suggested before it went in.

Working that way on something this size (about 54,000 lines in the end) taught me more than anything else I have tried to learn Rust. What made it work:

  • Tests as guardrails. Around 350 of them. When code is cheap to write, the thing that matters is knowing whether it’s right. Every feature came with checks, and CI runs them on Linux and macOS on every change.
  • Small steps I could follow. Asking for one change at a time, and asking why when something surprised me, kept me in charge of the design instead of just accepting whatever arrived.
  • Rules that don’t bend. Some things were never up for negotiation: the API key never goes into the browser, nothing places a real order, and nothing in the tests costs money. Writing those down early meant every new piece got checked against them.
  • Being willing to throw things away. An early version of the built-in test market accidentally had a pattern in it that some strategies could exploit. It was caught, cut, and a test now stops it creeping back.

What I learned about Rust along the way

I didn’t learn Rust from a book first. I learned it because of what I was building, and wrote it down as I went: the repo includes 25 short lessons, from ownership and borrowing through traits, async and channels, to how a game engine organises a world and how to work with an AI model like Jev from Rust.

  • The compiler is a teacher. The borrow checker felt like a wall at first and like a reviewer after that. Whole classes of bug just don’t compile.
  • One codebase, two targets. The floor is built with Bevy, a Rust game engine, and the same code runs as a desktop app or in a browser tab via WebAssembly.
  • Data first. Bevy uses an entity-component-system design: instead of objects that own their behaviour, you write systems that run over data. A pit’s crowd, a trader’s walk and a price board are all just queries over the same world.

How it fits together


How it fits together

The tape is the floor’s only source of prices: one small server with one simple protocol. The relay exists so an API key never ships inside a web page. And the evolving pit generates trading strategies by the thousand, backtests them on years of price history, and seats the survivors on the floor as paper traders.

Real data, and running without it

My own floor ran on a live feed from a cTrader demo account. The floor doesn’t care where prices come from: anything that can make an HTTP request can drive a pit. The repo has an adapter that streams real Bitcoin, and its order book, from Kraken’s free public API, plus a template and a walkthrough for wiring in your own source.

When I prepared the public version, I also wanted it to run for anyone, without an account or a price feed. So I added a synthetic market: it makes up realistic-looking prices for all nine pits, with busy and quiet hours, sudden jumps and an order book.

I made sure it had no hidden patterns: the direction of every move is pure chance. That started as a practical choice, but it turned out to be useful. Anything that “makes money” on it did so by luck, so it shows you what luck looks like. There’s plenty of room to develop it, whether that’s making it behave more like a real market (panic selling, realistic reactions to news) or deliberately hiding a pattern in it, to see whether the strategies can find one.

Honest about money

Nothing here makes money, and I’m not claiming it does. PitCrowd trades on paper only.

When I ran 39 paper strategies on real prices, 10 of them were in profit. That sounds promising until you think about coin flips: get 100 people to flip a coin ten times, and a few will get eight or nine heads with no skill at all. Ten winners out of 39 was no more than luck would give you.

That’s why the evolving pit works the way it does. The more strategies it tries, the higher the bar a strategy has to clear, and only its record going forward, not its backtest, can earn it a permanent place. I wrote those rules down before its first real run, so I couldn’t move the goalposts once results came in.

And as for my original question, whether seeing a market as a crowd gives you an edge over a chart: I found that I if I spent a fair amount of time on one market watching the comings and goings of the traders I could start to get a small feel for that market. Maybe that is the same as looking at a chart, but this is a far more intuitive and fun way to watch a market. Maybe with more data being fed in and more market mechanics it could develop into something that could help traders get more of a feel, like the tape readers of the past. Of course the question is still open for anyone who wants to explore it.

The part I’m least sure about: Jev

Jev classifies market conditions from the context you give it. I’m new to it, and I doubt I used it as well as it can be used. My experiments didn’t find an edge, but I’d put that down to my inputs and inexperience before I’d put it on the model. Someone who knows Jev well could do far more here.

Jev is optional and paid. Without a key, the floor uses a simple free rule in its place and labels it as such.

Where it could go

I’ve taken it as far as I can alone. The roadmap is a menu, not a promise:

  • Configurable markets: today the nine pits are fixed. Making the list configurable would let any feed bring its own instruments.
  • A browser demo: run the synthetic market inside the page, so anyone can try it from a link.
  • A better synthetic market: more realistic behaviour, or hidden patterns to test the strategies against.
  • Use Jev better: better inputs, or Jev as a filter on a strategy that already works.
  • More adapters: OANDA, Interactive Brokers, Binance, Alpaca.

There are good first issues, a contributing guide, and Discussions are open. If you build on it, a link back is appreciated.

PitCrowd on GitHub : https://github.com/Bwizrd/PitCrowd

Paul Leppard is a senior software engineer who builds things outside his day job to learn. PitCrowd is a research and visualisation project, not trading software, and nothing in it is financial advice.

title: Pearson VUE & OnVUE Exam Booking Checklist: 5 Common Mistakes That Cause Check-In Failures
description:
Clearing an enterprise IT certification—whether it is AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, CompTIA, or Fortinet—requires weeks of hands-on lab practice. Yet every week, prepared candidates lose their exam slots before answering a single question due to avoidable registration and proctoring errors.

Based on common Pearson VUE and OnVUE check-in issues, here is a practical pre-exam troubleshooting checklist to ensure your appointment goes smoothly.

1. Government ID Name Mismatch

The single most common reason proctors cancel an exam during check-in is a character-level discrepancy between your exam registration profile and your government-issued photo ID.

  • What goes wrong: Registering with a nickname, omitting a middle name that appears on your passport/driver's license, or inverting first and last names.
  • How to fix it: Open your Pearson VUE profile at least 72 hours before exam day and verify that your First Name and Last Name match your physical ID character for character. If a name change is required, submit a support ticket immediately rather than waiting until check-in.

2. Running OnVUE System Diagnostics on the Wrong Network or Device

Many candidates run the OnVUE system test on a personal home laptop and then attempt to take the exam on a corporate workstation or a different Wi-Fi network.

  • What goes wrong: Corporate firewalls, VPN clients, background endpoint security agents, or strict router ports block the OnVUE video stream during launch.
  • How to fix it:
    • Run the official OnVUE diagnostic test on the exact laptop, webcam, microphone, and internet connection you will use on exam day.
    • Disable all VPNs, firewall extensions, and background screen-recording tools before launching the check-in client.
    • Keep a mobile hotspot ready as an emergency backup if your primary broadband drops.

3. Ignoring Workspace and Multi-Monitor Restrictions

Online proctoring rules are strict about desk environments, and failing a room scan can terminate a session immediately.

  • What goes wrong: Leaving a secondary monitor plugged into a dock, keeping notebooks or phones within arm's reach, or taking the exam in a room with glass walls where people walk behind you.
  • How to fix it: Unplug secondary displays completely (turning them off is not enough—disconnect the HDMI/DisplayPort cable), clear everything off your desk except your valid ID, and close doors/blinds to maintain a quiet, private space.

4. Logging In at the Exact Scheduled Start Time

The appointment time listed in your confirmation email is when your exam timer begins—not when you should start checking in.

  • What goes wrong: Starting the mobile photo upload (ID photos + 4 workspace photos) at the exact start time leaves no buffer if the queue is busy, causing the check-in window to expire.
  • How to fix it: Launch your check-in link 30 minutes prior to your scheduled appointment. This gives you sufficient buffer for mobile check-in, ID verification, and proctor queue wait times.

5. Redeeming Exam Vouchers Without Checking Region & Expiration Rules

Prepaid exam vouchers are a great way to manage certification budgets, but they come with strict validity rules.

  • What goes wrong: Applying a voucher tied to a specific country/currency to an account set to a different billing region, or booking an exam date past the voucher's expiration deadline (even if the checkout system temporarily accepts it).
  • How to fix it: Confirm your voucher's exact exam code, regional validity, and final expiration date before scheduling. Ensure your exam appointment date falls on or before the voucher expiration date.

Additional Study & Exam Scheduling Resources

  • Official Proctoring Guidelines: Review the latest workstation and ID requirements directly on the Pearson VUE OnVUE Official Page before running your system test.
  • Domain-Wise Study Blueprints: For structured preparation roadmaps across AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, CompTIA, and Fortinet, explore the guides on EvolveSkill.

title: Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 Startup Failure on Windows: Fixing Netigso Errors and Recovering Database Connections
description:
Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 Fails To Start On Windows – Fixing Netigso Errors & Recovering Connections

A practical example of troubleshooting an Oracle SQL Developer error when launching the application. This includes checking the ZIP archive, Java libraries, user profile and moving connections.

Windows x64 Environment

Oracle SQL Developer 26.2.0.186.2220

Previous version SQL Developer 24.3

Date: 15th November 2026

Topic: Oracle Database tools & Windows Troubleshooting.

Introduction

Oracle SQL Developer is a tool used by DBAs and Developers to interact with Oracle databases. This allows SQL to be run, database objects managed and general administration tasks performed.

Although upgrading to a newer version of SQL Developer should be a simple task, sometimes the application can have issues launching.

Example

When attempting to install Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 on a Windows workstation.

Upon trying to launch the application there were errors relating to multiple software modules failing to be loaded.

The application raised an initial warning:


Warning - could not install some modules

There were also additional messages relating to Netigso and missing software bundles.

At first this appeared to indicate that there was an issue with the archive not being fully downloaded, or the application missing some files.

Further investigation showed that the downloaded archive had the correct checksum when compared to Oracle. The chosen Java libraries were also present.

The issue was resolved by backing up and refreshing the SQL Developer user profile.

This article covers how the issue was investigated, the commands used, the results and how DBAs should be cautious when dealing with similar errors.

  1. Understanding The Issue

The version of Oracle SQL Developer we had was:


26.2.0.186.2220

Installed on Windows using the ZIP archive.

ZIP Archive:


sqldeveloper-26.2.0.186.2220-x64.zip

Extracted application folder:


C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper

Upon attempting to launch the application there were errors relating to several modules not being initialised.

Errors:


Warning - could not install some modules

org.netbeans.InvalidException: Netigso

Not found bundle: oracle.jewt_core

Not found bundle: oracle.external.jdbc

Not found bundle: oracle.ide.editor

Not found bundle: oracle.javatools_jdk

What Is Netigso?

Netigso is used by NetBeans to allow modules to be integrated into the application.

Oracle SQL Developer uses multiple modules.

If some modules are not loaded or initialised correctly then SQL Developer will raise warnings and fail to launch.

It is important to note that just because there is an error related to a missing bundle does not mean that the file is not present.

The module may be present however there may be another issue preventing it from loading.

It may not be best practice to replace the files.

  1. Checking The ZIP Archive

The first thing to do was check that the SQL Developer ZIP file had been downloaded correctly.

The issue with modules failing to load could be due to the archive being corrupt.

Oracle will provide checksums for their downloadable archives.

A checksum is used to help confirm that the file you have downloaded is the correct one.

Step 1 – Launch PowerShell

Open PowerShell on your Windows workstation.

Navigate to the folder containing the Oracle SQL Developer archive file, or enter the full path.

Step 2 – Get File Checksum

Run:


$zip = "C:\oracle\sqldeveloper-26.2.0.186.2220-x64.zip"

Get-FileHash -Path $zip -Algorithm SHA1

The SHA1 value for this example was:


6A1BCA6CD756B821C11E92B821DB73A6AEB67D02

Which matched the value provided on Oracle’s download page for the x64 Windows version.

What Does This Mean?

This confirms that the ZIP file was the same as the one provided by Oracle.

This makes it less likely that the issue was to do with the download being incomplete or modified.

Lesson learnt

Always check the software package has the correct checksum provided by the vendor. This will help to avoid having to reinstall, or download multiple times.

  1. Checking Application Libraries

Now we know that the ZIP has the correct checksum we can now check that some of the important .jar files are present.

.java Archive Files normally use the .jar extension.

There are many .jar files within SQL Developer.

Multiple errors were raised relating to modules and Java libraries.

Step 1 – Find Installation Folder

The application had been extracted to:


C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper

Step 2 – Check 5 JAR Files

The below PowerShell script will check that 5 JAR files are present.


$base = "C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper"

@(

"external\oracle.jewt-core.jar",

"external\oracle.external.jdbc.jar",

"external\oracle.external.woodstox.jar",

"ide\lib\annotations.jar",

"jdev\lib\jdkver.jar"

) | ForEach-Object {

[PSCustomObject]@{

File   = $_

Exists = Test-Path (Join-Path $base $_)

}

}

Results

Java Library | Present

--- | ---

oracle.jewt-core.jar | True

oracle.external.jdbc.jar | True

oracle.external.woodstox.jar | True

annotations.jar | True

jdkver.jar | True

All 5 JAR files were present.

What Does This Prove?

That all 5 JAR files are present.

Although it does not prove that they are all correct, or that the modules can all be loaded, when combined with the ZIP having the correct checksum it shows that there may be an issue with something else.

We do not need to copy random JAR files from another SQL Developer installation.

  1. Understanding SQL Developer User Settings On Windows

Oracle SQL Developer stores some user settings in a separate folder.

This may be your application settings, connections, UI settings etc.

The user settings on Windows are usually located in:


%APPDATA%\SQL Developer\

For the SQL Developer 26.2 version this was:


%APPDATA%\SQL Developer\system26.2.0.186.2220

This is important as even though the application files may be correct, the user settings may have an impact on the application launching.

The next controlled action we can take is to refresh the user profile for this version.

Why Backup?

The user settings folder may contain important settings.

Removing this folder straight away may make it difficult to get back to your previous settings.

It is better to rename the folder.

This will make it easier to revert.

  1. Fixing The Issue By Refreshing User Profile

Ensure SQL Developer is closed.

IMPORTANT! These commands will affect your chosen version user profile. Ensure you backup any settings or connections you need.

Step 1 – Close SQL Developer

Ensure that SQL Developer 26.2 is closed.

If you need to, ensure that no processes are running for the application before renaming the configuration folder.

Step 2 – Find User Profile Folder

Open PowerShell and run:


$profile = Join-Path $env:APPDATA `

"SQL Developer\system26.2.0.186.2220"

Test-Path -LiteralPath $profile

If the folder exists you will receive:


True

Ensure that this is the correct version of SQL Developer.

Step 3 – Rename User Profile

Rather than delete the folder, we will rename it with a timestamp.


$profile = Join-Path $env:APPDATA `

"SQL Developer\system26.2.0.186.2220"

if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $profile) {

$backupName = "system26.2.0.186.2220.backup-" +

(Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMddHHmmss")

Rename-Item -LiteralPath $profile `

-NewName $backupName

Write-Host "Profile backed up as:" $backupName

} else {

Write-Host "Profile folder not found."

}

Step 4 – Launch SQL Developer 26.2

Launch the application from the installation folder.

E.g:


C:\oracle\SQLDeveloper26.2\sqldeveloper\sqldeveloper.exe

You will be asked if you want to import settings from a previous installation. In this example we chose No to ensure we had a clean configuration.

A new user profile was created.

Step 5 – Confirm Application Launched Successfully

The application launched successfully.

The Welcome Page opened, and we could confirm that we had the correct version installed.


Help > About

The version shown was:


26.2.0.186.2220

What Was The Fix?

By renaming and replacing the user profile we were able to get the application to launch successfully.

Although we do need to be careful with our conclusions.

We were unable to confirm what the exact cause was of the Netigso error on launch.

We can confirm that the previous user profile had an impact on the issue however we cannot confirm what file in the configuration was causing the error.

  1. Confirm Previous Version Of SQL Developer Works

We also had Oracle SQL Developer 24.3 installed on the workstation.

Sometimes when upgrading an application you may worry that the new version will affect the previous working version.

In this case we were able to use SQL Developer 24.3 as the new installation was in a separate application folder, and we only renamed the user settings folder for version 26.2.

Best Practice

When testing a new version of SQL Developer:

Have a separate installation folder.

Keep the previous working version until you have confirmed the new version works.

Backup any user configuration folders.

Ensure that any critical connections are still working.

Only remove older versions once you have accepted the upgrade (based on your maintenance policy).

This means that if the new application does not meet your requirements you can go back to your previous tools.

  1. Moving Connections From 24.3 To 26.2

Once we had launched SQL Developer 26.2 we needed to ensure that we kept our connections.

SQL Developer allows you to export connections from one installation and import them.

This should only be done for authorised connection profiles.

Step 1 – Launch SQL Developer 24.3

Launch SQL Developer 24.3.

Navigate to the Connections panel.

Step 2 – Export Connections

Right click on the Connections node and select:


Export Connections

Select the connections you wish to move.

Complete the wizard and save the connections in a JSON file.

Store this file somewhere secure. Connection files may contain sensitive information.

Where possible ensure that you have password protection enabled.

Step 3 – Launch SQL Developer 26.2

Launch the recovered SQL Developer 26.2.

Navigate to the Connections panel.

Step 4 – Import Connections

Right click on the Connections node and select:


Import Connections

Select the connection file you wish to import and complete the wizard.

Your connections should now appear in the Connections navigator.

Step 5 – Confirm Connections

Check all important connections.

Ensure that the connection properties are correct. If authorised, check the connections work.

Pay particular attention to connections using:

TNS Aliases

Oracle Wallet files

SSH or network tunnels

External authentication

Custom JDBC properties

Connection settings for the environment.

Just because you have moved a connection profile does not mean that all external files, passwords, network access and authentication have been moved.

Other Things To Consider

There may be other things you want to keep from SQL Developer. This can include:

SQL History

Snippets

Reports

Templates

Preferences

These should be checked separately as the connection export is not intended to move all application user data.

Note: The original troubleshooting confirmed that SQL Developer 26.2 launched successfully and that SQL Developer 24.3 was still working. The export/import process is guidance to help you move your connections, it was not confirmed that all connections were tested.

  1. Summary Of Troubleshooting

Below is a summary of what we found.

Step | Findings | Outcome

--- | --- | ---

Launch SQL Developer 26.2 | Module installation warnings | Fail

Review Netigso messages | Multiple bundles not available | Error

Check ZIP | SHA1 matched Oracle | Pass

Check 5 JAR files | All 5 JAR files present | Pass

Backup old 26.2 profile | Renamed existing settings folder | Complete

Launch with fresh profile | Application launched | Success

Check Help > About | Version 26.2.0.186.2220 | Confirmed

Check previous version | SQL Developer 24.3 still works | Confirmed

The main thing we found was that by refreshing the user profile for version 26.2 we were able to use the application. Despite the warnings suggesting modules were not available.

This shows that it is important to investigate multiple factors when troubleshooting an application.

  1. Screenshots & Evidence

Including screenshots in a technical troubleshooting article helps to make it more useful. Below are the screenshots we should include from the original issue.

Screenshot 1 – Application Error

A screenshot of the initial warning. This should show that some modules couldn’t be installed.

Include Netigso messages if available.

Remove any personal details from your Windows account.

Screenshot 2 – Check ZIP

A screenshot of the Get-FileHash command in PowerShell. This should show that the checksum matches Oracle.

Screenshot 3 – Check JAR Files

A screenshot of the PowerShell output confirming that the 5 application libraries are present.

Screenshot 4 – Application Launched

A screenshot of the Welcome Page for SQL Developer 26.2.

Screenshot 5 – Application Version

A screenshot of the Help > About screen confirming the version.

Ensure that the screenshots are original, clear and relevant. Do not fake any screenshots showing a success. Do not include any connection details for your live databases.

  1. Lessons Learnt

We learnt a few lessons from this troubleshooting.

Missing Bundle Doesn’t Mean Missing File

The initial error suggested that the application couldn’t find the required modules. However by checking we confirmed that the chosen JAR files were present.

Always Check The Archive

Comparing the checksum is a great first step. Often you will be able to avoid downloading the package multiple times as it will match the published checksum.

Backup Before Refreshing

It is better to rename the user settings folder. This means that if you need to get back to your previous settings you can.

Keep Previous Working Application

By keeping SQL Developer 24.3 we were able to investigate the new version. This is useful when troubleshooting tools used for operational activities.

Document Troubleshooting

When troubleshooting an issue it is important to document what you have done. This will help other DBAs understand what was checked to resolve the issue. Avoid assuming anything without verifying it.

Application May Be Recovered But Not Root Cause

Whilst we were able to recover the application we were unable to prove what the exact root cause was. By creating a fresh profile we were able to resolve the issue. A deeper investigation would be required to determine what part of the profile was causing the Netigso error.

  1. Troubleshooting Checklist

When troubleshooting an Oracle SQL Developer launch error on Windows:

Check what version & package you have installed.

Check relevant Java requirements.

Compare download checksum to vendor.

Check application files have been extracted into the correct folder.

Check what error you are receiving.

Check relevant application libraries.

Backup version specific user profile.

Test application with fresh profile.

Do not overwrite previous working installation.

Confirm application launched & version.

Carefully restore required connection profiles.

Document & remove sensitive details.

Not all launch errors will have the same cause. Refreshing the profile may be one option.

Conclusion

Oracle SQL Developer launch errors can be tricky to troubleshoot. In this article we looked at an example of Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 on Windows. We had issues with the application not launching and had errors relating to Netigso modules.

We confirmed that the downloaded installation ZIP had the correct checksum from Oracle. We also confirmed that the 5 JAR files were present.

By renaming the version specific user profile and creating a fresh profile we were able to get the application to launch successfully. We also confirmed that the previous SQL Developer 24.3 installation was still working.

The main takeaway from this is by taking a methodical approach, being cautious when recovering the configuration and keeping the existing settings we can have a safer and more effective solution.

By documenting the steps taken this can be a useful reference for DBAs in the future.

References

Oracle SQL Developer Downloads

https://www.oracle.com/database/sqldeveloper/technologies/download/

Official installation packages, versions & download checksums.

Oracle SQL Developer 26.2 Installation Guide

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/sql-developer/26.2/rptig/index.html

Installation requirements & guidance.

Migrating Information From Previous Releases

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/sql-developer/26.2/rptig/migrating-information-previous-releases.html

Oracle guidance for keeping connections & information when moving between versions.

SQL Developer Concepts & Usage

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/sql-developer/26.2/rptug/sql-developer-concepts-usage.html

Abdulrawof Totakhil

title: dail: running services in FreeBSD jails, Docker-style
description:
I'm new to FreeBSD. Most of my experience is with Linux, but at some point the FreeBSD philosophy caught my eye:
stability, a coherent system, and the fact that many things were done there long ago — well before Linux. Jails, for example — they've been around since 2000.
So I decided to build my home server on FreeBSD.

The first question was: how do I run services in isolation? On Linux there's Docker — describe it and run it.
I wanted the same here: keep the host clean and skip the hassle.

Why build my own

FreeBSD already has jails — isolation built right into the system. What was missing was a convenient way to use them.

I looked at the existing tools, but none of them clicked. Bastille looked decent, but like most of the others it's a set of scripts around jails.
I like the idea of a static binary: download it and run it.

And of course I wanted to build my own (what's life without reinventing the wheel).

That's how dail — daily jail management (github) came about.

Sensible defaults

I carried over what I liked about Docker, with a focus on having to specify almost nothing.
If something can be reasonably guessed, dail guesses it.

For example, here's the entire file for zid, my home OIDC server:

FROM 15.0-RELEASE

SERVICE zid

EXPOSE 5555

COPY target/release/zid /usr/local/bin/zid
COPY .env /usr/local/etc/zid/zid.env

And to run it:

doas dail run zid.dail --ip 10.100.0.4 --rebuild

What I didn't have to write:

  • the jail name — taken from the file name
  • the start command — SERVICE zid runs /usr/local/bin/zid by default
  • the user, group, rc.conf — SERVICE handles them

An IP is assigned automatically by default, but I keep zid on a fixed one — other services depend on it.

The defaults came from practice. Most of what I run are services, so SERVICE was the first directive.
With it I needed to create a user inside the jail — and every time I named it after the service.
So I made that the default.

How I use it day to day

The usual loop looks like this:

# edit the code
cargo build --release
doas dail run zid.dail --ip 10.100.0.4 --rebuild
doas dail logs zid

Even though the name says daily, I actually don't use dail that often.
I log in, build the service, rebuild the jail with one command — and forget about it. After that it just keeps running:

$ dail ls
NAME          STATUS   JID  IP              PORTS                           BASE          TYPE  UPTIME
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
valkey        running  2    10.100.0.6/24   6379->6379/tcp                  15.0-RELEASE  thin  44d 4h
pg            running  1    10.100.0.2/24                                   15.0-RELEASE  thin  44d 4h
filest        running  6    10.100.0.5/24   8090->8090/tcp, 8090->8090/udp  15.0-RELEASE  thin  44d 4h
zid-pg        running  7    10.100.0.3/24                                   15.0-RELEASE  thin  44d 4h
cfgy-pg       running  9    10.100.0.7/24                                   15.0-RELEASE  thin  44d 4h
cfgy          running  22   10.100.0.8/24   8080->8080/tcp                  15.0-RELEASE  thin  21d 0h
aurora        running  72   inherit         4000->4000/tcp                  15.1-RELEASE  thin  9d 0h
zid           running  78   10.100.0.4/24   5555->5555/tcp                  15.0-RELEASE  thin  5d 7h
domdev        running  148  10.100.0.12/24  8300->8080/tcp                  15.0-RELEASE  thin  4d 0h

Some of these jails haven't been restarted in over 44 days.

I count that as a success. And it shows that same FreeBSD philosophy: set it up, start it, forget it.

What's running

Currently living in jails:

  • zid — identity provider (OIDC)
  • cfgy — configuration management
  • aurora — home media center
  • filest — a simple REST file server
  • domdev — this blog
  • pg, zid-pg, cfgy-pg — a separate postgres for each service
  • valkey — cache for the services

Each service in its own jail, the host stays clean.

What's still missing

Not everything is perfect:

  • Autostart. After a server reboot, all jails have to be brought up by hand. An autostart mode is planned — it will most likely need some kind of daemon.
  • Networking. By default a jail gets an IP alias on lo0, and dail writes port forwarding rules into PF itself. But outbound access (NAT) and the bridge for VNET are still configured by hand — I'd like dail to handle that too.

Wrapping up

dail is my way to run services on FreeBSD as easily as with Docker.
One binary, a short .dail file and one command to rebuild.

If you've also come to FreeBSD from the world of Linux and Docker — give it a try, feedback is welcome: github.com/zeslava/dail
