title: Putting a TTL laser rangefinder module on an RS-485 line: logic levels, direction control and one request at a time
description:
A reader asked me last week whether our laser rangefinder modules come with RS-485. They do not. I work at ERDI TECH LTD, we make the modules, and none of our published rangefinder module records lists RS-485 or RS-232 as the module's interface. The 905 nm modules and the compact 1535 nm ones speak UART at TTL level. The larger 1535 nm modules (LRF0815C and LRF1017C are examples) list RS-422.

That does not stop you from putting one on a 485 bus. The factory's answer for the LRF0305C was that any TTL-to-RS485 converter board works, and the wiring is the same for the other TTL models. What matters is what happens at the three joints: the logic level on the TTL side, the direction control, and the polling logic on the host. Here is how I would do each, with code I ran against a fake module before pasting it here.

1. The TTL side of the converter must match the module

"Runs from 5 V" does not tell you the UART level. Read the electrical table for the exact model:

  • LRF0305C: the datasheet says UART (TTL 3.3 V).
  • LR1200E4: TXD stays at 3.3 V logic even on a 5 V supply, and RXD must not be driven at 5 V. The absolute maximum input is 3.6 V.
  • LR1200E2: the factory says TXD/RXD work with 3.3 V or 5 V logic.
  • For several other models the manual does not state the level at all. I would not guess; ask before you wire.

Many cheap RS-485 breakouts use a 5 V transceiver, and the receiver-output pin of such a part swings to roughly 5 V. Wired straight to a 3.3 V module RXD pin, that can exceed the 3.6 V limit above. Pick a converter with a 3.3 V logic side, or put a level shifter between them. This is general electronics, not an ERDI claim, but it is the failure I would check first.

2. Direction control: let the last bit leave before you release the bus

RS-485 on two wires is half duplex. The host must enable the driver, send, then switch back to receive before the module answers. Two ways to do it:

  • Use a converter with automatic direction control. Nothing to write, and the module sees an ordinary UART.
  • Drive the DE/RE pin from the host (an RTS line on a USB adapter, or a GPIO).

If you drive it yourself, the classic bug is releasing DE when write() returns. The call returns when the bytes are in the OS buffer, not when the last stop bit is on the wire. The 8-byte frame used by the LR series (55 AA ...) is 80 bit times: 0.69 ms at 115200 baud, 8.3 ms at 9600. Wait that long, plus a small margin, before you drop DE. That is what time.sleep(self.frame_s + 0.0005) does in the code below.

3. Poll with exactly one request in flight

On a point-to-point UART you can get away with "read whatever arrives". On a bus with latency, or a radio link in the middle, you cannot. A late reply from request N can be taken for the reply to request N+1, and the distance is real but belongs to a different moment. Nothing in the log looks broken.

The simple fix is rule three from our request/response note: keep exactly one request outstanding, flush stale bytes before sending, accept the first valid frame inside the timeout, and treat a timeout as its own fault, separate from a checksum error.

The 8-byte frame, with its two checksums

The LR1000E2 to LR2000E4 family, LRF1200A1, LRF3000A1 and the SPD1200N0/N2/N4 use the same 8-byte frame, hexadecimal, 115200 baud by default:

55 AA  FN  D1 D2 D3 D4  SUM

Single-shot request: 55 AA 88 FF FF FF FF 84. Reply: 55 AA 88 STA FF DIS_H DIS_L SUM. STA = 1 means success; the distance is big-endian and the raw value is metres times ten.

The part that bites: the two directions use different checksums, and the manual says so.

  • Host to module: SUM = (FN + D1 + D2 + D3 + D4) & 0xFF
  • Module to host: SUM = (0x55 + 0xAA + FN + D1 + D2 + D3 + D4) & 0xFF

They differ by 0x55 + 0xAA = 0xFF, so a parser that reuses the transmit formula on replies is off by one on every frame. The manuals do not state stop bits or parity for this family; the code below leaves your serial library's 8N1 default, so confirm if your unit disagrees. Also note that LRF1200A1 and LRF3000A1 have an open protocol question on continuous ranging (the request function byte and the reply function byte differ in the manual), so this code sticks to single-shot, which is unaffected.

The code 

import time

HDR = (0x55, 0xAA)

def tx_checksum(fn, d):            # host -> module: sum(function + D1..D4) & 0xFF
    return (fn + sum(d)) & 0xFF

def rx_checksum(fn, d):            # module -> host: sum(0x55 + 0xAA + function + D1..D4) & 0xFF
    return (0x55 + 0xAA + fn + sum(d)) & 0xFF

def single_shot():
    d = (0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
    return bytes((*HDR, 0x88, *d, tx_checksum(0x88, d)))

def parse_reply(buf):
    """Return (distance_m or None, status, bytes_consumed). Resyncs on 55 AA, drops bad frames."""
    i = 0
    while len(buf) - i >= 8:
        if buf[i] == 0x55 and buf[i + 1] == 0xAA:
            f = buf[i:i + 8]
            if f[7] == rx_checksum(f[2], f[3:7]):
                sta, raw = f[3], (f[5] << 8) | f[6]
                return (raw / 10.0 if sta == 1 else None), sta, i + 8
        i += 1
    return None, None, max(0, len(buf) - 7)

class Rs485Lrf:
    def __init__(self, ser, de_pin=None, baud=115200, timeout_s=0.25):
        self.ser, self.de, self.timeout_s = ser, de_pin, timeout_s
        self.frame_s = 8 * 10 / baud          # 8 bytes x 10 bits per byte (start + 8 data + stop)

    def _send(self, frame):
        if self.de: self.de(True)             # driver enable on
        self.ser.write(frame)
        time.sleep(self.frame_s + 0.0005)     # wait until the last bit has left the shift register
        if self.de: self.de(False)            # back to receive

    def measure(self):
        self.ser.reset_input_buffer()          # exactly one request in flight: drop anything stale
        self._send(single_shot())
        deadline = time.monotonic() + self.timeout_s
        buf = b""
        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            buf += self.ser.read(8)
            dist, sta, used = parse_reply(buf)
            if sta is not None:
                return dist, sta
            buf = buf[used:]
        return None, None                      # timeout: different fault from "bad checksum"

I tested it with a fake serial object: the request bytes come out as 55 aa 88 ff ff ff ff 84; a reply built with the receive formula parses (55 aa 88 01 ff 04 d2 5d decodes to 123.4 m); a reply with one flipped checksum bit is dropped; a reply using the transmit formula is dropped; noise in front of the frame is skipped; STA = 0 returns None; an empty line times out; and DE goes high and then low around each request.

On real hardware, hook it up like this: import serial; s = serial.Serial("COM5", 115200, timeout=0.05), and pass de_pin=lambda on: setattr(s, "rts", on) if your adapter's RTS drives DE/RE (check the polarity of your board). I have not tested a specific converter board, so treat the bench check below as part of the job.

A short bench check before you trust the bus

  1. Power the module on the bench with a current-limited supply, and measure the TX idle level before you connect anything.
  2. Connect ground first, then TX/RX, then power.
  3. Capture raw bytes at the documented baud rate and check the header and checksum by hand before relying on your parser.
  4. Only then move to the long cable. Do not fix long-cable errors by lowering the baud rate alone; under motor noise the checksum still fails.

Where to look next

  • Our wiring and protocol notes (MIT-licensed drivers and docs): https://github.com/ErdiTech/erdi-lrf-drivers
  • The RS485 / RS232 question on the website: https://erdilrf.com/rs485-rs232-laser-rangefinder-module/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=devto-rs485-bus-202611
  • UART flow control notes: https://erdilrf.com/knowledge/rangefinder-uart-flow-control/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=devto-rs485-bus-202611

If your model is not in the list above, send the model name and a raw hex capture of 20 frames to tommy@erdimail.com. A smoothed plot cannot tell me whether the problem is timing or checksum; the raw bytes can.

Disclosure: I am Tommy Yu, an engineer at ERDI TECH LTD (erdilrf.com), which makes the modules discussed. Facts checked against our model documents on 2026-11-18.

title: Rendering X posts as PNGs in Rust with xeet (no headless browser)
description:
I tried xeet, a library that turns an X post into a PNG without using a browser.

I'm building a metronome app called Metronome.fm as a side project, and I wanted to show some X posts as cards on its landing page. Embedding them means loading X's script on my page, which I'd rather not do, and taking screenshots by hand is a chore. Then I happened to come across xeet and thought, this looks like exactly what I need.

From what I've seen, most tools that turn posts into images open x.com in headless Chromium and take a screenshot. xeet doesn't. It re-implements how X draws a post, from scratch, in Rust. The official site describes it like this:

X's own rules. X's fonts, emoji and line breaking, with its own text shaper, bidi engine and rasterizer.

Small and fast. A WebAssembly core under 3 MB compressed paints a post in a few milliseconds. Emoji, Japanese, math, Arabic and Hebrew fonts load in parallel as six cached packs.

Checked against Chrome. Zero line-break differences across 13,440 text layouts, all 192 card layouts matching, and byte-identical PNGs on Linux, macOS and WebAssembly.

Doing all of that without a browser is pretty bold. I tried the last two claims, "byte-identical" and "small and fast", on my own machine later in this post.

There are three ways to use it:

  • As a Rust library
  • As a CLI
  • As a WebAssembly build (@xeet/core on npm), from Node or the browser

You can also just paste an x.com URL into the box on the official site and it renders the image right there. That's the quickest way to play with it.

xeet

X posts rendered to PNG in WebAssembly. No browser.

xeet-rs.vercel.app

Since I was at it, I rendered the same post from Node, Rust and the CLI. I'm not that experienced with Rust, but it's a Rust library, so I wanted to call it from Rust too.

Environment

  • macOS (Apple M2 Pro)
  • Node.js 24.22.1, @xeet/core 0.1.2
  • Rust 1.99.0 (stable), xeet at v0.1.2

It's still a 0.1.x release, so the API may change.

Rendering from Node

xeet is split into two parts: resolve(), which fetches the post data, and render(), which draws an image from that data.

resolve() fetches the post's page on x.com without logging in, and turns what's in it (the text, the author, the like count, and so on) into the data needed to draw it (a Post). You don't need an X API key. On the other hand, it can't fetch deleted posts or posts from protected accounts, and it will probably break if X changes how its pages are built.

All network requests go through the fetch you pass in. When you run it on a server, you get to decide where it's allowed to connect and how to cache, which I appreciate.

render(), on the other hand, makes no network requests at all. A Post is just a plain object, so if you edit it you can make an image with an inflated like count (please don't).

pnpm add @xeet/core

// render.mjs
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { loadXeet } from "@xeet/core/node";
import { memoryCache } from "@xeet/core/resolve";

const xeet = await loadXeet();

// Fetch the post
const host = xeet.whatwgHost({ fetch, ...memoryCache() }); // the fetch to use, plus an in-memory cache
const { post } = await xeet.resolve(
  process.argv[2],
  { media: true }, // also fetch the image bytes (without this, media is drawn as placeholders)
  host,
);

// Render: synchronous, no network
const { png, report } = xeet.render(post, {
  surface: "web-timeline", // which screen. web-detail, ios-timeline and ios-detail also exist
  width: 600,
  theme: "light",
  dpr: 2, // draw at 2x resolution
});
writeFileSync("post.png", png);
console.log(report.warnings, report.attachment);

node render.mjs https://x.com/metronome_fm/status/2122562163147768224

This is the post I rendered:

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2122562163147768224-926'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2122562163147768224&theme=dark" }

And here's the result. The first one is the output of the code above, and the second one is drawn with a different surface and theme.

It honestly looks like a screenshot. The line breaks, the emoji, the hashtag color, the App Store URL shortened with "…", and even the video thumbnail with its duration are all there. The like count and other numbers are the values at the time of fetching, and the video becomes a still thumbnail.

It tells you why it drew things the way it did

Along with the PNG, render() returns a report. For this post, it printed this (the first line is warnings, the second is attachment):

["media is attached, so the link card will not render"]
{ shown: "media", url: null, why: "media is attached; the link card is suppressed" }

In other words: there's an App Store link in the text, but since a video is attached, it didn't show the link card. It decides based on how X behaves, and then tells you the reason. I found that pretty fun. The report also includes how many lines the text wrapped into, whether it was cut off with "Show more", and the character count the way X counts it (full-width characters count as 2).

Rendering from Rust

I'm not as comfortable with Rust as with Node, so from here on I'm feeling my way a bit.

First, exactly as the site says

The official site has a Rust tab with a Cargo.toml and sample code. The crates aren't on crates.io, so you point at the git repository directly.

# Cargo.toml: the renderer, and the resolver with its default network stack
[dependencies]
xeet-core = { git = "https://github.com/rauchg/xeet" }
xeet-resolve = { git = "https://github.com/rauchg/xeet" }
xeet-resolve-net = { git = "https://github.com/rauchg/xeet" }
serde_json = "1"

// src/main.rs
use xeet_core::model::{Post, RenderOptions, Surface, Theme};
use xeet_core::render;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // The same JSON shape as everywhere else; only `text` is required.
    let post: Post = serde_json::from_str(r#"{
        "text": "We just shipped the thing.",
        "author": { "name": "Vercel", "handle": "vercel", "verified": "business" }
    }"#)?;

    let options = RenderOptions {
        surface: Surface::WebTimeline,
        width: 390.0,     // viewport width in CSS pixels
        theme: Theme::Dark,
        dpr: 2.0,         // the PNG is width × dpr wide
        ..RenderOptions::default()
    };

    // In-process and synchronous: no network, no browser, no font files.
    let (png, report) = render::render(&post, &options)?;
    std::fs::write("post.png", png)?;
    println!("{} × {}", report.size.width, report.size.height);
    Ok(())
}

I pasted this into a project made with cargo new, ran cargo run --release, and it just worked.

The post written as JSON comes out as an image as-is.

Rendering from a URL instead

What I actually want, though, is to render from an x.com URL, so I changed it to fetch the post from a URL and then draw it. xeet-core does the rendering, xeet-resolve fetches the post, and xeet-resolve-net is the network implementation used for fetching. I kept the same Cargo.toml as above (serde_json isn't used).

While I was at it, I switched to the iOS timeline (dark) this time.

// src/main.rs
use xeet_core::model::{RenderOptions, Surface, Theme};
use xeet_resolve_net::{DirCache, Host};

fn main() {
    let url = std::env::args().nth(1).expect("pass an x.com URL");

    // Fetch the post
    let host = Host::new();
    let opts = xeet_resolve::Options {
        media: true,                    // also fetch the image bytes
        now: std::env::var("NOW").ok(), // reference time for relative timestamps (more on this later)
        ..Default::default()
    };
    let resolved = xeet_resolve_net::block_on(xeet_resolve::resolve(
        &url,
        opts,
        &host,             // fetch
        Some(&host),       // DNS lookup (used to block requests to internal networks)
        None::<&DirCache>, // cache (not used)
        None::<&Host>,     // clock for recording cache times (not used)
    ))
    .expect("the async task didn't finish")
    .expect("couldn't fetch the post");

    // Render: synchronous, no network
    let opts = RenderOptions {
        surface: Surface::IosTimeline,
        width: 390.0,
        theme: Theme::Dark,
        dpr: 3.0,
        ..Default::default()
    };
    let (png, report) = xeet_core::render::render(&resolved.post, &opts).expect("couldn't render");
    println!("{:?} {:?}", report.size, report.warnings);
    std::fs::write("post.png", png).unwrap();
}

NOW=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) cargo run --release -- https://x.com/metronome_fm/status/2122562163147768224

On iOS, the display name gets cut off with "…" to fit the narrower layout, while the web timeline shows it in full. It really does switch the layout per surface.

Rendering from the CLI

I built the CLI from source too. There's also @xeet/cli (0.1.2) on npm, which is probably easier.

git clone https://github.com/rauchg/xeet.git
cd xeet
cargo build --release --bin xeet

resolve writes the post out as JSON, and render draws it. --now sets the reference time for relative timestamps like "13m" (it was added in v0.1.2).

X=./target/release/xeet
$X resolve https://x.com/metronome_fm/status/2122562163147768224 --media --now "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" > post.json
$X render post.json --surface ios-timeline --width 390 --theme dark --dpr 3 -o post.png

Do all three produce the same PNG?

This is the "byte-identical PNGs on Linux, macOS and WebAssembly" claim from the quote at the top. I rendered the iOS timeline (dark) with all three and compared the SHA-256 hashes. I passed the same NOW to all of them so the relative time would match.

  • Node: read the post.json written by the CLI and passed its post to render()
  • Rust: rendered with the program above (fetching the post again on its own)
  • CLI: rendered with the commands above 
e071d6c8220d215e0cb4fd8d6cb0327b43a76bc11f694c758aafa8e323e64c3f  Node (WebAssembly)
e071d6c8220d215e0cb4fd8d6cb0327b43a76bc11f694c758aafa8e323e64c3f  Rust library
e071d6c8220d215e0cb4fd8d6cb0327b43a76bc11f694c758aafa8e323e64c3f  CLI

All three match, down to the byte.

Speed and size

I rendered the iOS timeline (width 390, 3x) 20 times from Node and timed render().

Post Median
The post above (with a video thumbnail) 14 ms
A short text-only post 1.4 ms

Only the very first render took about 74 ms; after that, a text-only post takes under 2 ms. So "a few milliseconds" holds for text-only posts, and it's more like 10–20 ms once an image is attached.

As for size, the WebAssembly in @xeet/core is 6.5 MB, and 2.2 MB with brotli. So "under 3 MB compressed" checks out too.

Thoughts after trying it

Getting an image that's indistinguishable from X in a couple dozen milliseconds at most, without spinning up a browser, feels really good. I also like how cleanly fetching and rendering are separated, with rendering using neither the network nor the clock.

For showing my own posts as cards on a landing page, this looks like plenty.

Here's the metronome I'm building:

metronome.fm

title: Get SEC insider trades (Form 4) for a stock as JSON
description:
When a director, officer or 10% owner of a US-listed company buys or sells its stock, they file a Form 4 with the SEC within two business days. The filings are public, but each one is an XML document somewhere in EDGAR, and a single filing can hold several transactions. Our SEC Insider Trading API on Apify reads them and gives you one row per transaction.

One stock, last 90 days

Say you want the open-market buys and sells by NVIDIA insiders over the last 90 days. The input:

{
  "tickers": ["NVDA"],
  "transactionCodes": ["P", "S"],
  "lookbackDays": 90,
  "maxResults": 3,
  "includeClusterSignals": false
}

P is an open-market purchase and S an open-market or private sale. Leave transactionCodes out to get every Form 4 code, including grants and option exercises.

One of the rows we got back on 17 November 2026, trimmed:

{
  "ticker": "NVDA",
  "issuer_name": "NVIDIA CORP",
  "insider_roles": ["officer"],
  "officer_title": "EVP, General Counsel and Sec",
  "transaction_date": "2026-09-21",
  "transaction_code": "S",
  "transaction_type": "Open-market or private sale",
  "shares": 4499,
  "price": 223.75,
  "value_usd": 1006651.25,
  "shares_owned_after": 2687660,
  "plan_10b5_1": true,
  "filing_date": "2026-09-23",
  "source_url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000169684126000014/0001696841-26-000014-index.htm"
}

The full row also names the insider and their SEC CIK, as the filing does.

Reading the row

  • plan_10b5_1 says the trade was made under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan, set up in advance. A planned sale says much less about what the insider thinks than a sale they chose to make that week.
  • filing_date and transaction_date differ: the trade happened on the 21st and was filed on the 23rd. If you backtest a signal, use the filing date (the row also has usable_from, the first day you could have acted on it).
  • source_url opens the filing on sec.gov, so you can check any number against the original.

The whole market, and clusters

Leave tickers empty to read every Form 4 in the date range. Set clusterBuysOnly to true to keep only open-market purchases where several insiders of the same company bought within a short window (clusterWindowDays); those rows say how many insiders and how much in total. Data goes back to 2006.

On a daily schedule, set onlyNewSinceLastRun to get, and pay for, only the transactions you haven't seen.

Run it

On the Store page, click Try for free, paste the input and press Start. From Python, with Apify's official client (pip install apify-client):

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("bosco_labs/sec-insider-trades").call(run_input={
    "tickers": ["NVDA"],
    "transactionCodes": ["P", "S"],
    "lookbackDays": 90,
})
for row in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(row["transaction_date"], row["transaction_code"], row["value_usd"])

From an AI agent, add this server URL to your MCP client (Claude, Cursor, VS Code):

https://mcp.apify.com?tools=bosco_labs/sec-insider-trades

The agent then has the Actor as a tool and reads the rows itself.

Price

$0.0018 per transaction row ($1.80 per 1,000) and $0.02 per cluster signal, through Apify's pay per event. The same data is on our own HTTP API if you'd rather not use Apify.

title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
description:
Vercel Blob can now delete blobs automatically. Pass ttlDays when you write a blob and it is deleted that many days after upload, from 1 to 730 days. The TTL counts from the blob's upload date.

Use TTLs for blobs you would otherwise delete yourself, such as session transcripts, exports, and temporary uploads.

ttlDays works on put(), copy(), putImage(), multipart uploads, and presigned upload URLs. Every write result and head() response now includes expiresAt, so you know when a blob is due for deletion.

setTtl() changes or removes the TTL of blobs you already have, one URL or up to 1,000 at a time, without re-uploading them.

In Vercel CLI 65.16.0 and later, pass --ttl-days to vercel blob put, put-image, copy or presign, and use vercel blob set-ttl on existing blobs.

Setting a TTL costs one Advanced Operation per started 60 days, on top of the write. A 7-day TTL costs one, and the 730-day maximum costs 13. Clearing a TTL and the deletions themselves are free. You can track TTL operations in the Blob section of the Observability tab.

npm install @vercel/blob@2.9.0

Learn more in the Vercel Blob documentation.

title: I tested my own WordPress plugin against two cache plugins and published the null result
description:
I publish a small WordPress plugin on wordpress.org. Peakspire Font Loading Optimizer does one thing: it preloads locally hosted WOFF2 files, capped at four, so the first font file starts downloading earlier. Its readme says it is safe to use alongside cache plugins. In November 2026, at version 1.2.0 and 400 downloads, I stopped trusting my own sentence and tested it.

The question

Preload tags live in the head. Cache plugins rewrite the head: they minify HTML, combine CSS, and serve stored copies of the page. Any of those steps could drop, mangle, or duplicate a preload tag. So the claim "cache plugin safe" is really six test conditions: my plugin on and off, crossed with no cache, W3 Total Cache, and WP Fastest Cache.

The test: those six conditions in a local lab. WordPress 6.9 on PHP 8.3, Apache, no other plugins. On one side W3 Total Cache 2.11.0 with page cache, HTML minification, CSS minify and combine all verified active. On the other WP Fastest Cache 1.5.5 with its cache, minify HTML, minify CSS, and combine CSS options verified active. Then 40 interleaved Lighthouse mobile runs across the cells, alternating conditions so a slow afternoon could not fake a win.

Getting WP Fastest Cache to actually turn on was its own lesson. Its master toggle checks for the literal string "on" from the settings form, and even correct form posts dropped the status key. The reliable path was a direct option write in the exact persisted shape. I only believed it was running when the cache files materialized and the page bytes changed.

What held

The headline finding is boring, which is the point. The preload tags survived every cell. Through W3 Total Cache's cached, minified, combined renders and through WP Fastest Cache's, the tags came out byte for byte intact, crossorigin attribute included. On a theme that already self-preloads, the plugin added nothing, which is the correct behavior: no duplication, no reordering.

The speed finding: the first font file finished about 620 ms earlier with the plugin on, roughly 27 percent. That is the whole performance claim, and it matches what the plugin is for.

What did not move

Largest Contentful Paint medians differed by less than 100 ms across all conditions, which I read as no clear improvement either way. I have no LCP win to sell. Preloading the font earlier helped the font fetch, but that earlier fetch did not translate into a clear LCP improvement in this test. Publishing a null result feels odd when the download graph is the only audience, but a self-audit that only reports its wins is marketing. This one reports both.

The test has limits and they are on the page: one theme, one lab host, free tiers of both optimizers, local network. I am not claiming your stack behaves the same. The method is the deliverable: name the claim, build the matrix, interleave the runs, publish the cells including the flat ones.

Why a 400-download plugin deserves this

Nobody was asking. That is exactly why it was worth doing. The WordPress ecosystem runs on readme promises, and the cheapest trust signal a small author can offer is a public test of their own promise with the negative finding left in. The full matrix, the run logs, and the limits are on the proof page: peakspire.ca/font-plugin-cache-compat-test/

If you ship a plugin with a compatibility claim, the test is an afternoon plus a lab container. The null result costs nothing but the afternoon.

title: Why does my Lambda function hit "Too many connections" on Amazon RDS?
description:
Consider a hypothetical pipeline where a set of AWS Lambda functions processes incoming event streams from an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream. Each time a record arrives, the Lambda function spins up, opens a new TCP connection to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance, executes a small INSERT query, and closes the connection. During steady state, this works fine. However, during a traffic spike, the number of concurrent Lambda executions exceeds the database's max_connections parameter, causing the database to reject new connections. The system starts failing with connection timeout errors, leading to data loss in the ingestion layer.

This article explains how to mitigate connection exhaustion by introducing Amazon RDS Proxy between your serverless compute and your relational database. We will cover the mechanics of proxying, how to configure it to manage connection pooling, and the operational trade-offs involved.

Symptoms

Engineers often observe these symptoms when connection saturation occurs:

  1. Application Errors: The logs show psycopg2.OperationalError: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections or generic "connection refused" messages.
  2. High Database Load: Even if CPU usage is low, the DatabaseConnections metric in Amazon CloudWatch shows a flat line at the max_connections limit.
  3. Latency Spikes: Queries wait in a queue or time out while trying to establish a connection, not because the query itself is slow.

A common false lead is to simply increase the max_connections parameter on the RDS instance. While this provides temporary relief, it increases the memory pressure on the database server, as each connection consumes RAM for buffers and thread management. This approach fails to address the underlying architectural issue: the mismatch between the short-lived, bursty nature of serverless compute and the overhead of establishing stateful TCP connections to a relational database.

flowchart LR
    lambda["AWS Lambda (Compute)"]
    proxy["Amazon RDS Proxy"]
    db["Amazon RDS / Aurora"]

    lambda -- "Pooled Connection" --> proxy
    proxy -- "Persistent Connection" --> db

1. Connection Saturation

The most common cause is the "one-request, one-connection" pattern. Every time a Lambda function initializes, it performs a TCP handshake and a TLS negotiation, followed by a database authentication handshake. This process is computationally expensive for the database.

How to confirm: Check the DatabaseConnections metric in CloudWatch. If it consistently hits the limit defined in your RDS Parameter Group, you have reached your capacity.

How to fix: Introduce Amazon RDS Proxy. It maintains a pool of established connections to the database. When a Lambda function requests a connection, the proxy assigns an existing, idle connection from the pool rather than forcing the database to spawn a new backend process.

Verify: Monitor the DatabaseConnections metric after enabling the proxy. You should see a lower number of connections to the RDS instance, as the proxy multiplexes many client connections over a smaller number of established server connections.

2. Incorrect Proxy Target Configuration

A common error occurs when Lambda functions attempt to connect to the RDS endpoint directly instead of the RDS Proxy endpoint. The proxy cannot pool connections if the traffic bypasses it.

How to confirm: Inspect your Lambda environment variables. Ensure the DB_HOST variable points to the proxy endpoint (e.g., proxy-name.proxy-xyz.region.rds.amazonaws.com), not the RDS instance endpoint.

How to fix: Update your infrastructure-as-code to route application traffic to the proxy endpoint. If using AWS CDK, reference the proxy endpoint programmatically:

# Example: AWS CDK snippet
proxy = rds.DatabaseProxy(self, "Proxy",
    proxy_target=rds.ProxyTarget.from_db_instance(my_db_instance),
    secrets=[my_secret],
    vpc=my_vpc
)

# Use proxy.endpoint in your application config

Verify: Use netstat or check the application logs to confirm the connection is being routed to the proxy’s DNS name.

3. Excessive Connection Idle Timeout

If the IdleClientTimeout in your proxy configuration is too high, the proxy might keep too many connections open, preventing the database from reclaiming resources. Conversely, if it is too low, the proxy constantly creates and destroys connections, negating the performance benefits.

How to confirm: Check the ClientConnections and DatabaseConnections metrics in the RDS Proxy CloudWatch namespace. If ClientConnections is high but DatabaseConnections is also near the limit, your pooling efficiency is low.

How to fix: Tune the IdleClientTimeout parameter based on your workload's inter-arrival time. For bursty workloads, a value that matches your average event interval is ideal.

Verify: Observe the DatabaseConnections metric. You want to see it remain stable even as ClientConnections (the incoming Lambda requests) fluctuates.

4. Authentication Mismatch

RDS Proxy requires the Lambda function to have access to the database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager. If the IAM role attached to the Lambda lacks secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permissions, the proxy cannot authenticate the connection on behalf of the function.

How to confirm: Check CloudWatch Logs for Access Denied errors or authentication failures during the connection phase.

How to fix: Ensure the IAM policy for the Lambda function follows the principle of least privilege:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
            "Resource": "<your-secret-arn>"
        }
    ]
}

Verify: Run a test invocation of the Lambda function. If the connection succeeds, the proxy successfully retrieved the secret.

Preventing it

To prevent these issues systemically:

  1. Use Connection Pooling: Never allow serverless functions to open connections without a proxy in a high-concurrency environment.
  2. Monitor Early: Set up CloudWatch Alarms on the DatabaseConnections metric before you reach your limit.
  3. Decouple with Queues: If possible, introduce an Amazon SQS queue between your event source and the Lambda function to throttle the rate at which connections are requested, effectively smoothing out the bursts.
  4. Implement Exponential Backoff: Ensure your application code uses a connection retry strategy with exponential backoff to avoid overwhelming the proxy during a recovery phase.

Clean up

If you have created an RDS Proxy for testing purposes, ensure you delete it to avoid ongoing costs:

  1. Navigate to the RDS Console.
  2. Select Proxies from the navigation pane.
  3. Select the proxy and choose Delete.
  4. Remove the associated Secrets Manager secret and the RDS instance if they are no longer required.

Conclusion

Amazon RDS Proxy solves the problem of connection exhaustion by decoupling the number of incoming client requests from the number of established database connections. By correctly routing your traffic to the proxy endpoint and ensuring your IAM roles have the necessary permissions to access database secrets, you can maintain system stability even under high, bursty traffic. As a next step, audit your existing Lambda functions to ensure they are using persistent connection objects defined outside the function handler, which allows the Lambda execution environment to reuse connections between invocations.

References

  • Amazon RDS Proxy documentation
  • Managing connections with RDS Proxy
  • AWS Secrets Manager documentation

title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
description:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: Decision-1.1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Decision-1.1 from Microsoft AI is now available on AI Gateway. It is more accurate, better calibrated, and faster than Decision-1.

The decision model returns structured answers instead of free-form text for tasks such as routing support requests, choosing which model should handle a request, selecting the next step in a workflow, or grading AI responses.

  • Boolean: the probability that a condition is true

  • Choice: a selected category and probabilities for each option

  • Score: a numerical rating on a scale you define

Multiple questions can share the same input in one request. Better calibration means the model's probabilities track how often it is right, so your application can set thresholds for when to act, flag a case for review, or escalate.

Decision-1.1 accepts the same request format as Decision-1. To switch, change the model ID to microsoft/decision-1.1.

Call it through the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Decisions API, or the AI CLI. The examples below require ai 7.0.128 or later for TypeScript, or the OpenAI Python SDK 3.26.0 or later for Python.

Decision requests appear in request logs, count toward budgets, and support decision fallbacks.

Try Decision-1.1 in the model playground, or see the decision models documentation for request formats and question types.

title: Faster SSDs for PostgreSQL: From Read I/O to WAL Waits
description:
The baseline in the previous post reached 50,648 NOPM, with most active-client observations at IO:DataFileRead. To understand the next bottleneck, I first increased the storage budget, then checked the next boundary in the commit path: acknowledgment from another availability zone. The objective was to distinguish device capacity from waiting higher in the path.

The 95,000-warehouse dataset, 512 workers, 15-minute ramp-up, and 45-minute measurement remained. The primary still had 64 vCPUs, 512 GiB RAM, and 128 GiB of shared buffers.

What changed on the primary

I changed storage only on the primary because this step targeted the benchmark's foreground read I/O (IO:DataFileRead). In this HammerDB TPROC-C run, all transactions, including their SELECT statements, used the primary endpoint. The workload did not offload reads to replicas. Doing so would require changing the tested execution and checking its consistency assumptions.

I migrated the existing data to an Ultra disk, which supports up to 400K IOPS and 10 GB/s throughput at low latency. The IO limits are then determined by the non-bursting E64bds_v5 with NVMe: 294,800 IOPS and 7,800 MB/s throughput.

Original primary (previous post) Higher-I/O primary (this post)
VM E64ds_v5 E64bds_v5, NVMe
CPU / memory 64 vCPUs / 512 GiB 64 vCPUs / 512 GiB
Data disk Premium SSD v2 Ultra Disk
Capacity 20,480 GiB, or 20 TiB 20,480 GiB, or 20 TiB
Provisioned IOPS 80,000 294,800
Provisioned bandwidth 1,200 MB/s 7,800 MB/s
Filesystem ext4 ext4

Both data and WAL were on that remote disk.

The two replicas retained their Premium SSD v2 disks at 80,000 IOPS / 1,200 MB/s, as my goal was only to accelerate the reads on the primary. Each benchmark used the same-zone D64ds_v5 client with 64 vCPUs / 256 GiB. The standbys still performed I/O to receive, flush, and replay WAL. Their storage could affect synchronous commit. The local-commit diagnostic below separates their acknowledgments from the primary's own synchronization.

Keep in mind that the usable budget depends on both the disk and the VM. Ultra Disks support up to 400,000 IOPS / 10,000 MB/s, but the E64bds_v5 NVMe configuration lists 294,800 IOPS / 7,800 MB/s for Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 without bursting. That's sufficient for my test, as long as I don't encounter a bottleneck. Ultra Disk has been generally available since August 2019 and can be used with self-managed PostgreSQL on Azure VMs. It's now also generally available for Azure Database for PostgreSQL (the community PostgreSQL running as a managed service).

Premium SSD v2: waiting for reads

The first result covered in the previous post in this series was 50,648 NOPM (new orders per minute). During measurement, the primary data disk delivered approximately 51,130 read + 30,469 write IOPS, with 429 MiB/s reads + 412 MiB/s writes. Its guest busy-time counter was approximately 100%, and mean read/write completion times were 7.98 / 10.95 ms. The active-backend sample observations were:

Wait Share
IO:DataFileRead 79.6%
LWLock:WALWrite 10.8%
IPC:SyncRep 5.2%

That is the read-I/O-heavy baseline from part 1, with guest IOPS close to the provisioned 80,000-IOPS budget. The guest counters describe device activity. The wait percentages are shares of sampled active-client observations.

Ultra Disk: faster reads, then WALWrite

After moving the primary to Ultra, I got 55,784 NOPM, a 10.1% increase. Read/write completion times were about 0.31 / 0.23 ms. DataFileRead dropped to 2.56% of active-backend observations. But the wait mix had changed:

Wait Share
LWLock:WALWrite 83.18%
IPC:SyncRep 7.53%
IO:DataFileRead 2.56%

WALWrite was now the dominant wait, and that's why it doesn't fully benefit from the faster disks.

The Ultra primary delivered about 81,221 combined read/write IOPS and 976 MB/s, below its provisioned 294,800 IOPS / 7,800 MB/s. Guest busy time was 99.95%: I/O was almost continuous while the totals remained below the provisioned limits.

WALWrite means a backend is waiting for PostgreSQL's WAL write lock. The holder may be performing writes or waiting for synchronization. A long wait can therefore originate above device execution, even when admitted requests complete quickly.

Faster standby storage could reduce acknowledgment time, but that was a separate part of the path. Before attributing the remaining limit to cross-zone synchronization, I removed that wait from the diagnostic.

Remove the standby wait, for the investigation

The replicas were still on Premium SSD v2. I used session-level synchronous_commit set to local to remove their required acknowledgments from the commit path while retaining local durability and streaming replication. In the benchmark, the override was supplied through the workload's PGOPTIONS, so the worker connections inherited the setting.

Patroni automatic failover was separately paused for this bounded diagnostic. It's a lab to investigate what happens, not a production setup.

The result was that the throughput didn't increase, with 54,556 NOPM, versus 55,784 in the preceding run:

Active-client observation Ultra, commit on Ultra, commit local
LWLock:WALWrite 83.18% 87.29%
IPC:SyncRep 7.53% 0 observed
IO:DataFileRead 2.56% 3.93%

This change tested whether waiting for standby acknowledgments was holding back the workload. SyncRep disappeared from the samples, but throughput stayed near 55,000 NOPM and WALWrite remained dominant. Both standbys continued streaming, with a lag.

The name local explains why. It still waits for local durable WAL flushing. The WAL synchronization counter averaged 25.44 ms in the normal-HA run and 29.55 ms in the local-commit run.

The PostgreSQL commit path flushes local WAL before waiting for synchronous replication. WALWriteLock is released before the standby-acknowledgment wait reported as IPC:SyncRep. SyncRepLock protects the shared queue and state updates and is released while the backend waits on its latch. Group commit can make several transactions durable with a single synchronization.

What faster storage changed

The initial read waits fell substantially. WALWrite remained prominent after acknowledgment waits were removed. The investigation had moved from the device-read budget to what happened inside the primary's write/flush path.

These runs reused the dataset. Cache contents, dirty pages, checkpoint phase, and vacuum state evolved between tests. What we have proved is that even with the fastest disk and the lowest replication latency, we gained only 10%, far from the 8x throughput observed in HorizonDB.

HorizonDB maintains cross-zone durability using its shared WAL service, rather than waiting for a PostgreSQL standby to flush its private WAL disk. WAL replication happens outside the SQL writer, which explains why the workload achieves higher throughput than this PostgreSQL configuration can support.

I next traced the lock holder's path to understand why local synchronization averaged tens of milliseconds while device requests completed in fractions of a millisecond. Part 3 follows that delay into the Linux writeback path.

title: ByteChef Embedded, Part 12: Ship a Full Automations Page With One React Component
description:
Originally published on the ByteChef blog. Part 12 of the ByteChef Embedded series.

TL;DR: <AutomationHub jwtToken={token} /> from @bytechef/embedded 0.4.0 puts a complete automations page inside your product. Your users browse the templates you release, connect their own accounts, switch automations on and off, see why one stopped, and manage their connections. On your side: publish a project, release it with an enabled configuration per environment, drop in the component.

The page every integration product ends up building

Once users can create workflows, they need a page to come back to. That page has to answer the everyday questions:

  • Which account is this using?
  • Is it on?
  • Why did it stop?
  • How do I change it?

Building it yourself means a catalog, an activation flow that cleans up after itself when something fails, an on/off switch that explains why it won't turn on, a settings form, a connections list and a way into the builder. That's weeks of work nobody on your team wants to own.

The Automation Hub is that page, already built. It runs in an iframe served by your ByteChef instance, picks up your colors, and only shows what belongs to the user whose JWT you pass in.

Five terms you need

Term What it is Who manages it
Automation project A set of workflow templates you build, e.g. "Lead routing" You, in Embedded → Automations
Version A frozen, read-only snapshot of a project, created when you Publish You
Configuration Releases one version of a project to one environment. Has an on/off switch, per-workflow switches, a hub visibility toggle, an assignment rule and provided values You, per environment
Reference A user's automation that points at your template and stores only their connections and inputs Created when the user activates a template
Copy A user's own editable workflow, cloned from your template Created when the user picks Edit workflow

If you remember one thing: publishing doesn't release anything. Users only see a project once an enabled configuration releases it in their environment.

Step 1: Build and publish a project

Projects and templates are only editable in the Development environment. Switch to it at the bottom of the left sidebar, then open Embedded → Automations.

  1. Click New Project. Name and Description are required. Category, Tags and a Permission Expression like metadata['plan'] == 'pro' are optional.
  2. On the Workflows tab, click Create Workflow (or Import Workflow for .json, .yaml, .yml).
  3. Build the template. Every component that needs an app account gets a connection slot. Anything each user fills in themselves, like the Slack channel to post to, goes in the workflow inputs. The hub asks for those during activation.
  4. Publish. The badge goes from V1 DRAFT to V1 PUBLISHED.

Step 2: Release it with a configuration

A configuration puts a published version in front of users in one environment. Create one from New Configuration in the project's ⋮ menu, the Configurations tab, or the editor header.

The key fields:

Field What it does
Version Defaults to the latest published version. Pick an older one to roll back
Assignment rule Optional expression for which new users get this configuration, e.g. metadata['beta'] == 'true'. Empty means everyone
Show in Automation Hub On by default. Off hides the project from the catalog, though its workflows can still be activated by UUID

On the Workflows step, each workflow has its own switch. Turn one off and that template disappears from the hub in this environment.

Now the step that catches most people: new configurations are saved switched off. Users see nothing until you flip Enable Configuration.

Provided values

Some settings shouldn't be up to the user. Maybe every customer should post through your Slack bot. Open a workflow's ⋮ Edit in a saved configuration and you get two tabs:

  • Connections: pick Let each user connect or one of your own embedded connections.
  • Inputs: pick Let each user fill it or set a value. Inputs tied to a component property (like a Slack channel) get a real dropdown, loaded through one of your connections.

In the hub, provided values show Provided by your administrator instead of a picker. The server rejects any attempt to override them.

Several configurations, one environment

You can run Everyone on V3 and Beta on V4 side by side. Each user lands on exactly one, decided the first time they activate or copy a workflow: ByteChef picks the enabled configuration whose rule matches, preferring the highest version, then the newest configuration.

The rule is checked once. Changing a user's metadata later doesn't move them. To move users on purpose, use Move Users… on a configuration, Upgrade automation in Connected Users, or Change configuration… for a single user.

Rolling out a new version

Publishing V2 changes nothing for your users. To roll it out, use Change Project Version on the configuration. Before you save, the dialog tells you exactly what will happen:

Version 2 adds required input channel to New lead alert:
14 connected users will pause until they fill it.

On save, references move to the new version and keep each user's connections and inputs. Anything now missing pauses with a reason. Copies stay where they are.

Other actions that touch running automations:

  • Switching off a configuration or workflow pauses its references with "turned off by your administrator". Switch it back on and they resume.
  • Deleting a configuration deletes its references (the dialog tells you how many). Copies keep working.
  • Removing a workflow from the released version leaves dangling references, disabled until the user removes them.

Outside Development you get Automation Configurations instead of Automations: same row actions, no editor. Typical launch: build and publish in Development, test through a Development configuration, then create Staging and Production configurations for the version you tested.

One more prerequisite: every app your templates use needs an embedded integration with an enabled integration configuration in that environment (see part one). Without it, users can't finish activating.

Step 3: Allow your app's origin

Tell the ByteChef server which origins may embed the hub:

BYTECHEF_EMBEDDED_ALLOWED_PARENT_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com

or in application.yml:

bytechef:
  embedded:
    allowed-parent-origins: https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com

Exact origins only: scheme, host and port, no paths or wildcards. ByteChef uses the list three ways:

  1. Sends it as Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors, so browsers won't render the hub inside any other site.
  2. Sends its EMBED_READY message only to those origins.
  3. Only accepts EMBED_INIT (your props and token) from them.

Leave it empty and any site can embed your hub. Worse, the hub has to guess your page's origin from document.referrer, which breaks when:

  • your page sends Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, or
  • your app is on HTTPS and ByteChef on plain HTTP.

In both cases the hub sits on its loading dots forever. Set the origins and both problems go away.

Step 4: Drop in the component 

'use client';

import {AutomationHub} from '@bytechef/embedded';

export function AutomationsPage({jwtToken}: {jwtToken: string}) {
    return (
        <AutomationHub
            baseUrl="https://bytechef.example.com"
            className="h-[800px] w-full"
            environment="PRODUCTION"
            jwtToken={jwtToken}
            tabs={{connections: true, newWorkflow: false}}
            theme={{borderRadius: '0.5rem', mode: 'light', primaryColor: '#2563eb'}}
        />
    );
}

It renders a <div className={className}> with a full-size iframe inside. Give the wrapper a height or the iframe collapses.

Props

Prop Default What it does
jwtToken required The connected user's token from part one
baseUrl https://app.bytechef.io Your ByteChef host
environment 'PRODUCTION' Which environment's catalog and connections to show
tabs all true automations, connections, newWorkflow
editWorkflowAllowed true Shows Edit workflow and Customize
includeComponents none Limits which components the builder offers
defaultLayout 'grid' 'grid' or 'list'
layoutSwitcherAllowed true Shows the grid/list toggle
theme none Colors, font, corner radius
connectionDialogAllowed true false stops users creating connections in the hub

No callbacks. Everything is saved through the embedded API with the user's JWT.

Lock down connection creation in the token, not the prop

connectionDialogAllowed as a prop only hides buttons. To have the server enforce it, put it in the JWT:

const payload = {
    sub: externalUserId,
    name: userName,
    connectionDialogAllowed: false,
};

With the claim set to false, connection-create calls get a 403 and the hub hides its Connect buttons, whatever the prop says. Creation is allowed only when both allow it. The claim must be a boolean, or ByteChef rejects the token.

Token refresh is just a re-render

On load, the hub sends EMBED_READY and the component replies with EMBED_INIT carrying its props. When any prop changes, including jwtToken, the component sends a new EMBED_INIT without reloading the iframe. New token or environment means the hub reloads its data for that identity. So refreshing a token is passing a new value.

Theming

theme accepts mode, primaryColor, fontFamily, borderRadius, surfaceColor, cardColor, activeBorderColor, enableColor, disableColor, onAccentColor, segmentColor, plus cssVariables for any other custom property. It applies to dialogs and the builder too.

One catch: the hub is a separate page, so your @font-face rules don't reach it. Stick to fonts the system already has, like system-ui, Arial or Georgia.

What your users get

The catalog

A toolbar (All / Active / Enabled filter, search, grid/list toggle, optional New Automation button) and one card per template the user is allowed to see. Activated cards show the version badge, an Enable/Disable button, a ⋮ menu with Settings, Customize and Remove, and a Needs attention badge with a one-line reason when something blocks it.

The activation dialog

Clicking Use opens up to three steps:

  1. Connect: one account picker per app that isn't provided by you, with a + to connect a new account inline.
  2. Configure: one typed field per input (date, email, number, URL…).
  3. Activate.

Under the hood that's at most four calls:

GET    /api/embedded/v1/automation/workflows
POST   /api/embedded/v1/automation/workflow-templates/{templateUuid}/provision
POST   /api/embedded/v1/automation/workflows/{templateUuid}/enable
DELETE /api/embedded/v1/automation/workflow-templates/{templateUuid}/provision   # only on failure

The provision body:

{
  "connections": {"slack": 42, "hubspot": 17},
  "inputs": {"channel": "#sales"}
}

Connections you leave out are matched automatically to the first usable connection for that app. If provisioning or enabling fails, the dialog deletes the half-created reference so the user retries from a clean state, then maps the error to a human message (a 409 with missingConnectionComponentName jumps back to Connect and highlights the row).

That cleanup logic is the part people usually get wrong when they build this themselves.

Needs attention, explained

Each card's reason comes from attentionReason:

attentionReason What the card says
MISSING_CONNECTION:<component> Connect <component> to keep this running
INPUT_REQUIRED:<input> Fill in <input> to keep this running
INVALID_WORKFLOW:<count> Fix the <count> errors in this workflow to turn it on
TURNED_OFF_BY_ADMINISTRATOR Turned off by your administrator
UPDATE_PENDING Turn it on again to apply the latest update

When the user fills a missing input in Settings, a reference that was only waiting for it starts running again on its own.

Edit workflow

Edit workflow copies the template and opens the copy in the embedded builder from part eleven, inside the same iframe and theme. A new copy has to be published in the builder before it can be enabled.

The Connections tab

The user's connections with a Reconnect needed badge when credentials stop working. Reconnect replaces credentials but keeps the connection ID, so automations using it keep working. Delete is blocked with a 409 if an enabled automation still uses it.

References vs copies

Reference (from Use) Copy (from Edit workflow)
User owns Their connections and inputs A whole workflow
Editable in the builder No Yes
Gets your new versions Yes No
Provided values Applied and locked Not applied
You switch the workflow off Paused Keeps running

References are what let you fix a template once and roll the fix out to everyone. Want users on references only? Set editWorkflowAllowed={false}.

Building your own hub instead?

Every call goes to /api/embedded/v1 with Authorization: Bearer <JWT> and X-ENVIRONMENT:

Purpose Request
Catalog GET /automation/projects
One template GET /automation/workflow-templates/{uuid}
User's automations GET /automation/workflows
Activate / remove reference POST / DELETE /automation/workflow-templates/{uuid}/provision
Copy POST /automation/workflow-templates/{uuid}/copy
Blank automation POST /automation/workflows
Enable / disable POST / DELETE /automation/workflows/{uuid}/enable
Inputs PUT /automation/workflows/{uuid}/inputs
Publish a copy POST /automation/workflows/{uuid}/publish
Connection picker GET /components/{componentName}/connections
Connections tab GET /connections, DELETE /connections/{id}, POST /connections/{id}/reauthorize

Every /automation/... call also has a server-to-server version at /{externalUserId}/automation/..., authenticated with your environment's API key. Use it to set up automations from your backend, for example right after signup, before the user ever opens the hub.

Gotchas

  • Publishing shows nothing to anyone. You need an enabled configuration, and new ones are saved off. Development included, which is what the sample app uses by default.
  • New configurations don't move existing users. Move them with Change Project Version, Move Users… or Upgrade automation.
  • newWorkflow: false also hides My Automations, which is where users clean up references to templates you removed.
  • The token wins on connections. connectionDialogAllowed: false in the JWT can't be undone by the prop.
  • Custom fonts don't cross the iframe.
  • Set allowed origins before going live, or the hub depends on the browser's referrer to find your page.

Before you go to production

  • Enabled configurations in Staging and Production pointing at the version you tested
  • Hub visibility, workflow switches and provided values set per configuration
  • An enabled integration configuration for every app your templates use
  • Assignment rules based on metadata you actually set
  • BYTECHEF_EMBEDDED_ALLOWED_PARENT_ORIGINS set to exact origins
  • connectionDialogAllowed as a JWT claim, not just a prop
  • Tokens refreshed before expiry and passed in as a new prop
  • environment passed explicitly (it defaults to PRODUCTION)
  • A wrapper with a real height
  • A theme that works in light and dark mode
  • A rollout routine: Change Project Version, read the warnings, then save

What you own, what ByteChef owns

You own the templates, which versions are released where, provided values, assignment rules, enabled apps, allowed origins, the JWT and its claims, the page around the iframe, and the theme.

ByteChef owns the catalog, activation and its cleanup, automatic connection matching, version upgrades, attention reasons, the settings form, the connections list, the builder, credential storage, and the engine that runs every automation.

On your side it's one component and a token. Behind it is the whole lifecycle of an automation: release, assign, activate, upgrade, pause, retire.

Try it

Publish a project in Development, create a configuration and switch it on. Run the embedded sample app, open Automation Hub, click Use on a template, connect an account, and watch the card turn into a running automation.

Next up, part 13: the Integration Marketplace, where users browse and connect your integrations without hunting for a template.

ByteChef is open source (Apache 2.0). If this was useful, a star on GitHub helps a lot. The full reference version of this post, with every dialog message and error case, is on the ByteChef blog.

title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
description:
Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :)

What it does today:

- Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router.

- Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks.

- Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance.

We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results.

But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now.

We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions:

- 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency)

-The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps.

Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels.

So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8.

The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within

There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections.

You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:

https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...

Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback.

Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai.

We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

title: Kasm Developer API Keys Cross the Workspace Control Plane
description:
Kasm Developer API Keys Cross the Workspace Control Plane

Kasm Workspaces delivers browser-based desktops and applications through a control plane that manages users, sessions, images and infrastructure zones. A ZoomEye count-only query on November 18, 2026 found 36 matches for title="Kasm Workspaces" and no matches for app="Kasm Workspaces". The small result set makes ownership review practical, but it also means a custom title or a reverse-proxy page can remove a deployment from the inventory.

The query used page 1, page size 1 and sub_type=all. It did not retrieve asset records. The 36 matches are candidate services, not proof of public access, current version or configuration. Any investigation should verify the hostname and contact the owning team before probing the application.

Kasm's Developer API uses an API key and secret with HTTP Basic authentication on every request. API keys are generated under the administrative Developer settings. The documentation lists granular permissions for operations including user sessions, settings, images and zones. It also notes that performing actions as another user requires two specific permissions. That combination matters because an integration key can become a powerful impersonation mechanism if it is broader than its business purpose.

Inventory keys by integration and permission. Identify whether a key can create sessions as another user, modify authentication settings, manage images or view zones. Separate read-only monitoring keys from administrative automation. Store the secret outside source code and rotate it when an integration is retired. The secret is displayed at creation and should not be copied into a browser, notebook or public CI log.

Zones can separate deployment trust boundaries, but the separation must be configured and verified. Review which zones hold workspaces for different tenants or security enclaves and which API keys can view or change zone settings. A user who can select a workspace image must not automatically be able to run that image on a host with broader network access. Test the routing and network policy from the workspace itself, not only from the Kasm web UI.

Session actions are a separate authority path. The API can create, inspect and act on sessions. Review whether a compromised integration key can terminate another user's session, start a new session with a sensitive image or access a session URL. Log key identity with each action and alert on changes to developers, API permissions and zone assignments.

If external identity is used, the identity provider authenticates the user, while Kasm groups and image permissions determine what that user can launch. A valid directory account should not imply access to every workspace. Test group removal and session revocation with a non-admin account. Review whether a fallback local administrator remains enabled and whether its emergency use is monitored.

The title-only count is small enough to compare with internal deployment records one by one. Map each external hostname to a zone, owner, image catalog, identity provider and API-key inventory. If a host is a test system, document its expiration and network restriction. If it is production, verify that the public login page does not expose an administrative path or a development image.

Kasm is a control plane for remote execution. The distinction between a user session and an API key is important, but both can cross into the same workspace infrastructure. Treat the Developer API as privileged infrastructure and use the search result to find deployments, not to infer their security posture.

References

  • Kasm Workspaces Developer API
  • Kasm deployment zones
  • ZoomEye Kasm Workspaces title query

title: The refresh failed. Why did the whole screen disappear?
description:
You open an app to check your orders. The list loads, so you pull down to see if there are any updates.

The refresh fails. The list disappears, and the app shows a full-screen error.

I find this frustrating. The app had a useful list a moment ago. Why take it away just because the latest request failed?

A failed refresh tells us that the app couldn’t get an update. It doesn’t mean the information already on screen has stopped being useful.

Keep the list on screen

If the user already has a list in front of them, I think the app should usually keep it there while it tries to refresh. If the request fails, leave the list in place and say what happened:

Couldn’t refresh. Showing your last saved orders.

That gives the user something to work with. They can check the existing list or try again. If the app knows when it last updated the list, it can show that too.

There are limits, of course. An old list of articles is different from an old bank balance or an appointment slot that someone else may have booked. If the age of the data matters, make that clear. And before an action that depends on current information, check again.

Keeping old data visible should not mean pretending it is current.

A refresh error is different from an empty screen

It helps to keep the data and the refresh status separate in the screen state. For example:

data class OrdersUiState(
    val orders: List<Order> = emptyList(),
    val isRefreshing: Boolean = false,
    val refreshError: Boolean = false
)

When a refresh fails, the app can set refreshError and leave orders alone.

This is only a small example. An empty list could mean the user has no orders, or it could mean the app has never loaded them. If the screen needs to show those cases differently, it needs to track that too.

What if the user closes the app?

A list held in memory may be available while the app stays open. Once the app is stopped and reopened, it may be gone.

If it makes sense to save the information on the device, the app can read it from local storage and update it when a fresh response arrives. Android’s offline-first guidance explains this approach and the need to account for data that may be out of date.

Not every screen needs a full offline-first design. But every screen that fetches data should have a considered answer for a failed request.

Try this with one of your own screens: load it successfully, turn off the connection and refresh. Then close and reopen the app and try again.

What can the user still see?
