title: Hand Tracking vs Controllers in VR: How to Choose
description:
The short answer

Choose controllers when your app needs precision, speed, buttons or haptic feedback: action games, shooters, sports and tools. Choose hand tracking when ease of use matters more than precision: training, onboarding, casual experiences, mixed reality and public demos. If you can, support both through one input layer and let the user pick.

Side by side

Controllers Hand tracking
Learning curve Buttons must be learned Almost none
Tracking reliability Very high, including out of view on some systems Good in view, lost when hands are hidden or out of camera range
Precision High, steady pointing Moderate, some jitter
Speed Handles fast swings and punches Very fast motion can break tracking
Buttons and sticks Yes No. Everything is a gesture
Haptic feedback Yes None
Finger expression Limited to sensors Full fingers, natural gestures
Fatigue Arms can rest, small movements work Arms raised more often
Setup Charge, pair, hold Nothing to hold
Accessibility Needs grip and button presses Helps some users, excludes others with limited hand mobility

Where controllers win

  • Action and shooters. A trigger pull is immediate and certain. Pinching to fire is neither.
  • Locomotion. Thumbsticks are the standard for smooth movement and turning. Gesture-based movement exists but tires users.
  • Fast physical games. Rhythm, boxing and racket games move hands faster than cameras track reliably. See VR fitness app development.
  • Feedback. Vibration confirms a hit, a grab or a surface. Without it, players rely on sight and sound alone.
  • Hands out of view. Reaching behind the back or to the hip works better with tracked controllers.

Where hands win

  • First-time users. People understand reaching and touching at once. This matters in training rollouts where every minute of instruction is multiplied by hundreds of employees. See VR employee onboarding.
  • Training real hand skills. Procedures that depend on finger positions feel closer to reality with bare hands, as in VR healthcare training.
  • Mixed reality. When users see their real room, they also expect to use their real hands, and may need them free to handle real objects. See mixed reality app development.
  • Public spaces. Kiosks, museums and trade shows avoid lost, flat or unhygienic controllers.
  • Social presence. Real finger movement makes avatars far more expressive.
  • Productivity and media. Browsing, watching and light interaction do not justify picking up hardware.

Some platforms are built around this. Apple Vision Pro uses eyes and hands as its primary input, as we describe in Apple Vision Pro development, and Android XR headsets also treat hands as a first-class input.

Design rules for hand tracking

  1. Use a small set of gestures. Pinch to select, poke to press, grab to hold. Invented gestures are hard to remember and trigger by accident.
  2. Make targets large. Buttons should be bigger and further apart than on a controller-driven interface.
  3. Direct touch up close, ray and pinch at distance. Do not force users to stretch.
  4. Replace haptics with sight and sound. Buttons should depress visibly, highlight on approach and click audibly.
  5. Stop hands passing through objects where possible, or show clearly when they do.
  6. Design for tracking loss. When a hand disappears, hold the last state briefly and recover gracefully.
  7. Keep interactions low and close. Arms held high tire within minutes, an effect often called gorilla arm.
  8. Avoid system gestures. Platforms reserve some gestures, such as a palm pinch for the menu.
  9. Test in different lighting. Dim rooms and strong sunlight both reduce tracking quality.

Design rules for controllers

  1. Follow platform conventions for grab, trigger and menu buttons.
  2. Show a short tutorial with the controller model highlighted.
  3. Offer left-handed and one-handed modes.
  4. Use haptics sparingly and meaningfully.
  5. Provide comfort options for movement and turning. See VR comfort and motion sickness.

Supporting both

Most apps benefit from supporting both, because headsets switch between them automatically when the user puts controllers down.

  • Build on OpenXR, the cross-vendor standard, so the same code reaches multiple headsets.
  • Write an input abstraction layer: the app asks for select, grab and point, and each input method supplies them.
  • Design interface layouts that work for both, sized for the less precise method.
  • Decide what happens to features that have no hand equivalent, such as thumbstick movement. Teleport by pinch is the usual substitute.
  • Test every flow with each method. Supporting both doubles interaction testing, which should be in the budget.

For performance-critical games, it is reasonable to require controllers and say so on the store page.

Cost implications

Hand tracking itself is provided by the platform, so it adds no licence cost. It adds design and testing time: gestures, feedback, larger interfaces and edge cases. As a rough guide, supporting both methods well adds 10 to 20 percent to interaction work. General budgets are in VR development cost.

What is coming

Tracking keeps improving, wrist-worn input devices are appearing alongside smart glasses, and eye tracking combined with a pinch is becoming a common pointing method. Building on an abstraction layer today makes adopting these later much cheaper. See smart glasses app development.

Getting started

List the ten most frequent actions in your app and ask which input each needs. That list usually answers the question. We prototype interactions on Quest with both methods at fixed prices on the VR offer page.

Sources: Khronos Group: OpenXR · Meta Horizon developer documentation · Apple: visionOS. Checked November 11, 2026.

Related: VR game development · VR and AR packages · Get a quote

Originally published on A Plus Games Studio, a game, AR and VR development studio in Sacramento, CA.

title: Taming a 14.6 GB RAM Cliff and 4 GB GPU VRAM Limits in a Local-First AI Desktop App (Tauri v2 + Node.js + PyTorch)
description:
Whenever I tried using cloud LLMs to get through 500-page technical textbooks or multi-thousand-chapter web serials, I ran into the same two failure modes:

  1. Lossy summarization flattens nuance: Standard AI summaries strip out equations, drop edge cases, and hallucinate connective tissue.
  2. Zero source traceability: When a summary makes a surprising claim, there is no deterministic link back to the exact paragraph in the original PDF or EPUB.

Over the past 9 months, I built Omnitome—an open-source (AGPL-3.0), local-first Windows desktop application that performs loss-bounded semantic compression (with a documented target of ~7:1) where every synthesized sentence carries a clickable citation back to the immutable source paragraph.

🎥 3-Minute Architecture & UI Walkthrough: https://youtu.be/Nmb-qiZpnrk

Here is how the multi-process architecture works under the hood, and the four hardest systems bugs I had to solve to make the entire pipeline run offline on a 4 GB NVIDIA RTX 3050 laptop GPU.

1. Multi-Process Isolation & The Sole SQLite Writer Law

Packaging a modern React UI, an asynchronous orchestration layer, and heavy CUDA PyTorch models into a single desktop app without freezing the UI required strict process boundaries:

  • Tauri v2 Desktop Shell (Rust): Native window supervision, OS lifecycle management, and child process teardown.
  • Node.js 22 LTS Orchestrator (better-sqlite3): Pipeline coordinator and sole writer to data.db in SQLite WAL mode.
  • Python FastAPI Sidecar (PyTorch FP16 CUDA): Runs BGE-M3 (1024-dim embeddings), BGE Reranker v2, and Kokoro-82M neural TTS.

Why Node.js Is the Sole SQLite Writer

While SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode supports concurrent readers, allowing Rust, Node.js, and Python processes to write directly to data.db triggers SQLITE_BUSY lock contention during heavy ingestion. In Omnitome, Python sidecars and the React frontend have zero direct database write access—every mutation flows strictly through Node.js REST boundaries.

2. Crushing the 14.6 GB Node.js RAM Cliff (F65 Sequential Await Barrier)

In early builds, ingesting a 10-book, ~508,000-word multi-format test corpus caused Node.js heap memory to spike to 14.6 GB, crashing consumer laptops.

  • Root Cause: Unbounded Promise.all concurrency queued hundreds of document chunks, embedding payloads, and DOM parsing buffers in memory simultaneously while waiting on the GPU sidecar.
  • The Fix (F65 Sequential Await Barrier): I refactored the 5-stage ingestion pipeline (Parse -> Vectorize -> Classify -> Plan -> Compress & Attribute) behind a strict chunk-by-chunk asynchronous await gate with explicit buffer release.
  • Verified Result: Peak Node.js RSS dropped by 98%—from 14.6 GB down to 296 MB—processing all 508,000 words in 5.9 minutes.

3. Running 3 Neural Models on a 4 GB GPU (LifecycleManager VRAM Eviction)

Omnitome's local neural stack runs three models:

  • BGE-M3 (FP16): ~2.1 GB VRAM
  • BGE Reranker v2: ~2.2 GB VRAM
  • Kokoro-82M Neural TTS: ~0.6 GB VRAM

Keeping all three resident requires ~4.9 GB of VRAM, immediately crashing a 4 GB RTX 3050 laptop GPU.

To solve this without tearing down the Python sidecar process between tasks, I implemented an asynchronous LifecycleManager state machine (UNLOADED -> READY -> EVICTED) with a sliding-window TTL governor:

  • Models load in FP16 precision on demand.
  • When a stage completes or sits idle past its TTL window, the governor evicts the model weights and flushes the CUDA cache, reclaiming 3.2 GB of VRAM.

4. Calibrating BGE-M3 Retrieval & Fixing the CJK Token Explosion

  • CLS Pooling Calibration: Switching BGE-M3 vector extraction to calibrated CLS pooling improved our retrieval-separation metric 1.68x (from 0.2520 to 0.4225) across our 19-suite regression harness.
  • CJK Multilingual Token Safety: When testing unspaced Japanese texts, naive whitespace word counters treated entire paragraphs as a single "word," bypassing chunk guards and causing context-window overflows. Adding script-aware regex weighting (~0.7 words per CJK glyph) and sentence-boundary splitting (。！？\n) eliminated the overflow completely.

Try Omnitome v1.1.1 (Open Source)

Omnitome v1.1.1 is live today as a single 1.95 GB Windows x64 installer (bundling the Python + CUDA runtime so no local Python setup is needed):

  • 📂 GitHub Repository & Installer: https://github.com/ayumu-ml/Omnitome
  • 🚀 Product Hunt Launch Page: https://www.producthunt.com/products/omnitome
  • 🎬 3:44 Video Walkthrough: https://youtu.be/Nmb-qiZpnrk

If you're building local-first AI tools with Tauri, Rust, or PyTorch on constrained hardware, I'd love to hear how you handle sidecar supervision and VRAM residency!

title: Java Virtual Threads: Solving the Thread-per-Request Problem
description:
Introduction

For years, Java developers have relied on the traditional thread-per-request model to build scalable backend applications.

Every incoming HTTP request gets assigned a thread. That thread handles the request, executes business logic, communicates with databases, calls downstream services, and finally sends the response.

This model works well for many applications.

But what happens when your application receives thousands of concurrent requests?

Traditional platform threads are relatively expensive resources. Creating and managing thousands of threads consumes memory, increases context switching, and can eventually limit application scalability.

This is where Java Virtual Threads, introduced as a preview feature in Java 19 and finalized in Java 21 (JEP 444), change the game.

Virtual Threads allow Java applications to handle large numbers of concurrent tasks with significantly lower thread-management overhead.

Let's understand how they work and why they matter for modern microservices.

1. The Problem with Traditional Platform Threads

Traditionally, Java applications use platform threads.

A platform thread is backed by an operating-system thread.

Consider a Spring Boot REST API handling customer account requests.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/accounts")
public class AccountController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Account getAccount(@PathVariable Long id) {

        return accountService.getAccount(id);
    }
}

Under a traditional thread-per-request model:

  1. A request arrives.
  2. The server assigns a platform thread.
  3. The thread executes business logic.
  4. It queries the database.
  5. It waits for the database response.
  6. It returns the response.

The biggest problem is that the thread may spend most of its time waiting for I/O operations.

For example:

  • Database queries
  • REST API calls
  • Kafka-related blocking operations
  • External payment gateway calls
  • File operations

While waiting, the platform thread remains occupied.

What happens under high concurrency?

Imagine:

  • 10,000 concurrent HTTP requests.
  • Each request takes 500 ms.
  • 400 ms is spent waiting for external I/O.
  • 100 ms is spent executing business logic.

A large number of platform threads may remain occupied while waiting for I/O.

Increasing the thread pool size is not an unlimited solution.

It introduces additional overhead:

  • Higher memory consumption.
  • More operating-system thread scheduling.
  • Increased context switching.
  • Thread pool saturation.
  • Reduced application throughput under heavy load.

The real challenge is not necessarily CPU processing.

It is managing concurrency efficiently when requests spend significant time waiting.

2. What Are Java Virtual Threads?

Virtual Threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than being directly mapped one-to-one to operating-system threads.

They were finalized in Java 21 through JEP 444.

Unlike platform threads, millions of virtual threads can potentially be created without requiring millions of operating-system threads.

The JVM schedules virtual threads onto a smaller number of platform threads called carrier threads.

Think of it this way:

  • Virtual Thread: Represents an application task.
  • Carrier Thread: Platform thread that executes a virtual thread.
  • JVM Scheduler: Coordinates scheduling of virtual threads.

When a virtual thread performs a supported blocking operation, it can be suspended, allowing its carrier thread to execute another virtual thread.

When the operation completes, the suspended virtual thread becomes eligible to resume.

This makes blocking-style code much more scalable for I/O-intensive workloads.

3. Platform Threads vs Virtual Threads

Feature Platform Threads Virtual Threads
Managed by OS/JVM JVM
OS thread mapping Typically 1:1 M:N scheduling
Creation cost Relatively high Very low
Memory overhead Higher Much lower
Large concurrency Resource-intensive More efficient
Best suited for CPU-intensive tasks I/O-intensive tasks
Programming model Blocking or asynchronous Blocking-style code

Important: Virtual Threads do not make CPU-intensive operations faster. They primarily improve scalability when many tasks spend time waiting.

4. Creating Virtual Threads in Java 21

Java 21 provides simple APIs for creating virtual threads.

Approach 1: Thread.ofVirtual() 

public class VirtualThreadExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        Thread thread = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {

            System.out.println(
                "Running on: " +
                Thread.currentThread()
            );

        });

        thread.join();
    }
}

Approach 2: Thread.startVirtualThread() 

public class VirtualThreadExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> {

            System.out.println(
                "Hello from Virtual Thread"
            );

        });
    }
}

Approach 3: Virtual Thread Executor

For application-level task execution, Java provides a dedicated executor.

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class VirtualThreadExecutorExample {

    public static void main(String[] args)
            throws Exception {

        try (ExecutorService executor =
                 Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

            for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {

                executor.submit(() -> {

                    System.out.println(
                        Thread.currentThread()
                    );

                });
            }
        }
    }
}

Each submitted task gets its own virtual thread.

Unlike a fixed-size thread pool, this executor is designed around creating a new virtual thread per task.

5. How Virtual Threads Work Internally

Understanding the internal architecture is important for experienced Java developers.

Virtual Threads use a scheduling mechanism involving carrier threads.

Consider this execution flow:

  1. A virtual thread is created.
  2. The JVM schedules it onto a carrier platform thread.
  3. The virtual thread starts executing application code.
  4. It reaches a supported blocking I/O operation.
  5. The virtual thread is suspended.
  6. The carrier thread becomes available for another virtual thread.
  7. Once the I/O operation completes, the virtual thread becomes runnable again.
  8. The scheduler assigns it to a carrier thread to continue execution.

This process is called unmounting and mounting.

  • Mounting: A virtual thread runs on a carrier thread.
  • Unmounting: A virtual thread temporarily releases its carrier thread.

This is one of the fundamental mechanisms that makes virtual threads efficient.

Important internal concepts

Carrier Threads

These are ordinary platform threads that execute virtual threads.

Continuation

A continuation represents the execution state of a virtual thread, allowing it to suspend and resume.

ForkJoinPool Scheduler

The default virtual thread scheduler uses a ForkJoinPool implementation to schedule virtual threads onto carrier threads.

6. Using Virtual Threads in Spring Boot 3.2+

Spring Boot 3.2 introduced built-in support for virtual threads.

With Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.2+, enabling virtual threads is straightforward.

Add the following configuration to application.properties:

spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true

That's it!

Spring Boot can configure supported task execution and scheduling infrastructure to use virtual threads.

For Spring MVC applications using embedded Tomcat or Jetty, supported request-processing infrastructure can also use virtual threads.

Example: Spring Boot REST Controller 

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/payments")
public class PaymentController {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    public PaymentController(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<String> processPayment(
            @RequestBody PaymentRequest request) {

        paymentService.processPayment(request);

        return ResponseEntity.ok(
            "Payment processed successfully"
        );
    }
}

The controller can continue using a familiar synchronous programming model.

Virtual threads help the application manage concurrent blocking requests more efficiently.

Note: Enabling virtual threads does not automatically make every component of an application virtual-thread-aware. Verify the behavior of your server, task executors, libraries, and integrations.

7. Real-World Fintech Example: Payment Processing

Consider a banking application processing payment requests.

A single payment request may involve:

  1. Customer authentication.
  2. Account balance validation.
  3. Fraud detection service invocation.
  4. Database transaction.
  5. External payment gateway integration.
  6. Transaction status update.
  7. Response generation.

Several operations involve waiting for external systems.

Traditional platform thread model 

Incoming Payment Request
          |
          v
   Platform Thread
          |
          v
   Account Validation
          |
          v
   Fraud Detection API
          |
          v
   Database Operation
          |
          v
   Payment Gateway
          |
          v
   Response

During blocking operations, the platform thread may remain occupied.

Virtual thread model 

Incoming Payment Request
          |
          v
    Virtual Thread
          |
          v
   Account Validation
          |
          v
   Fraud Detection API
          |
          | Waiting
          v
   Virtual Thread Suspended
          |
     Carrier Released
          |
          v
   I/O Operation Completes
          |
          v
   Virtual Thread Resumes
          |
          v
   Database + Payment Gateway
          |
          v
       Response

The application can support more concurrent requests without requiring a corresponding number of platform threads.

However, database connection pools, payment gateway rate limits, and downstream service capacity still impose limits.

Virtual Threads improve concurrency management, not the capacity of external dependencies.

8. Virtual Threads vs CompletableFuture vs Reactive Programming

This is a common interview discussion.

Feature Virtual Threads CompletableFuture Reactive Programming
Programming style Synchronous Asynchronous Non-blocking reactive
Code readability Simple Can become complex Requires reactive concepts
Blocking operations Supported Depends on execution strategy Generally avoided
Thread management JVM-managed Executor-managed Event-loop based
Best use case Blocking I/O workloads Async task composition End-to-end non-blocking systems

When should you choose Virtual Threads?

Choose virtual threads when:

  • Your application uses blocking JDBC.
  • You have many synchronous REST API calls.
  • Your existing codebase uses imperative Spring MVC.
  • You want to improve concurrency without rewriting everything into reactive programming.

When should you consider Reactive Programming?

Consider reactive programming when:

  • You need end-to-end non-blocking I/O.
  • You are using reactive database drivers.
  • You have complex streaming pipelines.
  • Backpressure is an important requirement.

Virtual Threads and Reactive Programming solve related but different problems.

They are not direct replacements for every other concurrency model.

9. Important Limitations and Best Practices

Virtual Threads are powerful, but they are not a magic solution.

1. CPU-intensive workloads

Virtual Threads do not increase CPU capacity.

If your application performs heavy encryption, image processing, or complex calculations, CPU cores remain the primary limitation.

2. Database Connection Pool Limits

Suppose your application creates 10,000 virtual threads but has only 50 database connections.

Only 50 operations can actively use those connections at a time.

The remaining operations may wait for connection availability.

Tune database connection pools according to database capacity and workload.

3. Avoid Thread Pooling Virtual Threads

Virtual Threads are designed to be created per task.

Avoid treating them like scarce platform threads that need to be reused in a fixed-size pool.

4. Avoid Excessive ThreadLocal Usage

Virtual Threads support ThreadLocal variables, but creating millions of virtual threads with large ThreadLocal values can increase memory consumption.

Review existing ThreadLocal usage before migration.

5. Understand Pinning

Pinning happens when a virtual thread cannot unmount from its carrier thread during certain operations.

In Java 21, synchronized blocks and methods can cause pinning when a virtual thread blocks while holding a monitor.

Native or foreign function calls can also pin virtual threads.

Review long-running blocking operations inside synchronized sections.

Do not blindly replace every synchronized block with another synchronization mechanism.

6. Virtual Threads Do Not Replace Rate Limiting

If a downstream payment gateway supports only 500 concurrent requests, creating 10,000 virtual threads will not increase its capacity.

Use:

  • Rate limiting.
  • Bulkheads.
  • Timeouts.
  • Connection pooling.
  • Circuit breakers.

Concurrency management must still respect downstream system limits.

10. Monitoring Virtual Threads in Production

Before introducing virtual threads into production, monitor the application carefully.

Important metrics include:

  • Active virtual thread count.
  • Request throughput.
  • API response time (P95/P99).
  • Database connection pool utilization.
  • CPU utilization.
  • Heap memory consumption.
  • GC frequency and pause times.
  • Downstream API latency.
  • Thread pinning events.

Useful tools:

  • Java Flight Recorder (JFR).
  • Java Mission Control (JMC).
  • Thread dumps.
  • Spring Boot Actuator.
  • Micrometer and Prometheus.
  • Grafana.

For Java 21, JFR includes virtual-thread-related events that help investigate pinning and scheduling behavior.

11. When Should Enterprises Adopt Virtual Threads?

For enterprise Java applications, virtual threads are particularly useful when workloads are I/O-bound and use a blocking programming model.

Examples include:

  • Banking transaction APIs.
  • Payment processing systems.
  • Customer account services.
  • Loan processing applications.
  • Insurance policy services.
  • Enterprise integration services.

Before migration, evaluate:

  1. Current thread pool saturation.
  2. Request concurrency.
  3. Blocking I/O patterns.
  4. Database connection pool limits.
  5. Downstream API capacity.
  6. Performance under realistic load.

Run controlled load tests comparing platform threads and virtual threads.

Measure throughput, latency, memory consumption, and resource utilization rather than assuming virtual threads will always improve performance.

Conclusion

Java Virtual Threads represent one of the most significant improvements to Java concurrency in recent years.

They make it possible to write simple, blocking-style code while efficiently managing large numbers of concurrent tasks.

For organizations running Spring Boot microservices, virtual threads provide an opportunity to improve concurrency without completely redesigning existing applications around asynchronous or reactive programming.

But remember:

Virtual Threads improve scalability for I/O-bound workloads. They do not eliminate resource limits, replace proper system design, or make CPU-intensive operations faster.

As Java developers and architects, understanding when and where to use virtual threads is becoming an important skill in designing scalable enterprise applications.

References

  • JEP 444 – Virtual Threads
  • Java 21 Documentation
  • Spring Boot Virtual Threads Documentation

What about your applications?

Are you planning to adopt Java Virtual Threads in your Spring Boot microservices, or are you still using traditional thread pools and CompletableFuture?

Share your experience in the comments!

title: China-Nexus Actors Deploy Cairn in AI-Driven Attacks on 10 Organizations
description:
Originally published on satyamrastogi.com

China-linked threat actors leveraged the Cairn autonomous attack platform to breach 10 organizations spanning advanced manufacturing, defense, and human rights sectors. Analysis reveals AI-driven reconnaissance and exploitation techniques.

Executive Summary

China-nexus threat actors have demonstrated sustained operational capability by conducting coordinated attacks against 10 organizations using the Cairn autonomous attack framework. The campaign targeted critical infrastructure operators in advanced manufacturing and defense sectors, alongside civil and human rights organizations. This represents a significant escalation in adversary sophistication-the integration of autonomous AI-driven exploitation with traditional APT tradecraft signals a shift in attack velocity and target breadth.

Cairn, previously observed in campaigns attributed to Chinese state-sponsored groups, functions as an autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation platform. Its redeployment across diverse vertical sectors suggests threat actors are optimizing for operational efficiency while maintaining attribution flexibility through shared tooling.

Attack Vector Analysis

The Cairn framework operationalizes several MITRE ATT&CK techniques within an autonomous execution model:

Reconnaissance (T1592, T1595)

  • Automated network scanning and asset discovery
  • Passive information gathering from public sources (LinkedIn, GitHub, job postings)
  • SSL certificate enumeration and domain registration tracking

Vulnerability Assessment (T1046)

  • Autonomous port scanning and service enumeration
  • Known vulnerability mapping against exposed assets
  • Zero-day candidate identification through signature-less detection

Initial Access (T1190, T1200)

  • Exploitation of unpatched internet-facing applications
  • Supply chain compromise vectors targeting integrators
  • VPN and remote access solution targeting (Palo Alto, Fortinet, Citrix derivatives)

Persistence & Execution (T1547, T1059)

  • Scheduled task creation and registry modifications
  • PowerShell/Bash command execution via compromised credentials
  • Webshell deployment for sustained access

Technical Deep Dive

Cairn Architecture

Cairn operates as a distributed autonomous framework with these operational components:

  1. Sensor Layer: Passive reconnaissance module that continuously scans target environments. Fingerprints technologies (web servers, databases, IoT devices) and maps network topology without triggering WAF/IDS signatures.

  2. Analysis Engine: ML-driven vulnerability correlation linking CVE databases, exploit-db repositories, and zero-day threat intelligence feeds. The system prioritizes high-impact entry points (edge devices with low patch velocity).

  3. Exploitation Module: Autonomous payload generation and delivery. Notably, Cairn adapts shellcode and obfuscation techniques based on detected defensive postures (endpoint protection, behavioral analysis). This adaptive capability reduces alert fatigue and extends dwell time.

  4. Post-Exploitation Handler: Automated lateral movement, credential harvesting, and data exfiltration staging. Prioritizes lateral paths toward defense/manufacturing environments (OT networks) where visibility gaps are endemic.

Targeting Pattern Intelligence

The 10 compromised organizations span three distinct victim profiles:

  • Advanced Manufacturing (3 orgs): Semiconductor suppliers, aerospace component manufacturers. High interest in CAD/design intellectual property and supply chain documentation.
  • Defense Industrial Base (4 orgs): Primes and tier-1 contractors. Focus on weapons system specifications, logistics networks, and procurement data.
  • Civil/Human Rights Organizations (3 orgs): NGOs and advocacy groups. Likely collection targets for counter-intelligence, donor networks, and operational security patterns of foreign nationals.

This mixing of industrial espionage with political intelligence suggests compartmentalized tasking-separate operational branches within Chinese state apparatus coordinating through shared Cairn infrastructure.

Evasion Techniques

  • Living-off-the-Land Binaries: Exploitation chains favor native OS tools (certutil, bitsadmin, reg.exe) to minimize malware signatures.
  • C2 Obfuscation: DNS tunneling through legitimate CDNs (Cloudflare, Akamai) to blend exfiltration traffic with legitimate business activity.
  • Fileless Execution: Registry-stored PowerShell scripts and in-memory .NET assemblies bypass disk-based detection.
  • Timing Jitter: Autonomous framework implements random dwell periods between reconnaissance phases to evade behavioral baselining.

Detection Strategy

Network Layer

  • Monitor for anomalous outbound connections to known malicious ASNs (BGP hijacking infrastructure)
  • Establish baseline for external scanning activity; flag port sweeps targeting non-standard services (3389, 5985, 22)
  • Implement DNS sinkholing for known Cairn C2 domains (coordinate with CISA threat feeds)

Endpoint Layer

  • Alert on suspicious PowerShell execution with encoded payloads (Base64 strings > 1KB)
  • Track process creation chains: explorer.exe → cmd.exe → powershell.exe (high-confidence indicator)
  • Monitor scheduled task creation with SYSTEM privileges and randomized names
  • File integrity monitoring on web directories and config files (aspx, php, jsp uploads)

Behavioral Analytics

  • Correlate rapid privilege escalation attempts with subsequent file access patterns
  • Flag lateral movement spikes: failed authentication followed by successful SMB/WinRM within 60 seconds
  • Detect data staging: large volumes written to temp directories then exfiltrated

SIEM Rules

  • Event ID 4688 (Process Execution) with parent process spoofing
  • Event ID 7045 (Service Installation) with binary paths in %temp% or %appdata%
  • Event ID 5156 (Windows Filtering Platform) connections to private IP ranges from edge systems

Mitigation Framework

Immediate Actions (0-7 days)

  • Asset inventory for all internet-facing systems; prioritize patch gaps in Palo Alto, Fortinet, Citrix, Microsoft Exchange
  • MFA enforcement for all remote access solutions (VPN, RDP, SSH)
  • EDR deployment on critical assets if not present; ensure real-time threat intelligence integration
  • Egress filtering rules: block outbound DNS queries to non-approved resolvers

Short-term Controls (1-4 weeks)

  • Network segmentation: OT/manufacturing environments isolated from corporate IT via air-gapped DMZ
  • Credential rotation for service accounts and local admin passwords (avoid AD reuse patterns)
  • Threat-hunt for Cairn IOCs: file hashes, C2 domains, process signatures (coordinate with CISA/FBI)
  • Implement YARA rules for webshell detection across web-accessible directories

Strategic Hardening (1-3 months)

  • Zero-trust architecture: micro-segmentation based on asset sensitivity (CAD systems, finance databases)
  • Adversary emulation: hire red team to simulate Cairn attack chain against your infrastructure
  • Supply chain risk assessment: audit integrators, MSPs, and contractors for Cairn compromise
  • Threat intelligence sharing with ISACs (manufacturing ISAC, defense ISAC)

Key Takeaways

  1. Autonomous attack frameworks are operational reality-not theoretical. Organizations must assume adversaries have deployed self-learning exploitation platforms. Traditional perimeter defense is insufficient.

  2. Attribution complexity increases with shared tooling-Cairn's reuse across political and economic espionage missions creates false attribution trails. Focus on behavioral patterns and victimology rather than tool provenance.

  3. Defense industrial base faces compounded risk-the mixing of supply chain targeting (semiconductor, aerospace) with direct defense prime attacks suggests adversaries are building knowledge graphs of your end-to-end ecosystem.

  4. Dwell time remains adversary advantage-Cairn's adaptive evasion techniques enable 6-12 month undetected periods. Assume breach and implement assumption-of-compromise hunting protocols.

  5. Civil society targeting signals escalation-inclusion of NGOs in campaign scope indicates geopolitical competition leveraging cyber as espionage tool. Monitor your organization's digital footprint for reconnaissance indicators.

Related Articles

  • Red Team vs Blue Team vs Purple Team: Complete Cybersecurity Guide
  • FBI Warns ARTEX AI Hacking Tool Fueling Global Cyberattacks
  • AI-Powered Ransomware: Volume Up, Payments Down
  • Penetration Testing Cost in India 2026 - Complete Price Guide

CISA References: Review CISA APT Advisories and NSA Cybersecurity Advisories for official IOC lists and mitigation guidance.

title: How to Test AI Responses Against Changing Customer Context
description:
Imagine your AI customer-support application generates this response:

Your refund has been completed.

Your evaluator checks the response and returns pass.

That sounds good. But there is one important question:

What was the verified refund status when the response was evaluated?

If the status was completed, the response is supported.

If the status was processing, the response is incorrect.

The generated sentence is identical. The evidence is different.

This is a testing problem that becomes important when AI applications generate responses using customer records, transaction data, order histories, or other changing application state.

An evaluator should not approve a response simply because it sounds reasonable. It needs to check whether the claims in that response agree with the relevant verified information.

In this article, I'll walk through a practical regression-testing approach I use in my AI Customer Support Response Evaluator.

1. Start with a realistic failure scenario

Suppose an application provides an AI assistant with the following verified customer information:

const customerContext = {
  refund_status: "processing"
};

The assistant generates:

Your refund has been completed.

A response-quality evaluator might recognize this as a clear and professional answer.

But a reliable factual evaluator needs to check the actual claim.

The response says the refund is completed. The verified context says it is still processing.

Those two pieces of information contradict each other.

The expected result should therefore be:

fail

Now change only the verified status:

const customerContext = {
  refund_status: "completed"
};

Keep the generated response exactly the same.

The expected result becomes:

pass

This gives us a useful testing principle:

Hold the response constant and change the verified context. The evaluator's verdict should change when the evidence changes.

I use the term context-contrastive testing to describe this practical test-design approach.

2. Build a contrastive regression test matrix

Before writing tests, define the expected behavior.

For the refund example, the test matrix looks like this:

Response claim Verified status Expected result
Refund completed processing Fail
Refund completed completed Pass
Refund failed processing Fail
Refund failed failed Pass

This matrix covers four relationships:

  • A claim contradicted by the verified status.
  • A claim supported by the verified status.
  • Another contradicted claim.
  • Another supported claim.

Why test both directions?

Because an evaluator that rejects every response is not reliable. Neither is one that approves every response.

We need to establish that its decisions follow the evidence.

3. Turn the scenarios into regression tests

The following is an illustrative JavaScript example of how a test matrix could be structured. It demonstrates the test-design pattern, not the exact implementation or API of my evaluator.

const cases = [
  {
    response: "Your refund has been completed.",
    refundStatus: "processing",
    expected: "fail"
  },
  {
    response: "Your refund has been completed.",
    refundStatus: "completed",
    expected: "pass"
  },
  {
    response: "Your refund has failed.",
    refundStatus: "processing",
    expected: "fail"
  },
  {
    response: "Your refund has failed.",
    refundStatus: "failed",
    expected: "pass"
  }
];

describe("refund claim evaluation", () => {
  test.each(cases)(
    "returns $expected for refund status $refundStatus",
    async ({ response, refundStatus, expected }) => {
      const result = await evaluateSupportResponse({
        response,
        context: {
          refund_status: refundStatus
        }
      });

      expect(result.verdict).toBe(expected);
    }
  );
});

The important part is the structure:

  1. Define the response.
  2. Supply the verified context.
  3. Define the expected verdict.
  4. Run the evaluator.
  5. Assert that the actual verdict matches the expected one.

The function name and result shape above are illustrative. In a real project, use the evaluator's actual interface and verdict schema.

4. What I implemented in my evaluator

This testing approach is already part of my AI Customer Support Response Evaluator.

I implemented four separate regression scenarios covering the refund-state relationships in the test matrix.

The tests check that:

  • A completion claim fails when the verified status is processing.
  • The same completion claim passes when the status is completed.
  • A failure claim fails when the status is processing.
  • The failure claim passes when the status is failed.

These tests are useful because they check more than whether the evaluator recognizes particular words.

They check whether the evaluator distinguishes between a claim and the verified state that supports or contradicts it.

They also give the project a concrete regression boundary: changes to evaluation logic should not silently break these expected decisions.

5. Expand beyond supported and contradicted claims

The four scenarios provide a foundation, but real applications have more complicated contexts.

I would extend this test strategy in three directions.

Test irrelevant context changes

Suppose the customer's preferred communication channel changes, but the refund status remains completed.

That unrelated change should not alter whether a refund-completion claim is supported.

This checks whether the evaluator is relying on relevant evidence rather than arbitrary context.

Test missing evidence

What happens when the refund status is unavailable?

The evaluator should not confidently approve the completion claim without evidence.

An unknown or equivalent outcome can be more appropriate than forcing an unsupported decision into pass or fail.

Missing evidence does not automatically prove that a claim is false.

Test conflicting evidence

Imagine a customer record contains multiple refund events or conflicting transaction information.

Which record should the evaluator use?

A reliable system needs a defensible way to identify the relevant transaction and handle ambiguity. It should not silently choose whichever record makes the generated response appear correct.

These are additional test dimensions to develop and verify. They are not claims about what the four existing refund regression tests already cover.

6. Apply the same method to other AI workflows

The pattern is not limited to refund support.

Application AI-generated claim Context to verify
Delivery support "Your order has been delivered." Verified delivery status
Payments "Your payment was successful." Transaction status
Subscriptions "Your subscription has been cancelled." Subscription state
Account support "Your account is verified." Verification record
Booking systems "Your appointment is confirmed." Booking status

For each workflow, identify the claims an AI assistant can make, the authoritative source of truth, and the context changes that should alter the expected verdict.

Then design tests around those relationships.

7. A checklist for context-aware AI evaluation

Before trusting an evaluator in a real application, ask:

  • Does it check claims against verified application data?
  • Can the same response pass in one context and fail in another?
  • Does irrelevant context leave the verdict unchanged?
  • Does it handle missing evidence without inventing certainty?
  • Can it distinguish conflicting records?
  • Are these behaviors protected by regression tests?

These questions help make evaluation more concrete and testable.

They also encourage a shift away from measuring only how good an AI response sounds.

Final takeaway

A successful AI response is not necessarily a correct AI response.

For context-aware applications, the evaluator must establish whether the generated claims are supported by the information the application has actually verified.

In my AI Customer Support Response Evaluator, testing the same refund claim against different verified refund states gave me a practical way to check this behavior.

The engineering principle is worth carrying into other AI applications:

Don't just test whether an AI response can pass. Test whether it knows when that same response should fail.

Further reading

  • Gardner et al., Evaluating Models' Local Decision Boundaries via Contrast Sets
  • OpenAI: Evaluation Best Practices

Context-contrastive testing is the practical term used here for holding a generated response constant while varying the verified application context. The four refund-state scenarios described are implemented regression tests in my AI Customer Support Response Evaluator.

title: Our logs put one order's email failure under another order's number because a pooled thread remembered it
description:
Our order service puts the order number into every log line through the logging context, the MDC, so that one search shows everything that happened to an order. A servlet filter puts the number in when a request arrives and clears it when the response goes out. On the request thread that works perfectly.

In September we moved label printing and customer emails off the request path into a Spring thread pool, so checkout would not wait for them. Two weeks later a customer complained that her confirmation email had never arrived. Support searched for her order number and found the checkout and nothing after it. Searching for email errors in that minute found a failure logged against a different order, belonging to a customer who had received his email without any trouble.

Logback keeps the MDC in a ThreadLocal. It belongs to the thread that set it, and a pool thread does not inherit it from the thread that submitted the work. So the async tasks started with an empty context and their lines carried no order number at all. That alone would have been merely unhelpful. The worse part came from the label task, which put the order number into the MDC itself and never removed it. Pool threads are reused, so the next email task on that thread logged under whatever order the last label had left behind. Some lines had no order number, some had the wrong one, and nothing in the line told you which.

For two weeks every search by order number had silently missed the async half of an order's life, and now and then shown someone else's.

The executor now has a TaskDecorator that copies the submitting thread's MDC into the task and clears it in a finally block when the task ends, whatever happened inside. Tasks may no longer call MDC.put themselves, and an architecture test in the build enforces that. Every log line also carries the thread name, and a dashboard counts log lines without an order number by logger, a number that should be zero outside startup.

A context that lives on a thread is only as accurate as the last piece of code that ran there.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Floci: llevar la nube al entorno local sin perder el control arquitectónico
description:
Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.

Un desarrollador necesita validar un cambio en un servicio que guarda archivos en S3 y publica eventos en SQS. La aplicación levanta en su máquina, pero probarla de verdad requiere credenciales de una cuenta de desarrollo, permisos que gestiona otro equipo, una VPN y un ambiente de integración compartido que a esa hora usan otras tres personas. Cada uno de esos pasos agrega espera y variabilidad a un ciclo que debería durar segundos. Este artículo analiza Floci, un ecosistema open source de emuladores cloud locales, a partir de una tesis: la velocidad del feedback es una propiedad del diseño de la plataforma, no un esfuerzo individual de cada desarrollador. Las capacidades que se mencionan son las declaradas en los repositorios oficiales al 15 de noviembre de 2026; las conclusiones son propias y se señalan como tales.

La dependencia invisible de la nube

En un equipo que desarrolla aplicaciones cloud-native, levantar el servicio en local no equivale a poder probarlo. El código arranca, pero cada llamada a almacenamiento, colas, secretos o identidad sale de la máquina hacia una cuenta remota. Esa dependencia rara vez aparece en los diagramas de arquitectura y, sin embargo, determina buena parte de la experiencia de desarrollo.

Sus efectos se acumulan en cuatro lugares. En el onboarding, porque una persona nueva no puede ejecutar las pruebas de integración hasta tener acceso a la cuenta correcta. En el debugging, porque reproducir un error que depende del estado de un ambiente compartido es difícil y a veces imposible. En el testing, porque las pruebas que tocan servicios reales son lentas, costosas o inestables, y terminan desactivándose. Y en la autonomía, porque cada ajuste de permisos o de infraestructura de desarrollo pasa por la cola de otro equipo.

Desde Platform Engineering, el problema no es que los desarrolladores tengan que esperar, sino que la plataforma convierte esa espera en el camino por defecto. Si la forma más fácil de probar un cambio es abrir un pull request y esperar al pipeline, el ciclo de feedback se mide en decenas de minutos aunque el cambio sea trivial. El principio de que el camino correcto debe ser el más fácil aplica también acá: probar contra dependencias realistas debería ser más fácil que no probar.

Qué es Floci

Floci es una familia de emuladores open source, publicados bajo licencia MIT, que exponen APIs con la forma de los servicios de cuatro nubes en un entorno local. El repositorio principal, floci, emula AWS en el puerto 4566. Lo acompañan floci-az para Azure (puerto 4577), floci-gcp para GCP (4588) y floci-oci para Oracle Cloud (4599). Alrededor de ellos hay una CLI (floci-cli), una consola web (floci-ui) que muestra solo lo que devuelven los emuladores, y módulos de Testcontainers para Java, Node.js, Python, .NET y Go.

Emular una API cloud significa implementar el protocolo de red del servicio, de modo que un cliente estándar, como el AWS SDK, la CLI o Terraform, funcione sin cambios salvo la URL de destino. Conviene distinguirlo de otras tres opciones. Un mock reemplaza al cliente dentro del proceso de pruebas y verifica que se lo llamó, pero no ejecuta el protocolo. Un contenedor con la tecnología real, como PostgreSQL detrás de una API con forma de RDS, ejecuta el motor auténtico pero no la capa administrada del proveedor. La infraestructura de producción es la única que reproduce el comportamiento completo, con sus permisos, cuotas y fallas. Floci combina las dos primeras: emula en proceso la mayoría de las APIs y delega en contenedores reales los servicios donde la fidelidad depende del motor.

Arquitectura: cómo funciona por dentro

Según el README y el código del repositorio, el emulador de AWS es una aplicación Java construida con Quarkus (versión 3.40.1.1 al momento de esta revisión) y compilada a Java 25, que se distribuye como imagen nativa de GraalVM y como binario independiente. Un enrutador HTTP basado en JAX-RS y Vert.x recibe todas las peticiones en un único puerto y las dirige al servicio correspondiente según el protocolo de AWS de cada llamada.

Los servicios se dividen en tres grupos. La mayoría, como SQS, SNS, IAM, KMS, Secrets Manager o Step Functions, se emulan en proceso. S3 y DynamoDB también corren en proceso, pero con estado persistible. Un tercer grupo, que incluye Lambda, RDS, ElastiCache, MSK, ECS, EKS y OpenSearch, levanta contenedores Docker reales a través del socket del host: RDS usa postgres:16-alpine o mysql:8.0, MSK usa Redpanda y EKS usa k3s. Athena ejecuta SQL real mediante un sidecar basado en DuckDB.

Arquitectura del emulador de AWS, según la documentación del repositorio: el diagrama se puede ver en el artículo original.

El estado se configura con FLOCI_STORAGE_MODE: memory para pruebas efímeras, persistent con escritura inmediata a disco, hybrid con volcados asíncronos cada cinco segundos y wal con un registro previo a cada respuesta. El emulador también aísla recursos por cuenta: si la access key tiene doce dígitos, se usa como ID de cuenta, lo que permite probar flujos entre cuentas en local.

Los trade-offs del enfoque

  • Un proceso para muchos servicios simplifica la configuración, pero concentra el riesgo: un defecto en el enrutamiento afecta a todos los servicios a la vez.
  • La emulación en proceso es rápida y liviana, pero su fidelidad depende de cuánto del comportamiento real se haya reimplementado. Los contenedores reales mejoran la fidelidad del motor a cambio de más recursos y de requerir el socket de Docker, que otorga privilegios amplios sobre el host.
  • La imagen nativa reduce el tiempo de arranque y la memoria. El proyecto declara alrededor de 24 ms de arranque y 13 MiB de memoria en reposo, frente a 3,3 s y 143 MiB de LocalStack Community; son cifras del propio proyecto, no mediciones independientes.

Del concepto a la práctica: S3 y SQS con Spring Boot

El ejemplo implementa un caso frecuente: un servicio recibe un documento por HTTP, lo guarda en S3 y publica un evento en SQS para que otro componente lo procese de forma asíncrona. Usa Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5.16, AWS SDK for Java v2 (2.59.1), JUnit 5, Testcontainers 1.21.4 y testcontainers-floci 1.16.0, la línea compatible con Testcontainers 1.x. Para Spring Boot 4 y Testcontainers 2 corresponde la línea 2.x del módulo, cuyo artefacto es testcontainers-floci-aws.

Qué se verificó: El proyecto del ejemplo compila con esas versiones, resueltas desde Maven Central. La prueba de integración no se ejecutó en el entorno donde se escribió este artículo, porque no tenía Docker disponible; por eso no se informan resultados de ejecución.

El ejemplo en local y en pruebas: el diagrama se puede ver en el artículo original.

Dependencias

pom.xml (fragmento): el BOM del SDK y las dependencias de prueba

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.5.16</version>
</parent>

<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId>
      <artifactId>bom</artifactId>
      <version>2.59.1</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>s3</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>sqs</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>  <!-- 1.21.4, gestionada por Spring Boot -->
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.floci</groupId>
    <artifactId>testcontainers-floci</artifactId>
    <version>1.16.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Configuración: el mismo código en local y en la nube

La decisión de diseño más importante del ejemplo es que el código no sabe si habla con Floci o con AWS. La URL del emulador llega por configuración y, cuando está vacía, el SDK usa su resolución estándar de endpoints y credenciales. Así se evita mantener un perfil de código distinto para desarrollo.

application.yml

app:
  aws:
    region: ${AWS_REGION:us-east-1}
    endpoint: ${AWS_ENDPOINT_URL:}   # vacío en la nube real
    bucket: ${DOCUMENTS_BUCKET:documents}
    queue-name: ${DOCUMENTS_QUEUE:document-events}

AwsConfig.java: clientes del SDK con endpoint opcional

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.aws")
public record AwsProperties(String region, String endpoint, String bucket, String queueName) {
    boolean hasEndpointOverride() { return endpoint != null && !endpoint.isBlank(); }
}

@Configuration
@EnableConfigurationProperties(AwsProperties.class)
class AwsConfig {

    @Bean
    S3Client s3Client(AwsProperties props) {
        S3ClientBuilder builder = S3Client.builder().region(Region.of(props.region()));
        if (props.hasEndpointOverride()) {
            // Solo en local o en pruebas: emulador y URLs path-style.
            builder.endpointOverride(URI.create(props.endpoint())).forcePathStyle(true);
        }
        return builder.build();
    }

    @Bean
    SqsClient sqsClient(AwsProperties props) {
        SqsClientBuilder builder = SqsClient.builder().region(Region.of(props.region()));
        if (props.hasEndpointOverride()) {
            builder.endpointOverride(URI.create(props.endpoint()));
        }
        return builder.build();
    }
}

DocumentService.java: guardar y publicar

@Service
public class DocumentService {

    private final S3Client s3;
    private final SqsClient sqs;
    private final AwsProperties props;

    DocumentService(S3Client s3, SqsClient sqs, AwsProperties props) {
        this.s3 = s3;
        this.sqs = sqs;
        this.props = props;
    }

    public String store(byte[] content, String contentType) {
        String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        String key = "documents/" + id;

        s3.putObject(b -> b.bucket(props.bucket()).key(key).contentType(contentType),
                RequestBody.fromBytes(content));

        String queueUrl = sqs.getQueueUrl(b -> b.queueName(props.queueName())).queueUrl();
        sqs.sendMessage(b -> b.queueUrl(queueUrl).messageBody(
                "{\"documentId\":\"%s\",\"bucket\":\"%s\",\"key\":\"%s\"}"
                        .formatted(id, props.bucket(), key)));
        return id;
    }
}

El controlador que expone POST /documents solo delega en este servicio y responde 202 Accepted con el identificador. En un sistema real, el evento debería publicarse con una garantía explícita, por ejemplo mediante el patrón outbox, porque el código anterior puede guardar el archivo y fallar antes de publicar el mensaje. La emulación local no cambia esa responsabilidad de diseño.

Docker Compose para desarrollo

compose.yaml: emulador, inicialización de recursos y aplicación

services:
  floci:
    image: floci/floci:2.5.0          # versión fija para entornos reproducibles
    ports:
      - "4566:4566"
    environment:
      FLOCI_HOSTNAME: floci           # las URLs devueltas (QueueUrl) apuntan al servicio, no a localhost
      FLOCI_STORAGE_MODE: hybrid      # conserva el estado entre reinicios

  init:
    image: amazon/aws-cli:2.17.0
    depends_on: [floci]
    environment:
      AWS_ENDPOINT_URL: http://floci:4566
      AWS_REGION: us-east-1
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: test
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: test
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    command: >
      "until aws s3 ls >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done;
       aws s3 mb s3://documents || true;
       aws sqs create-queue --queue-name document-events"

  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    depends_on:
      init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    environment:
      AWS_ENDPOINT_URL: http://floci:4566
      AWS_REGION: us-east-1
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: test
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: test

El servicio init crea los recursos con la AWS CLI estándar. En un equipo que ya define su infraestructura con Terraform u OpenTofu, la alternativa más coherente es aplicar los mismos módulos contra Floci, que el proyecto declara compatible con el proveedor oficial de AWS: así el entorno local se deriva de la misma fuente que producción.

Prueba de integración automatizada

DocumentServiceIntegrationTest.java: un emulador aislado por ejecución

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class DocumentServiceIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    static FlociContainer floci = new FlociContainer("floci/floci:2.5.0")
            .withDockerSocket(false); // S3 y SQS corren en proceso: sin socket de Docker

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void awsProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("app.aws.endpoint", floci::getEndpoint);
        registry.add("app.aws.region", floci::getRegion);
        // La cadena de credenciales por defecto del SDK lee estas propiedades del sistema.
        System.setProperty("aws.accessKeyId", floci.getAccessKey());
        System.setProperty("aws.secretAccessKey", floci.getSecretKey());
    }

    @Autowired DocumentService documents;
    @Autowired S3Client s3;
    @Autowired SqsClient sqs;
    @Autowired AwsProperties props;

    @BeforeAll
    static void createResources(@Autowired S3Client s3, @Autowired SqsClient sqs,
                                @Autowired AwsProperties props) {
        s3.createBucket(b -> b.bucket(props.bucket()));
        sqs.createQueue(b -> b.queueName(props.queueName()));
    }

    @Test
    void storesTheDocumentAndPublishesAnEvent() {
        String id = documents.store("hola".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), "text/plain");

        String stored = s3.getObjectAsBytes(b -> b.bucket(props.bucket()).key("documents/" + id))
                .asUtf8String();
        assertThat(stored).isEqualTo("hola");

        String queueUrl = sqs.getQueueUrl(b -> b.queueName(props.queueName())).queueUrl();
        var messages = sqs.receiveMessage(b -> b.queueUrl(queueUrl)
                .waitTimeSeconds(2).maxNumberOfMessages(1)).messages();
        assertThat(messages).extracting(Message::body).singleElement().asString().contains(id);
    }
}

Dos detalles merecen atención. El primero es fijar la versión de la imagen: FlociContainer() sin argumentos usa floci/floci:latest, y el proyecto publica versiones estables dos veces por mes, de modo que una prueba sin versión fija puede cambiar de comportamiento sin que cambie el código. El segundo es withDockerSocket(false): el módulo monta el socket de Docker de forma automática cuando algún servicio habilitado lo necesita, y todos están habilitados por defecto. Para un servicio que solo usa S3 y SQS, desactivarlo reduce los privilegios que la prueba otorga al contenedor.

Ejecución en CI

.github/workflows/ci.yml: Testcontainers en un runner con Docker

name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
          cache: maven
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify

Los runners de GitHub Actions basados en Ubuntu incluyen Docker, por lo que Testcontainers puede crear el emulador sin pasos adicionales. Cada ejecución obtiene una instancia aislada, sin estado compartido con otras ramas ni con otras personas.

Floci como componente de una Internal Developer Platform

El valor de un emulador crece cuando deja de ser una herramienta que cada equipo configura por su cuenta y pasa a formar parte de un golden path. La experiencia deseada se puede describir en una frase: una persona crea un servicio desde una plantilla, ejecuta un comando y obtiene una aplicación funcional con sus dependencias cloud emuladas y sus pruebas de integración en verde.

Conviene separar lo que existe de lo que es una propuesta. Lo que el ecosistema ofrece hoy, según sus repositorios, incluye la CLI con comandos start, wait, env y stop pensados para CI; los módulos de Testcontainers en cinco lenguajes; compatibilidad declarada con Terraform, OpenTofu y CDK, respaldada por pruebas automatizadas en el repositorio; un chart de Helm para Kubernetes; compatibilidad con la configuración y los scripts de inicialización de LocalStack; y una skill para agentes de programación. Lo que sigue es una propuesta de arquitectura, no una integración existente.

  • Plantilla en Backstage (u otro portal interno) que genere el servicio con compose.yaml, la prueba de integración con Testcontainers y la versión de Floci fijada por la plataforma.
  • Módulos de Terraform u OpenTofu compartidos que se apliquen contra Floci en local y contra la cuenta real en los ambientes, de modo que el entorno de desarrollo y el de producción provengan de la misma definición.
  • Un workflow reutilizable de CI que ejecute las pruebas contra el emulador y deje para una etapa posterior las pruebas de humo en la nube.
  • Una versión de Floci gestionada por la plataforma, actualizada de forma deliberada y con pruebas de regresión propias, porque el ritmo de cambios del proyecto es alto.
  • Onboarding automatizado: la primera tarea de una persona nueva es ejecutar las pruebas de integración en su máquina, sin solicitar ningún acceso.

Impacto en Developer Experience

No hay datos públicos e independientes que cuantifiquen el impacto de Floci en la productividad, y este artículo no los inventa. Lo que sí puede hacerse es identificar dónde debería notarse y cómo medirlo antes y después de adoptarlo.

Dónde debería notarse el cambio y cómo medirlo

Dimensión Hipótesis Cómo medirla
Tiempo hasta el primer entorno funcional Baja, porque no requiere solicitar accesos Tiempo desde el alta hasta la primera ejecución verde de las pruebas de integración
Tiempo de feedback Baja, porque las pruebas corren en la máquina Duración de la suite de integración en local y en CI
Dependencia de ambientes compartidos Disminuye Cantidad de reservas o conflictos en el ambiente de integración
Reproducibilidad Mejora, con versiones fijas Tasa de pruebas inestables (flaky) en CI
Autonomía Aumenta Tickets a plataforma por accesos o recursos de desarrollo
Costo cloud de desarrollo y testing Puede bajar Gasto de las cuentas de desarrollo y CI, por servicio

Estas métricas se conectan con las de DORA: el tiempo de entrega de cambios incluye el tiempo que un cambio espera a ser validado, y la tasa de fallas de cambio es la contracara que hay que vigilar. Si la emulación acelera el feedback pero deja pasar más errores a producción, el resultado neto es negativo. Por eso conviene medir las dos cosas a la vez, junto con una encuesta breve de experiencia de desarrollo.

Floci frente a LocalStack y otras alternativas

La comparación más inmediata es con LocalStack, el emulador de AWS más difundido. En marzo de 2026, LocalStack anunció que su emulador pasaba a distribuirse como una imagen unificada que requiere un token de autenticación, y que ya no podía comprometerse a actualizar con regularidad la edición Community. Floci se presenta explícitamente como reemplazo directo de esa edición: usa el mismo puerto, traduce variables de entorno de LocalStack y ejecuta sus scripts de inicialización sin cambios.

Ese origen explica parte de su crecimiento, pero también obliga a leer sus comparaciones con cuidado. La tabla de su README contrasta Floci con LocalStack Community, no con las ediciones comerciales, y las cifras de arranque y memoria son del propio proyecto. Además del emulador de AWS, existen alternativas consolidadas para otros contextos.

Alternativas de emulación local, sin un ganador universal

Criterio Floci LocalStack Moto Azurite Emuladores de gcloud
Alcance AWS, Azure, GCP y OCI; más de cien servicios de AWS declarados AWS, con una larga trayectoria AWS, como biblioteca de Python o servidor Azure Storage: Blob, Queue y Table Pub/Sub, Firestore, Datastore, Bigtable, Spanner
Fidelidad Protocolo en proceso y contenedores reales para motores A evaluar por servicio Mocks del protocolo; menor fidelidad en servicios complejos Alta para el alcance que cubre Oficial, para cada servicio
Licencia MIT Imagen unificada que requiere token desde marzo de 2026 Apache 2.0 MIT Parte del SDK de Google Cloud
Integración con SDK SDK estándar con endpoint configurable SDK estándar con endpoint configurable Decoradores en Python o modo servidor Connection strings de Azure Variables de entorno del emulador
CI y Testcontainers Módulos propios en cinco lenguajes Módulo oficial de Testcontainers Sin contenedor en modo biblioteca Módulo de Testcontainers Módulos de Testcontainers para varios servicios
Madurez Proyecto de nueve meses, con ritmo de cambios muy alto Producto establecido Proyecto maduro Mantenido por Microsoft Mantenidos por Google

Los indicadores de madurez de Floci son llamativos y ambiguos a la vez. El repositorio principal se creó el 18 de febrero de 2026 y, al 15 de noviembre, tenía más de 31.000 estrellas, unos 170 contribuidores, más de 5.300 pull requests fusionados, más de 2.400 issues cerrados y alrededor de 170 abiertos, con 63 versiones publicadas y un tren de releases los días 15 y último de cada mes. El directorio de compatibilidad declara 2.576 pruebas automatizadas sobre cinco SDKs y tres herramientas de infraestructura como código. Es evidencia de actividad y de una comunidad amplia, pero un proyecto de nueve meses no tiene todavía un historial de estabilidad a largo plazo, y la cadencia de cambios exige fijar versiones.

Los límites de la emulación

La emulación local reduce dependencias, pero no reproduce la nube. Algunas diferencias son de diseño y la propia documentación las declara; otras son inherentes a cualquier emulador.

  • IAM y seguridad. Por defecto, Floci no verifica firmas SigV4 y acepta cualquier credencial no vacía. La evaluación de políticas IAM existe, pero se activa de forma explícita con FLOCI_SERVICES_IAM_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED, y la documentación recomienda dejarla desactivada en la mayoría de los escenarios locales. Una prueba verde en local no demuestra que los permisos de producción sean correctos.
  • Networking. VPC, grupos de seguridad, endpoints privados, DNS y TLS de producción no se reproducen con fidelidad. En el emulador de Azure, la mayoría de los servicios corre por HTTP plano salvo que se habilite TLS.
  • Latencia, cuotas y límites. El emulador responde en milisegundos y su catálogo de cuotas usa valores estáticos generosos. Un sistema que funciona en local puede encontrar throttling, límites de tamaño o latencias reales que cambian su comportamiento.
  • Consistencia y fallas. Las fallas parciales, los reintentos del lado del proveedor y los comportamientos de consistencia de un servicio distribuido no aparecen en un proceso local. Incluso la emulación de AWS FIS es, según su documentación, una simulación del plano de control que no inyecta fallas en otros servicios.
  • Servicios administrados y stubs. Varios servicios están implementados como stubs: Bedrock Runtime devuelve respuestas ficticias y Textract o Transcribe completan trabajos sin procesar contenido real. Sirven para probar el flujo de integración, no el resultado.
  • Performance. Ninguna medición hecha contra un emulador local es representativa del rendimiento en la nube.

Una estrategia de pruebas por capas

Qué valida cada capa y dónde conviene ejecutarla

Capa Qué valida Dónde corre
Unit tests Lógica de negocio sin dependencias externas Local y CI, en cada cambio
Integración con emulación local Uso correcto del SDK, serialización, flujos entre servicios Local y CI, en cada cambio, contra Floci
Contrato y compatibilidad Formato de eventos y APIs entre productores y consumidores CI, en cada cambio
Smoke tests en la nube real Permisos IAM, networking, configuración real Ambiente de staging, en cada despliegue
Resiliencia y performance Cuotas, latencias, comportamiento ante fallas Ambientes dedicados, de forma periódica

La emulación mueve hacia la izquierda la mayor parte de las pruebas de integración, que son las más frecuentes, y deja en la nube real las que dependen de lo que solo la nube real tiene. El error de adopción más probable no es técnico: es eliminar las pruebas en la nube porque las pruebas locales pasan.

Cloud local y desarrollo asistido por agentes

Los agentes de programación necesitan lo mismo que las personas para trabajar con autonomía: un entorno aislado, reproducible y con feedback automático. En términos de harness engineering, una suite de integración contra un emulador local es un sensor computacional: determinista, barato y ejecutable en cada cambio. En términos de Loop Engineering, es el verificador que cierra cada iteración del ciclo.

Un flujo posible: el agente recibe una especificación, implementa la funcionalidad, ejecuta las pruebas contra Floci, lee los errores, corrige el código y repite hasta que las pruebas pasan o se agota un límite de iteraciones; recién entonces propone un pull request para revisión humana. El aislamiento tiene además un beneficio de seguridad: el agente trabaja sin credenciales reales, de modo que un error no puede crear ni borrar recursos de una cuenta. La CLI de Floci incluye una skill para agentes, compatible con herramientas como Claude Code, Codex o Cursor, que les indica cómo configurar los clientes contra los emuladores en lugar de la nube real.

El límite de este ciclo: Un agente que valida contra un emulador comprueba que su código usa bien las APIs, no que el sistema funcione en la nube. Los permisos, la red, las cuotas y las fallas reales quedan fuera de su verificación, y por eso la revisión humana y las pruebas en un ambiente real siguen siendo parte del ciclo.

Conclusión: plataformas que eliminan fricción

Desde la gestión de ingeniería, la pregunta no es si Floci es mejor que otra herramienta, sino qué dependencia elimina y qué responsabilidad nueva introduce. Elimina la necesidad de una cuenta cloud y de un ambiente compartido para la mayoría de las pruebas de integración. Introduce la responsabilidad de gestionar la versión del emulador, de conocer qué servicios se emulan con fidelidad suficiente y de mantener las pruebas en la nube real donde la emulación no alcanza.

La adopción conviene hacerla de forma gradual: empezar por un servicio con dependencias simples, como S3, SQS o DynamoDB; medir el tiempo de feedback y la tasa de pruebas inestables antes y después; fijar la versión del emulador en la plataforma; y recién entonces incorporarlo a la plantilla de servicios. Si las métricas no mejoran o aparecen más fallas en producción, la decisión correcta es revisar el alcance, no extenderlo.

La lección transferible va más allá de esta herramienta. La velocidad del feedback no depende solo de la disciplina de cada equipo: es una propiedad que la plataforma habilita o impide. Una plataforma que logra que probar contra dependencias realistas sea más fácil que no probar está haciendo, en la práctica, que el camino correcto sea el más fácil.

Referencias

  • Floci. floci-io en GitHub: floci, floci-az, floci-gcp, floci-oci, floci-cli, floci-ui y testcontainers-floci. Consultados el 15 de noviembre de 2026.
  • Floci. Documentación oficial.
  • LocalStack. The Road Ahead for LocalStack.
  • Moto. Mock AWS Services.
  • Microsoft. Azurite.
  • Google Cloud. Emuladores locales de gcloud.
  • Testcontainers. Documentación para Java.
  • DORA. dora.dev.

En síntesis: Floci reduce la dependencia de cuentas y ambientes compartidos para la mayoría de las pruebas de integración, y lo hace con un enfoque que combina emulación en proceso y contenedores reales. No reemplaza la nube: IAM, networking, cuotas y fallas siguen requiriendo pruebas en un ambiente real. Su valor depende de integrarlo en la plataforma con versiones fijas, una estrategia de pruebas por capas y métricas que confirmen que el feedback más rápido no se paga con más fallas en producción.

title: I kept rebooting my machine to run local LLMs, so I built canfit
description:
The frustration

While building my previous open-source project, Knemora, I was running local LLMs on my Mac alongside Docker, a browser with too many tabs and everything else a developer keeps open. Memory kept running out.

Every time, the same question: what can I close safely, without killing something macOS needs?

The classic top shows you numbers, not answers.
It doesn't tell you whether the model you're about to load will fit, and it doesn't tell you which of those hundreds of processes are safe to close. More than once I just gave up and rebooted.

So I built the tool I wanted.

Meet canfit

canfit is the top command for people running local LLMs and apps.
It tells you if a model or an app can launch right now and, if it can't, what you can safely close to make room. System processes are never touched.

It's a single Rust binary for macOS, Windows and Linux, MIT licensed, with no telemetry: all data stays on your machine.

What it does

Can I launch it?

Point canfit at a GGUF model or an app and it checks it against the memory you have right now:

canfit model.gguf                    # can I launch this model?
canfit model.gguf --ctx 32768        # ...with a 32k context
canfit "Docker Desktop" model.gguf   # both together?

For GGUF files it reads the header (parameters, quantization, layers, tensor sizes) and estimates weights + context cache + overhead. On Apple Silicon it also checks the GPU wired limit, because the GPU can only use part of unified memory.

What should I close?

If it doesn't fit, canfit suggests the smallest set of apps to close:

canfit free model.gguf

Every process is classified as safe, caution or never. System processes are never suggested, unknown processes default to caution, and nothing is closed without your confirmation.

A friendlier top

Run canfit with no arguments and you get a live monitor that starts with a sentence instead of a table ("Memory under pressure: Chrome is using 9 GB"), with processes grouped by app.

Watch 

canfit watch -- llama-server -m model.gguf

Launch a command through canfit and it measures its real memory usage, so the next estimate is based on what actually happened.

Script-friendly

Every command supports --json, and the fit check returns an exit code (0 fits, 1 tight, 2 doesn't fit):

canfit model.gguf && llama-server -m model.gguf

Features overview

Install

canfit is available through Homebrew, Scoop, curl, PowerShell, .msi, .deb, .rpm and cargo install --git.

The exact commands for each platform are in the README:

👉 https://github.com/federicolaterra/canfit

Help me make the estimates better

This is 1.0.0, and memory estimates are the part I care about most.

And if you find it useful, a ⭐ on GitHub helps a lot.

Thanks for reading!
