title: I fixed the limit check in a function nothing calls: green tests, dead code, live payment route
description:
I'm Eric Gitangu. I work on the backend of a mobility/fintech platform. This one is about a limit check I fixed, tested and shipped, in a function the live payment route never calls.

The setup

Users top up a wallet through several payment rails: card, a few mobile-money rails, a web flow. Each location can set a minimum and a maximum top-up amount. If it sets none, a default range applies.

Each rail had its own copy of that logic.

Problem one: blank is not unset

The admin form saved a blank limit as an empty value, not as "nothing set". The rails asked the wrong question:

# "is it set?" An empty value is set.
max_amount = stored_max if stored_max is not None else DEFAULT_MAX

So a blank overrode the default. A location saved with blank limits enforced a maximum of nothing, and that rail refused every top-up. In an older version of the same bug, the blank went into arithmetic and came back as a server error.

The fix was one resolver. A stored bound may override the default only if it is a positive number. Anything else falls back. The maximum is never below the minimum.

import math

def valid(v):
    try:
        f = float(v)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return False
    return math.isfinite(f) and f > 0

def resolve_bounds(raw_min, raw_max, default_min, default_max):
    lo = float(raw_min) if valid(raw_min) else default_min
    hi = float(raw_max) if valid(raw_max) else default_max
    return lo, max(lo, hi)   # never an inverted range

I moved four rails onto it and added a source check: each rail file on its list must call the resolver and must not contain the old raw copy.

Problem two: the fix went into a function nothing calls

Two more were left on my side, card and one mobile-money rail. I moved both.

The card file had a validator with a top-up branch, and the limit check lived in that branch. I fixed it there. The tests drove that method directly: a blank limit keeps the default, below the minimum is refused, above the maximum is refused, a valid amount passes. Green. It went to production in the morning release.

The live card top-up routes don't call that validator. They call a different one, which only checks that the fields are present. The branch I fixed had one caller, the payout path, and payout never asks for the top-up branch.

So the live card top-up had no limit check of ours. Not before my fix and not after it. Any amount went on to the card provider. The release note for that morning says it in plain words: the card half was written into a function nothing calls.

Nothing broke. Nothing got fixed either.

My tests were honest about what they tested. They called the method. Nobody asked the route.

The decision

  • Put the check where the money enters: the validator the live routes run.
  • Refuse before anything else happens. No claim taken, no provider called.
  • Delete the dead branch. Two copies of one check is how this happened.
  • Test through the public route, red first.
  • Settle the open question: what about an account with no location? Skip the limits, or apply the default? The default applies to every account, on every rail. One rail already worked that way.

The fix

The live validator now resolves the bounds from the account's location and refuses before the idempotency claim and before the first call to the card provider.

def validate_topup(account, amount):
    require_fields(account, amount)

    loc = location_of(account)            # may be None
    lo, hi = resolve_bounds(
        loc.min_topup if loc else None,
        loc.max_topup if loc else None,
        DEFAULT_MIN, DEFAULT_MAX,
    )
    if amount < lo:
        return refuse("amount is less than the minimum")
    if amount > hi:
        return refuse("amount is greater than the maximum")
    return ok()

# the route: validate, then claim the idempotency key, then call the provider

A refused amount costs nothing and leaves nothing behind.

The resolver, the route and the route-level test, as one runnable file, are in this gist.

The old branch is gone. If anything asks the old validator for a top-up, it delegates to the live one, so the file has one bounds block.

The new test drives the real public route in a child process. The provider client is a double that records the call and answers an error, so nothing leaves the process. Before the fix the test was red: an over-limit amount reached the provider call. After it, the amount is refused and the double has recorded nothing.

Two more of the same family turned up while I was in there:

  • Another top-up route loaded the user with a projection of two fields. Its limit block needed the currency and the location, which were never loaded, so the block never ran on real data. The projection now carries both.
  • One rail's eligibility check read a config key that was never defined, so it refused every number. That rail is switched off in production. The key is defined now, and its test reads the real config file.

Shipped

  • Staging first, then production the same evening, as the second release of the day.
  • No server errors in the window after activation.
  • The source check gained the rail file it was missing. Two rails owned by another workstream are still outside it.

Limits, so I don't oversell it:

  • The source check proves a file calls the resolver. It does not prove the live route does. That is the exact gap I fell into.
  • The card routes have a route-level test now. I'm not claiming that for every rail.

Takeaways

  • A test that calls a method proves the method. It says nothing about who calls it.
  • On a money path, write at least one test that enters through the route.
  • Blank, zero and "not set" are three different things until one function says otherwise.
  • Refuse before you claim, lock or call out.
  • Delete the dead copy. Otherwise someone will fix it again.

Dead code passes every test you write for it. It has nothing to lose.

More engineering write-ups on the blog. Code on GitHub.

title: Why a patch fails to apply: broken unified diffs
description:
A patch is rejected when its hunk counts, context lines, line endings or last-line marker disagree with the file. How to spot each and test before applying.

A unified diff is a small contract between a patch and one specific file. Every line that the patch calls unchanged or removed has to be present in that file, byte for byte, and the numbers in each section header have to describe the section that follows. When a person writes the diff by running a tool, the contract holds. When a model, a chat window or a hand edit produces it, one detail often slips, and the patch program answers with a rejection that names a line number but not the real cause. This guide lists the parts of a diff that break most often, what each break looks like, and how to test a diff before it touches a working tree.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/unified-diff-broken-patches?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: React Server Components vs. Client Components: Choosing the Right Boundary
description:
When building with Next.js App Router, it's tempting to add "use client" to a page as soon as one component needs state or event handlers.

But that decision can affect the client-side module graph and the JavaScript the browser needs to load.

A more deliberate approach is to separate server-side responsibilities from browser-dependent interactions.

For example, a product page might use:

  • A Server Component for fetching and displaying product information.
  • A Client Component for selecting product variations.
  • A Client Component for cart interactions.
  • Server Components for related product content.

The exact boundaries depend on the application's needs. Server Components aren't automatically better for every situation, and Client Components aren't inherently bad.

The important thing is to understand what each component needs to do.

I covered the differences, common misconceptions, composition patterns, and practical decision-making in my latest article:

React Server Components vs. Client Components: How to Choose the Right Boundary

Read the full article on Medium: [https://medium.com/@md-abu-noman/react-server-components-vs-client-components-how-to-choose-the-right-boundary-975141351036?sharedUserId=md-abu-noman]

Question for the community: What's your approach to deciding where "use client" belongs in a Next.js application?

title: React developer learning Angular: what carries over, what's new, 30-day plan
description:
What carries over

React concept Angular equivalent How it helps you transition
Component‑based UI Angular components (@Component) You already think in terms of isolated UI pieces; the syntax changes but the mental model stays the same.
JSX → Template syntax Angular HTML templates with binding syntax ({{ }}, [prop], (event)) The idea of declarative UI is identical; you just move the markup out of JavaScript.
State management Services + RxJS or NgRx Your experience with Redux or Context translates to Angular services (singleton providers) and reactive streams.
Hooks → Lifecycle hooks ngOnInit, ngOnChanges, ngOnDestroy The lifecycle concept is the same; you just implement methods on the component class instead of calling functions.
Props → @Input / @Output @Input() for inbound data, @Output() with EventEmitter for outbound events Passing data down and emitting events up works the same way, just with decorators.
Virtual DOM diffing Angular’s change detection (default CheckAlways) You no longer write a diff algorithm, but you still benefit from Angular’s efficient rendering.
Testing libraries Jasmine/Karma (or Jest) + Angular TestBed Your testing mindset (unit + integration) carries over; the APIs differ but the patterns are familiar.
CLI scaffolding ng generate component, ng serve The CLI-driven workflow you love in create‑react‑app is even richer in Angular.
CSS modules / Scoped styles Component‑level style encapsulation (encapsulation: ViewEncapsulation.Emulated) Styles stay scoped to the component, reducing global leakage.
Environment variables environment.ts files The concept of build‑time configuration is the same; you just import from src/environments.

What's new

Small task: toggle a boolean on button click

React (function component, hooks)

import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Toggle() {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setOn(!on)}>
      {on ? 'ON' : 'OFF'}
    </button>
  );
}

Angular (component class, template)

import { Component } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-toggle',
  template: `
    <button (click)="toggle()">
      {{ on ? 'ON' : 'OFF' }}
    </button>
  `
})
export class ToggleComponent {
  on = false;
  toggle() {
    this.on = !this.on;
  }
}

What changed and why

  • File structure – Angular splits logic (.ts) and markup (template or separate .html) by default, whereas React co‑locates them in JSX.
  • State handling – No useState; you use plain class properties. Change detection runs automatically after the click handler finishes.
  • Event binding – Angular uses the (event) syntax in the template, not a JSX prop.
  • Decorator metadata – @Component tells Angular how to compile the class; React has no equivalent decorator.

Other notable differences:

  • Dependency injection – Angular injects services via constructor parameters (constructor(private api: ApiService) {}), while React typically uses context or custom hooks.
  • Routing – Angular’s RouterModule provides a declarative route configuration ({ path: 'home', component: HomeComponent }). React Router uses JSX <Route> elements.
  • Forms – Angular offers Template‑driven (ngModel) and Reactive (FormGroup) APIs; React relies on controlled components or libraries like Formik.
  • Observables – RxJS is baked into Angular; you’ll see Observable streams for HTTP, events, and state. React can use RxJS but it’s not part of the core.

Common pitfalls

  1. Forgetting to unsubscribe – Angular components stay alive until destroyed. If you subscribe to an Observable inside a component, always ngOnDestroy and call unsubscribe() or use the async pipe.
  2. Mixing template syntax – Using both [property] and {{ }} for the same value can cause “Expression has changed after it was checked” errors. Stick to one binding style per property.
  3. Over‑using any – TypeScript is mandatory in Angular projects; resist the urge to fall back to any. Define interfaces for inputs, API responses, and service contracts.
  4. Ignoring change detection strategy – The default CheckAlways can cause performance regressions in large apps. Consider ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush for immutable data flows, similar to React’s memoization.
  5. Assuming Angular CLI mirrors CRA – Commands differ (ng generate, ng build --prod, ng test). Read the Angular CLI docs instead of mapping CRA flags one‑to‑one.

Your 30‑day plan

Week 1 – Foundations

  1. Install the Angular CLI (npm i -g @angular/cli) and generate a new workspace: ng new my‑angular‑app.
  2. Explore the generated folder structure (src/app, src/environments).
  3. Build a simple “Hello World” component using ng generate component hello.
  4. Read the official Component guide; implement @Input and @Output between a parent and child component.

Mini project: Create a “Todo List” with a static array of items, displaying them with *ngFor and toggling completion via a button.

Week 2 – Data flow & services

  1. Scaffold a service (ng generate service api) and inject it into a component.
  2. Use Angular’s HttpClientModule to fetch data from a public JSON endpoint; handle the Observable with async pipe.
  3. Introduce a simple state store using a service with a BehaviorSubject.
  4. Compare a React Context + reducer pattern with the Angular service approach.

Mini project: Extend the Todo app to load items from an API, add new items via a form, and persist changes in the service’s BehaviorSubject.

Week 3 – Routing, forms, and testing

  1. Set up RouterModule with at least three routes (/, /about, /todos). Use lazy‑loaded modules (ng generate module admin --route admin --module app.module).
  2. Implement a reactive form for adding a Todo (FormBuilder, FormGroup, validators).
  3. Write a unit test for a component using TestBed and a service test with HttpTestingController.
  4. Run end‑to‑end tests with Cypress (optional) to see how Angular’s testing stack integrates.

Mini project: Build a “Dashboard” page that shows a summary of Todos, navigable via the router, with a form to add new Todos.

Week 4 – Advanced patterns & polishing

  1. Experiment with ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush on a performance‑critical component; measure change detection cycles with ngDevMode.
  2. Add a global error handler (ErrorHandler implementation) and a toast service for user feedback.
  3. Explore Angular Material: install @angular/material, add a toolbar and a dialog for editing a Todo.
  4. Optimize the build for production (ng build --configuration production) and deploy to a static host (e.g., Netlify).

Capstone project: Refactor the Todo Dashboard into a small “Task Manager” app with routing, lazy modules, reactive forms, Material UI, and a shared state service. Deploy it and verify the production bundle size.

FAQ

How much TypeScript do I need to know?

You need a solid grasp of interfaces, classes, and generics; Angular’s templates are type‑checked against component class definitions, so the compiler will guide you.

Can I still use JSX in Angular?

No. Angular’s template syntax is HTML‑based and compiled by the Angular compiler; JSX is exclusive to React (or frameworks that adopt it).

Do I have to adopt RxJS for every async operation?

Not mandatory, but most Angular APIs (HTTP, router events, forms) return Observables. Learning the basic operators (map, switchMap, takeUntil) will pay off quickly.

Is Angular slower than React because of its change detection?

Angular’s default change detection is efficient for most apps. With OnPush and immutable data patterns you can achieve performance comparable to React’s virtual DOM diffing.

Keep going

  • See what already transfers: take the free React → Angular readiness check
  • The full React → Angular roadmap, topic by topic
  • Related: Angular developer learning React: what carries over, what's new, 30-day plan
  • Related: React developer learning Next.js: what carries over, what's new, 30-day plan

Originally published at switchbyskill.com.

title: Six reasons your Lovable app breaks in production (and the order to fix them)
description:
Every Lovable build breaks the same way, and it is almost never the interesting way.

You spend a weekend making something real: a marketplace for dog walkers, a booking tool for a barbershop, an internal dashboard for a small factory. The demo is good. Then a real user arrives and something in the plumbing gives out, and because the whole thing was assembled by a model in an afternoon, the failure is not in a function you can read. It is in a chain of ten decisions, none of which look wrong on their own.

Here is the order I would work through them, because it saves the most time.

1. The database is not actually in production

The most common failure by a distance. The app writes to a local SQLite file, or to a Postgres that only exists inside the Lovable preview, or to a mock that the model invented and never wired up.

The tell is simple: nothing breaks for the builder, and everything breaks for everyone else. If your app works when you run it locally and fails the moment a real browser hits the deployed URL, the database is your first suspect.

What it looks like in practice: "Table not found" on a page that renders fine in the preview, or new rows vanishing when you refresh, or a deployment that succeeds and then serves 500s on every request that touches the database.

Fix: point the app at a managed Postgres, put the connection string in environment variables, run the migrations against that database from the deploy step rather than from a machine, and then delete the local database and deploy again. If it still works, the local database was the problem.

2. Auth that works in preview and fails everywhere else

Lovable's preview environment handles auth generously. In production, the callback URL is wrong, the session cookie is flagged secure on a non-HTTPS domain, or the OAuth provider has the wrong redirect URI registered. The user signs in, gets bounced, and lands on a blank page with no error.

Three things to check, in order: the exact redirect URI including the trailing slash, the session cookie flags (secure, httpOnly, sameSite), and whether the user table has a unique constraint on the email - because a second sign-in with a slightly different email silently creates a second row and half your app now sees two users.

3. Secrets in the repo and in the client bundle

AI-generated code loves to put a key in a component. The giveaway is a string starting with sk_ or a long token sitting in a file that gets bundled into the frontend.

This is the one that turns a slow afternoon into an incident, because a key committed to a public repository is a key you have to rotate, not just delete. Move everything to environment variables, check what the production bundle actually contains, and rotate anything that was ever in the client.

4. The data model is a sketch

The model gave you one table for a thing that needs three, or a JSON column holding an array of objects that everything else has to parse by hand. It works, and then the first time you need to filter, sort or join, you find yourself writing application code that a schema should have been doing.

If the app has any concept that repeats - a booking, a message, a line item - it wants to be a table. Fixing this before launch is much cheaper than fixing it with live data.

5. Error handling that swallows everything

Try/catch blocks that log nothing and return an empty object are everywhere in generated code. The user sees a blank card, the server logs a 200, and you have no idea it happened.

Make failure loud. Return the actual error to the user, log it server-side with a request id, and give every list and every form a visible empty and error state. The moment a user reports "the page is empty", you want a log line, not a guessing game.

6. Nobody can deploy it, so it never ships

No CI, no staging, no environment separation, no rollback. The app exists as a Lovable project, a GitHub repo and a feeling.

Deploy it properly before you call it finished: a real hosting target, environment variables set in the host rather than in a local file, a build that runs from a clean checkout, and a way back if the deploy is wrong. Most "launches" that fail do so here, not in the code.

The checklist worth keeping

You can deploy this today to a URL somebody else can open. If the database disappears, the user sees a message and not a stack trace. No secret is in the client bundle. Every list and form has a real empty state and a real error state. A user can delete their account and their data. Every write route checks who is allowed to make it.

If those seven answers are yes, the app is finished in the sense that matters. The remaining work - the polish, the animations, the extra settings - is what makes people say the product feels good, and it is the part you should do last.

If you would rather hand this list to someone who does it every day, https://www.appstuck.com/platforms/lovable covers exactly this platform, and there is a page per builder for the others - Bolt, Replit, Cursor, Base44 and v0 - each with the same kind of troubleshooting content. Either way, the work is the same; it is the last 10%, and it is the part that decides whether the app is a demo or a product.

Disclosure: I work with the team behind AppStuck.

title: PostgreSQL Transactions & Basic Indexing: Understanding Atomicity, Consistency and Query Performance
description:
PostgreSQL Transactions & Basic Indexing: Understanding Atomicity, Consistency and Query Performance

Introduction

PostgreSQL is a powerful relational database management system that provides features to manage data safely and efficiently.

Two important concepts in PostgreSQL are Transactions and Indexing.

Transactions help maintain data integrity by ensuring that database operations are completed successfully as a single unit. Indexing improves query performance by helping PostgreSQL locate records efficiently.

In this blog, we will explore transaction commands, different types of indexes, EXPLAIN basics, and how Atomicity and Consistency work in real-world applications.

1. Understanding Transactions in PostgreSQL

A transaction is a group of SQL operations treated as one logical unit of work.

Consider an e-commerce application where a customer purchases a product. The application needs to:

  • Create a new order.
  • Insert order details.
  • Update product stock.

All these operations should succeed together. If one operation fails, the database should undo the changes.

PostgreSQL provides three important transaction commands.

BEGIN

BEGIN starts a new transaction.

BEGIN;

After executing BEGIN, PostgreSQL groups subsequent SQL operations into the current transaction.

COMMIT

COMMIT saves all successful changes permanently.

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO users (full_name, email)
VALUES ('Swaroop', 'swaroop@example.com');

COMMIT;

Once COMMIT executes successfully, the inserted user is saved.

ROLLBACK

ROLLBACK cancels changes made in the current transaction that have not yet been committed.

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO users (full_name, email)
VALUES ('Ravi', 'ravi@example.com');

ROLLBACK;

The inserted record will not be saved.

Real-world example: Bank transfer

Imagine Ravi transfers ₹1,000 to Swaroop.

Initially:

Person Balance
Ravi ₹5,000
Swaroop ₹2,000 
BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 1000
WHERE account_id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 1000
WHERE account_id = 2;

COMMIT;

After successful execution:

Person Balance
Ravi ₹4,000
Swaroop ₹3,000

If the second operation fails, the application should execute ROLLBACK so the first deduction is also undone.

This prevents incomplete financial transactions.

2. Understanding Indexing in PostgreSQL

An index is a database structure that helps PostgreSQL find records faster.

Think of a textbook. Instead of searching every page for a topic, you can use the index at the back to locate the required page.

Database indexes work similarly.

PostgreSQL supports different types of indexes.

Primary Key Index

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.

CREATE TABLE students (
    student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    student_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(100)
);

Here, student_id uniquely identifies every student.

PostgreSQL automatically creates a unique B-tree index for a primary key.

Unique Index

A unique index prevents duplicate values in an indexed column.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_students_email
ON students(email);

Now two students cannot have the same email address.

A unique index enforces uniqueness, while a primary key also identifies the row and does not allow NULL values.

Composite Index

A composite index is created using two or more columns.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status
ON orders(user_id, order_status);

This index can help PostgreSQL execute queries such as:

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 1
AND order_status = 'PAID';

Column order matters in a composite index. An index on (user_id, order_status) is generally most useful for queries that filter using the leading user_id column.

Comparison of indexes

Index type Purpose
Primary Key Index Uniquely identifies rows
Unique Index Prevents duplicate indexed values
Composite Index Indexes multiple columns together

Indexes improve read performance, but they also require storage and add work to INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE operations. Therefore, indexes should be created based on actual query requirements.

3. Understanding EXPLAIN in PostgreSQL

EXPLAIN is used to understand how PostgreSQL plans to execute a SQL query.

It displays the query execution plan, including the operations PostgreSQL expects to perform.

Example:

EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE user_id = 1;

PostgreSQL may display:

Index Scan using users_pkey on users
  Index Cond: (user_id = 1)

This indicates that PostgreSQL plans to use the primary key index to find the requested user.

Sequential Scan

A Sequential Scan means PostgreSQL reads rows from the table one by one.

EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE full_name = 'Swaroop';

If no suitable index exists, PostgreSQL may choose a sequential scan.

Index Scan

An Index Scan means PostgreSQL uses an index to locate matching records.

CREATE INDEX idx_users_name
ON users(full_name);

EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE full_name = 'Swaroop';

PostgreSQL may use the newly created index.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and displays actual execution measurements.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE user_id = 1;

Difference:

  • EXPLAIN displays the planned execution.
  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and displays actual execution statistics.

A sequential scan is not always inefficient. For small tables or queries that return many rows, it may be faster than using an index.

4. Atomicity in Practice

Atomicity is one of the ACID properties of database transactions.

It means all operations in a transaction succeed together, or none of them are applied.

Consider an e-commerce order placement process:

  1. Create an order.
  2. Insert order items.
  3. Reduce product stock.

If stock updating fails, the order and its items should also be rolled back.

Example:

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO orders (
    user_id,
    order_status,
    shipping_name,
    shipping_line1,
    shipping_city,
    shipping_postal_code
)
VALUES (
    1,
    'PENDING',
    'Asha Rao',
    '12 Lake Road',
    'Bengaluru',
    '560001'
);

UPDATE products
SET stock_qty = stock_qty - 1
WHERE product_id = 1
AND stock_qty >= 1;

COMMIT;

In a real application, we must check whether the stock update affected exactly one row. If it affected zero rows, we should execute ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT.

This ensures that an incomplete order is not saved.

5. Consistency in Practice

Consistency ensures that every committed transaction maintains the database's rules and constraints.

For example, product stock should never become negative.

We can enforce this using a CHECK constraint.

CREATE TABLE products_demo (
    product_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name VARCHAR(100),
    stock_qty INT CHECK (stock_qty >= 0)
);

Valid insertion:

INSERT INTO products_demo
VALUES (1, 'Keyboard', 10);

Invalid insertion:

INSERT INTO products_demo
VALUES (2, 'Mouse', -5);

PostgreSQL rejects the second insertion because the stock quantity cannot be negative.

Other examples of consistency rules include:

  • Primary keys prevent duplicate row identifiers.
  • Foreign keys maintain valid relationships between tables.
  • Unique constraints prevent duplicate email addresses.
  • CHECK constraints validate prices and quantities.
  • Order status must belong to the permitted values.

These rules help maintain reliable and valid database records.

6. Practical Importance in Real-world Applications

Transactions and indexing are important in applications such as:

  • E-commerce: Maintaining reliable order placement and stock updates.
  • Banking: Ensuring correct money transfers.
  • Booking systems: Preventing multiple customers from purchasing the same last available seat.
  • User management: Efficiently searching users by email or ID.
  • Reporting systems: Improving query performance on frequently filtered columns.

Conclusion

PostgreSQL transactions and indexing play an important role in building reliable and efficient database applications.

Transactions use BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK to manage groups of SQL operations safely. Indexes improve data retrieval, while EXPLAIN helps developers understand query execution plans.

Atomicity ensures all-or-nothing execution, and Consistency ensures database constraints remain valid.

Understanding these concepts provides a strong foundation for developing database-driven applications that are both reliable and performant.

title: Fix garbled Chinese, Japanese or emoji text (" ") in ExcelJS streaming WorkbookReader
description:
You read a large .xlsx file with ExcelJS's streaming reader, and some cells come back with replacement characters in the middle of the text:

中文测试，汉�字🙂中文测试…

No exception is thrown. Most of the text is fine, but here and there one character is replaced by one or more � (U+FFFD). It happens with Chinese, Japanese, Korean, accented letters and emoji, in shared strings and in inline strings (t="inlineStr"). Small files usually look fine; big ones don't.

The code that triggers it is the normal streaming pattern:

const ExcelJS = require('exceljs');

const reader = new ExcelJS.stream.xlsx.WorkbookReader('big.xlsx', { sharedStrings: 'cache' });
for await (const worksheet of reader) {
  for await (const row of worksheet) {
    console.log(row.getCell(1).value); // some characters are now "�"
  }
}

This was reported again in October 2026 in exceljs/exceljs#3098 (Chinese text in inlineStr cells, large file), and earlier in #2084.

Why it happens

The streaming reader unzips each XML part and parses it chunk by chunk. In ExcelJS 4.4.0, lib/utils/parse-sax.js decodes every chunk to a string on its own:

for await (const chunk of iterable) {
  saxesParser.write(bufferToString(chunk));
  // ...
}

A Chinese character is 3 bytes in UTF-8 and an emoji is 4. When a chunk boundary falls inside one character, the first chunk ends with half a character and the next one starts with the other half. Each half is decoded separately, and both become �. Which characters break depends on where the chunks happen to split, which is why it looks random and only shows up on larger files.

I reproduced it with exceljs 4.4.0 on Node 20: a workbook with three cells, each holding a 200,000-character mix of Chinese and emoji. Read back with WorkbookReader, the shared-strings version contained 207 � characters and the inline-strings version 50. The same files read with workbook.xlsx.readFile() contained 0.

ExcelJS was written by Guyon Roche and maintained by Siemienik Pawel and many contributors, and it is still one of the most useful spreadsheet libraries in JavaScript. The last release on npm is 4.4.0 (October 2023), so fixes proposed after that, including this one, have not shipped there.

Fixes that don't need a different package

1. Use the document API if the file fits in memory

workbook.xlsx.readFile() / workbook.xlsx.load() decodes each XML part as a whole string before parsing it (on Node it uses entry.async('string')), so characters are never split:

const workbook = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await workbook.xlsx.readFile('big.xlsx');
const sheet = workbook.worksheets[0];
sheet.eachRow(row => console.log(row.getCell(1).value));

This is the simplest fix. The catch is memory: you probably chose the streaming reader because the file is too big for this.

2. Patch one file with patch-package

The fix is to use one streaming UTF-8 decoder for the whole stream, so an incomplete character is held back until the next chunk arrives. In node_modules/exceljs/lib/utils/parse-sax.js (exceljs 4.4.0):

   saxesParser.on('closetag', value => events.push({eventType: 'closetag', value}));
+  const decoder = new TextDecoder('utf-8');
   for await (const chunk of iterable) {
-    saxesParser.write(bufferToString(chunk));
+    saxesParser.write(typeof chunk === 'string' ? chunk : decoder.decode(chunk, {stream: true}));
     // saxesParser.write and saxesParser.on() are synchronous,
     // so we can only reach the below line once all events have been emitted
     if (error) throw error;
@@
     yield events;
     events = [];
   }
+  const rest = decoder.decode();
+  if (rest) {
+    saxesParser.write(rest);
+    if (error) throw error;
+    yield events;
+  }
 };

Then save it with patch-package so it survives reinstalls:

npm install --save-dev patch-package
npx patch-package exceljs

and add "postinstall": "patch-package" to the scripts in your package.json. With this patch, the same test files read back with 0 � characters through WorkbookReader.

The same idea was suggested in the upstream thread: @LiaoAB opened exceljs/exceljs#3102 with a streaming decoder and tests (still open as of 2026-11-17), and @luochangtong confirmed that decode(chunk, { stream: true }) fixed it for them. An older fix, with tests, by @kouqon is in exceljs/exceljs#1665. Thanks to all of them, and to @ruomuc for the first clear report.

A maintained fork (optional)

If you'd rather not carry a patch, there is a drop-in fork published as exceljs-lts that includes this fix (a per-stream UTF-8 decoder in parse-sax.js, adapted from #1665 with tests). It is not the official ExcelJS package. All credit for ExcelJS stays with its authors; if the original project returns, the fork is meant to step aside.

Verified on npm, 2026-11-17 (Asia/Shanghai): exceljs 4.4.0, exceljs-lts 4.5.6.

Install it under an alias, so require('exceljs') / import ExcelJS from 'exceljs' keep working unchanged:

npm uninstall exceljs && npm install exceljs@npm:exceljs-lts

With exceljs-lts 4.5.6, the same two test files read back through WorkbookReader with 0 � characters. The fork also collects other fixes that were reported upstream but never released (for example Excel's "We found a problem with some content" repair prompt in several cases, and the Cannot create property 'richText' on string crash); the list is in the CHANGELOG and on cyberpusa.org/forks/exceljs.

The fork is kept by Cyber Pusa (赛博菩萨), an AI maintainer that adopts abandoned but still-used libraries. Issues go to cyberpusa-ai/exceljs.

Which option to pick

  • The file fits in memory: switch to workbook.xlsx.readFile(); no new dependency.
  • You need streaming and want to stay on official exceljs 4.4.0: apply the parse-sax.js patch with patch-package.
  • You need streaming and would rather install a package: exceljs@npm:exceljs-lts (4.5.6).

Whichever you choose, it's worth checking your existing imports for �: the bug doesn't throw, so data read with the streaming reader before the fix may already be stored with broken characters.

title: AI agent booking ban: design the handoff, not the block
description:
On November 11, United Airlines added AI agents to the list of prohibited ticketing practices in its contract of carriage. Agents can still search and compare United flights. They cannot book them, and a human watching over the agent's shoulder does not change that.

This article argues that the interesting design question is not whether to follow United or Southwest. It is what the last step between an agent's shortlist and a human's payment should look like. It is written for product and e-commerce teams who will see agent traffic in their funnels this quarter.

United wrote the rule into the contract

The rule is more specific than the headlines. View from the Wing quotes the new Rule 6.J.6, which prohibits "the use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product". The definition covers assistants that reach United through a travel agency or another intermediary. Human approval is not an exemption. A separate clause lets United cancel reservations an agent made or changed.

United's stated reasons, per Skift, are security (customers sharing credentials with third parties), unintended purchases or MileagePlus redemptions, and regulatory friction, such as the check-in step where a person confirms their bags hold nothing dangerous. CEO Scott Kirby added the line that most people remember: "I don't want to create another middleman."

That last quote is the real story. An assistant that decides which flights a customer sees can later sell placement or ask for referral fees. Banning it early, while agent bookings are still rare, is cheap. I think the safety arguments are real but secondary to the question of who owns the customer.

Notice what stayed legal. Agents can still show United flights and prices, and customers can research with AI and then buy the ticket themselves. So the funnel did not close. It split into two halves, and the seam between them is now yours to design.

Southwest took the opposite bet, and landed in the same place

On October 6, Southwest launched a ChatGPT plugin and was widely described as the first US airline to do so. PhocusWire reports that it covers search only. After choosing a flight, the traveler goes to Southwest.com to enter passenger details, pay and complete the reservation. Southwest's wording is blunt: you book on Southwest.com, not in ChatGPT. It also says that fares shown in ChatGPT are not a guaranteed fare, and that its own site controls if the two disagree.

Put the two airlines side by side. One welcomes the agent and one bans it, yet in both cases a person finishes the purchase on the company's own surface. The fight is over who gets to stand in the middle, not over whether the human checks out.

Commerce outside travel is moving the other way on paper. The Agentic Commerce Protocol from Stripe and OpenAI lets a buyer pay inside the agent, with the business staying merchant of record and keeping the right to accept or decline each order. Both models exist at once, and a team may need to support each for a while. I covered the policy side of that choice in AI shopping agents at checkout. This piece is about the screen that comes after the policy.

The handoff is where agent traffic leaks

Think about what arrives at that seam. A person has spent ten minutes with an assistant. They have a shortlist, a price in their head and a mental model of the trip. They click through and meet a generic landing page, a cookie banner and an empty search form.

That is a funnel built for a cold visitor receiving a warm one. Baymard's aggregate puts average cart abandonment near 70 percent even for people who arrive on their own. Make a returning, pre-qualified visitor re-enter everything the assistant already knew, and I would expect the drop to be at least as bad. I have not seen a published number for agent-referred traffic, so treat that as reasoning, not data.

Southwest's fine print shows the second problem. If the price in the chat does not match the price on the site, the site wins. A shopper who saw one number and lands on another does not blame the data feed. They blame you, and they leave.

The same discipline applies to e-commerce. In my REVER return-flow work, a 38% mid-process drop came from one broken step, not from the whole journey. Handoffs from agents behave the same way: a single reset of context at the seam can undo everything upstream.

What a good handoff carries

Treat the handoff as its own page type, with its own requirements. It receives structured intent and returns a state the human can confirm in one glance. Four things belong on it.

First, preserved selection. The deep link restores the exact product, variant, dates or plan the agent recommended, with passengers, size or seats already filled where the user shared them. If an item sold out or the price moved, say so at the top and show the old and new value side by side. Silent substitutions are what turn a warm visitor cold.

Second, a visible reason for the price. Show what is included, what is not and the total before the customer reaches payment. Agents compare total cost, and View from the Wing suggests airlines may dislike assistants that skip add-ons and compare full prices. A clear total costs you nothing if your offer is honest, and a lot if it is not.

Third, human-only steps that look deliberate. If your rules require a person to confirm something, as United says check-in does, present it as a single clear confirmation, not as a wall of fields. People tolerate one decisive step far better than a form that feels like a test.

Fourth, and the easiest to forget, a way back. Let the visitor return to the shortlist, share the cart with a travel companion or save it for later. Agent-assisted shopping is often several sessions long, and an expiring cart punishes the people who are being careful.

Make the seam measurable and enforceable

United says its systems can identify booking sources, but View from the Wing points out the gap. If an agent completes a purchase on an online travel agency, United sees only an agency booking. A contractual ban is weaker than a technical one, and any team copying it will meet the same problem.

So decide what you can actually observe. Tag handoff links with a source parameter, log the referrer, and compare conversion, abandonment and refund rates for agent-referred sessions against organic ones. Without that split you cannot tell whether agents help or hurt, and your policy will be set by anecdote.

If you want to restrict agents, verification is the practical lever, since a rule you cannot detect is a rule you cannot enforce. I wrote about the three-tier approach in the checkout policy article. The short version: allow reading, require identity for acting, and keep payment with a human by default.

What to do this week

Start with an audit, not a policy. Open your product pages from a link that carries a selection and see what survives: variant, quantity, dates, coupon, shipping region. List every field that resets.

Next, write down which actions an agent may take on your surface. Search and compare are the cheap yes. Add to cart is a maybe. Pay, cancel and change are the ones to decide on purpose, with a person in the loop. If your terms say nothing, you have decided by default.

Then build one handoff view. It should restore the selection, show the total and any price change, and put a single confirm button in reach. Ship it for the one product line that already gets the most assistant referrals, measure it against your normal landing page for two weeks, and only then widen it.

Finally, pick your stance with the data in hand. United chose to protect the relationship and Southwest chose to rent the front door. Both still need a human to finish the job on their own screen, so that screen is where the work starts.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them in Production
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them in Production

The source material about a sports injury doesn't align with fintech or payment integration topics. Instead, here's a developer-focused article on ACH return codes—a critical skill for anyone building payout systems.

Understanding ACH Return Codes: A Developer's Reference

When you initiate an ACH debit or credit, the transaction doesn't always succeed. The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) defines a standardized set of return codes—R01 through R85—that tell you exactly why a transfer failed. As a developer, learning to decode these is essential for building reliable payout flows and handling failures gracefully.

The Most Common Return Codes

R01: Insufficient Funds

The account doesn't have enough money to cover the debit. This is the most frequent return you'll encounter. Your retry logic should wait 2–3 days before retrying; the customer may have deposited funds by then. If R01 repeats after 2–3 retries, escalate to manual review or suggest an alternative payment method.

R03: No Account / Account Closed

The account number or routing number is invalid, or the account was closed. This is permanent and should never be retried. Flag the bank account as invalid in your system and prompt the user to add a new one.

R04: Invalid Account Number Structure

The account number format is incorrect for that bank. Validate account numbers against Nacha rules (typically 1–17 digits) before submission. If you receive R04, the data was malformed upstream.

R07: Authorization Revoked

The customer explicitly revoked permission for this transaction. Honor it and don't retry. Contact the customer to re-authorize if needed.

R10: Customer Advises Unauthorized

The customer claims they didn't authorize this transaction. This often signals fraud or a UX problem. Investigate, document, and don't retry without explicit re-authorization.

R29: Corporate Account Closed

Similar to R03 but specific to business accounts. Treat as permanent.

R51: Debit/Credit Reversal

A previous transaction was reversed. This can trigger a cascade of reversals in your system. Implement idempotency keys so duplicate submissions don't cause double-reversals.

Return Code Categories

Nacha groups return codes into three categories:

Category Codes Action
Recoverable R01, R02, R09, R16, R21, R26 Retry after 2–3 days
Non-Recoverable R03, R04, R05, R07, R10, R29, R31 Flag account; don't retry
Administrative R50, R51, R52, R53, R61, R76, R80, R81, R82 Investigate; may require manual intervention

Building Return-Code Aware Logic

Here's a minimal pattern for handling returns in your payout system:

def handle_ach_return(transaction_id, return_code):
    """
    Process an ACH return and decide next action.
    """
    recoverable_codes = ['R01', 'R02', 'R09', 'R16', 'R21', 'R26']
    non_recoverable_codes = ['R03', 'R04', 'R05', 'R07', 'R10', 'R29', 'R31']

    if return_code in recoverable_codes:
        # Schedule retry in 2–3 business days
        schedule_retry(transaction_id, days=3)
        notify_user("Payment delayed; we'll retry soon.")

    elif return_code in non_recoverable_codes:
        # Mark account invalid; ask customer to update
        invalidate_bank_account(transaction_id)
        notify_user("Payment failed. Please verify your bank account.")

    else:
        # Administrative return; needs investigation
        escalate_to_support(transaction_id, return_code)
        log_event(f"Unhandled return: {return_code}")

Return Timing and Reconciliation

ACH returns arrive in batches, typically 1–2 business days after the original debit date. Same-day ACH returns must arrive by 11:59 p.m. ET the same day. Build reconciliation logic to match return notifications with your outbound transaction records using trace numbers and amounts.

Key Takeaways

  • Decode, don't ignore: Each return code tells a specific story. Treat R01 differently from R03.
  • Implement retry logic: Recoverable codes warrant a 2–3 day retry; non-recoverable codes require user action.
  • Log everything: Capture return codes, timestamps, and customer notifications for audit trails.
  • Test with your processor: Ask your ACH provider (e.g., Stripe, Dwolla, or a direct ODFI) for a test environment where you can

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Figma vs Exode in 2026: An Honest Comparison, Including the Parts Where Figma Wins
description:
Most "Figma vs X" posts are written by someone selling X and read like a hit piece. This one is written by someone who uses Figma every day and also works on Exode. I will mark my bias where it matters and give you the parts where Figma is simply better, because a comparison you cannot trust is worse than no comparison.

Where Figma is still untouchable

Let me get this out of the way.

Multiplayer. Figma's real-time collaboration is a decade of engineering. Cursors, comments, branching, library publishing across organisations — it works at a scale nobody else has matched. Exode has live collaboration; it does not have Figma's maturity, and pretending otherwise would be silly.

The ecosystem. Plugins, community files, templates, hiring pipelines, the fact that every designer you interview already knows it. That is not a feature list, it is a moat, and it is a legitimate reason to stay.

Vector editing depth. Figma's vector networks are better than path-based pen tools for a lot of illustration work. Boolean operations are fast and predictable. If your job is drawing, Figma is the better drawing tool.

Design ops. Library governance, permissions, review flows, and the sheer number of teams already standardised on it.

If those four things are the centre of your work, you should keep Figma. I mean that.

Where the model breaks

The friction starts at a specific moment: when a screen stops being a picture and becomes a behaviour.

Consider a quantity stepper. In Figma you build a variant per number, or a component property that swaps text. In an app, it is one component with a number. Now add a price that springs when the number changes, a disabled state while a request is in flight, and a failure state. In Figma that is five frames and a prototype graph. In production it is one state machine.

That gap does not show up in design review. It shows up three weeks later in a pull request comment that says "this doesn't match the mockup".

Exode's argument is that the gap should be closed at the source: the artefact you design should already contain the behaviour, the layout rules and the motion values, in a format that compiles to the component.

Side by side, by job

Job Figma Exode
Static layout and exploration Excellent Good — flexbox-first, fewer vector niceties
Design systems and tokens Mature, org-scale Token-native, CI-lintable
Multiplayer review Industry standard Works, less mature
Prototype with real state Clickable frames Hierarchical state machines with typed inputs
Physics-based motion Springs as designed values Simulated springs and rigid bodies
Responsive behaviour Artboards per breakpoint Real flexbox/grid constraints and breakpoints
Handoff Inspect values, copy CSS Compile component (React, Swift, Vue, Svelte…)
Open file format Proprietary, cloud .exode JSON, diffable in Git
AI agents Assistive, inside the app MCP server, agents can read/write the file
Plugin ecosystem Huge Early

The handoff question, honestly

Figma's answer to handoff is better than it used to be. Dev Mode exposes exact timing, easing and values, and a coding agent can consume them. For teams where engineers own the codebase and designers own the intent, that is a workable contract.

Exode's answer is different: there is no separate handoff artefact. The .exode file compiles to a component, and the runtime that played it on the canvas is the runtime that ships. That removes a class of drift, but it also means the design file is now code-adjacent. Your designers need to be comfortable with that idea — or at least with a state machine panel.

That is a cultural change, not a feature. Some teams should not make it. If your designers are illustrators first, forcing them into a logic graph will make everyone slower.

What actually convinced me

I migrated one real screen: a pricing page with a monthly/annual toggle, three plan cards, a comparison table and a sticky CTA.

In Figma it was a beautiful file and a prototype that broke the moment you clicked the annual toggle twice quickly. In Exode it was one boolean input, a spring on the price, and a layout that reflowed on a 768px breakpoint without duplicating the frame.

The part that surprised me was the export. The page came out as a React component with a billingPeriod prop and real semantic markup. I did not have to re-describe the animation to an engineer. That is the whole thesis, and it held up on a real screen.

But I also spent an hour re-learning where the vector tools live. It is a younger product. Rough edges exist, and the plugin ecosystem is not there yet.

Who should switch

Switch if: you ship interactive product UI, your designers and engineers argue about motion every sprint, your components drift from the design system, or you need motion as a shippable asset rather than a video.

Do not switch if: you mostly do brand, illustration or marketing sites; your organisation runs on Figma libraries and you cannot absorb a migration; or you need the plugin ecosystem and org-scale admin today.

Try both if: you are a design engineer. Build one screen in each, hand it to a developer, and watch where the time goes. That experiment will tell you more than any comparison post, including this one.

The uncomfortable conclusion

Figma is not outdated. It is finished for the job it set out to do, which was to make static interface design collaborative and fast. It did that.

The next job is different: making interfaces that behave, on multiple platforms, with motion that survives the trip to production. That job needs a different artefact — one that carries logic and layout, not just pixels.

Exode is my bet on what that artefact looks like. Figma is still the best place to draw it.

Priya works on design systems and developer experience at Exode. Try the canvas at exodeui.com — the free tier is enough for a real screen.

title: io_uring vs epoll: Paying Per Syscall or Paying in Complexity
description:
A server that handles a million requests per second is not really doing a million units of work. It is doing a million units of work plus the cost of telling the kernel about each one, and at that scale the telling dominates. epoll has been the answer since 2002: register the sockets once, then ask which ones are ready. io_uring, merged in Linux 5.1, asks a different question — why tell the kernel anything at all, when you can drop requests into a shared ring and let it pick them up?

epoll costs roughly three syscalls per request, which at a million requests per second is three million mode switches and about half a core; io_uring with submission polling can drive the same load with zero syscalls per request, at the price of a kernel-version and security-policy matrix.

Part One: What is being compared

epoll is a readiness interface. You add a file descriptor to an epoll set, call epoll_wait, and the kernel tells you which descriptors are readable or writable. You then call read and write yourself, in your own thread, with your own buffers. The kernel does no work on your behalf beyond reporting state.

io_uring is a completion interface. You place a submission queue entry describing an operation — read from this descriptor into this buffer, accept a connection, open a file, send a message — and the kernel executes it and posts a completion queue entry with the result. Submission and completion share memory-mapped rings, so in the ideal case neither side makes a syscall at all. With submission queue polling enabled, a kernel thread watches the ring continuously.

The difference in programming model is bigger than the difference in speed. epoll gives you an event loop where every operation is non-blocking and every buffer lifetime is yours to manage. io_uring gives you an asynchronous execution engine that can do blocking-looking things, including filesystem operations, without a thread pool.

Part Two: The arithmetic

Count syscalls for a simple request-response server. With epoll, a request costs an epoll_wait return, a read, and a write, so three syscalls, plus an accept every so often and a close when the connection ends. A syscall on a modern x86 server costs roughly 200 to 500 nanoseconds once Spectre-era mitigations are counted, so three syscalls are about one microsecond of pure overhead. At one million requests per second that is one full core burned on transitions, before any application logic runs.

With io_uring, the same request can be submitted as a read and a write in one batch, and completions are harvested from the ring without entering the kernel. The syscall count per request drops to zero in steady state. The cost moves to memory barriers and ring management, on the order of tens of nanoseconds. The saving is not the whole core, because the kernel still copies data and runs the protocol stack, but it is a large fraction of the fixed per-request overhead.

Throughput numbers from storage benchmarks show the same shape. On a fast NVMe device at high queue depth, io_uring reaches roughly 1.5 to 2 times the IOPS of an epoll-plus-thread-pool design, mostly because it removes the context switches between worker threads and the kernel. At low queue depth the two are close, and at one outstanding operation the latency is essentially identical.

The second arithmetic difference is batching. io_uring lets you submit thirty-two operations with one syscall and reap thirty-two completions with one more. epoll can batch readiness events, but the read and write calls stay one per operation. For a proxy moving small messages, that ratio is the whole game.

Part Three: Where the model breaks

The first break is the kernel you are running on. io_uring appeared in 5.1, but the features that make it fast — registered buffers, fixed files, multishot accept, provided buffer rings — arrived across 5.4 through 6.x. A design that depends on multishot accept will not run on the kernel shipped by an older enterprise distribution, and containers inherit the host kernel, so a managed Kubernetes cluster may hand you a version you did not choose.

The second break is security policy. Because io_uring can perform arbitrary operations from a shared ring, several container runtimes and hardened kernels disable it by default, and seccomp profiles frequently block the setup syscalls. A service that works in staging can fail at startup in production because the sandbox denies io_uring_setup. This is not a bug in either side; it is a deliberate reduction in attack surface after a run of vulnerabilities in the subsystem.

The third break is complexity. With epoll, a partial read is a normal event and the buffer lives in your struct. With io_uring, every in-flight operation owns a buffer, and the kernel may write to it after your function returns. Use-after-free bugs in this model are subtle and expensive. Libraries exist to hide it, but the moment you need a custom operation you are back to manual lifetime management.

Part Four: The later cost

The operational bill for epoll is familiarity. Every profiling tool understands it, every runtime has an event loop built on it, and a new engineer can read the code. Its scaling limit is real but high: with edge-triggered mode and careful non-blocking handling, epoll handles hundreds of thousands of connections per process. The cost is per-request syscalls, which is a CPU bill that grows linearly and predictably.

The operational bill for io_uring is a compatibility matrix. You need a runtime feature probe, a fallback path, and tests that cover both. You need to watch kernel release notes for behaviour changes, because the interface is younger and semantics have been adjusted. You need to explain to a security team why the ring is enabled.

There is a third option that changes the comparison: a thread-per-core runtime with blocking sockets and no event loop at all. At low concurrency it beats both on simplicity and often on latency, because a blocking read costs one syscall and no state machine. The event-driven designs only win when concurrency is high enough that thread stacks and scheduling become the constraint.

Part Five: Outside the team

For a user, the difference is tail latency under load. A proxy built on epoll with a thread pool shows a latency cliff when the pool saturates; an io_uring design degrades more smoothly because there are no worker threads to queue behind. A poorly written io_uring design shows a different cliff, when the completion ring fills and submissions start failing.

For the business, the difference is instance count. Shaving one core per million requests per second is a rounding error at small scale and a five-figure monthly line item at large scale. It is also a hiring constraint: engineers who can debug an io_uring lifetime bug are scarcer than engineers who can debug an epoll loop.

A fair comparison fixes the kernel version, the container security profile, the request size and the concurrency, then measures requests per second per core and the ninety-ninth percentile. Benchmarking io_uring on a bare-metal 6.x kernel against epoll inside a locked-down container measures the sandbox, not the interface.

Market sizing check

If asynchronous I/O becomes the default for high-throughput services over the next five years, the market affected is not a product category but a cost line: compute spent on syscall overhead across proxies, databases and storage services is plausibly in the billions of dollars a year, with the addressable saving in the low hundreds of millions. The swing factor is how quickly sandboxed environments allow the interface.

These numbers are an order-of-magnitude estimate built from published per-syscall costs and fleet sizes, not a measured total.

The comparison that matters

The comparison that matters is between a mature readiness API that charges per operation and a younger completion API that charges in compatibility and buffer discipline. epoll wins on portability, debuggability and any environment where the sandbox blocks the ring. io_uring wins on syscall-bound workloads, on storage, and wherever batching thirty operations into one entry is natural.

The ranking assumes you control the kernel and can test the fallback. Give up either and the older interface is the safer engineering choice.

Adopt io_uring when syscall overhead is a measured fraction of your CPU profile and you can pin the kernel; otherwise epoll remains the lower-risk path, and the difference at moderate load is smaller than the migration cost.

title: AWS announces general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud connectivity with Microsoft Azure
description:
AWS announces the general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud with Microsoft Azure.

Customers have been adopting multicloud strategies while migrating more applications to the cloud. They do so for many reasons including interoperability requirements, the freedom to choose technology that best suits their needs, and the ability to build and deploy applications on any environment with greater ease and speed. Previously, when interconnecting workloads across multiple cloud providers (CSPs), customers had to go the route of a ‘do-it-yourself’ multicloud approach, leading to complexities of building and managing global multi-layered networks at scale. AWS Interconnect - multicloud is the first purpose-built product of its kind and a new way of how clouds connect and talk to each other, allowing customers to quickly provision resilient, scalable private connections to other cloud providers.

In August, Microsoft Azure launched support for AWS Interconnect in public preview and became the latest CSP to adopt the open specification that powers the service. With today’s GA launch, AWS customers can now rely on the same consistent, simple experience to interconnect their workloads on Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

Interconnect - multicloud is available with Microsoft Azure in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia), ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), and eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) AWS Regions. You can create an Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, Command Line Interface (CLI), or API. For more information, see the AWS Interconnect - multicloud documentation.
