title: Deletion Deadlines Explained: 429 Queue Backoff for Node.js AI Image Object Storage
description:
Short answer: keep image generation and object storage as separate queue steps, persist the generated bytes, and retry each step with exponential backoff; use an idempotent object key so a 429 rate limit or upload timeout cannot create a second artifact.

That rule also works for a marketplace that stores signed documents and must delete them on a deadline. An AI image is just a different payload. The durable sink is useful only when the handoff is explicit: a worker records the generation result, then another worker owns the upload and retention metadata.

How should a Node.js pipeline retry a 429 rate limit after an image upload fails?

Treat the generated bytes as an input to a new job, not as a reason to call the image model again. The first worker writes a short-lived local or database-backed blob reference with the job id. The upload worker derives marketplace/{jobId}.png (or a document key with the same deterministic pattern), checks whether that key already exists, and then performs the write. A retry sees the same key and the same payload.

Here is a minimal TypeScript worker using the two verified storage routes. It retries 429 responses and other transient HTTP failures, honors Retry-After, and never sends the platform authorization header to the presigned URL because this example writes directly to the API.

const baseUrl = process.env.STORAGE_API_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) throw new Error("STORAGE_API_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");

type StoredImage = { bytes: Uint8Array; contentType: string };

async function requestWithBackoff(url: string, init: RequestInit): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 6; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, init);
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) return response;
    if (attempt === 5) return response;
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
  throw new Error("retry loop exhausted");
}

async function putImage(bucket: string, jobId: string, image: StoredImage) {
  const key = `marketplace/${jobId}.png`;
  const auth = { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` };
  const existing = await requestWithBackoff(
    `${baseUrl}/storage/object/head/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
    { method: "GET", headers: auth },
  );
  if (existing.ok) return { key, status: "already-present" };
  if (existing.status !== 404) throw new Error(`HEAD failed: ${existing.status} ${await existing.text()}`);

  const upload = await requestWithBackoff(
    `${baseUrl}/storage/object/put/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
    {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: { ...auth, "Content-Type": image.contentType, "x-infrai-acl": "private" },
      body: image.bytes,
    },
  );
  if (!upload.ok) throw new Error(`PUT failed: ${upload.status} ${await upload.text()}`);
  return { key, status: "uploaded" };
}

The queue must make the worker at-least-once safe: acknowledge only after putImage succeeds, cap attempts at six, and retain the bytes long enough for the retry window. For signed documents, store the deletion timestamp beside the job row and let a separate daily lifecycle process enforce it; the storage lifecycle minimum is one day, so an hour-level deadline needs an application queue or database scheduler. In a Node.js practice run, I also inject a restart between those two acknowledgements; that is where a superficially successful pipeline usually reveals a missing handoff record.

Keep it boring.

Which storage trade-offs matter for marketplace records?

The access-control versus delivery-simplicity choice is the real fork. Private objects and short-lived signed links keep a contract or generated image out of a public feed. A browser upload is less work when CORS is configurable, but this storage surface has no independent set_cors route, so direct browser writes need an application-controlled path or a different provider.

There is no If-Match conditional write. Two workers targeting one key therefore need a database lease or queue partition; a HEAD check reduces duplicate work but is not a mutual-exclusion primitive. There is also no object versioning or WORM lock, so an accidental overwrite cannot be recovered by the bucket itself. Those are capability boundaries, not retry bugs.

Option Delivery model Access and retention fit Choose it when
Amazon S3 SDK or signed URL Fine-grained IAM, versioning, Object Lock Legal hold and mature replication are requirements
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Private buckets and signed URLs Egress economics and edge adjacency matter
Google Cloud Storage Google SDK and signed URLs Versioning and retention policies Your workload already lives in GCP
Infrai storage Plain REST, one platform key Private/signed-only objects; lifecycle starts at one day You want the storage contract and other backend capabilities behind one REST API

Infrai's practical advantage here is the stable contract: the same plain HTTP conventions let you swap the service behind the capability without rewriting the queue, while one key reaches 295 routes across 20 modules. That can simplify a solo team's integration boundary, but it does not add version recovery, cross-region replication, or public-read hosting.

How do you make 429 backoff and deletion deadlines observable?

Record the job id, attempt number, HTTP status, Retry-After, object key, and the final response body. A 429 rate-limit response should move the message to a delayed queue; a 4xx other than 429 should usually go to a review path instead of burning all attempts. Keep generation and upload metrics separate, because a healthy model provider cannot tell you whether the storage account has credits for persistent writes. That separation is the useful practice: it tells you whether the failed stage was image creation, queue delivery, or object storage.

One easy-to-miss boundary: trial credits cannot fund persistent writes. If a trial upload is rejected for that reason, adding more retries only delays the same outcome. Move the job to a clearly labeled billing-required state and preserve the generated bytes according to your retention policy.

For a signed-document marketplace, my operational checklist is short prose: derive keys from immutable job ids, coordinate same-key writers in the queue or database, make deletion deadlines an explicit field, and test a worker restart between generation and upload. Keep private ACLs, issue signed URLs only at read time, and verify the object with a HEAD request before marking the business record complete.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://www.fedramp.gov/
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • Set STORAGE_API_BASE_URL to your storage provider's /v1 API base; the route paths above are the discovery-verified contract.

title: I built a Node.js toolkit for India's DPDP Act, so compliance can't quietly drift
description:
If your app has Indian users and stores even a phone number, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 applies to you. The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025, and most of their obligations start 18 months later, in May 2027: notices, security safeguards, breach reporting, erasure, and rights requests. The maximum penalty is ₹250 crore.

Most teams will handle this with a privacy policy page and a spreadsheet. Nothing in the code enforces either. Six months later someone adds an aadhaar_number column, nobody updates the spreadsheet, and the data is kept forever.

So I built dpdp-kit: an open-source, Node.js-native toolkit that builds the DPDP Act into your backend. Version 0.2.0 is out today.

npm i dpdp-kit

Not legal advice. dpdp-kit helps you put compliance into practice; it doesn't make an app compliant on its own. Every Section and Rule reference in it was checked against the official Gazette texts, but your lawyer still signs off.

What the law asks of your code

The law says Where dpdp-kit
Process data only for a stated purpose, with consent or a legitimate use Sections 4, 6, 7 Typed data map: every field lists its purposes
Prove a notice was given and consent was given Section 6(10) Hash-chained consent records with notice version and language
Notice in English or any Eighth Schedule language Sections 5(3), 6(3) All 22 languages built in
Erase when consent is withdrawn or the purpose ends, unless another law says keep it Section 8(7) Erasure plans + a runner, with legal holds
Keep data, traffic data and logs of processing for at least a year Rule 8(3) minimumRetention, enforced by the audit
Answer access, correction, erasure, grievance and nomination requests Sections 11–14 Rights requests with due dates
Answer grievances within 90 days Rule 14(3) Default due date, enforced by the audit
Tell processors to stop and erase Sections 6(6), 8(7)(b) Processor hooks

1. Declare your data, with types

Everything starts from one config file. Purposes are typed, so a typo in a field's purpose list is an error in your editor:

// dpdp.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "dpdp-kit";

export default defineConfig({
  fiduciary: { name: "Acme Pvt Ltd", grievanceUrl: "https://acme.in/privacy/grievance" },
  purposes: {
    account:       { basis: "legitimate-use", retain: "while-active" },
    order_updates: { basis: "consent", retain: "while-active" },
    marketing_sms: { basis: "consent", retain: { afterWithdrawal: "0d" } },
  },
  data: {
    users: {
      table: "users",
      subject: "id",
      fields: {
        phone: { category: "contact", purposes: ["account", "order_updates", "marketing_sms"] },
        name:  { category: "identity", purposes: ["account"] },
      },
    },
    orders: {
      table: "orders",
      subject: "user_id",
      fields: { address: { category: "contact", purposes: ["account"] } },
      legalHold: { reason: "GST records", keep: "8y", then: "anonymise" },
    },
  },
  processors: { msg91: { purposes: ["order_updates", "marketing_sms"] } },
  minimumRetention: "1y", // Rule 8(3)
});

2. Catch schema drift in CI

This is the part I'm proudest of. A data map is only useful while it matches the database, so the audit reads your real Drizzle schema and checks both directions:


npx dpdp-kit audit --schema src/db/schema.ts

✖ error    schema.users.aadhaar_number
             Looks like personal data (identity, matched "aadhaar") but isn't in the data map.
✖ error    data.orders.fields.address
             Column "address" isn't in table "orders". Fix the name, or remove it if the column was dropped.
⚠ warning  schema.users.gender
             Looks like personal data (identity, matched "gender") but isn't in the data map.

It recognises phone and email columns, Aadhaar, PAN, passport and voter IDs, dates of birth, names, addresses and PIN codes, UPI, IFSC and bank details, IP addresses and device IDs, and health, biometric and location data. Clear cases are errors; maybe-personal ones like name or city are warnings. Columns that describe data rather than hold it, like email_verified_at or address_type, are left alone.

In GitHub Actions, each problem lands on the pull request as an annotation:

- run: npm ci
- uses: yogesh2902/dpdp-kit@main
  with:
    schema: src/db/schema.ts

3. Consent records that show tampering 

import { createDpdp } from "dpdp-kit";
import { drizzleData, drizzleStore } from "dpdp-kit/drizzle";

const dpdp = createDpdp({ config, store: drizzleStore(db), data: drizzleData(db, { schema }) });

await dpdp.consent.grant(userId, ["marketing_sms"], {
  noticeVersion: "2026-11",
  language: "hi",
  channel: "android",
});
await dpdp.consent.has(userId, "marketing_sms"); // true
await dpdp.consent.verify(userId);               // { ok: true, events: 1 }

Each person's grants and withdrawals form a SHA-256 hash chain. verify() catches an edited, deleted or reordered event, which matters because Section 6(10) puts the burden of proving consent on you.

4. Erasure that actually happens

Withdrawing consent schedules the erasure. A daily retention.run() carries it out:

await dpdp.consent.withdraw(userId, ["marketing_sms"]);
await dpdp.retention.run(); // from a daily cron
  • Processors are told to stop immediately (Section 6(6)), through hooks you provide.
  • Fields are erased only when none of their purposes remain. phone stays while account still needs it.
  • Rule 8(3)'s one-year minimum is respected. The data is restricted now and deleted after a year, which is what the Rule's own example asks ("even if X deletes her account").
  • Legal holds win. Invoices kept for GST wait 8 years, then get anonymised.
  • It's safe with several servers. Tasks are claimed atomically, retried on failure, and a processor without a hook becomes a manual task.

5. Rights requests on a clock 

const request = await dpdp.rights.open(userId, "grievance", { text: "Too many promo SMS" });
// due 90 days later (Rule 14(3))

await dpdp.rights.list({ overdue: true }); // your inbox of late answers
await dpdp.rights.summary(userId);         // Section 11: what you hold, why, and who you shared it with
await dpdp.rights.erase(userId, { keepFor: ["account"], requestId: request.id }); // Section 12(3)

Why Node-native

dpdp-kit is a library, not a service. It runs inside your Node process, writes to your own Postgres through the Drizzle setup you already have, and makes no network calls. There's no server to deploy, no API key, and personal data never leaves your infrastructure. It works with ESM, require() and TypeScript, with Express and Hono middleware included.

How it's tested

  • 85 tests, including full flows against real Postgres (PGlite): withdraw → processor stopped → column nulled a year later, account deletion with an 8-year GST hold, and three runners racing for the same tasks
  • CI on Node 20.19, 22 and 24, plus a job that runs the GitHub Action against a sample project
  • Legal references checked against the Act (Gazette, 11 August 2023), the Rules (G.S.R. 846(E)) and their corrigendum (G.S.R. 892(E))

What's next

Recording objections to a Section 7(a) use, React components for notices and a privacy centre, MySQL and SQLite data access, children's data and guardian consent (Section 9, Rule 10), and breach records with the 72-hour Board report (Rule 7).

Try it 

npm i dpdp-kit
  • GitHub: github.com/yogesh2902/dpdp-kit (MIT)
  • npm: npmjs.com/package/dpdp-kit

If you build for Indian users, I'd really like to hear what's missing. Issues and PRs are welcome, and a star helps other developers find it.

title: ISC Stormcast For Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10182, (Tue, Nov 17th)
Every deploy gave a full share of traffic to JVMs that had not compiled anything yet
description:
Our stock lookup service answers in about twelve milliseconds at the ninety ninth percentile, and the shop calls it with a timeout of two hundred and fifty. It runs as eight pods behind an Application Load Balancer that sends traffic straight to the pods. For a year, every deploy produced a small burst of timeouts in the shop: a few hundred failed lookups, products shown as unavailable for a minute, then nothing. We had filed it under deploys being a bit noisy.

In October we started deploying several times a day, and the bursts became a visible share of the shop's errors, so I looked properly. Every timeout came from a new pod, in its first forty to sixty seconds.

A JVM starts by interpreting bytecode. Methods that run often get compiled, quickly by the C1 compiler first and later, after many more invocations, into optimised code by C2. Until the hot paths are compiled, a request costs many times what it will cost a minute later, and class loading and the first database connections add to it. Our readiness probe said ready as soon as Spring had started, so the load balancer gave each new pod its full share of traffic immediately. The pod was correct, only slow, and slow was enough to cross the shop's timeout.

The rollout replaced pods two at a time, so at every step a quarter of the traffic was going to cold code.

The service now warms itself before it reports ready. At start it replays a few thousand recorded stock lookups through the real code path against the real database, and readiness turns true only when that is done and the last batch has a p99 within twice the normal figure. The target group has slow start set to ninety seconds, so the load balancer ramps a new pod's share of requests up over that time instead of handing it everything at once. The deploy bursts have gone, and each rollout takes two minutes longer, which nobody has noticed.

Ready meant the process was up. It needed to mean the process was fast.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Cascading Failure Deep Dive: How a Months-Old Bug and One Router Took Down Email and Air Travel
description:
On November 12, Microsoft 365 email and collaboration services failed for about a day across dozens of countries. On November 13, the FAA held every departing flight in the United States for more than four hours. Officials said there was no sign they were related, and neither has been tied to a cyberattack.

They do share a shape. In both, a small, local fault became a system-wide outage because of how the system reacted to it. This post walks through each failure stage by stage, using the preliminary public explanations, then maps each stage to a defense you can apply to your own systems.

Two caveats up front. Both explanations are preliminary: Microsoft's final post-incident report is due November 20, and the FAA hasn't finished its root-cause review. And I wasn't inside either incident. Everything here comes from public statements and reporting, cited inline. (I used AI tools to help research and draft this, and checked every factual claim against those sources.)

Part 1: Microsoft 365, November 12 to 13

What happened

Exchange Online and Outlook were hit hardest, with Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, and other services affected. Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million. Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report, covered by GeekWire, The Register, and BleepingComputer, describes a chain of events.

Stage 1: a latent defect

A fix rolled out to Microsoft 365's networking gateway servers in July contained a defect. Under heavy load, it caused lock contention: threads waiting on each other for a shared lock, burning CPU and memory without doing useful work. Microsoft says the contention was inside an internal Windows process and got worse on newer machines with more cores. My reading is that more cores means more threads competing for the same lock.

The defect sat in production for more than three months without causing an outage, because normal load never pushed the gateways into the state where contention ran away.

Stage 2: headroom erodes

Two unrelated things removed the safety margin before the failure:

  • About 14% of gateway capacity was already out of service because of an earlier, separate issue.
  • Roughly 15 hours before the outage, according to GeekWire, Teams traffic had been moved onto the Exchange gateway pool.

Neither was an incident on its own. Microsoft says the reduced capacity alone left enough headroom. The combination is what tipped the gateways into the defect. Microsoft also says its load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores than production.

Stage 3: overload spreads through rerouting

Once some gateways crossed into runaway contention and stopped responding, automatic rerouting did what it was designed to do: it moved their traffic to the healthy gateways. That extra load pushed those gateways into the same state. The failure spread until more than 80% of gateway servers were unresponsive.

This is the classic shape of a cascading failure. The mechanism meant to contain a failure, moving work away from a broken node, spreads it when the cause is load itself.

Stage 4: recovery fights itself

When engineers restarted servers, clients that had been failing all reconnected at once. The restarted servers were overwhelmed before they could stabilize, a pattern usually called a thundering herd. GeekWire's summary of the report names it explicitly.

Stage 5: containment boundaries leak

Microsoft's design is meant to keep a problem in one region from spreading to others. The preliminary report says safeguards meant to keep a problem in one region didn't hold, and it doesn't yet explain why. That's one of the details the final report should clarify.

Microsoft resolved the outage by rolling out an update that reverted the defective change.

Part 2: the FAA ground stop, November 13

What happened

Around 3:30 to 3:36 p.m. Eastern, air traffic controllers began seeing radar and radio inconsistencies. At 3:54 p.m., the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop. Instability reached 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage high-altitude traffic, along with several approach control facilities. The stop was lifted at about 8:15 p.m. FedScoop reported it was only the second nationwide ground stop since 2001. The FAA's own Q&A covers the basics.

Stage 1: a change at the edge

L3Harris, which runs the FAA's telecommunications network, was replacing copper circuits with fiber at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas. A new router was installed as part of that work. AeroTime reports it was a Juniper unit replacing an older Cisco device. HPE, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer.

Stage 2: one device floods a shared network

The new router began generating connection attempts across the FAA's telecommunications network. The FAA describes about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Whether the cause was a configuration error or a faulty unit is still undetermined, according to Duffy.

Stage 3: older equipment can't absorb it

Legacy equipment elsewhere on the network couldn't handle the flood. Radar and communications feeds to most en-route centers degraded. A fault at one small site became a national event because the network was shared and the legacy equipment apparently couldn't protect itself from a misbehaving peer.

Stage 4: diagnosis is slow

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency spent about 45 minutes trying to find the cause without success before issuing the ground stop, partly because this kind of maintenance is logged by hand on paper (FedScoop). When you don't have a fast, searchable record of what changed and where, the first hour of an incident goes to finding the change.

Stage 5: isolation, then a fleet-wide fix

Isolating the El Dorado router, and a second one at a site in Amarillo, Texas, stabilized the network. The FAA then disabled the suspect function on about 60 similar routers across its network. The FBI is examining the router at an L3Harris lab, which officials describe as a precaution rather than evidence of an attack.

The shared shape

Stage Microsoft 365 FAA Defense
Trigger July fix with a load-dependent defect Router installed during a fiber upgrade Staged rollouts, plus load testing at degraded capacity
Hidden precondition 14% of capacity already out; extra traffic moved in Shared network; legacy equipment with no protection from a noisy peer Treat degraded capacity as an incident; per-peer rate limits
Amplifier Rerouting moved load onto healthy servers, which then failed Connection storm propagated across the network Load shedding and admission control instead of unlimited failover
Recovery problem Thundering herd on restarted servers Slow diagnosis; paper logs Retry backoff with jitter; searchable change records
Containment Regional isolation didn't hold Two sites affected 17 of 22 centers Cell-based isolation with tested boundaries

Defenses you can apply

None of these would have been easy for either organization. They're the standard toolkit for this failure shape, and most are cheaper to add before an incident than during one.

Load-test at degraded capacity, not full capacity. A system tested with every server healthy can pass every test and still fail when 14% of the fleet is out. Run load tests with a meaningful slice of capacity removed, because that's the state your system will be in when the next problem arrives.

Count lost headroom as an incident. "Some servers are down but we're fine" is the most dangerous status in operations. Alert on remaining headroom, not just on errors, so a reduced fleet gets attention before something else lands on top of it.

Shed load instead of moving all of it. Failover assumes the survivors have spare capacity. When the cause is load, moving all of a failed node's work onto its neighbors spreads the failure. Admission control (rejecting some requests quickly when a server is near its limit) keeps the rest of the fleet alive. Google's SRE book covers this in its chapter on addressing cascading failures.

Make clients back off with jitter. If every client retries immediately when a service comes back, the service goes down again. Exponential backoff with random jitter spreads the reconnections out. Server-side, ramping traffic back gradually to restarted nodes does the same thing from the other direction.

Rate-limit peers, not just users. A shared network should assume any device can misbehave. Per-port or per-peer limits on connection rates turn one noisy device into a local problem.

Keep a searchable record of every change. The first question in nearly every incident is "what changed?" If the answer lives in a ticket system, a spreadsheet, and someone's paper notes, diagnosis time goes up. A single timeline of deploys, config changes, and hardware work is one of the highest-value tools an operations team can have.

Test your isolation boundaries. Regions and cells only contain failures if nothing shared crosses them. Shared control planes, config systems, and dependency services are where boundaries leak. The only way to know a boundary holds is to break something on one side on purpose and watch the other side.

Where I landed

The scariest week of outages this year came down to a load-dependent defect, a router installed during an upgrade, and recovery mechanisms that amplified the damage. None of that is exotic. It's the same set of failure modes every large system has, which is why the defenses are well known, and also why they're worth revisiting before your own version of this week.

I'll update this post when Microsoft publishes its final report and the FAA completes its review.

Disclosure: I work at Control Plane, a cloud infrastructure company.

Originally published on Hashnode.

title: PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation: Building IBAN-Name Verification and a Fraud-Liability Decision Engine in Spring Boot
description:
Last year a friend almost wired a rental deposit to a fraudster. The invoice looked right, the IBAN was copied from an email, and the bank app accepted it without a murmur. Nothing in the flow asked the one question that would have saved them: does this account belong to the person I think I'm paying?

That question is now a legal requirement, and the next wave of EU rules also decides who pays when the answer is ignored. I build payment backends for a living, so this post is the version I wish I had when the compromise texts landed: first the plain explanation, then the architecture, then the code.

Part 1: The idea in plain words

Let me define the terms before I use them.

  • IBAN (International Bank Account Number): the long account identifier used for European transfers.
  • PSP (Payment Service Provider): a bank, payment institution or e-money company that moves money for customers.
  • PSD3 (Payment Services Directive 3): the third generation of the EU directive that licenses and supervises payment providers.
  • PSR (Payment Services Regulation): a companion law. A directive has to be converted into national law, while a regulation applies directly. The PSR carries the operational rules that engineers actually feel.
  • VoP (Verification of Payee): the name check. You type a name and an IBAN; the sending bank asks the receiving bank whether they belong together.
  • IPR (Instant Payments Regulation): the 2024 law that already forces euro-area providers to offer VoP on instant euro transfers.
  • APP fraud (Authorised Push Payment fraud): the customer themselves approves the payment, but only because a scammer deceived them. The customer did nothing "unauthorised" in the technical sense, which is why refund rules for it are contested.

Verification of Payee has three possible answers:

  1. Match: the name fits the account holder.
  2. Close match: the name is nearly right, for example a typo or a missing middle name. The receiving bank may reveal the correct name to the payer.
  3. No match: the name does not fit, or the account cannot be verified.

If I only had to explain it to a relative: it is the "are you sure this is the right person?" prompt that a bank is obliged to show, powered by a short conversation between two banks.

The IPR applies this to euro instant payments. According to the Council's published compromise texts from April 2026, the PSR package extends the idea to credit transfers in euro more broadly, and it links fraud liability to how the check was handled. The package was still in its final adoption stage when I wrote this, so please read the official text for the final article wording before you freeze any rule in production.

Part 2: What the law asks the engineer to prove

Two requirements turn into code.

Requirement one: do the check. Before the payer confirms, the system must ask the payee's bank, wait a short time, and present one of the three outcomes clearly.

Requirement two: remember everything. Liability depends on events: was the check offered, was the result shown, did the customer proceed despite a warning? A bank that cannot reconstruct those events months later has no defence in a refund dispute, whatever the law says.

I want to be honest about a gap. Different commentators describe the scope of impersonation-fraud liability differently. Some read it as covering only a scam where the fraudster poses as the customer's bank, others read it more widely. I am not going to pick a reading for you. In my design the liability rules live in configuration, with the text version they were built against recorded next to every decision. That is the only responsible way to build against a moving target.

Here is the shape of the whole system.

The flow has two halves. The synchronous half sits inside the payment journey and must answer in about a second. The asynchronous half classifies liability later, when a claim arrives, using the evidence the first half stored.

Part 3: The VoP service

Modelling the outcome

I start with types, because the whole design depends on never confusing "no match" with "we could not check". These are different legal facts.

public enum VopOutcome {
    MATCH,
    CLOSE_MATCH,
    NO_MATCH,
    UNAVAILABLE   // we asked and got no usable answer in time
}

public record VopRequest(
        String checkId,
        String payerPspRef,
        String payeeIban,
        String payeeNameAsTyped,
        Instant requestedAt) {}

public record VopResult(
        String checkId,
        VopOutcome outcome,
        String suggestedName,   // only for CLOSE_MATCH, if the payee bank shares it
        int score,              // 0-100, our own similarity score
        String source) {}       // "PAYEE_PSP", "LOCAL_RULE", "TIMEOUT_FALLBACK"

UNAVAILABLE is the type that saves you later. If a payer proceeds after an unavailable check, the liability story is different from proceeding after an explicit no-match.

Fuzzy name matching

Names are messy. "Müller", "Mueller" and "MULLER" are the same person. Company names carry suffixes like "GmbH" or "B.V.". Banks also differ in how they store a name, so I normalise first and compare second.

@Component
public class NameMatcher {

    private static final Set<String> NOISE = Set.of(
            "gmbh", "bv", "b.v.", "ltd", "sa", "sas", "ag", "srl", "mr", "mrs");

    public int score(String typed, String registered) {
        String a = normalise(typed);
        String b = normalise(registered);
        if (a.isEmpty() || b.isEmpty()) return 0;
        if (a.equals(b)) return 100;

        int tokenScore = tokenOverlap(a, b);
        int editScore = editSimilarity(a, b);
        return Math.max(tokenScore, editScore);
    }

    String normalise(String raw) {
        String folded = Normalizer.normalize(raw, Normalizer.Form.NFKD)
                .replaceAll("\\p{M}", "")
                .replace("ß", "ss")
                .replace("ue", "u")
                .toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)
                .replaceAll("[^a-z0-9 ]", " ");
        return Arrays.stream(folded.split("\\s+"))
                .filter(t -> !t.isBlank() && !NOISE.contains(t))
                .sorted()                       // order-insensitive: "Anna Meyer" == "Meyer Anna"
                .collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
    }

    private int tokenOverlap(String a, String b) {
        Set<String> sa = Set.of(a.split(" "));
        Set<String> sb = Set.of(b.split(" "));
        long common = sa.stream().filter(sb::contains).count();
        return (int) Math.round(100.0 * common / Math.max(sa.size(), sb.size()));
    }

    private int editSimilarity(String a, String b) {
        int dist = levenshtein(a, b);
        int longest = Math.max(a.length(), b.length());
        return (int) Math.round(100.0 * (longest - dist) / longest);
    }

    private int levenshtein(String s, String t) {
        int[] prev = new int[t.length() + 1];
        int[] curr = new int[t.length() + 1];
        for (int j = 0; j <= t.length(); j++) prev[j] = j;
        for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++) {
            curr[0] = i;
            for (int j = 1; j <= t.length(); j++) {
                int cost = s.charAt(i - 1) == t.charAt(j - 1) ? 0 : 1;
                curr[j] = Math.min(Math.min(curr[j - 1] + 1, prev[j] + 1), prev[j - 1] + cost);
            }
            var tmp = prev; prev = curr; curr = tmp;
        }
        return prev[t.length()];
    }
}

Two cautions from experience. First, the sort-the-tokens trick makes "Anna Meyer" and "Meyer Anna" identical, which is correct for payee checks but would be wrong for a fraud model that cares about order. Second, thresholds are policy, not maths. In real deployments the payee bank usually does the matching against its own records, so my matcher is mostly for the case where I am the receiving side, or where I post-process a vague answer. The thresholds below are therefore configuration.

vop:
  thresholds:
    match-min: 95
    close-match-min: 70
  timeout:
    payee-psp-ms: 900
    max-retries: 0
  fallback:
    on-timeout: UNAVAILABLE
    allow-proceed-on-unavailable: true
  liability-ruleset: "psr-compromise-2026-04-config-v1"

Timeout and fallback policy

An instant payment has a tight budget. If the receiving bank is slow, the payer is staring at a spinner while the clock runs. I give the remote call a hard deadline, no retries inside the payment journey, and an explicit fallback. This is the same discipline I describe in my post on idempotent payment pipelines with the transactional outbox: in payments, every timeout path must be a designed path.

@Service
public class VopService {

    private final PayeePspClient client;
    private final NameMatcher matcher;
    private final VopAuditLog audit;
    private final VopProperties props;

    public VopService(PayeePspClient client, NameMatcher matcher,
                      VopAuditLog audit, VopProperties props) {
        this.client = client; this.matcher = matcher;
        this.audit = audit; this.props = props;
    }

    public VopResult verify(VopRequest req) {
        VopResult result;
        try {
            var reply = CompletableFuture
                    .supplyAsync(() -> client.lookup(req.payeeIban()),
                            Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor())
                    .orTimeout(props.timeout().payeePspMs(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
                    .join();
            result = classify(req, reply);
        } catch (CompletionException ex) {
            result = new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.UNAVAILABLE,
                    null, 0, "TIMEOUT_FALLBACK");
        }
        audit.recordCheck(req, result);   // always, before returning anything to the payer
        return result;
    }

    private VopResult classify(VopRequest req, PayeeReply reply) {
        if (!reply.accountFound()) {
            return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.NO_MATCH, null, 0, "PAYEE_PSP");
        }
        int score = matcher.score(req.payeeNameAsTyped(), reply.registeredName());
        var t = props.thresholds();
        if (score >= t.matchMin()) {
            return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.MATCH, null, score, "PAYEE_PSP");
        }
        if (score >= t.closeMatchMin()) {
            String hint = reply.mayDisclose() ? reply.registeredName() : null;
            return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.CLOSE_MATCH, hint, score, "PAYEE_PSP");
        }
        return new VopResult(req.checkId(), VopOutcome.NO_MATCH, null, score, "PAYEE_PSP");
    }
}

I use virtual threads here because the call is pure waiting on network I/O. If you want the production background, my write-up on Java virtual threads in Spring Boot covers pinning and pool behaviour. In a real build I would create the executor once as a bean rather than per call; I inlined it to keep the example short.

Notice the ordering: the audit record is written before the method returns. If the audit write fails, the payment journey should fail closed or degrade to a documented manual path. A check that happened but left no trace is worth nothing in a dispute.

Part 4: An immutable audit trail

"Immutable" is a strong word, so let me be precise. I mean append-only at the application level, tamper-evident through hash chaining, and protected at the database level with permissions that deny updates and deletes.

Each event captures one fact. The facts I record per payment attempt are:

  1. The check was offered (the payer was given the chance).
  2. The result was displayed (with the exact wording version shown).
  3. The payer acted: confirmed, edited the name, or cancelled.
  4. For a warning, the payer overrode it, explicitly. 
public record AuditEvent(
        UUID eventId,
        String checkId,
        String type,          // CHECK_OFFERED, RESULT_SHOWN, PAYER_CONFIRMED, MISMATCH_OVERRIDDEN ...
        String payloadJson,
        String uiTextVersion, // which warning copy the customer saw
        Instant occurredAt,
        String prevHash,
        String hash) {}

@Repository
public class VopAuditLog {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public VopAuditLog(JdbcTemplate jdbc, ObjectMapper mapper) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc; this.mapper = mapper;
    }

    @Transactional
    public AuditEvent append(String checkId, String type, Object payload, String uiTextVersion) {
        String prev = jdbc.query(
                "select hash from vop_audit where check_id = ? order by seq desc limit 1",
                rs -> rs.next() ? rs.getString(1) : "GENESIS", checkId);
        String json = toJson(payload);
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        String hash = sha256(prev + type + json + uiTextVersion + now);
        var event = new AuditEvent(UUID.randomUUID(), checkId, type, json,
                uiTextVersion, now, prev, hash);
        jdbc.update("""
            insert into vop_audit(event_id, check_id, type, payload, ui_text_version,
                                  occurred_at, prev_hash, hash)
            values (?,?,?,?::jsonb,?,?,?,?)""",
            event.eventId(), checkId, type, json, uiTextVersion,
            Timestamp.from(now), prev, hash);
        return event;
    }

    public void recordCheck(VopRequest req, VopResult res) {
        append(req.checkId(), "CHECK_PERFORMED", res, "n/a");
    }

    private String toJson(Object o) {
        try { return mapper.writeValueAsString(o); }
        catch (JsonProcessingException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }

    private String sha256(String s) {
        try {
            var d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return HexFormat.of().formatHex(d);
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }
}

Hash chaining per check means an auditor can recompute the chain and spot a deleted or edited row. Pair it with a database role that only has INSERT and SELECT on the table. Concurrent appends for the same check are rare, but add a unique constraint on (check_id, prev_hash) so a fork fails loudly instead of silently.

Storing uiTextVersion matters more than it looks. When a customer says "your app never warned me", the strongest answer is the exact copy, the exact version, and the timestamp of the screen that carried it. If you run feature flags on warning text, version those strings like code. I took the same stance with compliance artefacts in my DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code post: evidence you generate at runtime beats evidence you reconstruct during an audit.

Part 5: The fraud-liability classifier

Now the part that makes finance teams lean forward. When a customer claims a refund after a scam, someone has to decide whether the PSP refunds, pushes back, or shares the loss with the payee's PSP. The compromise text ties that to the payee-check handling. My engine does not decide law. It reads the evidence and applies a ruleset that compliance owns.

The inputs I feed the classifier:

Evidence Where it comes from
Was the check offered? CHECK_OFFERED event
What was the outcome? CHECK_PERFORMED payload
Was it shown to the payer? RESULT_SHOWN event plus UI text version
Did the payer override a warning? MISMATCH_OVERRIDDEN event
Claimed fraud type Claims intake form

Rules are data, not code. A small interface keeps them swappable, and the active ruleset id is stamped on every verdict.

public enum Verdict { REFUND_PSP, CONTEST_PAYER_LIABLE, SHARE_WITH_PAYEE_PSP, MANUAL_REVIEW }

public record Evidence(
        boolean checkOffered,
        VopOutcome outcome,
        boolean resultShown,
        boolean warningOverridden,
        FraudType claimedType,
        List<UUID> supportingEventIds) {}

public record Decision(Verdict verdict, String ruleId, String rulesetVersion,
                       String rationale, List<UUID> evidence) {}

public interface LiabilityRule {
    String id();
    boolean appliesTo(FraudType type);               // keeps scope configurable
    Optional<Verdict> evaluate(Evidence e);
}

@Component
public class LiabilityEngine {

    private final List<LiabilityRule> rules;
    private final VopProperties props;

    public LiabilityEngine(List<LiabilityRule> rules, VopProperties props) {
        this.rules = rules; this.props = props;
    }

    public Decision decide(Evidence e) {
        for (LiabilityRule rule : rules) {
            if (!rule.appliesTo(e.claimedType())) continue;
            var v = rule.evaluate(e);
            if (v.isPresent()) {
                return new Decision(v.get(), rule.id(), props.liabilityRuleset(),
                        explain(rule, e), e.supportingEventIds());
            }
        }
        return new Decision(Verdict.MANUAL_REVIEW, "NO_RULE_MATCHED",
                props.liabilityRuleset(), "No configured rule covered this evidence.",
                e.supportingEventIds());
    }

    private String explain(LiabilityRule r, Evidence e) {
        return "Rule %s fired: offered=%s outcome=%s shown=%s overridden=%s"
                .formatted(r.id(), e.checkOffered(), e.outcome(),
                        e.resultShown(), e.warningOverridden());
    }
}

Here are two example rules. They illustrate the mechanism; the verdicts they return are a reading, not a statement of what the regulation says.

@Component
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "liability.rules.check-not-offered.enabled", havingValue = "true")
class CheckNotOfferedRule implements LiabilityRule {
    public String id() { return "CHECK_NOT_OFFERED"; }
    public boolean appliesTo(FraudType t) { return t == FraudType.IMPERSONATION; }
    public Optional<Verdict> evaluate(Evidence e) {
        // If the PSP never offered the check, defending a refusal is hard.
        return e.checkOffered() ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of(Verdict.REFUND_PSP);
    }
}

@Component
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "liability.rules.warning-overridden.enabled", havingValue = "true")
class WarningOverriddenRule implements LiabilityRule {
    public String id() { return "WARNING_OVERRIDDEN"; }
    public boolean appliesTo(FraudType t) { return t == FraudType.IMPERSONATION; }
    public Optional<Verdict> evaluate(Evidence e) {
        boolean warned = e.outcome() == VopOutcome.NO_MATCH || e.outcome() == VopOutcome.CLOSE_MATCH;
        if (e.checkOffered() && e.resultShown() && warned && e.warningOverridden()) {
            return Optional.of(Verdict.MANUAL_REVIEW); // flag for a human; do not auto-deny
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }
}

Two design choices deserve explanation.

Overridden warnings go to manual review, not automatic denial. The sources I read disagree on how far a customer's override should cut the refund right, and a wrong automated denial in a consumer-protection area is expensive. If your legal team settles on a firm reading, flip the rule through configuration and bump the ruleset version.

The appliesTo hook carries the scope argument. If the final reading covers only bank-impersonation scams, you narrow the FraudType list in configuration. If it covers wider impersonation, you widen it. The code paths stay the same, and historical decisions remain explainable because each carries the ruleset version that produced it.

Defending or conceding a claim

When the engine returns a verdict, I generate an evidence bundle: the ordered audit events, the hash chain proof, the UI copy shown, and the rule rationale. If the verdict is to concede, the same bundle supports the recovery claim against the payee's PSP. It is far better to concede quickly with clean records than to fight with half a file.

Part 6: Operational lessons from running payment systems

I have worked on high-traffic systems (AirAsia's booking platform handled around 130 million requests a day) and on open banking APIs, and the lessons repeat. Some I would apply here:

  • Measure the check as its own service. Track p95 latency and the share of UNAVAILABLE results per counterparty bank. A single weak partner can quietly push your unavailable rate up. The tracing setup from my distributed tracing guide works well here: one trace id from the payer tap through the VoP call to the audit write.
  • Treat the UI as part of the compliance system. The best backend cannot prove a warning was shown if the front end never reports it. Make the RESULT_SHOWN event a server-confirmed acknowledgement, not a fire-and-forget log.
  • Replay your rules. Keep a corpus of anonymised past claims and run every ruleset change against it before release. This is the same idea as deterministic replay I use for market data, described in my market-data replay article.
  • Keep personal data narrow. Names and IBANs are personal data. Retention periods for audit rows should be decided with your data-protection officer, and the hash chain can outlive payload deletion if you hash a salted payload digest rather than the clear text.

If you have read my notes on Open Banking PSD2 API development, this will feel familiar: the previous generation asked you to expose and secure APIs, and this one asks you to prove, afterwards, what each customer was told.

What I would not hard-code

After building this, here is my short list of things that should stay configurable:

  1. Match and close-match thresholds.
  2. Timeout length and the fallback behaviour on UNAVAILABLE.
  3. Which fraud types each liability rule covers.
  4. The verdict for an overridden warning.
  5. The ruleset id and the text version it was derived from.

Everything else, such as the three outcomes, the append-only audit and the evidence bundle, is stable under any reading of the text I have seen.

Your next step

Pick one live transfer journey in your system, add a CHECK_OFFERED and a RESULT_SHOWN audit event to it this week, and stamp each with the UI text version. That single change gives your compliance team real evidence to work with, whichever way the final liability wording lands. If you want help designing this for your payment stack, reach out through my contact section, see the payment systems I have shipped in my experience, or browse my projects.

title: Architecting a Serverless Telegram & WhatsApp Neobank Backend on Cloudflare Workers
description:
The traditional playbook for launching a fintech application involves spinning up containerized instances, wrestling with VPC configurations, and provisioning expensive database clusters just to handle basic API webhooks and request routing. For early-stage founders and developers building conversational banking solutions inside messaging apps like Telegram and WhatsApp, that infrastructure overhead eats up margins before the product even ships.

In modern fintech architecture, shifting execution to the edge using serverless infrastructure changes the economics entirely. By leveraging serverless edge workers, teams can build automated payment gateways, crypto off-ramping logic, and virtual card routers that run globally with zero server management and a monthly overhead of under $30.

The Core Technical Challenge: Edge Routing and Webhook Validation

When processing financial transactions or interacting with banking-as-a-service (BaaS) providers, the backend needs to validate incoming webhooks instantly, manage state securely, and route payloads without latency bottlenecks.

A traditional Node.js server requires constant monitoring, patching, and scaling. In contrast, a Cloudflare Worker handles incoming requests at data centers closest to the user.

Below is an example of how an edge routing handler processes incoming webhooks cleanly in standard JavaScript:

export default {
  async fetch(request, env, ctx) {
    if (request.method !== 'POST') {
      return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405 });
    }

    try {
      const update = await request.json();

      // Parse incoming platform message payload
      if (update.message) {
        const chatId = update.message.chat.id;
        const text = update.message.text;

        // Route through banking gateway / AI intent parser
        await processFinancialPayload(chatId, text, env);
      }

      return new Response(JSON.stringify({ status: 'ok' }), {
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      });
    } catch (err) {
      return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: err.message }), {
        status: 500,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      });
    }
  },
};

}

Integrating Conversational AI & Multi-Platform Support

Modern fintech users expect instant responses. By embedding natural language intent parsing into the edge function, the system can interpret unstructured text—such as fund requests, balance checks, or asset swaps—and execute the correct API call.

Because the architecture relies on modular JavaScript, the same core backend logic can be adapted across multiple messaging environments simultaneously, making it an ideal boilerplate for localized fintech solutions, trading communities, or automated customer support portals.

Resources & Getting Started

For developers looking to experiment with this architecture without building the boilerplate from scratch, the complete unencrypted starter framework—including the core worker script, dependency definitions (package.json), environment configuration templates (wrangler.example.toml), and documentation—is available for implementation.

title: CSS Grid Lanes: native masonry, now in Safari
description:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

Masonry layouts, the Pinterest-style wall of cards with different heights, finally have a native CSS value: display: grid-lanes. Safari ships it, and Safari 27.2 (WebKit's release post is from October 26) just renamed the one property that controls how it behaves. Chrome and Firefox aren't there yet, so this is a good moment to learn how it works and how to use it today without breaking anything.

What it is and why it matters

For years, a masonry wall meant a JavaScript library measuring every card and positioning it absolutely. CSS Grid alone can't do it: rows force every card in a row to share the same height, so short cards leave holes under them. Multi-column layout packs things tightly, but it fills the first column top to bottom before moving to the next, so items 1, 2 and 3 end up stacked on the left instead of reading across.

Grid Lanes, defined in CSS Grid Layout Level 3, sits in between. One axis is a real grid (your columns), and the other axis is a stacking axis with no rows. MDN sums it up well: "each row of items loads into the column with the most room, causing a tightly packed layout without strict row tracks."

The demo above lets you switch between grid and grid-lanes with the same cards. Watch the board height drop and the gaps disappear.

How it works

This is the whole thing, and it's the same CSS the demo uses:

.board {
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(120px, 1fr));
  gap: 10px;
}

You define columns exactly as you would in a normal grid. The browser then places each card, in order, into "whichever grid track is currently the least filled", in the spec's words. Everything you know from Grid still works on the grid axis: grid-column-end: span 2 makes a card cover two columns, and cards with a definite position (grid-column: 2 / 4) are placed before the rest. If you define grid-template-rows instead of columns, the layout turns sideways and items flow into rows. There's also inline-grid-lanes for the inline-level version.

fit-tolerance: tightness against order

Here's the subtle part. If the browser always picked the strictly shortest column, a 2 px difference would send card 5 to the far left while card 4 sits on the right, and the reading order would zigzag for no visible benefit. So the spec treats columns whose heights are within a threshold of the shortest one as tied. Among tied columns, the browser takes the first one at or after an "auto-placement cursor", which points just past the previous card. In plain terms: when it doesn't matter much, keep going left to right.

That threshold is fit-tolerance:

.board {
  fit-tolerance: normal;   /* 1em in grid lanes layout */
  fit-tolerance: 4em;      /* tolerate bigger differences, keep more order */
  fit-tolerance: infinite; /* strictly in order, ignore column heights */
}

The initial value, normal, resolves to 1em in grid lanes layout. infinite, according to the spec, makes items "distribute themselves strictly in order, without considering the length of the tracks at all", which can leave very uneven columns. Move the fit-tolerance slider in the demo and turn on "Tab order": the line connecting the cards in DOM order gets straighter as the tolerance grows, and the "cards out of turn" counter drops to zero.

The property used to be called flow-tolerance. The spec renamed it, and Safari 27.2 adopted fit-tolerance, keeping flow-tolerance as a deprecated alias. The 27.2 notes also explain why this matters beyond looks: a higher value keeps consecutive items in neighbouring columns, so keyboard focus moves more predictably.

Browser support and gotchas

  • Safari supports display: grid-lanes since 26.4, according to MDN's compatibility data, and fit-tolerance under its new name since 27.2.
  • Firefox has it only in preview builds. Chrome and Edge have no stable support: WebKit's January article said a variant had been behind a flag since version 140 and was being updated to the final syntax. MDN marks the feature as experimental and not Baseline.
  • The fallback is one extra line. Browsers ignore values they don't understand, so declare a normal grid first: 
.board {
  display: grid;
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(120px, 1fr));
  gap: 10px;
}

Without support you get a regular grid with holes, which is perfectly usable. WebKit also suggests @supports not (display: grid-lanes) rules to crop images or truncate text so the grid fallback looks tidy, or loading a JavaScript masonry library only when CSS.supports('display', 'grid-lanes') is false. The demo does a version of the latter: in browsers without support, it runs the spec's placement algorithm in JavaScript. I checked it against WebKit's native rendering (Playwright's WebKit build) at seven tolerances and three column widths, and every card landed in the same spot.

  • Order and accessibility. The spec itself warns that this layout "can switch between endward in the inline or block axis in a seemingly arbitrary manner". Tab order follows the DOM, not the visual position. If the order of your cards carries meaning (a timeline, ranked results), raise fit-tolerance or pick another layout. The spec points to reading-flow for content without an inherent order, but that property is currently only in Chromium-based browsers.
  • The spec is still moving. The latest published Working Draft is from January 2026, and the Editor's Draft changed again in October. The spec even notes that the property that controls orientation is still to be decided.

What to keep an eye on

  • When Chrome and Edge ship the final grid-lanes syntax, not the flagged prototype. That's the moment this stops being a progressive enhancement and becomes a default.
  • Firefox moving it out of preview builds.
  • Whether the orientation control and the other open issues in CSS Grid Level 3 change any syntax before then. For now, display: grid-lanes plus a display: grid fallback is the safe way to use it.

Sources

  • CSS Grid Layout Module Level 3 (Editor's Draft)
  • Grid lanes layout - MDN
  • WebKit Features for Safari 27.2 - WebKit blog
  • When will CSS Grid Lanes arrive? How long until we can use it? - WebKit blog

title: Google TPUs Are Coming to Oracle Cloud. Does That Change the AI Lock-In Problem?
description:
Google’s partnership with Oracle could let enterprises use TPUs without moving to Google Cloud. But does having the same AI accelerator available on different clouds make applications easier to move between them?

Imagine a company that runs its business applications and databases on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

The company is building an AI assistant to help employees find information, answer business questions and complete routine tasks. Its existing AI workloads run on NVIDIA GPUs, but the technology team wants to evaluate other accelerators, including Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).

Until now, accessing Google’s cloud-based TPU services has generally meant using Google Cloud. For a company already committed to OCI, that could mean introducing another cloud environment simply to use a different type of AI processor.

The team would need to consider connectivity, data access, monitoring, security and operating costs across both environments.

What if the company could use Google TPUs directly within OCI instead?

On October 27, 2026, Oracle and Google announced plans to bring TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, beginning in calendar year 2027.

That could give organizations another way to choose AI hardware without necessarily changing their primary cloud provider.

But it also raises a question that is more important than the announcement itself.

If the same AI accelerator becomes available through different cloud providers, does that reduce cloud lock-in, or simply change where the dependencies exist?

Why the Oracle agreement matters beyond another hardware option

In our earlier TechiesJournal article, Can Google TPUs Reduce AI’s Dependence on NVIDIA?, we examined how alternative accelerators and improving software support could reduce reliance on NVIDIA’s ecosystem.

That is one part of the infrastructure problem.

An organization may want access to different processors so it can compare performance, availability and operating costs. But choosing a different accelerator can also introduce dependencies on its software tools and supported cloud environments.

The Oracle agreement adds another dimension.

Google developed TPUs for machine-learning workloads and has offered cloud access to them through Google Cloud. The planned OCI deployment would make Oracle the first hyperscale cloud provider outside Google to offer these processors.

That changes the potential relationship between the company supplying the accelerator and the company operating the surrounding cloud infrastructure.

Google can extend the reach of its TPU systems beyond Google Cloud, while Oracle can add another accelerator architecture to its existing infrastructure portfolio.

For enterprise customers, the immediate significance is choice.

A company that already depends on OCI may eventually be able to evaluate Google’s specialized AI processors without establishing an entirely separate Google Cloud deployment solely for TPU compute.

However, the announcement establishes a future offering, not a finished customer deployment model.

Oracle and Google say TPU capacity will begin appearing in OCI in calendar year 2027, with expansion planned over multiple years. Oracle has also described an ambition to reach gigawatt-scale TPU deployment over that period.

As of November 16, 2026, the companies have not established publicly verifiable customer pricing, initial regions, provisioning details or complete service-level commitments for the planned offering.

Oracle’s own announcement includes a forward-looking statement warning that plans and expectations may change.

For architects, this distinction matters: an announced capability can influence a technology roadmap, but it cannot yet replace an available production service.

How Google TPUs would fit into Oracle’s infrastructure

The partnership is technically interesting because it brings together different parts of an AI computing system.

An accelerator does not work in isolation. It needs high-speed communication, data access, networking, cooling, power and software capable of coordinating computation across processors.

Google’s TPU systems include specialized technologies for communication between accelerators.

The Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) enables communication among TPU chips, while Optical Circuit Switching (OCS) helps manage communication paths in large TPU systems.

This becomes particularly important during the training of large AI models. Thousands of processors may need to exchange information repeatedly, and slow communication can leave expensive computing resources waiting for data.

Google’s technical explanation of the partnership describes how ICI and OCS form part of its system-level approach to accelerator communication and resilience.

Oracle provides the surrounding cloud infrastructure.

OCI will supply data-center power, cooling and networking, with Oracle Acceleron providing the network foundation that connects TPU capacity to other OCI resources.

Google specifically describes Acceleron’s SmartNIC-based isolation, High Performance Fabric and Zero Trust Packet Routing as technologies intended to support those connections.

These responsibilities operate at different levels.

Google’s TPU communication technologies connect and coordinate the accelerators within the TPU system. Oracle’s infrastructure connects that computing capacity to the wider cloud environment, including storage, databases and applications.

The result is not simply a Google processor installed in an ordinary server.

It is a planned integration of Google’s specialized AI computing systems with Oracle’s data-center and cloud networking infrastructure.

Even so, the companies have not published every detail an enterprise architect would need to deploy and operate the service.

The exact customer provisioning model, management interfaces, monitoring integrations and operational limitations will need to be evaluated when Oracle makes the offering available.

Following an enterprise AI request through the proposed architecture

Consider the fictional enterprise introduced earlier.

Its employees use an internal AI assistant to retrieve approved information from business databases.

The assistant must respond quickly, respect access permissions and avoid exposing confidential information.

Suppose the company eventually runs its AI inference workloads on Google TPUs hosted in OCI.

A request could follow this illustrative path.

First, the employee submits a question.

An application running on OCI receives the request, authenticates the employee and determines which business information the employee is permitted to access.

Next, the application retrieves relevant information.

The application queries the appropriate Oracle database or retrieval service using established access controls.

Only information that the employee is authorized to access should be made available to the AI workload.

The AI model then processes the request.

The application sends the relevant input to a model running on TPU compute. The TPU performs the numerical calculations required to generate the model’s response.

For a large model distributed across multiple TPU chips, Google’s TPU interconnect technologies may be involved in coordinating computation inside the accelerator system.

Oracle’s networking infrastructure provides connectivity between TPU capacity and the surrounding OCI services.

Finally, the application returns the answer.

The application processes the model output, applies any required validation or business rules, and returns a response to the employee.

This is an illustrative application architecture, not a published Oracle deployment specification. The exact networking, security and inference-service interfaces for OCI TPUs have not yet been confirmed.

The example nevertheless shows why the partnership could matter.

The business application, enterprise database and AI compute could potentially operate within the same cloud environment, rather than requiring a separate Google Cloud deployment to access TPU hardware.

That may simplify certain network designs and reduce some cross-cloud transfers.

But those benefits will depend on the actual deployment.

If the application and TPU capacity are in different regions, or if relevant data still resides outside OCI, network delays and transfer costs may remain significant.

Similarly, hosting components within one cloud does not automatically establish secure access. Identity, permissions, data isolation, logging and operational controls must still be designed and verified.

A useful architecture is not determined merely by where the accelerator is installed. It is determined by how the entire workload behaves.

Does having TPUs on two clouds make AI workloads portable?

This is where the distinction between more infrastructure choice and genuine portability becomes important.

An application can depend on three different layers of technology.

Dependency What it means What the OCI agreement changes
Accelerator hardware The processor architecture used to execute AI workloads TPUs are planned to become available through another hyperscaler
AI software Frameworks, compilers, libraries and model execution tools Existing TPU software support may help, but compatibility must still be verified
Cloud services Networking, identity, storage, deployment, monitoring and operations OCI becomes another hosting option, but its surrounding services remain distinct

These dependencies are related, but they are not interchangeable.

Consider the company’s AI assistant.

Its model may be developed using PyTorch, a widely used machine-learning framework. Google’s TorchTPU project aims to support TPU execution through familiar PyTorch workflows.

Google announced that TorchTPU is available as open-source software and describes an ecosystem that includes tools such as vLLM, SGLang and Ray.

The objective is to make TPU adoption easier for developers using established AI software.

That is meaningful progress.

However, three different claims must not be confused.

Model-code compatibility means developers can use familiar programming interfaces and potentially reuse substantial parts of their model code.

Performance portability means a workload continues to perform competitively when moved to different hardware. This may require tuning, alternative kernels, different memory-management approaches or changes to model execution.

Cloud deployment portability means the complete application can move between cloud environments while preserving its necessary security, networking, storage, monitoring and operational behavior.

TorchTPU can improve the first of these. Google presents broader portability as an intended benefit of its software ecosystem.

But neither open-source framework support nor the Oracle agreement proves that all three are achieved automatically.

For example, even if the enterprise runs the same model code on TPUs in Google Cloud and OCI, its surrounding application may still depend on OCI networking, Oracle databases, provider-specific access controls and deployment automation.

Moving the model is only one part of moving the application.

Therefore, the Oracle partnership can reduce one form of restriction, the need to use Google Cloud for access to cloud-hosted Google TPU capacity, without eliminating software or operational dependencies.

That is a useful improvement, but it is not the same as making AI infrastructure cloud-independent.

Why reduced lock-in is not always the right objective

Before deciding whether the agreement solves a dependency problem, enterprises should ask whether that dependency was creating a meaningful business problem in the first place.

Cloud portability has costs.

An organization might deliberately build applications around technology supported by several providers. That can make future migration easier, but it may also require additional engineering, testing and operational expertise.

Another organization may prefer services closely integrated with one cloud because they are easier to manage or better suited to its workloads.

Neither approach is automatically superior.

For the fictional OCI enterprise, adding a separate cloud platform solely to access another accelerator could increase operational complexity.

If TPUs become available within OCI, the organization may gain another hardware choice while retaining its existing cloud operating model.

It would still depend on Oracle for important infrastructure services and on Google’s TPU technology for accelerator execution.

That may be a reasonable trade-off.

For an organization with strict multicloud resilience requirements or a need to relocate workloads between providers, the same arrangement may not offer enough independence.

The goal is not to eliminate every specialized technology.

It is to understand whether the benefits justify the resulting dependencies and whether the organization can change direction when necessary.

Why Google and Oracle would pursue this arrangement

The technical partnership also reflects the commercial interests of both companies.

For Google, extending TPU availability beyond its own cloud could increase adoption of its accelerator architecture.

Organizations already committed to OCI may be more willing to evaluate TPUs if they can use them alongside their existing applications and data.

A broader installed base could also encourage software developers, framework maintainers and AI platform providers to improve TPU support.

These are plausible strategic benefits, not independently established business outcomes from the Oracle deployment.

For Oracle, the advantage is a broader range of compute options.

OCI already supports several computing architectures. Oracle’s October 2026 infrastructure strategy describes plans involving NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and additional specialized AI hardware.

Adding TPUs would allow Oracle to offer another option for training and inference workloads.

Different workloads may benefit from different accelerator architectures. A large training run, a low-latency chatbot and a batch inference process do not necessarily have the same priorities.

Providing multiple options could help customers select infrastructure based on their requirements rather than forcing every workload onto a single architecture.

However, the partnership does not establish that Google TPUs on OCI will be cheaper, faster or more reliable than competing alternatives.

Nor does it demonstrate that customers will reduce their NVIDIA spending.

To make those claims, enterprises would need comparable workloads running on available infrastructure, with measured performance and complete costs.

The business opportunity is credible. Its magnitude remains unproven.

What should an architect evaluate before making a decision?

Return to our enterprise AI assistant.

The organization wants reliable answers, acceptable response times, strong data protection and predictable operating costs.

Its decision should start with those requirements, not with the availability of a new processor.

When OCI TPUs become available, a useful evaluation would compare the complete application against its existing deployment.

Evaluation Question to answer
Model compatibility Does the model run correctly with its required software libraries and execution tools?
Performance Does it meet response-time and throughput targets under realistic demand?
Data access Can the workload access enterprise data securely without unnecessary transfers?
Operational support Can the organization deploy, monitor, scale and recover the service reliably?
Capacity Are suitable TPU configurations available in the required region and quantity?
Economics Is the total cost better than the existing practical alternative?
Future flexibility Which components would need to change if the organization later chose a different accelerator or cloud?

The comparison needs to include more than accelerator rental charges.

A deployment with lower compute pricing may still cost more when engineering effort, network charges, storage, operational support or application changes are included.

Similarly, an accelerator that produces faster results under one test may not deliver better economics under actual production demand.

A useful evaluation should therefore use the organization’s own workload and a credible alternative it could actually deploy.

Until Oracle publishes service details and customers can measure the resulting platform, several of these questions remain unanswered.

What should organizations do now, and what should wait?

The partnership does not require an immediate infrastructure change.

Organizations already running AI workloads successfully should continue improving and benchmarking their existing systems. They should not delay necessary deployments solely because another option is planned for 2027.

Companies evaluating TPU technology today can use currently available platforms to understand model compatibility, software requirements and the effort needed to operate their workloads.

For enterprises committed to OCI, the planned TPU service is worth including in future infrastructure evaluations, especially where AI workloads depend heavily on data already held in Oracle systems.

But organizations should wait for actual OCI service availability before assuming particular performance, prices, regions or operational capabilities.

A practical distinction is:

Decide now: Which workloads might benefit from alternative accelerators? What performance and cost measures matter? Which application dependencies would make a future change difficult?

Evaluate when available: OCI TPU pricing, supported hardware, software compatibility, regional capacity, network architecture, operational tooling and measured production performance.

Do not assume: That using TPUs on OCI automatically reduces total costs, eliminates cloud lock-in or makes existing Google Cloud TPU workloads portable without modification.

This approach keeps the organization prepared without committing to capabilities that have not yet been delivered.

More choice does not mean complete independence

Google’s decision to bring TPUs to Oracle Cloud is significant because it begins separating access to Google’s specialized AI hardware from the requirement to use Google’s own cloud infrastructure.

For enterprises already using OCI, that could remove an important obstacle to evaluating TPU-based workloads.

It may also create more competition among accelerator options within the same cloud environment.

But the infrastructure surrounding an AI processor remains important. Models still depend on software. Applications still depend on data, networking, identity and operational services. Businesses still need evidence that a different deployment delivers measurable value.

The Oracle partnership changes where Google TPUs may become available. It does not yet demonstrate that AI workloads can move freely between clouds.

For technology leaders, the useful question is not how to eliminate every dependency. It is which dependencies are worth accepting, which limit future choices, and what evidence would justify changing them.

That is the decision this partnership makes more interesting.

Go deeper

  1. Oracle: Oracle Brings Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: October 27, 2026. The official announcement covering the planned OCI offering, timing, infrastructure responsibilities and intended AI workloads.
  2. Google Cloud: Bringing Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: October 27, 2026. A technical explanation of TPU communication, the planned role of Oracle Acceleron, software ecosystem support and potential deployment benefits.
  3. Oracle: Building the Next Decade of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: October 27, 2026. Oracle’s wider infrastructure strategy, its plans to support multiple specialized computing architectures and its plan to ramp TPU capacity to gigawatt scale over multiple years.
  4. TechiesJournal: Can Google TPUs Reduce AI’s Dependence on NVIDIA?: November 14, 2026. Related reading on AI accelerator competition, software dependencies and the practical considerations involved in choosing alternatives to NVIDIA.

Source review: November 16, 2026. The OCI TPU offering remains a future commitment. Product specifications, timing, availability and commercial terms should be rechecked against official documentation before any deployment decision.
