title: Rendering 25 Mermaid diagrams into a print PDF (and what broke)
description:
I maintain a free book, Networking with Go, Made Easy, that ships as a web reader, a PDF and an EPUB from the same Markdown sources. The web reader renders Mermaid diagrams in the browser. The PDF did not: it printed 25 blocks of flowchart TB and sequenceDiagram as literal source code.

This is the story of the build step that fixed it, including the parts that were not obvious.

Three constraints, one conclusion

The PDF is produced by go-pretty-pdf, which composes the MDX into HTML and prints it with headless Chrome. Three details of that pipeline ruled out the obvious fixes:

  1. It has no Mermaid support. A `mermaid fence becomes an ordinary code block.
  2. It blocks subresources by default. Network and file:// fetches are blocked, so an <img src="diagram.svg"> inside the composed page never loads.
  3. It prints immediately after the load event. There is no wait for JavaScript, so pulling in mermaid.js and letting the browser draw the diagram does not work either.

That leaves one shape that survives: the SVG must already be inline in the HTML before Chrome prints it.

Pre-render, then materialize

The book keeps Mermaid blocks in the chapters. That is the source of truth, and it is what the web reader still uses.

A small Go tool, tools/diagrams, does two things:

  1. It finds every mermaid block in docs/`.
  2. It writes a copy of the book to build/docs/ with each block replaced by the matching SVG from assets/diagrams/.

The PDF build then runs against build/docs instead of docs:

go run tools/diagrams/main.go
pretty-pdf build --source build/docs --out networking-with-go.pdf

A Makefile wraps both commands as make pdf and make epub.

The asset lookup is content-addressed. The SVG file name is the SHA-256 of the diagram source, so editing a diagram without re-rendering it is a hard build error, not a stale picture:

diagrams: 1 diagram(s) have no rendered SVG:
  d77887b698c1  docs/part1/03-types-of-networks.mdx
Run: go run tools/diagrams/main.go -render

Rendering itself uses the official @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli, pinned. It needs Node, so it is an authoring step only: CI never runs it, and the release pipeline stays Go-only.

What broke

1. Monospace text and sequence diagrams

The book is set in a monospace face, so the first render profile forced the same stack inside Mermaid. Flowcharts were fine. Sequence diagrams were not: actor boxes and note rectangles came out narrower than their labels.

Mermaid measures those boxes with its own font metrics. Forcing a different family makes the measurement and the rendered text disagree, and the labels spill outside the shapes. The fix was to stop overriding the diagram font and let Mermaid measure what it renders. The figures ended up proportional while the prose stays monospace, which is a normal distinction in books.

2. HTML labels are not XHTML-friendly

Mermaid uses <foreignObject> with HTML inside for labels by default. Chrome prints that fine, but the EPUB is generated as XHTML, and foreign objects are a portability problem in e-readers. Setting htmlLabels: false (and the classic look) produces plain <text> and keeps the EPUB well-formed.

3. A page break ate the figure's top margin

The first PDF build had one diagram sitting flush against the top of the page, with the running header printed over its first row. Chrome drops a block's top margin when a page break lands on it. Margins were the wrong tool; padding survives fragmentation, so the figure wrapper uses padding for the top gap.

4. One diagram was 1144 px wide

A flowchart LR with five nodes laid out in a single row is 1144 px wide. Scaled to a 649 px text column, its 15 px labels print at about 6.5 pt. It is legible, but it is the one diagram I would redraw vertically if I were editing content rather than tooling. The pipeline does not try to fix layout decisions.

The check that keeps it honest

A GitHub Actions job runs the materializer on every pull request touching docs/ or assets/diagrams/. If someone edits a diagram and forgets to re-render it, the check fails with the hash it is missing. The release workflow runs the same step before building.

The result: zero Mermaid blocks in the PDF, 25 diagrams printed as vectors, and the EPUB still valid. The only raster image left in the PDF is the cover.

What I would do differently

This logic belongs inside the PDF tool, not in a wrapper around it. A render.mermaid option that pre-renders with Chrome and inlines the SVG would remove the extra build step and the duplicated source tree. Until then, the wrapper is small, deterministic and easy to explain, which is the next best thing.

The book is free to read at sazardev.github.io/networking-with-go, and the pipeline lives in the repository. If you are generating PDFs from Markdown with diagrams, the content-addressed asset trick is the part I would steal first.

title: Data Lake vs Data Warehouse vs Lakehouse
description:
These three terms describe where analytical data lives, and what guarantees it has. A data lake is files in cheap object storage. A data warehouse is a database built for analytical SQL. A lakehouse adds a transactional table format on top of lake files, so they behave like warehouse tables. Most real platforms combine at least two of them, so the useful skill is knowing what each one gives you, and which one a workload needs.

The comparison

Data lake Data warehouse Lakehouse
Storage Files in object storage (Parquet, JSON, CSV, images, logs) Managed storage inside the warehouse Files in object storage plus a table format (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi)
Schema Applied when reading (schema-on-read) Enforced when writing Enforced when writing, with controlled evolution
Transactions None by default Yes Yes, through the table format's log or metadata
Updates and deletes Rewrite files yourself UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE through the format
Data types Anything, including unstructured Mostly structured and semi-structured Structured and semi-structured; other files alongside
Compute Any engine that reads files The warehouse's engine Multiple engines over the same tables
Performance tuning Up to you (file sizes, partitions) Mostly managed Partly managed (compaction, clustering, statistics)
Typical users Data engineers, data scientists Analysts, BI tools Both

Data lake vs lakehouse

A lakehouse is a data lake with a table format added. The data stays as Parquet files in the same object storage; the difference is a metadata layer (a Delta Lake log, Iceberg metadata or a Hudi timeline) that records which files make up each version of a table. That one layer changes what the files can do:

Data lake (plain files) Lakehouse (files + table format)
A write that touches 50 files Readers can see half of it Appears all at once or not at all
A file with the wrong columns Accepted; queries break later Rejected unless schema evolution is allowed
Update or delete one customer Rewrite files yourself UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE
Last week's version Gone once files are overwritten Time travel to an earlier version

This is also the answer to "Delta Lake vs data lake": Delta Lake is not a separate place to keep data. It is a table format that runs on top of your data lake, so an existing folder of Parquet files can be converted into a Delta or Iceberg table in place. See Delta Lake vs traditional lake tables for the details.

Lakehouse vs data warehouse

Both give you transactional tables, schemas and SQL. The differences are about ownership and operations:

  • Storage: a lakehouse keeps open-format files in your own object storage; a warehouse keeps data in its own managed, usually proprietary storage.
  • Engines: many engines (Spark, Trino, DuckDB, warehouses) can share one lakehouse table; a warehouse is queried mainly through its own engine.
  • Operations: in a lakehouse you (or the platform) run compaction, cleanup and catalog upkeep; a warehouse handles most of this for you.
  • Strengths: warehouses shine at high-concurrency BI with little to operate; lakehouses shine when BI, ML and engineering must share one copy of large data.

The two are converging: warehouses now read and write Iceberg tables in your storage, and lakehouse platforms offer warehouse-style SQL engines.

Data lake vs data warehouse

A data lake stores raw files in any format, applies a schema only when the data is read, and costs little; it suits engineers and data scientists who need flexibility. A data warehouse stores modelled tables, enforces the schema when data is written, and returns fast, consistent SQL results; it suits analysts and dashboards. They are usually used together: the lake as the landing zone for everything, the warehouse (or a lakehouse layer) for the curated tables people report from.

Data lake

Cheap, durable object storage (S3, ADLS, GCS) holding raw and processed files. It is flexible: store anything in any format, and process it with any engine, Spark, Trino, DuckDB, pandas. Storage costs little and scales without limits you will hit.

The weakness is reliability. A folder of files is not a table: there is no transaction to make a multi-file write atomic, no enforced schema, and no safe way to update a row. Concurrent writes and failed jobs leave readers seeing partial data, upstream type changes break queries months later, and without layers, ownership and a catalog the lake drifts into a "swamp" no one trusts.

Data warehouse

A database optimised for analytical SQL: columnar storage, a cost-based optimiser, statistics, caching and concurrency control. It enforces schemas, provides transactions, and is easy for analysts and BI tools. Cloud warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift separate storage from compute so each scales independently.

The trade-offs: data must be loaded into the warehouse's storage, which means one more copy and one more pipeline. The storage format is usually proprietary, so other engines cannot read it directly. And workloads that want raw files, such as ML training on images or heavy Python processing, fit less naturally.

Lakehouse

A lakehouse adds warehouse-like guarantees to lake storage through an open table format: metadata on top of Parquet files that records which files make up each version of a table. Delta Lake keeps an ordered transaction log of JSON commits; Iceberg keeps a tree of metadata and manifest files with an atomic pointer swap in a catalog; Hudi keeps a timeline of commits. All three give:

  • ACID commits: a write becomes visible all at once or not at all.
  • Schema enforcement and evolution: writes that do not match the schema fail unless evolution is requested.
  • Row-level changes: MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE, implemented by rewriting files or with deletion vectors.
  • Time travel: read an earlier version for audits, debugging or reproducible ML.
  • File-level statistics for data skipping, plus maintenance operations (compaction, clustering, cleanup of old files).

Many engines can read and write the same tables: Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, and the major warehouses, which now read (and in some cases write) Iceberg or Delta tables in your storage. A catalog (Unity Catalog, AWS Glue, Apache Polaris, Hive Metastore and others) maps table names to their metadata and enforces access. The Delta Lake lesson shows the transaction log working.

The cost of a lakehouse is operational: someone has to run compaction and cleanup, choose layouts, keep catalogs and engines on compatible versions, and decide which engine owns writes to each table.

Seeing the difference: files vs a transactional table

The example uses DuckDB, which can both query a folder of Parquet files (a lake) and manage its own transactional tables (a warehouse), so the two behaviours sit side by side. It runs in Python with pip install duckdb.

import os
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
os.makedirs("lake/orders", exist_ok=True)

# Lake: a job writes files into a folder. Readers see whatever files exist.
con.execute("""COPY (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 'c1', 120.50), (2, 'c2', 80.00)) t(order_id, customer_id, amount))
               TO 'lake/orders/part-0001.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)""")
# The next job should write two files but crashes after the first one
con.execute("""COPY (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (3, 'c1', 15.00)) t(order_id, customer_id, amount))
               TO 'lake/orders/part-0002.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)""")
partial = con.execute("SELECT count(*), sum(amount) FROM 'lake/orders/*.parquet'").fetchone()
print("lake after failed job:", partial)          # half of the failed job is visible
assert partial[0] == 3

# Upstream starts sending amount as text; nothing stops the file landing
con.execute("""COPY (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5, 'c3', 'n/a')) t(order_id, customer_id, amount))
               TO 'lake/orders/part-0003.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)""")
try:
    con.execute("SELECT sum(amount) FROM 'lake/orders/*.parquet'").fetchone()
    raise AssertionError("expected the read to fail")
except duckdb.ConversionException as e:
    print("lake read now fails:", str(e).splitlines()[0][:90])

# Warehouse: a typed table and a transaction. A failure rolls everything back.
con.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id TEXT NOT NULL, amount DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'c1', 120.50), (2, 'c2', 80.00)")
try:
    con.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (3, 'c1', 15.00)")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5, 'c3', 'n/a')")     # rejected by the schema
    con.execute("COMMIT")
except duckdb.ConversionException:
    con.execute("ROLLBACK")
committed = con.execute("SELECT count(*), sum(amount) FROM orders").fetchone()
print("warehouse after failed job:", committed)   # nothing from the failed job
assert committed[0] == 2

The lake showed half of a failed job to every reader, and then a bad file broke every query on the folder long after the job that wrote it. The warehouse rejected the bad row at write time and rolled back the whole job. A lakehouse table format gives lake files the second behaviour: the failed job's files are never committed to the log, so readers never see them, and a write with the wrong schema fails before it commits.

How to choose

  1. Who uses the data? Mostly SQL analysts and dashboards favour a warehouse. Mixed BI, ML and engineering workloads favour a lakehouse.
  2. What data? Large volumes of semi-structured or unstructured data push toward lake storage.
  3. Openness. Open table formats reduce lock-in and let several engines share one copy. If several engines must read the same tables, that requirement often decides the design.
  4. Team skills and operations. A managed warehouse has fewer moving parts. A lakehouse needs people who understand file layout, compaction and catalogs.
  5. Cost profile. Compare storage, compute and data movement for your workload rather than relying on general claims. Copying data into a warehouse costs pipelines and storage; running a lakehouse costs maintenance and engineering time.
  6. Latency and concurrency. High-concurrency BI with tight latency targets is where warehouses are strongest; both can serve it with the right engine.

Decision table

Scenario Leaning Reasoning
Startup with a few sources, analysts writing SQL, dashboards Warehouse Fastest path to trusted SQL; little to operate
Clickstream or IoT at large volume, Spark processing, ML features Lakehouse Cheap storage, many engines, streaming writes with transactions
Raw logs, images, documents kept for future use Lake (raw zone) No need for tables yet; keep it cheap and organised
Regulated reporting with strict access control and auditing Warehouse or governed lakehouse Both work if the catalog and access controls are strong; choose the one the team can govern
Several engines (Spark, Trino, a warehouse) must share one copy Lakehouse with one owning catalog per table Open formats avoid copies; one writer per table avoids conflicts
Existing warehouse that works, plus a new ML team Keep the warehouse, add a lake or lakehouse for ML Migrations are expensive; share curated tables through an open format if needed

Many organisations combine them: raw data in a lake, curated tables in a lakehouse format, and a warehouse or SQL endpoint for BI, often organised as bronze, silver and gold layers.

Warehouses increasingly read and write open table formats such as Iceberg in your storage, and lakehouse platforms offer warehouse-style SQL engines. Focus on the properties you need (transactions, schema enforcement, openness, performance, governance) rather than the label.

Trade-offs to name

  • One copy vs convenience. A lakehouse avoids copying data into a warehouse; a warehouse avoids running table maintenance.
  • Openness vs integration. Open formats let you change engines; a single vendor's storage is better integrated with its optimiser, caching and governance.
  • Flexibility vs trust. Schema-on-read accepts anything quickly and fails later; schema-on-write fails early and protects readers.
  • Multi-engine writes. Several engines can read a table safely; letting several engines write it through different catalogs is how tables get corrupted.

Common mistakes

  1. Treating a lake as a dumping ground with no layers, schemas, ownership or catalog.
  2. Choosing a lakehouse "because it is modern" when the team only needs BI on structured data.
  3. Copying the same data into a lake and a warehouse without a clear source of truth.
  4. Assuming a lakehouse needs no maintenance; small files and old versions accumulate.
  5. Pointing two writers at the same table through different catalogs.
  6. Saying "a lakehouse is just Parquet"; plain Parquet files have no transactions.

In an interview

See the interview answer. Strong answers name the deciding properties rather than reciting definitions: "A lake gives cheap, open storage but no transactions. A warehouse gives transactions, schema enforcement and fast SQL in managed storage. A lakehouse adds a table format to lake files to get most of both, at the cost of running maintenance." Then recommend for the scenario and mention how the layers fit together. Common follow-ups: "How does a table format make a multi-file write atomic?" (the commit to the log or catalog pointer is the atomic step), "Delta or Iceberg?" (Delta vs Iceberg vs Hudi) and "Snowflake or Databricks?" (Snowflake vs Databricks).

Key takeaway

A lake is flexible storage, a warehouse is reliable SQL, and a lakehouse adds reliability to lake storage through an open table format. Choose by users, data types, openness, operations and measured cost, and be explicit about which system owns each table.

title: Vercel MCP now renders deployments as an interactive card
description:
Vercel MCP can now show your deployments as an interactive card inside ChatGPT and other chat clients that support MCP Apps.

The card shows live deployment status, build logs, and source and commit details, with a Visit button once the deployment URL is ready. You can send logs into the chat to debug with the model, or open the fullscreen view to read them beneath the card. For repositories linked to multiple projects, a project list lets you switch between them.

The card is Vercel MCP's first MCP App, built on the MCP Apps extension. Clients without app support receive the deployment state, preview URL, and commit as text instead. The open_deployments tool looks up deployments by project, repository, or commit, with environment filtering. ChatGPT connects to Vercel MCP through its Connectors setup.

title: Branch isolation in a live Supabase app
description:
Short answer

To keep branches apart in one Supabase database, give every branch-owned table a region_id, fill it in for existing rows, make it NOT NULL, stamp it on the server, and let Row Level Security decide which rows each signed-in user gets back. Filtering in React isn't enough, because the browser holds a public key and can ask the database for anything. Check the result with row counts, because RLS hides rows without raising an error.

I built Zarrar Cooling Services (ZCS) on my own: a React and Supabase platform for an appliance repair and cooling business, with a public booking site, an admin panel, a technician panel, and branch views. Version 1 served one branch, Islamabad (which also covers Rawalpindi). Then the business opened a branch in Jhelum.

The requirement sounded simple. Staff in one branch must not see another branch's jobs, payroll, invoices, or stock. The owner must see everything. And the app was live, with real bookings coming in, so I couldn't rebuild it from an empty database.

Most Supabase guides start from an empty database. This one starts from 24 tables of real data: the model I chose, the migration in the order I ran it, the policies, and what I have and haven't tested.

Why the database has to enforce it

Three terms first:

  • Row Level Security (RLS): a PostgreSQL feature that attaches rules (policies) to a table, so every query only sees and changes the rows the rules allow.
  • Publishable (anon) key: the key the React app ships to every browser. Supabase's docs describe publishable keys as safe to expose because they "only reach what Row Level Security allows" (Supabase: API keys).
  • Secret (service_role) key: a server-only key that "bypasses every Row Level Security policy you have" and must never appear in a browser (same source).

So anyone can copy the publishable key from DevTools and query the Data API directly. A region dropdown in React is a convenience; only a policy in Postgres keeps Jhelum's payroll away from an Islamabad technician. In ZCS the /admin routes only checked that you were signed in, so RLS was already the real authorisation layer.

This isn't a theoretical risk. UpGuard found 16,326 Supabase databases with publicly readable tables among about 300,000 domains showing signs of Supabase use, and more than half had indicators of personal data (UpGuard, "Everything, everywhere: systemic data exposure in Supabase apps"; the page is dated 14 Oct 2026, and BleepingComputer covered it on 28 Sep 2026). BleepingComputer summarises the causes as "missing or ineffective row-level security policies and misuse of public keys." OWASP ranks broken access control first in its 2025 Top 10 and says access control "is only effective when implemented in trusted server-side code" (OWASP A01:2025).

Region isolation is not multi-tenancy, but it uses the same tools

A tenant is a separate customer organisation sharing your infrastructure. Tenants must never see each other's data, and nobody on the tenant side sees across tenants. ZCS isn't that. It's one company with several branches, which I'll call regions because that's the name in the schema.

Multi-tenant SaaS compared with ZCS regions

Aspect Multi-tenant SaaS ZCS regions
Who owns the data Different organisations One company
Can anyone see across the boundary? Normally no customer user can Super-admins see every region by design
Shared data Rare Customer records and the services catalogue are shared; each branch only sees customers it has worked for
Cross-boundary reporting Usually forbidden The owner wants it

What carries over is the mechanism: an ID column on every owned row, a table linking users to the IDs they may access, a SECURITY DEFINER helper for that lookup, and policies that use it. For real multi-tenancy the migration steps below still apply, but the trust model usually needs to be stricter, for example no cross-tenant super-users inside the app.

Choosing the model

Before writing any SQL, I compared five options:

The five options I compared

Option What isolates the data Why I chose or rejected it
region_id + RLS (chosen) A column and policies in one database Adding a branch is an INSERT. Existing hooks keep working, because RLS filters what they already ask for. One generated types file. Cross-region reports are a GROUP BY.
Schema per region Separate Postgres schemas Every new branch re-runs the DDL for ~50 tables plus functions and policies. Schemas drift, and the client would have to pick a schema on every request.
Project per region Separate Supabase projects Cost and migrations multiply per branch, and cross-region reporting inside the app becomes impossible.
Hybrid Some tables split, some shared The ops cost of both approaches.
Client-side filter Nothing Not isolation at all.

The deciding argument was "existing hooks keep working": my plan estimated that about 14 pages would need no code changes, because the same select simply returns fewer rows.

The model in the database

Regions are data, not an enum, so a new branch never needs a migration:

  • regions: code, name, tax rate, contact details. A partial unique index makes sure exactly one region has is_default = true; that's Islamabad, the head region.
  • region_cities: a region covers many cities (Islamabad and Rawalpindi are one region). The public booking form uses it to work out the region from the city.
  • user_regions: which region each staff user works in.
  • super_admins: the people who see every region.
  • user_active_region: a super-admin's current choice in the region switcher; NULL means "All regions".

24 tables are region-owned and get a region_id: work orders, invoices, expenses, staff, inventory, suppliers, purchase orders, assets, the payroll tables, notes, reports, activity logs, and invoice settings. Child tables such as attachments and invoice items take the region of their parent. Shared tables (services, system settings) stay global. Customers are a special case: the table has no region_id, and any branch can add to it, but a policy only shows a customer to a branch that has a work order for them.

One function answers "may the current user touch this region?":

Real ZCS helper (migration 20260906101730)

create or replace function public.can_access_region(_region_id uuid)
returns boolean
language sql stable security definer set search_path = public as $$
  select case
    when exists (select 1 from public.super_admins where user_id = auth.uid())
      then coalesce(
             (select region_id from public.user_active_region where user_id = auth.uid())
               = _region_id,
             true)                         -- no active region = "All regions"
    else exists (select 1 from public.user_regions
                 where user_id = auth.uid() and region_id = _region_id)
  end;
$$;

It's SECURITY DEFINER (it runs with its owner's rights) so it can read user_regions and super_admins without triggering their own RLS. A policy that queries another RLS-protected table can recurse into itself. ZCS had already been bitten by that on user_roles and fixed it with the same pattern, which is the standard answer in the Supabase community.

Figure: a request carries the user's JWT; Postgres runs the policy, which asks the helper whether this user may access the row's region. For super-admins, the region switcher narrows what the database returns, because the helper reads user_active_region. That's a scope they choose, not a security boundary. For everyone else, it's only a badge.

Migrating the live app

Working on a copy, then switching

I never migrated the database the website was using. I made a copy of it as a new Supabase project and ran every migration below on that copy. I tested the updated app against it on my computer, and ran the same changes on a local Supabase stack.

When everything passed, I put the site into maintenance mode during off-hours, so nothing new was being written. I copied across the data the live database had gained since the copy was made, then changed the production environment variables so the website points to the new project. The original database is untouched and kept as a backup.

The site was in maintenance mode during the switch, and I didn't time it, so I'm not claiming zero downtime.

A baseline before touching anything

The first step wasn't SQL that changed anything. I counted every row in the 24 region-owned tables as the postgres role, which bypasses RLS: a little under 300 rows in total, plus the customers and auth users. It's a small business; the method matters more than the size. Every later phase had to leave those numbers unchanged. Under RLS, a denied read returns an empty result with no error, so a broken policy looks exactly like an empty table, and "the page loads" proves nothing.

The phases

All of this ran on 6 September 2026. Each phase was its own migration file, created with supabase migration new, applied through the SQL editor, and written with a ROLLBACK block in its header.

The migration phases, all run on 6 September 2026

Phase Change Why it was safe Checked
1 Region tables, helpers, Islamabad seeded Nothing existing touched Total unchanged
2 region_id uuid nullable, no default, on 24 tables Adds a column only; v1 code never mentions it Total unchanged
3 Backfill every row to Islamabad Writes one column, guarded by where region_id is null 0 nulls, total unchanged
4 Every auth user gets an Islamabad user_regions row New table only; fails loudly if a user is missed Every user covered
5 Default, FK, NOT NULL, index, stamping trigger NOT NULL fails if phase 3 missed a row 24 indexes and triggers
6a–6d New region-aware policies next to the old ones Permissive policies combine with OR, so access is unchanged Counts unchanged per group
Tighten Drop the old policies Rolled-back dry run first Same counts afterwards

Adding a nullable column with no default doesn't rewrite the table in PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL: ALTER TABLE). It still takes a short exclusive lock, which is harmless at this size and something to plan for on large tables.

The backfill put every row in Islamabad, even jobs that were really Jhelum work; those moved later, one at a time, through a "Move to region" action. A uniform backfill kept every check to one question: is the total still the same?

Phase 3, abridged (migration 20260906120956).

do $$
declare isb uuid;
begin
  select id into isb from public.regions where code = 'ISB';
  if isb is null then raise exception 'run phase 1 first'; end if;

  update public.work_orders set region_id = isb where region_id is null;
  update public.invoices    set region_id = isb where region_id is null;
  -- … the same for the other 22 tables
end $$;

Phase 5 is where the column became enforced. The trigger matters as much as the constraint:

Phase 5, abridged (migration 20260906122629)

create or replace function public.enforce_region_id() returns trigger
language plpgsql set search_path = public as $$
declare override_txt text := current_setting('app.region_override', true);
begin
  if tg_op = 'INSERT' then
    if override_txt is not null and override_txt <> '' then
      new.region_id := override_txt::uuid;               -- trusted server path
    else
      new.region_id := public.default_region_for_user(); -- ignore what the client sent
    end if;
    return new;
  end if;
  if new.region_id is distinct from old.region_id and not public.is_super_admin() then
    raise exception 'region_id may only be changed by a super-admin';
  end if;
  return new;
end $$;

The browser never chooses a region: on insert the trigger overwrites whatever the client sent, and only trusted server-side functions (public booking, region provisioning) pass a region through a transaction-local setting. On update, region_id is immutable for everyone except super-admins.

Additive policies, then one tightening step

The riskiest part was the policies, so I did them in two moves. In phases 6a–6d, I added a new _rgn_ policy for every operation on every table, written in its final form: the existing role condition AND can_access_region(region_id). Because Postgres combines permissive policies with OR (PostgreSQL: Row Security Policies), the old policies still granted the same access, so nothing changed for users. Work orders went last, because every page touches them.

Then a single migration dropped the old policies, keeping a short list of deliberate exceptions: the public booking insert, staff reading their own record, and the personal notifications inbox. A count check in the step before had already flagged a real problem: every inventory transaction had no location, so none of them had a region, and the new policy would have hidden all of them. So the tightening migration first made that policy accept location-less rows, then dropped the old ones. Before applying it, I ran it inside a transaction as the owner and rolled it back. The dry run showed the expected counts, and I applied it for real.

After the migration

Opening Jhelum on 7–8 September turned up three more issues. The first two came from the row-count check, not from clicking around:

  • Islamabad showed one row more than the baseline. A per-table diff traced the extra one to a test admin account I had created after the baseline, so I updated the baseline instead of "fixing" real data.
  • The new region had no city mapping, so bookings from Jhelum couldn't have found it.
  • default_region_for_user() ignored a super-admin's active region, so anything I created while switched to Jhelum would have been stamped Islamabad. I fixed it and checked it inside a rolled-back transaction.

The policies I implemented

Every region-owned table follows one pattern. This is the work orders UPDATE policy, slightly simplified:

work_orders update policy (slightly simplified)

create policy work_orders_rgn_update on public.work_orders
for update to authenticated
using (
  (assigned_to in (select id from public.staff_members where auth_user_id = auth.uid())
   or public.has_role(auth.uid(), 'admin') or public.has_role(auth.uid(), 'manager'))
  and public.can_access_region(region_id))
with check (
  (assigned_to in (select id from public.staff_members where auth_user_id = auth.uid())
   or public.has_role(auth.uid(), 'admin') or public.has_role(auth.uid(), 'manager'))
  and public.can_access_region(region_id));
  • USING filters the rows you can see or target. A row that fails it is skipped without an error.
  • WITH CHECK tests the row as it will look after an insert or update. A row that fails it raises an error and aborts the whole command (PostgreSQL: CREATE POLICY).
  • TO authenticated keeps anonymous visitors out of these policies entirely.

Authorisation never comes from a value the client sends. The region comes from auth.uid(), the user ID inside the JWT that Supabase has already verified, looked up against user_regions on the server.

Child tables follow their parent through a second SECURITY DEFINER helper, region_of_work_order(id), so an attachment is visible only if its work order's region is.

What I'd change (recommended, not yet done):

  • Move the helpers out of public. Supabase says never to create SECURITY DEFINER functions in an exposed schema, because they become callable through the Data API (Supabase: Row Level Security). Mine only answer yes/no about the caller's own access, but they belong in a private schema.
  • Pin search_path to ''. They use search_path = public; PostgreSQL's guidance is to exclude any schema untrusted users can write to (PostgreSQL: CREATE FUNCTION).
  • Performance. Supabase recommends indexing policy columns and wrapping auth.uid() as (select auth.uid()) (Supabase: RLS performance). region_id is indexed on all 24 tables. I haven't benchmarked the policies; at this size there was nothing to measure.

The gap RLS can't close: foreign keys

PostgreSQL is explicit: "Referential integrity checks, such as unique or primary key constraints and foreign key references, always bypass row security" (PostgreSQL: Row Security Policies).

In practice, if invoices.work_order_id is a plain foreign key, a user in region A who knows the ID of a region B work order can create an invoice in region A that points at it. RLS checks the invoice's own region_id, which is A, so the insert passes. The foreign key check only asks "does this work order exist?", without RLS.

Status in ZCS: child tables inherit their parent's region through policy joins, but the foreign keys between region-owned tables are still plain. Same-region composite foreign keys were deferred during the migration. UUIDs make guessing impractical, but IDs leak through URLs and exports, so I treat this as an open gap. I haven't tested it on the real app.

The fix is to make the foreign key carry the region:

Simplified example (companion demo)

alter table public.work_orders add constraint work_orders_region_id_id_key unique (region_id, id);

alter table public.invoices
  add constraint invoices_work_order_same_region_fkey
  foreign key (region_id, work_order_id)
  references public.work_orders (region_id, id)
  on update cascade;   -- invoices follow when a super-admin moves the work order

In the companion demo (plain PostgreSQL 16 with a Supabase-style mock, not a real Supabase stack), swapping this back to a plain foreign key made the isolation test fail on exactly this case.

Attack scenarios

Attack scenarios and their status in ZCS

What could go wrong What ZCS does Status
Client sends another region's region_id Trigger overwrites it on insert Implemented; phase 5 checks confirmed inserts are stamped with the caller's region
Fetch another region's row by ID USING filters it out Implemented; checked indirectly by the region-removal test below
Move a row to another region Trigger rejects unless super-admin; WITH CHECK also applies Implemented; a region change by a user who isn't a super-admin was rejected in phase 5 checks
Cross-region link through a foreign key Plain foreign keys between region-owned tables Open gap; not tested on the real app
A table left out of the rollout user_roles was missed (see lessons) Found and fixed 12 Sep 2026
Storage The inventory-documents bucket allows any signed-in user Not region-scoped
Realtime postgres_changes checks RLS per subscriber, but Supabase says DELETE events aren't RLS-filtered (see Sources) Known limitation; not tested
Views and RPC The one view uses security_invoker = on; region-changing functions check super-admin status inside Implemented
Setting app.region_override from a client Only set inside server-side functions; the Data API doesn't run arbitrary SQL Reasoned, not tested
service_role key in the browser Only in two Edge Functions; the browser client has the publishable key only Verified by reading the code

Testing: what I did and what's still to do

Done, before the switch: on a local Supabase stack and on the migrated copy, I worked through every table, form and field by hand, including a newly created region. I didn't keep a written checklist of those runs, so I'm not listing individual results.

Done, on the migrated project (now the live one):

  • Row counts against the baseline after every phase, as listed above.
  • A structural check that every region-owned table has region_id NOT NULL, an index on it, and RLS enabled. I proved the check could fail by running it against a table that should fail.
  • The rolled-back dry run before dropping the old policies, then the same counts after applying it.
  • The region-removal test. An admin who isn't a super-admin, assigned to Islamabad, saw all of the roughly 160 work orders (at that point every work order was Islamabad's). With their region assignment removed inside a rolled-back transaction, the same admin saw 0. The role stayed the same; only the region changed, so the region check controls access.

Not done yet: a two-region test where an Islamabad user and a Jhelum user each try to read, insert, update, delete, move and cross-link the other's data. That's the next test I'd add:

  1. Run it on a local stack or a Supabase branch, never production.
  2. Act as real users (the authenticated role plus JWT claims, or real sign-ins). Running as postgres or with the service_role key bypasses RLS and proves nothing.
  3. Count rows: assert "0 rows affected", not just "no exception".
  4. Check each user still sees their own data; a policy that hides everything passes every isolation check.
  5. Cover anonymous access, joins, views, RPC functions and the foreign key case.

The companion demo does this on a simplified four-table schema: eight checks, including a super-admin moving a work order and its invoice following along. All eight pass. I also planted one leak per run to show the test can fail. A plain foreign key, an extra using (true) policy, a region helper that always says yes, and an anon grant were each caught. Making the stamping trigger a no-op did not fail the test, because WITH CHECK blocked the cross-region writes on its own. That's a useful result in itself: the trigger keeps data correctly filed; RLS is the security boundary.

Lessons

  1. Counts beat clicking around. Comparing row counts caught the location-less inventory rows, the extra admin and the missing city mapping. None of them would have shown up as an error.
  2. Add first, then tighten. Running new policies alongside the old ones made the risky step a single, reversible migration with a dry run.
  3. The table you forget is the hole. Phase 6 covered 24 region-owned tables and their children, but not user_roles. Until I fixed it on 12 September, any admin in any region could read and change any role row, including the owner's. The fix added region scoping and made super-admin rows untouchable by anyone else.
  4. Backstops have to actually stop. I expected NOT NULL to catch records created in "All regions" mode, where there's no single region to inherit. It didn't, because the default falls back to the head region, so a few create buttons the UI guard missed filed assets and suppliers into Islamabad without telling anyone. I've since routed every create button through the guard; a live walk-through in All mode is still on my list. Silent fallbacks need a visible marker; work orders that land in the head region by fallback now carry a "Default" badge.
  5. Authentication isn't authorisation. Being signed in got you into /admin. Only the policies decide what you see once you're there.

Checklist

  • Baseline row counts captured, unfiltered, before any change
  • region_id added nullable, backfilled with an idempotent update, then made NOT NULL with an index and a foreign key
  • Region stamped server-side; client-supplied values ignored; changes allowed only for trusted roles
  • New policies added alongside the old ones, then the old ones dropped after a rolled-back dry run
  • Every table checked, including role, audit and join tables
  • Foreign keys between region-owned tables include region_id
  • Helper functions are SECURITY DEFINER, in a non-exposed schema, with a pinned search_path
  • Views use security_invoker; Storage buckets and Realtime reviewed
  • service_role key on the server only
  • Isolation test as real users, counting rows, run before every schema change

Conclusion

Adding branches to a live Supabase app came down to a small number of database rules, applied in an order where each step could be checked and undone. The SQL was the easy part. The practical takeaway: write down your row counts before you start, and treat any count that changes unexpectedly as a stop sign, because under RLS a mistake doesn't throw an error. It just shows less data.

FAQ

Is the Supabase publishable (anon) key safe to put in the browser?
Yes, it's designed to be public, but only because Row Level Security decides what it can reach. With RLS off or a policy missing, anyone holding the key can read that table through the Data API. The secret (service_role) key bypasses RLS and must stay on the server.

Is region or branch isolation the same as multi-tenancy?
No. Multi-tenancy separates different organisations that must never see each other's data. Branch isolation separates parts of one company, often with super-users who see everything and some shared data. Both use the same tools: an ID column, a membership table and RLS policies.

Do foreign keys bypass RLS in Supabase?
Yes. PostgreSQL runs foreign key checks without applying row security, so a row can reference another branch's row if its ID is known. Including the branch column in the foreign key, (region_id, parent_id) → parent(region_id, id), keeps references inside one branch.

How do I test Supabase RLS policies?
Act as a real user by switching to the authenticated role with that user's JWT claims, never as postgres or service_role. Try to read, insert, update, delete and link another branch's rows, and assert on row counts, because RLS hides rows without raising errors. Also confirm each user still sees their own data.

Can I add a region_id column to a live Supabase table safely?
Adding a nullable column with no default only changes PostgreSQL's catalogue and doesn't rewrite the table, though it briefly takes an exclusive lock. Backfill existing rows next, then add NOT NULL, the foreign key and an index, which all validate the data and fail if anything was missed. Rehearse on a copy first and compare row counts before and after.

Code: the foreign key example comes from a simplified companion demo (four tables, not the ZCS schema), run on plain PostgreSQL with a Supabase-style mock.

AI note: I built ZCS with AI coding agents, mainly Claude Code, alongside Cursor and Antigravity. I made the design decisions, ran each migration and checked it with the counts described here.

Sources

  • UpGuard, Everything, everywhere: systemic data exposure in Supabase apps (page dated 14 Oct 2026; checked 4 Nov 2026)
  • BleepingComputer, Misconfigured Supabase apps expose data in over 16,000 databases (28 Sep 2026; checked 4 Nov 2026)
  • OWASP, A01:2025 Broken Access Control
  • Supabase, API keys
  • Supabase, Row Level Security
  • Supabase, RLS performance and best practices
  • Supabase, Postgres Changes (Realtime)
  • Supabase, Storage buckets: fundamentals
  • Supabase community, RLS recursion and security definer functions, discussion #4509
  • PostgreSQL, Row Security Policies
  • PostgreSQL, CREATE POLICY
  • PostgreSQL, ALTER TABLE
  • PostgreSQL, CREATE FUNCTION: writing SECURITY DEFINER functions safely
  • PostgreSQL, CREATE VIEW: security_invoker

title: Cleaning Up Stale Policy Routing: Removing Orphaned VPN Rules from the Kernel Table
description:
ip route says the box has a clean default route through the LAN gateway. Then you run ip route get 10.0.0.50 and the kernel picks a path that isn't in that output at all. That gap exists because ip route only shows you the main table. The kernel checks the policy rule list first, and a VPN that died without cleaning up can leave rules there that nobody is looking at.

This post is for anyone running Tailscale, WireGuard (wg-quick), OpenVPN with policy routing, or any homegrown split-tunnel setup on Linux hosts, LXCs, or routers. If you've ever had a host where "some traffic works and some doesn't" after a VPN restart, the policy routing database is where I'd look first.

How the kernel actually picks a route

A Linux routing decision has two layers, and most tutorials only teach the second one.

  1. The rule list (RPDB). An ordered list of rules, checked from lowest priority number to highest. Each rule has a selector (source, fwmark, input interface, etc.) and an action (usually "look up table N").
  2. The routing tables. Each table is a separate set of routes. main is the one ip route shows. There can be up to 2^32 of them.

Rules are evaluated in order. If a rule says lookup 52 and table 52 has a matching route, that route wins and evaluation stops. If table 52 has no match, the kernel falls through to the next rule. If the rule's action is unreachable, blackhole, or prohibit, evaluation stops right there and the packet dies.

A freshly booted box looks like this:

$ ip rule show
0:      from all lookup local
32766:  from all lookup main
32767:  from all lookup default

Three rules. Everything else on your system was added by something: a VPN client, a CNI plugin, NetworkManager, a script you forgot about.

What VPN clients add (and what they leave behind)

Here's what a host running Tailscale and a wg-quick tunnel looks like:

$ ip rule show
0:      from all lookup local
5210:   from all fwmark 0x80000/0xff0000 lookup main
5230:   from all fwmark 0x80000/0xff0000 lookup default
5250:   from all fwmark 0x80000/0xff0000 unreachable
5270:   from all lookup 52
32764:  from all lookup main suppress_prefixlength 0
32765:  not from all fwmark 0xca6c lookup 51820
32766:  from all lookup main
32767:  from all lookup default

The 52xx block is Tailscale: its own traffic (marked with 0x80000) goes via the normal tables, and everything else consults table 52, where Tailscale puts routes for tailnet IPs and advertised subnets. The 3276x block is wg-quick with AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0: unmarked traffic goes to table 51820 (the tunnel), and the suppress_prefixlength 0 rule lets more-specific routes in main still win.

When these tools shut down cleanly, they remove their rules. When they don't (SIGKILL, OOM kill, a container stopped hard, a binary run by hand in a tmux session that got nuked, an uninstall while the daemon was still running), the rules stay. The kernel doesn't know or care that the process that created them is gone.

Not every orphan is equally dangerous

This is the part the docs don't really spell out. When a network interface is deleted, the kernel removes every route whose nexthop device was that interface. So if tailscale0 disappears, table 52 typically empties itself out. A stale 5270: from all lookup 52 pointing at an empty table just falls through to the next rule. It's clutter, but it isn't actively breaking anything.

The orphans that actually hurt fall into a few categories:

  • Terminal action rules. A leftover unreachable, blackhole, or prohibit rule kills matching packets outright. Tailscale's 5250 rule only matches its own fwmark, so it's mostly inert once the daemon is gone. But a custom kill-switch rule like from 10.0.0.0/24 unreachable from an OpenVPN up-script will black-hole that whole source range forever.
  • Tables with gateway routes, not device routes. A route like default via 10.0.0.1 table 100 isn't bound to a VPN interface, so the kernel has no reason to remove it. The rule still points at it, and traffic quietly takes a path you thought you'd torn down.
  • Blackhole/throw routes inside the table. Some kill-switch setups put blackhole default in the VPN table so traffic fails closed when the tunnel drops. That's a great design until the VPN is uninstalled and the fail-closed route stays.
  • Duplicates from restart loops. Scripts that run ip rule add without checking first stack up identical rules on every restart. The behavior doesn't change, but cleanup stops being "delete one rule" and starts being "delete it until it stops existing".
  • Interface-bound rules on a recreated interface. A rule like iif wg0 lookup 200 stays around after wg0 is deleted and shows [detached]. If something later creates a new wg0 for a different purpose, the old rule reattaches to it.

That last one is a good canary, so it gets its own grep:

# Rules referencing an interface that no longer exists show [detached]
ip rule show | grep detached
ip -6 rule show | grep detached

Detecting stale rules

My forensic approach: check every rule's table against the actual route state, flag empty tables, and separately list anything with a terminal action. Here's a script I'd drop on any box that has run a VPN:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# audit-policy-routing.sh: flag policy rules that look orphaned
set -uo pipefail

for fam in -4 -6; do
  echo "=== IPv${fam#-} ==="
  # Rules that do a table lookup; skip the three built-ins
  ip "$fam" -j rule show | jq -r '.[] | select(.table != null)
    | "\(.priority) \(.table)"' |
  while read -r prio table; do
    case "$table" in local|main|default) continue ;; esac
    count=$(ip "$fam" route show table "$table" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
    [ "$count" -eq 0 ] && echo "prio $prio -> table $table is EMPTY"
  done

  # Rules that drop packets without consulting any table
  ip "$fam" rule show | grep -E 'unreachable|blackhole|prohibit' \
    | sed 's/^/terminal: /'

  # Rules bound to interfaces that no longer exist
  ip "$fam" rule show | grep detached | sed 's/^/detached: /'
done

An empty table doesn't automatically mean "stale" (Tailscale's table 52 is briefly empty during startup, for example), so treat the output as a list of suspects, not a list of things to delete.

The inverse check is just as useful: tables that hold routes but have no rule pointing at them. They're inert, but they tell you which tool was here.

# Every table that currently holds routes, with a route count
ip route show table all | grep -oE 'table [^ ]+' | sort | uniq -c

Once you have a suspect, ip route get answers the only question that matters: what does the kernel actually do with this packet right now?

# Which path does traffic to this destination take?
ip route get 10.0.0.50
# Simulate traffic carrying a specific fwmark
ip route get 10.0.0.50 mark 0x80000
# Simulate traffic arriving from a specific source
ip route get 1.1.1.1 from 10.0.0.20 iif eth0

If the output mentions table 51820 or a dev that's down and you aren't expecting it, you've found your culprit.

Removing them surgically

ip rule del deletes the first rule that matches whatever selectors you give it. Give it too few and it'll happily delete something you wanted to keep. My habit is to always pass the priority plus the full selector, copied straight out of ip rule show:

# Remove the stale wg-quick pair (copy selectors exactly from ip rule show)
ip rule del priority 32765 not fwmark 0xca6c table 51820
ip rule del priority 32764 table main suppress_prefixlength 0

# Then flush the table they pointed at
ip route flush table 51820

# Don't forget IPv6: it has a completely separate rule list
ip -6 rule del priority 32765 not fwmark 0xca6c table 51820
ip -6 route flush table 51820

The IPv6 side is the one people miss. ip rule without -6 only shows IPv4. wg-quick with ::/0 in AllowedIPs installs both, and if you only clean up v4 you get a host where IPv4 works and anything preferring IPv6 hangs. That's a fun one to debug from the application layer.

For Tailscale's set, the priorities are stable, so this is mechanical:

# Remove all four Tailscale rules (v4 and v6), then empty table 52
for fam in -4 -6; do
  for prio in 5210 5230 5250 5270; do
    ip "$fam" rule del priority "$prio" 2>/dev/null
  done
  ip "$fam" route flush table 52 2>/dev/null
done

Before doing this by hand, though: tailscaled --cleanup exists and does exactly this, plus its netfilter chains. Prefer the tool's own cleanup when it has one.

For duplicates, loop until the delete fails:

# Delete every rule at priority 100 (only if you're sure all of them are stale)
while ip rule del priority 100 2>/dev/null; do :; done

Afterwards, verify with the same commands you used to diagnose: ip rule show, ip -6 rule show, and an ip route get against the destination that was misbehaving.

Stopping them from coming back

Manual cleanup is fine once. If a VPN service crashes regularly, you want the unit itself to guarantee a clean state on both ends. The official tailscaled.service already does this with ExecStartPre and ExecStopPost calling --cleanup, and it's a pattern worth copying for anything that adds its own rules:

# /etc/systemd/system/my-vpn.service.d/routing-cleanup.conf
[Service]
# "-" prefix: don't fail the unit if the rule is already gone
ExecStartPre=-/usr/sbin/ip rule del priority 5000
ExecStartPre=-/usr/sbin/ip route flush table 100
ExecStopPost=-/usr/sbin/ip rule del priority 5000
ExecStopPost=-/usr/sbin/ip route flush table 100
ExecStopPost=-/usr/sbin/ip -6 rule del priority 5000
ExecStopPost=-/usr/sbin/ip -6 route flush table 100

ExecStopPost runs after the main process exits for any reason, including a crash or an OOM kill, which is exactly the case where the client's own cleanup never ran. ExecStartPre covers the remaining gap: whatever state the last run left behind, the next start begins clean. Run systemctl daemon-reload after adding the drop-in.

If you write your own up-scripts, make rule creation idempotent instead of relying on cleanup alone:

# Add the rule only if an identical one isn't already present
ip rule show | grep -q '^5000:.*lookup 100' \
  || ip rule add priority 5000 from 10.0.0.0/24 lookup 100

Gotchas

You're probably looking in the wrong namespace. Rules live in a network namespace. A VPN running inside an unprivileged LXC (like the setup in my Tailscale kernel TUN in unprivileged LXC post) writes rules into the container's namespace, not the host's. Running ip rule on the Proxmox host shows you nothing useful. Either exec into the container or enter its namespace from the host:

# Inspect the namespace of a container's init process from the host
nsenter -t <container-init-pid> -n ip rule show

The flip side is Docker containers with network_mode: host and NET_ADMIN. Those write straight into the host's rule list, and they never show up when you go looking at "the VPN config."

Rules that survive a reboot aren't orphans. Kernel rules are not persistent. A reboot clears them. If a stale-looking rule is back after a reboot, something is reinstalling it: a post-up line in /etc/network/interfaces, routing-policy in a netplan file, NetworkManager ipv4.routing-rules on a connection profile, or a forgotten systemd unit. Deleting it at runtime only fixes it until the next boot. grep -r for the table number across /etc is the fastest way to find the source.

Don't flush the wrong table. ip route flush table main on a remote box ends your SSH session along with everything else. Same with deleting priority 32766. If you're cleaning up over SSH, schedule a rollback before you start (systemd-run --on-active=5m systemctl restart networking, or the equivalent for your stack) and cancel it once you've confirmed you still have a shell.

Numeric vs named tables. If /etc/iproute2/rt_tables maps 51820 to a name, ip rule show prints the name, not the number. The JSON output does the same. My audit script handles both since it passes whatever it reads back to ip route show table, but grep patterns written for numbers will miss named tables.

Subnet routers amplify this. A stale rule on a laptop breaks the laptop. A stale rule on a box acting as a Tailscale subnet router breaks routing for everything behind it, and the symptom shows up on clients that have no VPN installed at all. That's where I'd run the audit script first.

Alternatives I considered. You can run each VPN in its own network namespace (or VRF) so its rules die with the namespace. That's the cleanest isolation and the right answer for anything multi-tenant. For a single host running one or two tunnels, it adds more moving parts than the problem deserves, and the systemd drop-in gets you 95% of the benefit.

Wrap-up

Policy routing is invisible plumbing. It's a lot like the DNS search-path layer I wrote about in Wildcard DNS + ndots:5: it works silently until it doesn't, and the standard diagnostic command (ip route, dig) doesn't show you the layer that's misbehaving. Get in the habit of running ip rule show, ip -6 rule show, and ip route get whenever traffic behaves differently from what the main table says it should.

Reach for this cleanup after any VPN crash or uninstall, when a host has partial connectivity that ip route can't explain, or when you inherit a box with an unclear history. Then fix it properly with a cleanup drop-in on the unit, so the next crash doesn't put you back here. If you're running into this sort of thing across a fleet rather than one box, it's the kind of Day 2 networking work I help with through GuatuLabs.

title: Java 17 y CVE-2026-114938, la falla de 9,2 sin confirmar
description:
Java 17 quedó este martes ante CVE-2026-114938, una falla de ejecución remota de código sin autenticación reportada con nota 9,2 que afectaría a OpenJDK 17.0.6 y posteriores. The Hacker News publicó la advertencia el 17 de noviembre con una precisión que manda en la historia: los detalles técnicos siguen sin confirmación oficial y el registro del fallo permanece reservado, sin descripción pública.

Ejecución remota de código, RCE por sus siglas en inglés, significa que un atacante ejecuta órdenes dentro de un sistema ajeno desde fuera. Si el reporte coreano se sostiene, la puerta quedaría abierta sin pasar por una pantalla de acceso: ni usuario ni contraseña. La raíz atribuida al fallo es una corrupción de memoria.

La primera señal salió de Corea del Sur. Seoul Economic Daily contó que el Centro Nacional de Ciberseguridad, bajo el Servicio Nacional de Inteligencia, envió el 17 de noviembre un aviso a las instituciones públicas titulado «Recomendaciones para prepararse ante el anuncio de una vulnerabilidad de Java». El aviso pide revisar los entornos donde corre Java y preparar las actualizaciones.

El alcance reportado preocupa por el calendario. OpenJDK 17.0.6 salió en enero de 2023, así que la falla cubriría casi cuatro años de actualizaciones de la rama 17, la de soporte extendido que más servidores mantienen en producción. Java sostiene finanzas, comercio electrónico y servicios públicos en Corea del Sur, y el patrón se repite en América Latina y Estados Unidos.

La empresa de superficie de ataque watchTowr reconoció los reportes en X y advirtió que los detalles técnicos seguían sin confirmarse. Esa cautela tiene base: ningún fabricante publicó una versión corregida ni una descripción técnica, no existe código de prueba público y ningún organismo reportó ataques en curso. El fallo tampoco aparece en el catálogo de vulnerabilidades explotadas de la Agencia de Ciberseguridad y Seguridad de Infraestructuras de Estados Unidos, una ausencia esperable mientras su registro siga sin publicarse.

Oracle confirma 11 parches para Java, con nota máxima de 8,1



Lo que Oracle sí confirmó es más estrecho y llega hoy mismo. The Hacker News revisó el aviso previo de noviembre y contó 11 parches nuevos para Java SE, todos explotables de forma remota sin autenticación, dentro de una tanda de 652 correcciones para el conjunto de productos de la compañía. La nota más alta del bloque de Java queda en 8,1 con la escala CVSS 3.1, la que usa Oracle.

Las dos cifras no se comparan de frente. El 9,2 atribuido a CVE-2026-114938 usa la escala CVSS 4.0 y viene del reporte coreano; el 8,1 de Oracle usa CVSS 3.1 y cubre solo los fallos que la empresa lista en su aviso. Nada en la documentación pública permite afirmar que el fallo de OpenJDK sea uno de esos 11, y Oracle no publica identificadores ni componentes antes del día de salida. El parcheo lento en Java ya dejó una factura medida este mes, con empresas que tardaron semanas en cerrar fallos conocidos.

Las versiones con parche anunciado cubren Java SE 8u511, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5 y 27.0.1, más GraalVM para JDK 17.0.21 y 21.0.13 y JavaFX 21.0.13, 25.0.5 y 27.0.1. El portal de operaciones de Java lista las compilaciones de reemplazo programadas: 17.0.21.1 para la rama 17, 21.0.13.1 para la 21, 11.0.33.1, 8u513, 25.0.5.1 y 27.0.1.1. Oracle recomienda dejar de usar las compilaciones actuales tras la actualización de hoy.

El hueco queda en el lado abierto. El aviso de Oracle habla de sus productos y no nombra a OpenJDK, la base de código abierto de la que salen las distribuciones que empaquetan Linux y otros fabricantes. El Grupo de Vulnerabilidades de OpenJDK, que coordina esos anuncios, no traía un aviso más nuevo que el del 24 de octubre, así que el estado del parche para esas distribuciones sigue sin respuesta escrita.

Inventario hoy, parche en cuanto salga la compilación



El aviso coreano deja tareas concretas para cualquier equipo que opere Java, viva o no en Seúl. Primero, inventario: versión exacta, compilación y sistema operativo de cada entorno en uso. Después, la lista de sistemas conectados a internet, con el acceso externo que no haga falta bloqueado antes de que el detalle técnico se haga público.

La preparación incluye dos pasos que suelen dejarse para tarde. Uno es revisar la compatibilidad de cada producto con la versión nueva, para que el parche no tumbe una aplicación el día que llega. El otro es dejar listos respaldo y recuperación, para actualizar en cuanto la compilación corregida aparezca.

El calendario ayuda a ordenar la urgencia sin inventarla. Los reportes coreanos sitúan la divulgación completa, con parches, a las 6 de la mañana del miércoles 18 de noviembre en hora de Corea, la 1 de la tarde del martes 17 en la costa del Pacífico. Oracle estrenó en mayo un ciclo mensual de parches entre sus actualizaciones trimestrales grandes, y el 17 de noviembre ya constaba como fecha de este mes en su plan de septiembre.

Para quien administra servidores, la lectura práctica es corta: Java 17 es el entorno a revisar primero, la nota de 9,2 es un reporte atribuido y no un hecho cerrado, y las 11 correcciones de Oracle sí tienen fecha y compilaciones de reemplazo con nombre propio. Cuando el Grupo de Vulnerabilidades de OpenJDK publique su aviso, se sabrá si CVE-2026-114938 era uno de los fallos de esta tanda o un problema aparte.

Fuente: The Hacker News

title: Vercel Connect adds webhook triggers for more providers
description:
Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend, X, Twilio, Notion, and Telegram.

Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you.

To get started:

  1. Open Vercel Connect in the dashboard. Enable triggers when creating a connector for your provider or in an existing connector’s settings. Connect registers webhooks automatically for Resend and Telegram.

  2. For Twilio, Notion, and X, use the webhook URL from Connect and follow its instructions to complete setup in the provider’s settings.

  3. Add a trigger destination to choose the project and endpoint that should receive events.

You can turn triggers on or off later in the connector’s settings.

In the connector’s Observability tab, select Live to watch incoming trigger events.

These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear.

title: Oracle AI Database 26ai(23.26.4): Streaming Windowing Table Functions
description:
Analyzing time-based data is a common requirement in modern database applications. Oracle AI Database 26ai(RU 23.26.4) introduces four SQL streaming windowing table functions that simplify this type of analysis by dividing table rows into time-based windows.

These functions are:

  • TUMBLE: Divides rows into consecutive, non-overlapping time windows.
  • HOP: Creates sliding time windows that can overlap or have gaps.
  • CUMULATE: Creates expanding time windows with a common starting point.
  • SESSIONS: Groups rows into sessions based on the time interval between consecutive events.

Each function accepts a datetime column and interval parameters to determine how rows are assigned to windows. The returned result includes two additional columns, WINDOW_START and WINDOW_END, which identify the time boundaries of each window.

In this article, we will explore how these four functions work and demonstrate their practical applications using customer activity data.

1. How Streaming Windowing Functions Work

Before exploring the individual functions, it is useful to understand how Oracle assigns records to time windows.

A windowing function takes a table, a datetime column, and interval values to divide records into time periods.

The general syntax is:

function_name (
    table_name,
    COLUMNS (datetime_column),
    interval_arguments
)

The result contains the original columns from the input table, together with two additional columns:

WINDOW_START: The timestamp representing the beginning of the window.
WINDOW_END: The timestamp representing the end of the window.
These two columns allow us to identify the time range associated with each record.

For example, the following query creates one-hour windows using the event_time column:

SELECT *
FROM TUMBLE (
    sales,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '1' HOUR
);

In this example, Oracle uses the value of event_time to determine which one-hour period contains each sales record.

An important detail is how Oracle handles the beginning and ending points of a window. The starting time is included, but the ending time is not.

In other words:

WINDOW_START <= event_time < WINDOW_END

For example, with one-hour windows, a record timestamped at 11:00 belongs to the 11:00–12:00 window rather than the 10:00–11:00 window.

This boundary rule ensures that records occurring exactly between two consecutive windows are assigned consistently.

2. Four Different Approaches to Time-Based Analysis

Although the four functions share the same general purpose, their behavior can produce significantly different results.

Let’s examine each one and see how it can be used in real-world scenarios.

2.1. TUMBLE: Organizing Data into Fixed Time Periods

Sometimes we need to summarize information within predefined time intervals. For example, a business might want to know how many transactions occurred during every 10-minute period.

It divides the timeline into consecutive windows of equal duration. Each record with a non-null datetime value is assigned to one window, so records are not repeated across different windows.

Consider the following timeline:

10:00 - 10:10
10:10 - 10:20
10:20 - 10:30
10:30 - 10:40

Each interval represents an independent reporting period.

Practical implementation

In our example, we have a table called user_activities containing customer information, activity timestamps, and transaction amounts.

SQL> CREATE TABLE user_activities (
  2      activity_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  3      first_name  VARCHAR2(30),
  4      last_name   VARCHAR2(30),
  5      event_time  TIMESTAMP,
  6      amount      NUMBER(10,2)
  7  );
Table created


SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (1, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:01:00', 120);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (2, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:04:00', 250);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (3, 'Masoud', 'Sori',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:06:00', 180);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (4, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:08:00', 300);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (5, 'Masoud', 'Sori',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:12:00', 200);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (6, 'Kourosh', 'Barmak',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:14:00', 150);
1 row inserted

SQL> 
SQL> INSERT INTO user_activities VALUES
  2  (7, 'Vahid', 'Yousefzadeh',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:25:00', 400);
1 row inserted

  2  (10, 'Masoud', 'Sori',
  3   TIMESTAMP '2026-11-14 10:40:00', 500);
1 row inserted

SQL> COMMIT;
Commit complete

We want to calculate the number of transactions and their total value for every customer within each 10-minute period.

The following query demonstrates this approach:

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS transaction_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM TUMBLE (
    vahid.user_activities,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
)
     GROUP BY
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
ORDER BY
    window_start,
    first_name; 

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     TRANSACTION_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ ----------------- ------------
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   1          180
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   3          670
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM                   1          150

Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   2          620
