7 rows selected.

As the results demonstrate, Oracle groups transactions according to their timestamps. For example, Vahid has three transactions in the first 10-minute period, with a combined amount of 670.

2.2. HOP: Analyzing Data Across Overlapping Periods

There are situations where fixed reporting periods are not sufficient. We may want to evaluate recent activity more frequently while still considering a longer time range.

For these requirements, HOP provides a different approach.

Instead of moving from one completed window to the next without overlap, HOP creates windows at regular intervals. The starting point of each new window is determined by the slide parameter, while the size parameter controls its duration.

For example, consider a configuration with:

Window size: 10 minutes.
Slide interval: 5 minutes.
The resulting windows can look like this:

09:55 - 10:05
10:00 - 10:10
10:05 - 10:15
10:10 - 10:20
10:15 - 10:25

Because each new window starts before the previous one has finished, a record may participate in multiple windows.

Practical implementation

Using the same user_activities dataset, we can examine the transaction results produced by overlapping 10-minute windows.

The following results demonstrate how the same customer’s activities can appear in different windows.

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS transaction_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM HOP (
    vahid.user_activities,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '5' MINUTE,
    INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
)
GROUP BY
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
    ORDER BY
    window_start,
    first_name;

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     TRANSACTION_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ ----------------- ------------
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 09.55.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM                   2          370
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   1          180
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   3          670
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   2          380
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   1          300
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM                   1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM                   1          200
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.20.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   2          620
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.35.00.000000 AM                   2          620
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.35.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.45.00.000000 AM                   1          500
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.40.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.50.00.000000 AM                   1          500

14 rows selected.

The output contains more rows than the TUMBLE example because the same activity can contribute to multiple overlapping time windows.

This behavior allows us to examine transaction activity from different time perspectives without changing the original dataset.

2.3. CUMULATE: Building Progressively Larger Time Windows
Another interesting requirement is comparing activity at different stages of a reporting period.

For example, we might want to examine transaction totals after 5 minutes, 10 minutes, and 15 minutes, while keeping the same starting point.

CUMULATE provides this capability.

It creates multiple windows that begin at the same timestamp. Each subsequent window extends the ending timestamp by a predefined step until the maximum configured duration is reached.

Consider a step of 5 minutes and a maximum duration of 15 minutes:

10:00 - 10:05
10:00 - 10:10
10:00 - 10:15

The next group of windows starts at the following 15-minute boundary:

10:15 - 10:20
10:15 - 10:25
10:15 - 10:30

This arrangement allows us to compare different stages of the same reporting interval.

Practical implementation

Using our customer activity table, the following query generates progressively expanding windows with a 5-minute step and a maximum size of 15 minutes.

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS transaction_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM CUMULATE (
    vahid.user_activities,
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '5' MINUTE,
    INTERVAL '15' MINUTE
)
GROUP BY
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
    ORDER BY
    window_start,
    window_end,
    first_name;

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     TRANSACTION_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ ----------------- ------------
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.05.00.000000 AM                   2          370
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   1          180
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.10.00.000000 AM                   3          670
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   2          380
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.00.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM                   3          670
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   1          350
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.15.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM                   2          620
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.30.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.45.00.000000 AM                   1          500

10 rows selected.

The results show how Oracle produces different window boundaries for the same starting period. This makes it possible to compare transaction activity over progressively longer durations.

An important configuration requirement is that the maximum window size must be an integer multiple of the step. For example, a 15-minute maximum size is compatible with a 5-minute step.

2.4. SESSIONS: Identifying Continuous Periods of Activity

The previous functions use predefined time intervals to organize records. However, some business requirements are based on user behavior rather than fixed clock periods.

Consider a website where a customer performs several actions. We may want to consider consecutive actions part of the same session as long as the customer does not remain inactive for too long.

This is where SESSIONS becomes useful.

Instead of relying on a fixed window size, it examines the timestamps of consecutive records. A configured inactivity gap determines whether a record continues an existing session or starts a new one.

For example, if the maximum gap is 10 minutes, activities separated by 3 or 5 minutes can remain in the same session. However, when the interval between consecutive activities exceeds 10 minutes, a new session begins.

Another useful feature is PARTITION BY. It allows us to separate records according to one or more column values before identifying sessions.

This is especially important when analyzing multiple customers because each customer should have an independent activity history.

Practical implementation

In our example, we use the customer’s first and last names as partitioning columns. This ensures that activities from different customers are evaluated separately.

The session gap is configured to 10 minutes.

SQL> SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name,
    window_start,
   window_end,
    COUNT(*) AS activity_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM SESSIONS (
    Vahid.user_activities PARTITION BY (first_name, last_name),
    COLUMNS (event_time),
    INTERVAL '10' MINUTE
)
GROUP BY
    first_name,
   last_name,
    window_start,
    window_end
ORDER BY
    first_name,
    window_start; 

FIRST_NAME   LAST_NAME      WINDOW_START                   WINDOW_END                     ACTIVITY_COUNT TOTAL_AMOUNT
------------ -------------- ------------------------------ ------------------------------ -------------- ------------
Kourosh      Barmak         14-NOV-26 10.14.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.24.00.000000 AM                1          150
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.06.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.32.00.000000 AM                3          730
Masoud       Sori           14-NOV-26 10.40.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.50.00.000000 AM                1          500
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.01.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.18.00.000000 AM                3          670
Vahid        Yousefzadeh    14-NOV-26 10.25.00.000000 AM   14-NOV-26 10.39.00.000000 AM                2          620

The output identifies separate activity sessions for each customer.

For example, Masoud has two sessions. His first session contains three activities, while the second contains one activity. Vahid also has two separate sessions because the inactivity between his activities exceeds the configured gap.

title: File Reader And Buffered Reader
description:
FileReader and BufferedReader in Java

Java provides different classes to read data from files. Two commonly used classes are FileReader and BufferedReader.

Let's understand them with simple examples.

  1. FileReader

FileReader is used to read characters from a text file.

Example:

Assume we have a file called sample.txt:

Hello Java
Welcome to File Handling

Java Code:

import java.io.FileReader;

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

    FileReader reader = new FileReader("sample.txt");

    int data;

    while ((data = reader.read()) != -1) {
        System.out.print((char) data);
    }

    reader.close();
}

}

Explanation:

FileReader opens the file.

read() reads one character at a time.

-1 indicates the end of the file.

close() closes the file.

  1. BufferedReader

BufferedReader is used to read text efficiently. It also provides a method called readLine() to read a complete line.

Java Code:

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.FileReader;

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

    FileReader file = new FileReader("sample.txt");

    BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(file);

    String line;

    while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
        System.out.println(line);
    }

    reader.close();
}

}

Explanation:

FileReader opens the file.

BufferedReader reads the file using a buffer.

readLine() reads one complete line.

null indicates the end of the file.

close() closes the reader.

title: Autopsy #10: The Multi-Tab WebSocket Storm & Backpressure Collapse
description:
80,000 Sockets From 10,000 Users

A dashboard feature PR enabled per-widget live ticker subscriptions inside useRealtimeFeed(). In single-tab local tests against a 5 msg/s mock stream, CPU usage stayed under 3% and every integration spec passed.

At market open, 10,000 power users with 6 to 10 open browser tabs hit a 400 msg/s price burst. Edge telemetry recorded 80,000 concurrent WebSockets, RUM p95 INP jumped to 1,840 ms, and when one gateway node recycled, all 80,000 sockets reconnected in lockstep and triggered a 14-minute 503 storm.

  • T+00:00: Market open triggers a 400 msg/s upstream price burst across 10,000 active browser sessions.
  • T+02:00: Edge telemetry records 80,000 concurrent WebSocket connections from users keeping 6 to 10 tabs open.
  • T+04:30: RUM p95 INP jumps from 38 ms to 1,840 ms as each browser runs 3,200 JSON.parse() calls/sec across 8 main threads.
  • T+07:00: A gateway node recycles, dropping 80,000 sockets and triggering a 14-minute 503 storm at the TLS terminator.

Why a Fixed 1-Second Reconnect Amplified the Outage

On Slack, the team shipped a quick patch: setTimeout(() => reconnect(), 1000) paired with a 100 ms React setState throttle. It lowered render counts in single-tab DevTools.

In production, it made the collapse worse. Every dropped socket waited the exact same 1,000 ms and slammed the TLS terminator in synchronized waves, while all 8 tabs per user still ran 3,200 JSON.parse() calls per second on the main thread before the throttle even saw a frame.

Five Layers From Multi-Tab Fan-Out to Gateway Collapse

Single-tab tests never saw the failure because three multipliers only appear in real multi-tab sessions: N open tabs multiplying socket count by N, unthrottled JSON parsing saturating every tab's main thread, no stream backpressure on background tabs, no leader election to share one connection, and deterministic reconnect timers synchronizing a thundering herd.

Simulate the 8-Tab Socket Storm and Jittered Recovery

Dissecting the Thundering Herd

01 → 02: Eight Identical Sockets in Chrome Task Manager

Opening Chrome's internal Task Manager (Shift+Esc) on a power user's machine showed 8 separate renderer tabs each maintaining an identical wss://stream.example.com connection and burning 40% CPU each. Instead of sharing one stream across the origin via BroadcastChannel & Web Locks, every tab opened its own socket and parsed the exact same 400 msg/s feed.

Moving the socket and JSON.parse() loop into Dedicated Web Workers isolates frame decoding from the UI thread so main-thread input latency stays flat even during 400 msg/s market bursts.

02 → 03: Background Tabs Queuing Stale Frames

Even inside a Worker, background tabs throttled by browser timers could not consume 400 frames/sec, causing unbounded message queues to back up in memory. Applying Streams API Backpressure with a CountQueuingStrategy and checking controller.desiredSize lets slow tabs coalesce or drop superseded ticker ticks instead of buffering stale prices.

03 → 04: Electing One Socket Owner Per Origin

To collapse 80,000 sockets down to 10,000, tabs must coordinate who owns the upstream WebSocket. Using Cross-Tab Leader Election via navigator.locks.request('ws-leader', ...), only the tab holding the lock opens the WebSocket and broadcasts normalized frames over BroadcastChannel; if the leader closes, the browser automatically releases its lock and the next waiting tab promotes seamlessly.

04 → 05: Breaking the Synchronized Reconnect Wave

Gateway access logs showed TLS handshake spikes every 1,000 ms on the dot after a node restart. Replacing fixed timers with Realtime Streams, Backpressure & Jitter (Math.random() * Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt)) spreads 10,000 reconnecting leaders across a smooth window so the gateway recovers cleanly.

Electing One Leader and Applying Full-Jitter Backoff 

navigator.locks.request('ws-stream-leader', async () => {
  let attempt = 0;
  const connect = () => {
    const ws = new WebSocket('wss://stream.example.com');
    ws.onmessage = (e) => channel.postMessage(JSON.parse(e.data));
    ws.onclose = () => {
      const delay = Math.random() * Math.min(30_000, 500 * 2 ** attempt++);
      setTimeout(connect, delay);
    };
  };
  connect();
  await new Promise(() => {}); // Hold lock until tab closes
});

Architectural Invariants:

  • One WebSocket per browser origin: Elect a single leader tab with navigator.locks.request() and fan out over BroadcastChannel.
  • Parse off the main thread: Decode and normalize high-frequency frames inside a Worker before posting to UI state.
  • Full-jitter exponential backoff: Randomize every reconnect delay between 0 and min(cap, base * 2^attempt).

Golden Rule: Single-tab tests hide multi-tab socket multiplication; elect one origin leader via Web Locks and jitter every reconnect.

title: Buy Software or Vibe-Code It?
description:
A few weeks ago a founder we will call Sam was evaluating our product. He runs an e-commerce startup with a twelve-person engineering team. He liked the demo, the pricing made sense to him, and then he said the thing every founder of a small software company eventually hears. His engineers could vibe-code the same thing in a couple of days with an AI assistant, so why would he pay a subscription for it. We build Idlefy, a tool that keeps development virtual machines off by default and starts them on a timed lease, so this question lands on our desk a lot. Our honest answer is that Sam is right about the couple of days and wrong about nearly everything that comes after them. The gap between those two statements is where companies quietly lose real money, and we have watched the build-it-ourselves math fail at enough teams that we think the pattern deserves a proper write-up. This isn't really an article about our product. It is an article about what software actually costs.

A Working Demo Is Not a Product

Let's be fair to the weekend build first, because the progress here is real. With modern AI tools a competent engineer can produce a script that stops VMs on a schedule, posts a message to Slack, and handles the happy path by Sunday night. Five years ago that was a two-week project, and the fact that it is now a weekend is one of the best things to happen to small teams in a long time. The problem is what the demo doesn't contain. It doesn't contain the teammate in another timezone whose machine got shut down in the middle of a deploy, or the exception list that grows out of that incident, or the override button someone needs at 2 a.m. It doesn't contain onboarding for the new hire, permissions for the contractor who should see staging but never production, or an answer for what happens when the script itself goes down. Every one of those is a feature request that arrives within the first month, and every one of them turns your weekend script into a product whether you planned it or not. Buyers see a price tag on commercial software and no price tag on the internal version. That second price tag exists. It just gets mailed to you later.

The Hidden Payroll

The internal tool now needs somewhere to live, and that is the first recurring bill. You need a small VM or a serverless setup to run the scheduler, a database for state, monitoring so you know it is alive, and backups so a redeploy doesn't wipe the exception list. Call it thirty to a hundred dollars a month, which sounds trivial until you notice it is already in the range of many SaaS subscriptions all by itself. The real cost sits on the payroll line. A loaded senior engineer in the US or Western Europe runs fifty to eighty dollars an hour, and an internal tool that people actually depend on consumes a few hours a month at minimum. Dependencies need upgrades, the cloud provider deprecates an API version, someone requests a small feature, something breaks after a Friday deploy. Four hours a month is two or three hundred dollars, which is more than most teams would ever pay for the commercial equivalent, and it comes out of your scarcest resource rather than your most abundant one.

Then the engineer who built it leaves, and we have watched this exact moment play out at more than one company. The tool keeps running, nobody dares touch it, and every request to change it gets politely deferred. Eighteen months later it is quietly turned off, and the machines just run around the clock again like they did before anyone cared.

Here is the napkin math in one place. Swap in your own rates and instance prices and see where you land.

The Boring Parts Are the Product

Once a company grows past three people, the feature list stops being about the core function and starts being about everything around it. Your new DevOps lead wants the tool behind SSO, because one more password floating around a shared vault is how security incidents start. Your first enterprise customer sends a security questionnaire, and suddenly you need an audit trail of who started which machine and when, exportable, with timestamps nobody can edit. Your finance person wants usage broken down by team so the cloud bill can be allocated properly. None of this is hard the way algorithms are hard, but all of it is slow, and it is exactly the work AI assistants help with least, because the difficulty lives in edge cases and organizational detail rather than in the code itself.

The clouds are the other trap. AWS and GCP look similar from a distance and behave differently up close, in how resources are tagged, how permission boundaries work, and what actually happens to disks when an instance stops. A machine type with local NVMe storage loses that data on a stop, and a weekend script that doesn't know this will one day delete a dataset someone needed. We learned these lessons across hundreds of small decisions over years, and so has every serious vendor in every category. That accumulated scar tissue is most of what you are actually buying.

The Price of One Bad Weekend

Here is the scenario that settles the argument for us, and versions of it are the reason Idlefy exists. A team builds its own shutdown scheduler and it works fine for months. Then one Friday evening a cloud credential expires, or an API call starts returning an error code the script has never seen, or someone spins up machines in a region the script never knew about. Nothing alerts anyone, because the tool's entire job is for nothing to happen, so a failure looks exactly like success. A few GPU instances run through the weekend at list prices north of thirty dollars an hour each. By Monday morning the team has burned a couple of thousand dollars, which for a small company is more than a year of fees for the commercial tool they decided not to buy. Run that math with your own instance types before you make the call, because the arithmetic is rarely kind to the weekend build.

The painful part isn't even the one bad weekend. It is that the homegrown tool fails silently and nobody truly owns it, while a vendor has paying customers, an on-call rotation, a status page, and an existential reason to make sure that failure mode never ships. When our product misbehaves, our company's survival is on the line. When your internal script misbehaves, it is a ticket in next sprint's backlog.

How We Decide Now

We sell software, so of course we have an interest here, and you should discount our opinion accordingly. But we buy plenty of software ourselves, and the test we use is the same one we offered Sam. First, is this tool part of what makes your company different, or is it plumbing. We build our own product, obviously, and we buy accounting, support desk, analytics, and email, because being slightly better at any of those wins us nothing. Second, who owns this tool in year two, by name. If the answer is a shrug, the tool is already dead and the money is already spent. Third, what does one failure cost compared with one year of fees. For anything that touches money, security, or compliance, a single bad incident usually outweighs a decade of subscription payments. And fourth, will it ever need SSO, audit trails, or anything a lawyer or an auditor might ask about. If yes, buy it, because that work is invisible, endless, and nobody vibe-codes it for fun on a Saturday.

Vibe coding changed the price of the first eighty percent of any internal tool, and that is worth celebrating. It didn't change the price of the last twenty, and the last twenty is the part your company actually runs on. We don't know yet what Sam will decide. If his weekend build runs flawlessly forever, we will be happy for him. We just wouldn't bet our cloud bill on it.

What was the last tool your team built instead of buying, and would you make the same call today? Tell us in the comments.

title: Packaging Java Apps for Xbox Developer Mode, and Why Consoles Need Help
description:
Codename One targets iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, the web, watches, TVs and now embedded boards. There's one major category missing: game consoles.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

The technical side looks manageable. A console is a computer with a GPU and a controller, and we already render through Metal, Direct3D and OpenGL ES and map controllers to game actions. They're hard because everything about them sits behind a non-disclosure agreement. This week we took the first step that doesn't need one.

One build hint

Any retail Xbox can be switched into Developer Mode, which lets you sideload UWP apps for testing. Codename One can now build that package:

codename1.arg.windows.xbox=true

That builds the native Windows port as a UWP app and packages it as a signed .msix. If you don't provide a certificate, the build makes a self-signed development one next to the package. Then:

  1. Install Dev Home on the console and turn on Developer Mode and Remote Access.
  2. Open the Device Portal at https://<console>:11443 in a browser.
  3. Under Home, add the .msix and pick the .cer the build produced.

You can try the same package on a Windows PC first: import the certificate into the Local Machine's Trusted People store, then run Add-AppxPackage on the .msix.

What changes on a console

A console app isn't a desktop app with a bigger screen. Three things had to change in the port:

The app container. There's no desktop window. The port runs on a CoreWindow and draws with Direct2D into a Direct3D swap chain. The build links against WindowsApp.lib alone, which proves at build time that every system call the port makes is allowed inside the container. If something isn't allowed, the build fails instead of the console.

The controller. The D-pad and the left stick arrive as the four directions, A as fire and B as back, through the same Display.getGameAction() your game already uses for arrow keys. A game written with com.codename1.gaming or imported from a Unity 2D project doesn't need console-specific input code.

The TV. Televisions crop the edges of the picture. The visible area the console reports comes through Display.getDisplaySafeArea(). Use it to keep the score and the menus where people can see them.

Here's how a game reads input, unchanged from phone to desktop to console:

public void keyPressed(int keyCode) {
    switch (Display.getInstance().getGameAction(keyCode)) {
        case Display.GAME_LEFT:  player.moveLeft();  break;
        case Display.GAME_RIGHT: player.moveRight(); break;
        case Display.GAME_FIRE:  player.jump();      break;
    }
}

Where it stands

This is experimental, and the limits are real.

  • CI cross-compiles the target on Linux, installs the package on a Windows machine and checks that it reaches its first frame inside the app container. We haven't run it on a real Xbox yet. Controller input and overscan only exist on the console, so both are untested.
  • Some things the desktop port does aren't available in the container: secondary windows, menus, the tray, native text editors, file dialogs, the clipboard, printing, the camera, audio recording and the share sheet. The only file root is the app's local folder.
  • Most important: Developer Mode is a test sandbox, not a store. You can't sell a game this way. Retail Xbox titles are built with Microsoft's Game Development Kit under a publishing agreement.

Why consoles need a different kind of help

Every console platform holder, Microsoft, Sony and Nintendo, keeps its SDK, its development hardware and its certification process behind an NDA. You get access by signing a publishing or developer agreement, and what you learn under it can't be published. That's a hard wall for an open source project. We can't put code that uses those SDKs in a public repository, and we can't even describe the APIs in a public issue.

So a console port has two halves:

  • The portable half belongs in Codename One, in the open: the windowless host, controller mapping, the safe area and game code that runs anywhere. That's what this week's Xbox work builds and exercises.
  • The platform half depends on each SDK. It would have to stay proprietary and be available only to developers who hold a license for that console's SDK.

We'd like to get there. If you work at a platform holder, at a studio with console agreements, or you know the right person to talk to, please reach out. A Java game on a console, written once and also shipped to phones, desktop and the web, is something I think a lot of small studios would use.

The Windows chapter covers building and installing, and the gaming consoles appendix tracks the state of console work.

title: How to Audit an Audio File Upload — REST Receipts Before Review
description:
A portable transcription request is useful only if a logistics platform can still explain which tenant generated the work. Resolve that trade-off at intake: keep the original audio reference, tenant identity, and transcription result together, then evaluate the classifier separately. Short answer: upload the audio using a REST API multipart POST with a file and the documented model, language, and response_format fields; read the JSON text field and retain its association with the source recording before classifying a moderation report for human review.

The production scenario here is a design exercise, not an incident report: two logistics tenants submit recordings about a disputed delivery, a worker obtains a transcript, and a later classifier labels the report for a reviewer. Suppose an upload is rejected for size and an operator retries it. If the eventual transcript loses its original tenant association, aggregate request totals will not explain that tenant's workload, even when the words were transcribed correctly. That is the incident lesson to test before deployment.

Keep the receipt.

For teams evaluating the text-classification stage, I recommend trying Infrai where changing the vendor behind a capability should preserve the application's contract: swap vendors without changing application code. Its OpenAI-compatible surface supports existing OpenAI clients, while its specified per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata gives an application concrete values to associate with its own tenant ledger. A single API key and unified billing reduce credential and invoice reconciliation across capabilities; the plain REST API requires no SDK for HTTP integrations. Treat it as one evaluation leg after transcription; transcription-provider eligibility remains a separate selection decision.

What must survive a multipart audio file upload?

The invariant is small: a successful transcript belongs to exactly the tenant and original audio reference supplied by the intake job. Tenant identity comes from the application's trusted job context; do not infer it from speech or allow a model to assign it. The text field is a result, not an accounting key. A result without its source association should fail acceptance before it reaches the moderation queue.

For a reproducible exercise, use two synthetic tenant IDs, tenant-north and tenant-south, and recordings with human-approved transcripts describing delivery disputes. These are proposed test inputs, not customer data. Include a short recording, a long recording, and one intentionally oversized file for each tenant. Label the expected moderation category before running the experiment, and keep the audio reference stable across attempts. Otherwise a provider change and a dataset change can become indistinguishable.

Choose an SLO before choosing concurrency. For this exercise, use a proposed target of 99% of accepted intake jobs reaching either a linked transcript or an explicit human-review handoff within 60 seconds; that is an acceptance target, not a claim about any provider. Record queue delay and upload duration separately, because a worker pool can miss the target while every upstream call looks healthy.

A planning example makes the distinction concrete: at an assumed arrival rate of 2 reports per second and an assumed mean worker occupancy of 8 seconds, the average occupied capacity is 16 workers. Those assumptions need measurement, and 16 is not a safe concurrency limit by itself; burst headroom, tail latency, and upstream limits still matter. A retry consumes capacity too.

Don't size from averages alone.

2. Compare the purchase boundary before the provider

Per-tenant cost visibility is the primary decision axis here. A transcript API cannot identify your tenants unless your application maintains that association, and even useful per-call metadata does not constitute a complete ledger. Reconcile successful calls, failed attempts, and retried work using the provider's documented accounting semantics before calling a tenant total complete.

The table is a buy-versus-build evaluation plan. It assigns work to the team rather than pretending to report an unrun benchmark. OpenAI, Deepgram, and AssemblyAI are real candidates to investigate; verify each candidate's current upload contract and account-level controls before implementing an adapter.

Option What to buy or evaluate Work the platform team owns Decision boundary
OpenAI direct Evaluate the direct transcription service against the audio fixtures Verify the upload contract; associate results and usage with tenant jobs Prefer the direct integration if its documented controls and measured results satisfy the workload
Deepgram Evaluate a speech-focused alternative using the same recordings Check request and response differences; implement and operate its adapter Prefer it if speech requirements justify a separate integration after testing
AssemblyAI Evaluate another speech-focused alternative against identical expected transcripts Validate its processing lifecycle and map it to the review deadline Prefer it if that lifecycle and the measured output fit the review queue better
Anthropic direct, for classification Evaluate classification using the fixed transcript set Validate its client contract, structured output, and tenant accounting Prefer a direct contract if it meets the classification gates and simplifies your existing operations
Gemini direct, for classification Evaluate another text-classification candidate on the same labels Verify model eligibility and output validation before integration Prefer it if measured classification behavior and operational controls fit the review process
Infrai, for transcript classification Evaluate a stable client contract across backend vendor choices Attach per-call metadata to trusted tenant context; score classification against labels Try it when vendor substitution and attributable calls matter at the text stage
Build the orchestration layer Keep intake receipts, evaluation fixtures, and tenant attribution under application control Operate the queue, retention rules, reconciliation, and reviewer handoff Build this boundary when those semantics are part of your product

A specialist or direct transcription provider is the better choice when the immediate requirement is a verified audio-upload contract and speech-specific behavior. Do not mistake a compatible text client for proof that every audio workflow has the same operational properties.

Infrai provides one key, one bill, and one REST API for 295 routes across 20 modules. Its public discovery surface provides request and response schemas without requiring a key, and there is no SDK to install for a plain HTTP integration. Use discovery to establish the text-stage contract before integrating it, and verify capability readiness when selecting any processing leg. For report classification, evaluate a chat model with a constrained JSON schema and validate the category before handing it to a reviewer. Keep final decisions with the human review process.

3. Exercise the preventative code path locally

Save the following as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It uses only the Go standard library and a local test server; the bytes are a synthetic transport fixture, not playable audio. No external service is contacted, no credential is needed, and a passing run proves request construction and source association only. It says nothing about recognition accuracy.

The program builds the multipart body with file, model, language, response_format, and optional prompt fields. Its local server checks the multipart request, returns the documented JSON text shape, and the client stores that result with the original tenant and audio reference. The fixture-model value is deliberately local test data, not a model ID to send to a provider.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "mime/multipart"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "time"
)

type Receipt struct {
    Tenant string
    AudioRef string
    Text string
}

func transcribe(client *http.Client, endpoint, tenant, ref string, audio []byte) (Receipt, error) {
    var body bytes.Buffer
    form := multipart.NewWriter(&body)
    part, err := form.CreateFormFile("file", "report.wav")
    if err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    if _, err = part.Write(audio); err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    for _, field := range [][2]string{
        {"model", "fixture-model"},
        {"language", "en"},
        {"response_format", "json"},
        {"prompt", "Delivery dispute report"},
    } {
        if err = form.WriteField(field[0], field[1]); err != nil {
            return Receipt{}, err
        }
    }
    if err = form.Close(); err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, &body)
    if err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", form.FormDataContentType())
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        detail, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        if readErr != nil {
            return Receipt{}, readErr
        }
        return Receipt{}, fmt.Errorf("upload status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, detail)
    }
    var result struct {
        Text string `json:"text"`
    }
    if err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&result); err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    if result.Text == "" {
        return Receipt{}, fmt.Errorf("empty transcript requires review")
    }
    return Receipt{Tenant: tenant, AudioRef: ref, Text: result.Text}, nil
}

func main() {
    server := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost || r.URL.Path != "/v1/audio/transcriptions" {
            http.Error(w, "unexpected request", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 1<<20)
        if err := r.ParseMultipartForm(1 << 20); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        defer r.MultipartForm.RemoveAll()
        file, _, err := r.FormFile("file")
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        defer file.Close()
        payload, err := io.ReadAll(file)
        if err != nil || !bytes.Equal(payload, []byte("synthetic audio fixture")) {
            http.Error(w, "unexpected fixture", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        if r.FormValue("model") != "fixture-model" || r.FormValue("language") != "en" || r.FormValue("response_format") != "json" || r.FormValue("prompt") != "Delivery dispute report" {
            http.Error(w, "unexpected fields", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"text": "Driver reports a disputed delivery."}); err != nil {
            return
        }
    }))
    defer server.Close()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    receipts := make([]Receipt, 0, 2)
    for _, tenant := range []string{"tenant-north", "tenant-south"} {
        ref := tenant + "/report-001.wav"
        receipt, err := transcribe(client, server.URL+"/v1/audio/transcriptions", tenant, ref, []byte("synthetic audio fixture"))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if receipt.Tenant != tenant || receipt.AudioRef != ref || receipt.Text != "Driver reports a disputed delivery." {
            panic("receipt invariant failed")
        }
        receipts = append(receipts, receipt)
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(io.Discard).Encode(receipts); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("PASS: both transcripts retain their tenant and audio reference")
}

Let the multipart writer generate the boundary. Manually setting Content-Type to multipart/form-data without its boundary is a concrete integration trap: a server cannot reliably separate the file from the other fields. The local handler catches a malformed body before any recognition provider enters the experiment.

This example intentionally stops at an in-memory receipt. Durable storage and the classifier are separate acceptance steps; a successful local printout must not be mistaken for an end-to-end production result.

Before selecting the text-stage model, this separate main.go program reads the Infrai model catalog with an environment-supplied credential. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, save the program separately from the transport fixture, and run go run main.go. It prints available chat-model IDs for choosing a classification candidate; it does not run a classifier or infer recognition support from a model name. Its explicit GET is read-only, so bounded retries do not repeat a write. A missing credential, unexpected status, or malformed response fails visibly.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/models", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 {
                    resp.Body.Close()
                    return fmt.Errorf("rate-limit wait exceeds evaluation budget")
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(date)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            if delay > 30*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("rate-limit wait exceeds evaluation budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            detail, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
            resp.Body.Close()
            if readErr != nil {
                return readErr
            }
            return fmt.Errorf("catalog status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, detail)
        }
        var catalog struct {
            Data []struct {
                ID string `json:"id"`
                Capability string `json:"capability"`
                Available bool `json:"available"`
            } `json:"data"`
        }
        err = json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&catalog)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        found := false
        for _, model := range catalog.Data {
            if model.Available && model.Capability == "chat" && model.ID != "" {
                fmt.Println(model.ID)
                found = true
            }
        }
        if !found {
            return fmt.Errorf("no eligible classification model in this response")
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Eligibility isn't quality.

4. Promote the experiment only when attribution survives failure

Next, run the real audio fixtures through each eligible speech adapter, using model IDs and upload limits from that provider's current documentation. Keep the application receipt shape constant. Fetch in JavaScript changes the client syntax, not the multipart requirement; the Go example makes the same request-body boundary visible without introducing another SDK.

A 413 response calls for compressing the audio or splitting a long recording before uploading again. Preserve the parent audio reference and segment order when splitting, or a transcript can remain attached to the right tenant while describing the wrong sequence of events. Repeating the identical oversized request is wasted capacity.

For production adapters, define bounded retries explicitly: honor Retry-After on 429, apply exponential backoff, and stop when the remaining review deadline cannot accommodate another attempt. Use provider-supported idempotency for billable writes where documented; do not assume that an arbitrary header deduplicates an audio request. Keep a durable application job identity across retries and make receipt persistence idempotent. An ambiguous timeout needs reconciliation, since deduplicating your database row does not prove the upstream work ran once.

The local example performs no retries. That keeps its evidence narrow and inspectable.

Use the same labeled transcripts to evaluate the classification legs, including Infrai, without allowing differences in transcription to contaminate the classification comparison. Define the permitted labels with the reviewers before the run, score against those labels, and reject malformed or out-of-schema output. Retain vendor and latency alongside the cost metadata where supplied, joined to the application's tenant and job identity; do not fabricate values when an integration lacks them.

The proposed pass criteria are strict: every completed fixture retains its exact tenant and source reference; every rejected or timed-out job has an explicit review disposition; every classification matches the pre-agreed label and schema for this small acceptance set. A missing cost attribution fails the visibility requirement even if the category is correct. Passing this fixture set qualifies an adapter for a larger evaluation, not for an accuracy claim across all logistics reports.

Choose the leg that passes those gates and meets the review SLO under the expected tenant mix. If none does, retain human handling while revising the capacity assumptions or dataset; do not loosen attribution to make a dashboard green. Short recordings also do not establish a case for long recordings, live conversations, or autonomous moderation decisions. Those require separate acceptance criteria.

Sources

References for checking candidate contracts and protocol behavior follow. They are starting points for the experiment, not evidence of benchmark results.

  • OpenAI speech-to-text documentation
  • Deepgram documentation
  • AssemblyAI documentation
  • Anthropic documentation
  • Gemini documentation
  • Multipart form-data specification
  • HTTP status and retry semantics

If the text-stage boundary fits your system, start with the public contract and examples in the Infrai documentation.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud on November 6, 2026.

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud production will take place on Friday, November 6, 2026, from 9:00 PM PT to 10:00 PM PT (Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 5:00 AM UTC to 6:00 AM UTC). This maintenance follows the monthly maintenance window schedule documented in the Apigee Edge release notes archive.

During the scheduled maintenance window, the following services will be temporarily unavailable, and attempts to access them will return a 4xx status code:

  • Management Services UI
  • Management Services APIs
  • Monetization Management APIs
  • New proxy deployments
  • DevPortal Service
  • Microgateway Services
  • Edge Query (Analytics Stats APIs)

Runtime API calls to deployed API proxies are unaffected. While access to analytics queries may be temporarily unavailable during the maintenance window, all analytics and metrics data from this period will be available once maintenance ends.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.14.10

On November 5, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.14.10.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.14.10.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.
432315283 Fixed an issue where changes to a multi-certificate truststore's trust anchors required a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled was toggled at runtime; the outbound SSLContext now rebuilds automatically.

Application Integration

Feature

The following Application Integration features are now generally available (GA):

  • Mask sensitive data in logs
  • Test cases
  • Manage Application Integration resources using custom constraints
  • Config variables
  • Data Transformer Script task and Data Transformer functions
  • View OpenAPI specification for an integration

Announcement

The iam.serviceAccounts.actAs check on run-as service accounts already applies when you publish or test any integration. Starting January 15, 2027 (UTC), the new authorization behavior also applies to existing integrations created before October 15, 2026. Specifically, you must have a run-as service account to publish or test an integration with a scheduled or event trigger. For more information, see Prepare for upcoming authorization changes and the GCP-2026-068 security bulletin.

BigQuery

Feature

In the query execution graph's query text heatmap, you can now view and navigate through a hierarchical list of context references, such as nested function calls or view references, for stage steps. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

In the query execution graph, the query text heatmap now supports displaying the SQL text for persistent and temporary user-defined functions (UDFs). This feature is generally available (GA).

Change

The BigQuery Metadata curation console page has been removed. You can now use Knowledge Catalog to schedule Cloud Storage discovery scans, manage data profiling and data quality, and perform related data governance tasks.

Feature

Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now available in the asia-northeast1 (Tokyo) location. For more information, see Locations.

M4N network performance improvements provide up to 400 Gbps maximum bandwidth for internal network communications, and up to 200 Gbps for external network communications. For more information, see M4N machine types.

Data Studio

Feature

You can now combine tables vertically in Data Studio blends by using the Union merge operator, which appends rows across up to five tables and removes duplicate rows. In addition, blend UI labels now use merge (such as Merge another table, Merge conditions, and Hide repeated merge fields) to encompass both join and union operations. For more information, see How blends work in Data Studio and Create, edit, and manage blends.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Prepaid credits for Pay-as-you-go subscriptions and usage above quota

Prepaid credits are generally available (GA) for self-serve (online) Cloud Billing accounts. You can buy credits to pay for usage without an invoiced billing account. Your billing account's credit balance covers usage in the Pay-as-you-go edition and pay-as-you-go usage above quota in the Gemini Enterprise app, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and AI developer tools, such as Google Antigravity. Pay-as-you-go subscriptions have no license fee because you pay for what you use at pay-as-you-go rates. Cloud Billing still bills your account directly for seat-based license fees in editions such as Standard and Plus.

  • Buy credits and configure auto-reload: Buy prepaid credits, track your balance and transactions, and configure auto-reload with an optional monthly auto-charge limit. Usage is blocked if your credit balance reaches zero or a project reaches its monthly spend limit. Because credits are deducted after usage occurs, your balance might briefly drop below zero if usage occurs before the deduction runs.
  • Use AI developer tools on self-serve accounts: With an upgraded paid self-serve billing account and an active non-trial Gemini Enterprise subscription, you can enable AI developer tools and pay with prepaid credits for Pay-as-you-go edition usage or pay-as-you-go usage above quota. Eligible editions include Standard, Plus, eligible Standard Emerging Market, and Pay-as-you-go. Free-trial subscriptions, free-tier billing accounts, and reseller-managed subaccounts aren't eligible.
  • Monitor costs and invoices: View 30-day costs across the Gemini Enterprise app, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and AI developer tools, and view and download prepayment and monthly consumption invoices.

For more information, see:

  • Manage prepaid credits
  • Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota
  • Quotas and pricing for the Pay-as-you-go edition
  • AI developer tools overview
  • View costs

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash (gemini-omni-1.2-flash) is available in General Availability (GA). Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is an omni-modal foundation model that processes text, image, and video inputs to generate text and high-definition video with synchronized audio through the Interactions API.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces the following capabilities:

  • Standalone video upscaling: Upscale previously generated videos from 360p to 720p or 1080p, and from 720p to 1080p or 4K using task: "upscale". See Upscale videos.

  • Extended video generation and editing duration: Generate or edit videos up to 15 seconds in length across text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and video editing tasks (up to 10 seconds for first-and-last-frame interpolation and video extension).

  • Reference-guided video editing and extension: Supply up to 2 reference images along with an input video when editing or extending videos. See Edit videos and Extend videos.

  • Deterministic generation and billing labels: Specify seed for reproducible video outputs and attach custom labels to Interactions API requests.

  • Standard PayGo and Provisioned Throughput: Available with Standard Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) and Provisioned Throughput (685 tokens per second per GSU).

Feature

Interactions API long decodes for Gemini 4 Argon

Long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus input tokens) on the Interactions API (v1beta1) are available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon and gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive). You can extend single-turn outputs beyond the per-segment limit (65,536 streaming or 32,768 non-streaming tokens) using automatic continuation in the Google Gen AI SDK (google-genai >= 2.34.0 for Python, @google/genai >= 2.32.0 for JavaScript/TypeScript, Go >= 1.77.0, and Java >= 1.80.0), server-managed background execution (background=true), or custom stored (store=true) and stateless (store=false) continuation_token loops.

For code samples, continuation options, and implementation rules, see Long decodes in the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Argon.
