title: The Complete 2026 Guide to Self-Hosting Private n8n + Local LLMs on Cloud VPS: Full Production Architecture & Cost Breakdown
description:
Published by PixelBrain Engineering Lab · Updated November 2026

Canonical URL: https://pixelbrain-tools.blogspot.com/2026/11/self-hosting-n8n-local-llm-cloud-vps.html

Executive Summary: The $500/Month SaaS Trap vs. The $18/Month Private Cloud

In 2026, autonomous workflow automation and local Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shifted from experimental curiosity to table-stakes infrastructure for engineering teams, digital agencies, and一人公司 (one-person unicorn companies).

However, teams scaling on hosted cloud solutions quickly hit an aggressive pricing wall:

  1. Per-Execution Cloud Tax: Mainstream hosted iPaaS platforms charge between $0.01 and $0.05 per task execution beyond their modest base tiers. A multi-step autonomous agent running scheduled scrapers, CRM updates, and webhook reconciliations easily burns through 150,000 tasks/month—translating to a $600–$1,200 monthly invoice.
  2. Token Leakage & Data Governance: Piping internal database records, customer support transcripts, and sensitive intellectual property into public commercial LLM APIs introduces compliance nightmares (GDPR, SOC2, HIPAA) and variable API billing spikes.
  3. Vendor Lock-in & Rate Limits: Relying entirely on multi-tenant cloud runners subjects your mission-critical operations to unannounced latency spikes, concurrency caps, and sudden API deprecations.

This production guide details the architectural blueprint for deploying a fully private, unlimited-execution automation fortress combining self-hosted n8n, containerized local LLMs (via Ollama & vLLM), PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector, Redis-backed BullMQ execution, and automated TLS reverse proxying on a low-cost, high-performance Cloud Virtual Private Server (VPS).

For under $20 per month in raw compute, this stack delivers zero per-execution fees, total data sovereignty, sub-millisecond local network latency, and complete enterprise auditability.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                  THE 2026 PRIVATE AUTOMATION STACK                                |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                                                   |
|  [ Inbound Webhooks & UI Traffic ]                                                                |
|                 |                                                                                 |
|                 v                                                                                 |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | Caddy / Traefik Ingress Controller (Automatic Let's Encrypt TLS / Reverse Proxy)             |  |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|         |                                              |                                          |
|         | Port 5678 (HTTPS Basic / OAuth2)             | Port 11434 (Internal Docker Bridge)      |
|         v                                              v                                          |
|  +-------------------------------------+      +------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | n8n Workflow Automation Engine      |      | Local LLM Inference Engine                     |  |
|  | (Queue Mode / BullMQ Executor)      |<---->| (Ollama / vLLM OpenAI-Compatible API)          |  |
|  +-------------------------------------+      | Models: Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B / DeepSeek-R1-14B   |  |
|         |                      |              +------------------------------------------------+  |
|         v                      v                               |                                  |
|  +--------------+      +---------------------------+           |                                  |
|  | Redis Queue  |      | PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector  |<----------+ (Embeddings / Long-term RAG)     |
|  | (Cache/Locks)|      | (State Storage / Vectors) |                                              |
|  +--------------+      +---------------------------+                                              |
|                                                                                                   |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1. Cloud VPS Hardware Sizing & Provider Benchmarks (2026)

The secret to hosting local LLMs without thousand-dollar enterprise GPU instances lies in modern quantized weights (GGUF Q4_K_M / Q8_0) coupled with high-frequency DDR5 memory and AVX-512 CPU offloading.

For automated agents running deterministic tasks (data transformation, routing, webhook handling, code formatting, and summarization), a 14B parameter dense model (such as Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B or DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) running on 4–8 modern CPU cores delivers 14–22 tokens per second—more than adequate for asynchronous background jobs.

Memory & VRAM Mathematics for 14B Models

Before purchasing server capacity, calculate exact memory consumption using the standard quantization formula:

$$\text{RAM Requirements (GB)} \approx \left(\frac{\text{Parameters} \times \text{Bits per Weight}}{8}\right) \times 1.25 + \text{KV Cache Footprint}$$

For a 14.7 billion parameter model:

  • FP16 (Unquantized): $14.7 \times 2 = 29.4\text{ GB}$ (Exceeds standard VPS tiers; requires expensive GPU instances).
  • GGUF Q8_0 (8-bit Quantization): $14.7 \times 1.05 = 15.4\text{ GB}$ (Near-zero quality loss, requires 24GB VPS).
  • GGUF Q4_K_M (4-bit Medium Quantization): $14.7 \times 0.58 = 8.5\text{ GB}$ (Industry standard sweet spot; 98.7% MMLU retention, comfortably fits inside an affordable 16GB VPS).
  • KV Cache for 8,192 Context Window: Consumes approximately $1.2\text{ GB}$ of additional RAM.
  • n8n + PostgreSQL + Redis Footprint: Allocates approximately $2.5\text{ GB}$ of baseline system memory.
  • Total Recommended Server RAM: 16 GB to 24 GB.

Tested VPS Configurations & Real-World Latency

Tier Target Workload Recommended Specs Monthly Cost Tested Providers
Starter Stack n8n + Webhooks + Fast Embedding Search + 7B Model 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB NVMe $6.50 – $9.50/mo Hostinger KVM 2 / Hetzner CPX31 / Contabo Cloud VPS S
Production Matrix (Recommended) n8n Queue Mode + 14B Model (Q4_K_M) + PostgreSQL pgvector 6–8 vCPU, 16–24 GB RAM, 200 GB NVMe $14.00 – $19.00/mo Hostinger KVM 4 / Hetzner CPX41 / OVHcloud VPS Comfort
Heavy Inference Multi-Agent Swarms + 32B Model + Local Whisper Audio 8 vCPU + Dedicated Nvidia RTX 4060 (16GB) $45.00 – $65.00/mo Vast.ai / RunPod Community / OVH Cloud GPU

Pro Tip on Storage Performance: Workflow state management and vector searches require high Random I/O operations per second (IOPS). Always choose NVMe PCIe 4.0 storage over standard SSD block storage to avoid transaction locking when running concurrent n8n webhooks.

2. Production Docker Compose Architecture

Below is the verified, single-command production deployment file. It configures:

  • Caddy v2: Lightweight reverse proxy with zero-config automatic HTTPS (Let's Encrypt).
  • n8n (v1.65+): Configured for high-concurrency production with PostgreSQL backend.
  • PostgreSQL 16: Bundled with the official pgvector extension for native vector embedding storage.
  • Redis 7 (Alpine): Providing atomic lock management and BullMQ execution queuing.
  • Ollama: Serving local quantized LLMs with hardware acceleration.
  • Internal Docker Network: Ensuring the LLM and database ports are never exposed to the public internet. 
version: '3.8'

services:
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2-alpine
    container_name: production_caddy
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./caddy/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config
    networks:
      - automation_net
    depends_on:
      - n8n

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: production_redis
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes --requirepass ${REDIS_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecureRedis2026!}
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    networks:
      - automation_net
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "-a", "${REDIS_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecureRedis2026!}", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  postgres:
    image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16
    container_name: production_postgres
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecurePassword2026!}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - automation_net
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin} -d ${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:latest
    container_name: production_ollama
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=24h
      - OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4
    volumes:
      - ollama_models:/root/.ollama
    networks:
      - automation_net
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 14G

  n8n:
    image: n8nio/n8n:latest
    container_name: production_n8n
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - N8N_HOST=${SUBDOMAIN}.${DOMAIN_NAME}
      - N8N_PORT=5678
      - N8N_PROTOCOL=https
      - NODE_ENV=production
      - WEBHOOK_URL=https://${SUBDOMAIN}.${DOMAIN_NAME}/
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=UTC
      - DB_TYPE=postgresdb
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST=postgres
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PORT=5432
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE=${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_USER=${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecurePassword2026!}
      - EXECUTIONS_MODE=regular
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST=redis
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT=6379
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_PASSWORD:-ChangeMeSecureRedis2026!}
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE=168
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE_MAX_COUNT=50000
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n
    networks:
      - automation_net
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:
  ollama_models:
  n8n_data:

networks:
  automation_net:
    driver: bridge

The Caddyfile Configuration (./caddy/Caddyfile) 

automation.yourdomain.com {
    reverse_proxy n8n:5678 {
        header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}
        header_up X-Forwarded-Proto {scheme}
    }

    # Security Headers
    header {
        Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload"
        X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
        X-Frame-Options "DENY"
        Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
    }

    log {
        output file /data/access.log {
            roll_size 10mb
            roll_keep 5
        }
    }
}

3. Step-by-Step Server Hardening & Zero-Downtime Deployment

Step 1: Base VPS Setup & Docker Engine Installation

Connect to your Ubuntu 24.04 LTS VPS instance via SSH:

# Update repository index and apply critical security patches
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y curl git ufw fail2ban jq htop libssl-dev

# Configure Uncomplicated Firewall (UFW)
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp comment 'SSH Port'
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp comment 'HTTP Let’s Encrypt Challenge'
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp comment 'HTTPS Encrypted Ingress'
sudo ufw --force enable

# Install official Docker engine & Compose plugin
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Step 2: Fail2ban Protection Against Brute-Force Attacks

Create an automated jail configuration for SSH and HTTP authentication:

sudo cat <<EOF > /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
[DEFAULT]
bantime = 1h
findtime = 10m
maxretry = 5

[sshd]
enabled = true
port = 22
mode = aggressive
EOF

sudo systemctl restart fail2ban

Step 3: Directory Layout and Cryptographic Secret Generation 

mkdir -p ~/automation-stack/caddy
cd ~/automation-stack

# Generate hardened environment file with random 32-byte credentials
cat <<EOF > .env
DOMAIN_NAME=yourdomain.com
SUBDOMAIN=automation
POSTGRES_USER=n8n_master_$(openssl rand -hex 4)
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '/+=')
POSTGRES_DB=n8n_production
REDIS_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '/+=')
EOF

chmod 600 .env

Step 4: Pulling the Highest-ROI Local Models

Once docker compose up -d completes container initialization, pull the verified open weights directly into the containerized Ollama instance:

# 1. Pull the 2026 Sovereign Workhorse: Qwen 2.5 Coder 14B (Instruct)
# Remarkable performance on JSON extraction, API calling, and logic validation
docker exec -it production_ollama ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b-instruct-q4_K_M

# 2. Pull the Advanced Reasoning Model: DeepSeek-R1 Distilled 14B
# Outstanding at chain-of-thought analysis, fraud detection, and complex routing
docker exec -it production_ollama ollama pull deepseek-r1:14b

# 3. Pull Fast Multilingual Embedding Model (for RAG & Vector Search in Postgres)
docker exec -it production_ollama ollama pull bge-m3:latest

4. Advanced Vector DB Tuning: PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector

By default, standard relational databases perform sequential scans on text queries. To enable true semantic retrieval across hundreds of thousands of customer support records, PDF manuals, and transaction receipts, configure HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) indexing inside PostgreSQL.

Connecting to PostgreSQL and Enabling Extension 

docker exec -it production_postgres psql -U n8n_admin -d n8n_production

Execute the vector setup commands:

-- Enable the vector extension
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

-- Create an enterprise document embeddings table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS enterprise_knowledge_base (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    document_id VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    chunk_index INT NOT NULL,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    metadata JSONB DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
    embedding vector(1024), -- Matches bge-m3 dimension
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Build high-speed HNSW Index for cosine similarity search
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_hnsw_kb_embedding 
ON enterprise_knowledge_base 
USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

Querying Vectors with Sub-10ms Latency 

-- Semantic search query retrieving top 5 most relevant documentation chunks
SELECT id, document_id, content, metadata,
       1 - (embedding <=> '[0.012, -0.043, ...]'::vector) AS cosine_similarity
FROM enterprise_knowledge_base
WHERE metadata @> '{"department": "engineering"}'
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.012, -0.043, ...]'::vector
LIMIT 5;

5. Connecting n8n to Local LLM Agents (Zero-Cost Inference)

Inside the n8n interface at https://automation.yourdomain.com:

  1. Go to Credentials -> New Credential -> Select OpenAI API.
  2. Configure custom Base URL:
    • Credential Name: Local Ollama Internal Gateway
    • API Key: Enter any placeholder string (e.g. ollama-local-bearer).
    • Base URL: Set to http://ollama:11434/v1.
  3. In any n8n Workflow, insert the AI Agent node:
    • Connect the OpenAI Chat Model sub-node.
    • Set Model Name to: qwen2.5-coder:14b-instruct-q4_K_M or deepseek-r1:14b.
    • Set Temperature to: 0.1 (for deterministic schema validation & SQL synthesis) or 0.6 (for narrative drafting).
  4. Connect the Vector Store sub-node:
    • Select Postgres Vector Store.
    • Host: postgres, Port: 5432, Database: n8n_production.
    • Table: enterprise_knowledge_base.
    • Connect Embeddings OpenAI node pointed to bge-m3:latest on http://ollama:11434/v1.

You now possess an enterprise-grade Autonomous Agent capable of processing millions of records without a single external API call or token surcharge.

6. Enterprise Queue Mode & Scaling Beyond 500,000 Executions/Month

When running massive batch jobs or high-frequency webhook listeners, single-process n8n can bottleneck on Node.js event-loop CPU starvation. The enterprise solution is Queue Mode.

In Queue Mode, n8n decouples the user interface from execution runners:

  1. Webhook Process: Listens for inbound HTTP payloads, immediately returns an HTTP 200/202 acknowledgment, and enqueues job parameters into Redis.
  2. Worker Processes: Autonomous Node.js containers that dequeue jobs from Redis, execute the nodes, communicate with PostgreSQL/Ollama, and log the state.

Adding Dynamic Workers in Docker Compose

To scale up worker capacity during flash campaigns or month-end reconciliations, append a worker definition to your docker-compose.yml:

  n8n-worker:
    image: n8nio/n8n:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: worker
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production
      - DB_TYPE=postgresdb
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST=postgres
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PORT=5432
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE=${POSTGRES_DB:-n8n_production}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_USER=${POSTGRES_USER:-n8n_admin}
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      - EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST=redis
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT=6379
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_PASSWORD}
    networks:
      - automation_net
    depends_on:
      - redis
      - postgres

Scale instantly from the CLI without taking down the web interface:

# Spin up 3 parallel workers for high concurrency
docker compose up -d --scale n8n-worker=3

7. Automated Disaster Recovery & Remote S3 Backup Pipeline

Never rely solely on local disks. A production system must automate database dumps, workflow JSON exports, and model configuration backups to off-site cloud object storage (AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, or Backblaze B2).

The Automated Backup Script (/opt/scripts/backup_automation.sh) 

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

BACKUP_DIR="/var/backups/automation"
TIMESTAMP=$(date +"%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
RETENTION_DAYS=14

mkdir -p "${BACKUP_DIR}"

echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Initiating PostgreSQL atomic backup..."
docker exec production_postgres pg_dump -U n8n_admin n8n_production | gzip > "${BACKUP_DIR}/n8n_db_${TIMESTAMP}.sql.gz"

echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Exporting active n8n workflows..."
docker exec -u node production_n8n n8n export:workflow --all --output=/tmp/workflows.json
docker cp production_n8n:/tmp/workflows.json "${BACKUP_DIR}/workflows_${TIMESTAMP}.json"

# Prune local backups older than retention window
find "${BACKUP_DIR}" -type f -mtime +${RETENTION_DAYS} -delete

echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Syncing encrypted archives to remote Cloudflare R2 / S3..."
# rclone copy "${BACKUP_DIR}" r2:my-company-backups/automation/
echo "[${TIMESTAMP}] Backup completed successfully."

Make executable and register with system crontab:

chmod +x /opt/scripts/backup_automation.sh
(crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo "0 3 * * * /opt/scripts/backup_automation.sh >> /var/log/automation_backup.log 2>&1") | crontab -

8. Financial ROI Comparison: Hosted SaaS vs. Private Cloud VPS

Let us examine the concrete economics of running 200,000 monthly automation tasks with an average of 450 tokens generated per task:

Metric Hosted SaaS Stack (Make.com Enterprise + OpenAI Tier 4) Private Cloud VPS Stack (Self-Hosted n8n + Ollama 14B)
Monthly Executions 200,000 tasks/month 200,000+ tasks/month (Uncapped)
Compute / Base Platform Fee $299.00 / month $16.50 / month (Cloud VPS 6-core 16GB)
LLM Inference Tokens Cost $180.00 / month ($2.00/1M tokens) $0.00 / month (Local hardware inference)
Data Privacy & Compliance Multi-tenant shared cloud; external logging 100% Private Isolated VPS; zero data egress
Custom Extension Freedom Restricted to pre-built marketplace apps Full Node.js/Python npm package support
Total Annual Cost $5,748.00 / year $198.00 / year
Net Annual Cashflow Savings — $5,550.00 (96.5% Immediate Reduction)

9. Production Troubleshooting & Deep Kernel Optimizations

When deploying autonomous agents in production environments, standard Linux defaults can cause memory thrashing, unexpected OOM (Out-of-Memory) kills, or unbounded log growth that exhausts VPS storage. Implement these battle-tested kernel and Docker tuning parameters.

9.1 Mitigating Kernel OOM Killer on Memory-Constrained VPS

Linux kernels aggressively terminate processes when memory runs tight. Because Ollama and n8n allocate large contiguous blocks of virtual memory, you must configure swap space and lower kernel swappiness to prevent sudden service crashes:

# Create an 8GB high-speed NVMe swapfile
sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile

# Ensure persistence across server reboots
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

# Tune Virtual Memory Subsystem
sudo cat <<EOF >> /etc/sysctl.conf
# Reduce aggressive swapping while preserving emergency buffer
vm.swappiness = 10
vm.vfs_cache_pressure = 50
vm.overcommit_memory = 1
EOF

sudo sysctl -p

9.2 Docker Global Daemon Log Rotation

By default, Docker preserves container standard output logs indefinitely. An automated agent logging thousands of JSON payloads per hour will fill a 100GB NVMe drive within weeks. Configure global log rotation in /etc/docker/daemon.json:

{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "25m",
    "max-file": "4"
  },
  "default-ulimits": {
    "nofile": {
      "Name": "nofile",
      "Hard": 65536,
      "Soft": 65536
    }
  }
}

Reload the Docker daemon:

sudo systemctl restart docker

9.3 GPU Passthrough Setup (Optional: Dedicated Cloud GPU VPS)

If you deploy on a cloud VPS equipped with an NVIDIA GPU (such as an RTX 4060, A4000, or T4), enable zero-overhead container passthrough via the official NVIDIA Container Toolkit:

# Add NVIDIA package repository
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg
curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | \
  sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nvidia-container-toolkit
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
sudo systemctl restart docker

Then simply update the ollama block in docker-compose.yml to request all available GPUs:

    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: all
              capabilities: [gpu]

10. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Can I run this stack on a 4GB RAM VPS?

While n8n and PostgreSQL will run smoothly on 4GB of RAM, local LLM inference requires a minimum of 8GB to 16GB of memory to load 7B or 14B quantized models without severe thrashing. For 4GB instances, we recommend offloading inference to hybrid endpoints while maintaining self-hosted n8n and Postgres.

How does this stack compare to cloud-hosted n8n Cloud?

n8n Cloud is an exceptional managed platform for rapid prototyping. However, self-hosting unlocks unrestricted execution volume, custom npm dependencies, direct LAN access to local databases and Ollama instances, and eliminates the per-workflow execution pricing cap.

Is Ollama fast enough on pure CPU without a discrete GPU?

Yes. On modern AMD EPYC or Intel Xeon processors with AVX-512 extensions, GGUF 4-bit quantized 14B models achieve 14 to 22 tokens per second. Because background automation agents operate asynchronously (processing emails, webhooks, and tickets in queues), sub-second conversational latency is unnecessary—throughput and reliability take precedence.

What happens if the server reboots?

Every service in our Docker Compose blueprint utilizes restart: unless-stopped. Upon server restart, Caddy automatically rebinds TLS certificates, PostgreSQL performs atomic write-ahead log recovery, and n8n resumes listening on all webhook endpoints without manual intervention.

title: Liquid Glass Shaders vs. Flat Figma Rectangles: Designing for Spatial UI in 2026
description:
Flat grey cards have defined web design since 2013. But with spatial computing and visionOS, users expect interfaces with physical optical presence.

CSS backdrop-filter: blur(20px) is flat. True liquid glass requires dynamic refraction, chromatic dispersion, and surface highlights.


Figure 1: Hardware-accelerated frosted glass refraction running on WebGL.

Snell’s Law in WebGL 

// Fragment shader dispersion
float r = texture2D(u_texture, uv + refractOffset * 1.04).r;
float g = texture2D(u_texture, uv + refractOffset * 1.00).g;
float b = texture2D(u_texture, uv + refractOffset * 0.96).b;


Figure 2: Smooth refractive theme transitions in ExodeUI.

While Figma can only draw static grey rectangles, ExodeUI compiles real-time shaders for production. Read our guide to Rive alternatives for advanced vector motion.

title: 💀 I Deleted My Kubernetes Pod… And Lost My Database Data! Understanding Kubernetes Storage
description:
Your Pod gets deleted. Kubernetes creates a replacement. Your application starts again. But where did your data go?

Imagine deploying a database on Kubernetes.

Everything works perfectly.

You create a database, insert 10,000 records, and verify that everything is running.

Then someone deletes the Pod.

kubectl delete pod mysql-pod

Kubernetes creates a replacement Pod.

You connect to the database.

And suddenly...

Database is empty.
No records found.

😭 What just happened?

You assumed Kubernetes would automatically preserve your database data.

But here's the problem:

Containers are designed to be replaceable. Your data needs a storage strategy of its own.

Let's understand Kubernetes storage, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, and how to protect application data.

🧠 1. Why Kubernetes Needs Persistent Storage

Containers are generally designed to be disposable.

When a container is removed, its writable container filesystem does not automatically survive as persistent application storage.

Consider this:

        Kubernetes Pod
              |
              v
        Application
              |
              v
       Container Filesystem
              |
              v
        Container Deleted
              |
              v
      Writable Data Lost

This creates a problem for stateful applications such as:

  • PostgreSQL
  • MySQL
  • MongoDB
  • Redis with persistence enabled
  • Applications that store uploaded files

These applications often need data to survive container restarts and Pod replacement.

That's where Kubernetes storage resources become important.

💾 2. What Is a PersistentVolume (PV)?

A PersistentVolume is a cluster resource representing storage available for use by workloads.

Think of it as storage that exists independently of an individual Pod.

Examples of possible storage backends include:

  • AWS EBS
  • Google Persistent Disk
  • Azure Disk
  • NFS
  • Local storage
  • CSI-compatible storage systems

A simplified architecture:

       Kubernetes Cluster
               |
               v
        PersistentVolume
               |
               v
        External Storage
               |
               v
          Application

A PersistentVolume describes the storage resource, including its capacity, access modes, and storage configuration.

Example:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: demo-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 2Gi

  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain

  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data
    type: DirectoryOrCreate

Save it as pv.yaml.

Apply it:

kubectl apply -f pv.yaml

Check:

kubectl get pv

Important This hostPath example is intended for local learning. It is not a production storage design. The data is tied to the node's filesystem and does not provide reliable cluster-wide storage.

🔗 3. What Is a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)?

Here's an important question.

Should every application developer need to understand the details of the underlying storage infrastructure?

Not necessarily.

That's why Kubernetes provides PersistentVolumeClaims.

A PVC is a request for storage.

The application requests storage, and Kubernetes attempts to find or provision suitable storage.

Think of it like this:

       Application
            |
            v
    PersistentVolumeClaim
            |
            v
     PersistentVolume
            |
            v
      Storage Backend

Example:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: demo-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi

Save it as pvc.yaml.

Apply:

kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml

Check:

kubectl get pvc

A PVC can remain Pending if no suitable PV exists and no compatible dynamic provisioner is available.

This is one of the most common Kubernetes storage troubleshooting scenarios.

🔥 4. Connect Persistent Storage to a Pod

Now let's use the PVC inside a Pod.

Create pod.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: storage-test
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.27

      volumeMounts:
        - name: storage
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html

  volumes:
    - name: storage
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: demo-pvc

Apply:

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

Check:

kubectl get pods

Now create a test file inside the mounted volume:

kubectl exec storage-test -- sh -c \
  'echo "Kubernetes Persistent Storage Works!" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'

Read the file:

kubectl exec storage-test -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

You should see:

Kubernetes Persistent Storage Works!

Now delete the Pod:

kubectl delete pod storage-test

Create it again:

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

Read the file again:

kubectl exec storage-test -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

If the PVC remains bound to storage that survives Pod replacement, the file should still be present.

That's the purpose of persistent storage.

The Pod can be replaced without automatically destroying the separately managed storage.

⚙️ 5. What Is a StorageClass?

Imagine you manage hundreds of applications.

Manually creating PersistentVolumes for every application would be difficult.

Kubernetes supports dynamic volume provisioning through StorageClasses.

A StorageClass describes how storage should be provisioned.

For example, a cloud provider may offer different storage classes for different performance or cost requirements.

A PVC can request a StorageClass:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: database-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  storageClassName: standard

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi

When a compatible StorageClass and provisioner are configured, Kubernetes can dynamically provision storage for this claim.

Check available StorageClasses:

kubectl get storageclass

Inspect one:

kubectl describe storageclass <storage-class-name>

Remember that standard is only an example name. Your cluster may use a different StorageClass or may not have a default provisioner configured.

🆚 6. PV vs PVC vs StorageClass

This is an important comparison to remember.

Resource Meaning
PersistentVolume Represents available storage
PersistentVolumeClaim Requests storage
StorageClass Defines dynamic storage provisioning
VolumeMount Mounts storage into a container

A simple way to remember:

  • PV = Storage resource
  • PVC = Storage request
  • StorageClass = Storage provisioning mechanism

The relationship looks like this:

       StorageClass
            |
            v
     Dynamic Provisioning
            |
            v
    PersistentVolume
            |
            v
    PersistentVolumeClaim
            |
            v
          Pod
            |
            v
       Container

🚨 7. What Happens When You Delete a PVC?

This is where things become particularly important.

Deleting a PVC does not have one universal outcome for the underlying storage.

The result depends on the PersistentVolume's reclaim policy and the storage provisioner.

Two important reclaim policies are:

Retain

The underlying storage is retained after the claim is released. An administrator may need to handle the volume manually before it can be reused.

Delete

The provisioner may delete the underlying storage asset when the claim is released.

Check the reclaim policy:

kubectl get pv

Example:

NAME      CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY
demo-pv   2Gi        RWO            Retain

For important workloads, understand your storage backend's behavior and configure backups independently.

A PersistentVolume is not a backup.

If someone deletes the storage or the underlying infrastructure fails, persistent storage alone may not protect your data.

☸️ 8. StatefulSet vs Deployment: Which One Should You Use?

Another important Kubernetes concept is the difference between Deployments and StatefulSets.

A Deployment is commonly used for stateless applications.

A StatefulSet is designed for applications that need stable identities and associated storage.

Feature Deployment StatefulSet
Pod identity Generally interchangeable Stable ordinal identity
Pod names Generated names Predictable names
Storage Can use PVCs Supports stable per-Pod PVCs
Typical use Web applications Stateful workloads
Scaling Replica-based Ordered scaling behavior

For example, a StatefulSet might create:

mysql-0
mysql-1
mysql-2

Each Pod can have its own persistent storage claim.

Example StatefulSet:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: database
spec:
  serviceName: database
  replicas: 2

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database

  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: database

    spec:
      containers:
        - name: database
          image: mysql:8.4

          volumeMounts:
            - name: database-storage
              mountPath: /var/lib/mysql

  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: database-storage

      spec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce

        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi

This example demonstrates the storage pattern, not a complete production MySQL configuration. A real deployment needs secure credentials, appropriate database configuration, backup procedures, and a properly configured storage backend.

🛠️ 9. Kubernetes Storage Troubleshooting Commands

When storage stops working, these commands are extremely useful.

List PersistentVolumes:

kubectl get pv

List PersistentVolumeClaims:

kubectl get pvc

Describe a PVC:

kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name>

List StorageClasses:

kubectl get storageclass

Inspect Pod volume configuration:

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

Check namespace events:

kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

Common problems include:

  • PVC stuck in Pending.
  • No matching PersistentVolume.
  • StorageClass not found.
  • Provisioning failures.
  • Volume attachment problems.
  • Permission errors when mounting storage.
  • Node or CSI driver issues.

A simple troubleshooting flow 

PVC Not Working
      |
      v
Is PVC Bound?
      |
   No | Yes
      |   |
      v   v
Check PV  Check Pod
and SC    Events
      |   |
      v   v
Check     Check Volume
Provisioner Mount
      |
      v
Investigate Storage Backend

Follow the evidence instead of randomly deleting storage resources.

🧪 10. Your Weekend Challenge: Build a Kubernetes Storage Lab

Want to become confident with Kubernetes storage?

Build this project in Minikube or another local Kubernetes environment.

Project: Kubernetes Persistent Storage Lab

Your tasks:

  1. Create a PersistentVolume.
  2. Create a PersistentVolumeClaim.
  3. Mount the PVC into a Pod.
  4. Write a file into the mounted directory.
  5. Delete and recreate the Pod.
  6. Verify that the data remains.
  7. Test what happens when a PVC cannot be bound.
  8. Explore Retain and Delete reclaim policies in a disposable test environment.
  9. Create a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates.

Suggested repository structure:

kubernetes-storage-lab/
│
├── pv/
│   └── pv.yaml
│
├── pvc/
│   └── pvc.yaml
│
├── pods/
│   └── storage-test.yaml
│
├── statefulset/
│   └── database.yaml
│
└── README.md

Document your commands, screenshots, errors, and solutions.

This project will help you understand storage concepts much more deeply than simply reading definitions.

🎯 Final Thoughts

Kubernetes makes it easy to replace failed Pods and maintain application availability.

But your application data needs a different level of protection.

Understanding PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, and StatefulSets is essential when working with stateful applications.

And remember these three lessons:

  1. Containers are replaceable.
  2. Persistent storage must be managed separately.
  3. Persistent storage is not a substitute for backups.

A successful Kubernetes deployment isn't just about getting Pods into the Running state. It's about ensuring your applications and their data behave correctly when failures happen.

👇 Let's discuss!

Have you ever lost application data because of an incorrect Kubernetes storage configuration?

Which topic do you find most confusing?

  • PersistentVolumes and PVCs
  • StorageClasses
  • StatefulSets
  • Reclaim policies
  • CSI drivers

Share your experience in the comments!

📘 Preparing for the Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) Exam?

Explore my CKA Complete Study Guide — Certified Kubernetes Administrator:

☸️ Get the CKA Complete Study Guide

Build your Kubernetes foundation, strengthen your understanding of important concepts, and prepare with a structured learning resource.

Don't just memorize commands. Understand Kubernetes deeply. Practice consistently. Become confident.

title: I built a live SMM panel on Cloudflare's free tier — Workers, D1, and a wallet that can't double-spend
description:
I built a live SMM panel on Cloudflare's free tier

I'm a 2nd-year BTech CSE student, and I wanted to learn the parts of web development that tutorials skip: real money, real orders, and what happens when a provider API says one thing and your database says another.

So I built Ampliva — a live social media services storefront — and shipped it. Not a demo, not a localhost screenshot. Real users, real wallet balances, real orders going to a real upstream provider.

This post is about the engineering, because that's the part worth sharing. The interesting problems had nothing to do with the catalogue and everything to do with payments, state, and auth.

Live links, if you want to poke at it first:

  • Storefront: https://ampliva-store.pages.dev
  • There's a free Instagram Profile Lookup tool on the site (no login) if you just want to try something quickly

The stack was chosen by a budget of zero

Every choice below exists because the free tier forced it, and most of them turned out better than the paid default I would have picked.

Layer Choice Why
Frontend React 19 + Vite on Cloudflare Pages Fast builds, free hosting, deploys on push
API Cloudflare Worker + Hono No server to keep alive, runs at the edge
Database Cloudflare D1 SQLite at the edge, generous free tier, no separate DB bill
Auth (new) Firebase Auth (Spark, $0) Email verification and Google sign-in without building either
Approvals Discord, with real buttons My admin panel is where I already live
Payments Manual UPI for now See the Razorpay section — this is deliberate, not lazy

The catalogue syncs from the upstream provider (CID Growth Media) into D1 — 316 services at last sync — and orders are placed provider-first, so I never take a user's money for an order the provider has already rejected.

Money is a ledger, not a number

This is the lesson I'd tattoo on every side-project that touches payments:

Never store a balance as a single number you increment and decrement.

Ampliva's wallet is an append-only ledger. Every credit, every debit, every refund is a new row that explains itself — what it was for, which order it belongs to, when it happened. The balance is derived from that history.

That one decision killed an entire class of bugs before they could happen:

  • A cancelled order refunds automatically, and the refund is a ledger entry you can point to, not a mysterious balance change.
  • If an order flow crashes halfway, the ledger shows exactly where it stopped. No guessing, no "the balance looks wrong."
  • When a friend who was testing the store asked where ₹3.40 had gone, I didn't debug anything. I just read the ledger back to him. (It was a cancelled order, refunded correctly.)

If you're building anything with a wallet, credits, or in-app currency: build the ledger first. The balance column is a cache, not the truth.

Ordering follows the same paranoia: provider first, then charge. The order goes to the upstream provider, and only a confirmed provider order touches the wallet. A provider rejection costs the user nothing.

No payment gateway? Discord buttons are the admin panel

I don't have Razorpay live yet — it needs a PAN reprint, then video KYC, then live keys. That's parked, on purpose, until the paperwork clears.

So top-ups are manual UPI:

  1. The user pays by UPI and submits their UTR (the transaction reference).
  2. I get a ping in a Discord channel — with Approve / Reject buttons, not just a notification.
  3. One tap credits the wallet, as a ledger entry, obviously.

The buttons were the fun part. A plain Discord webhook can't do buttons that actually work — a webhook has no application behind it, so Discord has nowhere to send the click. Working buttons need a bot/app-owned message and an interactions endpoint that verifies Discord's Ed25519 signature on every click. Once that was in place, approvals became: phone buzzes, tap Approve, wallet credited. Owner-only, signature-verified, no dashboard login needed.

Is manual UPI scalable? No. Is it the right call at zero revenue with a gateway blocked on paperwork? Absolutely. Ship the human-in-the-loop version, automate later.

A 15-minute sweep keeps order statuses honest

Provider order statuses drift. An order that's "processing" in my database might have completed, partially delivered, or been cancelled upstream an hour ago.

Instead of webhooks I may or may not get, Ampliva runs a sweep every 15 minutes:

  • Poll open orders, capped at 50 per run so a backlog can't turn into an API hammering incident.
  • Terminal states are explicit: Completed, Canceled, Partial, Refunded. Once an order reaches one, it never moves again.
  • A daily watch also flags two things I actually care about: provider balance dropping below ₹500, and any order stuck open for more than 24 hours.

It's boring infrastructure. It's also the difference between users trusting your statuses and users screenshotting them to argue with you.

Auth: the token you get at signup is lying to you

This is the bug I most want to save someone else from.

I added Firebase Auth alongside the existing local accounts — hybrid, no forced migration. New users sign up with email/password in Firebase, click a verification link, then hit an "I've verified — continue" button on my site. My Worker verifies the Firebase token server-side (signature, project, and the email_verified flag) before creating a session.

First live test: the user verified, clicked continue, and got rejected. Verified flag: false.

The problem wasn't Firebase. It was token freshness. The ID token issued at signup is minted before verification happens, and it keeps saying email_verified: false even after the user clicks the link. The fix is to force a fresh token after verification — only the refreshed token carries the updated claim. My server was doing everything right; it was faithfully reading a stale token.

Once that clicked, the whole flow passed end-to-end on the first try.

Then I closed the old door properly

With verified signup working, I tightened registration:

  • Direct local signup now returns 403 with a message pointing to the real routes. It creates nothing.
  • Google sign-in counts as verified — Google has already done that work.
  • Existing users are grandfathered. The login route didn't change by a single line. Wallets, orders, and sessions are untouched. Nobody wakes up locked out because I improved signup security.

That last point matters. "Tighten auth" is easy to say and easy to do cruelly. If your change punishes the users who trusted you early, you did it wrong.

Two smaller auth lessons, free of charge:

  • Verification mail from a new sender lands in spam. It just does. Put "check spam" on the pending screen, next to the waiting message, not in a FAQ nobody reads.
  • Old cached clients will hit your new endpoints. A user on a stale page bundle submitting to the now-closed signup route gets a clear 403 message explaining where to go — not a crash, not a silent failure. Design your rejections like you design your errors: for a confused human.

What I deliberately haven't built yet

Build-in-public should include the "not done" list, so here's mine, honestly:

  • Razorpay — parked until PAN → video KYC → live keys. Manual UPI until then.
  • Referral payouts — when they arrive, bonuses will only pay to verified accounts. Grandfathered users can link Google or verified email to qualify; nobody gets locked out of the store itself over it.
  • Catalogue curation — a synced catalogue of 316 services includes some junk I wouldn't sell to anyone. Hiding those before driving real traffic is on me, and it's next.
  • One auth combination is still untested end-to-end — an existing local user signing in via the new verified-email mode. Both halves are proven separately on the same endpoint (token acquisition, and link-by-email), but I haven't watched the full path, because doing so would mean triggering password resets on real accounts that aren't mine to poke. I'd rather disclose that than quietly claim 100% coverage.

What I'd tell myself before starting

  1. The ledger is the product. Everything else is UI over an honest record of money.
  2. Free tiers are an architecture. Cloudflare + Firebase Spark didn't just save money, they removed servers, SMTP, and a verification system from my maintenance list.
  3. Verify claims on fresh tokens, verify statuses with a sweep, verify deploys on the live bundle. The theme of this whole build is that cached, stale, and assumed states are where bugs live.
  4. Grandfather your early users. Security changes should close doors behind new signups, not in the faces of existing accounts.

Ampliva is live at ampliva-store.pages.dev — the free Profile Lookup tool needs no account if you want to try the least payment-shaped part of it.

I'm genuinely curious how others have handled two things: wallet/ledger design in small projects, and verification flows where the mail reliably lands in spam. What worked for you?

I'll keep building in public as the catalogue cleanup and referral work land. If you spot something broken on the site, that's useful too — early users breaking things politely has been half my QA.

— Arppith (Shadow), 2nd-year BTech CSE

title: Engineering a Football Intelligence Platform: Simulations, Statistical Models, Scanners and Automated Workflows
description:
Written by the Slipio team. Slipio is our product.

Football looks like a perfect machine-learning problem: decades of results, thousands of matches a week, and a clean target. In practice the hard parts are rarely the model. They are time, truth and honesty: knowing exactly what was knowable when, knowing when a number in your database is final, and knowing whether your model is actually any good.

This is a tour of how we built Slipio, a football intelligence web app that turns data, simulation and calibrated models into match probabilities with plain-English reasons. The stack is a Java 21 / Spring Boot backend on PostgreSQL, a Qdrant vector store, and React front ends. We will go layer by layer and say where things went wrong, because most of what we know came from that.

1. Ingestion: a feed is not the truth

Fixtures, odds, statistics, match events and line-ups come from a commercial data provider. The ingestion layer is a set of resource-specific workers behind a dispatcher, and every request passes through a rate budget. Each priority level has its own ceiling, so a backfill cannot starve the jobs that collect pre-match data.

Three rules came out of real incidents:

  • An empty response is not "not found". Throttling also returns an empty body. Treat empty as "unknown, retry later", never as proof that something does not exist.
  • A present row is not a final row. The provider writes match statistics while the match is being played. We once settled a corners selection against statistics captured 33 minutes into the match. Settlement now waits until the statistics were last updated at least three hours after kick-off. This costs nothing in practice, because the median statistics row lands about two days after kick-off anyway.
  • Never derive a season from a calendar year. A European 2024 season runs from August 2024 to May 2025. One historical odds import resolved every January–May fixture against the wrong season. Every miss came back as "skipped", which looks exactly like a competition we do not track. A third of the corpus went unpriced, and the job still reported COMPLETED. Resolve a fixture on its provider id alone, and take the season from the match you find.

2. Historical data and the leakage problem

A feature leaks when it carries information that did not exist, or that we had not recorded, at the moment the prediction is made. A leaking model looks excellent offline and cannot reproduce that in production.

We think about three instants for every read:

Instant Meaning
Decision When the prediction is made (a horizon from 72 hours to 5 minutes before kick-off)
Event time When the thing the row describes happened
Record time When we stored it

These give two clocks. A publication clock admits a row whose event time comes before the decision. A knowledge clock also requires that we had recorded it by then. Some of the rules are obvious: the result of the match being predicted is never admissible. Others are not. A weather feature may only be the forecast that existed at the decision. The measured weather the match was played in is knowable six hours after kick-off, and training on it while serving a forecast is a train/serve skew. Injury rows have no return date, so "currently injured" has to be bounded by recency. A player's "current club" pointer is overwritten on every sync, so it must never stand in for a past squad.

A time-bounded read looks like this (simplified):

SELECT s.team_id, s.corners, s.yellow_cards
FROM   match_statistics s
JOIN   fixtures m ON m.id = s.match_id
WHERE  m.status = 'FINISHED'
  AND  m.kickoff_at < CAST(:decision AS timestamptz)
  AND  s.updated_at >= m.kickoff_at + interval '3 hours'  -- final, not in-play
  AND  s.created_at <= CAST(:decision AS timestamptz);     -- knowledge clock

The CAST is there for a reason. PostgreSQL infers an untyped bind parameter from its neighbour, so :decision + interval '21 days' comes back as an interval and fails at runtime. So does (:x IS NULL OR col = :x) once a caller passes null.

The rules are not just a document. A catalogue in code lists every leakage rule, and an architecture test fails the build if a new loader query loses its time bound or if a feature source is not classified. Every training run writes a leakage audit first, and the gate refuses to train on a hash-based or out-of-order split. Stages that leak knowingly are quarantined with a reason and a probe, not hidden.

3. Feature engineering

The V1 feature vector has around 580 features: rolling form windows (season, last 10, last 5, venue splits), opponent-adjusted and time-decayed rates, expected goals, Elo ratings, rest and congestion, availability, and market features built from de-vigged prices.

One engineering habit matters more than any single feature.

  • Version the calculation separately from the schema. Adding features bumps a calculation version, and the regeneration pass rewrites vectors in place. Re-keying the stored vectors instead would have stranded every live prediction until regeneration caught up.

Prices need care too. A bookmaker's "Home / Draw / Away" labels are also used for Asian handicaps, half-time markets and corners 1X2, and over/under is quoted across many lines. Any "latest price per bookmaker" key must include both market and line. Without them, the query usually picks the wrong price instead of blending it.

To remove the bookmaker margin from three-way markets we use the power method rather than proportional normalisation:

implied_i = 1 / odds_i              # sums to more than 1: that excess is the margin
find k by bisection such that  Σ implied_i^k = 1
fair_i   = implied_i^k

Proportional de-vigging leaves the book's longshot loading in place and creates a false favourite–longshot edge. Two-way markets stay proportional, because there the power method measured neutral or worse.

4. Simulation: Poisson, over-dispersion and shared samples

Each match is played out many times in a Monte Carlo engine. Each side's goal rate λ combines attack and defence strengths, a league base rate, and a home-advantage ratio. It is then anchored to the de-vigged market total and to an Elo-based balance between the sides. The anchors do not commute: market-then-Elo and Elo-then-market give the same total but a different split. A test that asserted otherwise failed straight away.

Real goal counts are more variable than a pure Poisson allows, so the main engine adds a Gamma mixture, which gives a negative binomial:

rate  ~ Gamma(shape = k, scale = λ / k)   # mean λ
goals ~ Poisson(rate)
# marginal: negative binomial, mean λ, variance λ(1 + λ/k)

Things we learned the hard way:

  • Size truncation for the distribution you actually use. Twenty-five goals a side is generous for a Poisson but not for a negative binomial at high λ. The grid now grows adaptively to a tolerance and reports the probability mass it discarded.
  • Shuffle samples allocated from a grid. Allocating an exact score grid into samples emits them in probability order. If anything later pairs index i across arrays, sorted order quietly creates a false correlation.
  • Monte Carlo noise is real. An internal audit found that at 10,000 iterations, the "most likely score" for one fixture came out as 0–1 on 86 seeds out of 100 and 0–2 on the other 14, and the stored run held the 0–2. The fix is to compute the score grid analytically where you can, or to sample far more.
  • One world per fixture. The same audit found that reading different markets from separate runs gave inconsistent answers. The Prediction Set engine therefore draws one shared sample set per match and settles every selection against it.

Dixon–Coles, the low-score correction, exists in the codebase but is off. On our corpus it made log-loss worse, probably because it fights the over-dispersion over the 1–1 cell. We do not use a bivariate Poisson.

5. Machine-learning models and calibration

Five prediction types (match result, over/under 2.5 goals, both teams to score, corners and cards) each have a model. Where a market price exists, the served probability blends the learner's output with the de-vigged price (the blend weight is fitted on validation log-loss) and then calibrates it with vector scaling or Platt scaling.

The order matters: blend, then calibrate. A calibrator only works on the distribution it was fitted to, so it has to be fitted on the blended validation probabilities.

We publish the result. Every pre-kick-off prediction is checked against the final score on a public record. As of 16 November 2026 the record had checked 26,725 predictions since 5 September. For match result, the average stated chance was 52.7% and the pick happened 53.3% of the time. Calibration metrics have their own trap: one of ours called "ECE" was really the mean |confidence − correct|, on which a perfectly calibrated 1X2 model scores about 0.5. The corrected metric got a new name, not a new meaning under the old one.

The honest headline: measured against the closing price, our models reached parity and none beats it. We say so because it is the result, and because it shapes the product. Slipio explains probabilities. It does not promise an edge.

6. The Scanner: evidence with a baseline

The Scanner checks every upcoming fixture for patterns: goals and both-teams-to-score rates, form streaks, corners, cards and referee tendencies, player shots and cards, line-up changes and availability. Its central idea is that a frequency means nothing without a baseline.

A goals pattern qualifies only if the combined rate is at least 20 points above the same pattern's rate in that competition over its last 150 finished matches with the statistic known, each team is at least 10 points above it, and the combined rate is at least 50%. Every insight is then ranked by one formula:

rank     = signal × sampleReliability × freshness × (0.7 + 0.3 × dataConfidence) × certainty
strength = round(100 × rank)    # "insight strength", never a probability

Small-data traps are handled explicitly. A 0–0 match with zero cards is treated as unknown rather than "no bookings", because some feeds report goals but not bookings. Only provider-confirmed line-ups with eleven starters count as "official". A whole scan is about fifteen bulk SQL statements (LATERAL joins over unnest(uuid[])), cached per window with stale-while-revalidate and single flight. The UI calls these patterns history, not predictions, and shows the sample behind each one.

7. Building a Prediction Set

A Prediction Set combines several selections. Two pieces of code make it honest:

  • Settlement-aware maths. Lines settle the Asian way: half lines win or lose, whole lines can push (stake returned), and quarter lines split into two half-stakes. Expected values go through the same settlement code the result checker uses, never through win-or-bust arithmetic.
  • Correlation from shared samples. Same-match selections are evaluated together on each simulated match, so "over 2.5 goals" plus "both teams to score" correctly comes out more likely than the product of the two. Contradictory selections come out at zero.

A rules layer decides what may share a set at all: no match result together with double chance, one outcome per market, and no correct score alongside a market the score already decides. Quoted prices go through a plausibility filter first, because the odds feed contains stale outlier quotes.

8. Retrieval and context, honestly scoped

Slipio stores news and match reports, embeds them (a 1024-dimension multilingual model served locally) and keeps the vectors in Qdrant. The rule is simple: structured platform data is authoritative, and retrieved documents are context. They can be quoted and dated. They never change a number. A stricter knowledge index adds as-of bounds and version checks. That index is still an internal preview, so we do not present it as a product feature.

Where Slippy, the in-app assistant, uses a language model to write prose, a guard drops any number that is not in the facts it was given. The language model never computes a probability.

9. Agent pipeline orchestration

Slipio Agents (on eligible plans) run a fixed pipeline on a schedule:

Fixture Scout → Scanner Analyst → Price Validator → Simulation Analyst
             → Rules Guardian → Set Architect → Prediction Set

No step is a language model. Each one is a deterministic service with bounded settings, and the stages run in sequence even where the canvas draws a fork. Every run executes an immutable, saved version of the agent's settings, so a later edit never reaches a run in progress. The runner reports append-only stage events with sequence numbers, and clients poll them. The node-state rule is strict: a node's state comes only from reported events, never from elapsed time. The simulation step reads the normal pipeline's numbers, but it runs its baseline inside a rollback-only transaction, so automated runs never add rows to the public prediction record.

10. Freshness and performance: the partition lesson

Odds history is our largest table: tens of millions of rows, range-partitioned by season. A query that filters by match id alone gives the planner no way to prune partitions, so it scans all of them in parallel. One fixtures-with-odds endpoint took more than five minutes. Adding season = m.season to a correlated subquery does not fix it, because the value is not a constant at plan time. What works is a literal season plus a bounded list of ids, sent in chunks.

Then the data grew again. Recent fixtures carry tens of thousands of quote rows each, so a 100-id chunk became millions of rows, and the planner switched to a sequential scan. A read that took 62 seconds dropped to 143 ms with 10-id chunks. Size chunks by rows, not ids, and re-measure with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) whenever capture rates change.

11. Limits

  • Our models are at parity with the closing price, not ahead of it.
  • Some context, such as team news and line-ups, is shown beside the probabilities. Showing it does not mean the probability was adjusted for it. Our rule is that a signal the models train on is a feature and must not also be applied as a simulation modifier, which would count it twice.
  • Corners and cards are noisier than goals. On corners, a log-loss difference under about 0.02 is inside the noise a deterministic learner shows from an ordinary data refresh. Find a market's noise band before calling a difference a regression.
  • Probabilities are estimates: a quarter of the outcomes rated 75% should not happen.

The most useful engineering decision we made was to measure ourselves in public and write down every time we were wrong.

Slipio is for over-18s. Predictions are estimates, not certainties, and never betting advice. Slipio takes
no bets and never takes money on what happens in a match.

title: We Cloned Our Purchasing Server to Test an Upgrade and Our Suppliers Received Every Order Twice
description:
Our purchasing server runs the jobs that turn the morning's replenishment into purchase orders and send them to suppliers, some by email and some as files to their own systems. In May we needed to test an upgrade to the purchasing software, and the quickest way to get a realistic test machine was to clone the production server.

An engineer made the copy on a Friday afternoon and attached it to our test network. Our test network can reach the internet, because testers need to download things and reach suppliers' test portals. He planned to start the upgrade on Monday.

At six on Saturday morning, the clone woke up and did exactly what the original did. It read the same purchasing database, built the same purchase orders and sent them to the same suppliers, from the same addresses and under the same order numbers. Every supplier on that morning's run received each order twice.

Most of their systems rejected the repeats or someone noticed. Three did not. On Monday we received a second lorry of cement, a double delivery of roof battens and twice the copper fittings we had asked for. Returning them cost us collection charges and an awkward call to each supplier.

Nothing about the clone was faulty. A copy of a server includes its scheduled jobs, its credentials and its idea of who it is. We had taken great care that test systems never touch production data, and none that a copy of production never behaves as production.

Clones are now created switched off and started on an isolated network with no route out. The engineer disables every scheduled job and checks the list with a colleague before the clone is moved anywhere it can reach a supplier, a customer or a mail server. Every job that sends anything outside the company first asks a central setting whether the server it runs on is the named production server, and stops if it is not. We also asked our twenty largest suppliers to reject a purchase order number they have already received, and most of them now do.

Automation does not know it has been copied. Make sure the copy can tell.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Make the agent keep the existing z-index scale — no magic z-index values
description:
The modal is under the sticky header again. The agent “fixes” it with z-index: 9999 on the dialog, 10000 on the toast, and 1 on a tooltip that now punches through a drawer. The visual bug is gone in that one storybook story. The stacking scale is not.

I’ve started treating a magic z-index in an agent UI patch as a review comment, not a mergeable polish. If the repo already has --z-dropdown, --z-modal, and --z-toast, the model should pick one of those — or propose a new token in the same file — not invent 9999.

Why 9999 is a trap

A z-index scale is a contract. Once three components pick random four-digit numbers, every later overlay has to guess higher. Portals, sticky headers, and third-party widgets make the guessing worse. The next agent session cannot see the implicit “we already used 10000,” so it uses 10001.

The number also hides the real bug. A popover under a header is often a stacking context problem (isolation, transform, filter, or a parent z-index), not a missing 9999. A huge literal lets the PR look finished without asking which context actually won.

A simple scale policy

  • Tokens only — var(--z-modal) or the Sass/JS equivalent already in the theme
  • One scale file — new layers are added there, with a one-line comment for what sits above and below
  • No +1 arms races — do not “beat” a sibling by adding one to its computed value
  • Name the layer — modal, popover, toast, nav, not zIndex={50} next to an unexplained zIndex={40}

If the design system uses Tailwind, pin the agent to the configured z- utilities (z-modal, z-10 only if that is the scale). A raw z-[9999] is the same offense as a raw 9999 in CSS.

What to put in the prompt

Give the agent the scale, not a vibe:

Use only the z-index tokens in src/theme/z-index.css.
Do not invent a new numeric z-index.
If a new layer is required, add a named token in that file and say what it sits above.
If the bug is a stacking context, fix the context — don’t raise the number.

Paste the token file, or a 10-line excerpt, into the prompt. A screenshot of the broken overlay is not a substitute for the scale.

In the PR, ask for a one-line note: which token was used, or why a new token was added. If the diff contains a raw integer, send it back.

The same rule applies when the agent “fixes” a popover by adding z-index to a parent that already creates a stacking context. Raising the child does nothing useful, and raising the parent can lift a whole column of the page over the nav. Ask what element actually forms the context. A one-line DevTools note in the PR (“header is transform: translateZ(0), so the popover must portal to document.body”) is worth more than a new integer.

If the design system documents a portal target for overlays, use that. A modal that stays in the article flow and then tries to win with z-index is the usual source of these patches.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • z-index: 9999, z-[9999], or style={{ zIndex: 10000 }} in a repo that has a scale
  • A toast, modal, and popover each inventing their own number in the same PR
  • “I set it high so it always wins” as the only justification
  • Fixing an overlay by raising z-index when a parent transform created a new context

Accept

  • An existing token, correctly chosen for the layer
  • A new named token in the scale file, with a short comment
  • A stacking-context fix that leaves the scale alone
