title: Encontré 2 bugs reales en Django y decidí no reportarlos. La razón es más interesante que el bug.
description:
Encontré 2 bugs reales en Django y decidí no reportarlos. La razón es más interesante que el bug.

Un embudo de tres etapas para auditar fronteras de acoplamiento, con tres de mis propios instrumentos refutados por la ejecución real.

Pasé una noche midiendo si los ciclos de importación predicen fallos en producción. Al final tenía 1 449 módulos auditados en 5 paquetes, 2 rupturas reales en el backend de base de datos de Django, 0 reportes enviados. Este artículo es sobre por qué la tercera cifra es la correcta, y sobre los tres instrumentos que tuvieron que romperse para llegar a ella. El código, los datos y los falsadores están en auditor-toolkit.

La premisa

Los proyectos maduros acumulan invariantes implícitos: órdenes de carga, estado global, dependencias no declaradas. Sus propias suites de pruebas nunca los violan, porque las pruebas se escribieron obedeciendo esas reglas. Un consumidor externo —un adaptador, un plugin, un backend de base de datos de terceros— sí puede violarlas, y entonces el sistema falla de una forma que ningún linter detecta.

Los linters responden a «¿existe un ciclo?». La pregunta útil es otra: ¿existe una ruptura alcanzable?

Etapa 1 — el candidato: mi primer instrumento, refutado tres veces

Escribí un modelo posicional: una sentencia from M import n solo rompe si n no existe todavía en M en el instante en que la sentencia corre. Suena correcto. Sobre 17 componentes fuertemente conexos (SCC) en django, pydantic, sqlalchemy, celery y django-filter, emitió veredicto en 14 de ellos y predijo 11 rupturas (los otros 3 los dio por PASA, y 3 quedaron NO_MEDIDO). La ejecución real, ya con todos los drivers instalados, encontró 2 — y ninguna de las 11 estaba entre ellas.

Lo corregí tres veces, cada vez con evidencia:

versión defecto corregido predice ROMPE lecturas inseguras
v1 un submódulo se medía contra el SCC en vez de contra el paquete completo 14 / 17 1 107
v2 el corte de líneas se leía del módulo que lee, no del leído 14 / 17 1 050
v3 regla padre-primero: un submódulo nunca está a medio ejecutar cuando su padre lo importa 11 / 17 625

Y la razón por la que ninguna versión funciona no es un bug. Es estructural:

Dentro de un SCC, todo par de módulos se alcanza mutuamente. Por tanto «¿está t a medio ejecutar?» no es decidible desde el AST: depende de la pila de importación, es decir, del punto de entrada.

Comparado SCC a SCC contra la ejecución real: los 11 SCC que el modelo marcó ROMPE ejecutaron PASA. Las 2 rupturas reales están en los 2 SCC que declaró NO_MEDIDO. No acertó por exceso: falló por abstención justo donde hacía falta. Lo dejé en el código con un REFUTADO COMO PREDICTOR en el docstring, porque un instrumento refutado es evidencia de que fue refutado.

Etapa 2 — la ruptura: aquí sí hay hechos

Un ejecutor independiente importa cada módulo en un intérprete limpio, uno por proceso, y clasifica la causa del fallo (ORDEN / DEPENDENCIA / OTRO). Reduce los 909 módulos de Django a 71 imports con veredicto.

En la primera corrida reportó 0 rupturas por orden. Ese cero era un artefacto: tres SCC estaban marcados NO_MEDIDO porque faltaban drivers opcionales. NO_MEDIDO no es cero. Instalé oracledb 26.1.0 y psycopg2 2.9.13, y el resultado cambió de signo:

# intérprete limpio, driver presente
import django.db.backends.postgresql.introspection
# ImportError: cannot import name 'DatabaseIntrospection'
#   from partially initialized module 'django.db.backends.postgresql.introspection'

import django.db.backends.oracle.utils
# ImportError: cannot import name 'BoundVar'
#   from partially initialized module 'django.db.backends.oracle.utils'

import django.db.backends.oracle.operations
# ImportError: cannot import name 'DatabaseOperations'
#   from partially initialized module 'django.db.backends.oracle.operations'

El mecanismo, en tres líneas de código ajeno:

oracle/operations.py:16   from .utils import BoundVar, ...                  → entra a utils
oracle/utils.py:4         from .base import Database                        → entra a base
oracle/base.py:65         from .operations import DatabaseOperations  ← operations a medio construir

Entrando por base o por el paquete, Database ya está ligado antes de la línea 65 y todo pasa. Entrando por utils u operations, no. La ruptura es real. Lo que falta es quién la alcance.

Etapa 3 — el consumidor: donde mi instrumento me mintió dos veces

Busqué los tres imports en GitHub. total_count: 0 · 0 · 0. Un cero limpio. No abrí el ticket.

Antes de publicarlo corrí un control positivo sobre el buscador, con la misma forma de consulta:

gh api search/code -f q="from+django.db.backends.postgresql.base+import"   # → 0
gh api search/code -f q="from django.db.backends.postgresql.base import"   # → 11 696

0 contra 11 696 para la misma cadena. En un parámetro de query, + es un signo más literal, no un espacio. Mi instrumento devolvía cero para lo que existe.

Lo rehice con espacios: 19 520 / 9 872 / 14 080. Igual de inservible, ahora en la dirección contraria: la API de búsqueda empareja tokens, no sentencias, y los resultados caían en el propio postgresql/base.py de Django.

Tercer intento, instrumento distinto y exacto: censo sobre el árbol fuente de Django 6.1.3, población declarada —los 5 módulos que forman los dos SCC—, separando las aristas internas del ciclo (esas son el ciclo, no quien lo alcanza).

clase cuenta detalle
aristas internas del ciclo 7 oracle/base.py:65, postgresql/introspection.py:6…
consumidores a nivel módulo 5 los 5 en contrib.gis; 2 rompen al desenmascararlos, 3 están precedidos por su base
consumidores dentro de función 13 11 en tests/, 1 en oracle/client.py:12
documentados en docs/ref/ 0

Ejecuté los 5 como punto de entrada. Cuatro fallan por GDAL ausente, no por el ciclo:

import django.contrib.gis.db.backends.oracle.operations
# ImproperlyConfigured: Could not find the GDAL library

El quinto no llega al import roto porque su línea 4 ya cargó postgresql.base. Es decir: GDAL no enmascara un caso, enmascara cuatro de cinco. Y ésa no es una casilla vacía que se pueda dejar abierta: es la variable que decide si esta etapa tiene algún consumidor vivo.

Así que la desenmascaré

Instalar GDAL por Homebrew son 44 fórmulas. Usé una más barata y sin trampa: el wheel de rasterio embarca un libgdal.38.3.12.2.dylib real, y basta apuntarlo con GDAL_LIBRARY_PATH. No es un stub: es la misma biblioteca C que Django enlaza.

Al hacerlo apareció una capa que no había previsto: no era una máscara, eran dos. geos/__init__.py:16 importa .libgeos, así que sin GEOS el módulo muere igual, un piso más abajo. Dos bibliotecas C hay que satisfacer antes de que un solo import de contrib.gis llegue a ejecutar Python propio.

Con las dos presentes, y tras django.setup():

consumidor antes después
gis/oracle/operations.py:20 GDAL ausente ImportError: oracle.operations parcialmente inicializado
gis/postgis/introspection.py:2 GDAL ausente ImportError: postgresql.introspection parcialmente inicializado
gis/oracle/base.py:1 GDAL ausente pasa (es la entrada segura)
gis/postgis/base.py:4 y :8 cubierto pasa (la línea 4 precede a la 8)

Dos de los cinco consumidores llegan al ciclo y rompen. El hallazgo cambia de signo: ya no es «cero accionables», es «dos accionables que ninguna biblioteca nativa alcanzaba a mostrar».

Y aquí está la prueba que hacía falta

Mismo intérprete, misma configuración, mismo módulo. Lo único que cambia es el orden:

import django.contrib.gis.db.backends.oracle.operations
# ImportError: cannot import name 'DatabaseOperations' from partially initialized module

import django.contrib.gis.db.backends.oracle.base      # primero esto
import django.contrib.gis.db.backends.oracle.operations  # y ahora esto
# OK

Lo mismo con postgis.introspection y postgis.base. El control negativo está dentro de la misma medición: las dos secuencias «base primero» existen justamente para refutar que la causa sea el entorno. No lo refutan. La causa es el orden.

Esto no es un bug de instalación ni una rareza de mi máquina: es un módulo que se rompe según quién lo importe antes.

No abrí el ticket — pero no por lo que creía. El criterio que me dejó el wontfix («sin un consumidor nombrado y alcanzable, no hay bug: hay texto») se pone a prueba tres párrafos más abajo, y no sale como esperaba: al desenmascarar GDAL, el consumidor aparece. Que aun así no haya ticket tiene otra razón, y es la que vale.

Las tres reglas que me costaron la noche

1. NO_MEDIDO no es cero. Dos veces. Los drivers ausentes fabricaron un nulo; el + en la consulta fabricó el otro. Un cero con dependencias no declaradas es una mentira estadística.

2. Un cero que también da cero para lo que existe es un instrumento roto. El control positivo no es burocracia: es lo único que distingue «no hay» de «no miré». Y un control positivo no basta: mi modelo posicional lo pasaba —sabía emitir ROMPE— y aun así sus 11 candidatos salieron limpios. Hace falta también el control que debe salir limpio.

3. La etapa que convierte ruptura en hallazgo no es el análisis: es el consumidor. Sin ella habría publicado un hallazgo falso por segunda vez.

El embudo, y lo que queda abierto

etapa instrumento resultado control positivo control negativo
candidato AST estático 17 SCC · 11 predichos ROMPE · 625 lecturas sí no: 11/11 falsos
ruptura ejecución en intérprete limpio 2 SCC · 3 puntos de entrada sí, uno por proceso sí
consumidor censo del sdist 5 a nivel módulo · 2 rompen al desenmascararlos · 13 en función · 0 documentados sí sí

Y el veredicto de la predicción que quedaba abierta. La corrí. 3 de 4 acertadas, y la que falló es un defecto de mi pre-registro, no del modelo: predije PASA para postgis/base y sin django.setup() da AppRegistryNotReady, una tercera clase de fallo que no declaré como precondición. Con setup(), pasa, como estaba escrito. La lección no es «acerté»: es que un pre-registro sin sus precondiciones no es falsable, es una frase.

Las dos que importan acertaron, y acertaron en la dirección incómoda: el ciclo es alcanzable y rompe de verdad.

Nivel 7: la pregunta que sí tiene respuesta

Hasta aquí la pregunta era «¿el ciclo predice la ruptura?», y la respuesta es que no: mis once candidatos salieron limpios. Pero hay una pregunta mejor, y esta sí se contesta con números: ¿qué le permite a un paquete tener ciclos y no romperse?

Cambié la unidad de medida. En vez de contar ciclos, conté lectores: módulos fuera del ciclo cuyo import a nivel módulo resuelve a un miembro del ciclo. Un lector es la persona que entra por la puerta de atrás. Para cada uno, dos sondas en intérprete limpio: import R, y import <predecesor>; import R. Si la primera rompe por ciclo y la segunda pasa, la causa es el orden y nada más.

Sobre los mismos 17 ciclos:

celda qué significa cuántos
INERTE nadie de fuera entra por el ciclo 13
INMUNE_CONSTRUCCION entra alguien y rompe, pero hay una entrada que lo salva 4
MINA_VIVA entra alguien, rompe, y ninguna entrada lo salva 0

Cinco pares (ciclo, lector) rompen, sobre cuatro módulos distintos, todos en Django: db.backends.oracle.operations, db.backends.postgresql.introspection, contrib.gis.db.backends.oracle.operations y contrib.gis.db.backends.postgis.introspection. (Son 4 módulos y no «2 rupturas» como dice la tabla de arriba porque cuento poblaciones distintas: allí, ciclos que rompen; aquí, módulos que rompen al importarse primero.)

Y aquí está el dato que no esperaba. Esos cuatro módulos se reparan con dos: db.backends.oracle.base y db.backends.postgresql.base. El invariante que protege a Django no vive en el ciclo, vive en el paquete: entra por .base. Es una convención de una línea, y su API pública la impone en django/db/utils.py:116. En pydantic, sqlalchemy y django-filter, sus 7 ciclos no tienen ni un lector que rompa: cero convención necesaria.

También me equivoqué aquí, y conviene decirlo. Mi pre-registro afirmaba que sólo dos de los diecisiete ciclos rompían; rompen cuatro. Y el reparador ni siquiera estaba donde lo busqué: para dos de ellos ningún miembro del propio ciclo repara — el que repara pertenece a otro ciclo. Por eso la tabla final publica dos columnas, «repara en su vecindario» y «repara en todo el paquete». Quince de diecisiete predicciones correctas: fallé en los dos ciclos del bloque db.models.

Lo que cambia para el ticket: no es que Django sea inmune por no tener ciclos —tiene diecisiete—. Es inmune porque tiene una entrada declarada y la hace cumplir. Eso no lo arregla un if, y no lo descubre un linter. Es exactamente el tipo de invariante implícito que este embudo existe para encontrar.

Entonces, ¿por qué sigo sin abrir el ticket?

Porque medí también el consumidor real, y ese número es pequeño y preciso: django/db/utils.py:116 hace import_module("%s.base" % backend_name) — Django siempre carga base antes de operations. En el uso normal el fallo no puede ocurrir. Vive en el único hueco donde alguien importe operations primero: un paquete de terceros que herede DatabaseOperations a nivel de módulo. Que ese paquete exista o no lo sigo teniendo en NO_MEDIDO.

Es una mina, no un incendio. Y una mina sin denominador medido no se reporta: se documenta.

Y queda una casilla honesta: el consumidor externo de terceros es NO_MEDIDO. No tengo hoy un instrumento que pruebe una sentencia literal sobre GitHub, y no voy a rellenar esa casilla con un número que no se distingue de un instrumento roto.

Medido el 16 y 17 de noviembre de 2026 sobre django 6.1.3, pydantic 2.14.3, sqlalchemy 2.1.9, celery 5.7.0, django-filter 26.2, Python 3.14.8 en macOS, con GDAL 3.12.2 y GEOS 3.15.0. Los tres instrumentos de esta medición —con su pre-registro, sus datos y sus falsadores ejecutables— están publicados en auditor-toolkit v0.2.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24323318, bajo research/frontera-import/.

Nota del método: los códigos de retorno que uso aquí están indexados con su causa declarada y la huella que los sella en https://indice-rc.vercel.app — y la compuerta que los emite se mueve a mano, sin llamadas de red, en https://indice-rc.vercel.app/simulador.html

title: Graceful Shutdown in Node.js and NestJS on Docker: SIGTERM, Draining, and Hook Order — Field Notes
description:
Headline: A graceful shutdown means a Node.js process that receives SIGTERM stops taking new work, finishes what is in flight, closes its database and Redis connections, and exits before the orchestrator's grace period ends. In a Dockerized NestJS app that takes an exec-form CMD, app.enableShutdownHooks(), and cleanup placed in the lifecycle hook that runs after the HTTP server drains.

Redeploying my containerized NestJS APIs used to cost a handful of 502s and, now and then, a queue job that ran twice. The logs showed no errors. The clue was in docker ps -a: the old containers ended with Exited (137). Exit code 137 is 128 + 9, meaning the process was ended by SIGKILL and my shutdown code never ran.

Key takeaways

  • docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits 10 seconds by default, then sends SIGKILL; Kubernetes waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, which defaults to 30 seconds.
  • Exit code 137 (128 + 9) means SIGKILL: the process overran its grace period or was OOM-killed.
  • Shell-form CMD, npm start, and Node.js running as PID 1 can each keep SIGTERM from reaching your code; use exec-form CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"] plus Docker's init: true.
  • NestJS ignores termination signals until you call app.enableShutdownHooks(), then runs onModuleDestroy → beforeApplicationShutdown → HTTP server close → onApplicationShutdown.
  • Close database pools and Redis clients in onApplicationShutdown, not onModuleDestroy, because onModuleDestroy runs while requests are still in flight.

What happens when Docker stops a Node.js container?

docker stop sends SIGTERM (or the image's STOPSIGNAL) to the container's PID 1, waits a grace period, and then sends SIGKILL. The default grace period is 10 seconds; docker stop --time and the Compose key stop_grace_period change it. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so anything unfinished is cut off: open HTTP responses, half-committed transactions, and queue jobs that were picked up but never acknowledged.

Kubernetes uses the same contract with terminationGracePeriodSeconds, 30 seconds by default, plus one race: a terminating pod is removed from Service endpoints in parallel with SIGTERM, not before it, so the pod can still receive new requests for a moment after shutdown starts.

The container's exit code tells you which path shutdown took:

Exit code Meaning What it says about shutdown
0 The process exited on its own Your handler ran and called process.exit(0)
143 128 + 15 (SIGTERM) The process ended on SIGTERM; NestJS re-raises the signal after its hooks, so a clean Nest shutdown usually lands here
137 128 + 9 (SIGKILL) The grace period expired or the OOM killer struck, and work was cut off mid-flight

docker inspect reports "OOMKilled": true only in the out-of-memory case, which separates the two causes of exit code 137.

Why doesn't my Node.js app receive SIGTERM in Docker?

Docker delivers SIGTERM to PID 1, and three common setups put something other than a signal-aware Node.js process there:

  • Shell-form CMD. CMD node dist/main.js runs as /bin/sh -c "node dist/main.js", so the shell becomes PID 1 and may not forward SIGTERM to Node.js.
  • npm start as the container command. npm sits between Docker and your app; the Node.js Docker best-practices guide recommends running node directly.
  • Node.js as PID 1. Linux ignores signals sent to PID 1 unless the process installed a handler for them, and Node.js was not designed to run as PID 1.

The fix is an exec-form command plus a tiny init process:

# Exec form: Docker starts node directly, no shell in between
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

services:
  api:
    build: .
    init: true              # tini runs as PID 1, forwards signals, reaps zombies
    stop_grace_period: 30s  # Docker's default is 10s

init: true in Compose (or docker run --init) runs tini as PID 1; tini forwards signals to Node.js and reaps zombie processes. It matters even when a handler is installed, because NestJS finishes shutdown by re-raising the signal, and a PID 1 process can ignore that re-raised SIGTERM too.

How do I enable graceful shutdown in NestJS?

NestJS does not listen for termination signals by default; you opt in by calling app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts. Without that call, onModuleDestroy, beforeApplicationShutdown, and onApplicationShutdown never run on SIGTERM — they only run when your own code calls app.close().

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.enableShutdownHooks(); // SIGTERM, SIGINT, ... now run lifecycle hooks

  // Hard deadline: fail loudly before the orchestrator's SIGKILL does it silently
  process.once('SIGTERM', () => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.error('Graceful shutdown timed out after 25s, forcing exit');
      process.exit(1);
    }, 25_000).unref();
  });

  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}
void bootstrap();

The hard deadline is the part I skipped the first time. If a cleanup step hangs — a Redis client stuck reconnecting, a job that never ends — SIGKILL arrives with no log line explaining why. A timer set a few seconds below the grace period exits with a message instead, and .unref() stops the timer itself from holding the process open.

NestJS 11 re-raises the original signal after the shutdown hooks finish, which is why a clean shutdown exits with code 143. Recent NestJS 11 releases also accept app.enableShutdownHooks([], { useProcessExit: true }), which calls process.exit(0) instead — useful when an async logger such as a Pino transport needs the exit event to flush.

Which NestJS lifecycle hook should close the database connection?

Close database pools and Redis clients in onApplicationShutdown, the only NestJS shutdown hook that runs after the HTTP server has stopped. On a termination signal, NestJS 11 runs this sequence:

  1. onModuleDestroy() runs immediately, while the HTTP server is still serving requests.
  2. beforeApplicationShutdown(signal) runs after every onModuleDestroy() handler has settled.
  3. The HTTP server closes: NestJS calls Node's server.close() through the HTTP adapter and waits for in-flight requests.
  4. onApplicationShutdown(signal) runs after the server has closed.

Most NestJS examples disconnect the database in onModuleDestroy, which runs before step 3, so an in-flight request can lose its database mid-query; with node-postgres, every pool.query() after pool.end() throws. I moved each step to the hook that matches its moment:

// shutdown.service.ts
import {
  BeforeApplicationShutdown, Inject, Injectable,
  OnApplicationShutdown, OnModuleDestroy,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';
import type { Pool } from 'pg';
import type Redis from 'ioredis';
import type { Worker } from 'bullmq';
import { EMAIL_WORKER, PG_POOL, REDIS } from './tokens';

@Injectable()
export class ShutdownService
  implements OnModuleDestroy, BeforeApplicationShutdown, OnApplicationShutdown
{
  isShuttingDown = false;

  constructor(
    @Inject(PG_POOL) private readonly pool: Pool,
    @Inject(REDIS) private readonly redis: Redis,
    @Inject(EMAIL_WORKER) private readonly worker: Worker,
  ) {}

  onModuleDestroy() {
    this.isShuttingDown = true; // readiness endpoint starts returning 503
  }

  async beforeApplicationShutdown() {
    await Promise.all([
      sleep(Number(process.env.DRAIN_DELAY_MS ?? 0)), // let the load balancer notice
      this.worker.close(), // BullMQ: take no new jobs, finish active ones
    ]);
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown() {
    // The HTTP server has drained; nothing else needs these connections
    await Promise.allSettled([this.pool.end(), this.redis.quit()]);
  }
}

A GET /health/ready endpoint throws ServiceUnavailableException once isShuttingDown is true, so load balancers and Kubernetes readiness probes stop sending new traffic. BullMQ's worker.close() stops taking new jobs and waits for active ones — that ended my duplicate runs, because a job killed by SIGKILL is later detected as stalled and processed again. DRAIN_DELAY_MS only helps when something in front of the container routes by health; behind a reverse proxy that ignores health checks, I leave it at 0.

Why does my Node.js HTTP server hang on close()?

Node.js server.close() stops accepting connections and waits for open ones, and before Node.js 19 that included idle keep-alive sockets, which could hold shutdown open until keepAliveTimeout expired. Since Node.js 19, server.close() also closes idle connections, and Node.js 18.2 added server.closeIdleConnections() and server.closeAllConnections() for manual control. Without NestJS, the whole drain pattern is a few lines:

import http from 'node:http';
import { app } from './app';
import { pool } from './db';

const server = http.createServer(app);
server.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

process.once('SIGTERM', () => {
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25_000).unref(); // hard deadline
  server.close(async () => {
    // Node 19+: idle keep-alive sockets are closed too
    await pool.end();
    process.exit(0);
  });
});

NestJS also offers NestFactory.create(AppModule, { forceCloseConnections: true }). With the Express adapter, that option calls socket.destroy() on every tracked socket at shutdown — including sockets with a request still in flight. On Node.js 24, the current LTS, I treat forceCloseConnections as a last resort, not a default.

How long should the shutdown grace period be?

The grace period must cover the drain delay, the slowest request or job you are willing to wait for, and connection cleanup, plus a margin. Docker's 10-second default rarely fits once a queue worker is involved, so my Compose files set stop_grace_period: 30s with the in-app hard deadline at 25 seconds. Any job that can outlast the grace period must be resumable or idempotent.

Graceful shutdown protects work already in flight; it does not create zero-downtime deploys. With one container, requests that arrive between the old container stopping and the new one becoming ready still fail at the proxy, so zero downtime needs a second instance serving traffic while the first one drains.

FAQ

Q: Why does my Docker container take 10 seconds to stop?

A: The process is not exiting on SIGTERM, so Docker waits out its 10-second default grace period and then sends SIGKILL. The usual causes are a shell-form CMD, npm start as the container command, or Node.js running as PID 1; use an exec-form CMD and init: true.

Q: What does exit code 137 mean for a Node.js container?

A: Exit code 137 is 128 + 9: the process was killed with SIGKILL, either because shutdown overran the grace period or because the kernel's OOM killer ended it. docker inspect shows "OOMKilled": true only in the second case.

Q: Is enableShutdownHooks() on by default in NestJS?

A: No. NestJS runs its shutdown lifecycle hooks on a termination signal only after app.enableShutdownHooks() is called; otherwise they run only when your code calls app.close().

Q: Does graceful shutdown give me zero-downtime deploys?

A: No. Graceful shutdown lets in-flight requests and jobs finish; zero-downtime deploys also need another healthy instance serving new traffic while the old one drains.

title: Our winery cost calculator quoted a quarter of the real price. The catalogue next to it knew better.
description:
wine.equipment is a catalogue of winery equipment: crushers, presses, tanks, filters, bottling lines. It also has a cost calculator. You pick how many cases a year you make, the wine type and how automated you want to be, and it gives you a budget range per production stage.

The calculator was wrong, and the page itself showed it. Below each stage's estimate it printed what listings on the site actually cost. The two numbers sat a few pixels apart and disagreed.

The rule of thumb

The estimate was a per-case rule. Each stage has a dollar-per-case range, and the result is scaled for wine type and automation:

const STAGES = [
  { stage: "grape-processing", rate: [8, 15] },
  { stage: "fermentation",     rate: [12, 25] },
  { stage: "pressing",         rate: [6, 18] },
  { stage: "wine-transfer",    rate: [4, 10] },
  { stage: "filtration",       rate: [3, 8] },
  { stage: "bottling",         rate: [5, 15] },
];

const autoMult = automation === "manual" ? 0.6 : automation === "semi-automatic" ? 1 : 1.8;
const typeMult = wineType === "red" ? 1.1 : wineType === "sparkling" ? 1.5 : 1;
const m = autoMult * typeMult; // estimate = volume × rate × m

For a commercial winery that's reasonable. Equipment cost does grow with volume.

For a small one it breaks. At the default setting (500 cases, red, semi-automatic) the rule priced pressing at $3,300 – $9,900. The cheapest semi-automatic press in the catalogue was $24,975. A winery needs at least one press whatever its volume, and a press doesn't come in a size that costs $3,300 just because you make less wine.

The total came out at $20,900 – $50,050. That was roughly a quarter of what the listings said.

The fix: let the catalogue set a floor

The data was already there. The page loaded catalogue prices per stage to show the "Listed here" line. It just wasn't used for the estimate.

Two changes:

  1. Group prices by automation level, not only by stage. Comparing a semi-automatic estimate to the cheapest press of any kind would mix basket presses with full pneumatic lines.
  2. Use them as bounds. A stage's range never starts below the cheapest listing at the chosen level, and never tops out below their median. 
export const calculateBudget = (
  volume: number,
  wineType: string,
  automation: string,
  catalogue?: StagePrices, // stage -> { lo, hi, median } at this automation level
): BudgetItem[] =>
  STAGES.map(({ stage, rate }) => {
    const ruleLow = Math.round(volume * rate[0] * m);
    const ruleHigh = Math.round(volume * rate[1] * m);
    const listed = catalogue?.[stage];
    const low = listed ? Math.max(ruleLow, listed.lo) : ruleLow;
    const high = listed ? Math.max(ruleHigh, listed.median, low) : ruleHigh;
    return { stage, low, high, raisedToCatalogue: low > ruleLow };
  });

Everything is Math.max. The catalogue can only raise a number, never lower it, so large wineries where the rule already beats the listings are untouched. Both bounds come from real listings, so there's no made-up minimum anywhere in the code.

The automation level needed one more step. The automation_level column holds whatever the importers wrote: semi-automatic, semi-auto, automatic, fully-automatic and so on. The site already had a map of spellings for its filters, so the calculator reuses it rather than keeping a second list:

export const automationOption = (value: string | null | undefined): string | null => {
  if (!value) return null;
  for (const [option, spellings] of Object.entries(AUTOMATION_VARIANTS)) {
    if (spellings.includes(value)) return option;
  }
  return null;
};

When the floor kicks in, the stage says so: "Raised to the cheapest semi-automatic machine listed". A visitor can see why the number moved and click through to that machine.

What changed

Setup Before After
500 cases, red, semi-automatic $20,900 – $50,050 $78,940 – $163,410
5,000 cases, red, semi-automatic $209,000 – $500,500 $209,000 – $500,500

The large winery doesn't move, which is the point. The tests pin both cases. One feeds in a catalogue and checks that pressing goes to $24,975 – $44,800. Another checks that 10,000 cases is exactly what the rule says.

The stage where the data said no

Bottling didn't follow. At semi-automatic it stayed at $2,750 – $8,250, while the line under it said listings run $13,440 – $114,750.

The obvious move was to apply the same floor using every bottling listing. Then I looked at what those listings were. Nearly every priced bottling machine is an automatic line: monoblocs, rotary labellers, volumetric fillers. The one exception, the $13,440 labeller at the bottom of the range, has no automation level recorded at all. The kit a 500-case winery would actually buy, a vacuum bottle filler and a bench corker, is in the catalogue too, but without a price.

So raising the estimate would have told a small winery it needs at least $13,440 for bottling, based on machines it would never buy. The rule's $2,750 – $8,250 was the better guess. The problem was the label, which put automatic-line prices next to a semi-automatic estimate as if they were the same thing.

That row now reads:

No semi-automatic machine priced here. Other levels: $13,440 – $114,750

Same numbers, honest framing.

What I'd take from it

  • If your page shows two numbers that disagree, one of them is a bug. Users notice before you do.
  • Check what the data actually holds before you build on it. 53 of 156 listings have no automation level, and nearly every priced bottling machine was automatic. A fix that looked general only held for five stages out of six.
  • Prefer bounds over replacements. Math.max(rule, catalogue) kept everything that already worked and only corrected what was too low.
  • When you have no comparable data, say so. A clear "nothing priced at this level" is more useful than a confident number built from the wrong machines.

Try it at wine.equipment/calculator, or browse the equipment catalogue by production stage. Figures there are budgeting estimates, not quotes. Only a manufacturer can price a real configuration.

title: axe-core found 10 accessibility issues in a health app. Manual testing found 7 more
description:
In October I audited OpenMRS O3, an open source electronic health record, against WCAG 2.2 level AA. I ran it locally from the official Docker images, pinned to version 3.7.1, and scanned eight screens with axe-core 4.13.0: login, location picker, the service queues home, patient search, patient registration, the patient chart, the vitals form and appointments.

axe reported ten distinct problems. Then I put the mouse away and went through the same screens with the keyboard, 200% zoom, a 320-pixel viewport and two screen readers. That found seven more failures. axe had not reported any of them, although it had flagged one of the elements for a different reason.

This article is about that gap: what the scanner saw, what it could not see and why, and how I still run axe on every pull request without the suite turning into noise. The full audit, with the raw scan, the evidence screenshots and the source verification, is public in accessibility-audits. The CI code comes from playwright-qa-showcase.

What axe found

I ran the WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 A and AA rule tags. Per screen, the counts look like this:

Screen Violations (rules) Checks axe could not decide
Login 0 1
Location picker 1 0
Home (service queues) 3 15
Patient search 4 14
Patient registration 4 15
Patient chart 6 54
Vitals form 5 52
Appointments 5 14

Added up, that is 28 rule hits, which overstates the problem. Nineteen of them involve two global components, the help button and the user menu, which show up on almost every screen. Grouped by cause, they come down to ten findings under five success criteria: 1.3.1, 1.4.1, 1.4.3, 2.5.8 and 4.1.2. A few examples:

  • The floating help button has no accessible name, so a screen reader announces only "button".
  • The user menu puts <div> elements directly inside a <ul>, which breaks the list semantics on six of the eight screens.
  • The date placeholders on the registration form have a contrast ratio of 1.72:1, against a minimum of 4.5:1.
  • "Vitals history" is 16 pixels tall, below the 24-pixel minimum target size that WCAG 2.2 added.

All of these are real, and axe found them in seconds. When I checked the findings against the current OpenMRS source, two of the ten were already fixed upstream, including the help button. This is what automated scanning is good at, and it costs nothing to run again after every change.

The third column matters too. axe marks a check as "incomplete" when it cannot decide by itself. On these eight screens, that was 165 checks: 76 for color contrast (mostly text over the colored alert bands in the vitals tables), 87 for ARIA attributes and two others. A scan that passes with 165 undecided checks has not shown that the page is accessible. It has handed you a to-do list.

What it missed

The manual pass ran in Firefox and Chrome on Linux (keyboard, zoom, responsive mode, DOM inspection), with Orca on Linux and TalkBack on an Android phone as screen readers. I did not test NVDA, JAWS or VoiceOver in this round, and the report says so.

These are the seven failures, grouped by the reason a scanner cannot catch them.

The page had to change first. axe looks at the DOM at the moment you call it. Two failures only happen after an interaction:

  • 2.4.3 Focus Order. The vitals, biometrics and conditions tables are paginated. When you change the page with the keyboard, the table re-renders, the page selector (a <select>) is recreated with a new id, and document.activeElement drops from the selector to <body>. A keyboard or screen reader user loses their place.
  • 2.4.7 Focus Visible. In the date-of-birth calendar, Tab moves focus into the grid of days and the arrow keys change the date, but the focused day has no visible style. The date in the field changed from 06/02/1959 to 26/03/1959 while I watched nothing move on screen.

The viewport had to change. I scanned at 1280×800. Both of these failures appear only in a different layout:

  • 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), new in WCAG 2.2. At 200% zoom, the chart's actions become a fixed bar at the bottom of the screen. Tabbing through the vitals card puts focus behind that bar, first partly and then completely hidden. The browser does not scroll, because as far as it knows the element is already in view.
  • 1.4.10 Reflow. At 320 pixels wide, the registration form keeps its two-column layout and gets cut off on the right: half-labels, a clipped "No" button, an unreadable date field. There is no horizontal scrollbar to reach the rest, so registering a patient at that width is impossible.

Something had to be announced. In the global patient search, the "N search results" counter updates on every keystroke, but it is a plain <p> with no role="status" or aria-live anywhere above it. Sighted users see the count. Screen reader users have to leave the field to find out whether the search found anyone. That is 4.1.3 Status Messages, and no static scan can hear what is not announced.

No rule exists for it. Each result in that same search is a link that contains a button ("Active Visit"). Interactive content inside a link is invalid HTML, and screen readers handle it inconsistently. I wondered whether axe missed it only because I never scanned the open search panel, so I tested a minimal page with a <button> inside an <a> against axe-core 4.13.0. It passed. axe's nested-interactive rule only applies to roles whose children are presentational, such as button or checkbox, and in axe's ARIA table the link role does not have that flag.

The element was flagged, for a different reason. The header of the vitals card is a div with role="button" and tabindex="0" that contains a link and a button. axe did flag it, as nested interactive controls. What axe could not tell is what happens when you reach it with Tab: focus lands on it with no visible indicator, Enter does nothing, and Space scrolls the page. It is a dead tab stop that announces itself as a button. The manual finding (2.4.7 and 4.1.2) is the one a keyboard user actually feels.

So the seven failures are four about focus, two about semantics and announcements, and one about reflow. The focus failures share a pattern: OpenMRS works with the keyboard almost everywhere, but it does not always show where the focus is. One consistent :focus-visible style and scroll-padding on the fixed bars would fix most of them.

Running axe in CI without drowning in it

None of this makes axe less useful. It makes it a regression guard, not an audit. I use it that way in my showcase suite, which scans four pages of SauceDemo on every pull request.

The first decision is which rules to run:

export const AXE_TAGS = ['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa', 'wcag22aa', 'best-practice'];

export async function runAxe(page: Page) {
  return new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(AXE_TAGS).analyze();
}

I include best-practice, which is advisory and not a WCAG failure. SauceDemo has no WCAG A or AA violations on these pages, so without the best-practice rules the mechanism below would have nothing real to work on.

The second decision is what to do with the violations you already know about. If the suite fails on all of them, people learn to ignore the red. If you skip the rules that fire, a new problem under the same rule goes unnoticed. I keep a baseline file with the violations I knowingly accept, one entry per rule per page, each with a reason and a date:

"login": [
  {
    "ruleId": "page-has-heading-one",
    "reason": "Best practice: the page has no level-one heading; the 'Swag Labs' logo is a plain div.",
    "since": "2026-09"
  },
  {
    "ruleId": "region",
    "reason": "Best practice: the logo text sits outside any landmark region.",
    "since": "2026-09"
  }
],

The reason is required. An entry that says only "known issue" does not tell the next person whether it is still acceptable. The file is validated with zod when the suite loads it, so an empty reason, a malformed date or a duplicated rule on the same page fails before any test runs.

The comparison is a pure function, with its own unit tests:

export function diffAgainstBaseline<T extends ViolationLike>(
  pageKey: string,
  violations: readonly T[],
  baseline: Baseline,
): BaselineDiff<T> {
  const entries = baseline[pageKey] ?? [];
  const entryByRule = new Map(entries.map((entry) => [entry.ruleId, entry]));
  const firedRules = new Set(violations.map((violation) => violation.id));

  const diff: BaselineDiff<T> = {
    newViolations: [],
    stillPresent: [],
    resolved: entries.filter((entry) => !firedRules.has(entry.ruleId)),
  };

  for (const violation of violations) {
    const entry = entryByRule.get(violation.id);
    if (entry) {
      diff.stillPresent.push({ violation, entry });
    } else {
      diff.newViolations.push(violation);
    }
  }
  return diff;
}

Three outcomes come out of it. A violation that is not in the baseline fails the test. A known one passes and becomes an annotation in the HTML report. A baseline entry whose rule stopped firing is annotated as stale, so someone removes it in a pull request instead of letting the file rot. A Playwright fixture runs the scan, attaches the raw axe JSON and a short markdown summary to every test, and makes the assertion:

// Only rule ids are compared; the details go in the message.
expect(
  diff.newViolations.map((violation) => violation.id),
  formatNewViolations(pageKey, diff.newViolations),
).toEqual([]);

Each test then reads as one line, await auditPage('login'), after the test has navigated to the page.

I chose two trade-offs on purpose. There is no "update baseline" mode: every entry is written by hand and goes through review, because an automatic update is how a real failure gets accepted without anyone reading it. And the baseline is keyed by rule per page, not by element selector. That keeps the file small and stable when the markup changes, but it means a second element breaking an already-baselined rule on the same page is not flagged. Keying by selector would catch it, at the cost of an entry that breaks whenever the markup changes.

The latest run, on 16 November 2026 with axe-core 4.13.0: no new violations on the four pages, five best-practice findings in the baseline (the missing level-one heading on all four pages and content outside a landmark on the login page), and three color contrast checks on the inventory page that axe could not decide. Those three go on the manual list, like the 165 on OpenMRS.

Narrowing the gap

Some of the seven manual failures can become automated checks once a human has found them. The cheapest step is to scan states, not only URLs. The scanner I used for the audit takes an optional selector to click before the scan, which opens a panel or a dialog first:

for (const { name, url, waitFor, click } of pages) {
  // SPAs that poll never reach "networkidle": wait for the page's own selector plus a short render pause.
  await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: 'load' });
  if (waitFor) await page.locator(waitFor).first().waitFor({ timeout: 60_000 });
  await page.waitForTimeout(2_000);
  if (click) {
    await page.locator(click).first().click();
    await page.waitForTimeout(2_000);
  }
  const result = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(TAGS).analyze();
   // ...write result to disk
  }

That is how the vitals form got scanned at all: it is a side panel that only exists after clicking "Add".

The next step is to write a plain Playwright test for the behavior a manual finding describes. The focus order failure is a good candidate: change the table page with the keyboard and assert that the focused element is still the page selector. The reflow and focus-not-obscured failures need the same flows run at 320 pixels and at 200% zoom. I have not written those tests yet. When I do, each one will start from a finding a person made with a keyboard, not from a scanner rule.

What does not automate is the judgment. Whether the counter needs to be announced, whether the focus indicator is visible enough, whether a cut-off form is still usable: those calls need someone who uses the page the way a disabled user would.

How I split the work now

On every pull request, axe runs with the baseline, and a new violation blocks the merge. It is fast, and it keeps fixed problems from coming back.

Before a release, or when a team is about to sign an accessibility conformance report, someone does the manual pass: keyboard only through the main flows, 200% zoom, 320 pixels wide, and at least one screen reader. On OpenMRS that pass produced seven of the seventeen findings in the report, and every one of the four focus failures. If a product only has the scanner, those are the failures its keyboard users meet first.

title: Java and Kotlin news: value classes arrive in JDK 28 and Kotlin 2.5
description:
Java’s Integer and LocalDate lose their identity in JDK 28 previews, and patched Java runtimes may still trust compromised eMudhra certificates.

This digest covers 20 to 28 October 2026.

Java

1. Integer and LocalDate lose their identity in JDK 28 previews (JEP 401)

Every Java object has an identity: two objects with the same fields are still two objects, and == tells them apart. Value classes give that up so the JVM can store them flat, like primitives. JEP 401 brings them to JDK 28 as a preview, and OpenJDK’s Quality Outreach asked library maintainers to test now.

With preview features on, 30 JDK classes become value classes. Integer and LocalDate are among them, even in code compiled on older JDKs:

var x = LocalDate.of(2026, 7, 31);
var y = LocalDate.of(2026, 7, 31);

var identical = x == y;
// without value classes: false
// with value classes:    true

Synchronizing on these objects or using them as WeakHashMap keys throws IdentityException. Record constructors that call instance methods stop compiling once you build with preview features. Without the preview flag, JDK 28 should behave as before, but OpenJDK asks you to test that too. Run your tests on the latest JDK 28 early access build with and without it:

java --enable-preview -jar app.jar

JDK 28 is planned for 9 March 2027, with the feature freeze on 3 December.

Sources: Inside Java, Nicolai Parlog, JEP 401, JDK 28 early access, JDK 28 project page.

2. Small off-heap allocations get 6 to 18x faster

The Foreign Function & Memory API calls native code from Java. A call usually allocates a few bytes of native memory in a confined arena, which only one thread can use, and frees them when the arena closes. Each allocation used to go to the native allocator. In JDK 28 small allocations come from a per-thread pool instead, with no source change:

try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment result = arena.allocate(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT);
    nativeFunction.invokeExact(result);
    return result.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 0);
}

On an Apple M4, a 5-byte allocation fell from 15.9 to 1.05 ns, about 15x. Pools hold 64 bytes, so larger allocations run as before. It helps most where a binding opens a confined arena around each native call, such as jextract-style wrappers.

Source: Inside Java, Per-Ake Minborg.

3. Spring Boot 4.2.0-RC1

The first Spring Boot 4.2 release candidate came out on 23 October with 113 changes. It moves to Spring Framework 7.1 and Spring Security 7.2 (see item 15). The changes you notice first:

  • Buildpacks images now build on Ubuntu 26.04 instead of 24.04 by default.
  • The properties migrator gets an opt-in setting that fails startup on errors or warnings, so you catch renamed properties in CI.
  • Startup is faster: classes and resources load straight from nested jars.
  • Caffeine caches can run in async mode.

To keep the old builder while you upgrade, set it in the plugin configuration:

<!-- pom.xml, spring-boot-maven-plugin -->
<configuration>
    <image>
        <builder>paketobuildpacks/builder-noble-java-tiny</builder>
    </image>
</configuration>

// build.gradle.kts
tasks.bootBuildImage {
    builder = "paketobuildpacks/builder-noble-java-tiny"
}

Spring Cloud 2026.0.0-RC1 is built on it, and Spring Cloud Bus is now part of Spring Cloud Stream with the same artifact coordinates. Bug-fix releases 4.1.2 and 4.0.9 also came out.

Sources: Spring Boot 4.1.2, Spring Boot 4.0.9, Spring blog, Moritz Halbritter, 4.2.0-RC1 release notes, Spring Cloud 2026.0.0-RC1.

4. Spring AI 2.1 keeps model reasoning between calls

Reasoning models return thinking blocks and signed reasoning items, and the provider wants them back unchanged and in order on the next call. Spring AI 2.0 stored a message as text plus side lists, so reasoning got lost in streaming and chat memory. Requests could then fail with HTTP 400 or lose context.

In 2.1.0-RC1 a message is an ordered list of parts: text, reasoning, tool calls and more. A new session API keeps every part across calls, and across restarts with its JDBC store:

String answer = chatClient.prompt()
    .user("Find the cheapest flight to Lisbon next Friday")
    .advisors(SessionAdvisors.session("session-42"))
    .call()
    .content();

Register SessionAdvisors.builder(sessionService) as a default advisor on the ChatClient first. Every call needs a session id: there is no default session.

ChatMemory is deprecated for removal in 3.0. Tools marked as requiring confirmation now pause until your app approves the call.

Sources: Spring blog, Eric Bottard, Spring blog, Dimitar Proynov.

5. TornadoVM 8 drops the Graal compiler

TornadoVM runs Java methods on GPUs. It turns your bytecode into GPU kernels and copies data between the Java heap and the device. Version 8.0 replaces the Graal compiler with TC, TornadoVM’s own bytecode-to-kernel compiler, and moves to the Apache 2.0 license.

The 7.x line had already swapped JNI for the FFM API and dropped the JVMCI dependency, so TornadoVM now runs on a stock JDK 21, 25, 26 or 27.

Sources: TornadoVM 8.0.0 release, InfoQ, Ben Evans.

6. WildFly 42 runs Jakarta Concurrency on virtual threads

WildFly is an open source Jakarta EE application server. Version 42 can back Jakarta Concurrency resources, the managed executors your EE code submits tasks to, with virtual threads. Every installation now ships a CycloneDX SBOM, so a scanner knows what is inside.

Java 25 is the recommended runtime. WildFly 43 is the last release on Java 17; WildFly 44 moves the baseline to 21. Plan the JDK upgrade now if you are still on 17.

Source: WildFly blog, Brian Stansberry.

7. Smaller releases

  • Apache POI 6.0.0: needs JDK 17, up from 8. DataFormatter now shows cached formula values by default, and some deprecated methods are gone.
  • Spring Modulith 2.2 RC1: Modulith checks and documents the module boundaries inside one Spring Boot app. In 2.2 RC1 an event is marked as completed inside the listener’s transaction, so both succeed or fail together.

Sources: Apache POI changes, Spring Modulith blog.

8. Worth reading

  • What jstack misses when your Java service uses virtual threads by Felipe Maschio: the dump shows idle carriers while 5,000 requests wait for a database connection.
  • What’s going wrong with my JVM?, a first-failure diagnosis guide on Inside Java.
  • Java Secure Coding Guidelines, Andrew Gross’s talk on the updated input validation and serialization advice.
  • Haskell-like type class resolution in Java by Gabriel Garcia: how far Java’s generics go when you emulate Haskell’s type classes.

Kotlin

9. Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2 brings full value classes

Kotlin’s value classes could hold one property and existed to wrap a value without the cost of an object. Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2 adds full value classes as an experimental feature: any number of properties, no identity, like JEP 401 in Java.

value class Complex(val real: Double, val imaginary: Double)

sealed interface UserResponse
value class UserFound(val user: User) : UserResponse
value object UserUnknown : UserResponse

The compiler generates the data class methods except copy and componentN. Full value classes can be sealed or abstract. Turn them on with a compiler flag. The flags in items 10 and 11 go in the same place:

<!-- pom.xml, kotlin-maven-plugin -->
<configuration>
    <args>
        <arg>-Xfull-value-classes</arg>
    </args>
</configuration>

// build.gradle.kts
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.add("-Xfull-value-classes")
    }
}

A plain value class will no longer be inline. A one-property inline class will need the inline modifier or @JvmInline. Kotlin 2.5.20 warns about unmarked ones, and a later release turns the warning into an error. JVM code already needs @JvmInline, so multiplatform code is where you look first.

Source: What’s new in Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2.

10. Companion blocks and companion extensions

A companion object holds a class’s static-like members, and on the JVM each needs @JvmStatic to become a real static. Beta2 adds companion blocks, whose members compile to statics, and companion extensions, which work even when the class has no companion object:

companion val Vector.UnitX get() = Vector(1.0, 0.0)

data class Vector(val x: Double, val y: Double) {
    companion {
        val Zero: Vector get() = Vector(0.0, 0.0)
    }
}

Both are experimental and need a flag:

kotlinc -Xcompanion-blocks-and-extensions Vector.kt

Source: What’s new in Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2.

11. The Kotlin 2.5 compiler needs JDK 17 to run

Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2 stops with an error when the compiler runs on a JDK older than 17. This is the JDK that runs the compiler, not your bytecode target. Until 2.5.20 or 2.6.0 makes JDK 17 mandatory, a flag turns the error off:

kotlinc -Xallow-pre-17-runtime-jdk Vector.kt

CI images still on an older JDK break with the upgrade. The same beta can generate Java 28 bytecode. Kotlin 2.5.0 is planned for December.

Sources: What’s new in Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2, Kotlin releases.

12. Swift export goes Beta

Kotlin Multiplatform shares Kotlin code with iOS. Swift export generates Swift from that code directly, without the Objective-C header in between. In 2.5.0-Beta2 it is Beta with a new Gradle DSL: the swiftExport block becomes export with a swift block inside, and dependencies you declare with api are exported on their own.

Library authors can try a new publication format, where each platform artifact (except JVM and Android) is a single archive. The cryptography-kotlin library went from 7,539 files and 91 MB to 1,036 files and 23 MB.

Source: What’s new in Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2.

13. Smaller news

  • Kotlin DataFrame 1.0.0-rc02: the typed table library for data work in Kotlin reaches its final release candidate before 1.0 (release).
  • Bootiful Kotlin: Josh Long builds a Spring Boot backend in Kotlin.
  • Flake-free Flow tests: Touchlab on why coroutine tests break with real threads and dispatchers.
  • Deezer’s Kotlin Multiplatform case study: one codebase for phones, browsers, cars and watches.
  • The KotlinConf 2027 call for papers closes on 27 November.

Security

14. eMudhra: patch your Java runtime again

A certificate authority (CA) signs the certificates your TLS clients trust. On 17 October a researcher showed that the private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CAs could be recovered from the certificates themselves. Whoever holds them can issue a certificate for any site, so a man-in-the-middle can fool any Java client that trusts these CAs.

Browsers blocked the certificates within days, but Java clients rarely check revocation. The first JDK fixes blocked the intermediates by fingerprint. Sonatype then showed that a re-encoded copy of a blocked certificate gets a new fingerprint and still validates. OpenJDK updated its advice on 24 October: act now, “even if you have updated your runtime in the past few days”.

The preferred fix is a runtime whose release notes list JDK-8395690. Until your vendor ships one, remove the affected roots. Removing the Comodo AAA root can also break services with certificates from it, so test those connections first. On JDK 11 and later:

keytool -delete -cacerts -alias "emsignrootcag1 [jdk]"
keytool -delete -cacerts -alias "emsignrootcag2 [jdk]"
keytool -delete -cacerts -alias "emsigneccrootcag3 [jdk]"
keytool -delete -cacerts -alias "comodoaaaca [jdk]"

Ignore errors that an alias does not exist, and restart every running JVM afterwards. On JDK 8, point keytool at the keystore under your JDK’s install directory ($JDK_HOME below), the same way for all four aliases:

keytool -delete -keystore $JDK_HOME/jre/lib/security/cacerts -alias "emsignrootcag1 [jdk]"

On Debian and Ubuntu, updating the ca-certificates packages doesn’t refresh Java’s keystore. Rebuild it as root:

rm -f /etc/ssl/certs/java/cacerts && update-ca-certificates --fresh

OpenJDK’s page has a CheckCerts program that tells you whether a runtime is still at risk.

Sources: OpenJDK guidance, OpenJDK advisory, Sonatype research, reporter’s incident page.

15. Locked accounts still log in with a one-time token

One-time token login is Spring Security’s magic link: the user gets a link with a token and logs in without a password. The password provider rejects locked and disabled accounts. The one-time token provider never checked them, so a user you banned yesterday can log in with a magic link today:

class MagicLinkLogin {

    Authentication login() {
        var users = new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(User.withUsername("alice")
            .password("{noop}secret").roles("USER")
            .accountLocked(true) // banned yesterday
            .build());
        var tokens = new InMemoryOneTimeTokenService();
        var token = tokens.generate(new GenerateOneTimeTokenRequest("alice"));
        var provider = new OneTimeTokenAuthenticationProvider(tokens, users);
        // Spring Security 7.1: no account status check, alice gets in
        return provider.authenticate(
            OneTimeTokenAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(token.getTokenValue()));
    }
}

Spring Security 7.2.0-RC1 adds the check, but it stays off by default to keep the old behavior. Turn it on yourself:

@Bean
OneTimeTokenAuthenticationProvider oneTimeTokenAuthenticationProvider(
        OneTimeTokenService tokens, UserDetailsService users) {
    var provider = new OneTimeTokenAuthenticationProvider(tokens, users);
    provider.setUserDetailsChecker(new AccountStatusUserDetailsChecker());
    return provider;
}

On 7.1 and older, check the account in your token generation handler before you send the link.

Sources: Spring Security 7.2 what’s new, one-time token docs, issue 17655.

16. Patch list

  • Java October Critical Patch Update: JDK 27.0.1, 25.0.5, 21.0.13, 17.0.21, 11.0.33 and 8u512. OpenJDK’s eMudhra advisory lists these builds as affected (CVSS 9.1), so take the next build whose release notes list JDK-8395690 (item 14).
  • Micronaut 5.2.3: a security release for Micronaut Core and Micronaut Security. On Micronaut 4, update to Platform 4.10.22; on Micronaut 3, to Core 3.10.17.

Sources: OpenJDK advisory, BellSoft release notes, Micronaut 5.2.3.

Do you use magic links in your Spring apps, and did you check what they do with locked accounts?

At the end

If you like this digest, follow me on LinkedIn and Telegram to get the next one. The previous digest: JDK 28 gets structured concurrency and AOT code.

Found this useful? Follow me on social media to stay updated.

Telegram · LinkedIn

title: Logs Aren't an Audit Trail: Debugging Business Data in Spring Boot
description:
A production support ticket comes in:

"Why was this account deactivated?"

You check the database:

id     = 1042
status = DEACTIVATED

Then you search the application logs:

2026-10-12T09:42:18Z INFO AccountService
Account 1042 updated successfully

The application processed an update.

But that doesn't answer the question.

What was the previous status? Who initiated the change? Did the transaction actually commit? Was this the first transition, or had the account changed several times?

This is a distinction that becomes important when supporting production applications:

Application logs describe execution. Audit trails describe changes to business data.

They are related, but they aren't interchangeable.

1. A Log Message Isn't Proof of a Committed Change

Consider a typical Spring Boot service:

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class AccountService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepository;

    @Transactional
    public void deactivate(Long accountId) {
        Account account = accountRepository.findById(accountId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(accountId));

        account.setStatus(AccountStatus.DEACTIVATED);

        log.info("Account {} deactivated", accountId);

        validateAdditionalRules(account);
    }
}

Suppose validateAdditionalRules() throws an unchecked exception.

By default, Spring rolls back the transaction.

But the log message has already been emitted.

You might end up with:

APPLICATION LOG
09:42:18 Account 1042 deactivated

DATABASE
Account 1042
status = ACTIVE

The log is not necessarily incorrect. It tells us that execution reached the logging statement.

But it doesn't prove the database change was committed.

This is one of the reasons not to treat application logs as authoritative business history.

What About Logging After Commit?

We could use Spring transaction synchronization to log only after a successful commit.

That avoids premature success messages, but introduces another limitation.

What happens if the database commits and the process crashes before the log is delivered?

The business change exists, but the corresponding log message might not.

Moving logging after commit does not make the database update and log delivery atomic.

For important business-data history, we need a different persistence guarantee.

2. Hibernate Envers Provides Transactional Revision History

Hibernate Envers provides a foundation for entity revision history in applications using Hibernate ORM.

Instead of manually logging every entity modification, we can configure entities for auditing.

@Entity
@Audited
@Table(name = "accounts")
public class Account {

    @Id
    private Long id;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private AccountStatus status;

    private String reasonCode;
}

With Envers configured, changes made through Hibernate's audited persistence lifecycle can produce corresponding revision records.

Those records normally participate in the same database transaction as the entity modifications.

Conceptually:

BEGIN TRANSACTION
    |
    +-- Update Account
    |
    +-- Persist Audit Revision
    |
COMMIT

If the transaction rolls back, the entity modification and associated audit revision roll back together.

The audit revision is tied to the committed business-data change.

There are still limitations.

Direct SQL modifications outside Hibernate, unsupported write paths, incorrect mappings, and incomplete revision metadata can compromise audit completeness.

Envers is not a universal database change-data-capture mechanism.

But for audited Hibernate-managed entities, it provides a solid foundation.

3. Logs and Audit Trails Have Different Data Models

Consider these application logs:

09:41:12 Account update requested
09:41:12 Validating account 1042
09:41:12 Validation successful
09:41:13 Updating account 1042
09:41:13 Account updated successfully

They help us reconstruct execution.

Now compare that with an audit history:

Account #1042

Revision 18
2026-10-12T09:41:13Z

status:
ACTIVE -> SUSPENDED

reasonCode:
null -> CUSTOMER_REQUEST

changedBy:
admin-17

The second representation is organized around the business entity.

It provides a history of what changed, rather than messages describing application execution.

Over time, the audit history might look like:

Oct 12
ACTIVE -> SUSPENDED

Oct 15
SUSPENDED -> ACTIVE

Oct 21
ACTIVE -> DEACTIVATED

That is much easier to consume when someone asks:

How did this account reach its current state?

It also opens the door to building administrative interfaces and support tools around revision history.

4. Why Not Just Log Every Field Change?

It's possible to write structured logs containing old and new values.

For some applications, that may be sufficient.

But there are several challenges.

Consistency: Every write path must follow the same logging convention, including scheduled jobs, message consumers, and administrative operations.

Transaction boundaries: Logging a change does not necessarily prove the corresponding transaction committed.

Retention: Application logs may be deleted long before business history is no longer needed.

Queryability: Searching logs is not the same as querying entity revisions, changed properties, and historical values.

Security: Logging complete entity snapshots can expose sensitive information.

These concerns deserve explicit architectural decisions.

If historical business-data changes are important, they should not depend entirely on developers remembering to add the correct log statements.

5. Audit History Still Doesn't Explain Everything

Suppose we have the following revision:

Account #1042

status:
ACTIVE -> SUSPENDED

changedBy:
account-service

changedAt:
2026-10-12T09:41:13Z

We know what changed.

But do we know why?

Not necessarily.

Hibernate Envers cannot automatically infer the business intent behind a state transition.

To capture that, the application needs relevant context.

For example:

reasonCode:
CUSTOMER_REQUEST

correlationId:
c5d8f1e2-7a40-4d9c-8b1e-9f1c02d5a611

The reason code provides explicitly recorded business context.

The correlation ID may connect the revision to related logs and traces, provided the identifier was propagated consistently.

This is where audit history and observability complement each other.

Audit history tells us what changed. Logs and traces help investigate the execution that produced the change.

Neither should invent information that was never captured.

6. Distributed Systems Need Both Event History and Audit History

Consider a simple asynchronous workflow:

Account API
    |
    v
Account Service
    |
    v
Database
    |
    v
Transactional Outbox
    |
    v
Kafka
    |
    v
Notification Service

Suppose an account is suspended.

Several things may happen:

  1. The account status changes from ACTIVE to SUSPENDED.
  2. An audit revision records the state change.
  3. An outbox event is persisted.
  4. The transaction commits.
  5. The event is published asynchronously.
  6. A downstream consumer processes the event.

Each step raises different operational questions.

Was the account state committed?

Was the event persisted?

Was the event published?

Did the consumer process it?

Was the notification delivered?

A single logging mechanism should not be expected to answer all these questions.

This is where two of my open-source libraries complement each other.

NERV Event: What Happened to the Message?

NERV Event focuses on reliable event-driven processing through patterns such as transactional outbox, inbox processing, retries, and idempotency.

These capabilities help applications reason about asynchronous message delivery and processing.

NERV Audit: What Happened to the Data?

NERV Audit focuses on making historical changes to business entities easier to inspect and consume.

It builds on Hibernate Envers rather than replacing it.

The goal is to make revision history usable by applications, support tools, and administrative interfaces.

For example:

Account #1042

Revision 18
ACTIVE -> SUSPENDED

Revision 19
SUSPENDED -> ACTIVE

Revision 20
ACTIVE -> DEACTIVATED

The audit trail helps reconstruct committed entity changes.

The event infrastructure helps investigate the asynchronous workflow.

Both are useful, but they provide different evidence.

7. What Should a Production System Capture?

I find it useful to think about production diagnostics in terms of questions.

Question Useful source
Why did this request fail? Logs, exceptions, traces
Was this event published? Outbox and messaging records
Was the message processed? Consumer and inbox records
What was the previous entity state? Audit history
Who changed this entity? Audit actor metadata
Why was the change requested? Explicit business context
How was the system performing? Metrics

These mechanisms work best when their responsibilities are clear.

We don't need to audit every field or retain every log indefinitely.

We do need to identify which business changes matter and design reliable ways to investigate them.

8. The Engineering Principle

After years of working on enterprise Java systems, one lesson has become increasingly important to me:

A production system should make important business changes explainable through evidence, not guesswork.

That doesn't mean a single tool can explain everything.

It means having the right evidence available when an investigation begins.

Application logs help reconstruct execution.

Audit history helps reconstruct business-data changes.

Event-processing records help reconstruct asynchronous workflows.

Distributed tracing connects execution across services.

And explicit business context helps explain why particular decisions were made.

That's the philosophy behind NERV Audit and the broader NERV ecosystem.

Final Thoughts

Logs are essential for production support.

But they are not an audit trail.

A log statement may describe an operation that eventually rolls back.

A structured log message may not survive as long as the business needs its history.

And a sequence of application events may still be insufficient to reconstruct an entity's committed state transitions.

For Spring Boot applications using Hibernate, Envers provides a strong starting point for transactional revision history.

NERV Audit builds on that foundation to make historical changes easier to query, inspect, and consume.

Because when production support asks:

"Why is this account in this state?"

We should have better tools than searching through thousands of unrelated log messages.

Logs tell us what the application was doing. An audit trail tells us what happened to the data.

This is Article #2 in my NERV Audit series, exploring practical approaches to production-ready auditing in Java and Spring Boot.

Explore the open-source NERV projects: GitHub — CzetsuyaTech

title: Our site and our desktop app use 58 colours between them and share 15, and three the site owns alone are a fake window's traffic lights
description:
Notifio exists as two pieces of front end. There is the website, 38 pages of Next.js that explain the product and sell it, and there is the desktop app itself, an Electron renderer you install from the download page. Same product, same person writing both, a few weeks apart.

I have counted the colours on each of them separately before. The website's stylesheet turned out to lean on #a3a3a3 138 times, a value Tailwind dropped from its own palette. What I had never done is put the two sets side by side and ask how much of the brand is actually shared, rather than remembered.

The two sets

For the website I counted every six-digit hex in what it actually serves: all 38 live pages plus the single stylesheet they link.

cat p_*.html site.css | grep -oE '#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}\b' | tr 'A-F' 'a-f' | sort -u

For the app, the same expression over the renderer source.

                        distinct   occurrences
served website                34         9,800
Electron renderer             39           322
union                         58
shared                        15
website only                  19
app only                      24

Fifty eight colours for one product, and a quarter of them are on both surfaces.

The part that agrees

The shared 15 are, almost exactly, the greyscale:

#fafafa  #e5e5e5  #a3a3a3  #737373  #525252
#404040  #3a3a3a  #262626  #1a1a1a  #0f0f0f  #0a0a0a

#4ade80  #f87171  #facc15  #14532d

Eleven neutrals and four status colours, green, red, amber, and one dark green panel background. The ranking agrees too. #fafafa is the most used value on both surfaces, 2,171 times in what the website serves and 60 times in the app's source, and #a3a3a3 and #525252 are in the top five on both. That is the Tailwind neutral ramp typed out as literals in two repos, which is a boring kind of consistency but it is real consistency: text, borders and panels do look like the same product.

The part that does not

The 24 the app has alone are the ones that surprised me least once I saw them:

#1e3a8a  #60a5fa  #93c5fd  #0a1229   a blue and a navy panel, neither on the site
#450a0a  #2a0a0a  #3a0f0f  #7f1d1d   darker reds and their borders
#422006  #2a1f04  #241a04  #3a2c06   darker ambers
#854d0e  #a1850a  #7a6a10  #7c5212   more amber borders and text
#052e16  #166534                     darker greens
#ef4444  #fb923c  #fca5a5  #fcd34d   brighter status text
#d4b106  #171717                      one more amber, and one more grey

Twenty three of those 24 are a palette the website never needed. A row in the app sits in one of several states, and each state needs a tinted panel plus a border plus a text colour that stays legible on it. The website writes sentences about those states and never has to paint one, so the dark tints had nowhere to come from. That is a genuine asymmetry rather than drift. The twenty fourth, #171717, is just a grey that got typed once.

The 19 the website has alone are a different story:

#0d0d0d  #141414  #1c1c1c  #1e1e1e  #252525  #2a2a2a  #2e2e2e
#383838  #4a4a4a  #6a6a6a  #c0c0c0  #d0d0d0  #d4d4d4
#a855f7  #ff6568  #0a1a0a
#ff5f57  #ffbd2e  #28c840

The first thirteen are greys between the greys in the shared ramp, which is the kind of thing that happens when you are drawing a mockup and want a panel slightly darker than the one next to it. Those are drift, and they are cheap to fix.

The last three are my favourite finding in the batch. #ff5f57, #ffbd2e and #28c840 are the macOS close, minimise and maximise buttons, and they appear in three components:

HeroDemo.tsx        h-3   w-3   rounded-full
BrowserDemo.tsx     h-2.5 w-2.5 rounded-full
AutoReplyDemo.tsx   h-2.5 w-2.5 rounded-full

The website draws a picture of a Mac window, three times, on the homepage and in the demos, with hand-typed traffic lights at the top of it. The actual app opens a real window with titleBarStyle: 'default', which means macOS draws those buttons and the app never specifies their colour. So three of the colours unique to the website are a drawing of something the product gets for free, and those exact hex values will never appear in the app no matter how closely the two surfaces converge.

The typography is not shared at all

Colour at least half agrees. Type does not agree in the slightest.

                     font files   font-family declarations
served website                3   3 families via CSS variables
Electron renderer             0   1

The website self-hosts two variable faces and pulls in a third:

const spaceGrotesk = localFont({ src: "./fonts/space-grotesk-latin.woff2", ... });
const dmSans       = localFont({ src: "./fonts/dm-sans-latin.woff2", ... });
import { GeistMono } from "geist/font/mono";

which resolve through --font-display, --font-sans and --font-mono and really do render: the stylesheet applies each variable to real rules, so a visitor sees Space Grotesk in the headings and DM Sans in the body.

The app's entire typographic configuration is this, and there is not one font file anywhere in the bundle:

font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI",
             "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif;

So the headline a visitor reads on the website is Space Grotesk, and the same words in the app are San Francisco on a Mac and Segoe UI on Windows. Here, unlike the colours, I think the app is right and the mismatch is correct. A desktop app that imposes a brand typeface on its own chrome reads as a website in a window, which is the exact impression this product cannot afford: it is trying to be a small native utility that sits in the tray, not a web page that happens to be installed. Shipping zero font files is also the only typographic decision in the product that costs nothing to download.

What I would change 

13 near-duplicate greys on the website      merge into the shared ramp
24 app-only state tints                     keep, the website has no states
 3 traffic lights                            keep, they are a drawing
 0 shared font files                         keep, on purpose

The useful part of the exercise was that it separated drift from difference. Before counting I would have guessed the two surfaces had diverged generally. They have not: they share a ranked neutral ramp and the three status hues, and every real difference between them is traceable to something one surface has to do and the other does not. The one exception is thirteen greys that exist because nobody had a list.

The site is at notifio.app, where the three fake windows are on the homepage, and the real one comes from the download page. The download page itself carries one image and two inline SVGs, and not a single pixel of either palette beyond the shared ramp.
