title: The New York Times Is Coming for Jensen Huang — Starting With His Daughter
description:
Jensen Huang resigned last week. The New York Times has now published its fourth story about him in six days. Today's target: his daughter.

Madison Huang, 35, is officially senior director of product marketing for physical AI. In practice, she was her father's de facto chief of staff.

In February, Jensen was supposed to keynote a conference in New Delhi. He pulled out and sent his longtime deputy Jay Puri instead. On a prep call, Madison tore into Puri for being unprepared. Puri interrupted her: stop yelling at me and I can answer your questions. Less than six months later, Puri was gone.

Over the past three years, more than a dozen key executives have left because they didn't want to work with her, according to employees. Complaints piled up so high that HR had her in weekly coaching on her management style for months. Late last year, a vice president had a panic attack on a call with her and had to drop off. In March, she berated Ian Buck — the inventor of CUDA, now seen as a leading candidate to succeed Jensen — in front of the PR team, because he hadn't prepared slides for a press briefing.

The family footprint is the real story. Son Spencer, 36, runs product management for robotics after eight years running a cocktail bar in Taipei. Son-in-law Nico Caprez joined in 2024 and is already VP of AI infrastructure growth. All three are inside the company. Interim CEO Colette Kress now has to decide what to do with them.

Madison's resume is worth reading in full. Culinary school degree in 2012. Baking and wine at Le Cordon Bleu in Paris and London, 2013 to 2015. Four years managing LVMH luxury hotels and an Italian dessert shop. London Business School in 2019. Joined Nvidia in 2020. Six years from running a dessert shop to being her father's chief of staff.

Then there's "Toy Jensen," the cartoon version of her father she pushed as a marketing mascot. Hoodies at $178. Employees said it made the company look like a cult. After Jensen admitted to infidelity last week, the company stopped using it. Madison also led the hiring of crisis PR firm Heller in May 2025, and pushed the PR team to fight back hard when the Times reported on Nvidia's Megaspeed business that October.

Harvard Business School professor David Yoffie put it bluntly in the piece: nepotism is almost always a bad idea, and even barely successful examples are few and far between.

But the daughter isn't the real point. The timing is. Jensen's allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street are pushing for his reinstatement. Trump just said he "wouldn't mind" Jensen coming back. And the Times drops this piece. November 12: his wife in the spotlight. November 13: the interim CEO. November 16: how the affair leaked. November 17: his daughter. Four stories in six days, all aimed at the same man.

This isn't news coverage anymore. It's a serial. First the affair, then the daughter — the message is that the problem isn't one mistake, it's the family. And once the press has set the frame, the politics follows.

Whether Jensen comes back won't be decided by whether his daughter yelled at people. It'll be decided by how far this fight goes. Nvidia doesn't need a new chip right now. It needs a CEO everyone can live with.

title: The best AI visibility MCP servers
description:
Key takeaways

  • AI visibility is three separate observations: whether an engine mentions your brand, whether it cites one of your pages, and whether it recommends you for a specific buying question.
  • Answers change between runs, so one answer proves little. Look for a server that lets you repeat the same question and keep every raw answer.
  • A single visibility score hides the evidence. Prefer a server that returns the answer text, the brands named and the cited URLs.
  • Check whether your site lets answer engines read it at all before you measure anything. A blocked crawler explains many missing mentions.

What AI visibility actually measures

When a buyer asks ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity for a recommendation, the answer may name brands, link to sources, or do both. AI visibility tracking records what those answers say about you and your competitors so you can see where you appear and where you do not.

An MCP server brings that tracking into your assistant. Instead of pasting questions into several chat windows by hand, you ask the assistant to run a set of questions on several engines and report back, with the evidence attached.

Three AI visibility signals and what each one tells you

Signal What it tells you What it does not tell you
Mention The engine named your brand in its answer That the answer was positive or that anyone clicked
Citation The engine linked to one of your pages as a source That your brand was recommended
Recommendation The engine suggested you for a specific buying question That the same answer will appear next time

What to look for in an AI visibility MCP server

  1. Engines you can name. Know exactly which engines the server queries, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, and whether each result comes from a live run or a stored sample.
  2. Raw answers, not just scores. You need the answer text, the brands it named and the sources it cited so you can read what a buyer would have seen.
  3. Repeatability. The same question should be runnable again with the same settings, so you can compare this month with last month.
  4. Location and language control. Answers differ by country and language, so these must be explicit.
  5. Prices you can see first. Every question on every engine costs something. Choose a server that quotes the cost before it runs.
  6. Honest failure handling. If one engine fails, the report should say so rather than silently averaging the rest.

Do not read one answer as a ranking

AI answers vary from run to run and are not a ranked list. Sample the same question more than once, and report how often you appear instead of a single yes or no.

Types of AI visibility MCP servers

Answer-tracking servers

Best for: Running your buyer questions on several engines and recording mentions and citations.

Watch out for: Check which engines are covered and whether answers are fresh runs or cached samples.

Search-data servers with AI features

Best for: Teams that already use a search data provider and want AI Overview data alongside keywords and rankings.

Watch out for: AI Overview coverage does not include chat engines like ChatGPT or Claude.

Site-readiness and crawler-access checks

Best for: Finding out whether answer engines are allowed to read your site at all.

Watch out for: Access is necessary but not sufficient. Passing a readiness check does not mean you will be cited.

Observed-prompt servers

Best for: Finding which questions people actually ask AI engines about a topic, so you track the right ones.

Watch out for: Prompt data is a sample from a provider’s index, not every question ever asked.

Where MARqentic fits

MARqentic includes three AI visibility tools alongside its search, social, ad and marketplace research.

  • aeo_run_ai_answers runs your prompts on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, and reports which brands each answer mentions and which sources it cites.
  • aeo_search_prompts finds prompts people ask ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews about a topic or brand, from a provider index of observed answers.
  • aeo_get_site_readiness checks whether your site is set up for answer engines, including robots.txt access for known AI crawlers and CDN or firewall rules that can block them.

Pricing is per prompt per engine, and answer runs are never cached, so each run reflects a fresh answer. A dry run quotes the cost before you spend. A failed engine result is not charged.

A repeatable AI visibility workflow

  1. Write ten to twenty buyer questions. Include unbranded category questions as well as direct comparisons, because a question that names your brand measures something different.
  2. Check site readiness first, so a blocked crawler does not distort the results.
  3. Run the questions on the engines you care about and keep every raw answer.
  4. Record, for each question, whether you were mentioned, cited or recommended, and which competitors appeared.
  5. Repeat the same set on a schedule, such as monthly, with the same settings.
  6. Look for patterns in the sources that get cited, then improve those pages or earn coverage on those sources.

A prompt to adapt

Replace the bracketed items with your own details and ask for the cost before anything runs.

Starter prompt

Check whether [domain] is readable by AI answer engines. Then, for [country] in [language], quote the cost of running these buyer questions on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Google AI Overviews: [question 1], [question 2], [question 3]. After I approve, run them and give me, for each question, the answer text, the brands mentioned, the cited URLs and whether [brand] appeared.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Judging visibility from a single answer instead of a repeated sample.
  • Asking only questions that already contain your brand name.
  • Reporting a score without keeping the answers behind it.
  • Ignoring whether answer crawlers can reach your site.
  • Comparing results across different countries or languages.

Questions people ask

What is an AI visibility MCP server?

It is a service that lets an AI assistant run questions on AI answer engines and report which brands and sources appear in the answers. It brings brand mention and citation tracking into your assistant conversation.

Which engines should I track?

Track the engines your buyers actually use. Many teams start with ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, then add Claude and AI Mode as needed.

How often should I measure AI visibility?

Monthly is a sensible start. Answers change, so repeating the same question set on a schedule shows the trend better than a single check.

Can I guarantee ChatGPT will cite my site?

No. Nobody can. You can make your pages accessible and useful, then measure whether engines cite them, but citations are not controllable.

Does AI visibility replace SEO?

No. They overlap, since engines often draw on pages that rank well, but they measure different things. Track both.

Originally published on the MARqentic blog. MARqentic connects Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and other MCP apps to live marketing research: SEO, backlinks, AI-answer visibility, ad libraries and social data. Try it free.

title: Cloud CI Email Tests Need an AWS Boundary
description:
Email verification tests often fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the application. A shared inbox is slow, an old message is read by the wrong test, or a CI retry consumes a token that the first attempt already used. The result is a red pipeline and very little evidence about what really happened.

In cloud work, I treat test email as an infrastructure boundary. The application under test should send to a short-lived fixture owned by that job, while the rest of the AWS environment should have no path to real customer mailboxes. This makes failures easier to classify and keeps test data from drifting into places nobody checks.

Why cloud email tests need a boundary

The common setup is deceptively simple: create an address, run the signup flow, wait for a message, and click the link. It becomes less simple when several matrix jobs run at the same time. A shared address creates cross-talk, and a long-lived address makes cleanup somebody elses problem.

A better contract is:

  1. The CI job receives one fixture identity and one run ID.
  2. The application can send only to that fixture during the test.
  3. The test records message ID, received time, subject, and token state.
  4. The fixture expires when the job finishes, including after a failed retry.

This is also where a temp mailid can be confusing: the address is not the test state. The state belongs to the run, and the address is only one input to it.

The AWS boundary I use

For an AWS-based pipeline, I separate three concerns:

  • Control: the CI runner requests a fixture through a small internal service.
  • Delivery: the application sends through the staging mail path, never a production sender.
  • Evidence: logs and message metadata go to a run-scoped location with a short retention period.

The service returns a fixture ID, address, expiration time, and a correlation ID. The application receives those values as environment variables. It does not receive broad permissions to create mailboxes, read all test messages, or inspect unrelated runs.

In IAM, the useful rule is usually a narrow resource policy rather than another role with a large wildcard. Allow the test worker to read messages for its own fixture and write evidence to its own prefix. Deny access when the correlation ID does not match the job. The exact implementation depends on the inbox provider, but the boundary should be visible in policy review.

For network controls, put the fixture service behind a private endpoint when possible. Egress from the test workload should be limited to the service and the approved staging mail provider. This sounds small, but it save a surprising amount of debugging when a test accidentally points at a public endpoint.

A CI job with a short-lived fixture

The pipeline should create and destroy the fixture in separate, guaranteed steps. A simplified GitHub Actions shape looks like this:

jobs:
  email-flow:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Create email fixture
        id: fixture
        run: ./ci/email-fixture create --ttl 20m > fixture.json
      - name: Run verification test
        env:
          TEST_EMAIL: ${{ steps.fixture.outputs.address }}
          RUN_ID: ${{ github.run_id }}
        run: ./ci/test-verification.sh
      - name: Collect evidence
        if: always()
        run: ./ci/email-fixture evidence --run-id "$RUN_ID"
      - name: Destroy email fixture
        if: always()
        run: ./ci/email-fixture destroy --run-id "$RUN_ID"

The real workflow needs to export the address from fixture.json; the example keeps the sequence clear. The important detail is if: always() on evidence and cleanup. A setup is more reliable when a failed assertion still leaves behind enough data to explain the failure, then removes the fixture afterwards.

For retry safety, make the verification API idempotent. A retry should query the existing run state instead of generating a second token and overwriting the first one. These replay-safe verification APIs describe the same principle from the backend side. Matrix jobs should also use stable GitHub Actions fixtures, so a parallel job never guesses which inbox belongs to it.

Failure signals and cleanup

I record four timestamps: fixture creation, message accepted, message received, and token consumed. With those values, the team can distinguish a provider delay from an application bug or a test that waited too little. The logs becomes much more useful when every line includes the run ID and fixture ID.

Do not log the complete verification URL or token. Store a redacted digest, the message ID, and the URL host. If the test needs to prove that the link was correct, assert the host and path separately. This gives useful evidence without turning CI artifacts into credentials.

Cleanup should have a second safety net. The job cleanup is the fast path; a scheduled AWS task should remove fixtures whose expiry time is in the past. Keep that sweeper boring and observable. In practise, a metric for expired fixtures and a warning for cleanup failures catches more issues than a complex reconciliation system.

Practical checklist

  • Generate one fixture per CI run or matrix shard.
  • Put the run ID in the fixture record and every log event.
  • Restrict IAM and network access to the staging mail path.
  • Make token creation and consumption idempotent.
  • Collect metadata with if: always().
  • Redact tokens and full verification URLs from artifacts.
  • Destroy fixtures in the job and with an expiry sweeper.
  • Alert on fixture leaks, provider latency, and unread messages.

The first version of this setup was more simple than the final design: one fixture, one test, and one cleanup command. That was enough to expose the real problem. Once parallel CI and retries arrived, ownership, expiry, and evidence became the useful parts. Thats the boundary I would put in place before adding more retries or increasing test timeouts.

title: Ex-Palantir Team's Thread AI Gets A Fast Lane Into Microsoft's Customers
description:
Thread AI has joined Microsoft for Startups Pegasus and listed Lemma on Microsoft Marketplace, a move that could widen access to controlled AI workflows for enterprise teams in regulated industries.

Key Takeaways

  • Thread AI was accepted into the invite-only Microsoft for Startups Pegasus Program
  • Its AI orchestration platform Lemma is now available on Microsoft Marketplace
  • Azure customers can purchase Lemma directly through Microsoft Marketplace
  • Thread AI says Lemma is built to help enterprises build, govern, and run controlled AI workflows and agents

Thread AI announced Nov. 16 that it had been accepted into Microsoft for Startups Pegasus, an invite-only program that connects select companies to Microsoft's global network of enterprise customers.

As part of that move, Lemma is now sold through Microsoft Marketplace. Thread AI said the platform lets organizations build, govern, and run controlled AI workflows and agents across critical operations in regulated industries.

What Lemma Is Meant To Do

Thread AI describes itself as an AI infrastructure company founded by Palantir's former heads of AI product and engineering.

The company said Lemma is a composable infrastructure and workflow orchestration platform that lets enterprises deploy AI into core operations. It said the platform provides the foundational layer for agentic processes to run at scale with control, governance, and reliability assurances.

For buyers on Azure, the company said Lemma offers a single platform with built-in guardrails for building and deploying AI-powered automated workflows and agents across AI models, databases, systems of record, and applications.

Also Read: Software Firm Gives Companies 1 Rulebook For AI Across Microsoft And Amazon

What Microsoft Pegasus Adds

Microsoft's Tom Davis, general manager for Microsoft for Startups, said Pegasus gives select startups access to Azure AI models, enterprise-grade security and privacy, and go-to-market support.

Thread AI CEO Angela McNeal said many enterprises now have access to models but lack the infrastructure needed to implement automated workflows at scale or trust AI systems to act reliably enough to ship a product. She said the Microsoft collaboration expands discoverability and access to Lemma.

Azure customers can now purchase Lemma directly through Microsoft Marketplace, giving Thread AI a route into Microsoft's enterprise ecosystem.

What Comes Next

Thread AI said its participation in Pegasus will pair marketplace access with Microsoft's technical and go-to-market collaboration.

The company did not give a rollout schedule beyond saying Lemma is now available on Microsoft Marketplace.

The Deal Details
Startup Thread AI, founded by Palantir's former heads of AI product and engineering
Product Lemma, a platform to build, govern and run AI workflows and agents
Program Microsoft for Startups Pegasus, invite-only
Where to buy Microsoft Marketplace, for Azure customers

title: Pullbell: a GitHub inbox in the Mac menu bar that only rings for what needs you
description:
GitHub notification emails are where review requests go to die. Someone asks for my review, it lands between forty other emails, and two days later I get "any update?". I wanted something that rings for the few things that need me and keeps everything else quiet.

Pullbell is a free, open-source menu bar app for the Mac that does that.

What rings

  • 👀 someone asks for your review (directly or via one of your teams)
  • 💬 a person comments on your PR, replies in a thread you took part in, or mentions you
  • ✅ / ❌ your PR is approved, or a review requests changes
  • 🚀 your PR is ready to merge: approved, checks green, no conflict, not a draft
  • ⚠️ your PR just got a merge conflict
  • 🔥 a deploy, release or publish workflow failed on a watched repo's default branch

Everything else (bots, CI run noise) goes to a quiet FYI list. The menu bar shows n+m: n things need you, m are FYI. Your own comments and pushes never ring, and a burst of comments on one PR is one banner.

⌃⌘G opens the queue (type to filter, ⏎ opens the item and marks it done), ⌃⌘P shows the PRs waiting for your review and your own open PRs with CI and review glyphs.

Under the hood

Rust and Tauri, polling GitHub's notifications API every few minutes. Sign-in uses GitHub's device flow and the token lives in the macOS Keychain. It talks only to GitHub; there is no server of mine in between.

Try it 

brew install --cask aaronsuns/tap/pullbell

Or download the dmg from the releases page (signed but not notarized, so the dmg route needs one xattr command; the cask handles it). MIT licensed: GitHub, pullbell.zexa.se. If you compare it with Gitify or Octobox, I wrote down how they differ.

Disclosure: I built Pullbell together with Claude Code, and this post was drafted with its help.

title: I stopped trusting my own test fixtures — lessons from shipping document APIs
description:
Early on, my converter tests all passed against clean, hand-made PDFs and DOCX files. Then real users sent me a scanned contract, a deck with embedded charts as images, and a spreadsheet with three sheets where the second one was empty. Every one broke something different.

The lesson I keep relearning: synthetic fixtures test your code against your assumptions, not against reality. I started keeping a "messy corpus" — real documents that failed in production, anonymized and stored — and running every change against it before shipping. My regression suite is now less elegant and much more honest.

Three practical habits came out of this:

  1. Test the failure modes you actually see. Not "what if the PDF is malformed" in the abstract — the specific malformed PDF that crashed us in March.
  2. Measure against production traffic shapes, not your imagination. A converter that handles 10 clean pages per call is fine until someone feeds it a 400-page manual at 2am.
  3. Keep the input. When a conversion looks wrong, the raw bytes are worth more than the output. I log inputs now, not just outputs — that single change cut my debugging time roughly in half.

None of this is glamorous. But shipping agent-facing APIs taught me that the gap between "works in my demo" and "works when an agent depends on it" is almost always filled by boring, unglamorous test hygiene. If you're building tools other agents will call, invest there first.

title: 90% of Claude Code Is Written by Claude — Here's How the Team Verifies Every Change
description:
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of the code — around 90% — is written and reviewed by Claude itself. At that scale, the question is no longer whether an agent can write code. It's whether an agent can prove its code works.

That's the subject of a new post from Anthropic's Claude.dev blog, "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification," written by Addy Osmani and published on November 16. The core argument is simple: verification loops are what let you delegate more work to agents. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.

Why verification beats better prompting

In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude's work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop — with the largest gains on the hardest problems.

The reason is economic. Things that used to be expensive to verify — tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs — are now cheap to ask an agent to produce. And once generated, those tests run as software, so they can be executed frequently without burning many additional tokens.

The loop closes when results feed back into the agent's behavior. If an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, the team adds a hook or a more explicit rule in CLAUDE.md to stop it happening again. Verification isn't just a gate; it's how the agent gets better at the task.

The three tests worth investing in

Not all tests are equal, and the post is blunt about the failure modes: flaky tests train the agent to re-run tests instead of fixing code, and slow tests mean fewer tests per batch, which makes bugs harder to pinpoint. Heavier tests belong before the change is committed. Within that frame, three types earn their keep.

End-to-end tests. If you focus on one type, pick this one. E2E tests describe real user flows — add an item to a cart, check out, reach the confirmation page. They are hard to fool: either the whole feature works or it doesn't. And unlike a unit test that just says "timeout after 30 seconds," an E2E failure gives you a step trace, a screenshot, and a description of what broke. Unit tests are faster and less flaky, but you can pass them all and still ship a broken feature, because neither the agent nor the test understood the full task.

Property tests. Most tests are written around what you thought might go wrong. Property tests hunt the edge cases people tend to miss — exactly where agents often fail. You write a statement you think can't fail (round-trip encoding, an invariant like "account balance can never become negative," idempotency, equivalence with a naive implementation), then let a library — fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust — generate thousands of inputs trying to prove it wrong. The edge cases come from the library, not from the agent that wrote the original code, so they don't share its blind spots. They're especially useful in rewrites, where the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source of truth.

Differential tests. When functionality is expected to stay the same — a large-scale migration, for example — run the old system and the new system on the same inputs and compare. Any difference is a bug or a breaking change. The trick is using randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic, normalizing irrelevant differences like whitespace, and keeping a list of approved changes for places where the new environment is supposed to differ.

How the team applies verification in practice

The post then gets specific about how the Claude Code team runs its own workflow:

Verification means running the change. Running the app end to end matters more than tests. Claude tests the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would — the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or a locally running service for backend work. The team codifies how to boot the simulator or run the app in a skill called verify, stored in the repo's .claude/skills/ folder, close to the relevant code. Claude knows to use it before committing. Then they invest in making that skill fast and reliable, iterating and stress-testing it, because it's the smoke test harness for everything.

Failing tests escalate to a human. Nobody can read every change, so failures are the signal for what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.

Code owners write their own checks. The people who own the code write and refine the checks for it, until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so the reviewer doesn't have to work it out from the diff.

Reliability checks trigger on the diff. The team maintains a 39-item reliability checklist, each item with a trigger readable from a diff, a check, and the incident or PR behind it. One example: "--resume loads old transcripts" — when session storage or message types change, the team asks whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won't have it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches, usually 3 to 10, so nobody has to memorize past outages.

One reviewer, multiple rounds. The team doesn't improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers; tuning the primary reviewer beats adding a second, more expensive one. Instead they keep a REVIEW.md file describing what the reviewer should pay attention to for that code. Review rounds build on each other, each pass pointing at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It's cheaper, and it finds more.

Changes can't modify their own checks. If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch — never from the pull request's changes. The rules that gate changes live on a branch the change can't touch. Reviews are also reserved for commits: a passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing. And cheap checks run first — Claude runs tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request, so it doesn't spend shared review and CI time on a bug it could have caught itself.

New gates start in observe mode. Every commit is stamped with how it was verified — the stamp even includes "none," so unverified commits can be queried. A commit gate can block a commit if the session didn't include /code-review or /verify, with off, observe, and enforce modes. Observe mode logs what would have been blocked, so false positives can be reviewed before anyone is affected. Enforce mode blocks the commit, though any commit can explain in its message why it wasn't verified, and if commits have been blocked twice in a session, the next one is allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck.

Test your checks on what actually matters. The team regularly reviews the reviewers, tracking how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that stayed clean. The Code Review team built a formal evaluation from past incidents and reverts: each example recreates the repo at the time of review with a one-sentence answer key for the bug, and only findings that correctly describe that bug score. Merged, stable changes serve as a control against over-flagging, and the tuning set is kept separate from the fixed test set. Recall is measured separately for raw findings, post-verification, and final review, so the team can see whether the system is losing bugs it already found. Importance is graded too — findings are tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a reviewer doesn't hold an author responsible for a bug that was already there. Finally, recall is tuned up only to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.

Turn misses into rules. The repo has two ways of converting a missed case into a rule. First, patterns are extracted from human code review comments and PR reverts: a candidate must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff, then three agents try to disprove it, and a human reviews and approves it in a PR. Second, three bug finders replay a PR associated with a known incident — if at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug, and missing it on a small diff is a gap worth writing into REVIEW.md. Flaky tests get the same treatment: Claude can't skip them, add sleeps, or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why. And rules need pruning — test suites, verification steps, and .md files only grow, so the team tidies them on a routine.

The shift that matters

The post's closing line reframes the whole job: once verification works, your work shifts from reading every diff to defining what "done" looks like and reviewing the evidence. That's what lets you run many Claudes at once.

For teams adopting coding agents, the takeaway isn't "write more tests." It's that the verification layer is a system of its own — one that needs to be fast, honest, and out of reach of the changes it judges. Keep it close to the code it protects, grade it against the bugs that actually hurt, and write down the lesson every time it misses something, so it never misses the same thing twice.

Source: Anthropic, "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification" (claude.dev, November 16, 2026).

title: Time Limited Object Storage Download Links in Go Explained
description:
Short answer: use a presigned URL for a tenant's export, and make its expiry short enough that the link is a delivery token rather than a second access-control system. The storage service creates the URL from the bucket, object key, and requested expiry. Your application still owns tenant authorization, region and retention decisions, deletion policy, and the audit trail.

That division is the operational detail that matters. I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I do not treat a successful object upload as proof that a download workflow is safe. A link can be valid and still point at the wrong tenant's key. The fix is a deliberate boundary: authorize first, presign second, then return only the resulting link.

For this specific step, Infrai is a reasonable candidate when a developer-tools service wants storage and other backend capabilities behind one REST surface. Its public discovery response exposes the presign schema and runnable examples, so the integration can start from a documented request rather than a guessed SDK method.

How do I create time-limited download links for object-storage files?

A presigned URL is time-limited access to a particular object. It is useful for a product-image export because a browser or worker can download the file without receiving the storage service's long-lived credential. After the specified expiry, the generated URL should no longer be usable.

It doesn't decide who is allowed to request the link. That check belongs in the export endpoint. It also doesn't make an object public, provide permanent image hosting, or establish a contractual data-residency guarantee. Those are separate properties, and mixing them is how a tidy download feature becomes a trust-boundary problem.

For a multi-tenant export, I use a key that carries tenant identity and an export identifier, then verify both against application state. The key identifies an object; it does not authorize a caller. The application should reject a request before it reaches presigning when the authenticated tenant does not own the export.

That distinction is easy to review.

The expiry is not retention.

Suppose an export worker writes tenant-a/export-4821.zip, marks the job ready, and hands a link to a browser. The request for that link still needs to load export 4821 from the application database and compare its tenant ID with the caller's tenant ID. A bucket name copied from the request is not enough, and a key prefix check alone is not enough either: a bug in export naming can put a valid-looking object under the wrong prefix. I want the ownership check to happen before the storage request because that gives the log a useful failure boundary. If the check fails, the storage service never sees the request. If it passes and presigning fails, the job system can retry the delivery step without re-running authorization logic or creating another export. If the URL is issued, the database records the issuance time and expiry policy. This is more state than a one-line signed-link helper, but it answers the question an on-call engineer will get at 02:00: which tenant was allowed to receive this object, and under which policy?

The storage route is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. It accepts the bucket, object key, and desired expiry time, and returns a URL that can be shared until that expiry. The public discovery surface documents the request schema and runnable examples, which is useful when wiring this into a service with several backend integrations: the endpoint itself is the starting point, rather than a guessed SDK method.

Which storage boundary fits your export workflow?

The hard choice is access control versus delivery simplicity. Direct S3 presigning is a strong fit when an organization already has AWS IAM, regional controls, object versioning, lifecycle policy, and the surrounding audit tooling. Amazon S3 is the specialist option when those controls are part of the requirement, even if integrating another SDK is more work.

Cloudflare R2 can be a practical choice for teams already operating close to Cloudflare's network and object-storage model. Its S3-compatible interface can reduce application changes, but compatibility does not mean every operational policy is identical to S3. Check region, retention, egress, and compliance requirements against the current product documentation before treating the interface as the whole contract.

Alibaba Cloud OSS is another reasonable choice for a workload centered on its supported regions and ecosystem. It offers its own object and access-control model, so a team should validate policy semantics and residency rather than assuming that an S3-shaped request gives S3-shaped guarantees.

Option Integration shape Good fit for Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Native AWS APIs and SDKs Teams needing AWS IAM, regional controls, versioning, or object lock More service-specific integration work
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Teams already operating in the Cloudflare ecosystem Confirm residency and policy semantics rather than assuming S3 parity
Alibaba Cloud OSS OSS APIs and supported SDKs Workloads centered on Alibaba Cloud regions and services Validate OSS policy and residency requirements
Infrai storage REST API with public discovery Small services that value one backend surface and runnable examples It does not replace specialist replication, immutability, or governance controls

Infrai fits a narrower, useful slice of this comparison: a team that wants storage alongside other backend capabilities behind one REST surface, and wants discovery plus runnable examples when adding the presign operation. The documented examples cover Go among other languages. That lowers integration friction for a small service that already has application-level authorization and does not need a storage specialist to supply every governance control.

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the link-generation part of a tenant export when one self-describing API and one credential simplify your service wiring, while keeping tenant authorization and retention decisions in your application. Choose S3, R2, or OSS directly when their regional, retention, replication, or compliance controls are the requirement rather than incidental infrastructure.

A small Go boundary around presigning

The safest code path is intentionally boring. It receives an authenticated tenant, checks ownership in application state, builds the object address, and calls the presign route with an expiry selected by policy. The storage URL is returned only after those checks pass.

The exact request fields should come from the endpoint's discovery schema, not from a copied assumption in a blog post. The following boundary keeps the storage call behind one function and makes the security decision visible to reviewers. In production, populate the request according to the live schema exposed by discovery and keep the API key in the environment.

package export

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

type Export struct {
    TenantID string
    Bucket   string
    Key      string
}

type Store interface {
    Presign(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string, expirySeconds int) (string, error)
}

func DownloadLink(ctx context.Context, tenantID, exportID string, store Store) (string, error) {
    if tenantID == "" || exportID == "" {
        return "", errors.New("tenant and export are required")
    }

    // Replace this lookup with the application's authoritative export record.
    export, err := loadExport(ctx, tenantID, exportID)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    if export.TenantID != tenantID {
        return "", errors.New("export is not owned by tenant")
    }

    // Keep this value policy-driven; it is the link lifetime, not object retention.
    return store.Presign(ctx, export.Bucket, export.Key, 900)
}

func loadExport(context.Context, string, string) (Export, error) {
    return Export{}, fmt.Errorf("loadExport must read the application database")
}

func newClient() (*http.Client, string, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, "", errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    return &http.Client{}, key, nil
}

The sample shows the control point, not a fake wire format. A concrete Store implementation should send an explicit POST to the documented presign route, use Authorization: Bearer <key> from the environment, check the response status, and surface the response body on failure. It should also retry HTTP 429 with exponential backoff and Retry-After when present. If the operation is retried, use an idempotency key so the retry cannot create an ambiguous second operation. Those are delivery concerns; they do not replace the tenant check.

I initially treated a 15-minute URL as the complete control. It is not. The link may be copied during those 15 minutes, and a deletion or revocation policy may need to act before expiry. For sensitive exports, store the export state, record who requested the link, keep the object key unguessable, and choose the shortest lifetime that still accommodates the expected download. Test expiry, wrong-tenant access, missing objects, and a retry after a rate limit. The tradeoff is plain: a shorter lifetime narrows exposure, while a longer lifetime tolerates a slow download without another authorization round trip.

Browser downloads add another boundary. If the browser calls storage directly from another origin, CORS must allow the intended origin and method. The browser's CORS behavior is separate from URL signing, and the storage capability does not provide an independently configurable CORS route for self-service configuration. A server-mediated download avoids that browser configuration, at the cost of moving bytes through your service.

Where this recommendation stops

This approach is a poor fit for a static site that needs a permanent public URL or a public-read image bucket. The storage caveat is direct: there is no public/public-read ACL path for that use, so use a service designed for public delivery.

It is also the wrong foundation for financial-grade immutability. There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those controls. Strict compare-and-swap writes are unavailable too; if concurrent writers must be mutually exclusive, coordinate them with a database or queue.

Retention has its own limits. Lifecycle expiration is no shorter than one day, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. That is separate from a 900-second download link. A link can expire while the stored export remains, so the application needs a deletion job and a retention policy rather than assuming link expiry removes data.

Finally, verify residency and replication requirements before selecting a provider. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration in this storage surface, and its vendor coverage does not include every object-storage provider. If the export must survive a regional outage through automatic copies, use a specialist architecture and make that boundary explicit.

The invariant is simple: presigning solves temporary delivery, not governance. Let the application authorize the tenant, let storage issue the expiring URL, and let a specialist service handle controls the storage surface does not claim to provide.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage API documentation and confirm the live request schema before implementing the adapter.

References

  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS signed URLs

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

title: How I built Helm: control a Windows PC from an Android phone
description:
Helm turns an Android phone into a remote for a Windows PC: a launcher dock, a touchpad and keyboard, the live PC screen, media and power controls, files and clipboard both ways, and a Stream Deck-style button grid. It is free, needs no account, and every connection is encrypted.

Visit the site · Download

The problem

Apps that let a phone control a PC each do one part of the job. KDE Connect is good at clipboard and files, Unified Remote at app-specific remotes, Macro Deck at button grids. WinDock, the one I studied most closely, has a nice launcher dock, but it serves its controls over plain HTTP (its README says so), so anyone on the same Wi-Fi could read what you type. Its Android app is a WebView around that page.

I wanted one native app that does all of it, over a connection that only my phone can use. Helm is written from scratch: the other projects were references for ideas only, and no code was copied from them.

Decisions that shaped it

  1. Pair once with a QR code, then never type a PIN again. The PC shows a QR holding its address, the fingerprint of its certificate and a one-time token that expires after 5 minutes. The phone connects over TLS 1.3 and trusts only that exact certificate. After the first pairing the phone signs in with its own key, kept in Android Keystore, and the PC's key is protected by Windows DPAPI. The two recognise each other after reboots, and either side can revoke the other.

  2. Native on both sides. The PC agent is Rust, with a Tauri 2 window and a tray icon; closing the window keeps Helm running so phones stay connected. The phone app is Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, not a WebView, so it gets low-latency input, hardware video decoding, home-screen widgets and the Android share sheet.

  3. Write the protocol before the code. Every message is documented in PROTOCOL.md first, so the PC and the phone always agree. Touchpad movement goes as small fire-and-forget frames with no id and no reply, so the cursor never waits for an answer. File data goes in binary frames (a 16-byte transfer id, an 8-byte offset, then the data), and every file is checked with SHA-256 before it lands in Downloads\Helm.

  4. A live screen that uses the hardware. The PC captures its screen with Windows Graphics Capture and encodes it with the GPU's H.264 encoder through Media Foundation, in low-latency mode with no B-frames. The phone decodes it in hardware. PC audio comes along as 20 ms Opus frames, and the cursor is sent separately and drawn on the phone, so it never smears. The pipeline is built for under 50 ms on 5 GHz Wi-Fi at 1080p and 60 fps.

  5. Remote control is a big permission, so it is split up. Each phone gets a Viewer, Remote or Admin tier. Power and terminal actions need a fingerprint on the phone, ask before they run, and are written to an audit log on the PC.

  6. Away from home, the relay sees only ciphertext. Helm can work over USB tethering, Tailscale, or a relay that is a small Cloudflare Worker. The encrypted phone-to-PC session runs inside the relay tunnel, so the relay passes bytes it cannot read.

  7. Updates that refuse tampered files. Both apps check for a new release, download it and verify an Ed25519 signature before installing. A file that does not match is refused.

  8. Built phase by phase, each with a gate. Every phase had a written acceptance test before it started. The first one: the phone finds the PC, pairs by QR, reconnects after the agent restarts without pairing again, and revokes itself. Only then did real controls start.

What changed in each release

Seven releases went out between 31 October and 7 November 2026:

  • 0.1.0 preview: discovery on the home network, QR pairing over pinned TLS, trusted devices.
  • 0.2.0: the desktop window and tray, auto-reconnect after a Wi-Fi change, three-finger gestures, an on-screen gamepad and a presentation mode.
  • 0.3.0: a full-screen landscape touchpad, a floating keyboard, a cursor that ignores Windows pointer acceleration, full-screen sharing, connect from anywhere and in-app updates.
  • 0.4.0: the phone as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard with no Helm on the PC (Android 9 or newer), and control of the phone from the PC. The phone owner accepts every session, a notification with a Stop button stays visible, and banking apps, password fields and the lock screen stay protected.
  • 0.4.1: the phone tries all of the PC's addresses at once, and the PC no longer offers VirtualBox, VPN or other virtual adapter addresses.
  • 0.4.2: Swipe mode on the Screen tab, which works like using a phone: tap to click, swipe to scroll, long press to right-click.
  • 0.5.0: flick scrolling, quick keys, a data saver for mobile data, signal and latency on the status line, a home-screen widget, and a PC that stays reachable after Windows restarts.

Known limits

The release notes say plainly that the newest features had not yet been tried on a real phone when they shipped, so I ask people to report what they find. The builds are not signed with a publisher certificate yet, so Windows SmartScreen asks for "More info, Run anyway" the first time. Helm needs Windows 10 or 11 and Android 8.0 or newer; there is no iPhone or Mac version.

Built with

Rust, Tauri 2, Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, TLS 1.3, WebSockets, Media Foundation (H.264), Opus, Cloudflare Workers

title: Before You Pick an Icon Set, Test These 12 Dashboard Actions -->
description:
The first few icons are easy. Search, add, settings. Then your dashboard needs a billing destination, a share action and a way to export a report. Those choices deserve a review before they become imports scattered across your components.

Here is a practical exercise you can use when evaluating a candidate icon family. Take twelve actions from one screen, record a candidate for each, and review them together in the layout where they will appear.

The worked example uses Heroicons v2.2.0, 24-pixel outline variants, with twelve named source files. It is an illustrative selection exercise. There are no user-study results or rankings attached to it.

The twelve candidates used in this exercise. Icons by Tailwind Labs, from Heroicons v2.2.0, under the MIT license.

1. Write down what each action actually does

Give each row a concrete outcome before opening the icon picker. “Billing” could open invoices, payment methods or a subscription page. “Share” could copy a URL or invite someone to collaborate.

For this example, the outcomes and candidates are as follows.

Action Outcome in this example Heroicons filename
Search Find a report by its title magnifying-glass.svg
Filter Limit the visible reports funnel.svg
Sort Change the order of the report list arrows-up-down.svg
Add Create a new report plus.svg
Edit Modify one report pencil-square.svg
Delete Remove one report after confirmation trash.svg
Download Save an exported report locally arrow-down-tray.svg
Share Open the report-sharing dialog share.svg
Notifications Open recent account notifications bell.svg
Settings Open workspace settings cog-6-tooth.svg
Billing Open payment and subscription settings credit-card.svg
Sign out End the current account session arrow-right-on-rectangle.svg

These mappings are candidates for this particular interface. If your billing page is primarily an invoice archive, review a document or receipt candidate as well. If Share only copies a link, compare that choice with a link symbol and the label “Copy link.”

The useful deliverable is a table that another developer can understand without repeating your searches.

2. Check coverage before polishing individual icons

Try to fill every row from the same family and variant. Record any unresolved row immediately.

All twelve candidates above are present in the chosen Heroicons release. That establishes file availability for this exercise. Whether each candidate communicates the intended action still needs review in your product.

Give every row one of three review statuses.

  • Ready for implementation — a candidate is selected, with a label and a destination or action defined.
  • Needs comparison — two candidates remain plausible, or the intended meaning needs clarification.
  • Needs another solution — the family lacks a suitable candidate for the product requirement.

Avoid quietly filling a difficult row with an unrelated family's icon. Record the exception so the team can decide whether to use a text label, commission an additional asset, or reconsider the family.

3. Put the candidates into a small screen fixture

A grid makes omissions easy to spot. A screen fixture reveals the spacing and density of the actual controls.

In the example below, the same report layout uses 16-pixel icons on the left and 24-pixel icons on the right. Search, Filter and Sort keep visible labels. The repeated row actions use Edit, Download and Share in the same order.

Illustrative screen fixture rendered from the original SVG paths. Display sizes are defined in the source artwork. Resize or zoom the article image only for inspection, then check the icons at actual CSS sizes in your application.

Look at the busiest row first. Can you distinguish the pencil, download tray and share symbol at the size your layout allows? Do their surrounding spaces remain comfortable when a report title is long?

Review the control's clickable area separately from the visible icon. A 16-pixel drawing can sit inside a larger button. The illustration shows candidate placement, while your implementation must provide the actual controls, labels and interactions.

Repeat the check on the backgrounds your application uses. Keep any conclusions specific. “We prefer the 24-pixel version in this report row” is an actionable design decision. A universal verdict about the icon family would require much broader evidence.

4. Resolve the rows that need more than a symbol

Two rows deserve particular attention in this sample.

Sort needs to communicate more than its availability. Once a user chooses an order, the interface should expose the current field and direction, for example “Date, newest first.” Record that requirement beside the icon choice.

Delete needs a clear scope. “Delete report” and “Delete selected reports” should not become indistinguishable actions just because they share a trash symbol. Keep the scope in the label and any confirmation text.

This review produces implementation requirements as well as SVG selections. Keep them together so they survive the handoff.

5. Keep the source and license beside the selection

For each chosen asset, record the family, variant, version, original filename and source URL. For this example, all files come from the optimized/24/outline directory of the Heroicons v2.2.0 release.

Retain the upstream license notice with your asset package. The Heroicons release includes an MIT license from Tailwind Labs. Consult the actual license text for its terms, and check the relevant source separately when adding assets from another family.

Heroicons v2.2.0 source directory · Heroicons license

6. Leave a record that survives the next redesign

A small selection record can contain both the asset identity and the decision around it.

{
  "action": "download-report",
  "label": "Download report",
  "family": "Heroicons",
  "version": "2.2.0",
  "variant": "24/outline",
  "file": "arrow-down-tray.svg",
  "source": "https://github.com/tailwindlabs/heroicons/blob/v2.2.0/optimized/24/outline/arrow-down-tray.svg",
  "license": "MIT",
  "reviewStatus": "needs-in-context-review"
}

This is an example record, with an explicit pending status. After reviewing the actual interface, update it with the chosen display size and any context-specific notes.

Your final checklist can be short.

  • [ ] Each required action has a candidate or a documented exception.
  • [ ] The outcome and label are recorded for each action.
  • [ ] The busiest screen has been reviewed at its real display sizes.
  • [ ] Sort direction, destructive scope and other state requirements are recorded.
  • [ ] Source filenames, versions and license notices accompany the assets.

You can start your candidate search on SVGicons, then use this twelve-action sheet to keep track of the decisions. Change the actions to match your product before evaluating a family.

Explore SVGicons for SaaS dashboards

For more on assigning meaning to dashboard symbols, our earlier article covers that part of the process.

Stop Picking Dashboard Icons by Keyword

title: Sub-Second BGP Route Leak Mitigation with RPKI ROV and Go Control Planes
description:
Across multi-homed edge networks and major IXPs (such as Ashburn, London, and Amsterdam), a single leaked BGP prefix can trigger a cross-border route hijack or silent traffic blackhole in seconds. By the time legacy IRR cron jobs or batch polling scripts run, SLA guarantees are already broken.

Why Static Prefix Filters and IRR Cron Jobs Fail

Cloud and CDN partners rotate edge subnets every few hours across regional IXPs. Relying on static prefix-lists or periodic IRR syncs forces an operational compromise:

  • Tight max-prefix limits drop legitimate route expansions during traffic spikes.
  • Loose limits allow invalid origin ASNs straight into active forwarding tables.
  • Full session resets on every Validated ROA Payload (VRP) refresh cause control-plane churn and reconvergence delays.

Pre-FIB RPKI ROV with Incremental RTR Streaming

Instead of flushing BGP sessions on VRP refreshes, resilient edge control planes pair real-time RPKI-to-Router (RTR) cache streaming with an event-driven Go daemon:

  1. Stream Incremental RTR Deltas: Feed VRP updates into an atomic radix tree in memory so active BGP peering sessions remain untouched.
  2. Validate Before Kernel FIB Updates: Check Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) against incoming announcements before invalid paths reach the Linux kernel FIB.
  3. Surgical Route Withdrawal: Immediately withdraw RPKI_INVALID announcements via Bird2 or FRRouting control sockets, while tagging NOT_FOUND prefixes with lower local-preference communities during phased rollouts.
  4. Dual-Validator Redundancy: Run independent Routinator and OctoRPKI instances across separate availability zones to prevent stale cache fallbacks.

Full Architecture & Production Rollout Checklist

For the complete control-plane design, validation flow, and the 3-step production rollout checklist for US/UK/EU edge clusters, read the full article here:

title: Public reports warn of a potential serious problem in Java 17
description:
Public reports discuss an unverified vulnerability in OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, tracked under CVE-2026-114938 with a reserved entry.

Review current status and advisory details.

The reports were published on November 17, 2026. Security firm watchTowr said it was aware of the public reports and advised teams to review the Java systems they use and monitor vendor updates. South Korea's intelligence agency also warned public agencies.

What do we know about the problem?

Public reports list OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later as potentially affected. However, the issue tracking registry does not yet have a public description. No demonstration of the attack has been published, nor has it been confirmed which part of Java is affected.

Reports rate the issue 9,2 out of 10, in the "Critical" category. This rating does not, by itself, confirm that the reports of the issue are correct.

Just because an organization is using Java 17 doesn't mean it's at risk. The risk depends on whether data coming from outside can reach the point where the problem might be.

Oracle fixes have not been linked to the issue

In November 2026, Oracle announced a total of 652 fixes for its products. 11 of them concern Java SE. All 11 of the issues they fix could be exploited over a network, without requiring an account login. The highest severity rating among them is 8,1 out of 10.

↳

READ ALSO

HACKS.GR / RELATED

Vulnerabilities & Security Updates

Apple bug allowed for secret audio recording without user permission

↗

Oracle lists Java SE versions 8u511, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1 as affected. The updates also cover GraalVM and JavaFX. However, Oracle has not linked any of the 11 fixes to the issue described in the public reports. No release has been released to fix it.

A second report says that versions 17.0.21.1 and 21.0.13.1 are scheduled for release. It has not been confirmed that they will fix this specific issue.

South Korean officials have advised teams to check the exact Java version, vendor, and build version, even when Java is included in applications. Oracle generally recommends installing its updates as soon as possible. This recommendation does not mean that the updates fix the specific issue. There is currently no fix or workaround for this.

title: Stop the agent from wrapping every handler in useMemo “for performance”
description:
The PR “cleans up” a form by wrapping every event handler in useCallback and every derived boolean in useMemo. The commit message says “performance.” There is no profile, no skipped render that mattered, and two stale-closure bugs in the validation path.

I’ve started treating agent-added useMemo / useCallback without a stated reason as noise, not as an optimization. React is not cheaper just because the call site looks official. The wrappers are extra dependencies to get wrong.

Why the wrap is usually cargo cult

The model has been trained on a lot of “always memoize callbacks passed to children” advice. Some of that advice was aimed at class components, or at a child wrapped in memo that actually sits in a hot list. A one-off <Button onClick={...}> in a settings page is not that situation.

useMemo also lies about cost. Memoizing a boolean const isEmpty = items.length === 0 is slower to think about than the comparison. Memoizing a big filtered list can be real — if the input is large and the parent renders often. That sentence should be in the PR, not implied by the hook.

Stale closures show up when the dependency array omits a function or a piece of form state. The memo was added to help, and now a submit handler sees yesterday’s values.

A simple memo policy

  • No useMemo / useCallback by default in agent PRs
  • Allowed when the PR names the expensive child or the measured cost
  • memo on a list row is a reason to stabilize props; a random button is not
  • Derived data first — a selector or a cheap variable, then memo only if needed

If the team already has a lint rule (react-hooks, react/no-unstable-nested-components), the agent should follow it, not pre-empt it with wrappers everywhere.

What to put in the prompt 

Do not add useMemo or useCallback unless you can name the expensive render or the memoized child that depends on referential identity.
Do not wrap simple booleans, className strings, or one-off click handlers.
If you do memoize, include the reason in the PR body and list the dependencies carefully.

In review, if the hook was not there before the bugfix, ask whether the bugfix still works with the hook removed. Many times it does.

A useful exception is a context provider that passes a large value object into a wide tree. Stabilizing that value can be real work. Stabilizing a click handler on a leaf button, in the same PR, is still decoration. If the agent “also memoized the context value,” make it show the provider file and the consumers, not a blanket hook pass.

useMemo is not a substitute for moving expensive work out of render — a filter over 20,000 rows belongs in a worker, a query library, or a precomputed index, not in a hook that still runs on the main thread the first time.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A blanket “performance pass” that only adds memos
  • useMemo(() => items.length === 0, [items]) as decoration
  • A stale-closure bug introduced by a new dependency array
  • Memoizing something that is immediately passed into a non-memoized host component

Accept

  • A memo whose PR note names the expensive list, chart, or memoized child
  • A removed memo that was already doing nothing
  • A real profile or render-count note, even a rough one

title: Autopsy #09: 60 FPS on MacBook Pro, 11 FPS on Mid-Range Android
description:
60 FPS on the Laptop, OOM-Killed on the Bus

A storefront redesign added multi-stop box-shadow elevation and a parallax hero banner to an 80-card catalog grid. On an M3 MacBook Pro during design review, the scroll held a locked 60 FPS.

Four minutes after shipping to mobile web traffic, Android RUM telemetry collapsed. Scroll frame rates dropped to 11 FPS on Moto G and Pixel 6a devices, GPU process memory climbed past 380 MB on initial load, and 14% of mobile tabs crashed with RESULT_CODE_HUNG within 30 seconds of scrolling.

  • T+00:00: Deployed the catalog update to 100% of mobile web traffic.
  • T+04:00: Android RUM telemetry flags scroll collapsing to 11 FPS, with main-thread frame times exceeding 88 ms.
  • T+11:00: Mobile GPU process memory climbs past 380 MB on initial page load.
  • T+18:00: Chrome crash reporting records a 14% tab OOM-kill rate (RESULT_CODE_HUNG) within 30 seconds of catalog scroll.

Why will-change: transform Doubled the Crash Rate

In #perf-triage, the team assumed Blink was software-rasterizing cards because they lacked GPU acceleration. An engineer shipped will-change: transform; transform: translateZ(0); on .product-card to force hardware compositing.

It looked smooth on a 16 GB desktop GPU. On mid-range Android with shared system RAM, promoting all 80 cards upfront allocated 80 persistent backing textures in VRAM, dropping scroll FPS even further and doubling tab OOM kills.

Five Steps From Soft Shadows to GPU Tile Exhaustion

The MacBook Pro hid the problem with raw memory bandwidth. On mobile, five rendering layers compounded: expensive box-shadow rasterization on the CPU, blanket will-change exploding GPU tile memory, uncontained badge updates invalidating the whole grid, offscreen cards staying in the active layout tree, and a main-thread scroll listener mutating hero transform every frame.

Compare Blanket GPU Promotion Against Containment and Scroll Timelines

Dissecting the Frame Budget in the Layers Panel

01 → 02: Green Paint Flashing Across 80 Cards

Enabling Paint flashing in Chrome DevTools during a scroll revealed the entire grid pulsing green whenever a hover badge or countdown updated. Multi-stop box-shadow blurs combined with border-radius forced Paint & Rasterization to re-rasterize large CPU tiles on every invalidation.

Adding will-change: transform to every .product-card moved each card into its own GPU Compositor Layer. In the DevTools Layers tab, each 360x420 card at devicePixelRatio: 3 consumed ~1.8 MB of uncompressed RGBA texture memory; 80 promoted cards ate 144 MB of tile memory before the user even touched the screen.

02 → 03: One Card Badge Invalidates the Entire Grid

Profiling a single badge timer tick showed Layout and Paint recalculating all 80 cards even though only one card's text changed. Without CSS Containment (contain: layout paint), Blink had to assume a geometry change inside card #1 could affect sibling grid tracks down to card #80.

03 → 04: Paying Layout Cost for Cards 4,000 Pixels Below the Fold

Even with containment, initial load and scroll frames still styled and laid out all 80 cards. Adding Content Visibility (content-visibility: auto) with contain-intrinsic-size: 360px 420px lets the browser skip layout and paint work for offscreen cards until they approach the viewport, cutting initial layout work by 78%.

04 → 05: Moving the Parallax Hero Off the Main Thread

The final culprit in the Performance flamegraph was a window.addEventListener('scroll', ...) handler setting hero.style.transform on every frame. Replacing that JS listener with Scroll-Driven Animations (animation-timeline: scroll()) binds the parallax transform directly to the compositor thread, holding 60 FPS even during main-thread JS bursts.

Containing Cards and Moving Scroll to the Compositor 

.product-card {
  contain: layout style paint;
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 360px 420px;
}

.hero-banner {
  animation: hero-parallax linear both;
  animation-timeline: scroll(root block);
}

Architectural Invariants:

  • Never apply will-change: transform to list items: Only promote active, bounded animations; remove will-change when idle.
  • Contain and skip offscreen subtrees: Pair contain: layout style paint with content-visibility: auto and contain-intrinsic-size on large grids.
  • Bind scroll effects to scroll() timelines: Replace main-thread scroll listeners with compositor-driven CSS Scroll-Driven Animations.

Golden Rule: Desktop GPUs hide layer explosion; never promote an entire card list to VRAM when contain and content-visibility: auto keep offscreen work at zero.

title: A Viewing Window, Not A Key To The Cage
description:
An admin screen may look at any table of any service - through glass. Read only, a timeout, caps, a log line, one at a time, and the glass is shut until someone opens it on purpose.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

The guarded query is built into the shared library and is off by default. No service imports it directly yet; everything below describes what is built, not how much it is used.

This is part 2 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

Ember, the small dragon of our zoo, guards the gold. That is what dragons do, and in our zoo the gold is the data: every resident keeps its own pile in its own cave, and nobody else is supposed to touch it.

Nora, the keeper, wants to count the coins. Not take them - just count. "Give me a key, I'll just count." Ember's answer is the answer every database owner has given: "Nobody touches my gold." And Ember is right. A key does not know the difference between counting and carrying.

So the zoo puts a viewing window into the cave wall. Pickle presses a nose to the glass and is delighted: "I can see every coin!" Biscuit tries to pass a bone through - "can I feed it?" - and learns what glass is for: look only. And when too many faces press against the window at once, Pip does the one thing that keeps the dragon calm: "Full. No waiting. Come back later."

That is the whole part in four panels. The admin screen can look at any table - through the service, through glass, one look at a time.

The key nobody should have

Admin screens want data. A list of records, a count, a join to check one thing on a Tuesday. The easy answer is a database address per service in the admin's configuration, and from then on the admin holds a key to every cave. A key does not know the difference between a SELECT and an UPDATE, does not know when to stop, and leaves no trace in the service that owns the data.

The library's answer is a guarded query that lives inside the service. The admin screen asks the service; the service runs the query on its own terms; the database address never leaves the resident. The line in the library's description says it plainly: the admin gets the schema and any selection through the service, not through a direct database address.

Six panes of glass

Every query that comes through the window passes the same guards.

Guard What it stops
a read-only transaction any write, however it is spelled
a statement timeout a query that would run all afternoon
a row cap a result that would not fit on any screen
a byte cap a few rows with huge values
its own small pool, or a replica the window starving the service's real work
one log line per query a look nobody can account for later

The settings, as a form - the names here are illustrative, the shape is what the library takes:

data_query:
  enabled: false              # off by default
  concurrency: <n>            # over it: busy at once, no waiting
  pool: <small own pool | replica>
  statement_timeout: <duration>
  max_rows: <n>
  max_bytes: <n>
# every query: a read-only transaction, the timeout, one log line

Two choices in that form matter more than the rest.

Off by default. The window is a wall until someone turns it into glass on purpose, for one service, with a switch in that service's environment. A new service does not get an open window because it was born.

Busy means no. When the number of running queries reaches the concurrency limit, the next one is refused at once - not queued, not made to wait. A queue in front of a database is a queue that grows exactly when the database is slow. Refusing at once keeps the cost of a look bounded and moves the waiting to the person who can decide whether to come back.

A key versus a window

The difference is not only safety. A key spreads knowledge of a service's database into every tool that holds it: the address, the credentials, the shape of the tables. A window keeps that knowledge in the service, which already describes its own tables through the sign from the previous part. The admin screen asks "what do you have" and "show me" - and both answers come from the resident.

Who looks through it yet

The window is new. The package is small - around forty files - and it reached the library late in October. No service imports it directly, and on every server it is off unless switched on. That is the state I can describe: the glass is installed, the switch is in the off position, and the first visitor is the admin screen it was built for.

What went wrong

The thing this part answers is a habit rather than an incident: when a screen needs data from a service, the fastest path is always a direct database address, and every such shortcut is a key handed out for good. The window exists because "just give the admin read access" kept being the easiest answer, and easy answers are the ones that stay.

The second lesson is in the busy refusal. A first instinct for "too many queries" is a queue. A queue in front of a struggling database makes everything slower at the worst moment, so the library refuses instead and lets the caller decide.

What I do not claim

  • Not that any service runs with the window open today. It is off by default and imported by none directly.
  • Not that the guards are measured under load. They are built.
  • Not that read only is enough on its own. It is one guard of six, on purpose.
  • Not the exact names of the settings. The form above shows the shape.

What of this is method

  • Look through the owner, not around it. The service holds its database address; tools ask the service.
  • Every look is bounded and written down. Read only, a timeout, caps, a log line.
  • Shut until opened, busy means no. Off by default; over the limit, refuse at once.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 2. Next: The Error That Escaped Without A Collar.

If your admin tools hold database addresses, how many caves do they have keys to? If you route queries through the service, what guards did you put on the glass? If you queue queries when busy, what happens to the queue when the database is slow? Who in your zoo has a key that should be a window?
