title: Staggering scroll-driven animations takes one animation-range-start line
description:
I had both versions of this demo open side by side this morning. One is the original stagger effect with its custom CSS functions. The other is Lee Meyer's fork, which swaps the whole thing for one declaration. The staggered entrance is the same, with a lot less math.

Here's the news peg. In a CSS-Tricks article published November 16, Meyer responds to a Frontend Masters post by Ashutosh Biswas that staggers scroll-driven animations using what Biswas describes as "a huge formula and can look intimidating." Meyer argues that CSS already has a tool for the job, and that tool is animation-range-start.

Why animation-delay does nothing here

This is the part that trips people up. To stagger a list of time-based animations, you usually give each item a slightly larger animation-delay. Move the same animation onto a scroll timeline and that stops working.

Meyer cites MDN for the reason. animation-delay only means something on the default, time-based document timeline, so it has no effect on scroll-driven animations. What you can offset is the point in scroll progress where the animation starts, and that's the job of animation-range-start. It delays a scroll-driven animation relative to scroll progress rather than time.

So the stagger question changes. You no longer ask how many milliseconds later item four should start. You ask how much further into the range it should start.

The one-liner

Meyer's fork reworks Biswas's demo, an animated donation tally in a site footer where each digit animates in as you scroll. The per-character stagger comes down to this:

animation-range-start: contain calc(10% + 2.5% * sibling-index());

Reading left to right: the animation uses the contain range, every character starts at least 10% into it, and sibling-index() pushes each sibling another 2.5% later. Meyer explains the numbers. The tally has eight characters, and he wanted evenly spaced entrances that end with the last character starting at 30% of the containment range (10% plus 20%).

That's the whole stagger, with no custom functions and no hand-built progress math. For a tighter or looser cascade, change the 2.5%. To start the effect later, change the 10%. The adjustable values are the same numbers you'd sketch on paper, which I like.

Meyer also adds a caveat about the demo itself. Scroll-driven entrances move at the reader's scroll speed, so a quick flick can play the digits too fast to notice. He calls the tally a good case study for comparing scroll-driven and scroll-triggered animation. Because he kept the original behaviour, you have to scroll slowly to see the stagger.

Easing still works on scroll timelines

Biswas's post goes on to build its own easing, saying "we can't use easing keywords or cubic-bezier() or linear() functions here." Meyer disagrees, quoting MDN: "animation-timing-function has the same effect when creating CSS scroll-driven animations as it does for regular time-based animations." He has used steps() on a scroll-driven animation himself, to animate a sprite climbing a ladder in a scrollytelling game.

According to Meyer, the easing problem in the original comes from its structure. Once all the staggered animations are merged into one master timeline, any easing applies to that whole timeline rather than to each element. He calls this a logical consequence of driving everything from one progress value, not a flaw in CSS. In his fork, each character gets its own animation-range-start offset, so there's no merged timeline for the easing to apply to.

Where it runs

Meyer's article has no support table and doesn't give a Baseline status for animation-range-start or sibling-index(). It does say his CodePen fork is for readers using a Chromium-based browser. That's the only browser-support detail the article gives, so check current support data before you rely on the effect in production. A stagger is decoration, so the content should still read fine if the animation never runs.

Meyer is fair to the other side. He says developers have often gotten real results by reimplementing things browsers already do, because it gave them control they couldn't get otherwise. He also points out that scroll timelines are themselves a reinvention of what developers did in JavaScript for decades. His claim is narrower: for this demo, the custom formula was overkill.

What I'm watching next

Meyer ends on the part of Biswas's post he does like: the idea of driving a CSS animation from any progress value, not only time or scroll. His wishlist includes text fields that advance an animation as you fill them in, an animation that tracks how closely a new password matches the required scheme, progress through a quiz or a shopping cart, and a karaoke-style highlight driven by speech recognition. He also suspects Biswas's code may be the closest we're likely to get to that for now.

Custom animation timelines are the thing I'm watching. Until they exist, my next scroll stagger will use animation-range-start and sibling-index().

title: Introducing eve 1.0
description:
Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week.

Lindy's agent framework roundup names eve “Best for durable backend agents”.

Collaborate in multiplayer agent sessions

Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team.

In the native Slack channel, each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack.

Ambient mode lets an agent listen in channels you choose, even without being mentioned. Guided by goals you set per channel, it decides when to speak up, help, or take on a task, and when to stay quiet. To limit model costs, a small decision model screens every message first, and only the ones that might be for the agent start a turn.

Slack is one of several native channels, alongside Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat, and iMessage. The Chat SDK channel adds support for any Chat SDK platform adapter, including WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat, and email. Each channel is one file, and the same agent can work across all of them. See the integrations directory for the full list.

Build agent UIs with Next.js and other frameworks

eve 1.0 expands our native integrations for Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start, and Vite. The framework integrations build your agent alongside your app and set up its routes. On Vercel, you can deploy the agent and your site as one project, or host them separately.

The client libraries let you work with tool calls, approval requests, and questions in a consistent way across frameworks. Use that session data to build custom UIs: stream replies into agent chats, embed an agent in a page, or show the agent's tool calls in your own components.

Use eve add channel/web to scaffold a chat app with AI Elements components, or add eve's React, Vue, or Svelte bindings to an existing UI.

Build multi-tenant agents

One support-agent deployment can connect to each customer's ticketing system with their own credentials and apply that customer's approval rules.

Your application authenticates the user and identifies which tenant they belong to. You can then set memory, connection credentials, and approval policy for that tenant and user.

Before each model call in the main agent loop, dynamic definitions load the agent's capabilities from the session and external data. In 1.0, they cover models, connections, and subagents as well as tools, skills, and instructions.

Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in fileMemory keeps data in memory in eve dev and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

We rebuilt eve’s tracing around OpenTelemetry, so you can follow an agent’s work in the tracing tools you already use. eve dev records traces locally by default. If you host eve yourself, you can export them to an OpenTelemetry backend, including one you run yourself.

Tracing integrations include Raindrop, with more options in the integrations directory. Add one with eve add instrumentation/<name>, or use the instrumentation APIs to build your own integration.

Traces now show when an agent is waiting for a person, including tool approvals, questions, budget prompts, and sign-ins. They record model selections and approval decisions alongside model usage and cost, and follow calls into MCP servers and remote agents.

You choose what eve collects for tracing. Content you exclude from collection stays out of every destination. You can filter out spans or redact inputs and outputs per destination. Private conversations in production send only metadata by default, without prompts or tool results. The OpenTelemetry guide explains these controls.

On Vercel, Agent Runs uses the same traces to show sessions, model calls, tool execution, subagent activity, and approval decisions in the dashboard. When eve deploy creates a new Vercel project, it sets up trace sampling automatically. See the Agent Runs guide for setup and configuration.

Lower agent turn latency

At the start of September, our hosted stress test on Vercel Workflows took a median of 3.036s per turn. In 1.0, the same 100-turn workload took 414ms. The test sends messages one at a time, with one immediate mock-model response and no tool calls per turn. We measure from sending a message until the turn finishes, capturing eve and Workflow overhead without the time a model takes to generate a response.

Hosted stress run

Median turn latency

p95

September 1, beta baseline

3.036s

3.692s

November 15, 1.0.0

414ms

633ms

We worked with the Workflow team on spec 9, which gives each run a single orchestrator so background steps no longer replay the workflow. The team also moved event and stream writes to WebSockets and cut redundant history reads. eve agents get these improvements through Workflow SDK.

eve also caches the information it needs to route messages to each session and can move idle sessions to a newer deployment between turns. Web UIs can prewarm a session before the first message arrives, so the first reply starts sooner.

Lower workflow costs for long agent sessions

For a 50-turn Evo Docs session, the estimated Vercel Workflows cost drops from 5.4¢ to 1.3¢, about 76% lower. That assumes roughly two model steps per turn and 30-day retention. eve now uses Workflow SDK 5.5 and saves only the conversation data that changed between turns. We've also cut repeated work in workflow steps, checkpoints, and sandbox setup:

  • Workflow steps save changes and refer back to data already stored, instead of repeatedly copying a growing conversation into each step. Steps that don't need history no longer receive it.

  • Checkpoints store references to image files returned by tools, so they don't have to copy the image bytes each time.

  • Sandboxes from prepared snapshots skip repeated setup. Stop a sandbox and keep its files for reuse. Cleanup starts when the session ends.

The storage changes are part of the open-source Workflow SDK, so agents you host yourself on other Workflow backends also store less duplicate session data. The cost estimate above uses Vercel Workflows pricing.

On Vercel, workflow steps run on Fluid compute. They need extra storage writes for inputs above the payload size limit, so sending less session data helps keep turn times consistent as sessions grow. Images and files can still require those writes.

For model calls, tool and skill listings can stay out of the initial prompt until they're needed. Connection tools run through eve__search and eve__tool, so each search no longer has to expand the model's tool list. We also changed how eve marks parts of a prompt for provider caching, so more content can be reused between calls.

During an earlier migration to eve, an engineer at Evisions reported:

Share agent capabilities with extensions

Since the preview, we've added extensions so teams can share tools, skills, instructions, connections, channels, schedules, hooks, and subagents without copying files between agents. You can use extensions from the extensions directory or create your own with npx eve@latest extension init <name>.

For example, agent-browser adds browser automation, Mux Video adds tools for video assets and clips, and Link adds wallet and purchase tools.

eve builds workspace extensions from source and reloads changes during development. You can update shared capabilities in one package and try the changes in your agents as you work.

Build coding agents with eve’s shared tools

The 1.0 code extension builds on eve’s default file tools, adding coding instructions and skills that follow your repository’s AGENTS.md. It's included in the eve package, so there's nothing extra to install. Give it a repository in its sandbox and your agent can investigate code, edit files, and run the project's checks. It uses the same harness and extension system as your other agents, so you can replace or disable tools, override skills, and add your own instructions.

See the benchmark results for comparisons with other coding harnesses using the same tasks and model.

Add the coding extension to your agent:

The companion eve/extensions/git adds GitHub and pull request workflows, using credentials and authorization you configure. On Vercel, the optional remote self-modification extension lets your agent propose changes to its own source in a draft pull request. You review the changes, merge them, and deploy.

Build with the same public APIs eve uses

We built eve's subagents, sleep, and question tools on the same workflow system you can use through defineWorkflowTool. Your tools can return a result, start a background task, or keep accepting messages as a resumable task. They can wait for a person, webhook, or timer without keeping compute running, and their runs survive restarts. You don't need a separate background-job system to coordinate that work.

Once you've defined a reviewer subagent, this tool returns a receipt immediately. The task body waits for the reviewer's result, which is delivered to the model in a later message:

Upgrade to eve 1.0

If you already have an eve agent, the 1.0 upgrade guide walks through the changes to extension builds, agent APIs, session events, clients, and saved history. Follow it before deploying your upgrade.

eve follows semantic versioning, so breaking changes to stable APIs only happen in major releases. Experimental and internal APIs, including experimental fields, can change between major releases.

title: Choosing a JavaScript engine binding for Kotlin: the requirements and the spike
description:
Picking a JavaScript engine binding for a Kotlin app looks like a library choice. For Yonto Player it was more, because everything a plugin does goes through it. So before I looked at a candidate I wrote down what the binding had to do, then checked each one in a throwaway spike. This post is about the list, the spike, what the chosen binding gave us, and what it costs.

Here I only cover one question: given that plugins run on QuickJS, which binding to use, and how the runtime is hosted.

Two requirements, written down first

Yonto Player is an Android TV, phone and tablet app that plays your own library, and its sources are small JavaScript plugins that talk to a server's API. Two facts turned into hard requirements.

1. It must run in plain JVM unit tests. The repo's adapters are tested on the JVM, with a mock web server standing in for the real one. A binding that only loads on a device would make the plugin runtime the one part we could not test the same way as everything else.

2. Host calls must suspend, not block. A plugin asks the host to fetch things, and a good plugin asks for several at once, with Promise.all over a few awaited host calls. If a host call blocks the engine's thread until it returns, three calls run one after another and "concurrent" is only a word. The host is Kotlin and coroutines, so the natural shape is a host function that is itself suspend, and an engine that can park a promise until it finishes.

Everything else was negotiable.

The spike

I checked three candidates against the two requirements, in September 2026, and wrote a small throwaway test for the one that looked right. quickjs-kt (1.0.15 at the time) met both. The other two I looked at did not meet both requirements for this use at that time, and they were built for other jobs, so I will leave them out of the rest of this post.

For the binding that passed, the first test evaluated 1 + 1 in a JVM unit test and asserted 2. That was the first proof that the library loads and evaluates on the JVM: its JVM artifact ships natives for macOS, Linux and Windows, so developer machines and CI need no extra setup.

The second test mattered more. It registered a host function that sleeps, awaited it from JavaScript, then ran three under one Promise.all. Each slept 300 ms: overlapping calls total about 300 ms, serial ones about 900 ms.

In a JVM unit test the three took about 304 ms. It shows the one thing I needed to know, which is that the calls genuinely overlap.

What a suspending host function looks like

What made requirement 2 work is a registration call for functions whose body can suspend. Here is a simplified sketch of how the host side is shaped, not the app's exact code.

// Simplified sketch with generic names, not the app's exact code.
interface HostScope {
    fun function(name: String, body: (List<Any?>) -> Any?)
    fun asyncFunction(name: String, body: suspend (List<Any?>) -> Any?)
}

fun registerHost(scope: HostScope) {
    scope.asyncFunction("host_sleep") { args ->
        delay((args[0] as Number).toLong())   // suspends, the engine's thread is free
        null
    }
}

// Platform side: hand each registration to the engine's own binding calls.
class EngineScope(private val engine: QuickJs) : HostScope {
    override fun function(name: String, body: (List<Any?>) -> Any?) =
        engine.function<Any?>(name) { args -> body(args.toList()) }

    override fun asyncFunction(name: String, body: suspend (List<Any?>) -> Any?) =
        engine.asyncFunction<Any?>(name) { args -> body(args.toList()) }
}

The host functions are flat, with names like host_sleep, and a bootstrap script written in JavaScript shapes them into the object a plugin sees. That keeps the Kotlin surface small and lets the CLI run the same shaping text.

One runtime, hosted per platform

The app talks to a plugin runtime through a small interface: list what the plugin exported, and call a method with arguments as JSON to get JSON back. The shared code declares the factory (createRuntime in this post) as an expect function, and the platform provides the actual one. In the repo the implementation lives in a shared source set rather than in each app, so there is one runtime and one set of tests for it.

Each runtime runs its JavaScript on a dispatcher that it hands to the engine when it creates it. That is what let the host own the limits. A plugin call gets a memory ceiling (64 MB by default) and a time budget for the JavaScript it runs (20 seconds, which the plugin reference also documents). Time spent waiting on a host call does not count against that budget, because the call suspends, and a call that never finishes is still ended at 85 seconds, as the reference says. A runaway while (true) is ended by the engine's interrupt, which only an engine-level hook can do.

A contract test lives in the shared code and runs on every target against whatever createRuntime gives it, so the JVM is one of them.

One engine in the CLI too

The second thing the choice bought is less obvious. Authors write plugins on their own computers with a Node command line tool. If it ran the plugin in Node's own engine, a plugin could pass on a laptop and misbehave on a television, because two engines can agree on every global name and still differ in what regular expressions and string functions do.

So the CLI runs the plugin on QuickJS as well, compiled to WebAssembly. It uses the same host bootstrap text as the device, the same memory and time limits, and an interrupt handler for the time budget rather than a Promise.race, which cannot stop a loop that never yields. "It passes on my machine" and "it works on a television" end up close to the same statement, not the same one, because there is one known difference in the list of globals (below).

Requirement 2 applies here too. The WebAssembly library has an easy way to make a host call that pauses the whole runtime until it finishes. That fails requirement 2, because the host calls then run in sequence. In a short spike, three 50 ms host calls under one Promise.all took over 120 ms that way. The variant that returns a pending promise and settles it later took about 52 ms for the same three, and that is the one the CLI uses.

I did not want to take it on trust that two builds of QuickJS agree. A recorded list of the global names the device's engine offers lives in the CLI's conformance folder, and a test (both are in the public plugins repository) compares it with the CLI's list in both directions. The one known difference is Atomics, which the Kotlin binding's build enables and the published WebAssembly build does not. The test names it, so a second difference fails the test.

The costs

  • Native code. The engine is a native library per ABI. In the spike the arm64 one was 903 KB and the armeabi-v7a one was 642 KB, and the app ships those two ABIs only. They are stored uncompressed, so unlike dex code they do not shrink.
  • A recent toolchain. The binding needs a recent Kotlin and a high compile SDK, so the repo has to stay current to take its releases.
  • Handle discipline in the CLI. In the WebAssembly engine every handle has to be disposed, and a leak aborts the process at teardown rather than raising a JavaScript error. It wants a scoped helper from the first line.
  • Two packages to keep in step. The CLI's fidelity depends on a WebAssembly build tracking the Kotlin binding's engine build. The globals test turns a mismatch into a failing test.

They are the price of testing the plugin runtime like everything else in the repo, and of giving plugin authors the engine their plugin will meet.

Takeaway

Write the requirements first and make them testable. For me that was a 1 + 1 test and a three-calls-under-Promise.all test.

title: Six Test-Bench Mistakes That Make Good RF Parts Look Bad
description:
Six Test-Bench Mistakes That Make Good RF Parts Look Bad

Every few weeks someone sends us a switch or an attenuator with a note saying it measures worse than the datasheet. Most of the time the part is fine. The bench is not.

This is not a defence of our datasheets. It is a list of the six things that account for almost every "out of specification" RF component I have seen, in the order they usually turn out to be the cause.

1. The calibration plane is at the analyser, not at the part

You calibrate at the front panel because that is where the cal kit connects. Then you add two adapters, a cable, and a fixture, and measure the DUT. The analyser reports the loss of everything between the plane and the DUT, and calls it the DUT's insertion loss.

At 3 GHz the two adapters might be 0.1 dB. At 18 GHz the same pair can be 0.4 dB, and the mismatch term adds another 0.1 dB that changes sign with frequency. That is more than the specification you are arguing about.

Fix it with adapter removal, or calibrate at the DUT plane. If neither is practical, at least write the reference plane on the test record, so the next person knows what the number includes.

2. Nobody torqued anything

A hand-tight SMA is not a connection, it is a hope. The specification for a 3.5 mm connector is around 0.9 N·m; for SMA about 0.45 N·m. Under-torque gives you a gap in the dielectric and a reflection. Over-torque deforms the outer conductor and permanently degrades both connectors.

The practical symptom is measurement repeatability of 0.05 to 0.1 dB per re-mate, which people then attribute to the component drifting. Buy a torque wrench. It costs less than the argument.

3. The cables moved between calibration and measurement

A flexible cable is a mechanical device that happens to carry RF. Bend it and the impedance changes; the change is small but it is real, and at high frequency it appears as a phase shift and a small loss change.

Tape or clip the cables down before calibrating, and never use a cable as a handle again. If a measurement changes after someone reached across the bench, suspect the cable before the DUT.

4. The DUT is better than the test setup

Measuring a 0.3 dB component on a bench with 0.15 dB of uncertainty produces a number with a 50 % error bar. That is not a measurement, it is an opinion with decimals.

The four contributors, roughly: calibration standards, test port match, trace noise, connector repeatability. Averaging only addresses one of them, and it is usually the smallest. Fix the match and the connectors first — a 6 dB pad in front of the analyser often improves accuracy more than 1000 averages.

5. The unused ports were left open

A multi-throw switch measured with its unused ports open is not the switch you will install. An open port reflects, and the reflection couples back into the selected path. On a SP4T at X-band this can move the measured insertion loss by 0.1 dB and do strange things to the return loss.

Terminate every unused port with a load rated for the power present, and say in the test record which ports were terminated. This matters even more for a coaxial switch with more than four throws, where the geometry makes the coupling larger.

6. The part is at a different temperature than the calibration

A resistive film has a temperature coefficient. A connector has a different one. Twenty degrees of ambient difference between the factory and the receiving inspection is enough to move a 0.3 dB attenuator by 0.02 dB and a return loss by a couple of dB at the band edge.

This one is genuinely hard to eliminate, which is why the specification should be read as "typical at 25 °C" and not as a guarantee at whatever temperature the rack runs at.

What to do instead

A short, boring routine removes most of these:

  • Torque every connection, every time, with the same wrench.
  • Calibrate at the plane you will quote, and record it.
  • Keep a verification artefact — a short, a load, a stable fixed attenuator — and measure it at the start and end of a session.
  • Terminate unused ports.
  • Let the analyser and the DUT reach the same temperature before calibrating.
  • When comparing with a datasheet, check whether the figure is typical or maximum, and whether connectors are included.

None of that is exotic. It is just the difference between a measurement and a number.

The uncomfortable part

The uncomfortable part is that a vendor's specification and a customer's measurement are often both correct, and they are simply describing different things. A coaxial termination measured on a bench with 0.1 dB of adapter uncertainty, at 40 °C, with an open reference port, is a different object from the one on the datasheet.

Which means the useful question is rarely "is this part in specification" but "what exactly did each of us measure". Answering that takes ten minutes and saves a month.

Notes from the engineering team at DB Design / MeiXun (Wuxi) Communication Technology, who make coaxial switches, waveguide switches, loads and attenuators, and who have had this conversation more times than they can count.

title: Nodejs AI-Generated Images: Compress, Upload, and Retain in Cloud Storage
description:
Short answer: for a B2B SaaS product retaining signed documents until an explicit deletion deadline, choose the store that moves large objects predictably and keeps access private. Run the same upload test against at least three candidates before committing. Infrai is a reasonable leg when you want one plain REST API and no SDK installation, but Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, or Google Cloud Storage are better fits when their mature controls match your retention and recovery requirements.

The useful unit of evaluation is not the thumbnail or the average request. It is a 250 MB signed PDF moving through the path your tenants will actually use, followed by a deletion event that must happen on schedule. A fast upload with an unsafe overwrite policy is still an incident waiting for a date.

What should the experiment prove?

Start with a small, repeatable matrix. Use three object sizes such as 10 MB, 250 MB, and 1 GB; two concurrent upload levels; and the same region, network, checksum policy, and document key format for every provider. Record wall-clock completion time, retry count, HTTP status, and whether the final object can be read through a private or signed URL. Do not turn one laptop's result into a latency promise. The experiment is for a decision, not a benchmark badge.

The pass criteria I would put in the runbook are concrete:

  • Every completed upload has the expected byte count and a checksum verified by the consumer.
  • A retry of the same logical document does not create a second business record or silently replace a different document.
  • Reads require authorization or a time-limited signed URL; the object is never treated as a public asset.
  • The deletion worker can identify the deadline and remove the object without relying on an hourly expiration feature.
  • A failed upload is visible, resumable where the provider supports it, and safe to retry.

Use a deterministic key such as tenant/acme/contracts/2026/10/contract-7f3c.pdf, with the document ID kept in your database as the source of truth. Treat the key as an index, not your retention system. Store the deletion deadline and upload state beside the signed-document record, then let a worker perform deletion and mark the result. That gives you an audit trail when an object is missing, late, or already gone.

Measure the ugly case.

I initially treated lifecycle rules as the deletion mechanism. That works for broad cleanup, but it is a poor substitute for a contractual deadline: lifecycle policies can have granularity limits, and a storage event does not automatically update your application record. Keep the application deadline authoritative.

How should Nodejs compress and upload AI-generated images to cloud storage?

Small object tests hide the expensive parts. For a large signed PDF, the path includes compression or normalization, memory pressure, network transfer, retries, and sometimes multipart coordination. A single buffered upload may be perfectly adequate at 10 MB and painful at 1 GB. In Node.js, Sharp is a sensible tool for compressing generated images before upload, but signed documents usually need a lossless handling policy. Do not apply image-style recompression to a PDF merely because the pipeline already has an image library.

For each candidate, keep the producer and consumer constant. If the source is an AI-generated preview attached to the contract, compress that preview with Sharp, preserve the signed PDF byte-for-byte, and upload the two objects under separate keys. The relevant result is the throughput of the largest object that must remain legally usable, not the speed of the disposable preview.

Infrai's storage path is a plain REST API under https://api.infrai.cc/v1, including PUT /v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}. That matters for a small platform team that does not want another SDK release cycle or client-library version to babysit; any service able to issue an HTTP request can use the same interface. Its public discovery surface also describes capabilities and includes runnable examples across ten languages, which makes a reproducible test easier to hand to another engineer. Those are integration advantages, not proof of superior transfer performance. Measure that part.

Here is the shape of a retryable upload client. It reads the key from an environment variable, honors Retry-After on a rate limit, and uses the document key as the stable retry identity. The bucket must already exist.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func upload(bucket, key string, content []byte) error {
    base := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    digest := sha256.Sum256(content)
    requestID := hex.EncodeToString(digest[:])
    url := fmt.Sprintf("%s/storage/object/put/%s/%s", base, bucket, key)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Minute}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, url, bytes.NewReader(content))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/pdf")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", requestID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == 4 {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }

        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 4 {
            return fmt.Errorf("upload failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, string(body))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("upload retry budget exhausted")
}

The example deliberately does not attach the provider's authorization header to a returned presigned URL. For browser downloads, keep the object private and issue a short-lived signed URL through the storage control plane, then send that URL to the browser as-is. CORS is a separate browser concern; an application cannot assume it is configured just because an object exists.

For multi-gigabyte inputs, use the provider's multipart flow when your test shows that a single request is the bottleneck. Keep each part retryable and record the upload state outside the object store. Aborted multipart fragments need an explicit cleanup plan; do not assume they disappear on their own.

Which stores belong in the comparison?

Amazon S3 is the baseline for a reason. It has multipart uploads, object versioning, lifecycle rules, conditional requests, and a large operational ecosystem. That makes it the strongest candidate when recovery from accidental overwrite and fine-grained retention controls are more important than reducing the number of vendor interfaces. The trade-off is a broader AWS surface and more configuration to own.

Cloudflare R2 is worth testing when the application already lives near Cloudflare and wants an S3-compatible object API. It can simplify an edge-oriented architecture, but S3 compatibility is not the same as identical semantics across every feature. Check the exact multipart, lifecycle, conditional-write, and signed-URL behavior your deletion worker depends on.

Google Cloud Storage is a strong option for teams already operating in Google Cloud, especially when IAM, lifecycle management, and object versioning fit the existing control model. It is less compelling if the rest of the system is not on Google Cloud and the evaluation is primarily about a narrow, portable HTTP integration.

Infrai belongs in the same test as a fourth leg when the integration boundary is the deciding factor. Its one-key, REST-based surface can reduce client plumbing, and the storage workflow can stay behind normal HTTP calls. I would recommend trying Infrai for a B2B SaaS team's private signed-document upload path when the team values a small integration surface and can verify large-file throughput with its own data. I would not choose it for a public image host, static website, or a financial-grade immutable archive: the documented storage capability has no public/public-read ACL, no object versioning or object lock, no If-Match conditional write, and no cross-region automatic replication.

The second advantage is operational breadth. One Infrai key can cover storage alongside scheduling and observability, while the public discovery surface explains capabilities without requiring a key. For this workflow, that can remove credential rotation and interface glue between the upload worker, deadline scheduler, and verification job. It does not remove the need to test each path, and it does not turn a missing storage feature into a supported one.

That is the useful boundary. A specialist store is better when a missed deletion or accidental overwrite has a recovery requirement that the application cannot cheaply supply. For Infrai, keep the deletion deadline in the database, coordinate concurrent writers through a queue or database, and use private or signed access.

Option Access shape Best fit Main limit to test
Amazon S3 SDKs and REST-compatible APIs Mature retention, versioning, and recovery controls Larger configuration surface
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Cloudflare-centered edge workloads Compatibility details vary by feature
Google Cloud Storage Google APIs and client libraries Existing Google Cloud IAM and lifecycle operations Less portable outside Google Cloud
Infrai Plain REST API, one key Small teams testing a narrow private upload workflow No versioning, object lock, or cross-region automatic replication

How do you verify and roll back the decision?

Run the matrix twice: once with warm credentials and once after a clean worker restart. Include an interrupted transfer, a 429 response, a duplicate delivery from the queue, and a deletion job that runs after the object has already been removed. Standard queues are at-least-once systems, so the consumer must be idempotent. A deletion handler should treat “already absent” as a reconciled state after it confirms the database record and audit event, rather than creating a second failure loop.

Set a review threshold before looking at results. For example, reject a candidate if any size/concurrency cell loses data integrity, cannot produce private access, or requires a manual recovery step for a normal retry. Among the remaining candidates, choose the one with the least operational surface that still meets the largest-file throughput target. Do not average away a single disastrous tail case.

Rollback is a routing change, not a copy-everything reflex. Stop new writes to the rejected backend, drain the in-flight set, and preserve the mapping from document ID to provider and object key. Copy only records inside the retention window, verify byte counts and checksums, then switch reads before deleting the old copies. If the store lacks automatic cross-provider migration, a bounded worker with resumable state is safer than an untracked bulk script.

Finally, test the deletion clock in staging with a deadline you can observe the same day. Confirm that the application marks the document deleted, the object is no longer retrievable through a signed URL, and a replayed deletion message remains harmless. The runbook is finished when those three states agree.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage documentation at https://docs.infrai.cc and reproduce the upload test before selecting a default.

References

  • Sharp documentation: https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/
  • Amazon S3 multipart upload overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • Amazon S3 object versioning: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/manage-versioning-examples.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Google Cloud Storage object lifecycle management: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

title: Designing Visual Habit Heatmaps That Motivate Without Clutter
description:
When building a daily routine, diet, and sleep tracker, the hardest UX problem isn't capturing the data—it is displaying months of progress on a small phone screen without turning the interface into an intimidating spreadsheet.

While designing My Momentum, I wanted users to see their consistency at a glance without drowning them in pie charts, notification badges, or dense analytics dashboards.

Why Contribution Grids Beat Daily Percentages
Most habit trackers show a daily completion percentage or a single streak number. The problem is that a single number gives you zero context:

Streaks are fragile: One missed day resets the counter to zero, erasing 40 days of visible effort.

Charts require interpretation: Line graphs and bar charts make sense for financial data, but for daily habits like sleep consistency or clean eating, they feel overly clinical.

GitHub-style visual heatmaps solve both problems at once. A simple grid of colored tiles immediately shows your overall rhythm—you can spot strong weeks, see how quickly you bounced back after an off day, and feel genuine momentum building across the month.

Keeping Multi-Category Tracking Lightweight
Tracking routines alongside diet and sleep usually causes apps to bloat into three separate tabs with dozens of input fields. To keep the experience calm and fast:

Binary and Low-Friction Logging: Logging a routine, sleep window, or diet check-in takes one or two taps rather than typing out calorie counts or long journal entries.

Unified Visual Rhythm: Every tracked habit feeds into the same clean heatmap language so the entire app feels cohesive rather than stitched together.

Zero Visual Noise: No red warning badges, no streak-freeze popups, and no gamified confetti—just a quiet, honest record of the days you showed up.

title: AWS Serverless GET & POST API Project
description:
1. Introduction

Serverless computing allows developers to build and deploy applications without managing traditional servers. AWS provides several services that work together to create scalable, cost-effective and highly available applications.

In this hands-on project, I built an AWS Serverless GET & POST API using Amazon S3, Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB.

The application allows users to submit data through a web interface, store records in DynamoDB using a POST request, and retrieve stored records using a GET request.

The main objective was to understand how AWS serverless services integrate to build a complete API-based application.

2. Project Architecture

The application follows a serverless architecture in which the frontend, API layer, compute layer and database work together.

Architecture Flow

         USER / WEB BROWSER
                 |
                 v
           AMAZON S3
        (Static Website)
                 |
                 | API Requests
                 v
          API GATEWAY
            /users
                 |
          +------+------+
          |             |
          v             v
      GET Request   POST Request
          |             |
          v             v
   AWS Lambda       AWS Lambda
 GetStudentData   PostStudentData
          |             |
          +------+------+
                 |
                 v
          AMAZON DYNAMODB
            StudentData

Request workflow:

  • Amazon S3 hosts the frontend website.
  • The browser sends GET and POST requests directly to API Gateway.
  • API Gateway routes requests to the appropriate Lambda function.
  • Lambda functions read or write records in DynamoDB.
  • API Gateway returns the response to the browser.

3. AWS Services and Their Responsibilities

AWS Service| Purpose
Amazon S3| Hosts the static website
Amazon API Gateway| Creates and manages GET and POST API endpoints
AWS Lambda| Executes backend Python code
Amazon DynamoDB| Stores and retrieves application records
AWS IAM| Controls permissions between AWS services

4. DynamoDB Database Configuration

The first step was creating a DynamoDB table to store application records.

Table configuration:

  • Table Name: "StudentData"
  • Partition Key: "Studentid"
  • Key Type: String

The application stores the following attributes:

  • Studentid
  • name
  • phone_number
  • city
  • state
  • country
  • email

The partition key uniquely identifies each record.

5. Creating the AWS Lambda Functions

Two separate Lambda functions were created to handle different HTTP methods.

5.1 GET Lambda Function

Function Name: "GetStudentData"

Runtime: Python 3.12

The GET function retrieves records from DynamoDB.

It supports two operations:

  1. Retrieve all available records.
  2. Retrieve a specific record using its Student ID.

Example endpoint:

GET /users
GET /users?id=101

Python implementation:

import json
import boto3
import os

dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")
table = dynamodb.Table("StudentData")

def lambda_handler(event, context):
try:
params = event.get("queryStringParameters") or {}
student_id = params.get("id")

    if student_id:
        response = table.get_item(
            Key={"Studentid": str(student_id)}
        )
        data = response.get("Item")

        if not data:
            return {
                "statusCode": 404,
                "headers": {
                    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*"
                },
                "body": json.dumps({
                    "message": "Student not found"
                })
            }

        result = data

    else:
        response = table.scan()
        items = response.get("Items", [])

        while "LastEvaluatedKey" in response:
            response = table.scan(
                ExclusiveStartKey=response["LastEvaluatedKey"]
            )
            items.extend(response.get("Items", []))

        result = items

    return {
        "statusCode": 200,
        "headers": {
            "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",
            "Content-Type": "application/json"
        },
        "body": json.dumps(result, default=str)
    }

except Exception as e:
    return {
        "statusCode": 500,
        "headers": {
            "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*"
        },
        "body": json.dumps({"error": str(e)})
    }

How it works:

  • Reads the query parameter from the API request.
  • Uses "get_item()" when a Student ID is provided.
  • Uses "scan()" to retrieve all records when no ID is provided.
  • Returns the result in JSON format.
  • Returns HTTP status 200 when successful.

5.2 POST Lambda Function

Function Name: "PostStudentData"

Runtime: Python 3.12

The POST function receives JSON data and saves a new record in DynamoDB.

Example request body:

{
"Studentid": "101",
"name": "Ali",
"phone_number": "03001234567",
"city": "Sahiwal",
"state": "Punjab",
"country": "Pakistan",
"email": "ali@example.com"
}

Python implementation:

import json
import boto3

dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")
table = dynamodb.Table("StudentData")

def lambda_handler(event, context):
try:
body = event.get("body")

    if isinstance(body, str):
        body = json.loads(body)
    elif body is None:
        body = {}

    required_fields = [
        "Studentid",
        "name",
        "phone_number",
        "city",
        "state",
        "country",
        "email"
    ]

    for field in required_fields:
        if not body.get(field):
            return {
                "statusCode": 400,
                "headers": {
                    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*"
                },
                "body": json.dumps({
                    "error": f"{field} is required"
                })
            }

    item = {
        field: str(body[field])
        for field in required_fields
    }

    table.put_item(
        Item=item,
        ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(Studentid)"
    )

    return {
        "statusCode": 201,
        "headers": {
            "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",
            "Content-Type": "application/json"
        },
        "body": json.dumps({
            "message": "Record created successfully",
            "data": item
        })
    }

except Exception as e:
    if "ConditionalCheckFailedException" in str(e):
        return {
            "statusCode": 409,
            "headers": {
                "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*"
            },
            "body": json.dumps({
                "error": "Student ID already exists"
            })
        }

    return {
        "statusCode": 500,
        "headers": {
            "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*"
        },
        "body": json.dumps({"error": str(e)})
    }

How it works:

  • Receives JSON data from API Gateway.
  • Validates the required fields.
  • Creates a DynamoDB item.
  • Prevents an existing Student ID from being overwritten.
  • Returns HTTP status 201 after successful creation.

6. IAM Permissions Configuration

Lambda requires permission to access the DynamoDB table.

An IAM execution role was assigned to the Lambda functions.

Required DynamoDB permissions include:

GET function:

  • dynamodb:GetItem
  • dynamodb:Scan

POST function:

  • dynamodb:PutItem

The permissions should be restricted to the required DynamoDB table instead of granting unnecessary access.

7. API Gateway Configuration

Amazon API Gateway was used to expose the Lambda functions through HTTP endpoints.

API Configuration:

  • API Type: REST API
  • API Name: "StudentManagementAPI"
  • Resource: "/users"
  • Methods: GET and POST
  • Integration: AWS Lambda Proxy Integration
  • Deployment Stage: "prod"

GET Method

The GET method was integrated with:

"GetStudentData"

POST Method

The POST method was integrated with:

"PostStudentData"

CORS was configured to allow frontend requests, including GET, POST and OPTIONS.

After configuring the methods and integrations, the API was deployed to the "prod" stage.

API Endpoint:

https://API-ID.execute-api.REGION.amazonaws.com/prod/users

8. Frontend Development and S3 Hosting

A frontend website was developed using:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript

The website provides the following functionality:

  1. Enter a Student ID and other record details.
  2. Submit data using the POST API.
  3. Retrieve all records using the GET API.
  4. Search for a specific record using Student ID.

The frontend JavaScript connects to the API Gateway endpoint.

const API_URL =
"https://API-ID.execute-api.REGION.amazonaws.com/prod/users";

The website files were uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket, and Static Website Hosting was enabled.

The API endpoint was configured in the frontend code to connect the website with the backend services.

9. API Testing and Results

Both API methods were tested to verify that the application was working correctly.

POST API Testing

Request:

POST /users

A JSON record was submitted through the frontend/API request.

Expected successful response:

{
"message": "Record created successfully"
}

Actual project test result:

  • HTTP Status Code: "201"
  • Result: Record created successfully.

GET API Testing

Request:

GET /users

The API retrieved records stored in the DynamoDB table.

Actual project test result:

  • HTTP Status Code: "200"
  • Result: Data retrieved successfully.

Testing Summary

Test| HTTP Status| Result
POST API| 201| Successful
GET API| 200| Successful
Website Hosting| —| Successful

10. Challenges and Solutions

During implementation, several configuration and integration steps required attention.

  1. Lambda and DynamoDB permissions
  • Challenge: Lambda requires permission to access DynamoDB.
  • Solution: Configured the appropriate IAM execution role and database permissions.
  1. API and frontend integration
  • Challenge: The frontend must communicate with the correct API endpoint.
  • Solution: Configured the deployed API URL in JavaScript.
  1. CORS configuration
  • Challenge: Browser-based API requests require correct cross-origin configuration.
  • Solution: Configured CORS for the required API methods and response headers.
  1. API deployment
  • Challenge: Changes to API configuration must be deployed before they become available through the stage.
  • Solution: Deployed the API to the "prod" stage after configuration changes.

11. Key Learnings

Through this project, I gained practical experience with:

  • Building a serverless application on AWS.
  • Creating and configuring DynamoDB tables.
  • Developing Python-based AWS Lambda functions.
  • Implementing GET and POST API methods.
  • Integrating API Gateway with Lambda.
  • Configuring IAM permissions.
  • Hosting static websites using Amazon S3.
  • Connecting frontend applications with backend APIs.
  • Testing HTTP responses and troubleshooting integration issues.

12. Security and Production Considerations

This project demonstrates the basic serverless workflow. Before using it in production:

  • Add authentication and authorization.
  • Apply least-privilege IAM policies.
  • Validate and sanitize incoming data.
  • Restrict CORS to trusted website origins.
  • Avoid exposing personal or sensitive records through a public website.
  • Consider using Amazon CloudFront and HTTPS for production website delivery.
  • Enable appropriate logging and monitoring.

13. Conclusion

The AWS Serverless GET & POST API Project demonstrates how multiple AWS services can work together to build a functional serverless application.

Amazon S3 provides frontend hosting, API Gateway manages API requests, AWS Lambda handles backend processing, and Amazon DynamoDB stores application data.

The successful GET and POST tests confirmed that the frontend, API and database were integrated correctly.

This project provided valuable hands-on experience in serverless application development and strengthened my understanding of AWS cloud architecture.

Technologies Used: Amazon S3 | Amazon API Gateway | AWS Lambda | Amazon DynamoDB | AWS IAM | Python 3.12 | HTML | CSS | JavaScript

title: Your AI-coded app is not broken, it is unfinished: how to rescue a stuck Lovable, Bolt or Replit build
description:
Most AI-coded apps do not fail in the first week. They fail in the last 10%, which is usually 50% of the work.

That is the pattern I keep seeing: Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Cursor, Base44 or v0 produces something that looks finished in a demo, and then something real happens. A user signs up with Google and the OAuth redirect drops them on a blank page. A payment succeeds in the test environment and breaks in production. The database works until there are 400 rows. The app has a beautiful front end and no way to delete a user account, which is fine right up until a GDPR request arrives.

The coding agent did what it was asked. The product was never finished.

The five states a stuck AI app is usually in

1. It runs on your machine and nowhere else. Secrets in a .env file, a local database, a hardcoded API key, a backend that only exists inside a preview. This is the most common state by a distance, and it is also the cheapest to fix.

2. It has no error handling. The generated code assumes every call succeeds. You get a stack trace, a blank screen, or a silent failure that writes a bad row and moves on. Nobody tested it because there was no test to run.

3. The data model is a sketch. A JSON blob where a table should be, or three tables that describe the same thing. Fine for a prototype, painful the moment you need to filter, paginate or migrate.

4. The auth is half-wired. Sessions that do not expire, roles that exist in the UI but not in the backend, a password reset that sends to no one, an admin panel reachable by guessing an ID.

5. Nobody can deploy it. No CI, no staging, no environment separation, no monitoring, no way to roll back. The app exists only as a laptop and a feeling.

Why it stalls

An AI coding agent optimises for the visible thing. You asked for a working app, so it produced a working screen. It has no incentive to write the migration, add the retry, or check the ownership on the update route, because those produce no visible result. It also cannot tell you what it left out, because it does not have a model of your intent - only of the request.

So the last 10% is not a bug in the tool. It is the part of building software that was never a "build a feature" task: verification, error paths, deployment, and the boring correctness work that has no screenshot.

What a rescue actually involves

If you want an outside pair of hands, https://www.appstuck.com/ does this as a service: they take over an existing codebase, map what is there, work out what is missing, and take it to a launch. The useful part is not the code - it is the checklist. A rescue usually runs through:

  • Project takeover. Reading the codebase as it is, not as it was intended, and writing down what actually exists versus what the plan says exists.
  • Launch and deploy. Real environments, real secrets, real rollback. Most "launches" that fail do so on the deploy step, not the build step.
  • Code optimisation. Turning the prototype into something a second developer can work in.
  • The unglamorous checklist. Session expiry, input validation, ownership checks on every write, a delete-account path, error states in the UI, and a way to see what happened in production when it breaks.

The questions worth asking before you start

  • Can I deploy this today, to a URL somebody else can open? If no, you have a prototype, not a product.
  • If the database disappears, what does the user see? If the answer is a stack trace, that is your next afternoon.
  • Can I delete my own account and all my data? If not, you have a compliance problem, not a feature gap.
  • Who is on call, and how do they know? The alternative is that you find out from a user.

Where to start if you are doing it yourself

Work through the states in order. Get it deployable first - a public URL with real secrets and a rollback path, even if the app is ugly. Then make every failure visible, because a failure you can see is a bug and a failure you cannot see is a data-loss incident. Then harden the data model while you still remember what it means. Leave the polish, the animations and the extra settings for last, and accept that they are the part that makes people say the product feels good.

Most of the time, the honest answer to "is my AI-coded app finished?" is no, and the gap is smaller than it feels. It is about half a week of focused work for a small app, and considerably more for a large one. The question is only whether you want to spend it yourself.

Disclosure: I work with the team behind AppStuck.

title: Secure Your APIs: OAuth2 and JWT for Beginners
description:
Securing an API usually turns into one of the fiddliest parts of backend work, and this JetBrains tutorial by Mdu Sibisi breaks it down for Kotlin and Spring Boot developers. It starts with the basics of how OAuth2 and JWTs fit together: OAuth2 handles delegated access, JWTs are the signed tokens that carry the identity and permissions, and your API only needs to check the "badge," not issue it. From there it builds a small document API, adds a custom converter to pull roles and permissions out of the token, and uses @PreAuthorize so access rules stay out of controller code. It also covers checking the issuer and audience claims, so tokens meant for a different app or environment get rejected.

It's most useful for developers who understand Spring or Kotlin but haven't done token-based security before. One thing I'll use from it is validating the issuer and audience explicitly in every service, even when a provider is already configured, because it's a cheap extra layer of defense.

Read the full tutorial here: https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2026/07/secure-your-apis-oauth2-and-jwt-for-beginners/

title: Python | Looping Problems
description:
1. Chocolate Wrapper Problem

Problem

You have Rs. 100 /- One chocolate costs Rs. 5. Every time you buy a chocolate, you get one wrapper. You can exchange 3 wrappers for 1 additional chocolate. What is the maximum number of chocolates you can have with Rs. 100?

Flowchart

See the first flowchart below.

Algorithm

  1. Set the total money as 100.
  2. Set the chocolate price as 5.
  3. Calculate the number of chocolates we can buy.
  4. Store the number of chocolates in a variable called total_chocolates.
  5. Store the same number in wrappers, because each chocolate gives one wrapper.
  6. Use a while loop to check whether we have at least 3 wrappers.
  7. If the condition is true:
    • Exchange 3 wrappers for 1 chocolate.
    • Add 1 to the total chocolates.
    • Add the new chocolate's wrapper.
  8. Repeat the process until fewer than 3 wrappers remain.
  9. Print the total number of chocolates.

Python Program 

total_money = 100
chocolate_price = 5

total_chocolates = total_money // chocolate_price
wrappers = total_chocolates

while wrappers >= 3:
    wrappers -= 3
    total_chocolates += 1
    wrappers += 1

print("Total chocolates:", total_chocolates)

Output 

Total chocolates: 29

Explanation

First, we use ₹100 to buy 20 chocolates because each chocolate costs ₹5.

Now we have 20 wrappers. We can exchange 3 wrappers for 1 extra chocolate.

Whenever we exchange wrappers, we receive another wrapper from the new chocolate. So, the loop continues as long as we have at least 3 wrappers.

Finally, when we have fewer than 3 wrappers, the loop stops.

Therefore, the total number of chocolates we get is 29.

2. Chapathi Story

Problem

There is one person called Viyan. He is a Software Engineer. He employs a maid for cooking. One day, the maid prepared n number of chapathis and kept in a hot box. Viyan ate those chapathis and the count is as follows:

  • For Morning breakfast, he completed 1/3 number of chapathis in the hot box.
  • For Lunch, He had 1/3 of what was there in the hot box.
  • For Dinner, again he took and ate 1/3 number of chapathis present in the box.

The next day morning, When the maid checked the number of chapathis remaining, it was 8. What was the number of chapathis, She made - in total?

Flowchart

See the second flowchart below.

Algorithm

  1. Initialize remaining_chapathi = 8.
  2. Initialize count = 0.
  3. Use a while loop to repeat the calculation 3 times.
  4. Since Viyan eats one-third and leaves two-thirds, we need to reverse the calculation.
  5. Calculate the previous quantity by multiplying the remaining chapathis by 3 and dividing by 2.
  6. Increase the count by 1.
  7. Repeat until the count reaches 3.
  8. Print the original number of chapathis.

Python Program 

remaining_chapathi = 8
count = 0

while count < 3:
    remaining_chapathi = remaining_chapathi * 3 // 2
    count += 1

print("Total chapathis:", remaining_chapathi)

Output 

Total chapathis: 27

Explanation

Here, we know that 8 chapathis are left after breakfast, lunch and dinner.

Instead of calculating forward, we calculate backwards.

After each meal, Viyan leaves two-thirds of the chapathis. So, to find the previous quantity, we multiply the remaining chapathis by 3 and divide by 2.

We repeat this calculation three times because there were three meals.

  • Before dinner: 8 × 3 / 2 = 12
  • Before lunch: 12 × 3 / 2 = 18
  • Before breakfast: 18 × 3 / 2 = 27

Therefore, the maid originally prepared 27 chapathis.

Conclusion

In the chocolate problem, we use a while loop to repeat the wrapper exchange until the condition becomes false.

In the chapathi problem, we use a loop to calculate the original quantity by working backwards.

title: A job board that agents pay for: four x402 bugs we hit before a directory would list it
description:
We run a small job board for AI agents at agent-job-board.obtranzat.workers.dev. No accounts, no API keys: an agent pays 0.02 USDC to read the board, 0.50 to post a job, 0.01 for an aggregated feed of open bounties. The rail is x402 v2 with exact USDC on Base (eip155:8453).

The payment path worked the first afternoon. Everything around it did not. Four bugs, in the order they bit.

1. HEAD is not an afterthought

Every validator we tried — the x402 directory, uptime checks, link scanners — asks HEAD before GET. Our router matched methods literally, so HEAD /jobs fell through to the 404 handler, and so did HEAD /meta. From the outside the whole origin looked dead: the directory reported "no valid x402 resources found" while curl showed a perfectly good 402 with a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header.

The fix is small: answer HEAD with the same status and headers a GET would produce, and no body.

if (request.method === "HEAD") {
  const res = await handle(new Request(request.url, { headers: request.headers }));
  return new Response(null, { status: res.status, headers: res.headers });
}

Lesson: "endpoint not found" can be an artifact of the method you probed with. If a machine is expected to discover your API, it will use methods you did not think about.

2. Discovery is part of the product

x402scan parses openapi.json and only treats an operation as payable when it carries x-payment-info:

"x-payment-info": {
  "price": { "mode": "fixed", "currency": "USD", "amount": "0.02" },
  "protocols": [{ "x402": {} }]
}

Without it our paid endpoints were classified as "public/API-key" and the registration returned no_valid_resources, even though each one answered 402 correctly. With the block added, the same origin registered three resources in one pass.

The 402 challenge is the contract at request time; the OpenAPI extension is the contract at discovery time. Agents browse before they call.

3. One transaction, one purchase — across rails

We accept x402 signatures and, for humans without an x402 client, a plain transfer: send USDC on Base, resend the request with the hash in X-TX-HASH. A settlement transaction from the x402 rail is also a valid transfer. So the same on-chain payment could be replayed through the other rail and read as new money.

The fix is a ledger-level lock, not a handler check: the first time a transaction hash is seen, whatever the rail, it is written to a txbind table keyed by the hash. A second attempt answers 402 "already been used", and the fee counter stays at one sale. The negative test — settle once, then replay the same hash manually — is part of the suite.

Lesson: idempotency belongs where the money is recorded. Two payment paths will find each other eventually.

4. A wrong error is worse than a slow one

A nonexistent hash used to exhaust our RPC fallback and surface as "provider unavailable". Two consequences: an attacker could spray fake hashes without ever being counted, and a real outage looked the same as garbage input. Now the code distinguishes "transaction not found on Base" from a transport failure, and bad credentials are budgeted per client address: twelve guesses a minute, then 429 with Retry-After for two minutes.

Same principle for unknown paths: mapping the API costs a budget (eight misses a minute), and the 404 for a hidden route is byte-identical to the 404 for a typo.

What the board actually does

  • GET /jobs — 0.02 USDC. The answer carries a 15-minute read pass, so a client that refreshes does not pay again.
  • POST /jobs — 0.50 USDC. Validation runs before payment; a malformed post costs nothing.
  • GET /v1/bounties — 0.01 USDC. Live poidh bounties, normalised, min_usd and chain filters applied before the charge.
  • /meta, /stats, /llms.txt, /openapi.json are free.

The suite is 188 assertions, most of them negative: replay, guessing, filters, cross-rail double spend. If you want to try it, the discovery docs are at /llms.txt. If you buy a read and the feed is missing something, tell me what.

The payment rail is the easy part. The rest is making a machine able to trust you without ever talking to you.

title: AI Demand is Constant, Unpredictable, and Extreme. MongoDB is Built for It.
description:
When a huge surge in demand meets limited resources, an awful experience usually isn’t far behind. Fans feel it when trying to compete for concert tickets with bots and scalpers. Diners feel it when they try to get a reservation at a trendy restaurant that’s fully booked for months. Websites and applications feel it when they go viral and get an accidental DDoS from a “Reddit Hug of Death.”

Unpredictable spikes in demand are only becoming more common, and scaling resources to meet them is hard. In my lifetime, I’ve seen big shifts in the amount of demand systems need to handle. First, the internet era, then the cloud era, we saw increased demand that was often predictable. Think of an annual flash sale or regular seasonality. Things might speed up, with more frequent spikes, but they were still spikes you could plan around.

Then AI happened. And this is where we live now: demand that’s constant, unpredictable, and extreme, increasing in frequency and intensity at the same time. If the internet era taught customers to expect an instant response, then the AI era is teaching them to expect something else: instant value. You can snap a photo of something you want, and an agent can identify it, buy it, and have it on your doorstep tomorrow. Those capabilities cut both ways. Change now hits every layer underneath faster and harder than before. The user isn't only human anymore. Agents are in the product too.

Agents don’t ease in. The second they’re on, they hit your system with massive, simultaneous reads and writes. They also take in and act on more information at once than any team of people ever could. Enterprises need a data layer built for that reality, where the only predictable thing is how unpredictable the load will be. Teams that can scale into those spikes will be the ones that last.

Introducing Atlas Infinite

Today, we're announcing Atlas Infinite, the largest architectural innovation for MongoDB Atlas ever. Atlas Infinite is purpose-built to handle the speed of development and unpredictable demand of applications that customers expect, with independent scaling of compute and storage to absorb sudden bursts of traffic.

Atlas Infinite is not a new database. It's a new deployment option within Atlas. Same document model, same drivers and APIs, no code changes required. Also, the current deployment option you know and love as MongoDB Atlas is not going anywhere. It just has a new name, MongoDB Atlas Core. Atlas Core and Atlas Infinite are the two database deployment options within the Atlas platform. You pick the right one for each workload.

How does Atlas Infinite deal with four key scaling and future-proofing problems organizations are dealing with today?

  1. Scaling delay: Gone. Atlas Infinite cuts read scaling time by more than 96% compared to Atlas Core. Compute and storage automatically scale independently within minutes, not hours.

  2. Storage ceiling: 10x higher. Atlas Infinite grows with you, from prototype to a petabyte, on the same foundation. You scale on your terms, when you need more performance, not when you run out of room. Atlas Infinite supports replica sets that hold 10x the data of replica sets in Atlas Core. 

  3. Capacity planning: No more guesswork. Atlas Infinite meets your needs in real time as you scale up and down. Atlas Infinite also runs more efficiently on the same hardware compared to Atlas Core, so you get nearly triple the performance per dollar.

  4. Re-architecture: Not required. Zero application changes required. Enjoy more elasticity and scalability on literally the same database.

This isn't only a scalability story. It's a more capable, more performant engine. Internal tests* using MongoDB 9.0 have shown that Atlas Infinite provides 189% more throughput per dollar compared with Atlas Core. And customers like Icon Solutions are using it to drive more growth.

"Atlas Infinite let us process 55% more transactions per second than our equivalent previous setup on MongoDB 8.0, with zero application changes. In payments, that kind of headroom without a re-architecture means faster, more reliable experiences for the customers on the other end of every transaction," said Mike Wallis, Head of DevOps at Icon Solutions.

Atlas Infinite is available as a public preview, and I can’t wait for you to try out the next generation of MongoDB Atlas.

MongoDB 9.0: The best version of MongoDB ever

In addition, we just released the best version of MongoDB ever, MongoDB 9.0. We’ve hardened the core to ensure a rock-solid foundation for the most demanding enterprises, and we’re setting a new bar for security, durability, availability, and performance.

That bar was already high. MongoDB 8.0 was released just two years ago, and today, nearly 80% of our Atlas fleet has adopted it, with higher customer satisfaction and stronger retention among these customers.

We are proud of what 8.0 delivered, and 9.0 pushes further still. Here are some of my favorite enhancements in MongoDB 9.0.

Performance*: 

  • In our internal tests against MongoDB 8.0, MongoDB 9.0 delivers:

    • Up to 35% faster find-one queries

    • Up to 30% faster update-one queries

    • Up to 2x throughput on large instances

    • Up to 20% higher throughput for transactional workloads

Security:

  • Queryable Encryption now supports prefix, suffix, and substring searches, allowing organizations to query sensitive information without ever decrypting it. 

  • Expanded private networking capabilities make it easier to deploy MongoDB Atlas securely across complex enterprise environments.

Durability and Availability:

  • Intelligent Workload Management automatically protects clusters when they are overloaded with requests and ensures short-running operations continue when demand is unpredictable.

  • Enhanced backup, restore, and recovery capabilities help organizations to maintain application availability and speed recovery when disruptions occur.

Observability & Developer Productivity:

  • Expanded observability into application and database performance

  • New developer productivity features that make it easier to modernize applications with familiar tools and frameworks, without costly rewrites.

MongoDB 9.0 continues to give you the freedom to run anywhere. MongoDB 9.0 is available in MongoDB Atlas and in self-managed environments through MongoDB Enterprise Advanced and MongoDB Community Edition.

MongoDB 9.0 on Atlas Infinite changes the calculus on scale. It's not something you plan around anymore, it's just there when you need it. There's never been a better time to build on MongoDB.

*Performance results are based on internal MongoDB testing comparing MongoDB 9.0 and MongoDB 8.0 using public benchmark methodologies. Results may vary by workload, deployment, hardware, and configuration.

title: Daemons can now send traces to Vercel Tracing
description:
Vercel Daemons can now send OpenTelemetry traces to Vercel Tracing, allowing you and your agents to inspect background worker operations alongside the rest of your project's traces.

Vercel provides each daemon with a Unix socket for receiving OTLP/HTTP traces and sets the socket's path in VERCEL_OTEL_SOCKET_PATH.

Upgrading @vercel/otel to version 2.3.0 or later enables automatic trace export for Node.js daemons using the default configuration. The SDK detects this socket and sends the spans your worker records to Vercel.

These spans are available through the Vercel CLI, which can search by service name within a project and return JSON for your agents.

Learn more in the daemon tracing documentation.
