title: I patched the Postgres planner, found 8 bugs in my own patch, then proved Tom Lane's fix with one commit
description:
Who this is for: anyone who read my first Postgres article and wanted the rest of the story, or anyone who builds views on views.

The short version: I wrote a patch for the Postgres 15.8 planner. It took one report from 194,910 ms to 114 ms. I then found 8 bugs in my own patch. Then I found that Tom Lane had committed a better fix, so I tested that one against the same data and did not submit mine.

1. The order is 16 years old, and it was a choice

In my first article I showed that the planner splits a big join into groups of join_collapse_limit tables (default 8). Only after that does it remove the LEFT JOINs a query does not need.

That order dates from Postgres 9.0 (2010). Tom Lane put join removal right after the grouping step on purpose. Removal needs facts the planner only builds during that step. Moving it earlier, he wrote, would need "a massive rethinking of the order of operations in the planner". He also judged that removal helps only a minority of queries.

For most queries this is fine. Views on views are the exception.

2. What it did to one report

A reporting view at work expanded to about 435 table references. The query needed about 11 of them. But the groups were drawn while all 435 were still counted. Two tables that needed each other, so the planner could look one up through an index from the other, landed in different groups. That fast plan was no longer possible.

I am not the first to hit this. People have asked about slow nested views since at least 2010 (pgsql-performance, "problem with from_collapse_limit and joined views"). Tom Lane answered a similar question again in 2017. The usual advice is to raise the limit, and that works. It is the workaround I shipped.

I wanted to know if the cause could be removed instead.

3. My patch: remove first, then group

I wrote a pass for 15.8 that removes the unneeded LEFT JOINs from the query tree before the split. The groups are then drawn on the survivors only.

join_collapse_limit Before With my patch
9 194,910 ms 114 ms
8 (default) only about 1.5x faster

At 8 the gain was small. My reading: about 11 tables survive, and 11 is more than 8, so the survivors still get split. At 9 the groups happened to fall the right way. That is the same "holes" behaviour from the first article.

The speed was the easy part.

4. The 8 bugs in my own patch

Correct results were the real work. Here is what I found, in plain words.

# What my patch did wrong What happened
1 Treated t.a = t.b as proof that t matches one row Wrong rows. A test returned 2 rows instead of 6
2 Left a dead entry behind when it removed a join Planner error: "so where are the outer joins?"
3 Opened an index without taking a lock Assertion failure on debug builds
4 Missed a table used through a join alias "no relation entry for relid N"
5 Missed a table needed by a placeholder expression with no column of it Same error
6 Removed the target table of a MERGE Broken MERGE
7 Ignored references from LATERAL subqueries Same error, in system views
8 Registered the new setting without a flag that EXPLAIN needs One regression test failed

Most of these sat in checks I had rewritten myself. I wrote my own "is this table used?" walker and my own "is this row unique?" check. Postgres already has both, tested over many years.

The lesson: a table can be "used" in ways a simple walker misses. Join aliases, placeholder expressions, references from subqueries and the target of a MERGE are four of them. Postgres's own bookkeeping already knows all four.

Bug 1 is the dangerous kind. The others fail loudly. That one returned wrong rows, and nothing complained.

5. Tom Lane's commit

Then I read commit 2ebf25e7d7, committed on 28 August 2026. It uses the same core idea: replace the LEFT JOIN node by its left input.

The purpose is different. He was fixing bug #19560, where a query silently lost a WHERE condition and returned wrong results. The faster grouping is a side effect.

The approach is also different:

  1. Let Postgres decide what is removable, using its own join_is_removable.
  2. Edit the jointree to cut those joins out.
  3. Throw away the derived data and restart planning, so the grouping runs on the survivors.
  4. Repeat until nothing more can be removed.

It was back-patched to 16. It shipped in 16.16, 17.12 and 18.7 on 12 November 2026. It never went into 15.

So the part where my patch failed, the safety proof, is the part he reuses. The price is the restart. My version avoided that cost, but it paid with the bugs above. I did not submit mine.

6. The proof: one commit, nothing else changed

"18.7 is fast" is not proof. 18.7 holds other changes too. So I ran an A/B on a copy of the real data, with default limits (join_collapse_limit = from_collapse_limit = 8):

Build Result
Official 18.6 about 2 minutes
My own build of 18.6, plain over 2 minutes (153 s, 358 s, 678 s)
My own build of 18.6 with only Tom's commit 2.1 s on the first run, then 0.3 s and 0.2 s
Official 18.7 about 40 ms

Both own builds came from the same source tree. I built it plain, applied the 18.6 back-port of the commit to the same tree, and rebuilt. Then I ran both servers on the same copy of the data.

The plan shows why. Without the commit, the child table is read by a scan over the whole account:

Bitmap Heap Scan on enrollment      (all ~51k rows of the account)
  Recheck Cond: (<account filter> AND NOT is_deleted)

With the commit, the same table is read through an index, one lookup per course:

Index Scan on enrollment
  Index Cond: (course_id = course.id)

Index Cond: (course_id = course.id) only exists when course and enrollment sit in the same group. With the commit, my two tables finally landed together. No setting was needed.

7. Two more numbers

15.8 never gets the fix. On 15.8 the shipped workaround is still SET LOCAL join_collapse_limit = 64, with from_collapse_limit left at 8. Raising from_collapse_limit too made this query worse. On the 15.8 copy this gave about 24 ms. The setting stays scoped to one transaction.

What does the restart cost? A reader asked this under my first LinkedIn post. Part of the answer, from official images, same data, fresh statistics:

Version Planning time
18.7 0.5 to 0.8 s
18.6 0.9 to 2.3 s

On these views, 18.7 planned faster, not slower. That is not the full answer. Richard Guo measured the bad case on the mailing list. A chain of 64 removals that each depend on the last took 20.9 ms instead of 1.98 ms, because every link costs one full pass. Views on views can have that shape. I have not yet counted how many restart passes my views need. That is next.

8. Caveats

  • My own builds are slower and noisier than the official images, and plain 18.6 got slower on each run. Compare the ratio and the plan, not the milliseconds.
  • The own builds show a collation version warning, because the locale files came from the official image. It applies equally to both builds.
  • The data is a copy of real data. No names appear here, and the tables are renamed.
  • An early run of mine compared 15.8 with 18.7 and gave the wrong cause. The fresh statistics differed, and the collapse limit made no difference on 15.8. I dropped that comparison and ran the 18.6 A/B instead.
  • This is one query on one data set. It shows what the commit does here. It does not claim every nested view gets faster.

What I'd tell you

If you see a fast fix, find the cause. If you have a patch, look for a better one before you submit. Mine was right about the idea and wrong in eight places, and a Postgres committer had already done the same job with the checks the planner trusts.

Planner folks: beyond the regression suite, how do you test a change like this for wrong results?

Sources

  • Commit 2ebf25e7d7: https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commit/2ebf25e7d70a8fce31ace78d723fa9271ab8af72
  • Bug #19560 report: https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/19560-54cd7ede78d5e355%40postgresql.org
  • Discussion thread: https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/1186816.1784573544%40sss.pgh.pa.us
  • 2010 thread, "problem with from_collapse_limit and joined views": https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/201011241937.08622%40Mail-Followup-To
  • Tom Lane, 2017 reply: https://postgresql.org/message-id/20264.1486185381%40sss.pgh.pa.us
  • 2010 thread on join removal: https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/8212.1269701421%40sss.pgh.pa.us
  • PostgreSQL 18.7 release notes: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.7/
  • First article: https://depthfirst.hashnode.dev/changing-one-number-from-32-to-34-made-a-postgres-query-6-000-faster-here-s-exactly-why

title: Metrics Rollback Safety: How to Choose Free Dashboards for Small Teams
description:
Choose Grafana with Prometheus as the starting point for a small team's free metrics dashboard, and make rollback decisions depend on structured evidence from the nightly pipeline. A developer tools team searching logs after a release needs to distinguish a processing failure from a job that never ran; a chart alone cannot settle that distinction.

TL;DR: preserve the previous dashboard and its data path while evaluating a replacement, compare the same completed runs, and keep release decisions separate from the dashboard migration. Grafana supplies visualization, Prometheus supplies time-series collection, and a structured-log view supplies the detail needed to investigate a suspicious run. Treat rollback safety as the acceptance test.

Start with evidence.

1. What should free metrics dashboard software prove for a small team?

Suppose the nightly job builds a developer tools catalog and the next morning's dashboard looks different after a release. That is an investigation trigger, not proof that the release damaged the catalog: a changed view, an incomplete run, and an actual processing failure require different responses, so the first useful result is a run you can identify consistently in the chart and the underlying structured logs.

Define an SLO around the pipeline's consumer-visible outcome before choosing panels. A proposed acceptance policy might require each scheduled catalog build to complete before its delivery deadline, with matching expected and processed record counts; the deadline and error budget belong to the team, and neither is a measured service guarantee in this guide. Keep the run identifier, release identifier, completion status, and record counts together in your application logs. These are proposed application fields, not a vendor ingestion schema.

The trap is comparing two screenshots without checking that both represent the same completed run. A visually reassuring panel can still describe yesterday's work. Separately check that the scheduled job ran; use a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks for that signal, rather than treating an empty metrics result as a successful night.

For teams already connecting several backend capabilities, try Infrai for the read-only metrics-query portion of this evaluation: its unified API covers 295 routes across 20 modules with a single API key, which reduces the credential and client setup needed as the workflow expands. Public discovery adds a separate practical benefit: request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples can be inspected before provisioning credentials, so an engineer can evaluate the integration contract before changing the pipeline. That is a reason to test an adapter, not a reason to discard a working dashboard.

Infrai's integration contract is one REST API, one API key, one bill, and no SDK to install. For this pipeline, the useful consequence is fewer separate credentials and client libraries to maintain when adding another backend capability.

Don't migrate blind.

2. Choose the operating responsibility before the software

Free dashboard software still consumes platform capacity. Budget for the collection path, retained history, the time required to restore a useful view, and whoever answers when the view is misleading; choosing a deployment model without assigning those responsibilities merely moves work into the on-call queue.

The comparison below is a buy-versus-build decision aid for this pipeline, rather than a ranking of interchangeable products. Prometheus is a collection component, Grafana is a visualization option, and the log investigation remains a separate requirement.

Option First useful result and integration work Build-versus-buy boundary for this job
Grafana with Prometheus Grafana offers dynamic visualization and straightforward integration; Prometheus supplies time-series collection. Grafana is free to self-host. Prefer this starting point for a small team's metrics dashboard when the team can own the self-hosted collection and visualization path. Keep log evidence alongside it.
ELK Stack with Kibana Kibana is an open-source option to evaluate for the structured-log investigation side. Prefer a specialist log workflow when searching individual pipeline events dominates the job; account for the stack's potentially higher operating overhead.
Metabase Lightweight setup makes it a candidate for simple analysis; free availability depends on the usage tier. Evaluate it for straightforward analytical views. Its suitability for that work does not establish that it will satisfy this runbook's log-search and rollback requirements.
Airtable or Google Data Studio Both may suit simple analysis and visualization on a small budget. Consider them for a compact reporting task, then demonstrate the required run-level evidence before assigning operational decisions to that report.
Infrai A consistent REST contract spans backend modules; public discovery and examples in 10 languages help assess the client work. Try it for metrics access within a broader backend integration. Choose a specialist when the decisive requirement is deep log investigation, distributed trace exploration, or dashboard operations.

There is no measured time-to-first-result ranking here. Count the actual work in a trial: credentials issued, client dependencies introduced, schema mapping required, and the point at which an engineer can identify one completed catalog run. A small API client can reduce SDK surface, but the platform still owns the mapping from application evidence to a rollback decision.

The trade-off is operating responsibility: this API trial is not suitable as a replacement for a specialist log investigation stack. Choose Kibana when detailed structured-log investigation is the deciding requirement, and budget for its higher operational overhead. Use dedicated tooling for alert delivery, heartbeat checks, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay when those are acceptance requirements; log correlation identifiers should not be treated as a distributed span-tree investigation. For a system whose adoption criteria include per-user deletion, bulk log export or subscriptions, configurable retention, or audited feature-flag changes, make those separate tool-selection gates. This guide's query trial does not establish those capabilities.

3. Capture a read-only result before connecting the dashboard

Run this Go program with INFRAI_API_KEY set in the environment. It makes an explicit GET to the verified metrics-query route, sends no query parameters, and prints the successful response without guessing at its JSON envelope. This is the first adapter check, not a complete dashboard or a demonstration of structured-log filtering.

The program uses the standard library: no SDK is required. Save it as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It retries only rate-limited reads, honors either form of Retry-After, bounds the total wait with a context deadline, and surfaces the response body on other HTTP errors; the timeout is an illustrative client setting, not a latency claim.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func query(ctx context.Context, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retryAfter := strings.TrimSpace(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
        if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retryAfter, 10, 32); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                delay = wait
            }
        } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
            if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                delay = wait
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := query(ctx, key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Accept this step only when authentication succeeds and the returned data can be understood against the published response schema. An HTTP success establishes access; it does not establish coverage of the catalog run, dashboard compatibility, or correctness of the release.

Next, inspect the contract for the log-search integration before mapping your application fields. Keep the example above parameter-free: a run identifier in an application log is not permission to invent a similarly named remote filter. Preserve the previous search workflow until the candidate can recover the same run-level evidence.

4. Verify the decision rule with a local fixture

Before wiring a release action to any dashboard, test the evidence rule independently. The following complete program uses a deliberately small synthetic fixture with 120 expected catalog records; its fields are local examples, and its output is a test result rather than a production incident or an API response. Save it separately as verify.go, then run go run verify.go.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "os"
)

type Run struct {
    ID        string `json:"run_id"`
    Release   string `json:"release"`
    Status    string `json:"status"`
    Expected  int    `json:"expected_records"`
    Processed int    `json:"processed_records"`
}

func acceptable(r Run) bool {
    return r.ID != "" && r.Release != "" &&
        r.Status == "complete" && r.Expected > 0 &&
        r.Processed == r.Expected
}

func main() {
    fixture := `[
        {"run_id":"catalog-a","release":"previous","status":"complete","expected_records":120,"processed_records":120},
        {"run_id":"catalog-b","release":"candidate","status":"complete","expected_records":120,"processed_records":119}
    ]`
    var runs []Run
    if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(fixture), &runs); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if len(runs) != 2 || !acceptable(runs[0]) || acceptable(runs[1]) {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "evidence-rule test failed")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("Evidence-rule test passed; candidate requires investigation.")
}

A complete status with 119 processed records fails this proposed rule even though the status label looks healthy. That is the pitfall being tested. Record-count equality is only one check, however: this fixture says nothing about record contents, scheduling deadlines, or whether two dashboard views include the same events. Add domain validation to the real acceptance policy before allowing it to authorize a release.

For capacity planning, estimate query demand before scheduling dashboard refreshes. With 3 panels refreshed once every 60 seconds, a design that sends one query per panel would make 180 queries per hour per viewer, before retries; that is arithmetic for a proposed layout, not a vendor throughput limit. Multiply by the expected viewers and investigation traffic, then decide how much polling the platform is prepared to operate.

5. Rehearse the rollback before replacing the view

Keep the old dashboard configuration and collection path available while the candidate reads the same pipeline evidence. During verification, compare run identity, completion, counts, and freshness rather than panel colors, and deliberately test a missing run as well as the mismatched-count fixture. A successful query should never consume the pipeline's error budget on behalf of an unverified result.

Rollback the view first when the candidate cannot reproduce the previous evidence: restore the previous dashboard configuration, confirm the same completed run remains inspectable, and leave release rollback to the pipeline's own acceptance policy. If the catalog itself violates that policy, follow the release runbook and separately verify the data outcome; reverting a dashboard cannot undo pipeline side effects. Do not combine a dashboard cutover with a release change unless the team can independently reverse and verify both.

Preserve the evidence.

Grafana and Prometheus remain the starting recommendation for a small team's free metrics dashboard. Teams expanding an existing backend integration should try Infrai for read-only metrics access, while retaining their dashboard and log investigation tools until the acceptance checks pass. The useful alternative is determined by ownership: a specialist log stack for deeper investigation, a lightweight analytical tool for simple reporting, or a shared API contract when integrating additional backend capabilities is the work consuming the roadmap. Accept a replacement only after the team can explain and reverse its effect on the rollback decision.

References

  • OpenTelemetry, metrics signal concepts
  • Grafana documentation
  • Prometheus overview
  • Kibana documentation
  • Metabase documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If the shared API boundary fits your system, start with the first-party metrics workflow guide.

title: Media Queue Draining: 3 Audit Controls for Rate-Limited Webhook Recovery
description:
Short answer: retry failed webhook deliveries from a durable ledger, gate each attempt through a destination-level rate limiter, and reuse one idempotency key across every replay.

When a media worker pool is being drained, a failed webhook should become a durable delivery record, not an immediate retry loop. The practical choice is to combine a bounded retry schedule, a per-destination rate limiter, and an idempotency ledger that survives worker shutdown. That arrangement lets the pool stop accepting work while already-recorded attempts finish predictably.

The important distinction is between redelivery and replay. A queue can make a job visible again; it cannot prove that the remote system did not accept the previous HTTP request. I design the boundary as at-least-once transport with an exactly-once mindset: every attempt may happen again, while the business effect is committed once by an idempotent consumer. Auditability is the mechanism that makes that claim testable.

The queue is not the ledger.

What changes when the pool must drain?

A normal retry policy can hide an operational contradiction. If workers are asked to drain, but each failed callback immediately creates another runnable callback, the queue never reaches zero. A media pipeline makes this visible during a large ingest: thumbnail completion events, caption updates, and publication notifications can all target the same partner endpoint, while that endpoint advertises a small request budget.

I use three states for a delivery record: ready, in_flight, and settled. The record contains a stable event ID, destination ID, attempt count, next eligible time, and the last response class. A worker claims one record with a lease, sends at most one request, and writes the outcome before the lease expires. The lease is a recovery aid, not proof of exactly-once execution.

A drain begins by stopping new claims, then allowing already-claimed records to reach a short deadline. Records whose lease expires return to ready with their original event ID. This is more controllable than terminating processes and trusting a broker-specific redelivery detail, because the ledger preserves the reason for each transition and gives reconciliation something concrete to inspect.

Consider a batch of 240 caption-complete events for one destination when the pool enters drain mode. If 20 workers each reclaim five expired records, the destination can see a burst even though the queue itself is behaving correctly. The drain controller should therefore mark the generation as closed to new claims, let the destination limiter admit only its available tokens, and leave records beyond the deadline in ready with their next eligible timestamp intact. A worker that wakes after the deadline must release its lease without sending; otherwise the operational meaning of drain depends on process timing. That small rule also gives the next generation a clean starting point: it inherits durable work, not partially inferred work from a previous process lifetime.

Drain is a state transition.

How do I retry failed webhook delivery from a message queue?

They answer different questions. Retry asks when another attempt is eligible. Throttling asks whether the destination may receive it now. Idempotency asks what happens if the previous attempt actually succeeded. Collapsing these into one counter produces misleading dashboards and unsafe recovery.

For a transient response such as a timeout or a 5xx, I use exponential backoff with jitter and a hard attempt ceiling. A Retry-After value can move the next eligible time later, but it should not bypass the destination limiter. For a permanent 4xx, malformed payload, or an explicitly rejected signature, the record settles as failed and enters a review path rather than consuming the same retry budget forever.

The limiter belongs to the destination, not the worker. A pool of 20 workers must not accidentally turn a destination limit of 5 requests per second into 20 simultaneous requests. A token bucket or equivalent admission counter can enforce the rate, while a separate concurrency bound protects the connection pool. Rate and concurrency are related; they are not interchangeable.

The idempotency key should be derived from the immutable media event, for example media-asset-1842:published:v3, rather than from an attempt UUID. The receiver should persist that key with the applied result and return the same semantic result for a duplicate. If the receiver cannot offer that contract, the sender must treat a timeout after request transmission as an ambiguous outcome and reconcile by querying a read model or a partner-provided event status. Blind replay is not a correctness strategy.

I initially treated the retry count as the main safety control. The harder case is a timeout after the receiver commits but before the sender sees the response; the count says nothing useful there, while the event key still gives reconciliation a stable handle.

Here is the decision core in Go. It deliberately keeps transport, admission, and persistence separate, so a test can force a timeout between the request and the ledger write without pretending that a network call is transactional.

type Delivery struct {
    EventID       string
    DestinationID string
    Attempt       int
    NextEligible  time.Time
    State         string
}

func nextAttempt(d Delivery, now time.Time, retryAfter time.Duration) Delivery {
    const maxBackoff = 30 * time.Minute
    backoff := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<min(d.Attempt, 10))
    if backoff > maxBackoff {
        backoff = maxBackoff
    }
    if retryAfter > backoff {
        backoff = retryAfter
    }
    d.Attempt++
    d.NextEligible = now.Add(backoff)
    d.State = "ready"
    return d
}

func min(a, b int) int {
    if a < b {
        return a
    }
    return b
}

The production version needs jitter, durable compare-and-swap on the lease, and a transaction around the state transition. Those details matter because two workers can observe the same eligible record. The code is a policy sketch, not a claim that a queue acknowledgement and a remote HTTP side effect form one atomic operation.

Which queue behavior is relevant, and which is not?

Queue products expose different building blocks, but the design question stays stable: where are ownership, delay, acknowledgement, and deduplication recorded? Acknowledgement-based brokers such as RabbitMQ let a consumer explicitly acknowledge or negatively acknowledge deliveries; that is useful for recovering an unprocessed message, but it does not know whether a remote webhook was accepted before the consumer failed. Its publisher confirms and consumer acknowledgements solve broker delivery boundaries, not external side-effect atomicity.

BullMQ places delayed jobs and retry attempts in a Redis-backed job model, which is convenient when the application already owns that storage boundary. Its retry configuration still needs a destination-level limiter and an idempotency record, because a delayed job is not a receipt from the remote endpoint.

Amazon SQS offers visibility timeouts and redrive policies, which provide useful lease and poison-message controls. Those controls likewise do not turn an HTTP callback into an exactly-once operation; the application must persist the event key and settle its own outcome. These are objective boundaries, not a ranking. Pick the primitive that fits the existing operational model, then keep the delivery ledger explicit instead of outsourcing the business guarantee to queue terminology.

This design is a poor fit for a tiny, non-critical callback where a lost notification is acceptable; a durable ledger and reconciliation loop add operational weight. It is also the wrong place to promise exactly-once effects when the receiving system cannot store an idempotency key. In those cases, accept at-least-once delivery explicitly and document the duplicate-handling trade-off.

What should the drain and recovery runbook verify?

First, freeze new claims and record the drain generation. Workers from an older generation must finish or release their leases; otherwise a late process can keep producing attempts after the operator believes the drain is complete. Second, continue destination admission for already-claimed records until the deadline, but stop scheduling retries whose next eligible time exceeds that deadline. Those records remain durable and can be resumed by the next generation.

I would measure four separate quantities: eligible records, leased records, settled records, and ambiguous outcomes. A single queue-depth graph hides the most dangerous class. An ambiguous outcome means the request may have reached the receiver, so the recovery job should reconcile the event key before sending again. Log the event ID, destination ID, attempt number, limiter decision, response class, and ledger transition; exclude payload secrets and authorization headers.

The tests should include a 429 with Retry-After, a timeout after bytes leave the process, two workers claiming one record, a lease expiring during drain, and a duplicate event arriving with a new transport message ID. I would also run a property test that repeatedly crashes between each pair of state writes. The invariant is modest and defensible: no settled success is silently forgotten, and no retry bypasses the destination's admission rule.

A compact rollout path

Start by writing delivery records beside the existing job submission path, with the immutable event ID as the uniqueness constraint. Shadow the limiter and compare its decisions with current traffic before enforcing it. Then enable bounded retries for one destination class, measure ambiguous outcomes, and add reconciliation before raising concurrency.

During a drain, prefer a visible backlog over an unbounded retry storm. The backlog is recoverable state; duplicate external effects are often not. A queue can schedule work, but the ledger, receiver contract, and audit trail define what delivery means.

Sources

  • RabbitMQ, “Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms”: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • Amazon Web Services, “Amazon SQS visibility timeout”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/visibility-timeout.html
  • Amazon Web Services, “Amazon SQS dead-letter queues”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • BullMQ, “Retrying failing jobs”: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • BullMQ, “Rate limiting”: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/rate-limiting
  • RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: E-commerce Product Search Retrieval Architecture with Node.js Filters (Two Stages)
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval. Keep tenant, market, and access metadata on every product chunk, apply a bounded metadata filter in the first vector query, then rerank only the small candidate set before composing an answer with source identifiers.

That shape keeps retrieval quality and latency visible as separate choices. It also gives a solo team a useful escape hatch: you can change the vector backend or reranker without changing the product-search contract.

Start with a retrieval contract

Product search starts with an answer, not an index. For “show me waterproof trail shoes under $150 in the EU store,” define the contract before picking a database: the query embedding, hard constraints, maximum candidates, freshness expectation, and the evidence returned to the UI.

I keep hard constraints out of free text. A chunk carries tenant_id, storefront, country, category, price_cents, stock, and source_url as metadata. The authorization decision is repeated at query time. An item that is semantically perfect but belongs to another tenant is still a miss.

The contract has two invariants:

  1. Every candidate is eligible for the requesting tenant and storefront.
  2. Every displayed claim can be traced to a product document identifier or URL.

Those invariants matter more than a fashionable index setting. The RAG paper describes retrieval and generation as separate stages; product search benefits from the same boundary because catalog policy changes faster than embeddings do.

A small Node.js implementation

The following example uses the three vector operations exposed by Infrai's search surface. The payload fields are deliberately plain: a collection name and dimension, vectors with metadata, then a query with a metadata filter. Replace the sample embedding with the embedding produced by your chosen model.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function call(endpoint: string, body: unknown, write = false): Promise<unknown> {
  let delay = 250;
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const headers: Record<string, string> = {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    };
    if (write) headers["Idempotency-Key"] = `catalog-${endpoint}-${bodyHash(body)}`;
    const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers,
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1800),
    });
    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : delay));
      delay *= 2;
      continue;
    }
    throw new Error(`${path} failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
    throw new Error(`${endpoint} exhausted retries`);
}

function bodyHash(value: unknown): string {
  return Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(value)).toString("base64url").slice(0, 32);
}

await call("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/create", {
  collection: "catalog-eu",
  dimension: 3,
  metric: "cosine",
  metadata: { tenant_id: "shop-17", storefront: "eu" },
}, true);

await call("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/upsert", {
  collection: "catalog-eu",
  vectors: [{
    id: "sku-4817-description-0",
    values: [0.12, -0.44, 0.81],
    metadata: {
      tenant_id: "shop-17",
      storefront: "eu",
      country: "DE",
      category: "trail-shoes",
      price_cents: 12900,
      stock: true,
      source_url: "https://shop.example/products/sku-4817",
    },
  }],
}, true);

const result = await call("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query", {
  collection: "catalog-eu",
  embedding: [0.10, -0.40, 0.79],
  top_k: 20,
  filter: {
    tenant_id: "shop-17",
    storefront: "eu",
    country: "DE",
    category: "trail-shoes",
    stock: true,
    price_cents: { $lte: 15000 },
  },
  include_metadata: true,
});
console.log(result);

There are a few unglamorous details here. Every request has an explicit method and an 1.8-second timeout. Writes carry a client-generated idempotency key, so a retry does not duplicate an upsert. A 429 honors Retry-After when supplied and otherwise backs off. Any other non-success response includes its body in the thrown error.

The filter syntax above is the contract your application should validate and test against the live discovery schema. Keep the filter builder in one module; do not let UI strings become arbitrary query objects. Your mileage may vary across vector engines, so a staging test should verify numeric comparisons and boolean handling before launch.

How should metadata filters shape e-commerce product search architecture?

There are two viable system shapes.

The first is a specialist vector stack: a managed engine owns indexing and filtering, while your API layer owns tenant policy, embedding calls, reranking, and citations. Pinecone and Weaviate are strong fits when the team wants hosted operational tooling and their query semantics match the catalog. Qdrant is attractive when explicit payload filters and a self-hosting option matter. pgvector keeps vectors beside transactional Postgres data, which can simplify joins and consistency for a small catalog, at the cost of more tuning as traffic grows.

The second is a single contract across backend capabilities. Infrai fits this shape when you want vector operations and adjacent services behind one REST API, one key, and one billing surface. The breadth is practical here: adding a web-backed product source or another backend capability uses the same HTTP-oriented integration style instead of another SDK and credential set. That is an integration advantage, not a claim that its vector index will beat a specialist on every benchmark.

The pipeline stays the same in both shapes: normalize catalog records, chunk long descriptions, attach immutable access metadata, retrieve at most 20 filtered candidates, rerank five to eight of them, and pass only cited context to generation. A hard timeout should return a useful partial result or a clear “no matches” state; it should never let a slow source hold the checkout path open.

Option Where it fits Trade-off to test
Pinecone Hosted vector retrieval for a focused search service Vendor-specific filter and index behavior
Weaviate Teams wanting a broader hosted search platform More platform surface to operate and learn
Qdrant Payload-heavy filters with self-hosting flexibility You own more availability and upgrade work when self-hosted
pgvector Catalogs already centered on Postgres transactions Recall and latency tuning compete with OLTP resources
Infrai vector API A small team standardizing vector plus other backend calls over HTTP Specialist engines may offer deeper vector controls or ecosystem tooling

Where quality and latency actually move

Metadata filtering protects relevance before it improves it. If stock=true and country=DE remove 90% of the corpus, the remaining nearest neighbors are easier to rerank and cheaper to pass to a model. If the filter is too strict, recall collapses; expose a deliberate relaxation policy rather than silently dropping constraints.

I use a two-pass policy: strict tenant and access filters always stay on, while merchandising filters such as color or size can relax only after an empty result, with an event logged for review. This makes a quality regression diagnosable. It also keeps latency bounded because each pass has a fixed top_k and deadline.

Do not make web search the hidden third stage of every request. Fetch and index external product documents asynchronously, retain their URL, and refresh on a schedule appropriate to catalog volatility. The answer path should read the vector index first and attach the stored source context.

Limits, and when to choose differently

The catch is specialization. If you need engine-specific hybrid scoring, complex geo predicates, or a large team already operating Pinecone, Weaviate, or Qdrant, use that specialist directly and keep the same retrieval contract. If transactional joins and strict row-level policy dominate, pgvector may be the cleaner boundary.

Infrai is a deliberate option for the opposite constraint: a lean team that values a broad capability surface with a simple, consistent HTTP interface and wants to add adjacent backend calls without installing another SDK. It is not a reason to skip relevance evaluation. Run the same held-out query set, measure recall and p95 latency in your own region, and inspect whether every result carries the metadata your UI needs.

Before shipping, verify five things in prose: the indexer rejects missing tenant metadata; the query service caps top_k and total context bytes; retries are bounded and idempotent; source URLs are returned with the context shown to users; and timeout metrics distinguish embedding, vector, reranking, and generation. I am not sure which relaxation rule will win for your catalog without those traces, and pretending otherwise is how filters become accidental product policy.

If this system shape fits, the vector API reference is the sensible next step: https://docs.infrai.cc

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/search/filter-by-metadata
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate/search/filters
  • https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/filtering/
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector

title: pg_fastload 1.0.0 released: parallel bulk loading for PostgreSQL
description:
pg_fastload 1.0.0 is a parallel bulk loader for PostgreSQL, 1.58x faster than the best pg_bulkload mode and 6.07x faster than COPY.

It parallelises the loading pipeline across background workers while keeping the load inside a single transaction. It is a source-level fork of pg_bulkload 3.1.23, so control-file syntax, TYPE values, log format and WRITER modes are unchanged.

  • Repository: github.com/yuansong/pg_fastload
  • Release: pg_fastload v1.0.0
  • License: BSD 3-Clause, with the upstream pg_bulkload copyright notices retained

The problem

pg_bulkload and COPY both run the whole load in one backend: read, parse, form the tuple, write. On a 16-core machine that leaves 15 cores idle, and the parse step is usually the expensive one. For CSV it is a byte-at-a-time state machine followed by a type input function per column.

How it works

The load has four stages: read input, parse record and split fields, form the tuple, and insert. Stages 1-3 move to background workers; stage 4 stays serial in the backend that issued the load: one reader worker -> N parser workers -> leader writes

Design points that matter in practice:

  • The input file is read exactly once. A single reader scans sequentially and hands chunks to the workers over shm_mq; the workers never open the file. Total read volume stays at 1x the file size, so the speedup does not invert once the data is larger than the page cache.
  • It is still one transaction. No second connection, no early visibility of uncommitted rows, and a bad row aborts the whole load rather than leaving a worker-timing-dependent subset behind.
  • 13 conditions the parallel path cannot honour fall back automatically, with one INFO line saying why: FILTER and FORCE_NOT_NULL, explicit ENCODING, NOT NULL or CHECK constraints, PARSE_ERRORS tolerance, STDIN input, TUPLE and FUNCTION input, and others.
  • The serial path itself was optimised. Records without quotes or CRs take a memchr bulk split instead of the byte-at-a-time loop.

Progress reporting and export

Every load and export publishes progress into a cluster-wide view, pgfastload.pg_fastload_progress: rows, bytes, rates and elapsed time. When a row total is known (a finite LIMIT, or a TABLE= export estimated from pg_class.reltuples), it also reports a percent and an ETA. Long loads are trackable from any session, or streamed as NOTICEs with PROGRESS_NOTICE=ON.

Export logs additionally record the MVCC snapshot fingerprint (xmin/xmax/cid), so every output file is auditable back to the exact snapshot that produced it. pg_fastload_export() writes a table or any SELECT to CSV, BINARY or FIXED output.

Results

1 GiB TPC-H lineitem CSV, 7,375,042 rows, 16 vCPU, warm cache, WRITER=DIRECT, no indexes, median of 3 runs. Same file and same empty table for every row.

configuration                         time     vs serial   vs COPY FROM
PARALLEL=OFF                          5.81 s   1.00x       1.43x
PARALLEL_WORKERS=4                    1.58 s   3.68x       5.27x
default (15 workers)                  1.37 s   4.24x       6.07x
reference: upstream pg_bulkload       6.98 s
reference: COPY ... FROM              8.32 s
reference: COPY into UNLOGGED table   7.51 s

A full loader x writer-mode x format matrix (3 alternating rounds, medians):

                                     CSV   BINARY    FIXED
upstream pg_bulkload BUFFERED       9.22     4.08     3.95
upstream pg_bulkload DIRECT         6.98     1.62     1.59
upstream pg_bulkload PARALLEL       6.63     1.39     1.42
pg_fastload PARALLEL=OFF            5.84     1.58     1.63
pg_fastload 8 workers               1.42     0.88     0.90
pg_fastload default                 1.40     0.90     0.93
COPY ... FROM                       8.34    (n/a)    (n/a)

Upstream's own fastest writer mode is PARALLEL, about 13% ahead of its DIRECT, so the honest headline is 1.58x over the best upstream mode and 4.4-4.6x over its slowest, rather than the 2x+ that a DIRECT-only comparison suggests.

Export shows the same effect in the other direction: 7.4M rows (1.13 GiB) take 4.08 s serial and 0.42 s with 15 workers, i.e. 9.33x server-side COPY TO. The export scan runs under one MVCC snapshot, serialized to the parallel workers, so an export under concurrent writes is consistent and reproducible.

Method, fairness controls and the full result set (cold cache, fixed-length, export, historical tiers) are in docs/BENCHMARK.md in the repository, and all raw run logs ship with the release archive.

Differences from upstream pg_bulkload 3.1.23

  • Parallel CSV and parallel fixed-length loading, 4.7x and 1.6x over upstream's best mode. The serial path alone is 1.22x upstream with identical semantics.
  • Load and export progress view with percent and ETA, plus NOTICE streaming.
  • SKIP_INDEX=ON drops the target's secondary indexes inside the load transaction and prints the verbatim CREATE INDEX statements to re-create them, which recovers about half the load time on an indexed table.
  • No spool busy-work on unindexed tables.
  • Stage-level profiling build, and one branch for PostgreSQL 15 through 19.

Compatibility and limits

  • PARALLEL=ON, PARALLEL_WORKERS and SKIP_INDEX are additive; everything else is compatible with pg_bulkload.
  • PostgreSQL 15, 16, 17, 18 and 19 from one branch; differences are resolved at compile time with PG_VERSION_NUM.
  • Index maintenance during a load costs about 1.9 s per GiB for one btree and does not parallelise. SKIP_INDEX=ON automates the drop-and-recreate workflow; constraint-backed indexes (PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, EXCLUSION) are refused rather than silently removed.
  • The leader's serial insert is the floor: at 1.37 s/GiB the remaining bottleneck is page fill plus WAL, not parsing.

Feedback is very welcome, especially counter-examples on other hardware, larger-than-RAM datasets, or workloads where the parallel path falls back more often than expected.

Regards,

Yuansong

title: Autopsy #11: Anatomy of a Supply-Chain DOM XSS & How Trusted Types Stop It
description:
One Marketing Snippet, 3.8% of Sessions Exfiltrated

A marketing PR added a one-line <script> embed for a third-party support chat widget to the authenticated dashboard layout. Local smoke tests showed the chat bubble rendering cleanly with zero console errors.

Six minutes after deploy, an upstream compromise on the widget's CDN injected an HTML payload into its postMessage stream. WAF anomaly alerts flagged POST /collect beacons exfiltrating session tokens and CSRF nonces from 3.8% of active customer sessions—with zero server-side breach.

  • T+00:00: Widget embed ships to production. Upstream CDN compromise injects a payload into the widget's postMessage stream.
  • T+06:00: Widget assigns an attacker string directly to widgetRoot.innerHTML, executing <img src=x onerror=fetch(...)> inside the host origin.
  • T+14:00: WAF alerts flag POST /collect beacons exfiltrating session tokens from 3.8% of active sessions.
  • T+22:00: Audit logs confirm zero server-side breach; all exfiltration came from authenticated browsers executing injected DOM handlers.

Why Stripping <script> Tags With a Regex Failed

In #sec-incident, the team shipped an emergency regex stripper (html.replace(/<script/gi, '')) while keeping script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' in CSP. It blocked <script>alert(1)</script> in staging.

In production, exfiltration continued unabated. The attacker payload used <img src=x onerror=...>, not <script>, and unsafe-inline allowed every inline event handler to execute immediately with full access to document.cookie and localStorage.

Five Defense Layers Between a String and Execution

Supply-chain DOM XSS succeeds when raw strings flow straight into DOM sinks without type enforcement, CSP allows inline handlers, Object.prototype gadgets forge sanitizer configs, cross-origin windows share process groups, and postMessage payloads are trusted without schema validation.

Step Through the DOM XSS Takeover and Trusted Types Block

Dissecting the Sink Takeover

01 → 02: The Network Beacon That Started at innerHTML

Inspecting the captured WAF beacon showed Origin: https://app.example.com and a stack trace rooted in widget.js assigning event.data.html directly to widgetRoot.innerHTML. Because innerHTML accepts raw strings by default, any string containing an event-handler attribute executes JavaScript in the host origin. Enforcing DOM XSS & Trusted Types (require-trusted-types-for 'script') turns innerHTML = rawString into a synchronous TypeError unless the string passed through an explicit TrustedTypePolicy sanitizer.

Even if a script tag or inline handler slips past an older library, removing 'unsafe-inline' and enforcing CSP Nonces & strict-dynamic blocks unauthenticated inline execution at the parser level.

02 → 03: The Polluted Prototype That Disabled the Sanitizer

Forensic inspection of the widget's JSON.parse merge helper uncovered a secondary gadget: __proto__.ALLOW_UNKNOWN_PROTOCOLS = true was injected via a crafted config payload. Through Prototype Chain Lookup, the sanitizer read config.ALLOW_UNKNOWN_PROTOCOLS off Object.prototype, bypassing URL scheme checks until the merge helper switched to Object.create(null) and Object.hasOwn().

03 → 04: Isolating the Origin Context

To prevent compromised popups or embeds from reaching window.opener or sharing memory with the authenticated app, Cross-Origin Isolation (COOP/COEP) severs browsing context groups and blocks unauthenticated cross-origin subresources.

04 → 05: Validating Every postMessage Boundary

Finally, the widget listener accepted any window.addEventListener('message', ...) event without checking event.origin or payload shape. Enforcing Runtime Boundary Validation with a strict Zod schema and explicit origin allowlist drops malformed third-party messages before they ever reach a DOM sink or state store.

Enforcing Trusted Types and Strict Message Schemas 

const policy = window.trustedTypes?.createPolicy('widget-sanitizer', {
  createHTML: (dirty: string) => DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty, { RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE: false }),
});

window.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
  if (event.origin !== 'https://chat.vendor.example') return;
  const parsed = WidgetPayloadSchema.safeParse(event.data);
  if (!parsed.success) return;
  widgetRoot.innerHTML = policy ? policy.createHTML(parsed.data.html) : '';
});

Architectural Invariants:

  • Lock down DOM sinks with Trusted Types: Ship Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script' and route every HTML sink through one audited policy.
  • Ban 'unsafe-inline': Authenticate bundles with per-request cryptographic nonces and strict-dynamic.
  • Validate all postMessage boundaries: Verify event.origin and parse payloads with a strict schema before touching state or DOM.

Golden Rule: Regexes cannot sanitize HTML; enforce Trusted Types at every DOM sink and drop 'unsafe-inline' from CSP.

title: 7 small SEO bugs an audit found on my own site (and the fixes)
description:
I run a small launch directory. Last week I went through an SEO audit of it, expecting advice about content. Most of what it found were small technical bugs I had shipped myself. None of them were hard to fix, but every one of them was quietly costing crawl budget or clicks.

Here they are, with the fix for each.

1. /blog/ returned 404, /blog worked

My router matched exact paths. Anyone (or any site) linking with a trailing slash got a "not found" page.

Fix: one permanent redirect before routing.

if (path.length > 1 && path.endsWith('/') && !path.startsWith('/api/')) {
  const clean = '/' + path.replace(/^\/+|\/+$/g, '');
  res.writeHead(301, { Location: clean + search });
  return res.end();
}

Watch the '/' + ...replace(/^\/+/...) part. My first version kept leading slashes, so //evil.com/ would have redirected to //evil.com, which browsers read as another site. Collapse leading slashes and that open redirect can't happen.

2. /index.html returned 200 with an empty shell

The static file server happily served the raw template, with no content and no canonical. Now it is a 301 to /.

3. Old ID links still on two pages

Product pages moved from /tools/<uuid> to /tools/<slug> weeks ago, and the old addresses redirect. But two pages still built links from the ID, so 23 internal links went through a redirect. Internal links should point straight at the final address. The fix was passing the slug along with the ID in the data those pages use.

4. Lowercase category links were 404s

The real address is /categories/Development. People (and other sites) type /categories/development. Now the server compares a loose version of both and redirects:

const loose = v => v.toLowerCase().replace(/&/g, ' ')
  .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-').replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');
const match = categories.find(c => loose(c) === loose(requested));
if (match && match !== requested) return redirect301(categoryPath(match));

So sales-crm also finds Sales & CRM.

5. The sitemap had no dates and missed pages

No <lastmod>, and only categories used as a product's main category were listed. Now every category with at least one live product is in, and <lastmod> is added only where a real date exists (product updated or launched, post updated). I left it off pages with no honest date. A made-up date is worse than none.

6. Two pages shared one meta description

/directory and /categories used the same string, so in search results the two pages looked like the same thing. Each now has its own.

7. The Organization schema had no logo

The JSON-LD had a name, URL and one profile link. I added a logo with a stable file name (not a build-hashed one, which changes on every deploy) and the brand's real profiles in sameAs.

One more, outside the code

www redirected to the bare domain with a 302 (temporary). For a permanent move it should be a 301. That was one dropdown in the CDN's redirect rule.

What I took from it

None of this needed a new feature. It needed someone to request odd URLs: with a trailing slash, in lowercase, through /index.html, through www. If you have ten minutes, try those four on your own site.

For the meta description and share preview side, I use the free meta tag checker I built for the directory. It shows the title, description and share preview of any page, so you can compare two pages side by side.

Which of these would your site fail?

title: LosslessCut vs Electron
description:
TL;DR

  • LosslessCut uses Electron and suffers greatly from it
  • I'm developing a native alternative to address these issues

 

Recently, Discord officially announced[1] the move from Electron and React Native to Rust everywhere with GPUI on desktop, and the native toolkits on iOS and Android. I'm not sure about other people, but this very much surprised me. Discord out of everyone seemed like the last company that would ever do that. RIP to Vesktop I guess. Apparently they had been planning this change ever since 2018[2], so I guess they were technically early adopters of Rust, but why has it taken this long? Discord seems like the type of company to love LLM coding, so who knows. Discord aside, I hate Electron. My opinion might be skewed because I have never personally developed an Electron app, but that may be due to the awkward nature of JS apps on the desktop and just JS in general. Many features of Electron are quite useful, but there are libraries out there that provide that functionality, of which is not hard to wire up yourself. I can't really think of a proper argument for Electron as the default choice for apps. Maybe something like an email client, but even then you can just embed a web view (like KMail) like come on! The time you spend working around the limitations of your app just being a website can be better spent making your app better.

Electron apps are bloated too. Hundreds of megabytes in distribution, and they take up so much fucking RAM. This is a massive issue with Vesktop where at idle, it sometimes takes up over a gigabyte, reaching 1.5 sometimes. Discord is a special case for being a rich communication app, but still. The new Phoenix rewrite they announced was shown to be taking up 300 MB at idle[2], which is still leaning on the heavy side, but much better than before, and it most likely won't spike or fluctuate wildly. And for a desktop app, bringing an entire JavaScript runtime + HTML and CSS parsers is super overkill for most apps. You then have to make a tradeoff because Chromium is a massive project with security fixes all the time; do you update for most security fixes and have to push new versions constantly, or wait for them to accumulate, leaving vulnerabilities open (if that even matters for your app).

Tauri is a misleading solution to Electron. It definitely does solve many of the problems like distribution size, RAM consumption, library size, but makes the tradeoff of using the system web view. When I had first heart about Tauri, I was not too familiar with web views or even Rust in general, and to me it seemed that it was basically THE solution to Electron. Keep your UI and frontend in HTML/CSS, and write the backend in a language you don't hate. But, now you essentially depend on a system browser, that will have variations between OSes. I've also heard that WebKitGTK isn't very good, but take that with a grain of salt. Overall though, I do think Tauri is at least a step in the right direction. The effort to port an Electron app to it though is not worth it in my opinion, as you'd be rewriting your backend in Rust, so why not just rewrite your entire app too? Pull the bandaid off in one fell swoop?

Now let's finally get to the main point of this post, LosslessCut. If you don't know what it is, it's a simple lossless video editor (trimmer more accurately) written in Electron. Now, I don't dislike the maintainer of LosslessCut and I understand why Electron was chosen, but I think it was a big mistake. The main functionality of it shells out to FFmpeg, including piping video to it as a subprocess. The latter only occurs during FFmpeg-assisted playback, which is decoding a video with FFmpeg because Chromium's video player doesn't support it, which is an awfully large amount of videos. Most notably, hardware HEVC on Linux! That issue really hits me specifically as I record clips in stupidly high bitrates with the best possible hardware acceleration for 4:4:4 on my GPU, which is HEVC. FFmpeg-assisted playback with my videos is quite laggy and it pisses me off. Considering that LosslessCut is a polished wrapper over FFmpeg copy muxing, Electron does basically nothing for it as many of the issues in LosslessCut can be attributed to Electron or Chromium. Chromium's video element is quite limited in codec support and makes for a subpar video player.

Can we do anything about it? No, unless you want to go tell someone to completely abandon their longstanding project to rewrite it natively. I want to do something about it though, which is why I've started development on a native app very similar to LosslessCut, with some extra features where possible. I'm going to call it RustySlice (yes it's a cliche name I know), but development is currently not public. For simplicity, I chose to use Slint for UI since declarative UI is simple, and nothing more performant or architecturally cleaner is really needed. Video playback will be done utilising libmpv since from my own experience, it is the best video player technical-wise, and the only one to play back my stupidly high bitrate videos with no lag. mpv by default uses its new gpu-next backend for rendering, utilising libplacebo with Vulkan for HDR and such. The only problem being that the render API for embedding an mpv player into a canvas currently only supports the older regular gpu backend, which uses OpenGL and not libplacebo[3].

 

Sources

  1. Discord official announcement about Project Phoenix
  2. Discord CTO talking about Discord Phoenix
  3. A pending gpu-next pull request for mpv's render API
  • LosslessCut icon used in post artwork, by Dimi Kazak licensed under CC 3.0 BY.

title: Will Your Photo Come Out Sideways? A Python EXIF Orientation Preflight Before You Pay for a Bama Bound Clip (Tested)
description:
Checked November 17, 2026 (15:19–15:21 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, an independent studio that turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. It is not the University of Alabama, and the clip is not an admission letter.

The photo rule on the FAQ and the photo guide is short: one JPEG, PNG or WebP of one person, up to 10 MB, with the face uncovered. There is no prompt. Resolution is the only extra setting. The site does not publish a required aspect ratio, and it does not mention EXIF Orientation.

That last gap is the one that bites people who write their own "is this photo okay?" check before they pay. A phone held upright often stores the pixels as a landscape rectangle and writes Orientation 6 or 8. A naive width, height = Image.open(path).size then reports 1280×720 for a picture that displays as 720×1280. If your script rejects "landscape" uploads on that number, you will fail a perfectly ordinary portrait. If it only looks at the stored size, it can also miss the opposite mistake.

I wrote a local preflight that never uploads anything. It reads the file, applies ImageOps.exif_transpose, and tells you whether a size check that ignored the tag would have lied. Then I built a small fixture set and ran it.

What the tag actually does

EXIF Orientation 1 means the stored pixels are already the right way up. Orientation 3 is a 180° rotation: the axes stay put, so a 720×1280 file is still 720×1280 after a compliant viewer rotates it. Orientation 6 and 8 are the 90° tags. Those do swap the axes. The fixtures that honour the usual phone convention store those two as 1280×720 and display them as 720×1280.

The preflight flags exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read when the displayed picture is portrait and the stored pixels, read without the tag, look landscape (or the other way around).

The preflight


python

!/usr/bin/env python3

"""Preflight a still before you pay to upload it to a one-photo studio.

Checks: format, file size, pixel size, EXIF Orientation vs how Pillow opens
the file, and whether a naive dimension read (without applying Orientation)
would lie about portrait vs landscape.

This script never uploads anything. It only reads a local file.
"""
from future import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image, ImageOps, UnidentifiedImageError

ALLOWED = {"JPEG", "PNG", "WEBP"}
MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024
MIN_SHORT_SIDE = 256 # a practical floor, not a site rule

def exif_orientation(img: Image.Image) -> int | None:
try:
exif = img.getexif()
except Exception:
return None
if not exif:
return None
# 0x0112 is Orientation
value = exif.get(0x0112)
"format_allowed": False,
"mode": None,
"width_stored": None,
"height_stored": None,
"orientation": None,
"width_displayed": None,
"height_displayed": None,
"orientation_swaps_axes": False,
"looks_portrait_displayed": None,
"looks_portrait_if_you_ignore_exif": None,
"short_side": None,
"issues": [],
"ok_for_upload_shape": False,
}
if not rec["exists"]:
rec["issues"].append("missing_file")
return rec
rec["over_10mb"] = rec["bytes"] > MAX_BYTES
if rec["over_10mb"]:
rec["issues"].append("over_10mb")
try:
with Image.open(path) as img:
rec["format"] = img.format
rec["mode"] = img.mode
rec["width_stored"], rec["height_stored"] = img.size
rec["orientation"] = exif_orientation(img)
applied = ImageOps.exif_transpose(img)
rec["width_displayed"], rec["height_displayed"] = applied.size
except UnidentifiedImageError:
rec["issues"].append("unreadable_image")
return rec
except OSError as e:
rec["issues"].append(f"open_error:{e}")
return rec

rec["format_allowed"] = rec["format"] in ALLOWED
if not rec["format_allowed"]:
    rec["issues"].append("format_not_jpeg_png_webp")

rec["orientation_swaps_axes"] = (
    rec["width_stored"], rec["height_stored"]
) != (rec["width_displayed"], rec["height_displayed"])
rec["looks_portrait_displayed"] = rec["height_displayed"] >= rec["width_displayed"]
rec["looks_portrait_if_you_ignore_exif"] = rec["height_stored"] >= rec["width_stored"]
rec["short_side"] = min(rec["width_displayed"], rec["height_displayed"])
if rec["short_side"] < MIN_SHORT_SIDE:
    rec["issues"].append("short_side_under_256")
if rec["orientation"] in (5, 6, 7, 8) or rec["orientation_swaps_axes"]:
    if rec["looks_portrait_displayed"] != rec["looks_portrait_if_you_ignore_exif"]:
        rec["issues"].append("exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read")
rec["ok_for_upload_shape"] = (
    rec["format_allowed"]
    and not rec["over_10mb"]
    and "unreadable_image" not in rec["issues"]
    and "short_side_under_256" not in rec["issues"]
)
return rec

def main() -> int:
p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=doc)
p.add_argument("paths", nargs="+", type=Path)
p.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
args = p.parse_args()
rows = [inspect(path) for path in args.paths]
if args.json:
json.dump(rows, sys.stdout, indent=2)
sys.stdout.write("
")
else:
for rec in rows:
flag = "OK " if rec["ok_for_upload_shape"] and not rec["issues"] else "SEE"
print(
f"{flag} {rec['path']}
"
f" {rec['bytes']} bytes format={rec['format']} "
f"stored={rec['width_stored']}x{rec['height_stored']} "
f"displayed={rec['width_displayed']}x{rec['height_displayed']} "
f"Orientation={rec['orientation']}
"
f" issues={rec['issues'] or ['none']}"
)
return 0

if name == "main":
raise SystemExit(main())


python

MIN_SHORT_SIDE = 256 is a practical floor I put in the script so a obviously tiny test file gets a warning. It is not a published site rule. The live FAQ and guide only state JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 10 MB. A 200-pixel photo might still be accepted by the upload field; I would not use one, but I will not pretend the studio published a 256 px minimum.

A short fixture builder

A short fixture builder

The full fixture kit I used also writes a 73 MB JPEG so the 10 MB check has something to trip over. I am not shipping that file, and the script below does not create it. Point the oversize test at any JPEG larger than 10,485,760 bytes if you want that row. Everything else you need is here: the four orientation tags, a portrait and a landscape with no EXIF, PNG, WebP, a TIFF, and an 80×142 thumbnail.


python

!/usr/bin/env python3

"""Build a small set of orientation / format fixtures. Does not write an oversized JPEG."""
from future import annotations

from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image, ImageDraw

OUT = Path("fixtures")
W, H = 720, 1280 # same frame as a 9:16 720p clip

def upright() -> Image.Image:
img = Image.new("RGB", (W, H), (236, 232, 224))
d = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
d.rectangle((0, 0, W, 80), fill=(20, 20, 20))
d.rectangle((0, H - 120, W, H), fill=(165, 20, 30))
d.text((24, 24), "TOP", fill=(255, 255, 255))
d.text((24, H - 80), "BOTTOM BANNER", fill=(255, 255, 255))
return img

def save_jpeg_with_orientation(img: Image.Image, path: Path, orientation: int) -> None:
# Store pixels without applying the tag. Compliant viewers rotate on open.
exif = Image.Exif()
exif[0x0112] = orientation
exif[0x0131] = "bama-exif-preflight-fixture"
img.save(path, format="JPEG", quality=92, exif=exif, subsampling=0)

def main() -> None:
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
base = upright()
# Inverse-transform so ImageOps.exif_transpose restores the upright picture.
# EXIF 6: stored as landscape (1280x720); displayed 720x1280.
# EXIF 8: the other 90° tag. EXIF 3 is 180° and does not swap axes.
inv = {
1: lambda im: im,
3: lambda im: im.transpose(Image.ROTATE_180),
6: lambda im: im.transpose(Image.ROTATE_270),
8: lambda im: im.transpose(Image.ROTATE_90),
}
for orient, fn in inv.items():
save_jpeg_with_orientation(fn(base), OUT / f"orient-{orient}.jpg", orient)
base.save(OUT / "no-exif-portrait.jpg", format="JPEG", quality=92)
land = Image.new("RGB", (1280, 720), (236, 232, 224))
ImageDraw.Draw(land).text((24, 24), "LANDSCAPE", fill=(20, 20, 20))
land.save(OUT / "no-exif-landscape.jpg", format="JPEG", quality=92)
base.save(OUT / "portrait.png", format="PNG")
base.save(OUT / "portrait.webp", format="WEBP", quality=90)
base.resize((80, 142)).save(OUT / "too-small.jpg", format="JPEG", quality=92)
base.save(OUT / "portrait.tif", format="TIFF")
print(f"wrote fixtures in {OUT}")
for p in sorted(OUT.iterdir()):
print(f" {p.name:28} {p.stat().st_size:9} bytes")

if name == "main":
main()


markdown

What I measured

I ran exif_preflight.py on the fixtures. Displayed size is after ImageOps.exif_transpose.

File Stored Displayed Orientation Issues
orient-1.jpg / orient-1-upright.jpg 720×1280 720×1280 1 none
orient-3.jpg 720×1280 720×1280 3 none (180°, axes not swapped)
orient-6.jpg 1280×720 720×1280 6 exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read
orient-8.jpg 1280×720 720×1280 8 same issue
no-exif-portrait.jpg 720×1280 720×1280 None none
no-exif-landscape.jpg 1280×720 1280×720 None none
portrait.png / portrait.webp 720×1280 720×1280 None none
portrait.tif 720×1280 720×1280 None format_not_jpeg_png_webp (2,764,940 bytes, format TIFF)
too-small.jpg 80×142 80×142 None short_side_under_256
over-10mb.jpg 4000×6000 4000×6000 None over_10mb (73,278,492 bytes, 69.89 MiB)

A few things worth spelling out.

Orientation 3 is the easy one to over-think. The picture is upside down if you ignore the tag, but the stored size is already 720×1280, and the displayed size is the same. The script does not flag it as a naive-size lie, because a width/height check would not have been fooled. You still need exif_transpose (or a viewer that honours the tag) if you want the head at the top.

Orientation 6 and 8 are the ones that fool a size read. Stored 1280×720, displayed 720×1280. Both are allowed formats, both are under 10 MB, and both came back ok_for_upload_shape=true with that one issue noted. I would upload the transposed, upright JPEG if I were being careful, but the live pages do not require you to strip the tag first.

The landscape file with no EXIF is also not rejected. The script does not treat landscape as a failure, because the site asks for one person, not a required aspect. A group photo still does not create extra people in the clip; that is a different rule, on the FAQ, and this preflight does not try to detect it.

TIFF is rejected on format alone: format_not_jpeg_png_webp. The studio lists JPEG, PNG and WebP. A 2,764,940-byte TIFF of the same portrait does not become allowed just because it is under 10 MB.

The oversize fixture was 73,278,492 bytes, 4000×6000. The check is a raw byte count against 10 * 1024 * 1024, not a megapixel cap.

Flattening a copy, if you want to

If you prefer to upload a file whose stored size is already the displayed size, transpose and save a new JPEG with Orientation 1 (or with no Orientation tag):

from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

src = Path("phone-photo.jpg")
with Image.open(src) as im:
    upright = ImageOps.exif_transpose(im)
    upright.save(src.with_name(src.stem + "-upright.jpg"), format="JPEG", quality=92)

That is a local convenience, not a published requirement. The live FAQ and guide do not ask you to strip EXIF first. They ask for one JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 10 MB, with the face uncovered.

How I would use it

Run it on the photo you are about to upload, locally:

python3 exif_preflight.py portrait.jpg
python3 exif_preflight.py --json fixtures/*.jpg fixtures/*.png fixtures/*.webp fixtures/*.tif

If you see exif_orientation_would_fool_a_naive_size_read, open the file in anything that honours EXIF (Preview, Photos, a browser, or Pillow with exif_transpose) and confirm the person is upright. Saving a flattened copy with Orientation 1 is a reasonable habit. It is not a published requirement.

If you see format_not_jpeg_png_webp or over_10mb, that does match the published rule. Convert or compress before you pay. The studio still does the real check at upload time; this script is only a preflight.

One photo, face uncovered, then choose a resolution if you want more than the 480p default. That part has not changed.
