title: CrossTrace – crash-test your AI agent's model and MCP calls in CI
description:
TL;DR. After my earlier post I ran CrossTrace, the open-source tool that breaks a model call in your agent and
watches what happens, on the OpenAI Agents SDK, pydantic-ai and CrewAI. Two of them (pydantic-ai and CrewAI) handled a failure in a way my tool had
labelled as a bug: they re-prompted the model, refused a broken tool call, or summarised and carried on. Those aren't bugs, so I fixed the
tool, not the frameworks. (The Agents SDK simply raised an error, which the tool had judged right.) The fix changed how it decides pass or fail, and the changes are below. There are also real findings (cut answers
printed as complete, hangs, a tool call that ran twice), and it can now fault MCP tool calls, where the damage is a customer refunded
twice. https://github.com/mac146/crosstrace

What the tool does, in one paragraph

A local proxy sits between your agent and the model API (the agent only reads OPENAI_BASE_URL). CrossTrace records one healthy run,
replays it offline, and breaks one model call per trial at the byte level: a stream cut mid-tool-call, a stall, a 500, an empty reply.
Then it watches the agent's next move. No LLM judge.

Where it went wrong

My first version decided what the agent meant by looking at the first request it sent after the fault. If it didn't retry the same
call, and it carried on with something else, I called it SILENT: "the agent hid the failure". That fails your build.

Then I ran real frameworks:

  • pydantic-ai got a tool call cut in half. It refused to run it and told the model its arguments were invalid. That's the right behaviour. I labelled it SILENT.
  • CrewAI got a context-length error. It summarised the conversation and continued. I labelled it SILENT.
  • A re-prompt ("your last reply was empty, try again") looks exactly like an agent carrying on as if nothing happened, because both are "the failed reply plus one more user message".

I patched each one as it showed up, and each new agent needed another patch. That's when I stopped and asked what was common to all of them.

The root problem

The replay is a closed world: it can only answer the healthy conversation. Any request that is legitimately different gets an error,
the run dies there, and the verdict is a guess from the shape of one request.

Looking back at what I'd patched, the facts I measured on the wire never needed a patch: a hang, a retry storm, a retry that ignored
Retry-After, a surfaced error. Everything that inferred intent from a request's shape needed one, every time.

So two changes:

  1. A verdict fails the build only if it rests on something measured. Where all I can see is a different-looking request, the result is DIVERGED or REPROMPTED, shown for review with the facts: what the framework sent, what the error was, what the model was told.
  2. The run continues past the fault. After the fault, requests that match nothing recorded get the next healthy reply, so the agent reaches its real end. Then the verdict comes from how it ends: it finishes, it stops with an error, or it never stops (capped at 8 different requests, then RETRY_STORM).

The limit I put in the README: continuation shows that an agent stops, and how. It doesn't show that its re-prompt would work with a real
model. So I added --live: those requests go to the real provider with your own key (the agent never sees it, capped at 6 calls per
trial). On two frameworks, the recovery works:

  • pydantic-ai refused the cut tool call, the real model answered the re-prompt, and the run finished after 3 more requests.
  • CrewAI summarised after the context-length error, and finished after 4 more requests answered by the real model.

I ran only one or two trials per case, and a real model isn't deterministic, so treat those as demonstrations rather than a guarantee.

What the frameworks do (after the labels were fixed)

Framework Cut stream or cut tool call Stalled response
LangGraph ran the tool on the cut arguments hangs
OpenAI Agents SDK raised an error hangs
pydantic-ai refused the cut call and told the model; printed a cut answer as complete hangs
CrewAI printed a cut answer as complete hangs unless you pass a timeout

Each stall fix was run, not assumed (timeout= on the client, 10 s in my test). Three more things worth knowing: CrewAI retried a
persistent outage 7+ times in about 3 seconds, an empty reply made pydantic-ai re-prompt, and on the Agents SDK, --live showed the same
thing as the unlive run: it stops with an error and doesn't retry.

Tool calls: the failure that costs money

A model call that fails is annoying. A tool call that succeeded but whose reply was lost can be expensive: the email went out, the
card was charged, the response never reached the agent, and a retry does it again.

CrossTrace can now do this to MCP servers. The server is launched through crosstrace mcp-wrap, or for a remote server over HTTP you
list its URL in crosstrace.toml. In a test run it never starts or calls the real server. One tool call is made and counted, its reply is
replaced by a transport error, and every write the agent makes afterwards is counted against the healthy run.

On the example agent in the repo, a refund tool and a naive retry loop:

✗ lost_response   DUPLICATE 1/1
                  refund({"amount":129.99,"customer_id":"42",...}) ran 2 time(s), 1 in the healthy run;
                  the agent recovered and finished, but the write was repeated

The agent printed the right answer and exited 0. It also refunded the customer twice. I also ran it against the official Playwright MCP
server with a real Chrome and a local order form: recording placed one real order, replays placed none, and losing the response to the
click made the retrying agent a DUPLICATE. (That agent was scripted, so it tests the tool-call handling, not how well a model drives a
browser.)

For the claim "it really happens twice" there's --real-tools: the lost-reply trial runs the real server, and the report quotes what the
server answered to the repeat. I tested that against a remote server over HTTP, and the server refunded twice. It's opt-in because it does
the work for real, so point it at a sandbox.

What it still can't do

  • It tests model and MCP calls, not an agent's own HTTP calls to other APIs.
  • An agent that checks state before retrying ("did the refund go through?") gets the recorded answer in replay, so it shows as stopping with an error rather than as recovering safely.
  • MCP over stdio and streamable HTTP, but not servers that push messages on their own stream.
  • A real model's answer to a re-prompt varies, so --live is a demonstration, not CI.
  • I have no outside users yet. Everything above was run on agents I wrote or recorded myself.

Try it 

pip install git+https://github.com/mac146/crosstrace
crosstrace init --command "python agent.py {input}"
crosstrace record      # runs your agent for real, once per input
crosstrace test        # replays with faults, offline; exit code 1 if it hides a failure

A demo agent with a recording is in the repo (examples/broken_agents), so you can see the whole thing without a key. There's also a
GitHub Action for the report in a PR summary.

If it can't start your agent, or the replay isn't stable, it says why and, for a value that changes every run, prints the mask to paste.
If you try it on your agent, I'd really like to know what it found, or where it's wrong. Given this post, wrong verdicts are the most
useful thing you could send me.

title: Local SEO for Small Businesses: Add LocalBusiness Schema the Right Way
description:
Local SEO for small businesses is often described as a content problem, but a chunk of it is markup: search engines can only trust your location facts when the visible page and the machine-readable data say the same thing. This walkthrough shows how to add a single LocalBusiness (or a more specific subtype) JSON-LD block to a small-business website, how to test it, and how to avoid the errors that create a second, conflicting NAP.

I build and review sites for local service businesses. I also run North Fox Digital. The example below is fictional. Do not copy the names, phone numbers, or coordinates onto a live site.

You only need one canonical JSON-LD graph on the templates that represent the business as a whole, usually the homepage and the contact page. You do not need a unique LocalBusiness blob on every blog post. If you already have Open Graph tags, leave them; they do not replace schema.

A JSON-LD recipe you can adapt

Prefer JSON-LD in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag over microdata sprinkled through the HTML. JSON-LD is easier to review in a pull request, and you are less likely to break it when a designer edits the header.

Start with the most specific type Google documents for the business. LocalBusiness is the safe parent. A dental office can use Dentist, a shop can use Store, a trades firm can use HomeAndConstructionBusiness or a narrower subtype. Do not pick a type because it “sounds stronger.” If no subtype fits, stay with LocalBusiness.

Here is a compact example for a fictional service-area plumber. The @id values let the organization, the website, and the owner node point at each other without duplicating the telephone number in three disconnected objects.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@graph": [
    {
      "@type": "HomeAndConstructionBusiness",
      "@id": "https://example-plumbing.example/#business",
      "name": "Example Plumbing",
      "url": "https://example-plumbing.example/",
      "telephone": "+1-407-555-0142",
      "email": "hello@example-plumbing.example",
      "image": "https://example-plumbing.example/images/van.jpg",
      "priceRange": "$$",
      "areaServed": [
        { "@type": "City", "name": "Orlando" },
        { "@type": "AdministrativeArea", "name": "Orange County" }
      ],
      "openingHoursSpecification": [
        {
          "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
          "dayOfWeek": ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"],
          "opens": "07:30",
          "closes": "17:00"
        }
      ],
      "sameAs": [
        "https://www.facebook.com/exampleplumbing",
        "https://maps.google.com/?cid=0000000000"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

A storefront business should add a PostalAddress under address, with streetAddress, addressLocality, addressRegion, postalCode, and addressCountry. If the business is service-area only and hides the street address on the public profile, do not invent a public street in JSON-LD to look more complete. Use areaServed for the cities or counties the crew actually covers, and keep that list short and true. Listing every city in a metro area will not create a branch office.

telephone should be the public customer number in international format, not a tracking number that differs from the number on the contact page. sameAs should list official profiles you control, not directories you have not claimed. If you do not have a given profile, omit it.

Common implementation mistakes:

  • Two generators, two stories. A theme plugin emits one LocalBusiness block, a marketing plugin emits another, and the footer still shows a retired phone number. View source and keep a single graph.
  • Markup that does not match the page. If the visible heading says “Example Plumbing” and the JSON-LD says a different legal name, fix the source of truth first. Schema is not a place to try a keyword variation.
  • Coordinates for places you do not occupy. Do not drop a GeoCoordinates pin on a city you merely hope to rank in. If you have a real premises, use the real lat/long.
  • AggregateRating you did not earn on that page. Do not hard-code star ratings. If you later add review markup, it has to follow the current rich-result rules and represent reviews that are actually present.
  • Copy-pasted opening hours. A holiday exception that exists on the Google Business Profile but not in JSON-LD (or on the contact page) is a contradiction. Update the facts in one place, then regenerate the script.

When the script is in a staging build, validate it before you merge. I use three checks, in this order:

  1. The Schema.org Validator at validator.schema.org, to confirm the JSON is valid and the types exist.
  2. Google’s Rich Results Test at search.google.com/test/rich-results, to see whether the page is eligible for any documented rich result. A valid LocalBusiness graph can still produce “not eligible,” which is fine; you are aiming for accurate entity data, not a decorative badge.
  3. A visual diff of the rendered homepage and contact page against the JSON-LD: name, phone, hours, and area served must match.

If the site is a static or server-rendered app, generate the JSON from the same configuration file that prints the footer. That is the whole trick. In a Next.js or similar project I keep a business.json module and serialize it into the layout, so a hours change cannot land in the footer and miss the graph.

Local SEO for small businesses also depends on work that schema cannot do: service pages that name the offer clearly, a contact path that works on a phone, and public listings that repeat the same facts. Markup is the consistency layer, not a substitute for those pages. If you want a non-code walkthrough of the basic parts of local search visibility, that explanation is written for owners who will approve the facts you are about to encode.

Ship the script, run the three checks, and then leave it alone until a fact changes. A quiet, accurate LocalBusiness block is more useful than a quarterly rewrite of the same JSON.

title: AWS Security Hub now infers resource criticality from installed software and usage
description:
Today, AWS Security Hub adds installed software and resource usage as signals for resource criticality, which indicates how important a resource is to your business. Security Hub uses criticality to rank exposure findings, so that central security teams can prioritize the exposures that affect their most important resources.

Security Hub already infers criticality from resource tags and names, but inconsistently tagged resources often have an Unknown criticality, which makes their exposures harder to prioritize. With installed software and resource usage as additional signals, more of your resources receive a meaningful criticality with no tagging or configuration required. For example, an EC2 instance that runs a database engine and serves steady traffic receives a higher criticality than an instance that runs only monitoring agents and sits idle.

These signals are included with the Security Hub Essentials plan at no additional cost and require no new enablement. To learn more, see Resources in Security Hub in the AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page. For a list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available, see the AWS Region table.

title: 1.3 MB of class names in our HTML, and 69 per cent of the stylesheet they point at never reaches a public page
description:
Atomic CSS makes a trade that everybody describes and almost nobody measures: the stylesheet stops growing with your app, and the class names move into every document instead. I wanted the actual figures for that trade on a real site, so I counted the class attributes on all 76 public pages of Nakodo, and then counted what the stylesheet contains that those pages never use.

The two sides of the trade 

elements on 76 pages                      64,980
elements carrying a class attribute        24,118
bytes of class attributes                1,321,945
class tokens                                97,725
distinct class tokens, site-wide               540
distinct tokens on one page, median            265
stylesheet, two files                      154,378 bytes

1.3 MB of class names against a 154 KB stylesheet, which is 8.6 to 1 in favour of the markup. Per page it is about 17.4 KB of class attributes, repeated in every document, against a stylesheet downloaded once and then cached for a year because its URL contains its own hash.

Then the other direction. Parsing class selectors out of both CSS files gives 1,739 distinct ones, and only 540 of them appear anywhere on a public page:

class selectors in the CSS                   1,739
ever used on a public page                     540
never used on a public page                  1,206   (69%)

That 69 per cent is not dead code. It is the app behind the login, which shares one stylesheet with the marketing site, so a visitor who never signs in downloads the rules for the campaign table, the brief editor, the dialogs and the dropdowns. The sample reads exactly like the app you cannot see from outside:

**:data-[slot=kbd]:rounded-sm
*:data-[slot=select-value]:items-center
*:[svg:not([class*='size-'])]:size-4
*:data-[slot=alert-description]:text-danger

Splitting the stylesheet by route group would move perhaps 100 KB off the public pages, and it would also mean two cache entries and a second file on the critical path. Since the file is immutable and cached, and since an earlier measurement showed first paint on this site is bounded by font preloads rather than CSS, I am leaving it as one file. But "69 per cent of our CSS is for logged-in screens" is a much better thing to know than "our CSS is 154 KB".

The 714-character button

The longest class attribute on every single page is the same one, to the character:

longest class attribute per page: 714 characters (median across 76 pages: 714)
element: <a>

It is the button component rendered as a link. ui/button.tsx is 65 lines and holds a 482-character base string, and variants and sizes take the rendered attribute to 714:

group/button inline-flex shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-md border
border-transparent bg-clip-padding text-sm font-medium whitespace-nowrap
transition-colors outline-none select-none focus-visible:outline-2 ...

Seven hundred characters of attribute for one button. Across a sample of twelve pages there are 63 elements carrying that component's classes, 40,480 bytes between them, about 3.4 KB a page, and exactly one of them per page is the full 714. That is the clearest example of where atomic CSS puts its weight: not in the stylesheet, in every copy of the document. It is also why the compression ratio matters so much here: the glossary is 526,929 bytes of HTML and 47,715 bytes on the wire, an 11 to 1 saving, because a document full of repeated class strings is the easiest thing brotli will ever be handed.

540 tokens, and seven with nothing behind them

The most-used utilities are the boring ones, which is reassuring:

hover:text-foreground   3,016
text-muted-foreground   2,779
text-ink-700            2,661
dark:text-muted-foreground 2,661
shrink-0                2,350
flex                    2,333

58 tokens appear exactly once in the whole site, which is the long tail you would expect from one-off layout fixes.

Seven tokens in use have no rule anywhere in the CSS, and both reasons are worth knowing:

group/button
lucide-check  lucide-copy  lucide-mail  lucide-menu  lucide-plus  lucide-x

group/button is a named group marker. It never produces a declaration itself; it exists so that other selectors can say group-hover/button: and mean "when that specific ancestor is hovered". The six lucide-* classes are added by the icon library to every icon it renders, as a styling hook for people who want one. We do not, so they are 76 pages of bytes buying nothing, and the library has no option to turn them off.

Every inline style on the site is a coordinate

1,167 style attributes across the 76 pages, and only 42 distinct values. The frequencies give it away:

76  left:43.735%;right:45.776%
76  left:2%
76  left:9%
76  left:17%
76  left:24%

Exactly 76 occurrences each, which means one per page, which means they are in the footer. This site's footer is a drawn landscape, and the things standing in it are positioned as percentages that no utility class could express without generating a class per value. That is precisely the case the style attribute is for: a number that belongs to one element and will never be reused.

So the audit of inline styles came out better than I expected. Not one of the 1,167 is a colour, a font or a spacing value sneaking past the design system. They are all drawing coordinates.

1,178 comments, and we wrote none of them

The last count was the one I had never looked at:

comment nodes across 76 pages   1,178
  <!-- -->                        872
  <!--$-->                        153
  <!--/$-->                       153

The 872 empty ones are React's text separators, which it emits so that hydration can tell two adjacent text nodes apart. The median page has 10 and the terms has 82, which tracks exactly with how much interpolated prose a page contains: legal pages are full of sentences stitched together from constants.

The 153 pairs are Suspense boundaries, and the distribution is the interesting part: exactly two on 75 pages, three on the home page. The only <Suspense> written into a public page in this codebase is the one on the home page, around a notice that reads a search parameter. So two boundaries per page belong to the router itself, inserted around its own segments, and they are in the HTML of a page that streams nothing and has no fallback to show.

That is the whole shape of a modern document in three numbers. Of 1,178 comment nodes, one is mine.

What I am changing

Nothing in the markup, and one thing in the review checklist. The measurements that would have worried me came out clean: no inline styles carrying design values, no runaway one-off utilities, no duplicate ids. The numbers worth keeping are the two that contradict the usual framing of atomic CSS: the stylesheet is not the cost, the documents are, and most of the stylesheet is for screens the public never sees. Both are fine here because of compression and immutable caching, and both would stop being fine the moment this site started serving uncached HTML.

If you want to check any of it, every page is public: the glossary is the biggest document, the terms has the most React comments, and any guide will show you the 714-character button in its header.

title: PDF Summaries: Node.js Embeddings and Rerank Explained for Moderation Review
description:
Retrieving fewer PDF passages makes a moderation summary easier to constrain, but it can also hide the passage that changes the decision. Resolve that trade-off by making evidence selection explicit and letting an application validator decide whether the resulting classification can enter the human review queue. TL;DR: use embeddings for semantic search, rerank the retrieved passages, and summarize the selected evidence into a checked record; route missing or invalid evidence to human review. This is a focused summary, not a promise to cover every page.

Consider a developer tool that receives moderation reports with PDF attachments: abuse reports, exported conversations, or policy explanations. The job is to classify each report before a reviewer opens it. A Node.js service can own that workflow while a small Python example makes the acceptance rule concrete below. The decisive property is structured output correctness. An eloquent paragraph with an unusable category is still an unusable queue item.

Keep evidence attached.

A deliverability mindset helps here. A message being accepted for sending and actually reaching its recipient are different checkpoints; similarly, a model returning text and a review queue accepting a valid record are different checkpoints. Design for the second checkpoint. The report must reach a reviewer with its meaning and evidence intact.

How do embeddings and semantic search select PDF pages to summarize?

Start with an application contract: a report identifier, one category from a small allowed set, a short summary, and references to evidence selected from that report. These are application fields, not a vendor response schema. A category can be syntactically valid while the cited passage belongs to another report, so checking JSON syntax alone leaves the most consequential boundary unguarded. The worker should know which passages were eligible for this particular decision and reject references outside that set.

The data flow is straightforward. Extract PDF text while preserving page references, divide it into identifiable chunks, index their embeddings, and retrieve candidates for a report-specific question. Rerank those candidates before handing the strongest passages to the summary step. Embeddings support retrieval of likely relevant sections; reranking improves the ordering of the retrieved candidates. Neither step establishes whether an allegation is true.

That distinction matters for moderation. A passage saying “the reporter alleges credential spam” and a passage containing a quoted example of that spam need different treatment. Keep the allegation and quotation distinguishable in the evidence sent to the model. Ask for classification for review, with supporting references, rather than an automatic enforcement decision. A report's own instructions are evidence content, too; they should never acquire authority over the classifier's instructions. OWASP's LLM application guidance is a useful starting point for that trust boundary.

For teams maintaining this handoff across providers, try Infrai for the embeddings, reranking, and final summary stages when keeping the capability contract stable is the main integration requirement. Its common HTTP surface lets the application retain its integration boundary while the provider behind a capability changes. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas, which gives the adapter implementer a concrete contract to inspect instead of reconstructing each handoff from prose. These are two useful properties for this workflow: a stable application-facing integration and less schema investigation at the adapter boundary.

Infrai uses a single API key and a unified API across capabilities: one key, one wallet, one bill. Plain HTTP is sufficient, with no SDK required for the discovery call below. Changing the provider behind a capability doesn't require rewriting the application-facing adapter. Treat that as an integration recommendation. For moderation through this approach, use a chat model with a JSON Schema output contract and application validation. A specialist moderation product is a better fit when the requirement is a dedicated moderation decision interface. The general summary pipeline still needs its own policy definitions and review rules.

Derive the selection rule before choosing a provider

The natural retrieval question is narrower than “summarize this PDF.” For a report about unsolicited credential messages, ask which passages describe the alleged behavior and which passages qualify or contradict that description. Run selection against those needs. A generic document summary might faithfully describe the attachment while omitting the one quotation a reviewer needs.

Selection has a cost in coverage.

For large documents where only the relevant sections matter, embeddings followed by reranking can reduce the text sent to final summarization. That is a good fit for a focused report brief. A complete policy review has a different requirement: the system may need to consider every applicable section, including qualifications that semantic retrieval did not select. Do not label a selected-evidence summary a comprehensive assessment.

Keep stable chunk identifiers and original page references through the pipeline. The retrieval adapter returns candidates; the reranking adapter orders them; the summary adapter consumes selected text plus those identifiers. The application owns the mapping back to the report. A shared HTTP surface simplifies these handoffs, but it does not make embeddings from different models interchangeable. As an application migration rule, keep an index tied to its embedding configuration and rebuild it when that configuration changes, rather than silently mixing vectors.

Compliance belongs at this same boundary. PDF attachments may contain contact details, message contents, and identifiers that are unnecessary for classification. Decide what the classifier needs before sending text onward, and define retention and access rules for evidence. GDPR is a relevant legal reference where it applies; using a common API does not settle the application's obligations or establish a provider's suitability for a particular data flow.

Do not turn classification into an immediate notification trigger. A duplicated review item can become a duplicated email or SMS, and a queue full of repeated alerts teaches reviewers to ignore the channel. Keep report-level deduplication and any later notification decision in application logic. These are design requirements, not claims that the model or retrieval service provides delivery guarantees.

Compare the options at the boundary that matters

Choose a provider after the record and its acceptance rule are clear. The following are selection criteria, not benchmark results; they do not rank classification accuracy. Validate each candidate against the same report examples and the exact output constraints you need.

Option Reason to evaluate it here Trade-off to resolve
Direct OpenAI integration Consider it when the final structured generation step is the main provider boundary you want to own. Check the chosen model's structured-output support and retain the application's evidence validator.
Anthropic Claude Evaluate a direct Claude integration when your final classifier is intended to stay with that provider. Keep retrieval separate and verify the selected model's output contract against the same acceptance gate.
Google Gemini Evaluate Gemini when a Google-facing model integration fits the existing backend. Check its current structured-output interface rather than assuming another provider's schema settings transfer unchanged.
Cohere Consider it when reranking is the stage you want to evaluate independently. Decide who owns the embedding index and final summary integration around that stage.
Elasticsearch Consider it when document retrieval and index operations are already part of your backend responsibilities. Budget for index configuration and an explicit handoff into classification and summarization.
Infrai Consider it when embeddings, reranking, and summary calls should share an integration surface. A stable interface still requires separate checks for retrieval coverage and classification validity.

These choices can coexist. A search-oriented backend may keep retrieval close to its existing index and use a separate provider for generation. A team comparing rerankers may preserve its current summary adapter. If a direct provider's model-specific controls are the deciding requirement, a direct integration is a reasonable choice; an intermediary's cleaner boundary should not outweigh a required control. Consult the linked product documentation for the specific interface under evaluation.

The useful comparison is therefore about ownership. Who changes the adapter when a provider changes? Who verifies the category vocabulary? Who can explain why page evidence reached the reviewer? None of those questions is answered by a summary that merely sounds plausible.

A minimal acceptance gate, then a narrow rollout

The smallest useful implementation combines contract inspection with an acceptance gate after model output. The Python example below uses the standard library to fetch Infrai's public reranking capability schema, then validates a deliberately constructed candidate response locally. It does not perform retrieval or model classification. The local fields are an application contract, not an Infrai API payload. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, save this as a Python file, and run it; the discovery request itself is public and needs no key, but the example shows the Bearer authentication convention used by authenticated calls. In production, inspect the returned schema when implementing the adapter and pass the model's returned text and selected evidence map into the gate before writing a review item.

import json
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def read_rerank_contract():
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/ai.rerank",
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]},
        method="GET",
    )
    for attempt in range(3):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 2:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            delay = 2 ** attempt
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after:
                try:
                    delay = max(delay, float(retry_after))
                except ValueError:
                    retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                    delay = max(
                        delay,
                        (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds(),
                    )
            time.sleep(delay)


def accept_candidate(raw, expected_report_id, selected):
    candidate = json.loads(raw)
    required = {
        "report_id", "category", "summary", "evidence_ids"
    }
    if not isinstance(candidate, dict) or set(candidate) != required:
        raise ValueError("Unexpected record shape")
    if candidate["report_id"] != expected_report_id:
        raise ValueError("Report identity mismatch")
    categories = {"spam", "harassment", "needs_review"}
    category = candidate["category"]
    if not isinstance(category, str) or category not in categories:
        raise ValueError("Unknown review category")
    summary = candidate["summary"]
    if not isinstance(summary, str) or not summary.strip():
        raise ValueError("Missing summary")
    evidence = candidate["evidence_ids"]
    if not isinstance(evidence, list) or not evidence:
        raise ValueError("Missing evidence references")
    if any(not isinstance(item, str) for item in evidence):
        raise ValueError("Evidence identifiers must be strings")
    if len(set(evidence)) != len(evidence):
        raise ValueError("Repeated evidence reference")
    if any(item not in selected for item in evidence):
        raise ValueError("Evidence outside this selection")
    return candidate


contract = read_rerank_contract()
print(json.dumps({"capability": contract["id"], "params": contract["params"]}))

selected_evidence = {
    "report-17:p2:c1": {
        "page": 2,
        "text": "The reporter alleges repeated credential spam.",
    }
}
raw_candidate = json.dumps({
    "report_id": "report-17",
    "category": "needs_review",
    "summary": "The reporter alleges credential spam; review is required.",
    "evidence_ids": ["report-17:p2:c1"],
})
try:
    accepted = accept_candidate(
        raw_candidate, "report-17", selected_evidence
    )
except (ValueError, TypeError) as error:
    print(json.dumps({"review_required": True, "reason": str(error)}))
else:
    print(json.dumps(accepted, indent=2))

The read-only discovery request makes at most 3 attempts and backs off on HTTP 429, honoring Retry-After when supplied. It creates no review item. The local gate checks four fields, rejects unknown categories, and verifies that evidence references belong to the current selection. It doesn't prove that the summary follows from the cited text. Preserve that limit in the interface: passing the gate means the record is structurally admissible for review. It does not mean the allegation is confirmed.

An invalid response should create a review exception, not erase the original report. An empty retrieval result also needs an explicit review path; inventing a plausible category would hide the evidence gap. Keep those exceptions visible without copying sensitive attachment contents into routine logs.

Roll out with the existing human process still making the decision. Compare the selected passages with what reviewers actually need, inspect invalid records separately from disputed classifications, and include reports with quotations, contradictory passages, and no relevant evidence. Before changing providers, repeat those checks with the same report set and embedding configuration. This checks the contract where it matters: at the moment evidence becomes a review item.

Sources

References for the trust boundary, legal considerations, and the alternative interfaces discussed above:

  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
  • GDPR text
  • OpenAI structured outputs documentation
  • Anthropic Claude documentation
  • Gemini structured outputs documentation
  • Cohere reranking documentation
  • Elasticsearch documentation

If this boundary fits your review workflow, start with the first-party Infrai embeddings and reranking guide and keep the application acceptance rule beside your adapter.

title: How to build an Azure Landing Zone with Terraform (and the mistakes it saves you from)
description:
Every cloud journey starts the same way. Someone creates a subscription, deploys the first application by hand, and it works. Then a second team arrives. Then a third.

A year later, the same company usually has:

  • resources in regions nobody approved,
  • resource groups nobody owns, and a bill nobody can explain,
  • virtual networks with overlapping address ranges that can never be connected,
  • a database with a public IP "just for testing",
  • and a monthly cost that grows faster than the business.

None of these is a disaster on its own. Together, they make every change slow and risky, because everything is already in production.

After more than 20 years in infrastructure, including scaling cloud platforms for a global e-commerce company, I've learned that the cheapest moment to fix these problems is before the first workload lands. That is what a landing zone is for.

In this article I'll walk through how to build one with Terraform, the decisions behind each part, and the mistakes it protects you from. All the code is open source:

👉 github.com/diogosmoreira84/azure-enterprise-landing-zone

What is a landing zone, really?

A landing zone is the pre-built environment that workloads "land" in. When a new team arrives, the hierarchy, the rules, the network, the logging and the cost controls are already there. Teams move fast; the platform team keeps control.

Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework describes it through eight design areas. You don't need all of them on day one. The reference I built covers the six that matter most for getting started, and leaves identity and billing for later:

Design area Covered How
Billing and Entra tenant Decided once per organisation, outside Terraform
Identity and access A topic for its own article
Resource organisation ✅ Management groups, naming and tagging
Network topology ✅ Hub and spoke, NSGs, optional firewall, private DNS
Security ✅ Deny-by-default NSGs, no public IPs in Corp
Management ✅ Central Log Analytics and Activity Log export
Governance ✅ Azure Policy guardrails and budgets
Platform automation ✅ Modular Terraform, remote state, CI with security scanning

Let's go through them in the order I'd build them.

Step 1: Organise with management groups

Management groups are folders above subscriptions. Anything you assign to a management group, like a policy or a role, is inherited by every subscription below it. Get the hierarchy right and you configure governance once, instead of once per subscription.

The mistake it saves you from: building the hierarchy around the org chart. Departments change at every reorganisation. "Internal" versus "internet-facing" doesn't. Organise by the rules a workload needs, keep it shallow (three or four levels), and always have a place for the exceptions, so nobody has to bend the production rules.

Step 2: Guardrails with Azure Policy

A guideline is something people forget. A policy is something the platform enforces. I start with three guardrails:

Policy Where Why
Allowed locations Organisation root Data residency and a predictable footprint
Required tags on resource groups Organisation root Every cost and every incident has an owner
No public IPs on network interfaces Corp Internal stays internal

In Terraform, I look up built-in policies by name instead of hard-coding GUIDs, which keeps the code readable:

data "azurerm_policy_definition_built_in" "allowed_locations" {
  display_name = "Allowed locations"
}

resource "azurerm_management_group_policy_assignment" "allowed_locations" {
  name                 = "allowed-locations"
  management_group_id  = var.root_management_group_id
  policy_definition_id = data.azurerm_policy_definition_built_in.allowed_locations.id

  parameters = jsonencode({
    listOfAllowedLocations = { value = var.allowed_locations }
  })
}

The mistake it saves you from: switching straight to "deny" in an existing environment. You will break deployments on a Friday afternoon. In brownfield subscriptions, start with audit, fix what you find, then enforce.

Step 3: One place for logs

When something breaks, or an auditor asks who changed a firewall rule, the answer must be in one place. The landing zone creates a central Log Analytics workspace and sends the subscription Activity Log to it from day one.

The mistake it saves you from: discovering, during an incident review, that the Activity Log you needed is older than the 90 days Azure keeps by default.

Step 4: A network you won't have to rebuild

The landing zone uses a hub-and-spoke topology. Shared network services live in a central hub. Every workload gets its own spoke, peered to the hub.

Each spoke gets its own subnets, a deny-by-default NSG on every subnet, and, when the firewall is on, a route that sends all outbound traffic through the hub.

A few lessons I'd tattoo on every platform team:

  • Plan the address space once, for the whole company. Overlapping ranges are the one networking mistake you cannot fix without rebuilding. In the code, the hub subnets are calculated from a single range with cidrsubnet(), so there's no manual subnet maths to get wrong.
  • Reserve the special subnets on day one. Firewall, Gateway and Bastion need exact names and minimum sizes.
  • Peering is not transitive. Spoke A can't reach spoke B through the hub unless something routes the traffic. That's the firewall's job.
  • Make expensive things optional. Azure Firewall has a significant fixed monthly cost, so it's one variable away, but off by default.

And adding a new workload is data, not code:

spokes = {
  payments = {
    address_space = "10.20.0.0/16"
    subnets       = { api = "10.20.1.0/24", db = "10.20.2.0/24" }
  }
}

Step 5: Costs under control from day one

Cost is a design area like any other. Three things go a long way:

  1. Standard tags on everything, enforced by policy, so every euro can be traced to a team. Optional tags are missing within weeks.
  2. A monthly budget with alerts at 50%, 80% and 100%.
  3. A forecast alert, which is the one that actually helps: an alert at 100% of actual spend tells you about money that's already gone.

Step 6: Treat the platform like a product

A landing zone isn't a one-off project. It's a product the platform team runs and evolves, so it deserves the same engineering discipline:

  • Remote state in a hardened storage account: TLS 1.2, no public blobs, shared keys disabled (Entra ID only), versioning and soft delete. The repository includes a small bootstrap/ to create it.
  • One module per responsibility: governance, logging, connectivity, cost.
  • Validation on inputs that can be wrong, like CIDR ranges and naming prefixes.
  • CI on every pull request: terraform fmt, validate, TFLint and a Checkov security scan. Every skipped security check is skipped on purpose, with the reason written next to the resource.

What a production landing zone adds

This reference shows the patterns. For a real company, you'd add identity (Entra ID groups mapped to roles, Privileged Identity Management, break-glass accounts), subscription vending so every workload gets its own subscription, separate platform subscriptions, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and hybrid connectivity. For large estates, Microsoft's own Azure Landing Zones Terraform modules are a solid, supported baseline.

But the principles stay the same, and they are the part that matters: decide the rules before the workloads arrive, enforce them in code, and make the right thing the easy thing.

Key takeaways

  • Build the foundations before the first workload lands. Fixing them later means changing things that are already in production.
  • Organise by the rules workloads need, not by the org chart, and keep the hierarchy shallow.
  • Enforce, don't recommend. Policies, tags and budgets only work when the platform applies them.
  • Plan the network once. Overlapping address ranges are the mistake you can't undo.
  • Run the landing zone like a product, with code review, CI and security scanning.

Try it

The full code, with a step-by-step guide, is here:

👉 github.com/diogosmoreira84/azure-enterprise-landing-zone

With the default settings it costs very little to run, so you can deploy it in a personal subscription and explore.

In the next articles of this series I'll go deeper into each area, starting with Azure Policy: how to roll out guardrails without breaking production.

What was the first thing that went wrong in your cloud environment because the foundations weren't there? I'd love to hear it in the comments.

title: Autopsy #08: Surviving a 4-Hour Tunnel: Local-First Sync & Conflicts
description:
Three Hours of Teammate Commits Erased at Tunnel Exit

A two-line PR replaced the incremental patch endpoint with a "simpler" PUT /api/docs/:id full-document upload triggered on window online events. It passed QA on office fiber in 40 ms.

Then a product manager boarded a 4-hour train with a 14-page specification open in two browser tabs. While the train passed through dead zones, three office teammates merged 24 revisions (rev: 95 → rev: 118). When the train exited the final tunnel, both offline tabs woke up, flushed PUT /api/docs/42 with rev: 94, and silently overwrote three hours of work.

  • T+00:00: Deployed PR #1412. Traveler opens document 42 (rev: 94) in two tabs before entering tunnel LTE dead zone.
  • T+02:15: Three office teammates merge 24 consecutive revisions (rev: 95 → rev: 118).
  • T+04:08: Train exits the final tunnel; both tabs fire online simultaneously and send PUT /api/docs/42 with updatedAt: 1763318529000.
  • T+04:09: Gateway logs 200 OK, overwriting rev: 118 with rev: 94 + 1 local paragraph.

Why ETag 412 Inverted the Data Loss

In #inc-storage, the on-call engineer blamed missing optimistic locking and added an If-Match ETag check on PUT /api/docs/:id. Unit tests confirmed stale writes returned 412 Precondition Failed.

In production, that patch inverted the disaster. When the next offline laptop reconnected, the server rejected the PUT with 412, and the client's catch handler purged the local IndexedDB outbox, destroying the traveler's 4 hours of offline edits instead.

Five Layers Between Offline Edits and Clean Merge

Surviving a 4-hour disconnect requires five coordinated guarantees: durable IndexedDB outbox transactions, conflict-free delta merging instead of full-document replacement, Web Locks around multi-tab outbox reads, idempotent operation replay over flaky 4G, and a single elected sync leader per origin.

Step Through the Tunnel Reconnect Storm

Dissecting the Conflict Storm

01 → 02: The Outbox Transaction That Aborted Silently

Inspecting the traveler's IndexedDB outbox store showed gaps between local edits: a QuotaExceededError on an unawaited readwrite transaction had silently rolled back two paragraphs before the tunnel even ended. Under IndexedDB Transactions & Quotas, transactions auto-commit or abort when the microtask queue drains, and quota pressure requires explicit await tx.done handling.

Even for the deltas that persisted, the client threw away operation history on reconnect and serialized the entire document into PUT /api/docs/42 with a wall-clock updatedAt. Relying on full-snapshot Last-Write-Wins instead of Local-First Sync & CRDTs guarantees that whoever reconnects last erases every concurrent edit.

02 → 03: Two Tabs Draining One Outbox at Once

Server access logs showed two identical PUT /api/docs/42 requests arriving 6 ms apart from the same user_id and device_id. Both open tabs received the window.online event simultaneously, read the same IndexedDB outbox rows, and raced to flush them.

Wrapping outbox drains in navigator.locks.request('sync-doc-42', ...) via BroadcastChannel & Web Locks serializes access across tabs on the same origin so two tabs never read and mutate the same outbox cursor concurrently.

03 → 04: Flaky 4G Retries Replaying Non-Idempotent Deltas

Leaving the tunnel, cellular handoffs dropped two POST /ops responses after the server had already applied them. Without operation IDs, the retry loop re-appended the same text insertions twice. Attaching deterministic opId keys with Idempotency & Optimistic Queues lets the server deduplicate replayed deltas safely.

04 → 05: One Sync Leader Per Origin

Finally, having two tabs both open WebSocket sync streams doubled reconnection traffic and applied server snapshots out of order. Using Cross-Tab Leader Election (navigator.locks + BroadcastChannel), only one tab holds the live WebSocket and relays merged CRDT updates to sibling tabs.

Serializing Sync With Web Locks and CRDT Deltas 

async function syncOutbox(docId: string, ydoc: Y.Doc) {
  await navigator.locks.request(`sync-${docId}`, async () => {
    const ops = await readPendingOps(docId);
    if (ops.length === 0) return;
    const res = await fetch(`/api/docs/${docId}/ops`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Idempotency-Key': ops[0].batchId },
      body: JSON.stringify({ sv: Y.encodeStateVector(ydoc), ops }),
    });
    if (res.ok) await markOpsSynced(ops);
  });
}

Architectural Invariants:

  • Never overwrite concurrent history with full PUTs: Persist and sync operation deltas or CRDT state vectors, never wall-clock full-document snapshots.
  • Lock multi-tab outbox drains: Gate IndexedDB outbox reads and network flushes with navigator.locks.request().
  • Preserve local outbox on 4xx/5xx: Only delete outbox entries after an explicit server acknowledgment; rebase on conflict instead of purging.

Golden Rule: Offline-first sync fails when two tabs race or one snapshot overwrites another; merge CRDT deltas under a single Web Lock leader.

title: Reduce Codebase Complexity and Dependencies by Using Python's Standard Library Instead of External Packages
description:
The Dependency Trap: Why Modern Developers Overlook Built-In Power

Modern software engineering suffers from a pervasive cognitive shortcut: when faced with a structural requirement, the reflex is to query PyPI rather than inspect the Python installation already sitting on disk. This reflex is not accidental; it is engineered by the high-visibility marketing of third-party packages, searchable documentation indexes, and tutorial ecosystems that treat the standard library as a rudimentary set of primitives rather than a production-grade toolkit. When a developer defaults to external libraries for tasks already solved by native modules like pathlib, itertools, or collections, they introduce structural friction into the codebase.

The cultural habit of reaching for external dependencies first stems from a friction asymmetry. PyPI packages often present polished, specialized APIs tailored to a single niche, whereas the standard library offers general-purpose primitives that require composition. Developers mistake this requirement for compositional thought as missing functionality. Under high-velocity delivery pressures, the path of least resistance becomes pip install, bypassing any architectural evaluation of what Python ships with natively.

This habitual bypass exacts a severe mechanical toll on the software lifecycle:

  • Dependency Tree Expansion: Importing a single external utility package forces the package manager to resolve its transitive dependencies. A lightweight helper package often pulls in a dozen sub-dependencies, exponentially expanding the local module graph.
  • Supply Chain Attack Surface: Every external package introduces an uncontrolled vector for malicious code injection, typosquatting, or unvetted upstream maintainer updates. The build pipeline breaks or compromises security integrity when a third-party repository changes its internal namespace or gets abandoned.
  • Versioning Deadlocks and Rot: External packages age poorly against core Python interpreter updates. When downstream dependencies lock specific minor versions, the entire environment calcifies, halting Python upgrades and exposing the application to unpatched runtime vulnerabilities.

When evaluating whether to use a third-party package versus a native module, architectural decisions must be governed by mechanical clarity rather than API convenience. If a native module can implement the core logic with standard data structures, introducing an external package degrades maintainability by binding the system's runtime stability to external release cycles.

Hidden Gems: High-Performance Standard Library Modules You Are Probably Ignoring

The modern Python developer workflow suffers from a severe friction asymmetry. When faced with path manipulation, sequence iteration, or caching, the reflex is to execute pip install. PyPI packages present polished, highly specific domain APIs that require zero composition, whereas standard library modules offer general-purpose primitives that demand a small amount of structural thought. Under velocity pressures, developers bypass architectural evaluation entirely. Mechanically, this habit forces a transitive dependency resolution cascade. Pulling in a single external utility package drags along its entire local module graph, bloating your import tree and exponentially expanding the surface area for runtime state corruption.

This dependency bloat introduces direct supply chain vulnerabilities. External packages act as unvetted vectors for malicious code injection, typosquatting, and upstream namespace disruptions that instantly fracture build pipelines. Furthermore, downstream version locks calcify the virtual environment. As packages lock themselves to rigid interpreter constraints, they block core Python upgrades, leaving applications exposed to unpatched runtime vulnerabilities. Opting for native modules like pathlib, itertools, functools, and collections decouples system runtime stability from external release cycles, shielding your codebase from upstream rot.

When evaluating how to handle structural data transformations and filesystem operations, architectural choices must be governed by mechanical clarity over API convenience:

  • pathlib vs. string concatenation and os.path: Standard string paths handle file paths as raw byte streams, leaving your code vulnerable to cross-platform separator breaks (Windows backslashes vs. POSIX slashes). pathlib treats paths as rich objects, enforcing mechanical safety by abstracting OS-level translation directly through C-level system calls.
  • itertools vs. manual list comprehensions for heavy iteration: Manual loops allocate entire intermediate lists in RAM, causing memory pressure spikes and garbage collection thrashing. itertools operates via lazy evaluation, streaming items lazily through C-implemented iterators that maintain a near-zero memory footprint.
  • functools.lru_cache vs. custom dict-based memoization: Writing manual caching logic invites cache invalidation bugs and memory leaks from unbounded growth. functools.lru_cache provides a compiled, thread-safe least-recently-used eviction mechanism that automatically drops stale states before memory exhaustion occurs.

The optimal solution for high-performance operations is to default exclusively to these native primitives. They execute directly inside Python's C-layer runtime, bypassing the interpreter overhead associated with third-party Python wrappers. However, this native-first rule stops working under precise conditions: when you require complex asynchronous streaming primitives, enterprise-grade database serialization layers, or cryptographic primitives that demand specialized C extensions not present in the standard library.

A typical choice error occurs when developers reach for external utility libraries out of habit for tasks fully solved by collections.defaultdict or collections.Counter. The mechanism of failure here is unnecessary object instantiation overhead and polluted site-packages directories. Therefore, adopt this strict architectural rule: if a problem can be solved by composing standard library primitives without writing custom state management, you must reject external packages entirely. By enforcing this constraint, you eliminate supply chain vectors, guarantee interpreter upgrade paths, and preserve long-term maintainability.

Refactoring for Resilience: A Strategic Blueprint for LeanRefactoring for Resilience: A Strategic Blueprint for Leaner Codebases Eliminating preventable codebase complexity requires shifting from passive dependency accumulation to an aggressive architectural audit. When developers execute an unvetted pip install to solve a localized problem, they trigger a cascade of invisible mechanical failures within the virtual environment. The Anatomy of Dependency Bloat and Transitive Failure Every external package introduces a transitive dependency tree. Importing a single helper utility forces the local module graph to expand exponentially, pulling in dozens of unvetted third-party sub-packages. This mechanical expansion enlarges the attack surface area for runtime state corruption. If an upstream maintainer experiences a namespace hijack, typosquatting attack, or a breaking release, your build pipeline snaps instantly. Furthermore, downstream version constraints calcify the virtual environment. These version locks bind your application to rigid interpreter boundaries, blocking core Python upgrades and leaving production deployments permanently exposed to unpatched runtime vulnerabilities. Resilience demands decoupling system stability from external release cycles. The Systematic Native Refactoring Framework To purge this overhead, developers must systematically evaluate legacy patterns against Python's native C-layer primitives. Native modules bypass the interpreter overhead inherent to third-party Python wrappers by executing directly inside optimized C structures. * Path Manipulation: Replace fragile string concatenation and legacy os.path scripts with pathlib. Pathlib treats paths as rich objects, executing OS-level translations via low-level system calls to prevent cross-platform separator crashes between Windows and POSIX environments. * Memory-Efficient Iteration: Discard manual list comprehensions that pre-allocate bulky data structures in RAM. Use itertools to stream items via C-implemented iterators using lazy evaluation, maintaining a near-zero memory footprint by avoiding intermediate RAM allocations and garbage collection thrashing. * Compiled Caching: Drop custom dictionary memoization implementations prone to memory leaks. Deploy functools.lru_cache to leverage a compiled, thread-safe least-recently-used eviction mechanism that automatically purges stale states before RAM exhaustion occurs. * Optimized Data Structures: Swap custom lookup or counting logic for collections.defaultdict and collections.Counter, eliminating unnecessary object instantiation overhead and site-packages directory pollution. Decision Rules, Choice Errors, and Boundary Limits Adopting native primitives requires strict architectural boundaries to prevent engineering friction. The core decision rule is absolute: Reject external packages entirely if a problem can be solved by composing standard library primitives without introducing custom state management. Typical choice errors stem from friction asymmetry—the psychological trap where developers choose a polished, niche third-party API over a general-purpose standard library primitive simply to save a few lines of composition code. Bypassing architectural evaluation for immediate development velocity introduces long-term maintenance debt. However, the native standard library has strict functional boundaries. The standard library approach breaks down and must yield to external packages under specific, high-stress conditions: * Complex asynchronous streaming primitives that demand specialized event-loop scheduling beyond standard library concurrency models. * Enterprise-grade database serialization layers requiring heavy ORM relational mapping and complex transaction state machines. * Cryptographic primitives demanding specialized, heavily optimized C extensions completely absent from native distributions. Outside of these explicit exceptions, defaulting to Python's native standard library preserves runtime stability, minimizes security surface areas, and guarantees long-term codebase maintainability.

title: FaceScored: an AI face score you can audit, computed entirely in your browser
description:
FaceScored is a free AI face rating tool that performs the whole analysis inside your browser tab.

What happens to the photo

Nothing is uploaded. The app reads the photo locally, runs MediaPipe face landmark detection, measures facial symmetry and proportion ratios, then renders a score next to the formula that produced it. No account, no server-side copy of the image.

How the symmetry number is built

The symmetry test averages the horizontal imbalance across six landmark pairs, normalises it by face width, and applies the same formula the homepage rating uses. Two of the pairs are the inner and outer eye corners, measured against the vertical reference line through the face. The result also surfaces the two largest measured deviations, so the score can be read against the measurements behind it.

  • Face rater: https://facescored.com
  • Symmetry breakdown: https://facescored.com/face-symmetry/

Why two photos of the same face score differently

The calculation works on landmark positions in a 2D image, so camera perspective, head rotation, expression and landmark-detection noise all move those positions. The site states this itself and does not present the output as a medical assessment.

Free vs paid

Free: overall symmetry score, left and right mirrored comparisons, deviation list, browser-local processing.

Optional full report (currently listed at $16.99, one-time): six dimensions - symmetry, proportions, jawline, eye-angle balance, face shape, skin clarity - written feature notes, heuristic percentile estimates and a printable PDF. Percentiles are model heuristics, not measured population rankings.

title: SAP-C03 starts on 17 November: what actually changed
description:
If you're studying for the AWS Solutions Architect – Professional exam, the version changes next week. The last day to sit SAP-C02 is 16 November 2026. SAP-C03 starts on 17 November.

I went through AWS's new exam guide and their side-by-side comparison. This is the short version.

What stays the same

  • 75 questions (65 scored), 180 minutes, $300
  • Multiple choice and multiple response
  • Either version gets you the same certification

What's different

The passing score drops from 750 to 720. That surprised me. My guess is that it reflects the wider scope rather than an easier exam.

Five domains instead of four. The domains are now grouped by theme (design, security, cost, resilience and operations) instead of by type of project. Cost now has its own domain at 15%, so expect more questions on pricing models, data transfer costs, tagging and chargeback.

Generative AI is in, and it's the biggest new area. Amazon Bedrock covers RAG with Knowledge Bases, agents with Bedrock AgentCore, and Guardrails for content filtering. There's also monitoring and cost control for AI workloads: batching, caching and cross-Region inference.

Other new topics:

  • post-quantum cryptography with KMS
  • IAM Roles Anywhere for hybrid workloads
  • EKS Pod Identity
  • VPC Lattice and Cloud WAN
  • multi-tenant isolation
  • IPv6 and dual-stack networks
  • Resilience Hub and Fault Injection Service

Now out of scope:

  • all the IoT services
  • WorkSpaces and AppStream 2.0
  • Elastic Transcoder and Kinesis Video Streams
  • a long list of smaller services, including Lightsail, Pinpoint, Proton and Service Catalog

The individual AI services (Comprehend, Textract, Rekognition and so on) are no longer listed one by one. They now come under Bedrock and SageMaker AI.

Which one should you take?

  • Ready by 16 November? Take SAP-C02, because most study material still matches it.
  • Sitting on or after 17 November? Add Bedrock (RAG, agents and Guardrails) and the cost topics to your plan. Spend less time on IoT and end-user computing.

Practicing for SAP-C03

I built ExamPark, a free practice exam site. The Solutions Architect – Professional exam there already follows the SAP-C03 guide: a full 75-question exam, no sign-up, with an explanation for every option. The questions are original, AI-assisted, and checked against the AWS docs and exam guide. There are no exam dumps.

  • Full breakdown of the changes: https://exampark.app/guides/sap-c03-changes/
  • Free SAP-C03 practice exam: https://exampark.app/exams/aws-solutions-architect-professional/

Source for the changes: AWS, "Comparison of SAP-C02 and SAP-C03" in the AWS Certification docs.

Good luck if you're sitting it. If you've taken the new version, I'd love to hear how it went.

title: How Yoast SEO Actually Works Under the Hood: A Technical Breakdown for WordPress Developers
description:
Yoast SEO from a Systems Perspective

Hầu hết tài liệu về Yoast SEO mô tả nó từ góc độ người dùng cuối: điền focus keyphrase, chờ đèn xanh, đăng bài. Nhưng với người xây dựng hoặc quản lý WordPress từ góc độ kỹ thuật, câu hỏi thực sự là: Yoast SEO làm gì với database, với DOM và với HTTP response — và làm thế nào nó có thể tích hợp hoặc xung đột với các hệ thống khác trong stack?

Bài này phân tích cơ chế hoạt động thực tế của Yoast SEO: cách nó ghi metadata, tạo sitemap, inject schema, và những điểm cần chú ý khi triển khai trong môi trường có nhiều plugin hoặc automation pipeline.

Lớp metadata: Yoast ghi dữ liệu đi đâu?

Khi người dùng điền Tiêu đề SEO và Thẻ mô tả trong editor, Yoast không ghi vào bảng wp_posts. Toàn bộ metadata của Yoast lưu trong wp_postmeta với các key có prefix _yoast_wpseo_:

  • _yoast_wpseo_title — tiêu đề SEO tùy chỉnh (nếu khác template mặc định)
  • _yoast_wpseo_metadesc — thẻ mô tả
  • _yoast_wpseo_focuskw — focus keyphrase
  • _yoast_wpseo_linkdex — điểm SEO (0–100) được tính toán và cache lại
  • _yoast_wpseo_content_score — điểm khả năng đọc
  • _yoast_wpseo_canonical — canonical URL tùy chỉnh nếu có
  • _yoast_wpseo_meta-robots-noindex — chỉ thị noindex cụ thể cho bài

Đây là điểm quan trọng khi xây dựng automation pipeline: nếu muốn ghi metadata hàng loạt qua code (ví dụ từ một AI content pipeline), anh em cần update_post_meta() vào đúng các key này, không phải ghi vào post title hay excerpt thông thường.

Lưu ý khi dùng Yoast với WP-CLI hoặc REST API: Yoast có REST API endpoint riêng (/wp/v2/yoast_head) trả về rendered head HTML. Nhưng để ghi ngược lại metadata qua REST, cần đảm bảo schema của Yoast đã đăng ký field trong register_rest_field() — không phải mặc định của WordPress core.

XML Sitemap: cơ chế tạo và cập nhật

Yoast không tạo sitemap bằng cách generate file tĩnh vào filesystem. Thay vào đó, sitemap được serve động qua WordPress rewrite rules. Khi truy cập ten-website.com/sitemap_index.xml, WordPress xử lý request qua query var sitemap=1 và Yoast intercept để render XML output.

Cấu trúc sitemap index phân cấp như sau:

  • sitemap_index.xml — file index chứa danh sách sitemap con
  • post-sitemap.xml — tất cả bài viết (post_type=post)
  • page-sitemap.xml — tất cả trang (post_type=page)
  • product-sitemap.xml — sản phẩm WooCommerce nếu có
  • category-sitemap.xml, post_tag-sitemap.xml — taxonomy nếu được bật

Sitemap được cache trong wp_options với key wpseo_sitemap_cache_validator. Cache bị invalidate mỗi khi post được publish, update hoặc delete — trigger qua WordPress hooks publish_post, save_post, delete_post.

Ngoài ra, Yoast gửi XML-RPC ping đến Google và Bing mỗi khi sitemap được cập nhật — hành vi này có thể tắt bằng filter wpseo_allow_xml_sitemap_ping nếu không muốn.

Schema injection: Yoast xây dựng JSON-LD thế nào?

Yoast inject schema markup dưới dạng JSON-LD vào <head> của mỗi trang. Thay vì schema phẳng, Yoast dùng Graph approach — một JSON-LD object duy nhất chứa nhiều entity liên kết nhau qua @id:

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@graph": [
    { "@type": "WebPage", "@id": "https://example.com/post/#webpage" },
    { "@type": "Article", "@id": "https://example.com/post/#article" },
    { "@type": "Person", "@id": "https://example.com/#/schema/person/xxx" },
    { "@type": "Organization", "@id": "https://example.com/#organization" },
    { "@type": "WebSite", "@id": "https://example.com/#website" }
  ]
}

Graph approach này có ưu điểm là tránh khai báo entity trùng lặp và cho phép extend schema bằng cách thêm node mới vào graph thay vì sửa vào JSON đã có. Developer có thể hook vào wpseo_schema_graph_pieces để thêm custom schema piece hoặc modify piece đã có.

Focus keyphrase analysis: scoring engine hoạt động ra sao?

Hệ thống đèn màu của Yoast không phải heuristic đơn giản. Scoring engine chạy phía client (JavaScript) và phía server:

  • Client-side analysis: Chạy trong browser khi người dùng đang soạn thảo. Yoast dùng thư viện JavaScript yoastseo (open source, có trên npm) để parse nội dung bài, tách câu, tính mật độ từ khóa và score từng assessment.
  • Server-side scoring: Điểm cuối cùng được lưu vào _yoast_wpseo_linkdex và _yoast_wpseo_content_score khi save post.

Mỗi assessment (keyword in title, keyword density, text length, image alt tags...) trả về một trong ba trạng thái: GOOD, OK, BAD — ánh xạ ra đèn xanh, cam, đỏ. Điểm tổng là weighted average của tất cả assessments.

Điều quan trọng cần hiểu: scoring engine của Yoast là rule-based checklist, không phải mô hình ML. Nó không dự đoán khả năng xếp hạng — nó kiểm tra danh sách tiêu chí kỹ thuật xác định trước. Đèn xanh chỉ có nghĩa là bài pass checklist, không có nghĩa gì hơn.

Khi nhìn vào hệ sinh thái plugin SEO WordPress rộng hơn — không chỉ Yoast — và cách các plugin như Rank Math hay Yoast so sánh với nhau ở tầng kiến trúc, bài viết phân tích toàn diện về Yoast SEO cung cấp bức tranh rõ hơn từ góc độ người triển khai.

Xung đột plugin: vấn đề meta duplication

Vấn đề phổ biến nhất khi Yoast xung đột với plugin khác là meta duplication: hai plugin cùng output <title> tag hoặc cùng ghi og:title vào head, dẫn đến Google và Facebook đọc giá trị khác nhau.

Yoast handle việc này bằng cách:

  • Remove WordPress default title output: remove_action('wp_head', '_wp_render_title_tag', 1)
  • Remove theme title nếu theme dùng wp_title()

Rank Math và AIOSEO làm tương tự — đây là lý do không thể chạy song song hai plugin SEO: cả hai đều cố remove title của nhau và inject title của mình, kết quả là race condition không đoán được.

Cách kiểm tra xung đột: Inspect source HTML của bất kỳ trang nào, tìm trong <head> xem có nhiều hơn một <title> tag hoặc nhiều og:title không. Nếu có, đang có plugin conflict.

Tích hợp Yoast với AI automation pipeline

Khi xây dựng pipeline tự động hóa nội dung trên WordPress — ví dụ AI viết bài và điền metadata hàng loạt — cần hiểu cách Yoast expect data được ghi vào.

Có hai cách tiếp cận:

Cách 1: Ghi trực tiếp vào wp_postmeta

Dùng update_post_meta($post_id, '_yoast_wpseo_title', $seo_title) và update_post_meta($post_id, '_yoast_wpseo_metadesc', $meta_desc). Cách này nhanh và không phụ thuộc vào Yoast API, nhưng cần đảm bảo format đúng (plain string, không có HTML tags).

Cách 2: Dùng Yoast REST API hoặc plugin-specific hooks

Yoast expose một số filter cho phép can thiệp vào quá trình render: wpseo_title, wpseo_metadesc, wpseo_canonical. Dùng các filter này nếu muốn dynamic override mà không lưu vào database.

Onic AI SEO Automation xử lý vấn đề này bằng cách nhận diện Yoast tự động và ghi tiêu đề SEO, thẻ mô tả trực tiếp vào đúng trường của Yoast khi tối ưu hàng loạt — không cần can thiệp thủ công từng bài. Đây là ví dụ về cách một automation layer cần "biết" cấu trúc lưu trữ của từng plugin SEO để ghi đúng chỗ, thay vì ghi vào post title thông thường rồi bị Yoast override.

Sitemap và crawl budget: điểm cần lưu ý cho large-scale site

Với website có hàng trăm nghìn URL (WooCommerce lớn, news site), cần chú ý đến cách Yoast handle sitemap size:

  • Yoast tự động split sitemap khi vượt quá 1,000 URLs mỗi file (configurable qua filter wpseo_sitemap_entries_per_page)
  • Với large catalog, sitemap generation có thể gây timeout nếu chạy on-request. Nên pre-generate bằng WP-CLI: wp yoast index --reindex
  • Cân nhắc exclude post types không cần index (custom post type nội bộ, revision logs) khỏi sitemap qua Yoast Settings để giảm crawl budget lãng phí

Kết luận: Yoast SEO trong kiến trúc WordPress

Yoast SEO là một metadata management layer đặt trên WordPress core — không phải một công cụ "magic SEO". Hiểu cơ chế lưu trữ trong wp_postmeta, cách sitemap được serve động qua rewrite rules, Graph schema approach và scoring engine rule-based giúp developer tích hợp đúng, debug nhanh hơn và xây dựng automation pipeline không phá vỡ dữ liệu hiện có.

Khi kết hợp Yoast với AI automation pipeline, điểm mấu chốt là pipeline cần biết Yoast lưu metadata đi đâu (_yoast_wpseo_* keys trong wp_postmeta) và ghi vào đúng chỗ — đây là sự khác biệt giữa automation hoạt động đúng và automation tạo ra dữ liệu không nhất quán.

Bài gốc: https://onic.vn/kien-thuc/yoast-seo/

title: Introducing Ovie Lang
description:
A Systems Programming Language.

Ovie combines low-level programming capabilities with high-level language features, providing developers with direct control, expressive syntax and a structured development environment.

A Language with Its Own Identity
Ovie introduces its own declaration and output vocabulary:

oya name = "Shedrack"
oya language = "Ovie"
mut age = 31
seeAm "Hello, " + name
seeAm language
seeAm age
oya: immutable declaration.
mut: mutable declaration.
seeAm: output with a newline.
print: output without a newline.
Compiler Architecture
Ovie has two compiler implementations:

oviec: The Rust-based compiler.
oviev: The self-hosted compiler written in Ovie (.ov).
Aproko
Aproko (an Urhobo word) is the built-in analyser. It runs on every oviec run. It catches bad keywords, explains runtime errors, and teaches best practices.

The Official Project
Ovie Lang is the official organization for the language. Developed under Nashedy Ltd.

Official repository: https://github.com/Ovie-Lang/ovie X: https://x.com/Ovielang GitHub org: https://github.com/Ovie-Lang

title: Tyrus - TypeScript syntax. Rust semantics. A programming language made for devs.
description:
Four months ago, I got curious about building my own programming language.

All I wanted was for it to be written in Rust and compiled to native code. My initial goal was simply to print "Hello World" in the terminal. I pulled it off, and from there, I kept adding more features.

I knew absolutely nothing about compilers when I started. Along the way, I discovered a whole new world of concepts: parsing, semantic analysis, AST, ASan, LSan, UB, LLVM, IR, drop glue, double free, LSP, and so on.

Today, I feel like I know maybe 5% of it. Now it's time to fix all the bugs that will inevitably show up.

So I created Tyrus: TypeScript syntax. Rust semantics.

What is already implemented:

  • Lexer, parser, and AST
  • Type checker with inference and generics
  • Borrow checker with NLL
  • LLVM codegen
  • REPL with JIT
  • Async functions, async/await, and task management
  • Arrays, tuples, Map, Set, and collection methods
  • Option/Result, comptime, defer/errdefer, exhaustive pattern matching, and pipe operator
  • Validator Decorations
  • Automated tests and a CLI to create, check, build, run, and watch projects
  • LSP for VS Code, Neovim, Zed, Kate, and IntelliJ/WebStorm
  • WASM playground
  • Native modules: fs, os, net, http, process, temporal, crypto, algorithm, archive, compress, db, encoding, stream, task, and others

https://tyruslang.org

What feature would you implement if you were building your own programming language?
