title: Next.js vs React in 2026: Key Differences and When to Use Each
description:
If you're starting a new React project in 2026, the real choice usually isn't "React or Next.js". It's whether you need React on its own with Vite, or React plus a framework for routing, server rendering and backend endpoints. I build client sites and apps for a living, so this breakdown comes from the angle of SEO, first-load speed and long-term maintenance. It covers Next.js 16, React Router and Vite, with the current versions checked against npm and the official docs.

Next.js vs React is one of the first questions that comes up when a founder or developer plans a new web project, and it's a slightly unfair matchup. React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Next.js is a framework built on top of React that adds routing, server rendering, data fetching and a production build setup. So the real question isn't "which one?" but "do I need React on its own, or React plus a framework?" This guide answers that from the angle of building client sites and apps, where SEO, speed and maintenance all matter.

Versions and recommendations below were rechecked on November 17, 2026 against npm, the official React docs (react.dev) and the Next.js docs and release notes (nextjs.org).

Quick answer: React is the UI library; Next.js is React plus routing, server rendering, static generation and backend endpoints. Choose Next.js for public websites where SEO and fast first loads matter (marketing sites, blogs, e-commerce, SaaS landing pages). Choose plain React with Vite for apps behind a login, internal tools, or front ends that talk to a separate backend. If you're learning, learn React first, then Next.js. Every Next.js app is written in React, so nothing you learn is wasted.

What React and Next.js Actually Are

React gives you components, state and hooks. It doesn't decide how pages are routed, how data is loaded or how the app is served. You pick those pieces yourself, usually with a build tool like Vite and a router library. At the time of writing (November 2026), the latest stable React release on npm is 19.3.1.

Next.js is a React framework maintained by Vercel. Its App Router, built around React Server Components, lets parts of a page render on the server and send less JavaScript to the browser. It also handles file-based routing, layouts, image optimization and backend endpoints (Route Handlers). The latest stable version on npm is Next.js 16.4 (16.4.6 as of November 17, 2026). Next.js 16 made Turbopack the default bundler, added Cache Components and renamed middleware.ts to proxy.ts, and it needs Node.js 20.9 or newer.

The official React docs now recommend starting new apps with a framework. They list Next.js (App Router), React Router and Expo (for native apps) as the main options, and they still document how to build a React app from scratch with tools like Vite when a framework doesn't fit. Create React App is no longer the recommended way to start; the React team deprecated it in 2025.

Difference Between React and Next.js: Side-by-Side

Next.js vs React at a glance (November 2026)

Feature React (with Vite) Next.js
What it is UI library Full-stack React framework
Rendering Client-side rendering (CSR) by default CSR, SSR, SSG and ISR, plus Server Components
Routing Add a library (e.g. React Router) Built-in file-based App Router with layouts
SEO Needs extra work; content often loads after JavaScript runs Strong by default, since HTML is rendered on the server or at build time
Performance Fast for app-like UIs; larger initial JS bundle Less client JS with Server Components, built-in image and font optimization
Learning curve Lower: just React and a few libraries Higher: server vs client components, caching, rendering modes
Backend / API routes None; you need a separate backend Route Handlers and Server Actions built in
Build tool Vite (or Parcel, Rsbuild) Turbopack by default in Next.js 16
Hosting Any static host or CDN Vercel, any Node.js or Docker host; static export possible
Cost to run Usually free on static hosts Free tiers exist; server rendering can add hosting cost at scale
Best fit Dashboards, internal tools, apps behind a login Marketing sites, blogs, e-commerce, SaaS with public pages

Next.js vs React JS: Which Is Better?

Neither is better in general, because Next.js is React with extra structure. The better choice depends on who visits your app and how:

  • Strangers find it on Google or social media? Next.js. Rendered HTML, metadata APIs and fast first loads help search and link previews.
  • Users log in before they see anything? Plain React is usually enough, and simpler to host.
  • You need a small backend (forms, webhooks, payments)? Next.js keeps it in one project.
  • You already have a backend in Django, Laravel, Rails, Go or Node? React with Vite talks to it over an API without a second server layer.

Next.js can be overkill for small widgets or private apps, where its server model, caching rules and hosting needs add moving parts.

React vs Next.js Performance and SEO

This is where the difference matters most for a business site.

A plain React app built with Vite ships an almost empty HTML file and builds the page in the browser. Google can render JavaScript, but rendering costs time and other crawlers and link previews may see very little. Users on slow phones also wait for the bundle to download before seeing content.

Next.js sends real HTML first. Pages can be:

  • Statically generated (SSG) at build time, ideal for blogs and landing pages
  • Server-rendered (SSR) on each request, for personalized or frequently changing data
  • Incrementally regenerated (ISR), so static pages refresh in the background without a full rebuild

Server Components push more work to the server and keep client JavaScript smaller, which usually helps Core Web Vitals. Built-in metadata APIs make titles, descriptions and Open Graph tags easier to manage per page, and file-based routing gives every page a clean, readable path (our guide on what a URL is explains how paths and slugs fit together).

Is Next.js faster than React?

For the first page load of a public page, usually yes: the browser gets ready-made HTML instead of waiting for JavaScript. After the app has loaded, a well-built React single-page app can feel just as fast, because both run the same React code in the browser. Next.js isn't automatically fast either. Heavy client components, unoptimized images or careless data fetching can slow any site.

Is Next.js better than React for SEO?

Yes, for pages you want indexed. Search engines get full HTML with your title, headings and content on the first request. You can make a Vite React app SEO-friendly with pre-rendering or a framework, but at that point you're rebuilding what Next.js already provides. For a dashboard behind a login, SEO doesn't matter at all. If you are budgeting for search work rather than picking a stack, see how much SEO costs.

Next.js vs React Router v7 (and Vite)

Many "Next.js vs React" searches are really "Next.js vs React Router" or "Next.js vs React with Vite". These are the three most common ways to start a React web project in 2026:

Next.js vs React Router vs React + Vite

Item Next.js React Router (framework mode) React + Vite (from scratch)
Maintained by Vercel Shopify (the Remix team) Vite and React teams (separate tools)
Type Full-stack framework Full-stack framework or plain router Build tool plus libraries you pick
Server rendering Yes, plus Server Components Yes, per route No (client-side only)
Routing File-based App Router Config or file-based routes You add a router yourself
Data loading Server Components, Server Actions Loaders and actions per route Your choice (fetch, TanStack Query, etc.)
Static/SPA mode Static export SPA and pre-rendering modes SPA by default
Start command npx create-next-app@latest npx create-react-router@latest npm create vite@latest (React template)
Pick it when Public sites, SEO, React Server Components You like web-standard loaders/forms and deploying to many runtimes Learning, dashboards, apps with a separate backend

React Router is the long-time routing library for React; since v7 (when Remix merged into it) it can also act as a full framework. The React docs still call this option "React Router (v7)", while the current release on npm is v8. If you only need client-side navigation, you can use React Router as a plain library inside a Vite app.

Other React frameworks the React docs mention include TanStack Start and RedwoodSDK. They're worth a look, but Next.js and React Router have the largest ecosystems and the most tutorials.

Next.js vs React Native

These solve different problems. React Native builds real iOS and Android apps with React, rendering native UI instead of HTML. Next.js builds websites and web apps. If you need both a website and a mobile app, a common setup is Next.js for the web and React Native (often via Expo, which the React docs recommend for native apps) for mobile, sharing logic and design ideas between them.

Next.js vs React vs Node.js (and Angular)

  • Node.js is a JavaScript runtime that runs code on a server. It isn't a front-end tool. Next.js runs on Node.js when it renders pages on the server.
  • React runs in the browser (and on the server, when a framework uses it there).
  • Next.js combines the two: React for the UI and Node.js for server rendering and API endpoints.
  • Angular is a separate, all-in-one framework from Google with its own conventions and TypeScript-first setup. It competes with React plus a framework, not with React alone.

TypeScript isn't a competitor either. It's a typed version of JavaScript that works with React, Next.js, Node.js and Angular alike, and create-next-app sets it up by default.

Should I Learn React or Next.js First?

Learn React first. Next.js assumes you already understand components, props, state, hooks and JSX, and its extra ideas (server vs client components, caching, rendering modes) are easier once React itself feels natural. A practical path:

  1. Learn React basics with a small Vite project: components, props, state, effects and forms.
  2. Build one small app that calls a public API (our guide on what an API is covers the basics).
  3. Move to Next.js: routing, layouts, Server Components, data fetching and metadata.
  4. Deploy it on a free tier so you understand builds, environment variables and domains.

If you already know React well, you can start straight with Next.js. Most of what's new is about where code runs, not how React works.

When to Use Next.js

Next.js is usually the better call when:

  • Search traffic matters. Marketing sites, blogs, documentation and product pages benefit from server-rendered HTML.
  • You want one codebase for front end and light backend. Form handlers, webhooks and small APIs can live in Route Handlers.
  • The project will grow. Layouts, nested routes and conventions keep a larger app organized.
  • You want sensible defaults. Image optimization, code splitting and routing work out of the box.

A typical client scenario: a startup needs a fast landing page, a blog for content marketing and a signup flow. Next.js covers all three in one project.

When Plain React (Vite) Is Enough

Plain React with Vite is often the simpler, cheaper choice when:

  • The app lives behind a login (admin panels, internal tools, SaaS dashboards).
  • You already have a separate backend in another language or framework.
  • You want to host anywhere as static files, with no server to run.
  • The team is learning React and wants fewer concepts at once.

Another common scenario: a business needs an internal reporting tool for staff. Nobody searches for it on Google, so the extra rendering features of Next.js add complexity without much payoff.

Hosting and Cost

Both can be hosted for free when a project is small. A Vite React build is just static files, so any static host or CDN works. Next.js runs best on Vercel, but the React docs and Next.js docs both note you can deploy it to any provider that supports Node.js or Docker, or use static export with no server at all (you lose server-only features like SSR and Route Handlers). Costs mostly appear at scale, when server rendering, image optimization and bandwidth add up. For a plain-English breakdown of hosting options, real platform prices and a decision tree for a first stack, see cloud infrastructure explained. For a rough budget for a full site build, read how much a website costs, scope by scope or try the free Website Cost Calculator.

Which Should You Choose?

Next.js or React: quick picks

You are... Pick Why
Founder building a public product or marketing site Next.js SEO, speed and room to grow
Beginner learning front-end React + Vite, then Next.js Fewer concepts at first
Freelancer or agency building client sites Next.js Most client sites need SEO
Team with an existing backend React + Vite No second server layer
E-commerce or content site Next.js SSG/ISR and fast first loads
Internal dashboard or admin panel React + Vite No SEO needs, simple static hosting
Mobile app React Native (Expo) Native iOS and Android UI

AI coding tools can speed up either stack. If you're choosing one, see our Cursor vs Claude Code vs Codex comparison, Windsurf vs Cursor and this list of Cursor alternatives. For what the terminal-based option costs, see Claude Code pricing. If you'd rather prototype in the browser without a local setup, see our roundup of Replit alternatives.

FAQ

What is the main difference between Next.js and React?

React is a UI library; Next.js is a React framework that adds routing, server rendering, static generation and backend endpoints.

Next.js vs React JS: which is better?

Neither is better overall. Next.js is better for public, SEO-driven sites; plain React with Vite is often better for apps behind a login or with a separate backend.

Is React and Next.js the same?

No. Next.js is built on React, so every Next.js app uses React, but React on its own doesn't include routing, server rendering or a backend.

Should I learn React or Next.js first?

React first. Next.js builds on React's components, props, state and hooks, so learning React makes Next.js much easier.

Is Next.js better than React for SEO?

Usually, yes. Next.js sends rendered HTML to crawlers, while a client-rendered React app depends on JavaScript running first.

Is Next.js faster than React?

For the first load of a public page, usually yes, because the HTML arrives ready. Once loaded, a well-built React app can feel just as fast.

Is Next.js harder than React?

A little. You need to understand server vs client components, caching and rendering modes on top of React itself.

When to use Next.js instead of plain React?

Use Next.js for public websites, blogs, e-commerce and SaaS marketing pages. Use plain React for apps behind a login or with a separate backend.

What is the difference between Next.js and React Router?

Both can be full-stack React frameworks. Next.js uses file-based routing and React Server Components; React Router (v7 and later) uses route loaders and actions built on web standards, and can also be used as a plain client-side router.

Is Next.js frontend or backend?

Both. It renders the front end with React and can run backend code through Route Handlers, Server Actions and Server Components.

Does React recommend using a framework?

Yes. The official React docs recommend starting new apps with a framework like Next.js or React Router, while still supporting setups built with tools like Vite.

Do I need Vercel to host Next.js?

No. Vercel builds Next.js and offers the smoothest hosting, but you can run it on any Node.js or Docker host, or export a static site.

Need Help Choosing or Building Your Stack?

If you're weighing Next.js vs React for a new product, a site rebuild or a client project, I can help you pick the right setup and build it properly, from fast, SEO-ready marketing pages to full web apps. Get in touch here and tell me what you're planning.

Originally published at https://www.nilesharma.space/blog/nextjs-vs-react

title: I built a coupon search for AI assistants and Telegram: an MCP server, a bot, and posts that delete themselves
description:
Coupon sites have a reputation problem: half the codes are expired, the other half were never real. I wanted to build one that only shows what a store's affiliate program actually published, with end dates, and then make that data usable where people already are: in their AI assistant and in Telegram.

The result is Coupossum: a website, a public MCP server, a Telegram channel and a Telegram bot, all answering from the same PostgreSQL database. Right now that's about 35,000 codes and deals from about 5,000 stores, refreshed every two hours.

This post covers the parts that turned out to be interesting:

  1. One database, four front ends
  2. An MCP server that AI directories accept
  3. Telegram posts that disappear when the offer ends
  4. A Telegram bot without an AI model
  5. Links that are never opened by a machine

1. One database, four front ends

The data comes from Feedico's Partner API, which aggregates coupons and products from affiliate networks. Coupossum is my own product built on that data, not an official Feedico service.

A sync job pulls coupons every two hours, stores daily, products daily. Everything shown publicly goes through one file of read queries, so the visibility rules exist exactly once:

export const COUPON_VISIBLE = `
  c.is_active AND m.is_eligible AND NOT c.is_duplicate
  AND (c.ends_at IS NULL OR c.ends_at > now())
  AND (c.starts_at IS NULL OR c.starts_at <= now())
  AND (c.link_status IS NULL OR c.link_status NOT IN ${BAD_LINK})
  AND c.is_offer`;

Note ends_at > now() is checked at query time, not at sync time. An offer that ends at 14:00 disappears at 14:00, not at the next sync.

The website, the MCP server and the Telegram bot all import these queries. When I fix a ranking or filter bug, it's fixed everywhere.

Stack: Node 22, Fastify 5, PostgreSQL, the official MCP TypeScript SDK, node:test with PGlite (Postgres in WebAssembly) so the tests run against a real Postgres without Docker. pm2 and cron on a small VPS.

2. An MCP server that AI directories accept

The MCP server is public: https://coupossum.com/mcp, Streamable HTTP, no authentication, read-only. Four tools:

Tool What it does
search_coupons Codes and deals by keyword and/or store, optionally by country
get_store_offers One store's current offers
search_stores Stores by name or domain
search_products Products on sale, with max price and currency

Add it to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or VS Code as a remote MCP server and ask "any codes for Belleek?" or "running shoes under 80 euros on sale".

A few things I learned getting it into directories (Anthropic's connector directory, the official MCP Registry as com.coupossum/coupossum, Glama, LobeHub):

Tool descriptions must describe, not instruct. My first version had rules like "always show both links" inside the tool descriptions. Anthropic's directory policy doesn't allow that: tool descriptions are for what a tool does. The rules moved into the server's instructions, which every client receives on connect:

const server = new McpServer(
  { name: 'coupossum', version: '0.2.5', websiteUrl: SITE.origin },
  { instructions: INSTRUCTIONS },
);

Annotations matter. Every tool is marked readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false, idempotentHint: true and openWorldHint: false, with a human-readable title. Reviewers and clients both use them.

Cap and say so. Every tool returns at most 10 results and tells the model when there are more, with a link to the full list. That keeps answers short and stops a model from paging through the whole database.

Rate limit in memory only. A fixed window per IP, kept in a Map for a few minutes and never written anywhere. Search terms are logged for statistics, IPs are not.

3. Telegram posts that disappear when the offer ends

The Telegram channel @coupossum posts one offer an hour during the day. Each post is a generated image plus a caption:

The images come from @napi-rs/canvas with the Inter font bundled from @fontsource/inter, so the server doesn't depend on system fonts. Store names are text only: no logos, no product photos.

The interesting part isn't posting. It's un-posting. A deals channel full of expired codes is exactly the reputation problem I wanted to avoid, so every post is stored with its message id, and every hour the job checks which posted offers are no longer visible:

for (const p of await endedPosts(db, chat)) {
  try {
    await tg.deleteMessage(chat, p.message_id);
    await setStatus(db, p.id, 'deleted');
    continue;
  } catch (err) {
    if (notFound(err)) { await setStatus(db, p.id, 'gone'); continue; }
  }
  // Telegram may refuse: replace the post instead
  await tg.editPhoto(chat, p.message_id, await endedImage(p), endedCaption(p.store_name));
  await setStatus(db, p.id, 'ended');
}

Why the fallback? The Bot API docs say a message "can only be deleted if it was sent less than 48 hours ago", and in the same list that a channel admin with the delete right "can delete any message there". It's not clear which wins for old channel posts, and most offers run longer than 48 hours. Editing has no such limit for a bot's own messages, so if deletion fails, the post becomes an "offer ended" card without the code. I'm running a test post past the 48-hour mark to find out which path Telegram actually takes.

This is also why Telegram is the first social channel and not Pinterest or WhatsApp. On Pinterest, deleting pins through the API needs an approved developer app, and free schedulers like Buffer can't delete published pins. WhatsApp Channels have no official API at all. A channel only gets added once its expired posts can be removed automatically.

4. A Telegram bot without an AI model

@coupossum_bot answers in private chats: send "homary" and you get that store's current codes; send "shoes 20% off" and you get a keyword search. It also works inline: type @coupossum_bot nike in any chat and pick an offer to share.

No LLM involved. A store name match is checked first, then a plain keyword search over the same queries as the website. It's instant, free to run, and it can't hallucinate a code.

The bot runs on a webhook inside the existing Fastify app, not a separate process. Telegram sends a secret token header with each request, which I derive from the bot token so there's no second secret to manage:

export const webhookSecret = (token) =>
  createHmac('sha256', token).update('coupossum-telegram-webhook').digest('base64url').slice(0, 48);

app.post('/telegram/webhook', async (req, reply) => {
  const got = Buffer.from(String(req.headers['x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token'] || ''));
  if (got.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(got, expected)) return reply.code(403).send('forbidden');
  // handle the update, always answer 200 so Telegram doesn't retry our own errors
});

Nothing about Telegram users is stored. Search terms are logged without user or chat ids; user ids live in memory for a minute for the rate limit.

5. Links that are never opened by a machine

Every store link is an affiliate link, and affiliate networks treat automated clicks as invalid traffic. That shaped more of the design than I expected:

  • Website: store links point to /go/<token> on my own domain (disallowed in robots.txt), and the actual partner URL is opened by JavaScript on a real click. I added this after a crawler that ignores robots.txt started following plain affiliate links.
  • MCP: the server instructions tell assistants to show links and never open them.
  • Telegram: the bot and channel only ever link to the offer's page on coupossum.com, and link previews are switched off, so Telegram's servers never fetch a link on their own.

If you build anything on affiliate data, design for "a human clicked this" from day one.

Try it

  • Website: coupossum.com
  • MCP server: https://coupossum.com/mcp (setup guide) or if you're using Claude you can add it from the directory https://claude.ai/directory/coupossum
  • Telegram: @coupossum (channel) and @coupossum_bot (search)

I'd love feedback on the MCP tool design in particular: what would you want a shopping tool to return that it doesn't?

Disclosure: Coupossum's store links are affiliate links; if you buy through one, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Coupossum is independent: the stores don't run or endorse it. Offers come from the Feedico partner network; Coupossum is not an official Feedico product.

title: Amazon API Gateway REST APIs now support JWT authorizers
description:
Amazon API Gateway now offers a native JWT authorizer for REST APIs, a new authorizer type that validates JSON Web Tokens directly in the gateway. Until now, validating tokens from an OpenID Connect or OAuth 2.0 identity provider other than Amazon Cognito required a Lambda authorizer. You now configure token validation instead of writing and operating code for it.

You can define one or more issuers, the audiences accepted for each, the signing algorithms you permit, and any additional claims a token may present. API Gateway verifies each token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and claims on every request. You can attach one authorizer to many methods and require different scopes on each. This fits machine-to-machine APIs, mobile and web backends, and multi-tenant APIs that accept tokens from several identity providers.

The JWT authorizer works on Regional, edge-optimized, and private REST APIs, and is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see Amazon API Gateway documentation and AWS blog post.

title: How GPT‑6.2 Astra Slashed Robot Debug Time From Hours to Minutes – The 2026 Game‑Changer
description:
GPT‑6.2 Astra & Sol: The 2026 Launch That Turns Vision Into Action

Lead

OpenAI’s February 12, 2026 debut of GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol slashes the time it takes to turn video‑based problems into robot‑ready solutions from hours to minutes.

The GitHub Blog announced a single “GPT‑6.2” line, but the technical sheet quickly split the offering into a multimodal vision‑language engine (Astra) and a pure‑text, high‑throughput engine (Sol). Within weeks, pricing tables appeared, SDK v2.0 landed on the developer portal, and Microsoft, Adobe, and Autodesk began beta‑testing Astra‑powered assistants. By Q2 2026, peer‑reviewed papers on arXiv measured Astra’s performance on robotics and CAD tasks, while Sol set new records on long‑context reasoning benchmarks.

The launch did not happen in a vacuum. It arrived on the heels of Gemini 1.5’s diffusion‑transformer architecture and follows a year of OpenAI’s incremental scaling experiments. The result is a family that pushes the frontier of agentic multimodality while keeping the cost curve flat enough for broader commercial adoption.

Below, I break down the technical specs, benchmark numbers, real‑world use cases, and the risks that still linger.

Case Study: A Multimodal Debugger in Action

Imagine a robotics engineer named Maya who maintains a fleet of warehouse pick‑and‑place bots. Her daily routine involves three steps:

  1. Review video logs of a bot that failed to grasp an item.
  2. Identify the root cause—perhaps a misaligned gripper or a timing issue.
  3. Generate a corrected motion plan and push it to the robot’s controller.

Before GPT‑6.2 Astra, Maya would manually scrub through minutes of video, annotate frames, and then write a custom script to extract joint trajectories. The process could take several hours per incident.

With Astra, Maya uploads the 30‑second failure clip via the new “step‑wise agent” API (the user‑friendly name for OpenAI’s internal agentic‑step primitive). In a single request, Astra returns:

  • A visual summary highlighting the moment the gripper missed the object.
  • A textual diagnosis (“gripper angle deviated by −12° at t = 2.3 s”).
  • A proposed corrective plan expressed as a series of vision‑action tokens that encode new joint angles and timing offsets.

Maya reviews the plan, clicks “accept,” and the system pushes the updated trajectory to the robot fleet. The entire loop finishes in under two minutes, a ten‑fold speed‑up compared with the legacy workflow.

The same API call also triggers Self‑Check, a safety module that flags any motion that could exceed joint torque limits. In Maya’s case, Self‑Check approves the plan, allowing the robot to resume operation without human‑in‑the‑loop supervision.

This scenario showcases Astra’s hierarchical multimodal tokenization and the step‑wise agent primitive that SDK v2.0 introduced. Combining vision, proprioception, and planning in a single, low‑latency call represents a qualitative shift for industries that rely on embodied AI.

Hard Numbers & Technical Deep‑Dive

Architecture at a Glance

Feature GPT‑6.2 Astra GPT‑6.2 Sol
Core backbone 128‑layer Diffusion‑Transformer (DT‑128) 96‑layer Standard Transformer (TT‑96)
Parameters ~1.9 T (1.3 T vision‑language + 0.6 T planning) ~1.4 T
Training corpus 12 TB multimodal (video, image, audio, text) + 5 TB robotics logs (Dec 2025 cut‑off) 14 TB text + 2 TB agentic execution traces (Dec 2025 cut‑off)
Context window 64 k tokens (48 k text + 16 k visual patches) 128 k tokens (text‑only)
New primitives step‑wise agent, vision‑action token cost‑per‑step, stream‑checkpoint
Safety layer Self‑Check (physical‑harm veto) Fact‑Check (hallucination filter, 95 % precision)
Inference latency (A100‑80 GB) 180 ms / 1 k token vision‑language; 1 s / 4 k video frames 45 ms / 1 k token text; 120 ms / 8 k streaming tokens
Pricing (Mar 2026) $0.009 / 1 k vision‑language tokens (Pro) $0.004 / 1 k text tokens (Pro)

Diffusion‑Transformer (DT‑128)

  • Two‑stage processing – raw visual patches are first diffused into a latent space, then transformed jointly with text tokens.
  • Memory efficiency – the diffusion step compresses high‑resolution video, making a 64 k token window feasible on a single GPU.

Hierarchical Multimodal Tokenization

  • Visual sub‑tokens (e.g., “object‑center”, “edge‑gradient”) are produced first.
  • These feed into higher‑level action tokens that embed proprioceptive data (joint angles, forces).
  • The model can output a robot command and a caption in the same forward pass.

Step‑wise Agent Primitive

The API accepts a single prompt and returns a structured JSON payload:

{
  "plan": ["move_to(kitchen)", "pick(object)", "place(table)"],
  "substeps": [
    {"vision_action": "..."},
    {"text_explanation": "..."}
  ],
  "cost_estimate": 0.012
}

Developers can execute the plan step‑by‑step, pause with stream‑checkpoint, or let the model iterate autonomously.

Benchmark Performance

“Astra tops VLM‑Eval 2026 with 92.4 % accuracy, a full 8 points above GPT‑4‑V.” – arXiv 2026‑11‑04

Benchmark Astra Sol GPT‑4‑Turbo Gemini 1.5
VLM‑Eval 2026 (vision‑language) 92.4 % — 84.7 % 86.1 %
RoboMME (real‑world robot tasks) 78 % success — 61 % 65 %
CAD‑Task Suite (geometry generation) 0.89 mAP / 0.81 accuracy — 0.73 mAP 0.77 mAP
MMLU‑2026 (knowledge) — 92.1 % 88.3 % 89.6 %
Code‑Eval‑2026 (Python) — 84.7 % pass 78 % 81 %
Long‑Horizon QA (30‑step) — 78 % correct 65 % 70 %
TruthfulQA‑2026 (fact‑check) — 95 % precision 88 % 90 %
  • RoboMME showcases Astra’s embodied‑reasoning edge.
  • Long‑Horizon QA demonstrates Sol’s advantage from the 128 k token window.

Pricing Highlights

OpenAI’s cost‑per‑step model for Sol lets developers forecast spend per reasoning depth. A typical 10‑step planning request (≈5 k tokens) costs $0.02 on the Pro tier—half the price of GPT‑4‑Turbo. Astra’s video‑frame pricing (1 k frames per 1 k token) keeps multimodal workloads affordable for enterprise pilots.

Risks & Open Questions

  1. Hallucination in Action – Self‑Check blocks commands that could damage hardware, but it does not guarantee logical soundness. Early papers reported a 12 % failure rate when Astra suggested motion plans that obeyed safety limits yet violated task constraints (e.g., grasping the wrong object). The root cause is an implicit world model that still lacks explicit symbolic reasoning.

  2. Data Staleness – Both models train on data cut off at Dec 2025. Regulatory updates, new hardware specs, or API changes released after that date appear as unknowns. Enterprises must add a retrieval‑augmented layer to keep the LLM’s knowledge current.

  3. Compute Footprint – Running Astra at full capacity requires A100‑80 GB or comparable GPUs. Smaller instances can handle Sol’s text‑only workloads, but latency rises on consumer‑grade hardware. Companies lacking high‑end GPUs will need to rely on OpenAI’s managed inference, raising data‑residency and latency concerns.

  4. Alignment Trade‑offs – Fact‑Check achieves 95 % precision on TruthfulQA, but the strict filter reduces recall. In long‑form generation the model sometimes truncates factual statements to avoid a potential flag, yielding overly terse answers. Balancing safety with completeness remains an open research problem.

Outlook: GPT‑6.2’s Role in the 2026 AI Ecosystem

  1. Enterprise Automation – Astra’s multimodal step‑wise agent enables “vision‑to‑action” pipelines that replace hand‑crafted perception‑control stacks. Early adopters—manufacturing, logistics, and design—should pilot Astra in low‑risk scenarios (e.g., CAD suggestion bots) before scaling to safety‑critical robots.

  2. Developer Ecosystem – SDK v2.0’s new primitives lower the barrier for building step‑wise agents. The stream‑checkpoint feature lets developers pause long generations without losing context, a capability that will fuel more sophisticated autonomous assistants.

  3. Competitive Pressure – Google’s Gemini 1.5 and Anthropic’s Claude 3.5 still dominate pure‑text markets, but neither offers a unified multimodal‑agentic API. OpenAI’s pricing undercuts competitors by ≈30 % for comparable token counts, positioning GPT‑6.2 as the default choice for mixed‑modality workloads.

  4. Research Frontiers – The diffusion‑transformer backbone opens a research avenue: joint diffusion of visual and symbolic tokens. Academic groups are already publishing on “latent‑action planning” that builds on Astra’s architecture. Expect a wave of papers that push context windows beyond 256 k tokens and fuse reinforcement‑learning signals directly into the diffusion process.

  5. Regulatory Scrutiny – As Astra powers more physical agents, regulators will likely demand audit trails for each step‑wise agent execution. OpenAI’s API logs already capture step‑wise cost and decision metadata, but enterprises must build compliance layers that map those logs to industry standards (ISO 26262 for automotive, IEC 61508 for industrial safety).

Closing Thoughts

The Feb 12, 2026 announcement marked more than a product release; it signaled the arrival of a dual‑track LLM strategy that unifies vision‑language reasoning with high‑throughput text generation. Astra’s diffusion‑transformer and hierarchical tokenization give developers a single call that can see, think, and act. Sol’s massive context window and cost‑per‑step pricing make it a pragmatic engine for long‑form reasoning and code generation.

However, the launch also surfaces unfinished business. Hallucinations in physical plans, data staleness, and the heavy compute demand of the multimodal model all require careful engineering and policy work. Companies that treat GPT‑6.2 as a component—not a silver bullet—will extract the most value while mitigating risk.

If you’re evaluating AI upgrades for your organization, start by mapping existing pipelines to the step‑wise agent workflow. Run a pilot on a non‑critical visual task, measure latency and safety‑veto rates, then decide whether the 30 % price advantage justifies the hardware investment. In the fast‑moving 2026 AI ecosystem, the ability to prototype, test, and iterate quickly will separate early adopters from the rest.

Bottom line: GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol raise the bar for multimodal and long‑context AI, but they also demand a disciplined approach to safety, data freshness, and compute budgeting. The models are powerful tools; how you wield them will determine whether they become a competitive edge or a costly experiment.

title: Using CSS Masks to Improve Icons in Design Systems
description:
Design system icons often appear dozens of times on one screen, and inline SVG can create a separate subtree per instance. For our monochrome icons, CSS masks removed that markup, simplified updates, and made theming across Shadow DOM easier.

Here's how the approach works, where it scales, and when SVG may still be a better choice.

The problem with inline SVGs

Originally, every one of our icon components resolved to an SVG string. The component parsed the string, cloned an <svg> element, inserted it into its shadow root, and synchronized the node on updates.

That meant every icon on the page carried its own SVG subtree. On icon-heavy screens with lots of menus, tables, toolbars, trees, etc., the same small glyph was parsed, cloned, and stored over and over again.

It also created a fragile update path that produced real bugs, including an update loop and a viewBox regression.

The cost wasn't really about SVG being slow. It was about treating a repeated, static shape as a miniature document per instance.

A mask is the same shape, but cheaper

Our built-in icons are single-color paths using fill="currentColor". For that class of icon, the SVG document isn't the important part. The shape is. The color is just currentColor.

That's exactly what a CSS mask gives you: an image used as an alpha channel, painted with a background color.

So instead of rendering SVG per instance, we publish each icon once as a CSS custom property:

--ch-icon-warning: url("data:image/svg+xml,...");

and render the host as the masked shape:

:host([name]) {
  background-color: currentColor;
  mask: var(--_icon-src) center / contain no-repeat;
  -webkit-mask: var(--_icon-src) center / contain no-repeat;
}

--_icon-src points at the requested icon, with the question icon as a CSS fallback:

this.style.setProperty(
  "--_icon-src",
  `var(--ch-icon-${name}, var(--ch-icon-question))`,
);

One adopted stylesheet, one data URI per icon, and no SVG DOM per instance.

That buys us:

  • Less work per named icon. No DOMParser, no cloneNode, no per-instance SVG tree.
  • Cheaper updates. Changing name swaps a custom property instead of rebuilding DOM.
  • Better at scale. A menu or table with dozens of icons creates host elements, not SVG documents.
  • Simpler transforms. rotate and flip apply to the host through CSS variables, so the same transform path works for masked and SVG icons.

Does this scale to 100+ icons?

There are two kinds of scale here: many icon instances, and many unique icons in the set.

100+ instances

This is the sweet spot. Each instance still needs a host element, but it avoids an SVG subtree:

  • one host element
  • no SVG DOM
  • no parse or clone per instance
  • a CSS custom property that selects the icon
  • no SVG subtree rebuild when name changes, though style and paint work still occur

Whether you've got ten icons or a thousand instances drawn from those same ten, the basic DOM structure per instance is the same. Browsers can reuse cached image resources for identical data URIs.

This is exactly where masks shine: menus, tables, trees, toolbars, and buttons repeating the same monochrome glyphs.

100+ unique icons

The rendering path stays cheap. What grows is the registry: CSS payload increases with the number of custom properties for each icon.

Based on our current icon set — 15 icons, about 360 bytes of SVG each — here's a rough payload estimate. The CSS figures include the encoded data URIs and declarations, not the JavaScript icon registry; larger-set figures are extrapolations from the current set:

Current 15 100 icons 1,000 icons
Raw SVG 5.4 KB ~36 KB ~360 KB
Encoded CSS declarations 8.5 KB ~57 KB ~570 KB
Gzipped CSS 1.7 KB ~11 KB ~110 KB

The exact numbers depend on the icon's complexity, but there should be a fairly linear pattern. One hundred icons is comfortably in "ship it" territory: tens of KB of CSS, roughly 10 KB gzipped. A thousand icons is where I'd start splitting sets or generating CSS at build time.

Here's what to watch at that size:

  • :root inheritance. Every icon variable is declared on :root and is available through inheritance. The browser's actual style and memory costs are implementation-dependent. One hundred is usually fine; a thousand is worth profiling for style recalculation and memory.
  • Everything ships. The default icon set is a single record, so 100+ icons means all of them are bundled even if a page only uses five. Splitting by feature or route becomes worthwhile.

Splitting icons into sets

Icon splitting can happen at the CSS level. A charting feature could load a stylesheet with only its chart icon variables, while a WYSIWYG editor loads a separate set.

The component resolves name to a custom property, so it doesn't need to know which stylesheet supplied the icon. Add the matching variable and load its stylesheet; the existing component can render it unchanged.

The short version: masking avoids per-instance SVG DOM, but it doesn't make instance cost independent of page size. A page with hundreds of icons still creates one element per icon and does style and paint work for them, while sharing the same CSS assets.

A set with hundreds of unique icons is also manageable; what grows is the global registry and the fact that all icons ship together, not the per-instance SVG subtree.

The value in custom elements

The core benefit applies anywhere: rendering inline SVG for each icon creates an SVG DOM per instance, whether the app uses React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, or plain HTML. Frameworks can avoid some re-renders, but memoization doesn't remove the per-instance SVG DOM.

An SVG sprite using <symbol> and <use> is another way to reduce duplicated markup, though it still has its own rendering and browser costs.

Shadow DOM can make styling harder

An SVG inside a shadow root isn't reachable by ordinary consumer CSS. You end up exposing ::part(svg), CSS variables, or internal APIs.

A mask on the host is naturally themeable. Custom properties inherit through shadow boundaries, so a theme can override an icon without reaching into component internals:

--ch-icon-warning: url("...");

The icon set can be published once, globally

We write the icon set into an adopted stylesheet as :root custom properties. Every shadow root inherits the same variables, so no component needs its own copy of the SVG markup.

The same pattern also makes the component easy to extend. A separately loaded stylesheet can add another icon:

:root {
  --ch-icon-editor-bold: url("data:image/svg+xml,...");
}

As long as the variable name matches the component's name sanitization, <ch-icon name="editor-bold"> can use it. Apps can load smaller, feature-specific sets—or add their own icons—without changing the component.

You could do the same in any app, but custom elements make the "one global definition, many shadow roots" pattern especially useful.

It removed imperative DOM synchronization

The old icon component had to synchronize an SVG node into its shadow root on updates. That's where the update loop and viewBox problems came from. Mask mode removes the imperative sync entirely: a name change only updates a CSS variable.

A virtual-DOM framework would handle some of that diffing for you, but the underlying per-instance SVG would still be there.

Icons are nested inside other custom elements

An icon often lives inside a button, menu item, tab, or tree node, each with its own shadow root. Inline SVG gets duplicated at every level. A global CSS variable means you're not embedding the same markup into every component instance.

What we gave up

Masking is best suited to monochrome rendering. A mask can use a multicolor image as a silhouette, but it doesn't preserve the source's colors or gradients. If an icon needs path-level animation or internal structure that consumers must inspect or style, a mask is the wrong tool.

So we didn't remove SVG rendering entirely:

  • URL icons still render real SVG, because external icons can be arbitrary.
  • render="svg" opts a named icon back into SVG DOM for ::part(svg) or direct DOM access.

We also need -webkit-mask for compatibility and a forced-colors fallback so icons stay visible in high-contrast mode.

The takeaway

The best rendering strategy isn't "always SVG" or "always mask." It's matching the representation to the content.

For our named icon set, the icons are monochrome, decorative, and drawn in currentColor. The shape is the data, and CSS is the renderer. Masking opened the door for better performance and extensibility.

Masking was a performance optimization, but the more important win was conceptual: an icon became a styled element instead of a tiny document we had to manage. Custom elements added some additional flexibility, but the model itself works in any framework.

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

title: October 23, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Deprecated

Negative backend deadlines are deprecated

A negative backend deadline in an OpenAPI 2.0 x-google-backend extension or a gRPC BackendRule uses the default deadline, the same as 0. Negative values there are deprecated and will be rejected in a future release; until then, creating an API config with one returns a warning in the operation metadata. OpenAPI 3.x backends already reject a negative deadline. To use the default, omit the field or set it to 0.

For more information, see OpenAPI 2.0 extensions and OpenAPI 3.x extensions.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Security

On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed by AAA Certificate Services. Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked.

To continue connecting to a source database after its CA certificate is updated, upload the new CA certificate to the Database Migration Service source connection profile:

  • Update the connection profile using gcloud database-migration connection-profiles update or the connectionProfiles.patch API method.
  • Modify the connection profile in the Google Cloud console:
    • MySQL connection profiles
    • PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • PostgreSQL to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles
    • Oracle to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles
    • SQL Server to Cloud SQL connection profiles
    • SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connection profiles

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-071.

Cloud Monitoring

Fixed

Ops Agent version 2.73.0 includes patches for a Go vulnerability involving system root certificates, CVE-2026-111943. For more information, see Ops Agent 2.73.0 notes.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating Cloud SQL's managed components. No manual updates to the certificate store are required for Cloud SQL-managed instances. The fix is shipping in a new maintenance version that will be applied during scheduled maintenance. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance. An announcement will be published when the self-service maintenance fix is available.

What should I do?

  • If you use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, then upgrade the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to 2.26.3 or later and the Cloud SQL Proxy Operator to 1.8.4 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use a Cloud SQL Language Connector, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates used with the Cloud SQL Language Connector (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later, certifi 2026.10.19 or later).

  • If you're using the gcloud CLI to install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, then update the gcloud CLI to 590.0.1.

title: What Is XDBL and How Does Database-Independent Querying Work?
description:
Modern enterprise applications rarely operate with simple database requirements. They process financial transactions, manage customer records, coordinate business operations and generate analytical reports. As organizations grow, their applications may need to work with different database engines, support existing database infrastructure or separate transactional workloads from analytical processing.

However, supporting multiple databases introduces a technical challenge: each database engine has its own SQL dialect, data types, functions, sequence mechanisms and stored procedure implementations. An application written specifically for one database can require significant changes when deployed on another.

XDBL addresses this challenge by providing a unified, database-independent source for defining database structures, queries and procedural logic. Instead of maintaining separate database-specific implementations, developers define operations once and use a schema compiler to generate native SQL for supported database engines.

Understanding how this works requires looking at database independence, SQL dialect differences, schema compilation and the role of native SQL generation.

What Is XDBL?

XDBL is Airtool's XML-based, database-independent language for defining database operations and structures. It provides a unified format for expressing different aspects of database development without directly embedding the syntax of a particular database engine into application definitions.

Its scope includes four important database language categories:

  • DDL (Data Definition Language): Defines database structures such as tables, indexes and constraints.
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language): Defines operations for retrieving, inserting, updating and deleting data.
  • DCL (Data Control Language): Handles database permissions and access control statements.
  • SPL (Stored Procedure Language): Defines procedural database logic, including stored procedures and related database objects.

These definitions are maintained in a common source format. Airtool's schema compiler processes the XDBL definitions and generates SQL appropriate for the selected database engine.

The important distinction is that XDBL does not attempt to replace SQL inside database engines. It provides a higher-level source from which the compiler produces the SQL those engines actually execute.

Why Is Database-Independent Querying Important?

Different database engines implement SQL differently. Although SQL provides a common foundation for relational databases, individual vendors introduce their own syntax, functions, data types and procedural capabilities.

For example, a date calculation, string operation or sequence definition may require different SQL expressions depending on whether an application uses PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server or MySQL.

These differences create several challenges.

1. Database-Specific Code Increases Maintenance

When developers write queries directly for a particular database, the application becomes dependent on that database's syntax and behaviour. Supporting another database may require rewriting queries, procedures and schema definitions.

As the application grows, maintaining multiple versions of the same business logic becomes increasingly difficult.

2. Database Migration Becomes More Complicated

Organizations may change database platforms because of licensing decisions, infrastructure requirements, performance considerations or existing technology investments.

However, applications containing database-specific logic cannot always move easily between engines. Developers must identify incompatible statements, modify database objects and test the resulting application.

3. Different Workloads Require Different Database Engines

Transactional applications and analytical systems have different requirements.

Online Transaction Processing (OLTP) databases handle frequent business operations, such as sales orders, payments, inventory movements and employee records. Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) databases are designed for analytical queries involving large datasets, aggregations and reporting.

A business may need both types of database engines without wanting to maintain entirely separate application definitions.

Database-independent querying helps address these challenges by separating application definitions from database-specific SQL syntax.

How Does Database-Independent Querying Work?

Airtool uses XDBL and a schema compiler to translate unified database definitions into engine-native SQL.

The process can be understood through three main stages.

1. Define Database Operations in a Unified Format

Developers create database structures, queries and procedural logic using XDBL rather than writing separate SQL implementations for every supported database.

For example, a business application may need a table containing employee information, including employee IDs, names, departments and salary records.

Instead of manually creating different table definitions for each database, developers maintain one XDBL definition.

The same principle applies to queries, database functions, stored procedures and triggers.

2. Compile XDBL into Database-Specific SQL

The schema compiler interprets the XDBL definition and generates SQL according to the selected database engine.

This is where database-specific differences are handled.

The compiler accounts for variations in:

  • SQL syntax and dialects.
  • Data types and column definitions.
  • Date and time calculations.
  • String functions.
  • Sequence and identity handling.
  • Stored procedure structures.
  • Database-specific constraints and other capabilities.

Rather than requiring developers to maintain these differences manually, the compiler handles the translation.

3. Execute Native SQL on the Target Database

The generated SQL is executed using the target database engine's native capabilities.

This distinction matters because database independence does not have to mean restricting every application to the smallest set of SQL features shared by all supported databases.

Instead, the compiler can generate different SQL implementations for the same XDBL definition, allowing each database to use its own supported syntax and functionality.

The result is a common application source with database-specific SQL generated for execution.

Why Native SQL Generation Matters

Not all database-independent approaches work in the same way. Some rely on a common subset of SQL supported across multiple engines. Others use runtime drivers or abstraction layers to manage database communication and query differences.

These approaches can be useful, but they address different parts of the problem.

A database driver provides connectivity and communication with a database. An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) maps application objects to database records and may generate queries from application-level expressions. A query builder provides an abstraction for constructing SQL statements.

These tools do not automatically provide a unified source for every database definition, stored procedure and trigger.

A lowest-common-denominator approach can also restrict developers to features available across all supported databases. This may prevent applications from using certain engine-specific capabilities.

Airtool's XDBL approach takes a different direction: maintain one database-independent definition while generating SQL that uses the capabilities of the target engine.

For example, database engines may use different approaches to handle date arithmetic, string aggregation, sequence generation and data types. The compiler can produce the appropriate native expression rather than forcing every engine to execute an identical SQL statement.

The database optimizer can then work with SQL expressed in its own dialect.

This does not automatically guarantee identical query performance across engines. Actual performance still depends on query design, indexing, data distribution, execution plans and the underlying infrastructure. However, native SQL generation avoids making portability depend solely on a restricted common SQL subset.

A Practical Example: Handling Date Calculations Across Databases

Date arithmetic is a useful example of why database independence matters.

Suppose an enterprise application needs to calculate the number of hours between two timestamps. This calculation may be required for employee working hours, project duration, service response times or transaction processing.

Although the business requirement is identical, different databases can express the calculation differently.

One database may support direct timestamp subtraction, while another returns an interval that needs additional processing. Other engines may require different date functions or conversions.

Without a database-independent approach, developers may need to maintain separate SQL expressions for each database.

With XDBL, the date calculation is defined once. Airtool's schema compiler generates the appropriate SQL for each supported engine.

Airtool's published technical example demonstrates this difference across ten database engines. The generated SQL varies significantly in length and structure. For example, the SQL Server implementation requires substantially less SQL than the Oracle implementation because Oracle's interval result requires additional calculations to reconstruct the total hours.

The important point is not that every generated query looks identical. It is that the underlying operation can be defined once while the compiler handles the database-specific implementation.

This approach is also useful for string functions, sequence handling, table definitions and other operations where SQL dialects differ.

Supporting Both OLTP and OLAP Database Engines

Database independence becomes particularly valuable when an enterprise application needs to support transactional and analytical workloads.

OLTP and OLAP databases serve different purposes, and organizations may choose different engines for each workload.

Airtool's data architecture supports seven OLTP engines:

  • PostgreSQL
  • Informix
  • Oracle
  • IBM DB2
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • MySQL
  • SAP HANA

For analytical workloads, Airtool supports three OLAP engines:

  • Vertica
  • ClickHouse
  • Google BigQuery

The same application model can support these different database environments through the platform's compilation approach.

For example, an enterprise application may use PostgreSQL or Oracle for transactional operations while routing analytical workloads to ClickHouse, Vertica or BigQuery.

This separation allows organizations to select database engines according to their operational and analytical requirements without maintaining an entirely separate application definition for each database environment.

It is particularly relevant for businesses that need reliable transaction processing alongside large-scale reporting and analytics.

How Does Schema Compilation Simplify Database Maintenance?

Database independence is not limited to translating individual queries. Database structures and procedural objects also need to be managed consistently.

Airtool's schema compiler supports the import of existing customer database schemas into its metadata repository.

This includes objects such as:

  • Tables and columns.
  • Indexes and constraints.
  • Stored procedures.
  • Triggers.
  • Other supported database definitions.

Once imported, these objects can be managed through the platform's schema compilation process.

This is important for organizations with existing database investments. They do not necessarily need to approach database modernization as a complete rewrite of their existing data structures.

The compiler also processes different categories of database objects through its MODEL and CODE pipelines. MODEL handles table-related objects, while CODE processes stored procedure language objects in dependency order.

Dependency handling matters because database objects often rely on other objects being available first. A procedure, for example, may depend on a function or database structure that must be resolved before compilation.

By managing these relationships through a structured compilation process, the platform can support more consistent database deployment and maintenance.

What Does Database Independence Mean for Enterprise Development?

For developers, database independence reduces the need to maintain multiple versions of the same database logic.

For software architects, it provides greater flexibility when designing applications for different customer infrastructure environments.

For businesses, it helps reduce dependence on a single database engine and supports technology decisions based on operational requirements.

The practical advantages include:

Reduced Database-Specific Development: Developers maintain common definitions instead of repeatedly rewriting database structures and operations.

Simplified Database Migration: Changing the target database can become a recompile-and-migrate exercise rather than requiring the entire application to be rewritten. Migration still requires appropriate data conversion, validation and testing.

Greater Infrastructure Flexibility: Organizations can choose supported database engines according to existing investments, licensing arrangements and technical requirements.

Support for Different Workloads: Applications can use transactional and analytical database engines within the same broader platform architecture.

Consistent Application Logic: Business rules and database definitions remain centrally managed rather than being duplicated across separate database implementations.

XDBL and AI-Assisted Application Development

Database-independent development also has implications for AI-assisted software development.

AI coding agents often need to understand database structures, generate queries and interact with application data. When an agent must produce native SQL for every database engine, it needs to account for the differences between their dialects and capabilities.

XDBL provides a structured alternative.

Its grammar is described through an XML Schema Definition (XSD), allowing compatible AI development tools to work with a defined language structure.

An AI agent can generate XDBL definitions without independently implementing the SQL dialect of every supported database. The schema compiler then handles the translation into the appropriate native SQL.

This separates the AI agent's task of expressing database operations from the compiler's responsibility for handling database-specific syntax.

It can make AI-assisted development more consistent across supported database environments, although the generated definitions still need validation, appropriate permissions and testing.

Conclusion

Database independence is about more than connecting an application to different databases. It is about maintaining application logic without making every database-specific difference a development responsibility.

XDBL addresses this through a unified XML-based source format and a schema compiler that generates native SQL for supported database engines.

By supporting seven OLTP engines and three OLAP engines, Airtool provides a common application development approach across different transactional and analytical database environments.

For enterprise applications, this means greater database flexibility, reduced duplication of database-specific logic and a more consistent foundation for development and modernization.

The goal is straightforward: define database operations once, let the compiler handle engine-specific differences, and allow applications to work with the database technology that best fits the organization's requirements.

title: Best IT Certifications to Earn in 2027: AI, Cybersecurity, Cloud and Beyond
description:
The technology industry is evolving faster than ever. Artificial intelligence is transforming businesses, cybersecurity threats are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and cloud computing continues to reshape how organizations manage their infrastructure.

For IT professionals, students, and career changers, 2027 offers an excellent opportunity to develop new technical skills and earn industry-recognized certifications.

But with hundreds of IT certifications available, choosing the right one can be challenging.

Should you focus on artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud computing, networking, or IT governance? Which certifications are suitable for beginners, and which ones can help experienced professionals advance their careers?

In this guide, we'll explore the best IT certifications to earn in 2027, covering popular technology fields, career opportunities, professional development, and effective exam preparation strategies.

Whether you're starting your IT career or looking to strengthen your existing technical expertise, this guide will help you identify a certification path worth considering.

Why IT Certifications Matter in 2027

IT certifications provide a structured way to learn technical concepts, demonstrate professional knowledge, and validate skills against recognized industry standards.

They are particularly valuable in technology fields where tools, platforms, security requirements, and industry practices continue to change.

Some of the most important technology skills organizations are investing in include:

  • Artificial intelligence and machine learning
  • Cybersecurity and information security
  • Cloud computing and infrastructure
  • Data analytics and engineering
  • Networking and automation
  • IT governance, risk, and compliance

However, earning a certification alone does not guarantee employment or career advancement.

Employers also value practical experience, problem-solving abilities, communication skills, and the ability to apply technical knowledge in real-world situations.

The best approach is to combine certification preparation with hands-on learning and practical projects.

1. Best AI Certifications to Earn in 2027

Artificial intelligence is becoming an important part of software development, business operations, data analysis, cybersecurity, and enterprise technology.

As organizations adopt generative AI, machine learning, and AI-powered automation, professionals who understand these technologies can develop valuable skills.

Here are some AI certifications worth considering.

AWS Certified AI Practitioner

The AWS Certified AI Practitioner certification is a good starting point for individuals interested in artificial intelligence and machine learning.

It covers foundational AI and ML concepts, generative AI, responsible AI, and practical business applications.

Best suited for: Beginners exploring AI, business professionals working with AI solutions, and IT professionals interested in AWS AI services.

AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer – Associate

For professionals interested in building and maintaining machine learning solutions, this certification offers a more technical learning path.

It covers machine learning implementation, data preparation, model deployment, monitoring, and optimization using AWS services.

Candidates should have a reasonable understanding of cloud computing and machine learning concepts before beginning preparation.

Best suited for: Machine learning engineers, data professionals, cloud developers, and professionals working with AI-powered applications.

Microsoft AI Certifications and Applied Skills

Microsoft's AI learning and credential ecosystem is another area worth exploring.

Professionals can develop knowledge around Azure AI services, generative AI, machine learning, and AI-powered business solutions through Microsoft Learn.

These learning opportunities are particularly relevant for people already working with Microsoft technologies.

Best suited for: Azure professionals, developers building AI applications, data scientists, and professionals working with Microsoft AI technologies.

IAPP Artificial Intelligence Governance Professional (AIGP)

AI development is not just about building intelligent systems. Organizations also need professionals who understand AI governance, privacy, risk management, accountability, and responsible AI practices.

The IAPP Artificial Intelligence Governance Professional (AIGP) certification focuses on the governance and responsible implementation of AI systems.

It is especially relevant as businesses increasingly evaluate the legal, ethical, and operational risks associated with AI adoption.

Best suited for: AI governance professionals, compliance specialists, risk management professionals, privacy professionals, and technology policy specialists.

AI knowledge is becoming relevant across multiple technology careers. Even professionals who do not plan to become machine learning engineers can benefit from understanding AI systems, their limitations, security considerations, and business applications.

2. Best Cybersecurity Certifications to Earn in 2027

Cybersecurity remains one of the most important areas of information technology.

Organizations need professionals who can identify vulnerabilities, investigate security incidents, protect sensitive information, manage access controls, and develop effective security strategies.

The following certifications are worth considering.

CompTIA Security+

CompTIA Security+ is a widely recognized entry-level cybersecurity certification.

It introduces candidates to essential security concepts, including:

  • Threat detection
  • Risk management
  • Network security
  • Identity management
  • Incident response
  • Security operations

For someone entering cybersecurity, Security+ provides a structured foundation for understanding how organizations protect their systems, networks, and information.

Best suited for: Beginners entering cybersecurity, IT support professionals, junior security analysts, and network administrators transitioning into security.

ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity (CC)

ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity is designed for individuals who want to develop foundational cybersecurity knowledge.

It introduces essential concepts such as security principles, access controls, network security, security operations, and incident response.

It can be a useful starting point for students and career changers who want to understand the fundamentals before pursuing more advanced credentials.

Best suited for: Students, career changers, entry-level IT professionals, and individuals exploring cybersecurity careers.

Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP)

CISSP is an advanced cybersecurity certification for experienced professionals interested in security leadership and architecture.

Its broad coverage includes:

  • Security and risk management
  • Asset security
  • Security architecture
  • Network security
  • Identity management
  • Security operations
  • Software development security

Unlike beginner-level credentials, CISSP requires candidates to meet specific professional experience requirements.

It is important to review the official ISC2 eligibility criteria before pursuing this certification.

Best suited for: Experienced security professionals, security architects, security managers, and information security consultants.

The AWS Certified Developer – Associate certification focuses on developing, deploying, and maintaining applications on AWS.

Best suited for: Software developers, cloud application developers, backend engineers, and professionals building applications on AWS.

Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate (AZ-104)

AZ-104 is an important certification for professionals responsible for managing Microsoft Azure environments.

It covers:

  • Storage management
  • Compute resources
  • Virtual networking
  • Monitoring

Candidates develop the knowledge required to administer and maintain Azure infrastructure effectively.

Best suited for: Azure administrators, cloud engineers, system administrators, and IT infrastructure professionals.

Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert

Professionals who want to move beyond administration and focus on enterprise cloud architecture should consider the Azure Solutions Architect pathway.

It develops knowledge of designing cloud and hybrid solutions involving infrastructure, networking, security, data, and application architecture.

Best suited for: Experienced cloud engineers, solutions architects, enterprise IT consultants, and infrastructure specialists.

Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer

The Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer certification validates the ability to deploy applications, monitor operations, manage enterprise solutions, and maintain cloud infrastructure.

It provides a structured learning path for professionals interested in managing resources and workloads on Google Cloud.

Best suited for: Cloud administrators, junior cloud engineers, IT professionals exploring Google Cloud, and infrastructure specialists.

CompTIA Network+

CompTIA Network+ provides vendor-neutral networking knowledge.

It covers networking concepts, infrastructure, network operations, security, troubleshooting, and emerging technologies.

It can help candidates develop foundational networking knowledge before moving toward vendor-specific certifications.

They also require professionals who can manage technology risks, evaluate internal controls, oversee compliance, and ensure that IT systems support business objectives.

Certified Information Security Manager (CISM)

Artificial Intelligence Governance Professional (AIGP)

6. Best Data and Analytics Certifications to Consider

Microsoft Power BI Data Analyst Associate
