7. How to Choose the Right IT Certification in 2027

Choosing a certification should be a strategic decision rather than simply following popular trends.

A certification that works well for one professional may not be suitable for someone with a different background or career objective.

Consider the following factors before making your decision.

Identify Your Career Goals

Start by identifying your career goal.

  • Interested in artificial intelligence? Explore AI and machine learning certifications.
  • Interested in protecting systems? Consider cybersecurity.
  • Enjoy managing infrastructure? Explore cloud computing.
  • Interested in auditing and organizational risk? Consider CISA, CISM, CRISC, or AIGP.
  • Interested in working with data? Explore analytics and data engineering certifications.

Consider Your Existing Experience

Not every certification is designed for beginners.

Some credentials require professional experience, while others introduce foundational concepts.

Establishing the right knowledge before attempting an advanced certification can make preparation considerably more effective.

Review Official Exam Objectives

Another important step is reviewing the official exam objectives.

These documents explain which topics are covered, what technical skills are assessed, and how the examination is structured.

Certification providers sometimes revise their exams, so always check the latest official information rather than relying entirely on older study materials.

Consider Long-Term Career Value

Choose a credential that aligns with your intended job role, the technologies you want to work with, and the professional skills you want to develop over the next few years.

8. How to Pass Your IT Certification Exam on the First Attempt

Passing your IT certification exam on the first attempt requires a focused study plan, a strong understanding of exam objectives, and consistent practice.

Use reliable study materials, review important concepts, and test your knowledge regularly to identify areas that need improvement.

CertsTree can support your preparation with certification-focused practice questions, helping you evaluate your understanding, strengthen weak areas, and build confidence before exam day.

Start your journey today: https://www.certstree.com/exams

Here are some practical strategies to improve your exam preparation.

Understand the Official Exam Objectives

Before starting your preparation, download the latest official exam guide from the certification provider.

Review every exam domain and understand how much importance each topic receives.

This helps you prioritize your study time and avoid spending too much time on subjects that represent only a small portion of the examination.

For example, someone preparing for Microsoft AZ-104 should understand Azure identities, governance, storage, compute, networking, and monitoring rather than concentrating exclusively on virtual machines.

Create a Realistic Study Plan

A structured study schedule helps you maintain consistency and track your progress.

Divide the syllabus into smaller sections and assign realistic study goals.

For example, if you have six weeks to prepare:

  • Weeks 1–3: Understand the main concepts and exam objectives.
  • Weeks 4–5: Complete practical exercises, practice questions, and revision.
  • Week 6: Take mock assessments and review weak areas.

Your schedule should reflect your existing knowledge and available study time.

Avoid rushing through the material simply to finish the syllabus.

Use Quality Study Materials and Practice Questions

Choosing reliable preparation resources can make a significant difference.

Start with official documentation, training courses, and learning paths. Once you understand the fundamentals, use exam-style practice questions to evaluate your knowledge.

You can also explore CertsTree for certification-focused practice resources.

Use these questions to:

  • Identify knowledge gaps.
  • Understand scenario-based problems.
  • Evaluate your understanding of important concepts.
  • Become more comfortable with the examination format.

Remember that practice questions should support your learning rather than replace it.

Understanding why an answer is correct is much more valuable than memorizing a particular question.

Focus on Understanding Instead of Memorization

Modern IT certification exams frequently test how candidates apply knowledge to realistic situations.

A question may describe a cloud infrastructure problem, a cybersecurity incident, or a network configuration challenge and ask you to identify the most appropriate solution.

Instead of memorizing isolated answers, understand the underlying concepts and why different solutions may or may not work.

Gain Hands-On Experience

Practical experience is especially important for technical certifications.

Use cloud labs, virtual machines, networking simulations, and hands-on projects to reinforce your learning.

For example:

  • Azure candidates can practice configuring resources, managing identities, and monitoring services.
  • Networking candidates can use simulation tools to practice routing and switching concepts.
  • AWS candidates can explore cloud services and build practical infrastructure projects.
  • Cybersecurity candidates can use authorized lab environments to understand security concepts and incident response.

Hands-on learning makes theoretical topics easier to understand and helps prepare you for scenario-based examination questions.

Take Mock Exams Before Scheduling Your Test

Mock examinations help you evaluate your readiness under realistic time constraints.

After each assessment, review your incorrect answers and identify the topics that need more attention.

Do not focus only on your overall score. Understanding your weak areas is essential for making further progress.

Aim for consistent results across multiple practice assessments before scheduling your official examination.

Practice scores are useful indicators, but they cannot guarantee an actual exam result.

Explore realistic practice resources: CertsTree.com

Manage Your Time During the Examination

Even well-prepared candidates can struggle if they do not manage their examination time effectively.

  • Read each question carefully.
  • Identify the key requirements.
  • Avoid spending too long on a single difficult question.
  • Flag challenging questions and return to them later if the exam platform allows it.
  • Stay calm and select answers based on the actual scenario.

A focused approach can help you use your examination time more effectively.

9. IT Certification Roadmap for 2027

If you are unsure where to begin, the following roadmap can help you select a learning path based on your experience and career interests.

AI and Machine Learning

Cybersecurity

Cloud Computing

Microsoft Azure

Networking

IT Auditing and Governance

Data Analytics

10. Common Mistakes to Avoid When Choosing IT Certifications

Even motivated candidates can make poor certification decisions when they focus on collecting credentials rather than developing useful skills.

Here are some common mistakes to avoid.

Choosing certifications only because they are popular

A trending credential may not match your career interests or professional background. Consider whether the skills it develops are relevant to your intended job role.

Ignoring exam updates

Certification providers regularly revise their objectives, exam formats, and requirements. Always check the latest official information before beginning preparation.

Skipping practical exercises

Some candidates rely entirely on study notes or practice questions. This can create gaps in understanding, particularly for technical examinations involving cloud infrastructure, networking, and cybersecurity.

Collecting too many unrelated certifications

Avoid collecting certifications without developing practical expertise.

A focused certification pathway supported by hands-on experience is generally more valuable than earning several unrelated credentials.

Final Thoughts: Which IT Certifications Are Worth Pursuing in 2027?

The best IT certification for 2027 depends on your career goals, existing experience, and the technology field you want to pursue.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning offer opportunities for professionals interested in emerging technologies. Cybersecurity remains important for protecting digital infrastructure, while cloud computing continues to create demand for professionals who can design and manage modern IT environments.

Networking, data analytics, auditing, and IT governance also provide valuable career pathways.

Rather than trying to earn every popular certification, choose one professional direction, build the necessary foundational knowledge, and progress toward more advanced credentials as your experience grows.

title: LSM-Trees vs B-Trees: Which Side of the Disk You Tax
description:
Every storage engine has to put a new version of a record somewhere, and there are only two honest places: overwrite the old one in place, or append the new one and clean up later. B-trees overwrite. LSM-trees append. That single decision sets the write amplification, the read amplification, the space amplification and the tail latency of everything above it, and it is why two databases with identical SQL surfaces behave nothing alike under a write-heavy load.

A B-tree turns one logical update into two to four random page writes, while an LSM-tree turns it into one sequential append plus ten to thirty bytes of compaction rewrite per byte stored — the bill arrives on different hardware counters.

Part One: What is being compared

A B-tree keeps one sorted copy of the data. A write descends the tree, latches the leaf page, changes a few bytes, writes the page back, and records the change in a write-ahead log so a crash can be repaired. Pages are fixed size, usually 4 to 16 kilobytes, and the tree stays balanced by splitting pages when they fill.

An LSM-tree keeps many sorted copies. A write lands in a memory table and in a log, and when the table fills it is flushed as an immutable sorted run. Background compaction merges runs so the number of copies does not grow without bound. Reads consult the memory table and then the runs, newest to oldest, using Bloom filters to skip the ones that cannot contain the key.

Both are mature. InnoDB, PostgreSQL and SQL Server are B-tree engines at heart. RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB and the storage layer under many time-series systems are LSM. Neither is a research prototype, so the comparison is about workload shape rather than maturity.

Part Two: The arithmetic

Take a mainstream NVMe drive: about 3.5 gigabytes per second of sequential write, roughly 80,000 random 4-kilobyte write IOPS, and a few hundred microseconds of latency per random operation. Those two numbers differ by an order of magnitude, and the entire debate lives in that gap.

A B-tree update dirties a leaf page, and the write-back plus the log record plus the eventual checkpoint means roughly two to four physical page writes per logical update. At 80,000 random IOPS and four pages each, the ceiling lands near 20,000 updates per second, and each one costs a seek-equivalent stall. A page split doubles the work for that insert and briefly holds a latch that other writers queue behind.

An LSM-tree writes the record sequentially into the log and the memory table, then flushes a sorted file. Sequential bandwidth looks generous until compaction is counted: with a levelled policy and a size ratio of ten, each byte is rewritten roughly ten to twenty times over its life. Divide 3.5 gigabytes per second by fifteen and the sustainable user write rate is about 230 megabytes per second, which is roughly 58,000 four-kilobyte updates per second. That is two to three times the B-tree ceiling on the same device, and the writes arrive as large sequential batches rather than scattered pages.

Reads invert the picture. A B-tree lookup with the upper levels cached touches one or two pages, so a point read is close to one device access and a handful of microseconds of comparison work. An LSM lookup must check every level: five to seven Bloom filters at roughly 100 nanoseconds of hashing each, then usually one real read. The filters keep the average near 1.05 device reads, but the CPU cost is paid on every single lookup, and a filter with a 1 percent false-positive rate still sends one in a hundred reads to disk for nothing.

Part Three: Where the model breaks

The clean crossover assumes uniform keys and a device that behaves like its datasheet. Both assumptions fail in production.

B-trees fragment. Random inserts into a tree with 16-kilobyte pages leave pages half full, so space amplification drifts toward 1.5 to 2 times the logical data, and the working set that must stay cached grows with it. A tree that fit in 64 gigabytes of RAM at load time may need 100 gigabytes a year later, which is the quiet way a database stops being memory-resident.

LSM-trees stall. Compaction competes with foreground writes for the same device, and when incoming writes outrun compaction the engine applies back pressure: write stalls, throttling, or a hard slowdown at a level-size threshold. The average throughput looks excellent while the ninety-ninth percentile jumps by an order of magnitude during a compaction burst. Tombstones make it worse — a delete is a marker that must survive until every older version is compacted away, so a workload of insert-then-delete can hold disk space far above the live data size.

The crossover also depends on concurrency. A B-tree with a good buffer pool and group commit can push far past the naive IOPS estimate because many updates hit pages already in memory; the random writes only happen on eviction. An LSM-tree with a large memory table and a fast device can hide compaction entirely if the write rate stays under the compaction budget. The formula tells you which failure mode to expect, not the exact number.

Part Four: The later cost

The operational bill differs in kind. A B-tree is easy to reason about: one copy, one place to look, backups and point-in-time recovery map directly onto pages and logs. Its failure mode is contention — hot pages, latch waits, deadlocks between concurrent updates — and the fix is usually schema or access-pattern work that the application team owns.

An LSM-tree moves the complexity into tuning. Level count, size ratio, compaction strategy, Bloom filter bits per key, block size and compression all interact, and a change that improves write throughput usually worsens read latency or space. The failure mode is a background process, which means the person debugging it is reading compaction stats at three in the morning rather than reading a query plan.

There is also a hardware asymmetry that has grown sharper. Consumer and datacentre SSDs have much higher sequential than random write throughput, which favours LSM. But drives with power-loss protection and large DRAM caches, plus persistent memory and CXL-attached memory, narrow the gap by making random writes cheaper. On a device where random 4-kilobyte writes cost almost the same as sequential ones, the LSM advantage largely evaporates and its read and space costs remain.

Part Five: Outside the team

For the person using the product, the difference is whether the dashboard loads in 40 milliseconds or 400, and whether last month's data is still queryable after a bulk import. Write amplification becomes an infrastructure bill: an LSM engine that rewrites every byte fifteen times wears out drives faster and burns more write bandwidth, which on a metered cloud volume shows up as a line item.

For the team, the choice decides who is on call. B-tree problems surface as slow queries and lock waits that a database administrator can see in a familiar plan. LSM problems surface as compaction debt and read stalls that require understanding an internal scheduler. Neither is better; they are different jobs attached to the same feature.

A fair comparison fixes the device, the key distribution, the read-write ratio and the latency target, then measures bytes written per user byte and ninety-ninth percentile read latency. Comparing average throughput across two different drives is the most common way this decision gets made badly.

Market sizing check

If managed database spend keeps growing at low double digits and storage engines remain the core of that spend, the segment tied to engine choice — managed Postgres, wide-column stores, time-series platforms and the observability backends built on them — is plausibly $30B to $60B a year by 2030. The swing factor is how much of the workload shifts to append-only telemetry, which favours LSM, versus transactional records, which favour B-trees.

These figures are a synthesis of published market ranges and a stated model, not a forecast of any specific vendor.

The comparison that matters

The comparison that matters is between random overwrite and sequential append, priced on the device you actually run. B-trees win when the working set fits in memory, reads dominate, and space predictability matters. LSM-trees win when writes arrive faster than a tree can absorb them, when the data is append-heavy, and when sequential bandwidth is the cheap resource.

The ranking assumes the read-write ratio holds. Shift toward read-heavy traffic and the B-tree's single-copy lookup becomes decisive; shift toward ingest and the LSM's sequential path does.

Pick the engine by which amplification your workload can afford — random write IOPS for B-trees, compaction bandwidth and read CPU for LSM-trees — then measure the ninety-ninth percentile, because averages hide both failure modes.

title: tileserver: a small Rust server for PMTiles and MBTiles map archives
description:
If you host your own map, at some point you end up with a tile archive: one .pmtiles or .mbtiles file that holds every tile of a region. It may come from a vector tile generator, from an export of a raster layer, or from someone else's pipeline. The file is convenient to copy around. But a map library in the browser does not read archives from your disk. It asks for /{z}/{x}/{y} URLs and expects the right answer for each.

So something has to stand between the file and the map. That something has to get a list of small details right. Vector tiles are usually stored gzip-compressed, and the browser needs Content-Encoding: gzip to decode them. MBTiles numbers its rows from the bottom, while XYZ URLs count from the top. A missing tile in the ocean is not an error. And tiles should be cached, or every pan of the map hits your server again.

tileserver is a small tile server written in Rust with axum that handles those details for PMTiles and MBTiles archives. You put files in a directory, and the server exposes each one as XYZ tiles plus TileJSON, with correct content headers, ETags and a MapLibre preview page.

What it does

One directory, one source per file. Every *.pmtiles and *.mbtiles file directly inside --dir becomes a source named after the file: roads.pmtiles becomes roads. Unreadable files and duplicate ids are logged and skipped. They do not stop the server.

A short list of endpoints.

  • GET / is the preview page: the source list, auto-styled vector layers or raster, and a click shows a feature's properties. Adding ?debug shows tile boundaries.
  • GET /sources is a JSON list of sources with kind, format, zooms, bounds and TileJSON URL.
  • GET /{id}.json is TileJSON 3.0.0, with vector_layers for vector sources.
  • GET /{id}/{z}/{x}/{y}[.ext] is the tile. The extension is optional, but if present it must match (pbf/mvt, png, jpg, webp, avif).
  • GET /health answers ok.

Headers done properly. These are the details that decide whether the map shows up:

  • Content-Type comes from the archive's tile type: application/vnd.mapbox-vector-tile, image/png, and so on.
  • Content-Encoding: gzip (or br/zstd) is set when the archive stores compressed tiles. Tiles are served as stored, with no recompression. If a client does not accept gzip, the tile is inflated on the fly. Vary: Accept-Encoding is always set.
  • ETag is a strong validator, an FNV-1a hash of the stored bytes. A request with a matching If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified.
  • Cache-Control: public, max-age=N with a default of 3600, and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.

Status codes that map libraries expect. 204 No Content for a tile inside the zoom range that the archive does not contain, which MapLibre treats as empty. 404 for unknown sources or zooms outside the range. 400 for invalid coordinates or a wrong extension.

TileJSON URLs that work behind a proxy. They use --base-url when you set it, or else the Host header and X-Forwarded-Proto.

How to use it

Install it from GitHub with Cargo, generate the demo archives and serve them:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tileserver --locked
tileserver fixtures tiles && tileserver serve --dir tiles

Or from a clone of the repository:

cargo run --release -- fixtures tiles            # generate 4 small demo archives
cargo run --release -- serve --dir tiles         # http://127.0.0.1:3000/
cargo test

The whole command line fits in two lines:

tileserver serve [--dir DIR] [--addr 127.0.0.1:3000] [--base-url URL] [--max-age SECONDS]
tileserver fixtures DIR

The fixtures command is useful on its own. It needs no external data: a tiny PNG encoder draws a debug grid for zooms 0 to 3, with each tile's z/x/y shown as bar counts, and a hand-written MVT encoder produces point tiles for zooms 0 to 6 with six Algerian cities. Both are written as PMTiles and as MBTiles. That gives you a raster source and a vector source in each format to try the server with, before you bring your own files.

How it works inside

PMTiles v3 is read by a module written from the spec. The reader parses the 127-byte header, then the gzip-compressed root directory and the JSON metadata. A tile id is the count of tiles in lower zooms plus the tile's position on a Hilbert curve. The reader binary-searches the directory for the last entry less than or equal to the id. Entries with run_length > 0 point into tile data, and run_length == 0 points to a leaf directory. Leaves are cached. File reads use pread, so one open file serves concurrent requests without locking.

The same module has a writer. It deduplicates identical tiles, run-length encodes consecutive repeats, and splits into leaf directories when the root gets big. The tests and the fixtures command use it.

MBTiles files are SQLite databases, opened read-only through rusqlite with bundled SQLite. The XYZ y is flipped to the TMS row 2^z − 1 − y. The metadata table (format, bounds, center, minzoom/maxzoom, and json for vector_layers) feeds TileJSON. Gzip is detected from the first tile's magic bytes instead of being assumed.

HTTP is axum 0.8. Tile reads run in spawn_blocking, since both backends do blocking I/O.

Things to know

  • Sources are discovered at startup. Restart the server to pick up new files.
  • Local files only. There is no HTTP range or remote PMTiles support.
  • No brotli or zstd for PMTiles internal (directory) compression. Tile-level compression of any kind is passed through.
  • The leaf-directory cache is a simple bounded map, not an LRU.
  • The preview page uses external resources. It loads MapLibre from unpkg, OSM raster tiles as a backdrop, and glyphs from demotiles.maplibre.org for labels.

What is tested. cargo test runs 13 integration tests on freshly generated fixtures in a temporary directory. On the PMTiles side: tile ids against the spec's values, id to z/x/y round trips over zooms 0 to 6 plus deep zooms, directory encoding and decoding, entry lookup inside runs and gaps, and writer-to-reader runs with deduplicated "ocean" tiles, both root-only and with forced leaf directories. On the HTTP side: raster headers and body, ETag and 304, gzip pass-through versus inflation depending on Accept-Encoding, the 204/404/400 cases, TileJSON including X-Forwarded-Proto and --base-url, and MBTiles row flipping checked tile by tile against the generated PNGs.

Why I built it

Serving tiles from an archive is a narrow job, and it deserves a narrow tool: one binary, one directory, no configuration file. The difficulty is not the amount of code. It is that each small mistake produces a map that is blank with no error message: a missing Content-Encoding, a flipped row, a 404 where a 204 was expected. I wanted a server where each of those cases is written down and covered by a test.

Writing the PMTiles reader and writer from the spec was the other reason. It makes the format concrete: the header, the directories, the Hilbert curve ids, the run-length trick for repeated tiles. And having a writer means the tests need no downloaded data.

Get the code

The source and tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tileserver. It is MIT licensed. The generated fixtures contain no third-party data (city positions are approximate and typed by hand), and the preview backdrop is © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: We moved our cut-off service to a scratch image and it started working in UTC
description:
Our delivery promise service is a small Go program that answers one question for the website: if this order is placed now, which day will it arrive. The answer depends on the depot's cut-off, five o'clock UK time. In June we moved it from a Debian based image to FROM scratch with a statically linked binary. The image went from ninety megabytes to eleven, and every package our scanner had been complaining about disappeared.

The service loads Europe/London at start with time.LoadLocation. Go looks for the time zone database in the operating system's zoneinfo directories, among a few other places, and a scratch image has no operating system. LoadLocation returned an error. Years earlier someone had written the obvious defensive code around that call: log a warning and fall back to UTC so the service can still start. It started, the health check passed, and the warning went into a log nobody read.

In June the UK is on British Summer Time, an hour ahead of UTC. Five o'clock in UTC is six o'clock in London. For three weeks, every order placed between five and six in the evening was promised next day delivery from a depot that had already closed for the day. Roughly four hundred customers a week were told tomorrow and received their parcel the day after. Customer service found the pattern before we did, because every complaint came from the same hour.

The fix inside the binary was one line. Importing the time/tzdata package, available since Go 1.15, embeds the time zone database in the program for a few hundred kilobytes. We also removed the fallback. A service whose whole job is local cut-off times now refuses to start if it cannot load its zone, because a crash on deploy is found in minutes and a wrong answer took three weeks. The cut-off tests now run inside the built image, with a fixed clock set once to a summer date and once to a winter date.

A minimal image is minimal about everything, including the files your code assumed every machine would have.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Pixels vs the Accessibility Tree: I Measured What a Web Page Costs an AI Agent (67 Lines of Python)
description:
Vercel Labs open-sourced agent-desktop this month: a native CLI that lets AI agents control macOS, Windows and Linux by reading the accessibility tree instead of looking at pixels. Google's Computer Use also reached general availability. So there are now two serious ways for an agent to "see" a screen, and they bill you very differently.

I wanted numbers, not opinions. So I wrote 67 lines of Python that load real pages and measure what each view costs in tokens.

The three views

  1. Screenshot. One image of the viewport. Anthropic's published estimate for an image is width * height / 750 tokens, so a 1280x800 screenshot costs about 1,365 tokens regardless of what is on it.
  2. Full accessibility tree. Every role, name and link on the page, as text. I used Playwright's aria_snapshot().
  3. Viewport tree. Only the interactive elements (links, buttons, inputs) that are visible right now, one numbered line each.

The script 

"""What does a web page cost an agent: pixels vs the accessibility tree?"""
import os, sys, json, math
import tiktoken
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

ENC = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
VIEW = {"width": 1280, "height": 800}
URLS = sys.argv[1:] or [
    "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_Context_Protocol",
    "https://news.ycombinator.com",
    "https://github.com/microsoft/playwright",
    "https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html",
    "https://stripe.com/pricing",
    "https://www.bbc.com/news",
]

# Interactive elements that are actually visible in the current viewport.
VISIBLE_JS = """() => {
  const sel = 'a[href],button,input,select,textarea,[role=button],[role=link],[role=tab],[role=menuitem],[role=checkbox],[role=textbox],[role=combobox]';
  const out = []; let total = 0;
  for (const el of document.querySelectorAll(sel)) {
    const r = el.getBoundingClientRect(), s = getComputedStyle(el);
    if (r.width < 2 || r.height < 2 || s.visibility === 'hidden' || s.display === 'none') continue;
    total++;
    if (r.bottom < 0 || r.top > innerHeight || r.right < 0 || r.left > innerWidth) continue;
    const role = el.getAttribute('role') || el.tagName.toLowerCase();
    const name = (el.getAttribute('aria-label') || el.innerText || el.value || el.placeholder || '').trim().replace(/\\s+/g, ' ').slice(0, 60);
    out.push(`[${out.length}] ${role} "${name}"`);
  }
  return {lines: out, total, pageHeight: document.documentElement.scrollHeight};
}"""

def image_tokens(w, h):
    """Anthropic's published estimate: tokens ~= width * height / 750."""
    return round(w * h / 750)

def measure(page, url):
    page.goto(url, wait_until="domcontentloaded", timeout=45000)
    page.wait_for_timeout(2500)
    full_tree = page.locator("body").aria_snapshot()
    vis = page.evaluate(VISIBLE_JS)
    screens = math.ceil(vis["pageHeight"] / VIEW["height"])
    shot = image_tokens(VIEW["width"], VIEW["height"])
    return {
        "url": url,
        "screenshot_tokens": shot,
        "screens_to_scroll": screens,
        "whole_page_as_pixels": shot * screens,
        "full_tree_tokens": len(ENC.encode(full_tree)),
        "viewport_tree_tokens": len(ENC.encode("\n".join(vis["lines"]))),
        "interactive_total": vis["total"],
        "interactive_in_view": len(vis["lines"]),
    }

with sync_playwright() as pw:
    proxy = {"server": os.environ["HTTPS_PROXY"]} if os.environ.get("HTTPS_PROXY") else None
    browser = pw.chromium.launch(proxy=proxy)
    page = browser.new_page(viewport=VIEW)
    rows = []
    for u in URLS:
        try:
            rows.append(measure(page, u))
        except Exception as e:
            rows.append({"url": u, "error": str(e)[:80]})
    browser.close()

print(json.dumps(rows, indent=1))

Run it with pip install playwright tiktoken and playwright install chromium. Pass your own URLs as arguments.

The results

Measured on November 17, 2026, at a 1280x800 viewport. All numbers are tokens.

Page 1 screenshot Whole page as screenshots Full tree Viewport tree Interactive in view / total
Wikipedia article 1,365 10,920 (8 screens) 12,711 578 76 / 723
Hacker News front page 1,365 2,730 (2 screens) 9,905 1,516 167 / 229
GitHub repo page 1,365 15,015 (11 screens) 13,361 907 95 / 274
Python docs (asyncio) 1,365 5,460 (4 screens) 3,772 229 26 / 78
Stripe pricing 1,365 40,950 (30 screens) 19,737 903 98 / 445
BBC News 1,365 10,920 (8 screens) 8,144 260 33 / 119

What the numbers say

1. The full tree is not the cheap option people assume. It cost between 2.8 and 14.5 times one screenshot. On Hacker News the full tree was 9,905 tokens, while scrolling the entire page as screenshots was 2,730. Dense link pages are terrible as trees.

2. For reading a whole long page, the tree usually wins. On 4 of 6 pages the full tree beat scrolling through screenshots. Stripe's pricing page is the extreme: 19,737 tokens as a tree against 40,950 as 30 screenshots.

3. The viewport tree is the best default for acting. It beat a single screenshot on 5 of 6 pages: 229 tokens against 1,365 on the Python docs, a 6x saving. The one loss was Hacker News, where 167 links fit in one viewport and the list (1,516 tokens) cost slightly more than the image.

The part tokens do not show

Cost is half the story. The other half is what the agent does next.

With a screenshot, the model answers "click at (873, 659)". With a tree, it answers "click element 41". In our own browser automation runs, coordinate clicks went wrong whenever the window size changed between two steps: the same coordinates landed on a different button. References to tree nodes kept working, because they point at the element and not at a place on the screen.

That is the real argument for tools like agent-desktop. A tree is not only cheaper on most pages. It gives the agent handles that survive a layout change.

What I would build from this

  • Default to the viewport tree. Numbered, interactive elements only, re-read after every action.
  • Fall back to a screenshot when the tree is poor. Canvas apps, charts, image-heavy pages and custom widgets with no accessible names.
  • Fall back when the list is longer than the image. If the viewport tree passes roughly 1,400 tokens, the screenshot is cheaper. Hacker News is the proof.
  • Never send the full tree by default. Fetch it only when the task is to read the whole page.

Caveats

  • Six pages, one viewport size, one run each. Treat the ratios as a guide, not a law.
  • Image tokens use Anthropic's estimate. Text tokens were counted with OpenAI's o200k_base tokenizer as a stand-in, so the two columns are close but not from the same tokenizer.
  • The viewport tree drops static text on purpose. It is for acting, not for reading.

If you are building agents that drive real software, the loop around this matters more than the view itself. I wrote about that here: the agent loop architecture we use in production. And if you want an agent like this built for your product, that is what we do at Axionry.

Sources

  • Vercel Labs releases agent-desktop (emergent.sh)
  • AI agents news brief, November 2, 2026 (AI Agents Directory)

title: Getting Started with AI: A Practical Learning Roadmap for Beginners (2026)
description:
Artificial Intelligence is changing how developers, students, freelancers, and businesses approach everyday tasks.

From AI-powered writing assistants to image generators and productivity tools, there are many opportunities to explore.

But for someone new to AI, one challenge remains:

Where should you start?

Learning AI doesn't necessarily require advanced programming knowledge. You can begin by understanding basic concepts and experimenting with practical tools.

1. Start with AI Fundamentals

Before using different AI applications, understand the basics:

  • What is Artificial Intelligence?
  • How do AI assistants work?
  • What are generative AI tools?
  • What are the limitations of AI-generated outputs?
  • Why is human verification important?

These concepts provide a foundation for exploring more advanced applications.

2. Explore Beginner-Friendly AI Tools

Start experimenting with tools that solve practical problems.

  • ChatGPT: Brainstorming, explanations, and writing assistance.
  • Canva AI: Visual design and presentations.
  • Midjourney: AI-generated images.
  • Notion AI: Productivity and information organization.

Choose tools based on your interests instead of trying to learn everything simultaneously.

3. Learn Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering is the process of providing clear instructions and context to an AI system.

For example, instead of asking:

"Explain Python."

Try:

"Explain Python variables to a beginner using three simple examples and short code snippets."

A well-structured prompt helps communicate your requirements more effectively.

4. Build Practical Projects

Apply what you learn through small projects:

  • Create a blog outline using an AI assistant.
  • Generate a visual using an image-generation tool.
  • Prepare a YouTube script.
  • Organize research notes.
  • Create a social media content calendar.

Always review generated results for accuracy and quality.

5. Follow a Structured Learning Roadmap

A useful learning sequence is:

Beginner

  • AI fundamentals
  • ChatGPT basics
  • Prompt engineering
  • Google Gemini

Intermediate

  • AI image generation
  • AI video creation
  • AI content writing
  • AI for SEO

Advanced

  • AI automation
  • AI agents and workflows
  • AI chatbots
  • AI for business

Continue Learning

If you're looking for beginner-friendly AI learning resources, explore the AI Tutorials section at AIToolMind.

It brings together AI learning topics, popular tools, and practical guides in one place.

Explore the complete learning resource:

https://aitoolmind.com/ai-tutorials/

Final Thoughts

The best way to learn AI is to combine basic knowledge with practical experimentation.

Start with one tool, understand what it can do, build a small project, and gradually expand your skills.

You don't need to master everything at once. Consistent learning is what matters.

title: Detect Known VPN Traffic in Express and FastAPI Middleware
description:
A spike hits /account. Half the requests look scripted. Someone on the team suggests a one-line fix: block every VPN. That rule is tempting, and it is a good way to lock out people on a company VPN or a privacy relay, while anyone determined just switches networks.

A better pattern is middleware that looks up the client IP, attaches a few flags to the request, and steps up verification on sensitive paths. Log it, tighten a rate limit, or send a challenge. Don’t hard-block by default, and don’t treat a flag as a verdict that someone is hiding something.

This post is that middleware in Express and in FastAPI. A longer walkthrough, including a few more edge cases, is in the guide to detecting VPN traffic in Node.js and Python.

What the flags actually mean

One GET /v0/ip/{ip} call, with Authorization: Bearer, returns location, network and traits. This is not proxy detection. On a paid key, the traits that matter for live traffic are:

  • is_vpn — the IP belongs to a known VPN network, including major commercial VPN providers. Whole networks of VPN-heavy hosting providers are flagged, so other servers on those networks are flagged too. A new VPN range may still show false.
  • is_tor — a current Tor exit node (exits only, not guards, middle relays or bridges).
  • is_relay — privacy relay egress. It is kept separate from is_vpn, so you don’t treat privacy-relay users like VPN users by mistake.
  • is_hosting — hosting/datacenter detection: cloud, hosting and CDN networks where real users rarely browse from.

Behind a known VPN network, a Tor exit or a privacy relay, location is the egress, not the user’s. Use the flags as signals.

These risk flags (is_vpn, is_tor, is_relay, is_hosting) are paid-only; plans start at $9/month. A free key returns geolocation and ASN only — the flags are omitted — at 1,000 requests per UTC calendar month and 1 request/second, for personal and non-commercial use. Commercial use needs a paid plan. The flag reference is on the VPN detection API page.

Get the real client IP first

Behind Nginx, a load balancer or a CDN, the socket address is the proxy, not the visitor. In Express, set trust proxy to match your topology and use req.ip — never parse raw X-Forwarded-For yourself; a client can put any address there. In FastAPI / Uvicorn, start with --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips so request.client.host is the visitor. Strip the ::ffff: prefix from IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses before you look the IP up.

Express middleware

Keep the key in NDL_API_KEY on the server. This helper caches per IP, times out at 800 ms and fails open. Attach it after trust proxy is set:

// vpn-mw.js (Node 18+, global fetch)
const API = "https://api.networkdatalabs.com/v0/ip/";
const KEY = process.env.NDL_API_KEY;
const cache = new Map();            // swap for Redis/LRU in production
const TTL_MS = 6 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

function normalize(ip) {
  return ip && ip.startsWith("::ffff:") ? ip.slice(7) : ip;
}

async function lookup(ip) {
  const hit = cache.get(ip);
  if (hit && hit.exp > Date.now()) return hit.data;

  const res = await fetch(API + encodeURIComponent(ip), {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}` },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(800),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`lookup ${res.status}`);
  const data = await res.json();
  cache.set(ip, { data, exp: Date.now() + TTL_MS });
  return data;
}

function vpnTraffic() {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    try {
      req.ipIntel = await lookup(normalize(req.ip));
    } catch {
      req.ipIntel = null;           // fail open: never block the request
    }
    next();
  };
}

module.exports = { vpnTraffic };

// app.js
const express = require("express");
const { vpnTraffic } = require("./vpn-mw");

const app = express();
app.set("trust proxy", 1);          // one reverse proxy; see the Express guide
app.use(vpnTraffic());

app.get("/account", (req, res) => {
  const t = req.ipIntel?.traits ?? {};
  // Step up on known VPN networks, Tor exits or hosting IPs.
  // Privacy relay (is_relay) is usually a normal user — log it, don't block.
  if (t.is_tor || t.is_vpn || t.is_hosting) {
    res.set("X-Step-Up", "verify");
  }
  res.json({ ok: true });
});

The same policy in FastAPI

Tell Uvicorn which proxy to trust, then read request.state.ip_intel in the route:

# vpn_mw.py
import os, time
from urllib.parse import quote
import httpx
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware

API = "https://api.networkdatalabs.com/v0/ip/"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['NDL_API_KEY']}"}
_client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(0.8), headers=HEADERS)
_cache: dict[str, tuple[float, dict]] = {}
TTL = 6 * 3600

def normalize(ip: str) -> str:
    return ip[7:] if ip and ip.startswith("::ffff:") else ip

async def lookup(ip: str) -> dict | None:
    hit = _cache.get(ip)
    if hit and hit[0] > time.time():
        return hit[1]
    try:
        r = await _client.get(API + quote(ip, safe=""))
        r.raise_for_status()
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        return None                  # fail open
    data = r.json()
    _cache[ip] = (time.time() + TTL, data)
    return data

class VpnTrafficMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
        ip = request.client.host if request.client else ""
        request.state.ip_intel = await lookup(normalize(ip))
        return await call_next(request)

# app.py — FastAPI behind one trusted proxy
# uvicorn app:app --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips="10.0.0.5"
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from vpn_mw import VpnTrafficMiddleware

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(VpnTrafficMiddleware)

@app.get("/account")
async def account(request: Request):
    data = request.state.ip_intel
    t = (data or {}).get("traits") or {}
    step_up = bool(t.get("is_tor") or t.get("is_vpn") or t.get("is_hosting"))
    return {"ok": True, "step_up": step_up}

How to treat each flag

Signal What it means Suggested action
is_tor Current Tor exit node Step up or challenge; don’t hard-block unless you must
is_vpn Known VPN networks, including major commercial VPN providers Log it; step up on sensitive paths (account, payment)
is_hosting Hosting/datacenter IP: often scripts and bots Tighter rate limit or a challenge
is_relay Privacy relay: usually a normal, privacy-minded user Allow; don’t treat the location as precise

You can hard-block every known VPN network, but it usually backfires. Plenty of real users come from a known VPN network or a privacy relay. Leave is_relay alone unless you have a reason not to.

A fixture: 8.8.8.8 is hosting, not a VPN

A public US DNS resolver is a useful check. It should come back as US with is_hosting and is_anycast true, and is_vpn / is_tor / is_relay false. If your middleware would treat this IP as a VPN, the rule is too broad.

$ curl -s https://api.networkdatalabs.com/v0/ip/8.8.8.8 \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
    | jq '{country_code: .location.country_code, traits}'

{
  "country_code": "US",
  "traits": {
    "is_anycast": true,
    "is_hosting": true,
    "is_mobile": false,
    "is_satellite": false,
    "is_bogon": false,
    "is_vpn": false,
    "is_tor": false,
    "is_relay": false
  }
}

Documentation IPs like 203.0.113.10 are reserved TEST-NET addresses. The API returns them with traits.is_bogon true and no useful location. They’re fine for exercising fail-open; use a public US IP such as 8.8.8.8 when you want a real geolocation and traits fixture.

If the country looks “wrong” on a VPN, you’re seeing the egress. The IP belongs to the known VPN network, the Tor exit or the privacy relay, so location.country_code is that exit’s country, not the user’s.

Caching, timeouts and quota

  • Cache per IP for a few hours. Most traffic is repeat visitors, so the cache absorbs most lookups.
  • Skip paths that don’t need it — static assets, health checks — so you don’t spend quota on them.
  • Fail open on timeouts and errors; log that the lookup was unavailable.
  • Backfilling logs? Use POST /v0/bulk (paid plans) with up to 100 IPs per request. Each IP counts toward the monthly quota; a bad IP shows up under errors without failing the batch.

That’s the middleware we actually shipped: flags as signals, a short cache, and a fail-open path so a lookup outage never takes the app down.

— The Network Data Labs team

title: Building Production-Ready AI Agents: Data Quality, Observability & Security
description:
Building Production-Ready AI Agents: A Practical Architecture for Data Quality, Observability, and Runtime Security

An engineering guide to moving AI applications beyond successful demos and into dependable production environments.

Building an AI prototype has become considerably easier. Developers can connect a language model to external tools, add retrieval capabilities, integrate an image recognition model, and demonstrate an automated workflow in relatively little time. However, a successful demonstration is not the same as a production-ready application. Real-world systems must process imperfect data, recover from unexpected failures, manage access to sensitive resources, and provide enough operational visibility for engineers to understand what happened when something goes wrong.

These challenges become particularly important when AI applications combine computer vision with autonomous agents. A visual model may identify an equipment anomaly, while an agent retrieves maintenance records, evaluates possible causes, and recommends corrective actions. Each component introduces its own failure modes, and the combined system requires safeguards that extend beyond model accuracy.

A useful engineering approach is to organize production readiness around four complementary capabilities: data annotation and validation, computer vision reliability, agentic AI observability, and runtime security.

1. Start With Data Contracts, Not Just Model Accuracy

Many AI projects begin by selecting a model and measuring its performance against an evaluation dataset. Although this is necessary, production reliability also depends on whether incoming data meets the assumptions made during development.

Consider a visual inspection service trained on images captured at a particular resolution and lighting configuration. If a production camera begins delivering lower-resolution images, the model may continue producing predictions even though the input no longer resembles the data on which it was evaluated.

A data contract helps prevent this type of silent degradation by defining expected input characteristics and validation rules.

For example, a computer vision application might require images to meet minimum resolution thresholds, use supported file formats, and contain the metadata needed to identify the camera or production environment.

def validate_image_metadata(metadata):
    required_fields = ["width", "height", "camera_id"]

    for field in required_fields:
        if field not in metadata:
            raise ValueError(f"Missing field: {field}")

    if metadata["width"] < 640:
        raise ValueError("Image width below supported threshold")

    if metadata["height"] < 480:
        raise ValueError("Image height below supported threshold")

    return True

This illustrative validation function does not guarantee that an image is suitable for inference. It demonstrates how basic input assumptions can be checked before a model processes the data.

Training data requires similar discipline. Annotation guidelines should define how ambiguous examples are handled, how disagreements are resolved, and how labeling quality is evaluated.

These requirements are becoming increasingly relevant as the Data Annotation Tools Market expands alongside multimodal AI development.

For engineering teams, the objective should be reproducible datasets and documented validation procedures rather than simply maximizing the volume of labeled information.

2. Design Computer Vision for Real-World Variability

Computer vision models often perform well on benchmark datasets while struggling with unfamiliar operating conditions. This is particularly relevant in manufacturing, logistics, and infrastructure monitoring, where environmental changes can affect image quality.

A production vision service should therefore include mechanisms for monitoring input characteristics and detecting changes in model performance.

Useful signals may include changes in prediction confidence distributions, the frequency of rejected inputs, processing latency, and the proportion of cases escalated for human review.

A simplified inference workflow might look like this:

def inspect_image(image, model, metadata):
    validate_image_metadata(metadata)

    prediction = model.predict(image)

    if prediction.confidence < 0.80:
        return {
            "status": "human_review",
            "reason": "Low-confidence prediction"
        }

    return {
        "status": "completed",
        "label": prediction.label,
        "confidence": prediction.confidence
    }

The confidence threshold is illustrative. Production thresholds should be established through application-specific evaluation, including the costs of false positives and false negatives.

Developers should also avoid assuming that model confidence is equivalent to correctness. A model can be confidently wrong, especially when processing unfamiliar inputs.

These engineering challenges help explain why the AI in Computer Vision Market encompasses more than model development. Reliable deployment requires data pipelines, monitoring infrastructure, evaluation workflows, and integration with operational systems.

3. Treat Agent Execution as a Traceable Workflow

Autonomous agents introduce another layer of complexity because their behavior may depend on sequences of model decisions and external tool calls.

Suppose an agent receives an equipment alert from a computer vision system. It retrieves maintenance records, examines recent sensor readings, and recommends whether a technician should inspect the equipment.

If the recommendation is incorrect, engineers need to determine which information the agent used, which tools it called, and where the workflow diverged from expectations.

This requires structured observability.

At a minimum, an agent execution record should identify the workflow, its steps, relevant tool calls, execution outcomes, and error conditions. Sensitive payloads should be redacted or excluded according to organizational policies.

A simplified logging approach could be:

import logging
import uuid

logger = logging.getLogger("ai_agent")

def execute_agent_step(step_name, tool, arguments):
    trace_id = str(uuid.uuid4())

    logger.info(
        "step_started",
        extra={
            "trace_id": trace_id,
            "step": step_name,
            "tool": tool.__name__
        }
    )

    try:
        result = tool(**arguments)

        logger.info(
            "step_completed",
            extra={
                "trace_id": trace_id,
                "step": step_name
            }
        )

        return result

    except Exception:
        logger.exception(
            "step_failed",
            extra={
                "trace_id": trace_id,
                "step": step_name
            }
        )
        raise

In a real system, a workflow-level trace identifier should be propagated across related operations, while individual spans identify specific steps. The example above illustrates the basic logging concept rather than implementing distributed tracing.

Developers can use established observability approaches such as OpenTelemetry to support standardized telemetry collection and correlation.

The growing Agentic AI Observability Market reflects the importance of these capabilities as organizations move toward more autonomous applications.

Observability is not only about debugging. It also supports evaluation, cost management, reliability engineering, and the investigation of unexpected agent behavior.

4. Enforce Security at Every Tool Boundary

One of the most consequential mistakes in agent development is allowing a model to determine its own permissions.

An agent may be capable of generating a request to delete a record, transfer information, or modify an operational system. That does not mean the request should be authorized.

Permissions should be enforced by application logic and supporting infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on instructions embedded in the model prompt.

For example:

ALLOWED_TOOLS = {
    "maintenance_agent": {
        "read_equipment_status",
        "read_maintenance_history"
    }
}

def authorize_tool_call(agent_role, tool_name):
    permitted = ALLOWED_TOOLS.get(agent_role, set())

    if tool_name not in permitted:
        raise PermissionError(
            f"{agent_role} cannot execute {tool_name}"
        )

    return True

This simplified allowlist demonstrates a basic principle: authorization decisions should be explicit and independently enforced.

Production implementations should also consider user identity, resource-level permissions, request context, and audit requirements. High-impact actions may require human approval even when a tool is technically available.

Developers should pay particular attention to prompt injection, where untrusted information attempts to influence the instructions followed by an AI application.

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications provides useful guidance on risks including prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, and excessive agency.

These concerns are central to the emerging AI Model Runtime Security Market, which focuses on protecting AI systems during active operation.

Runtime security should complement conventional controls such as authentication, authorization, input validation, secure API design, and infrastructure monitoring.

5. Connect the Components Into a Production Architecture

The four capabilities become more useful when implemented as parts of a coherent workflow.

Consider an industrial inspection application in which a computer vision service analyzes images and an AI agent assists with investigating potential defects.

A production-oriented architecture could follow this sequence:

Image ingestion and validation: The application checks incoming data against supported formats, metadata requirements, and basic quality conditions.

Computer vision inference: A model evaluates the image and produces a prediction, with uncertain results routed for additional review.

Agent orchestration: An AI agent retrieves relevant equipment information and prepares a recommendation using approved tools.

Observability: The application records workflow events, tool calls, errors, and operational metrics using consistent identifiers.

Runtime authorization: Independent controls verify that the agent is permitted to access requested resources and execute proposed actions.

Human oversight: Consequential recommendations or actions are escalated according to established approval policies.

This architecture does not require every organization to adopt the same vendors or development frameworks. The implementation should reflect application requirements, existing infrastructure, and the consequences of system failure.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides a broader reference for incorporating risk considerations into AI development and deployment.

6. Production Readiness Is an Ongoing Engineering Process

AI production readiness should not be treated as a checklist completed immediately before launch. Models encounter new data, business workflows change, integrations evolve, and security risks develop over time.

Engineering teams therefore need repeatable procedures for evaluation, monitoring, incident response, and controlled updates.

A useful release process should verify that datasets meet documented quality requirements, computer vision models perform acceptably under representative conditions, agent workflows produce adequate telemetry, and tool permissions remain appropriately restricted.

After deployment, the same controls should support ongoing assessment. Unexpected behavior should lead to investigation and measurable improvements rather than ad hoc adjustments to prompts or model configurations.

The larger lesson is that dependable AI systems require more than sophisticated algorithms. They require well-designed interfaces between data, models, agents, monitoring infrastructure, and security controls.

As enterprise AI becomes more autonomous, the quality of these engineering foundations may become as important as the capabilities of the models themselves.

Production-ready AI is not simply AI that works during a demonstration. It is AI that can be evaluated, monitored, controlled, and improved under real operating conditions.

title: HTML & CSS for Beginners: Build Your First Website From Scratch
description:
If you've ever wanted to build your own website but didn't know where to start, HTML and CSS are the perfect place.

Every website you visit, from a simple personal portfolio to a complex web application, relies on technologies that structure and present information in a browser.

Two of the most important technologies are HTML and CSS.

In this tutorial, we'll start from zero and build a small, responsive profile card using HTML and CSS. You don't need previous programming experience.

By the end, you'll understand how webpages are structured, how CSS styles them, and how to create your first working web interface.

1. What Are HTML and CSS?

Before writing code, let's understand what these technologies actually do.

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) defines the structure and content of a webpage.

It tells the browser what elements exist, such as:

  • Headings
  • Paragraphs
  • Images
  • Links
  • Buttons
  • Forms
  • Navigation menus

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how those elements look.

It handles:

  • Colors and backgrounds
  • Fonts and typography
  • Spacing and alignment
  • Layouts
  • Borders and shadows
  • Responsive designs
  • Animations and transitions

Think of a website as a house:

  • HTML is the structure and rooms.
  • CSS is the interior design and appearance.
  • JavaScript adds interactive behavior.

You can build a webpage using HTML alone, but CSS makes it visually appealing and easier to use.

2. What Do You Need to Get Started?

You don't need expensive software or a complicated development environment.

You'll need:

  1. A computer.
  2. A modern web browser such as Chrome or Firefox.
  3. A code editor.

I recommend Visual Studio Code (VS Code).

Create a folder named my-first-website.

Inside that folder, create two files:

  • index.html
  • style.css

Your project structure should look like this:

my-first-website/
│
├── index.html
└── style.css

That's everything we need for our first project.

3. Create Your First HTML Page

Open index.html and add the following code:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport"
          content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

    <title>My First Website</title>

    <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
<body>

    <h1>Hello, World!</h1>

    <p>
        Welcome to my first website.
        I'm learning HTML and CSS!
    </p>

</body>
</html>

Let's understand the important parts.

<!DOCTYPE html>

Tells the browser to interpret the document using modern HTML.

<html lang="en">

The root element of the HTML document. The language attribute identifies the page language.

<head>

Contains information about the document, including its title, metadata, and stylesheet references.

<title>

Defines the browser tab title.

<body>

Contains the content displayed on the webpage.

<h1>

Creates the main heading.

<p>

Defines a paragraph.

Save the file and open index.html in your browser.

Congratulations! You've just created your first webpage.

4. Understand HTML Elements and Attributes

HTML uses elements to organize content.

For example:

<h1>Learn Web Development</h1>

<p>Start building websites today.</p>

<a href="https://example.com">
    Visit Website
</a>

<img src="image.jpg" alt="A sample image">

An HTML element generally consists of:

  • An opening tag.
  • Some content.
  • A closing tag.

Attributes provide additional information about an element.

For example, href specifies a link destination, while src specifies an image source.

Some elements, such as <img>, don't require a closing tag.

Understanding elements and attributes is fundamental to writing clean HTML.

5. Add CSS to Style Your Website

Our webpage currently looks very basic.

Let's improve it with CSS.

Open style.css and write:

* {
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
    box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    background: #f1f5f9;
    color: #1e293b;
    padding: 40px;
}

h1 {
    color: #2563eb;
    margin-bottom: 15px;
}

p {
    font-size: 18px;
    line-height: 1.6;
}

Save the file and refresh your browser.

You'll notice that the heading has changed color, the paragraph is easier to read, and the page has some breathing room.

Let's understand a few CSS concepts.

CSS Selectors

Selectors identify which HTML elements should receive styles.

h1 {
    color: blue;
}

This targets all <h1> elements.

CSS Properties

Properties define what you want to change.

Examples include:

  • color
  • background
  • font-size
  • margin
  • padding
  • border

CSS Values

Values determine how a property behaves.

For example:

font-size: 24px;

Here, font-size is the property and 24px is its value.

6. Build a Complete Profile Card

Now let's combine everything into a small project.

We'll create a modern profile card with:

  • A profile image.
  • A name and job title.
  • A short description.
  • A contact button.
  • A responsive layout.

Replace the contents of index.html with:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport"
          content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

    <title>My Profile Card</title>

    <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
<body>

    <main class="profile-card">

        <img
            src="https://placehold.co/120x120"
            alt="Profile placeholder"
            class="profile-image"
        >

        <h1>Alex Morgan</h1>

        <h2>Frontend Developer</h2>

        <p>
            I enjoy creating modern websites
            and learning new technologies.
        </p>

        <a href="mailto:hello@example.com"
           class="contact-btn">
            Contact Me
        </a>

    </main>

</body>
</html>

Now add the following CSS to style.css:

* {
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
    box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
    min-height: 100vh;
    display: grid;
    place-items: center;
    padding: 20px;
    background: #0f172a;
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
}

.profile-card {
    width: 100%;
    max-width: 350px;
    padding: 35px 25px;
    text-align: center;
    background: #1e293b;
    border-radius: 20px;
    color: white;
    box-shadow: 0 15px 40px
                rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3);
}

.profile-image {
    width: 120px;
    height: 120px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    object-fit: cover;
    margin-bottom: 20px;
    border: 4px solid #38bdf8;
}

.profile-card h1 {
    font-size: 26px;
    margin-bottom: 8px;
}

.profile-card h2 {
    font-size: 16px;
    color: #38bdf8;
    margin-bottom: 15px;
}

.profile-card p {
    color: #cbd5e1;
    line-height: 1.6;
    margin-bottom: 25px;
}

.contact-btn {
    display: inline-block;
    padding: 12px 25px;
    background: #2563eb;
    color: white;
    text-decoration: none;
    border-radius: 8px;
    transition: background 0.3s ease;
}

.contact-btn:hover {
    background: #1d4ed8;
}

What did we learn from this project?

We used several important CSS concepts:

  • display: grid to center the profile card.
  • max-width to control its maximum size.
  • border-radius to create rounded corners.
  • box-shadow to add depth.
  • transition to animate hover changes.
  • :hover to change the button's appearance.

We also used object-fit: cover to make the profile image fit its circular container.

Notice something important: We didn't need JavaScript to create this interface. HTML and CSS were enough.

7. Make Your Website Responsive

A website should work on different screen sizes.

Our profile card already uses a flexible width and a maximum width, which helps it adapt to smaller screens.

For more complex layouts, CSS media queries allow you to apply styles depending on the viewport size.

For example:

@media (max-width: 480px) {

    .profile-card {
        padding: 25px 18px;
    }

    .profile-card h1 {
        font-size: 22px;
    }

    .profile-image {
        width: 100px;
        height: 100px;
    }

}

This makes some elements smaller on mobile devices.

Responsive design is an essential skill for modern frontend developers.

8. Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

When learning HTML and CSS, beginners often make a few common mistakes.

1. Forgetting to link the CSS file

Make sure your HTML contains:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">

Also check that both files are in the correct folder.

2. Using too many <div> elements

HTML provides semantic elements such as <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, and <footer>.

Use elements that describe the purpose of your content whenever appropriate.

3. Ignoring mobile screens

Always test your webpages at different viewport widths.

4. Writing CSS without understanding selectors

Learn the difference between element, class, and ID selectors before moving into advanced styling.

5. Copying code without experimenting

Change colors, spacing, fonts, and layouts. Experimentation is one of the best ways to understand how CSS works.

9. What Should You Learn Next?

Once you understand the basics, follow a structured learning path.

HTML learning path

  1. HTML document structure.
  2. Headings and paragraphs.
  3. Links and images.
  4. Lists and tables.
  5. Forms and input fields.
  6. Semantic HTML.
  7. HTML accessibility.
  8. Metadata and SEO fundamentals.

CSS learning path

  1. Selectors and specificity.
  2. Colors and backgrounds.
  3. Box model.
  4. Display and positioning.
  5. Flexbox.
  6. CSS Grid.
  7. Responsive design.
  8. Transitions and animations.
  9. Advanced CSS techniques.

You can explore free HTML and CSS learning resources at MAKUIStudio.

The goal is to understand each concept, practice it, and gradually build more complex projects.

10. Practice With Free Code Examples

Reading tutorials is useful, but building things yourself is what develops practical skills.

Try creating these projects next:

  • Personal portfolio card.
  • Responsive navigation bar.
  • Login and registration form.
  • Pricing cards.
  • Landing page.
  • Responsive image gallery.
  • Modern dashboard layout.

You can also explore MAKUIStudio for free programming courses and reusable HTML/CSS code examples.

Use snippets as learning material: study the structure, experiment with the styles, and customize the code for your own projects.

Final Thoughts

Learning web development doesn't have to be complicated.

HTML gives your website structure, while CSS brings that structure to life through styling and layout.

Start with simple webpages, practice regularly, and gradually move toward more advanced projects.

You don't need to master everything in one day. Consistency and hands-on practice matter much more than memorizing hundreds of properties.

Your turn!

Have you already built your first website, or are you just starting with HTML and CSS?

Share your experience in the comments. I'd love to know what you're building!

Continue Learning: Explore free HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python learning resources at MAKUIStudio.

title: I built a self-hosted app to see all my Steam, PlayStation and Xbox games in one place
description:
I play on PC, PS5 and Xbox, plus a Switch that sits next to the TV. Every platform has its own library, its own stats and its own idea of what "played" means. I wanted one page where I could see everything: what I own, what I actually played, and the pile of games I keep buying and never start.

The existing tools didn't fit what I wanted. Some are desktop-only, some are hosted services where my data lives on someone else's server. I run a small homelab anyway, so I built Playroom, a self-hosted web app for your whole game collection.

Live demo (fake collection, read-only): https://hexguardsec.github.io/playroom-selfhosted/
Source: https://github.com/HexGuardSec/playroom-selfhosted

What it does

  • Syncs Steam, PlayStation (PS3 to PS5 trophies) and Xbox automatically. Nintendo games are added by hand, since there is no public API.
  • Covers, playtime, achievements and trophies, ratings and notes for every game.
  • An activity calendar built from each sync, so you can see when you actually played.
  • A backlog view with estimated time to beat, to face the pile of shame.
  • Public or private collection, 15 interface languages.

Things that were harder than expected

PlayStation has no public API. Playroom uses the same endpoints as the official PlayStation website, with an NPSSO token you get from your own account. It works, but it can break if Sony changes something, and the docs say so clearly.

Xbox history is noisy. On Windows, the Xbox app records PC games launched through Game Bar, even games that have nothing to do with Xbox. My first sync showed almost 200 "Xbox" games. Playroom now keeps a title only if it ran on a console or has Xbox achievements, and my list went down to the 95 games I really played.

PS4 and PS5 versions of the same game show up as two trophy lists. Playroom merges them into a single entry.

Built for people who self-host

  • One Docker container, no database to run. Data stays in a single folder you can back up.
  • No runtime dependencies: Node.js 22 and plain browser JavaScript, nothing from npm.
  • Security first: scrypt password hashing, strict Content Security Policy, CSRF protection, a non-root container with a read-only file system and no Linux capabilities. API keys never appear in logs or URLs.
  • No telemetry. Playroom never phones home.

Running it takes one command:

docker run -d --name playroom -p 8080:8080 \
  -v ./data:/app/data \
  ghcr.io/hexguardsec/playroom-selfhosted:latest

On first launch, the container logs print a one-time setup code, and the web page walks you through creating your account and adding your API keys.

A note on how it was built

I built Playroom with a lot of help from an AI assistant (Claude). I designed it, tested it on my own setup and reviewed the code, and the repository has an AI-DECLARATION.md file that explains what was AI-generated and what wasn't. I'd rather be upfront about it.

What's next

The next version (planned for mid-December) adds notifications (Discord, ntfy), JSON/CSV export, backup and restore, and an import from Playnite. The full roadmap is in ROADMAP.md.

If you try it, I'd love your feedback: issues and ideas are welcome on GitHub, and there's a Discord server for questions: https://discord.gg/xy9nYXxRvW

And if you also have a backlog that scares you a little, tell me how many unplayed games you have. Mine is not a number I'm proud of.

title: You Changed the Prompt and Your Score Went Up Four Points on Fifty Questions
description:
You had an evaluation set.

Fifty questions,
each with a correct answer.

The old prompt
scored seventy eight percent.

You rewrote the instructions
and the new one
scored eighty two.

Four points better.

You wrote it up,
shipped it,
and moved on.

Look at what four points means
on fifty questions.

Each question is worth two points.

Four points is two questions.

Two questions
out of fifty
went the other way.

That is not a result.

That is a coin
landing differently twice.

Here is the arithmetic.

At around eighty percent,
the standard error
on fifty questions
is close to six points.

A rough ninety five percent range
is plus or minus eleven.

Your true score
could be anywhere
from about seventy
to about ninety.

Both prompts
fit easily inside that.

And the model
is not perfectly repeatable either.

Run the old prompt again
and it may move
a question or two by itself.

Same prompt.

Same questions.

A different afternoon.

So do not compare totals.

Compare question by question.

How many did the new prompt fix?

How many did it break?

Fixed seven
and broke five
is not the same change
as fixed two
and broke none,
even though both
add up to plus two.

Read the five it broke.

They are often
the important ones.

Then make the set bigger.

To see a few points of difference
with any confidence,
you need hundreds of questions,
not dozens.

Run each version
more than once,
and look at how much
a version disagrees with itself
before you trust
how much it disagrees with another.

Keep a note of the noise.

If two runs of the same prompt
differ by three points,
a three point improvement
means nothing.

A score is a measurement.

Every measurement
comes with an error bar,
whether you draw it or not.

If you never draw it,
you will spend months
chasing changes
that were never there.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor now helps you find issues before your users notice them (Public Preview)
description:
When a WorkSpace is slow or won't connect, the IT administrator trying to help has traditionally had to dig through Amazon CloudWatch metrics, logs, and configuration data across multiple tools to find out why. And in the meantime, the user on the other end can't get their work done. In April this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor, an AI-powered agent that helps IT administrators diagnose and fix WorkSpaces performance, connectivity and provisioning issues and get users back to work faster. With Advisor, administrators can investigate a WorkSpace from the console and, in minutes, see the likely root cause and recommended actions they can take right away. Since then, we've continued to invest in Advisor so your team can spend less time chasing down issues one by one, and more time on the projects your business is counting on you to deliver.

Today, we're excited to announce the preview of proactive troubleshooting in WorkSpaces Advisor, which moves your team from reacting to individual tickets to staying ahead of issues across your whole environment. Advisor can identify issues across your WorkSpaces, explain the likely cause of each one and recommend a fix. You don't need to start an investigation, wait for a user to report a problem, or set alarm thresholds first.  

If the same problem affects many WorkSpaces, Advisor will show it as a single issue with the likely cause and a recommended fix.  Your team fixes the root cause once instead of chasing the same symptom one WorkSpace at a time. For example, Advisor can tell you when a group of WorkSpaces became unhealthy at the same time, when WorkSpaces are running low on CPU or memory, or when a certificate your users need to sign in is about to expire. That gives you time to act before a small issue turns into an outage or a queue of support tickets. You'll find these issues in the WorkSpaces console.

Proactive troubleshooting also extends Advisor to your users, which means fewer tickets reach your help desk and the ones that do come with better information. When a session is slow or won't connect, Advisor will tell users whether the problem is with their device, their network, or their WorkSpace. It then walks them through the fixes you've approved, such as restarting their WorkSpace. When an issue does need IT, the user gets a clear explanation to pass along, so your team starts from a diagnosis instead of "my WorkSpace is slow."  You stay in control because you decide which fixes users can make on their own, and you can turn this off for any directory.

Proactive troubleshooting is available in preview at no additional charge in AWS commercial Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Personal is available. Troubleshooting for end users requires version 5.37 or later of the WorkSpaces client for Windows, with the new experience turned on. Troubleshooting for users requires the WorkSpaces client for Windows version 5.37 or later with new experience. To get started, see the Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor Administration Guide.
