title: Human in the loop AI for client work: where to put the approval step
description:
A reminder goes to a client who paid last week. A client is told the wrong filing deadline. A draft engagement letter leaves the office with last year's rates still in it. Each one costs a partner an afternoon of apology and rework, and the client's trust takes longer to rebuild than the email took to send. So when we say human in the loop AI, we mean something specific: a person approves particular actions before they happen. Not a dashboard someone checks when they remember. Not a review screen that appears after the send. Approval that sits in the path of the action and stops it until a named person says yes.

That definition matters because a lot of the disappointment with agents in accounting and law practices isn't a model problem. It's a placement problem. The approval sits in the wrong place, or nowhere, or everywhere.

Place it nowhere and something leaves the building that should not have. Place it everywhere and people stop reading. Both failures cost money. The first costs clients. The second costs the automation, because the firm quietly stops using it and goes back to doing the work by hand.

Classify by reversibility and audience

We sort every action an agent can take on two axes. Can we undo it? Who sees it? A draft that stays inside the firm and can be deleted is a different animal from an email that leaves the building with a partner's name on it. A calendar hold is different from a payment instruction.

The default we have landed on is simple. If the action is client-facing, it waits for approval. If it is irreversible, it waits for approval. If it is both, it waits for approval from the person who is accountable for the outcome, not just anyone with a login.

  • Internal and reversible: let it run, keep a log.
  • Internal but awkward to unwind: let it run with a short undo window and a notification.
  • Client-facing: approve before send, every time.
  • Money, filings, deadline changes, permissions: approve, and name the role that owns it.

This is a policy, not a prompt. It lives in configuration that a partner or ops lead can read and change, not in the system message of an agent. If the policy is buried in a prompt, nobody can audit it and nobody can explain it to a client. It also has to be versioned. When the rules change, you want to know which items ran under the old ones, and the people who own the rules should be able to read the diff.

One more distinction helps. Some actions are safe to reverse technically but expensive to reverse socially. Sending a corrected invoice is easy. Un-sending the wrong one is not. We treat social irreversibility as real irreversibility.

Make the review worth doing

Approval screens fail in a predictable way. The reviewer has thirty items, each with a green button, and no reason to slow down. Click, click, click. The step exists, the signature exists, and the judgment does not.

So the screen has to give the reviewer three things at once: the draft that will go out, the source data it came from, and a plain statement of what happens on approval. If a reminder email is about to go to a client, show the invoice status next to it. If the status says paid, the reviewer should see that without opening another tab. We also put the consequence in plain language: this sends the attached statement to three named recipients at 9am tomorrow. Reviewers decide better when the result is stated rather than implied.

Editing has to be as easy as approving. If the reviewer has to reject, go back to the source, regenerate, and start again, they will approve a draft they know is mediocre. Let them fix a line, then send. Log the edited version as the version of record. Approval should not require a meeting either. If an approval needs a conversation, the action is not ready to be queued. Change the request until a busy person can decide it in under a minute.

Batching is where a lot of the time savings come from, and a lot of the risk. Twenty drafts reviewed on one screen beats twenty separate interruptions. But a batch should not flatten exceptions. Sort items where the source data conflicts with the draft, and make those the first thing a reviewer sees.

Then log it. Who approved, what they saw, when, and which version went out. We do not log this to catch people. We log it because a client will eventually ask, an auditor may ask, and because the log is the most honest record you have when deciding what to loosen later.

policy:
  internal_meeting_summary:
    requires_approval: false
    log: true
  client_email_send:
    requires_approval: true
    approver: engagement_partner
    show: [draft, source_data, recipients]
  payment_reminder:
    requires_approval: true
    approver: billing_lead
    block_if: invoice_status == paid
  filing_deadline_change:
    requires_approval: true
    approvers_all_of: [engagement_partner, compliance]
  payment_instruction:
    requires_approval: true
    approvers_all_of: [partner, second_partner]  # two different people

Loosen only with evidence

Two numbers tell you whether an approval step is earning its place: how often items are approved, and how often they are edited first. Look at them per action type. An overall average hides the one step that is failing.

If an action is approved almost every time and rarely edited, the step may be doing nothing except slowing the queue. That is a candidate for an undo window or a sampling review. If an action is edited often, the step is doing real work, and the better question is why the draft keeps arriving wrong. Track both numbers next to the log, so the review is a short read and not a project.

Be careful with the first case. A low edit rate can mean the work is good or the reviewers have stopped reading. Check for fast approvals on items that should take thought. We would rather keep a step too long than remove one people were quietly relying on.

And do not create approvals that only transfer blame. If a reviewer cannot evaluate the thing they are signing, their approval is not a control. It is a signature on a risk nobody looked at. Review the policy when the work changes, not on a calendar. A new template, a new filing rule, a new billing process, each one moves actions across the line. A step that was safe to auto-send last quarter may not be safe now.

Precision AI OS builds an Agent OS for professional service firms where agents prepare the work and anything that goes to a client waits for a person's approval by default.

title: Estados accesibles en formularios React con email
description:
Cuando un formulario de registro pide confirmar el email, solemos pensar primero en la API: enviar el mensaje, esperar el código y comprobarlo. En la interfaz, sin embargo, hay una pequeña máquina de estados que decide si la experiencia se siente clara o rota.

En mis formularios React intento tratar esa máquina como una parte del diseño, no como un detalle que se arregla al final. Un botón que cambia de texto, un error que empuja todo el layout o un foco que desaparece pueden hacer que una tarea sencilla se vuelva confusa. Esto suena pequeño, aunque cambia bastante cuando la persona navega con teclado o usa un lector de pantalla.

El problema: el email también tiene estados de interfaz

Un flujo de verificación suele tener, como mínimo, estos estados:

  • idle: el formulario está listo para recibir la dirección.
  • sending: la solicitud está en curso y no conviene duplicarla.
  • sent: el código fue enviado y aparece un campo para introducirlo.
  • verifying: se está comprobando el código.
  • success: la dirección quedó confirmada.
  • error: hay que explicar qué puede hacer la persona ahora.

Cuando estos estados se mezclan en varios booleanos (isLoading, hasSent, isValid), aparecen combinaciones imposibles. Por ejemplo, un mensaje puede decir “enviado” mientras el botón sigue bloqueado por un error anterior. Es facil que el código funcione en el caso feliz y se comporte raro al repetir el envío.

Un status único hace más visible la intención:

type EmailStatus =
  | "idle"
  | "sending"
  | "sent"
  | "verifying"
  | "success"
  | "error";

const [status, setStatus] = useState<EmailStatus>("idle");

Así, cada transición se puede revisar junto con su texto, su foco y su comportamiento visual. También ayuda a que el equipo de QA reproduzca el flujo sin adivinar qué combinación de flags provocó el fallo.

Si el flujo tiene más pasos, me ha resultado útil separar la lógica de red de la presentación y documentar los estados claros para un inbox temporal. La idea es la misma: una pantalla debe tener un estado que se pueda nombrar.

Accesibilidad y rendimiento en cada transición

El feedback no debe depender solo del color. Un mensaje de error puede usar role="alert" cuando necesita anunciarse de inmediato, mientras que una confirmación menos urgente puede vivir en un aria-live="polite". No pondría role="alert" en todo: si cada cambio interrumpe la lectura, la experiencia se vuelve cansada.

El foco también necesita una regla. Tras enviar correctamente, el foco puede ir al encabezado que explica cómo introducir el código. Si la solicitud falla, debe quedarse cerca del campo que se puede corregir. Sin esta decisión, el teclado queda perdido y toca volver a buscar donde estaba el problema.

Para el CSS, reserva espacio para los mensajes desde el principio. Un contenedor con min-height o una fila de ayuda estable evita que el formulario salte cuando llega la respuesta. Este enfoque complementa bien estas técnicas para mostrar errores de email sin CLS. El rendimiento percibido mejora aunque la red tarde lo mismo.

Un patrón sencillo para el botón puede ser:

<button type="submit" disabled={status === "sending"}>
  {status === "sending" ? "Enviando…" : "Enviar código"}
</button>

El texto debe explicar la acción actual, no solo mostrar un spinner. Un lector de pantalla necesita saber si la solicitud sigue en curso; una animación sola no cuenta toda la historia.

Cómo probar el flujo con un correo desechable

Para pruebas manuales y de staging, uso una dirección aislada que no mezcle mensajes reales con datos de QA. Un correo desechable permite revisar el mensaje, abrir el enlace y comprobar que la aplicación actualiza el estado correcto sin tocar una bandeja personal.

En una revisión de frontend compruebo también los casos menos comodos:

  1. Enviar dos veces con rapidez: el segundo clic no debe crear una carrera.
  2. Recargar después de recibir el código: la interfaz debe explicar qué se perdió.
  3. Introducir un código caducado: el error debe indicar el siguiente paso.
  4. Volver atrás y cambiar el email: el código anterior no debe validarse para la nueva dirección.
  5. Usar teclado y zoom alto: ningún mensaje debe quedar oculto ni cortar el botón.

En las notas de prueba suelen aparecer búsquedas extrañas como temp org mail o tamp mail com. Las trato como texto de QA, no como nombres de campos ni como enlaces: si el requisito está mal escrito, la interfaz aún puede seguir siendo clara.

Checklist final

  • ¿Existe un estado explícito para cada respuesta de red?
  • ¿El foco tiene un destino definido después de éxito y error?
  • ¿Los mensajes se anuncian sin repetir información innecesaria?
  • ¿El espacio de ayuda evita cambios bruscos de layout?
  • ¿El botón impide duplicar solicitudes mientras se envía?
  • ¿Se puede probar la dirección burner email address sin usar datos personales?
  • ¿La copia sigue siendo comprensible incluso cuando la red va lenta?

Una interfaz de verificación no necesita muchos componentes para ser sólida. Necesita estados con nombres claros, transiciones previsibles y una salida accesible para cada fallo. Cuando React, CSS y Accessibility se revisan juntos, el formulario se siente más tranquilo: la persona sabe qué pasó y cuál es el siguiente paso.

title: What makes a chat mockup look fake: the geometry details nobody mentions
description:
There is a moment in every mockup review where someone says "it doesn't look real yet", and the feedback usually is not about the content. It is about geometry.

If you have ever built a chat interface in Figma, Sketch or a component library, you already know the list of things that make it look fake. Here is that list, in the order that usually matters.

The bubble itself is not a rounded rectangle

A real chat bubble is a shape with at least four independent decisions: the corner radius of each corner, which corner carries the tail, the radius of the tail, and the padding around the text. Get the radius wrong by a few pixels and the bubble reads as "web UI" rather than "app".

The tail is the detail people notice without being able to name it. WhatsApp tails, iMessage tails and Telegram tails are different shapes. A tail that is too wide, too short, or attached to the wrong corner instantly reads as a sticker.

Then there is the grouping rule: consecutive messages from the same sender within a short window group into a single visual unit, with tighter spacing between them than between messages from different people. And the last message in a group often drops its tail entirely, because the bubble sits alone.

Status bar, carrier and clock

Every real phone has a status bar. Most mockups skip it and then look like a floating widget.

The status bar is not decoration either: the clock sits in a fixed position, the signal and battery icons have a specific weight, and the whole bar has a background tint that differs between light and dark mode. On Android it carries the carrier name and sometimes a second icon. On iOS the battery is on the right, on Android on the left.

Get one of these wrong and the screenshot reads as "a design mockup of a phone" rather than "a phone".

Light and dark are different layouts

The most common mistake in mockups is treating dark mode as a color swap. It is not.

A bubble in dark mode has a different radius in some apps, different padding, a different border, and a different shadow, because shadows do not exist on dark surfaces - separation comes from the background tint instead. Text colors, the timestamp gray, the read-receipt blue and the reaction pill all need their own dark-mode values.

If a set of mockups has to work in both appearances, budget for two separate renders, not one render plus a filter.

Timestamps, receipts and reactions

Read receipts live in one of two places: inside the bubble, or below it, and the position depends on the app and on whether the message is the last in the conversation. The color of "Read" versus "Delivered" versus "Sent" is another app-specific value, and mixing them up is instantly recognizable.

Reactions are a pill under the bubble with an emoji and a count, separated from the text by a small gap. They are not round avatars floating next to the message.

Line breaks, links and media

Message bubbles have a maximum width, and long messages wrap. Link previews expand into a card with a title, a domain and sometimes an image, and they sit flush with the bubble's edges rather than inside the text. Voice notes, images and files each have their own inline shape.

One detail that reads as "real": the content inside the bubble is not perfectly aligned to a grid of identical widths. Bubble widths vary with content, which is exactly what makes a real conversation look real.

The practical takeaway

Each of those details is cheap to get right once you know it is there, and expensive to discover one at a time. If you are producing these mocks repeatedly - for ads, product pages, onboarding screens, social posts - the details are worth encoding into a tool rather than re-measuring them per export.

That is the approach behind MockupChat: 16 messaging apps, each skin rebuilt bubble by bubble with its own radii, tail shapes, grouping rules, receipt positions and status bar, in light and dark, exported as PNG or as an animated MP4 from the browser. There is a public REST API and an MCP server if you want to script it, and the format documentation is on the developer page.

How to review a mockup in five minutes

  1. Look at the tail first, then the corner radii.
  2. Check the spacing between grouped messages against the spacing between different senders.
  3. Compare the status bar against a screenshot of a real phone of the same platform.
  4. Read the receipt colors out loud - sent, delivered, read - and check whether they are the right ones for that app.
  5. Then look at the content. If it survives that, the rest is copy.

Getting these details right is what turns "a screenshot of a chat" into something people read as a conversation.

title: Keep Video Preview UI Out of Your Rendered HTML
description:
The 3 AM Page: When Preview Chrome Becomes Render Artifact

You wake to an alert: the automated video pipeline produced 47 corrupted exports overnight. Frame one shows your application's sidebar. Frame twelve captures a modal mid-transition. The encoder did exactly what you asked—it rendered the HTML you gave it, including the preview interface you forgot was part of the DOM tree.

This is the failure mode I am addressing while evaluating heygen-com/hyperframes. Its premise, "Write HTML. Render video," makes HTML the production artifact. A preview dialog, responsive sidebar, or entrance animation must never quietly become part of that artifact.

For a React application using Tailwind CSS v4 and Radix primitives, my recommendation is straightforward: isolate the render document, and animate only the surrounding interface.

One Document, Two Consumers

The architecture has three responsibilities.

The application produces a self-contained HTML document. The preview interface displays that document without modifying it. A render adapter submits the same document, together with explicit viewport and timing settings, to the video-rendering workflow.

That adapter is where Hyperframes integration belongs. I am not assuming a particular repository command, rendering API, or timing contract here; those require verification against the version being adopted. The implementation below deliberately stops at the document boundary.

Do not export the React application root. That couples video output to navigation, portal placement, loaded application styles, and whatever animation happens to be running when capture begins.

Instead, treat the generated HTML as immutable input. Fonts, images, viewport dimensions, and the selected scene time are part of its rendering contract—not incidental browser state.

Why the Tutorial Version Breaks

A common preview implementation measures a panel with getBoundingClientRect(), writes a new width, then repeats that process on the next animation frame. The read after the write can force synchronous layout. Add text wrapping and image decoding, and a smooth-looking demo becomes a source of dropped preview frames and unstable measurements.

Moving the same animation into CSS does not automatically fix it: animating width or height still requires layout work. Use transforms and opacity for interface motion, and reserve fixed dimensions for the rendered document.

The related accessibility failure comes from treating a modal as an absolutely positioned <div>. Adding aria-modal="true" does not implement focus containment, Escape handling, or focus restoration. Keyboard navigation can continue behind the overlay while screen-reader users encounter a misleading dialog boundary.

Both failures come from giving preview chrome responsibilities it should not own.

A Reusable Preview Boundary

In an existing React/TypeScript application configured for Tailwind v4, install @radix-ui/react-dialog. Save this component as VideoPreview.tsx and import the stylesheet below through your application entry point.

import * as Dialog from "@radix-ui/react-dialog";

type VideoPreviewProps = {
  html: string;
};

export function VideoPreview({ html }: VideoPreviewProps) {
  return (
    <Dialog.Root>
      <Dialog.Trigger asChild>
        <button
          type="button"
          className="rounded-md bg-slate-900 px-4 py-2 text-white
            focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-4
            focus-visible:outline-blue-600"
        >
          Preview video document
        </button>
      </Dialog.Trigger>

      <Dialog.Portal>
        <Dialog.Overlay className="fixed inset-0 z-40 bg-black/60" />

        <Dialog.Content
          className="preview-dialog fixed inset-4 z-50 m-auto
            h-fit max-h-[calc(100dvh-2rem)] max-w-5xl
            overflow-auto rounded-xl bg-white p-4 shadow-xl"
        >
          <Dialog.Title className="text-lg font-semibold">
            Video document preview
          </Dialog.Title>

          <Dialog.Description className="mt-1 text-sm text-slate-600">
            Static visual inspection. Final timing is controlled by
            the render workflow.
          </Dialog.Description>

          <div className="preview-shell mt-4">
            <div className="preview-layout">
              <iframe
                title="Isolated video document"
                srcDoc={html}
                sandbox=""
                referrerPolicy="no-referrer"
                className="aspect-video w-full border-0 bg-slate-950"
              />
              <p className="text-sm text-slate-600">
                Preview chrome is excluded from the video document.
              </p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <Dialog.Close asChild>
            <button
              type="button"
              className="mt-4 rounded-md border px-3 py-2
                focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-4
                focus-visible:outline-blue-600"
            >
              Close preview
            </button>
          </Dialog.Close>
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog.Root>
  );
}

Radix supplies the modal interaction model and connects the title and description. The iframe gives the document a separate styling context; the surrounding Tailwind utilities cannot accidentally restyle its headings or captions.

Configure Motion Around the Artifact

This is the complete CSS configuration and micro-interaction:

@import "tailwindcss";

.preview-shell {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.preview-layout {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
}

@container (min-width: 48rem) {
  .preview-layout {
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 12rem;
    align-items: start;
  }
}

@keyframes preview-enter {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(0.5rem);
  }
  to {
    opacity: 1;
    transform: translateY(0);
  }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .preview-dialog[data-state="open"] {
    animation: preview-enter 160ms ease-out both;
  }
}

The container query responds to available dialog space rather than assuming the browser viewport describes the component's layout. The entrance animation never changes the iframe's document.

The Trade-offs Are Intentional

This preview is static. Its empty sandbox disables scripts, so it cannot faithfully preview a document that depends on JavaScript-driven animation. That limitation is preferable to silently executing arbitrary generated code inside the application's trust boundary. A scripted preview needs a separately designed isolation policy.

Likewise, aspect-video describes the preview box, not a guaranteed export resolution. For pixel-sensitive work, render the document at its exact production viewport and scale that surface for inspection. Otherwise, line wrapping can differ between preview and export.

The sandbox also does not make HTML network-isolated. External images and styles can still create requests. Use controlled assets and an appropriate content security policy when documents are untrusted.

Before adoption, test keyboard entry, Escape, focus restoration, reduced motion, and representative documents with a screen reader. Radix handles the outer dialog; it cannot repair inaccessible content inside the iframe.

The architectural payoff is modest but important: Hyperframes receives a document, not a screenshot of your application. Preview improvements remain interface changes instead of becoming accidental changes to the video.

The Isolation Dilemma

The empty sandbox solves the trust boundary problem but creates a fidelity gap. If your video document legitimately requires scripted animation—timed transitions, chart rendering, dynamic text layout—this preview cannot show it. The alternative, enabling scripts, means previewing untrusted or generated HTML inside your application's security context.

How are you solving scripted preview safely? Separate worker context? Sandboxed subprocess? Different trust model entirely? I would value hearing how production teams are navigating this trade-off."

Vercel Token Pass now includes $150 of tokens per month (up from $80) for the same $30 per team per month.

The credit applies to featured open-weight models served through AI Gateway, including Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

Credit resets each billing period with no rollover. When it runs out, requests using standard AI Gateway keys or OIDC tokens fall back to the team's AI Gateway balance, while requests using Token Pass-scoped keys stop with no overage charges.

Token Pass is an Early Access add-on for Pro teams, with limited spots and a waitlist when they fill. To connect your coding agent, run vercel token-pass in the Vercel CLI, or use a Token Pass API key if your agent supports AI Gateway.

Subscribe to Token Pass in your AI Gateway dashboard.

Read more

title: Pin agent color usage to semantic tokens — no raw hex in JSX
description:
The error text looks right on the default theme: #FF4D4F, close enough to the brand red. In dark mode it glows like a highlighter. In the high-contrast theme it fails the contrast check the design system already passed for --color-danger-text.

I’ve started treating a raw hex, rgb(), or Tailwind arbitrary color in an agent UI patch as a merge blocker, the same way a magic font-size should be. If the repo has semantic tokens — danger, text-muted, border-subtle — the agent should use those names, not repaint the brand by eye.

Why the hex always drifts

The model has seen #FF0000 and #111827 in a million examples. It does not know your --color-danger-text is slightly desaturated on purpose, or that background and text come in pairs. A one-off hex also skips dark-mode aliases, focus rings, and the forced-colors adjustments you already paid for.

It is also un-greppable in a useful way. You can find #FF4D4F. You cannot find “every unofficial danger color” after three agents have used #F00, red, and rgb(255 60 60).

A simple color policy

  • Semantic tokens only in product UI: var(--color-danger-text), text-danger, theme('colors.danger.DEFAULT')
  • No raw hex / rgb / hsl in JSX or CSS modules unless the file is the token source
  • Pairs stay paired — if you set a danger background, use the matching danger foreground
  • New colors go in the token file first, with a name and a theme variant, not in the component

If the request is “make this look like the mock,” paste the token names from the mock or the Figma inspect, not a screenshot alone.

What to put in the prompt 

Use only semantic color tokens from src/theme/colors.css (or the Tailwind theme keys listed below).
Do not add hex, rgb, or arbitrary color classes in components.
If a new color is required, add a named token with light and dark values in the token file and use that name.

Paste the token list — it is usually shorter than the component. In review, grep the diff for #, rgb(, hsl(, and Tailwind -[#. Those hits should all live in the token file.

The same gate applies to borders, shadows, and chart series. A one-off #E5E7EB border looks fine until the dark theme uses a different hairline token. Chart palettes should come from the same token file, or from a documented chart subset, not from a D3 example’s category10 colors pasted into a React component.

If the mock is slightly off-token, fix the mock or file a token change. Do not honor a screenshot by hard-coding the eyedropper value. That is how the design system and the running app diverge in a week.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • style={{ color: '#FF4D4F' }} or text-[#FF4D4F] in a component
  • A one-off red / rebeccapurple that ignores the scale
  • A dark-mode fix that adds a second hex instead of a token alias
  • “I picked a color close to the mock” without a token name

Accept

  • An existing semantic token, including its hover/disabled variants
  • A new token in the theme file, used by the component, with both themes filled in

title: October 30, 2026
description:
Agent Registry

Feature

Agent Registry supports cross-project management boundaries (Preview), letting you centrally discover, search, and govern AI agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and tools across multiple Google Cloud projects from a central management project. For more information, see Cross-project boundaries and Configure a management boundary for multiple projects.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Fixed

For AlloyDB clusters compatible with PostgreSQL 18 or later, an instance restart is no longer required when you enable or edit Advanced Query Insights settings, including changing the query length or enabling active query analysis. For clusters compatible with PostgreSQL 17 or earlier, saving changes still requires an instance restart.

For more information, see Use Advanced Query Insights and Monitor active queries.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.13

On October 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.13.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.16.13.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: Do not use Apigee hybrid v1.16.12 due to a potential regression in apigee-connect-agent (see known issue 578314600). Use v1.16.13 instead.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

New ApigeeValkey custom resource

Apigee hybrid v1.16.13 adds the ApigeeValkey custom resource definition (CRD), the apigee-valkey Helm chart, and the valkey configuration properties. ApigeeValkey is the replacement for the ApigeeRedis resource.

In version 1.16.13, the runtime continues to use ApigeeRedis. When you upgrade, install the new CRD with the other CRDs. Leave the new ao.args.valkeyBackend property set to its default value, false. You don't need to install the apigee-valkey chart or change your configuration.

For the supported upgrade sequence, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid. For more information about the resource, see Kubernetes resources.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
492041991 Fixed an issue where VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables from unmatched LLM operations; they are now set only from the LLM operations that matched the request.

Backup and DR

Feature

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.508. These fixes aren't rolled out to the 11.0.16 release. To receive these updates, upgrade the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17.

The following feature is available for the Backup and DR agent:

  • Expanded Linux Changed Block Tracking (CBT) support across kernel updates for Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8, RHEL 9, and RHEL 10 distributions. For more information, see Backup and DR supported operating systems and kernels.

Security

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.508. These fixes aren't rolled out to the 11.0.16 release. To receive these updates, upgrade the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17.

The following security updates are available for the backup/recovery appliance:

  • Addressed multiple input sanitization vulnerabilities, including SQL injection and OS command injection, across appliance backend services and management workflows.
  • Strengthened TLS, certificate truststore, and SSH host key validation across appliance and cluster communications.
  • Remediated authorization and validation vulnerabilities in policy option management and host lookup workflows.
  • Addressed memory safety and access control vulnerabilities in appliance storage management services.

The following security updates are available for the Backup and DR agent:

  • Strengthened local device access controls for Linux Changed Block Tracking (CBT) components to prevent unprivileged local access.
  • Improved temporary file creation, path verification, and file permission handling across Linux and Windows Backup and DR agents to mitigate symlink race conditions and local privilege escalation vulnerabilities.
  • Hardened Oracle and IBM Db2 database integration scripts on protected hosts to improve credential and directory permission handling during recovery and migration workflows.
  • Addressed memory handling vulnerabilities and refined system logging rules in Linux Backup and DR agent components.

The following library updates are available for the backup/recovery appliance:

  • Upgraded the Java runtime environment and third-party application libraries on the appliance to remediate reported security vulnerabilities.
  • Updated base operating system and database packages across backup/recovery appliance and management server images to mitigate reported vulnerabilities.

Feature

You can now back up Cloud SQL instances to a backup vault that's located in a different region to the instance. This approach enhances data resilience and helps meet strict compliance and disaster recovery requirements by storing backups in a separate geographic location.

Feature

You can now edit existing backup plans for Cloud SQL instances to update settings such as backup rules and maximum custom on-demand retention periods. To learn more, see Back up Cloud SQL instances to a backup vault.

Fixed

Note: The following fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.507. These fixes aren't rolled out to the 11.0.16 release. To receive the following updates, upgrade your backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17.

The following issues are resolved for the backup/recovery appliance:

  • Application discovery and management API requests can time out when multiple discovery operations run concurrently.
  • Hostnames containing special characters prevented active jobs from being accurately detected during Backup and DR agent upgrade pre-checks.
  • Excessive informational log messages in appliance service logs when replication optimization was turned off.
  • Appliance image packaging issue by including required system libraries for fresh appliance deployments.

The following issue is resolved for the Backup and DR agent:

  • Scheduling conflict where concurrent database log backups and full database backups, such as SAP Sybase IQ and SAP MaxDB backups, can interrupt an in-progress backup job.

Deprecated

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.508. These fixes aren't rolled out to the 11.0.16 release. To receive these updates, upgrade the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17.

The following deprecation applies to the Backup and DR agent:

  • Deprecated support for end-of-life and non-Extended Update Support (non-EUS) Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) and SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) releases. For more information, see Backup and DR supported operating systems and kernels.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, unpatched Cloud SQL for MySQL instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

  • Apply self-service maintenance (Recommended): If your applications rely on database functions to calculate, schedule, or display times in these Canadian time zones (such as Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, or Winnipeg), then update your instances to the latest maintenance release using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for MySQL maintenance release *.R20260726.00_36 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set the time zone for your database session without causing downtime for your instance. Set the default_time_zone flag for the database session to your target fixed numeric offset (for example, '-06:00' for Alberta, '-07:00' for British Columbia, or '-05:00' for Manitoba).

    For more information about configuring database flags, see Configure database flags.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, unpatched Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

  • Apply self-service maintenance (Recommended): If your applications rely on database functions to calculate, schedule, or display times in these Canadian time zones (such as Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, or Winnipeg), then update your instances to the latest maintenance release using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL maintenance release *.R20260712.01_44 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set your database session time zone without downtime to an anchor zone.

    ALTER DATABASE database_name SET timezone TO 'anchor_zone';

    Replace the following:

    • database_name: the name of your database.

    • anchor_zone: the anchor zone to use as the time zone for your database. Specify an anchor zone that operates on a permanent offset.

      For example, 'America/Regina' for Alberta and Northwest Territories (UTC-6), 'America/Whitehorse' for British Columbia (UTC-7), or 'America/Coral_Harbour' for Manitoba (UTC-5).

Cloud SQL for SQL Server

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

For SQL Server, Microsoft has published guidance, recommending updating each applicable instance's time zone to the Windows time zone with the matching fixed offset.

Update each instance's time zone to the Windows time zone with the matching fixed offset:

Jurisdiction Current time zone Recommended time zone Fixed offset
British Columbia Pacific Standard Time Yukon Standard Time UTC-07:00
Alberta / Inuvik, NWT Mountain Standard Time Canada Central Standard Time UTC-06:00
Manitoba Central Standard Time Eastern Standard Time (Mexico) UTC-05:00

You can make the change in the Google Cloud console (Edit instance > Flags and parameters > Time zone) or with gcloud:

gcloud sql instances patch INSTANCE_NAME \
  --project=PROJECT_ID \
  --time-zone="Yukon Standard Time"

This update includes the following changes and features. These features are generally available (GA):

  • Audio overview language selection: You can choose the language for the audio overview output. This lets you create an audio output in a language different from the notebook's language (Settings > Output language).

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Inference request metadata logging (GA)

Inference request metadata logging is generally available. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform can write one Cloud Logging entry for every inference request your project serves. Each entry records the model, region, consumption option, token counts, Provisioned Throughput usage, latency and error code. Entries record metadata only and never contain prompts or responses. Logging is supported for Gemini models that use generateContent and streamGenerateContent, and for Claude models that use rawPredict and streamRawPredict.

You can turn on logging in the Google Cloud console, from the Provisioned Throughput page, or with the REST API. Turning on logging in the console also turns on detailed metrics, which chart Provisioned Throughput traffic at one-second resolution. With logging on, the model observability dashboard adds 1-second resolution options to its charts for pay-as-you-go traffic. To attribute usage to a team, application or tenant, add request headers with the x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label- prefix, and query the entries with SQL in Observability Analytics.

For more information, see Log inference request metadata.

Feature

Computer use tool is available in General Availability

The Computer use tool is available in General Availability (GA). This release introduces comprehensive Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) safety governance, enabling developers to selectively configure or override specific confirmation policies (such as financial transactions or data modification) while allowing administrators to mandate organization-wide guardrails using the configurableComputerUseToolSafetyPolicies constraint.

Looker

Announcement

On November 1, 2026, several Canadian provinces and territories—Manitoba, Alberta, British Columbia, and parts of the Northwest Territories—transition to permanent daylight saving time (DST) or remain on their summer UTC offsets year-round. On unpatched Looker instances, these changes affect scheduled content delivery fire times and table calculations that use now() with the affected Canadian time zones (America/Winnipeg, Canada/Central, America/Rainy_River, America/Edmonton, Canada/Mountain, America/Vancouver, Canada/Pacific, and America/Inuvik). Patched Looker builds update the scheduler (Ruby) and browser (JavaScript) time zone data, while server-evaluated now() table calculations on the JVM still use the bundled JDK time zone database (tzdb 2026b). To learn how to upgrade to a patched Looker build or configure an alternative schedule delivery time zone, see 2026 Canadian time zone changes.

Starting October 24, 2026, Managed Airflow (Gen 3) and Managed Airflow (Gen 2) environments running Python 3.11 with google-api-core package versions 2.28.0 to 2.43.0 (including versions 2.30.3 to 2.43.0, which weren't previously affected) might experience degraded performance because of a Python 3.11 deprecation check that scans installed package metadata on every new Python subprocess import. You might observe increased DAG parsing times, longer task execution times, higher CPU usage on Airflow DAG processors and workers, and frequent FutureWarning log entries from google/api_core/_python_version_support.py about Python 3.11 support ending on 2027-10-24.

For the list of affected builds and available workarounds (installing google-api-core>=2.43.1 on compatible Airflow 3 builds or applying a sitecustomize.py runtime patch), see the known issue for Managed Airflow (Gen 3) or Managed Airflow (Gen 2).

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following regions:

  • northamerica-northeast1 (Montréal)

  • northamerica-northeast2 (Toronto)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Resource Manager

Feature

Preview: Management boundaries and capability configurations in Resource Manager are available in Preview. Management boundaries establish dynamic, tag-based or hierarchy-wide administrative perimeters across multiple Google Cloud projects. This feature lets you centralize resource discovery and governance from a designated management project. You can configure BoundaryConfig, Boundary, and CapabilityConfig resources using Google Cloud CLI to partition projects by Tags values and enable management capabilities for Agent Registry.

For more information, see Management boundaries overview and Configure management boundaries.

SAP on Google Cloud

Announcement

Google SecOps for SAP is generally available (GA)

Google SecOps for SAP is generally available (GA). This solution helps you protect your enterprise SAP applications by integrating business-critical telemetry into Google SecOps to provide unified visibility, threat detection, and security response capabilities.

This release includes:

  • Log ingestion from SAP RISE and self-managed SAP environments that run on Google Cloud, on-premises, or other clouds.
  • SAP-specific YARA-L threat detection rules available in the Google SecOps Detection Rules GitHub repository.
  • Automated threat response and containment capabilities by using the SAP RFC Gateway and SOAR playbooks (Preview).

For more information, see Secure SAP applications with Google SecOps.

Secure Source Manager

Feature

You can now enable vulnerability scanning to detect known vulnerabilities in your dependencies.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports equality and ordering comparisons on JSONB and JSON values. You can use these values in GROUP_BY and ORDER BY clauses without first converting them to another data type.

In GoogleSQL, you can also convert other data types to JSON using CAST(expression AS JSON) and compare JSON values directly with non-JSON values. Spanner can implicitly coerces the non-JSON value to JSON for comparison.

Additionally, you can use search indexes to accelerate equality comparisons such as = or IN on JSONB and JSON columns and subpaths.

For more information, see JSON comparison and sorting , JSON comparison coercion , CAST AS JSON , JSON search indexes , and Working with JSONB.

Feature

Spanner Graph supports the following enhancements:

  • You can create property graphs from SQL views that call remote functions (Preview) to compute node and edge properties. For more information, see Compute properties with remote functions.
  • You can write simplified queries on schemaless dynamic properties without explicit conversions to SQL data types. This lets you group and sort dynamic properties, and compare them directly with literal values or other dynamic properties. For more information, see Filter, compare, and sort by dynamic properties and JSON comparison and sorting.

reCAPTCHA

Change

Fraud Defense Mobile SDK v18.9.4 is available for Android. This version includes the following:

  • Fixes a memory leak where destroyed activities were retained by lifecycle callbacks (Issue #194).
  • Fixes a dependency compatibility issue with Kotlin Coroutines and POM API dependencies.

title: Once Upon Agentic AI (Part 2): Develop your own MCP server and cast its tools from Strands Agents
description:
Series: Once Upon Agentic AI.

Despite their new powers and fearless hearts, our heroes had not defeated all the foes. A greater monster was waiting for them, mightier than anything they had faced. This time, our heroes would need more than their own strength to prevail.

The series follows the adventure in three parts:

  • Part 1: Create your first agent, equip it with a Vended tool, then write a tool of your own.
  • This article: MCP (Model Context Protocol) explored via the MCP Inspector and Strands Agents Harness SDK.
  • Part 3: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), A2A (Agent2Agent) and Structured output with an orchestrator agent leading specialized agents.

You need Python, uv, a terminal, and AWS credentials with access to Amazon Bedrock.

The code lives in aws-samples/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai. The main branch contains skeletons with # TODO markers. Let's Learn and Be Curious together!

Use the same setup as Part 1:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai.git ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai
cd ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai
uv sync
export AWS_PROFILE=YOUR_AWS_PROFILE AWS_REGION=YOUR_AWS_REGION

No AWS profile yet? The Strands Agents Amazon Bedrock model provider guide shows how to set up AWS credentials (with aws configure, environment variables, a boto3 session, or aws login) and lists the IAM permissions your agent needs to invoke a model. Strands picks those credentials up on its own.

What is MCP?

In Part 1, the whole agent loop ran inside one Python process: the model read the tool specification, decided to call roll_dice, Strands ran the function, and the model read the result. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an agent use capabilities living in another program. Tools are one of them, and a server can also share data and reusable prompts, as the table below shows. In this post, we move the dice tool into a server. The agent loop stays as it is: the model still decides which tool to call, and only the place where the function runs changes.

Who talks to whom? MCP uses a client/server architecture: think HTTP, but for AI agents. A web browser sends requests to a web server and reads its responses; an MCP client does the same with an MCP server, which answers with its tools and their results. The host is the AI application, which here is a Strands agent. For every server it uses, the host creates one client that keeps a dedicated connection to that server. That client is TheWitcherish's green orb. The server is the program that offers capabilities: it lists its tools when the client asks with tools/list, and runs one when the client sends tools/call. Between those two requests, the agent loop runs exactly as in Part 1.

What can a server offer? A server has three primitives, grouped by who controls their use:

Primitive Controlled by Example
Prompts User System prompts, few-shot examples
Resources Application File contents, database schemas, API responses
Tools Model An API call, a database write

How are messages written? Every MCP message is JSON-RPC 2.0, a small standard for calling another program with JSON. A request carries an id, a method and params, and its response repeats the same id with either a result or an error. A notification has no id, because it expects no reply. Here is a tool call:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"search","arguments":{"q":"otters"}}}

How do messages travel? MCP defines two transports. With stdio, the client starts the server as a child process and exchanges messages through its standard input and output. It is the simplest option, with no network port and no authentication, but only that one client can use the server. With Streamable HTTP, the server runs as its own process and receives HTTP POST requests at one endpoint. Many clients can share it, on your machine or across a network, but it opens a port, and a server shared beyond your machine needs the authorization described in the MCP specification.

If you would like to Dive Deep, you can find the MCP specification right here.

Step 1: Is an MCP server just a tool in another program?

Almost. A server can offer any of the three MCP primitives we saw earlier: tools, resources and prompts. In our heroes' quest, we focus on tools. The green orb needs something to talk to, so TheWitcherish, Amagash and Tagazok build the server it will reach. They move Lady Luck's dice out of the agent and into their own file, dice_roll_mcp_server.py. They create the server with FastMCP(port=8002), put @mcp.tool() above the same roll_dice function from Part 1, and end the file with the line that starts the server:

import random
import logging
from mcp.server import FastMCP

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')

mcp = FastMCP(port=8002)

@mcp.tool()
def roll_dice(faces: int = 6) -> int:
    """Roll one die with a given number of faces and return the result.
    ...
    """
    if faces < 1:
        raise ValueError("Dice must have at least 1 face")

    result = random.randint(1, faces)

    logging.info(f"... DICE ROLL: d{faces} = {result}")

    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")

FastMCP comes from the official MCP Python SDK. Like Part 1's @tool, @mcp.tool() turns the docstring and type hints into a tool description and input schema. The function stays familiar, and only its home changes. Each roll now lands in the server's own log, giving us evidence outside the agent.

Then comes the question of how the orb will reach their server:

"Do we talk over stdio?"

"SSE?"

"I know, Streamable HTTP!"

They choose Streamable HTTP, which the server starts with transport="streamable-http".

Start the server in one terminal and leave it running:

cd ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai/4_mcp_integration
uv run python dice_roll_mcp_server.py

INFO - StreamableHTTP session manager started
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8002 (Press CTRL+C to quit)

It listens on 127.0.0.1, FastMCP's default host, so only your machine can reach it. No model lives here. The server waits for clients.

Step 2: Does the server answer before any agent calls it?

This step uses Node.js to run the MCP Inspector. If node --version doesn't print a version in your terminal, install Node.js from the Node.js download page first.

Test the server first. If an agent misbehaves, you want to know whether the server or the model is to blame, so check the server alone before any model joins in. The MCP Inspector is the reference tool for testing and debugging MCP servers. It is an MCP client with no model behind it, so it shows you exactly what an agent would receive. With your MCP dice server up and running, open a second terminal.

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector opens the web interface, where you add the server URL http://127.0.0.1:8002/mcp with the Streamable HTTP transport. The same tool also has a command-line mode, which prints each answer as text, so the traces below come from it. First, shake hands with the server:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://127.0.0.1:8002/mcp --transport http --method initialize

{
  "serverInfo": {
    "name": "FastMCP",
    "version": "1.30.0"
  },
  "protocolVersion": "2025-11-25",
  "capabilities": {
    ...
    "tools": {
      "listChanged": false
    }
  }
}

The server announces itself, the protocol revision it speaks, and the capabilities it offers. "protocolVersion": "2025-11-25" is the revision this version of the MCP Python SDK speaks. Now ask what an agent would ask during startup, tools/list:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://127.0.0.1:8002/mcp --transport http --method tools/list

{
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "roll_dice",
      "description": "Roll one die with a given number of faces and return the result.\n\n...faces: Number of faces on the die, 1 or more. ...",
      "inputSchema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "faces": {
            "default": 6,
            "title": "Faces",
            "type": "integer"
          }
        },
        "title": "roll_diceArguments"
      },
      "outputSchema": {
        ...
        "properties": {
          "result": {
            "title": "Result",
            "type": "integer"
          }
        },
        ...
      }
    }
  ]
}

This is the same comparison as Part 1's tool_spec, now read over the wire. The docstring became the description, the type hint became "type": "integer", and the default became "default": 6. The server also sends an outputSchema, which Part 1's local tool did not have. Look for the bound, though: "1 or more" appears only in the description text. The schema has no minimum, so the model learns the bound by reading, and the function enforces it. Call the tool once with a good value and once with a bad one:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://127.0.0.1:8002/mcp --transport http --method tools/call --tool-name roll_dice --tool-arg faces=20
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://127.0.0.1:8002/mcp --transport http --method tools/call --tool-name roll_dice --tool-arg faces=0

{
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "19"
    }
  ],
  "structuredContent": {
    "result": 19
  },
  "isError": false
}
{
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Error executing tool roll_dice: Dice must have at least 1 face"
    }
  ],
  "isError": true
}

The dice server's terminal records both visits, and the good roll matches:

2026-11-11 15:44:58,566 - INFO - Processing request of type ListToolsRequest
2026-11-11 15:44:58,570 - INFO - Processing request of type CallToolRequest
2026-11-11 15:44:58,570 - INFO - ... DICE ROLL: d20 = 19
...
2026-11-11 15:44:59,836 - INFO - Processing request of type ListToolsRequest
2026-11-11 15:44:59,839 - INFO - Processing request of type CallToolRequest

The Inspector read the tool list before each call, the same way an agent does. faces=0 passed the schema and stopped at the if faces < 1 check, so the server returned an error result with "isError": true rather than crashing, and the Inspector exited with code 5. Write your bounds into the docstring so the model reads them, and check them in the function so the server keeps them. The server answers. Now it is time for an agent to call it.

Step 3: Does the agent need the tool's code?

No. The server address is enough. gamemaster_mcp_client.py defines an agent called gamemaster that speaks as Lady Luck, and it contains no dice implementation:

from strands import Agent
from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient

mcp_dice_client = MCPClient(url="http://localhost:8002/mcp")

gamemaster = Agent(
    system_prompt="""You are Lady Luck, the mystical keeper of dice and fortune in fantasy role-playing adventures.
    ...""",
    tools=[mcp_dice_client]
)

gamemaster("Help me create a new fantasy character! Roll the strength, wisdom, charisma and intelligence abilities scores using 4d6 drop lowest method.")

Give MCPClient the server's url, then add it to tools. For Strands, an MCP tool is just a tool. MCPClient is a tool provider: when the agent starts, the client sends the same tools/list you just ran with the Inspector, and each tool it receives joins the agent's tool list with its name, description and input schema, exactly like a Part 1 @tool function. The model picks roll_dice, and Strands forwards the call to the server.

Of the three primitives, only tools reach the model. A server's prompts and resources stay available to your own code through the same client, with list_prompts_sync(), get_prompt_sync(), list_resources_sync() and read_resource_sync(), so you decide when to use them.

Time to roll Lady Luck's dice!

Make sure your MCP dice server is still running in its terminal. Then open another terminal and cast from there. This time the agent calls a model on Amazon Bedrock, so that terminal needs valid AWS credentials: export the same AWS_PROFILE and AWS_REGION as in the setup, and check them with aws sts get-caller-identity before you run the client:

cd ~/sample-once-upon-agentic-ai/4_mcp_integration
export AWS_PROFILE=YOUR_AWS_PROFILE AWS_REGION=YOUR_AWS_REGION
aws sts get-caller-identity
uv run python gamemaster_mcp_client.py

If aws sts get-caller-identity returns an error instead of your account and role, refresh your credentials first; otherwise the client stops at its first model call with NoCredentialsError or an expired-token error.

To see what the SDK does, reuse the logging line from the dice server at the top of gamemaster_mcp_client.py, with DEBUG instead of INFO:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')

DEBUG on the root logger also prints the AWS SDK's own requests and responses, so the output is long: search it for mcp and stop_reason. The trace follows the SDK step by step:

2026-11-12 13:41:13,578 - DEBUG - [...] transport connection established
2026-11-12 13:41:13,584 - DEBUG - [...] session initialized successfully
2026-11-12 13:41:13,591 - DEBUG - [...] received 1 tools from MCP server
2026-11-12 13:41:13,591 - DEBUG - tool_name=<roll_dice> | creating mcp agent tool
...
2026-11-12 13:41:16,639 - DEBUG - stop_reason=<tool_use> | model call succeeded, resetting retry state
...
Tool #1: roll_dice
Tool #2: roll_dice
...
Tool #16: roll_dice

The client connects, receives one tool, and wraps it as an agent tool. The model stops with stop_reason=<tool_use> and asks for sixteen rolls in one turn: four dice for each of four abilities. Lady Luck reports the first ability score, trimmed:

STRENGTH
Rolls: 3, 6, 4, 2 → 3 + 6 + 4 = 13

The server log follows the same path:

INFO - Created new transport with session ID: 6b20ac77014340f8b57cbd4fa3443214
INFO - Processing request of type ListToolsRequest
INFO - Processing request of type CallToolRequest
INFO - ... DICE ROLL: d6 = 3
INFO - Processing request of type CallToolRequest
INFO - ... DICE ROLL: d6 = 6
INFO - Processing request of type CallToolRequest
INFO - ... DICE ROLL: d6 = 4
INFO - Processing request of type CallToolRequest
INFO - ... DICE ROLL: d6 = 2
...

ListToolsRequest is tools/list; each CallToolRequest is one tools/call. Before roll_dice runs, FastMCP checks the arguments against the tool's input schema with Pydantic. That is the tower's "Request Validated".

Now place the two sides next to each other. The server logged sixteen rolls. The model's next request carried sixteen tool results:

Rolls 1 to 16
Server log 3 6 4 2 · 2 1 2 4 · 5 4 1 3 · 5 4 5 6
Model received 3 6 4 2 · 2 1 4 2 · 5 4 1 3 · 5 4 5 6

The same sixteen values appear on both sides. Rolls 7 and 8 swapped places because Strands runs one turn's tool calls concurrently. Neighbouring results can therefore return in a different order than the server logged them.

So every number existed in the timestamped server log before the model saw it. The model retold the result; it never rolled. When its reply and the server log disagree, trust the log.

Now you try: ask Lady Luck to roll dexterity and constitution too. Then count the new DICE ROLL lines in the server log. You should find eight more.

Follow the adventurers

In Part 3, the orchestrator agent consults the Rules of our Role-Playing Game, because Tagazok may not be allowed to wield a very specific power, while Amagash learns to give her tools a shape with Structured output.

Until then, keep two habits:

  • Test your MCP server before your agent does. The MCP Inspector shows what an agent will receive, with no model in the way.
  • Write bounds where both sides see them. The docstring tells the model, and the check in the function holds the line.

The comic book illustrations in this blog post were created and produced by Holy Bird, based on the AWS workshop.

title: Amazon Aurora DSQL now offers SQL statement statistics in Database Insights
description:
Amazon Aurora DSQL now records statistics for each SQL statement your cluster runs and publishes them as Amazon CloudWatch OpenTelemetry (OTel) metrics. You can view them in Amazon CloudWatch Database Insights. For each statement, you see how often it runs, how long it takes, the rows it scans, returns, or changes, and the DPUs it uses.

Statement statistics measure every successful statement rather than sampling activity. Use them to find the statements that take the most time, run most often, or cost the most. In Database Insights, choose a statement under Top SQL to see its normalized SQL text and per-call charts. You can also query the metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch. Turn on statement statistics for each cluster in the Aurora DSQL console or the API when you create or update the cluster.

Statement statistics are available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available. Standard CloudWatch metrics and Logs charges apply, with no additional Aurora DSQL charge. To learn more, see monitoring SQL statements with statement statistics in the Aurora DSQL User Guide and CloudWatch pricing.

title: Your Bug Report Says "iPhone". The Screen Is 448 by 364.
description:
Last Friday Safari arrived on a new device: Apple HomeView, which has a square 7-inch display that people mostly use with their voice. WebKit's announcement includes a line that will produce a particular kind of bug report for the next year:

Safari on HomeView also reports an iOS user agent.

So the report will say "iOS Safari". You will pick up an iPhone, open the page, and it will be fine. Not because the bug is not real, but because the report described the wrong thing. It classified the device, and the device class is the one fact that does not decide how a page renders.

A user agent is a claim. A viewport is a measurement.

Everything about how your layout behaves is decided by a handful of numbers the browser can measure directly: the width and height of the viewport, whether the primary pointer is precise, whether it can hover. The user agent is a string that a vendor chose, and on HomeView it says iOS.

WebKit is specific about what that hides. The screen is square, and "Some sites assume the viewport is always taller than 600px, while on HomeView it’s shorter." Its suggested test size is 448 by 364. Put a sticky header and a sticky footer on that and there is very little page left between them. Put a newsletter modal on it that is taller than the viewport, and its close button can sit below the bottom of the screen with no way to scroll to it.

None of that is in the words "iOS Safari".

Record the screen, not the category

The fix for the report is small. Capture what the page actually had to work with, at the moment it went wrong:

function describeScreen() {
  const vv = window.visualViewport
  return {
    viewport: `${window.innerWidth}x${window.innerHeight}`,
    visualViewport: vv ? `${Math.round(vv.width)}x${Math.round(vv.height)} @ ${vv.scale}` : null,
    devicePixelRatio: window.devicePixelRatio,
    pointer: matchMedia('(pointer: fine)').matches ? 'fine'
           : matchMedia('(pointer: coarse)').matches ? 'coarse' : 'none',
    hover: matchMedia('(hover: hover)').matches,
    orientation: screen.orientation ? screen.orientation.type : null,
    userAgent: navigator.userAgent,  // still worth keeping, just not trusting
  }
}

The media features are not guesses. The Media Queries specification defines pointer as reflecting "the characteristics of the “primary” pointing device, as determined by the user agent", and coarse as "a pointing device of limited accuracy. Examples include touchscreens". hover is defined the same way, for the ability to hover over elements with that primary pointer. They answer the question your CSS is actually asking, which is why they are the thing to log.

Do not assume what any of them will say on HomeView. WebKit's post does not tell you, and the point of measuring is that you no longer need to be told.

Reproduce with the numbers, not the device

Once a report carries 448x364, you do not need the device. Responsive design mode in any browser will give you that viewport, and WebKit's own advice for anybody without the hardware is the same idea: "test your site on a phone in landscape orientation", which is short in the same way.

Without the numbers, you are guessing at a device from a string that, on this device, names the wrong one.

The general version

HomeView is just the cleanest recent example of an old problem. Device names are categories, and categories are how people describe what they were holding. Layout bugs live in the dimensions, the input method and the zoom level, and none of those survive the trip into "it's broken on my iPhone" unless something captured them before the person started typing.

Ask for the numbers, or collect them. Treat "iPhone" in a report as the beginning of a question, not the answer to one.

title: Class and Object in Java
description:
Java is an object-oriented programming language. Two important concepts in Java are Class and Object.

Let's understand them with a simple example.

  1. What is a Class?

A class is a blueprint or template used to create objects.

It defines the properties (variables) and behaviors (methods) that its objects can have.

Example:

class Student {
String name;
int age;

void display() {
    System.out.println(name);
    System.out.println(age);
}

}

Here:

Student is the class name.

name and age are variables.

display() is a method.

The class describes what information and behavior a student object can have.

  1. What is an Object?

An object is an instance of a class.

We create an object using the new keyword in Java.

Example:

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {

    Student s1 = new Student();

    s1.name = "Arun";
    s1.age = 21;

    s1.display();
}

}

Output:

Arun
21

Here:

Student is the class.

s1 is the object reference variable.

new Student() creates a new Student object.

s1.name assigns a name.

s1.age assigns an age.

s1.display() calls the method.

  1. Creating Multiple Objects

We can create multiple objects from the same class. Each object can store different values.

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {

    Student s1 = new Student();
    Student s2 = new Student();

    s1.name = "Arun";
    s1.age = 21;

    s2.name = "Priya";
    s2.age = 22;

    s1.display();
    s2.display();
}

}

Output:

Arun
21
Priya
22

Both objects use the same class, but they maintain their own data.

title: Same CSS Rule, Different Font Weight: Auditing Type Drift Across Templates
description:
Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy by Design Den Solutions. Every number below was measured by us on our own live site, on one machine, one browser, one session — our results, not industry averages.

Your brand guidelines say one typeface. Your templates may be serving two.

We audited the eight public pages of our own site (designdensolutions.com) this week, and found that the same navigation rule — .nav-links a { font-weight: 500 }, byte-identical in both templates — renders a different font weight on the homepage than on every inner page. Not a different font family. The same family, different cut, decided by which weights each template happens to request.

This is template drift: the homepage gets a performance pass, the inner pages keep the old head, and nobody re-checks that the two still describe the same brand. Here is the whole audit, the numbers, and the two scripts we used, so you can run it on your own site in about ten minutes.

What the two templates actually request

Homepage 7 inner pages
Google Fonts request Plus+Jakarta+Sans:wght@400;600;700 Plus+Jakarta+Sans:wght@400;500;600;700
font-display optional swap
Font stylesheet loads 2 (one async media="print" trick, one plain blocking — same URL) 1, blocking
preconnect googleapis.com + gstatic.com googleapis.com only
Inline <style> 2 blocks, 57,014 bytes 0
External CSS files 0 (all inline) 6

Three separate drifts in one table:

  1. The weight sets differ. The homepage never requests 500. The inner pages do.
  2. The loading strategies differ. optional on the homepage, swap everywhere else.
  3. The homepage's async font-CSS optimization is cancelled by its own duplicate — the second <link> to the identical URL is render-blocking, so the media="print" onload trick on the first one buys nothing.

The rendered consequence, measured

Both templates style the nav with font-weight: 500. When a requested weight has no loaded face, the CSS font-matching algorithm picks the nearest available one — for 500 with only 400/600/700 present, that is 400. You can prove which face actually rendered without any visual guesswork, using canvas text metrics:

// Run in the console of each page, after document.fonts.ready.
const c = document.createElement('canvas').getContext('2d');
const sample = 'Services About Contact Pricing 0123';
const w = f => { c.font = f; return c.measureText(sample).width; };

console.log('400:', w('400 14px "Plus Jakarta Sans"'));
console.log('500:', w('500 14px "Plus Jakarta Sans"'));
console.log('600:', w('600 14px "Plus Jakarta Sans"'));
// If width(500) === width(400), the 500 request is being
// served by the 400 face. No 500 face exists on this page.

Our results, same browser, same session, same sample string:

Page 400 500 600 500 face loaded?
index.html 240.90 px 240.90 px 245.15 px no
branding.html 240.90 px 243.07 px 245.15 px yes

On the homepage, 500 and 400 are the same pixels. On branding.html, 500 is its own face, 2.18 px wider on a 34-character sample (~0.9%). Width is just the proxy — the visible difference is stroke weight: the nav is literally lighter on the homepage than on the pages it links to. document.fonts confirms it: three loaded weights on the homepage (400/600/700), four on the inner pages.

One caution if you run this: document.fonts.check('500 14px "Plus Jakarta Sans"') returned true on the homepage even though no 500 face exists — check() runs the same matching algorithm, so it reports the matched face, not the requested one. Canvas width equality is the honest test.

The slower-network divergence (spec-derived, not measured)

font-display: optional gives the font roughly a 100 ms block period; if it misses that window, the fallback renders for the rest of that page view (the font may still download for the next navigation). swap shows the fallback briefly, then swaps the brand font in whenever it arrives.

So on a cold cache over a slow line, a first-time visitor can read the entire homepage in system-ui, click through, and watch the brand typeface appear on the service page. One brand, two heads — mid-session. We did not measure this on a throttled connection; it follows from the two font-display values we did verify in the served HTML. Treat it as a mechanism, not a benchmark.

The audit script

Fetch your pages and diff their font requests. This is the actual script we ran (Node, no dependencies):

const pages = ['index', 'about', 'services', 'contact']; // your paths
const base = 'https://www.example.com/';
for (const p of pages) {
  const html = await (await fetch(base + p + '.html')).text();
  const links = [...html.matchAll(/<link\b[^>]*>/gi)].map(m => m[0]);
  const font = links.filter(l => /fonts\.googleapis/.test(l));
  console.log(p, {
    requests: font.map(l => (l.match(/family=([^&"']+)/) || [])[1]),
    display: [...new Set([...html.matchAll(/display=(\w+)/g)].map(m => m[1]))],
    duplicateFontLinks: font.length - new Set(font).size,
    preconnects: links.filter(l => /preconnect/.test(l))
      .map(l => (l.match(/href=["']([^"']+)/) || [])[1]),
  });
}

Then grep your CSS for every font-weight value and diff that set against each template's requested weights. Any weight in the CSS but not in the request is a silent substitution waiting to happen.

What we fixed vs what we're reporting

To be clear about scope: this article is the audit, not the fix. The fixes are queued for our own deployment review — align the weight sets, pick one font-display strategy per brand decision (not per template accident), delete the duplicate font link, and add the gstatic preconnect where fonts actually download from. We also found a dead rule declaring Instrument Serif for a component that no longer renders it — the font is never requested, and canvas metrics show the name resolves to Times New Roman. Dead type declarations are drift too; they just haven't bitten anyone yet.

What we are not claiming

  • No field data, no user-perception study, no conversion claim. One machine, one browser, one session.
  • The weight difference is measured in canvas text width, not visually assessed for "noticeability".
  • The slow-network behaviour is derived from the CSS spec and the observed font-display values, not throttled measurements.
  • This is our own site and our own audit — a self-published referral placement, not third-party coverage.

If your brand guidelines specify a typeface and weights, your templates should be testable against them — the same way you'd test a logo at six sizes. Typography is part of the brand system, and drift is a bug, not a style choice.
