title: Beyond “Push to Deploy”: Five Companies and the Engineering Behind Reliable GitOps
description:
A Git push can trigger a deployment. It cannot, by itself, prove that a customer can log in, complete a transaction, or connect an external service.

That gap matters when teams use GitOps to provision multiple environments. Declarative configuration makes infrastructure easier to reproduce, but applications still depend on databases, credentials, network policies, and recovery procedures.

A useful company shortlist therefore needs technical context. GeekyAnts, Red Hat, GitLab, AWS, and Microsoft offer relevant implementation experience or platform capabilities. They serve different roles, so this comparison examines their documented approaches rather than presenting a performance ranking.

What Can Go Wrong After a Successful Sync?

GeekyAnts’ engineering account describes a platform built with Argo CD, ApplicationSets, and Helm to provision isolated customer evaluation environments.

Its operational problems included applications starting before Redis and NATS accepted connections, new configuration requirements breaking existing tenants, integrations failing despite healthy deployment status, and resource quotas blocking migration work.

The team introduced deployment ordering and a TCP connectivity gate, while acknowledging that an open port does not prove functional readiness. The article also records approximately 110 seconds for one cold-provisioning run, rather than claiming a repeatable benchmark.

The GitOps deployment reliability breakdown provides the original incident context and explains the limits of those observations.

For developers, the distinction between ordering and readiness is especially useful. Argo CD sync waves apply resources in a defined sequence, with progression influenced by resource health. Their effectiveness still depends on what those health assessments actually check.

Which Five Companies Are Relevant to GitOps Delivery?

Custom Implementation and Operational Lessons

GeekyAnts contributes a documented implementation example rather than a standalone GitOps platform. Its account connects provisioning automation with tenant compatibility, integration validation, and recovery behavior.

For teams evaluating an engineering partner, this creates practical discussion points: how will existing environments receive configuration changes, how will failed migrations recover, and what evidence will establish that an environment is usable?

An Argo CD Platform Within OpenShift

Red Hat offers OpenShift GitOps, built on Argo CD, for declarative application delivery and cluster configuration management. Its documentation describes additional OpenShift integration, automation, and enterprise support around the upstream project.

This makes it relevant when OpenShift is already part of the architecture. Evaluation should examine how platform defaults fit the team’s release process, access controls, and troubleshooting responsibilities.

Flux Integration With the Development Workflow

GitLab recommends Flux for GitOps deployments and documents integration between Flux and its Kubernetes agent. The agent can detect relevant Flux repository resources and configure notification receivers.

For teams already using GitLab, the useful question is how repository review, build automation, and cluster reconciliation will connect. A pipeline should make it clear which artifact was built, which configuration references it, and which revision reached each environment.

GitOps Delivery on Amazon EKS

AWS documents Argo CD workflows for Amazon EKS and offers an EKS capability for managed Argo CD. Its published material describes configurable GitOps continuous delivery within that service.

Teams considering this option should separate controller management from application ownership. The evaluation should identify who maintains deployment definitions, investigates unhealthy workloads, and validates application behavior after reconciliation.

GitOps Across Azure and Connected Clusters

Microsoft documents Flux v2 configurations for Azure Kubernetes Service and Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes. Azure Policy can apply those configurations across supported clusters at scale.

This is relevant to organizations coordinating configuration across multiple clusters. Teams should examine repository boundaries, policy scope, credentials, and the process for handling an urgent exception.

What Should a Technical Evaluation Include?

Company names provide a starting point. A small failure exercise provides stronger evidence.

Ask the proposed team or platform owner to demonstrate:

  • A deployment while a required dependency is unavailable.
  • An upgrade to an older environment with missing configuration.
  • Recovery after a migration fails partway through.
  • A functional check that detects an incorrect API destination.

Capacity deserves a separate test. Kubernetes schedules workloads using resource requests and available node capacity. Low observed CPU consumption alone does not establish that another workload can be scheduled or safely operated.

A useful acceptance criterion is whether the team can explain a failure, recover predictably, and preserve enough evidence to prevent repetition. That makes a GitOps workflow easier to operate as applications and environments grow.

Discussion: Which has caused the most trouble in a GitOps setup: dependency readiness, configuration compatibility, or migration recovery?

title: Flexible Global Report Cron Job API in Go: Time-Zone-Safe Reconciliation
description:
Short answer: choose a time-zone-aware cron job API or durable workflow boundary that preserves each property's IANA zone and local report time; then enforce idempotency in the reconciliation service, because no scheduler can make an external payment query exactly once.

A nightly property-management reconciliation should be scheduled from each property's local reporting rule, but executed according to a canonical instant. The decision rule is straightforward: persist an IANA time-zone identifier and the intended local date, derive the UTC execution window at runtime, and make the reconciliation idempotent before adding retries. A cron API that accepts only a UTC expression cannot represent this policy safely for global users.

The report email is secondary. The ledger comparison is the durable operation, and the email should be an observable consequence of a completed reconciliation rather than the thing that defines success. This distinction prevents daylight-saving transitions, provider retries, and a delayed worker from producing a second financial result.

Identity determines the retry boundary.

This is not cosmetic.

Which cron job API allows flexible report timing across time zones?

“Run at 02:00” is incomplete. It needs a calendar, a location, a time-zone rule set, and a policy for dates on which 02:00 is absent or occurs twice. America/New_York is a durable business value; UTC-05:00 is merely an offset observed at one instant. The former can describe future civil-time behavior, while the latter cannot encode daylight-saving changes.

For a property record, I would keep the scheduling intent separate from execution state:

Field Meaning Why it matters
property_id Stable business scope Defines the reconciliation partition
local_time Civil trigger time, such as 02:00 Preserves the user's chosen wall clock
time_zone IANA identifier Lets the runtime apply the relevant rules
local_date Date being reconciled Makes retries address the same business period
attempt Delivery or execution attempt Supports audit without changing identity

The scheduler's contract should then say what happens when a local time is skipped or duplicated. A practical policy is to move a nonexistent local time forward to the first valid instant and to execute a repeated local time once, keyed by (property_id, local_date). That policy belongs in an architecture decision record because changing it after reconciliation data exists changes accounting behavior.

Consider a property whose rule is 02:00 in a zone that advances its clocks at that hour. There is no honest UTC timestamp for the missing wall-clock value, so silently converting the rule with a fixed offset would either run at the wrong local time or omit the report without an audit event. On the autumn transition, the same wall-clock label can occur twice; accepting both deliveries makes the provider comparison run twice, while rejecting both can erase a valid reporting day. The scheduler needs a declared policy, and the reconciliation key needs to make that policy enforceable after a worker restart.

This is where the usual cron-shaped answer becomes too narrow. Cron is a useful expression for recurring wall-clock work, but it is not automatically a business-calendar specification, a ledger lock, or a deduplication key.

Where should retries stop and idempotency begin?

The critical path has two distinct identities: the schedule occurrence and the provider query. Both need stable keys. A retry may repeat an HTTP request, a worker may restart after writing a result, and a scheduler may deliver the same occurrence twice. None of those events should create a second reconciliation.

The following Go sketch keeps the business key explicit. It assumes the database transaction enforces a unique constraint on property_id, local_date; the scheduler remains responsible for delivery, while the reconciliation service remains responsible for correctness.

package reconcile

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    PropertyID string
    LocalDate  string
    TimeZone   string
}

type Store interface {
    Begin(ctx context.Context) (Tx, error)
}

type Tx interface {
    InsertRun(ctx context.Context, propertyID, localDate, key string) (bool, error)
    SaveResult(ctx context.Context, propertyID, localDate string, matched bool) error
    Commit(ctx context.Context) error
    Rollback(ctx context.Context) error
}

func Reconcile(ctx context.Context, store Store, job Job) error {
    key := job.PropertyID + ":" + job.LocalDate

    tx, err := store.Begin(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer tx.Rollback(ctx)

    inserted, err := tx.InsertRun(ctx, job.PropertyID, job.LocalDate, key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !inserted {
        return nil // An earlier attempt owns this business occurrence.
    }

    matched, err := compareProviderLedger(ctx, job.PropertyID, job.LocalDate)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := tx.SaveResult(ctx, job.PropertyID, job.LocalDate, matched); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return tx.Commit(ctx)
}

func compareProviderLedger(context.Context, string, string) (bool, error) {
    return true, nil
}

The placeholder comparison is deliberately uninteresting: production code must define the provider query, pagination, settlement cutoff, and amount representation separately. The invariant is the important part. A failed attempt before commit can be retried; a committed occurrence is not repeated merely because the delivery layer does not know whether the worker finished. “Exactly once” is therefore an application property assembled from an idempotency key, a transaction boundary, and an audit record, not a promise that a scheduler can make for an external provider.

A report email needs its own key, such as the committed reconciliation identifier plus recipient, because notification delivery and ledger reconciliation have different retry behavior. Sending the email inside the same database transaction does not make the external side effect atomic. An outbox record committed with the result gives a worker a durable handoff and leaves a searchable audit trail.

Which scheduling boundary fits this workflow?

There are three reasonable boundaries. A system cron expression is adequate when every tenant shares one fixed UTC cadence and missing or repeated civil times have no business meaning. A time-zone-aware recurring scheduler is more suitable when the stored intent is “local time in this named zone.” A durable workflow engine is justified when the run includes long waits, explicit activity retries, human review, or recovery after process failure. The choice should follow the failure boundary, not the vocabulary used in a product's marketing page.

For a property portfolio, I would create or update one logical schedule per property and record the next computed occurrence. Recomputing that occurrence after a time-zone database update should be an explicit migration or reviewable event, because the same local rule can map to a different instant when civil-time rules change. The worker should receive the business key and expected local date, then verify that the trigger still corresponds to the current schedule version before it reads provider data.

That model also keeps global customization comprehensible. Users edit a local time and named zone; operators inspect UTC instants and schedule versions; auditors inspect the local date, reconciliation key, provider query window, result, and retry history. Each view has the representation appropriate to its job.

The option I would reject, and when is it valid?

I would reject storing only a UTC timestamp and calling it a recurring report rule. It is operationally simple, but it silently changes the user's local trigger when daylight-saving rules change. I would also reject a retry policy that creates a new reconciliation identifier for every delivery attempt; that turns scheduler noise into duplicate financial work and makes incident reconstruction harder.

The rejected UTC-only design has a limitation, but it is still valid for a different problem: a one-time maintenance action whose owner has explicitly chosen an instant rather than a local civil time. Likewise, at-least-once delivery is a reasonable scheduler contract when the receiving operation is idempotent and the audit log records every delivery. The error is treating those contracts as interchangeable with a global daily report.

Operationally, the minimum useful telemetry is the schedule version, named zone, intended local date and time, resolved UTC instant, occurrence key, attempt number, provider request correlation, and final reconciliation state. Alert on an absent completion, a duplicate-key conflict rate that changes suddenly, and a mismatch that remains unresolved past the reporting cutoff. Logs without the occurrence key are not an audit trail; they are fragments.

Conclusion

A global property report does not need a magical cron expression. It needs a scheduler that preserves local intent, a runtime that resolves named time zones, and a reconciliation endpoint that treats retries as expected input. Store the business occurrence, enforce uniqueness, separate ledger completion from email delivery, and make skipped or repeated civil times an explicit policy. Those rules are the selection criteria for any cron job API or workflow system, regardless of its interface.

References

  • https://docs.temporal.io/
  • https://pkg.go.dev/time
  • https://www.iana.org/time-zones
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5545

title: Taking ShopEase to 1,000 Concurrent Users: High-Concurrency Load Testing with k6
description:
Overview


A backend application may work correctly during normal development and functional testing, but its real behavior becomes clearer when multiple requests arrive simultaneously.

As part of my ShopEase e-commerce backend project, I performed high-concurrency load testing using k6 to evaluate how the application handled increasing request loads.

The objective was to simulate concurrent users, generate a significant number of HTTP requests, and observe whether the backend could continue responding successfully during the test execution.

This testing milestone helped me move beyond checking whether individual APIs work and start evaluating backend behavior under concurrent traffic.

Project Architecture

ShopEase is a full-stack e-commerce application built around a Java and Spring Boot backend.

The testing environment used a containerized backend setup involving:

Java & Spring Boot: Backend application and REST API processing.

MySQL: Relational database for application data.

Redis: Caching layer.

Docker: Containerized infrastructure.

k6: Load testing and traffic simulation.

The purpose of this test was to evaluate the backend under concurrent request execution within this environment.

Why High-Concurrency Testing?

Functional testing generally verifies whether an API returns the expected response for a given request.

However, it does not necessarily reveal how the application behaves when hundreds of virtual users send requests at the same time.

Some important questions I wanted to investigate were:

Can the backend continue processing requests as concurrency increases?

Does the application return successful HTTP responses during the test?

Are there dropped connections or server crashes?

Can the application handle a substantial number of requests during a short testing window?

These questions motivated the use of k6 for load testing.

Load Testing with k6

I used k6 to simulate concurrent virtual users against the ShopEase backend.

The test was configured with a gradual ramp-up period, allowing the number of virtual users to increase rather than immediately applying the maximum load.

Test Configuration

Parameter

Test Result

Testing Tool

k6

Maximum Virtual Users

1,000

Ramp-up Duration

3 minutes

Total Requests

15,946+

Reported Success Rate

100%

HTTP Response

200 OK

Reported Dropped Connections

0

Server Crashes

0

The test reached up to 1,000 concurrent Virtual Users and generated more than 15,946 requests during execution.

Test Results

The observed results were:

  1. Concurrent Virtual Users

The test simulated up to 1,000 virtual users, creating concurrent request traffic against the backend.

  1. Request Processing

More than 15,946 requests were processed during the test execution.

  1. Successful HTTP Responses

The reported success rate was 100%, with successful HTTP 200 responses.

  1. Connection Stability

No dropped connections were reported during the execution.

  1. Server Stability

No server crashes were observed during the test.

These results provided a useful indication of how the current ShopEase setup behaved under the tested workload.

What I Learned

This exercise helped me understand that performance testing involves more than simply sending a large number of requests.

Some important concepts I explored include:

Virtual Users (VUs): How load testing tools simulate concurrent users.

Concurrency: How multiple requests can be processed during overlapping execution periods.

Ramp-up: Why gradually increasing load is useful when observing application behavior.

HTTP Success Rate: How successful responses can be tracked during a test.

Backend Resilience: Why server stability and connection handling matter under load.

Performance Testing: Why functional correctness and performance behavior need separate evaluation.

It also reinforced the importance of measuring application behavior instead of assuming that a backend can handle increased traffic simply because its APIs work correctly.

Important Scope and Limitations

The results represent one load-testing execution in the tested environment.

A 100% reported success rate does not automatically establish production readiness or guarantee that the application can sustain 1,000 concurrent users indefinitely.

A more complete performance evaluation would also require additional measurements, including:

Average response time.

p90 and p95 latency.

p99 latency.

Requests per second (RPS).

CPU and memory utilization.

JVM performance and garbage collection.

Database connection pool utilization.

MySQL query performance.

Redis behavior under increasing load.

These measurements would help identify bottlenecks and provide a more complete picture of the system's performance.

What's Next?

The next stage of performance testing for ShopEase will focus on deeper analysis rather than only request success.

Planned areas of investigation include:

Response-time distribution and latency analysis.

Database connection pool monitoring.

JVM resource utilization.

Identifying potential bottlenecks.

Longer-duration stress and endurance testing.

Comparing performance across different load profiles.

Conclusion

This load-testing exercise was an important step in the development of ShopEase.

Using k6, I simulated up to 1,000 concurrent Virtual Users and processed 15,946+ requests, with a reported 100% success rate and no reported dropped connections or server crashes during the test.

More importantly, this exercise helped me understand how to evaluate backend behavior under concurrent workloads and why measurable performance testing is an essential part of backend engineering.

title: Stop Client User Spoofing in React Telegram Mini Apps with Backend HMAC Check
description:
Building a Telegram Mini App inside React feels straightforward: Telegram provides a native JavaScript script, developers load it, pull the user object from window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe.user, and render a custom storefront or checkout interface.

However, relying on initDataUnsafe for backend transactions opens a severe security vulnerability. The initDataUnsafe object is unverified front-end state. Anyone opening your Mini App in Telegram Desktop, a browser, or a custom webview can open Developer Tools or intercept network requests to override window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe.user.id with any arbitrary user ID. If your React app sends that unverified user.id to your backend checkout endpoint, an attacker can place orders, view private data, or deplete account balances under another user's identity.

To build a secure Mini App, you must transmit the raw, untouched initData query string to your server, verify its HMAC-SHA256 signature using your Telegram Bot Token, check the payload timestamp to block replay attacks, and only then enable native UI controls like the MainButton.

Loading the Telegram SDK and Extracting Raw initData in React

Developers often choose between importing @twa-dev/sdk from npm or loading the official https://telegram.org/js/telegram-web-app.js script via an HTML script tag. Both expose the exact same global window.Telegram.WebApp object. While @twa-dev/sdk provides TypeScript definitions, the underlying object is identical.

The key structural difference lies between two properties:

  • initDataUnsafe: A parsed JavaScript object containing user metadata (id, first_name, username). It is convenient for populating non-sensitive UI elements like profile avatars before network requests complete. Never use this property for API authorization.
  • initData: A raw, URL-encoded string generated and signed by Telegram's servers containing key-value pairs (including hash and auth_date). This exact string must be forwarded to your server in an HTTP header or request body.

Here is a custom React hook that initializes the Telegram WebApp context safely, handles SSR execution environments, extracts the raw initData string, and configures native viewport parameters.

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export interface TelegramUser {
  id: number;
  first_name: string;
  last_name?: string;
  username?: string;
  language_code?: string;
}

export interface WebAppInitState {
  isReady: boolean;
  initData: string;
  unsafeUser: TelegramUser | null;
  webApp: WebApp | null;
}

export function useTelegramWebApp(): WebAppInitState {
  const [state, setState] = useState<WebAppInitState>({
    isReady: false,
    initData: '',
    unsafeUser: null,
    webApp: null,
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    // Ensure window.Telegram is available (prevents SSR crashes)
    if (typeof window === 'undefined' || !window.Telegram?.WebApp) {
      return;
    }

    const tg = window.Telegram.WebApp;

    // Expand app to full height inside Telegram container
    tg.expand();

    setState({
      isReady: true,
      initData: tg.initData,
      unsafeUser: (tg.initDataUnsafe?.user as TelegramUser) || null,
      webApp: tg,
    });
  }, []);

  return state;
}

If a user launches your React app outside Telegram (for example, directly in Chrome during local testing), tg.initData will be an empty string (""). Your front-end logic must detect this state early and prevent authenticated API calls when initData is missing.

Cryptographic Backend Validation of raw initData

To verify that initData originated from Telegram and was not tampered with on the client, your server must implement Telegram's exact HMAC-SHA256 verification algorithm.

The validation sequence follows these strict steps:

  1. Parse the raw initData query string into key-value pairs.
  2. Extract and remove the hash parameter from the dataset.
  3. Sort the remaining key-value pairs alphabetically by key.
  4. Format sorted pairs into a key=value format separated by newline characters ( ). This string is the data_check_string.
  5. Create a secret key by calculating an HMAC-SHA256 hash of your secret Bot Token, using the constant string "WebAppData" as the key.
  6. Calculate an HMAC-SHA256 signature of the data_check_string using the generated secret key.
  7. Compare your calculated hex signature with the received hash using a timing-safe equality check (crypto.timingSafeEqual) to mitigate timing attacks.
  8. Check the auth_date unix timestamp against the current server time to reject stale payloads.

Here is a production-ready Express.js middleware implementation in Node.js using native crypto modules:

import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import crypto from 'node:crypto';

interface VerifiedRequest extends Request {
  telegramUser?: any;
}

export function validateTelegramInitData(botToken: string, maxAgeSeconds: number = 86400) {
  return (req: VerifiedRequest, res: Response, next: NextFunction): void => {
    const rawInitData = req.headers['x-telegram-init-data'] as string;

    if (!rawInitData) {
      res.status(401).json({ error: 'Missing Telegram initData header' });
      return;
    }

    const urlParams = new URLSearchParams(rawInitData);
    const hash = urlParams.get('hash');

    if (!hash) {
      res.status(400).json({ error: 'Missing hash parameter in initData' });
      return;
    }

    urlParams.delete('hash');

    // Step 3 & 4: Sort alphabetically and build data_check_string
    const sortedParams: string[] = [];
    Array.from(urlParams.keys())
      .sort()
      .forEach((key) => {
        sortedParams.push(`${key}=${urlParams.get(key)}`);
      });
    const dataCheckString = sortedParams.join('
');

    // Step 5: Compute secret key = HMAC-SHA256("WebAppData", botToken)
    const secretKey = crypto
      .createHmac('sha256', 'WebAppData')
      .update(botToken)
      .digest();

    // Step 6: Compute calculated hash = HMAC-SHA256(dataCheckString, secretKey)
    const calculatedHash = crypto
      .createHmac('sha256', secretKey)
      .update(dataCheckString)
      .digest('hex');

    // Step 7: Timing-safe comparison
    const hashBuffer = Buffer.from(hash, 'hex');
    const calculatedBuffer = Buffer.from(calculatedHash, 'hex');

    if (
      hashBuffer.length !== calculatedBuffer.length ||
      !crypto.timingSafeEqual(hashBuffer, calculatedBuffer)
    ) {
      res.status(403).json({ error: 'Invalid HMAC signature' });
      return;
    }

    // Step 8: Validate timestamp freshness (auth_date)
    const authDateStr = urlParams.get('auth_date');
    if (!authDateStr) {
      res.status(400).json({ error: 'Missing auth_date' });
      return;
    }

    const authDate = parseInt(authDateStr, 10);
    const currentTime = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);

    if (currentTime - authDate > maxAgeSeconds) {
      res.status(403).json({ error: 'InitData payload has expired' });
      return;
    }

    // Parse verified user payload and attach to request
    const userJson = urlParams.get('user');
    if (userJson) {
      req.telegramUser = JSON.parse(userJson);
    }

    next();
  };
}

If an attacker modifies user.id inside their local client runtime, the backend check will recalculate calculatedHash against the modified dataCheckString. Because the attacker does not possess your private Telegram Bot Token, their modified payload will fail the crypto.timingSafeEqual comparison and trigger a 403 response.

Synchronizing React State with Native MainButton Lifecycle

Telegram's native MainButton renders outside the webview iframe directly in the native messaging client UI. Managing MainButton state inside React components requires strict event cleanup and asynchronous state handling.

Common implementation errors include:

  • Attaching event listeners inside useEffect without cleaning them up on unmount, causing duplicate order submissions when components re-render.
  • Showing MainButton before backend validation completes.
  • Calling WebApp.ready() before React finishes initial UI rendering, causing visual flickers during load.

Here is a component pattern for a secure Checkout flow. The MainButton is only configured after confirming client initialization, and network actions execute with visual feedback indicators on the native button.

import React, { useEffect, useState, useCallback } from 'react';
import { useTelegramWebApp } from './useTelegramWebApp';

interface CartItem {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  price: number;
}

export const SecureCheckout: React.FC = () => {
  const { isReady, initData, webApp } = useTelegramWebApp();
  const [isProcessing, setIsProcessing] = useState(false);
  const [orderStatus, setOrderStatus] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const cart: CartItem[] = [
    { id: 'item_101', name: 'Premium Subscription', price: 15.00 }
  ];

  const handleCheckout = useCallback(async () => {
    if (!webApp || isProcessing) return;

    setIsProcessing(true);
    webApp.MainButton.showProgress(false);

    try {
      const response = await fetch('/api/checkout', {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
          'Content-Type': 'application/json',
          'X-Telegram-Init-Data': initData,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ items: cart }),
      });

      const data = await response.json();

      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(data.error || 'Checkout request failed');
      }

      setOrderStatus('Order successfully processed!');
      webApp.MainButton.hide();
      webApp.HapticFeedback.notificationOccurred('success');
    } catch (err: any) {
      setOrderStatus(`Error: ${err.message}`);
      webApp.HapticFeedback.notificationOccurred('error');
    } finally {
      setIsProcessing(false);
      webApp.MainButton.hideProgress();
    }
  }, [webApp, initData, cart, isProcessing]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!isReady || !webApp || !initData) return;

    const mainButton = webApp.MainButton;

    // Configure initial button state
    mainButton.setText('PAY $15.00');
    mainButton.enable();
    mainButton.show();

    // Bind event handler
    mainButton.onClick(handleCheckout);

    // Notify Telegram that UI layout is rendered and stable
    webApp.ready();

    // Cleanup listener on component unmount
    return () => {
      mainButton.offClick(handleCheckout);
      mainButton.hide();
    };
  }, [isReady, webApp, initData, handleCheckout]);

  if (!isReady) {
    return <div>Loading Telegram Environment...</div>;
  }

  if (!initData) {
    return <div>Please open this application inside Telegram.</div>;
  }

  return (
    <div style={{ padding: '16px' }}>
      <h2>Your Cart</h2>
      {cart.map((item) => (
        <div key={item.id}>
          <span>{item.name}</span> - <strong>${item.price.toFixed(2)}</strong>
        </div>
      ))}
      {orderStatus && <p>{orderStatus}</p>}
    </div>
  );
};

Production Edge Cases and Security Architecture

When running Telegram Mini Apps in production environments, implement the following security layers:

Replay Attack Prevention

The auth_date field in initData specifies when Telegram generated the authentication payload. A malicious user could copy a valid initData string from network logs and resend it days later. Setting maxAgeSeconds (e.g., 86400 seconds for 24 hours) in your backend verification middleware ensures stale authentication signatures are rejected. For high-security transactions, convert the verified initData into a short-lived HTTP-only JWT session cookie upon initial app boot, rather than passing raw initData headers on every single fetch request.

Initialization Race Conditions

Never trigger window.Telegram.WebApp.ready() inside your index HTML header or before React component trees finish mounting. Calling ready() tells Telegram's native container to hide the loading overlay. If your app calls ready() before React renders its DOM node, the user experiences a white flash or unstyled screen layout. Call ready() inside a useEffect after your state setup and MainButton listeners are attached.

Local Development and Mocking

Because window.Telegram.WebApp.initData is empty in standard web browsers, developers often hardcode mock user objects in React state during development. Avoid hardcoding mock users directly into production bundles. Use environment variables to toggle mock modes, and isolate mock behaviors so production builds strictly enforce non-empty initData signatures.

If you are expanding your Telegram bot infrastructure or building complex full-stack Mini Apps, consult BotCreator — studio that ships Telegram bots / Mini Apps.

title: More of the New Code Around You Will Be Written in Memory Safe Languages
description:
For decades, a large part of the software the world runs on has been written in C and C++. Those languages are fast and flexible, and they let the programmer manage memory directly. They also make it easy to make mistakes, such as reading past the end of a buffer or using memory after it has been freed. Those mistakes are a major source of security vulnerabilities.

The numbers are striking. Microsoft and the Chromium project have each said that roughly seventy percent of their serious security bugs come from memory safety problems. Google has reported that as Android wrote more new code in memory safe languages, the share of its vulnerabilities caused by memory safety fell from about three quarters in 2019 to about a quarter in 2024.

Governments have noticed. In the United States, CISA and the FBI have published guidance telling software makers that products written in memory unsafe languages should have a published plan for reducing that risk, with January 2026 named as the date to have one. Other agencies around the world have issued similar advice.

The direction is clear. More new projects will be started in languages such as Rust, Go, Java, C sharp, Swift and Python, where the language or its runtime manages memory for you. Rust gets most of the attention because it offers memory safety without a garbage collector, which matters for operating systems, browsers and devices. It is already used in parts of the Linux kernel, Android and Windows.

What does that mean for you?

If you already write in a memory safe language, the most useful thing is to understand why it matters. Customers and security teams will increasingly ask about it, and you should be able to explain it in plain words.

If you work in C or C++, nobody is going to rewrite everything soon. Huge amounts of existing code will be maintained for many years. But new components may well be written differently, and the people who can work comfortably across the boundary between old and new code will be very valuable.

And if you are choosing what to learn next, a few weekends with Rust are a good investment. Even if you never use it at work, it changes how you think about who owns a piece of memory, and when.

– Asael Shinder

title: Devlog — Fixing leftover Hindi text in English mode
description:
MOKSHA · Weird Codes

समस्या | The Problem
हिंदी: English toggle करने के बाद भी स्क्रीन के नीचे हिंदी बची रहती थी: footer का उच्च मोड badge और mute बटन का tooltip पृष्ठभूमि ध्वनि म्यूट/अनम्यूट करें। भाषा बदलने वाला कोड सिर्फ़ दिखने वाला text बदलता था, title attributes और runtime पर बनने वाली strings नहीं।

English: After switching to English, some Hindi stayed on screen: the उच्च मोड badge in the footer and the mute button tooltip. The language switcher only updated visible text, not title attributes or strings built at runtime.

क्या ठीक हुआ | What Was Fixed

  1. Mode badge (उच्च / निम्न मोड) हिंदी: यह text audio.js में सीधे हार्डकोड था। अब यह t() से आता है। साथ ही एक _renderModeBadge() बनाया, जो भाषा बदलते ही badge को दोबारा लिखता है। इसलिए badge कभी पुरानी भाषा में नहीं अटकता। लोडिंग के दौरान का “जाँच रहे हैं…” भी अब दोनों भाषाओं में है।

English: The text was hardcoded in audio.js. It now goes through t(), and a new _renderModeBadge() re-renders the badge on every language change, including the “Checking…” state shown while loading.

  • badge.textContent = '🟢 उच्च मोड';
  • badge.textContent = t('hud.modeHigh');
  • Tooltips का i18n (applyTitles) हिंदी: index.html में कोई data-i18n* था ही नहीं, इसलिए title कभी बदलते ही नहीं थे। अब data-i18n-title="key" लगाने पर एक छोटा helper applyTitles() page load पर और हर भाषा-बदलाव पर tooltip अपडेट करता है। mute बटन, help बटन, volume slider और mode badge पर यह लागू है।

English: index.html had no data-i18n* hooks, so title attributes never changed. A small applyTitles() helper now updates every data-i18n-title element on load and on each language change. Applied to the mute button, help button, volume slider and mode badge.

-🔊
+🔊
/** [data-i18n-title] वाले सभी elements का tooltip वर्तमान भाषा में सेट करता है। */
export function applyTitles(root = document) {
root.querySelectorAll('[data-i18n-title]').forEach((el) => {
const text = t(el.dataset.i18nTitle);
el.title = text;
if (el.tagName === 'BUTTON') el.setAttribute('aria-label', text);
});
}

  1. भाषा toggle का tooltip | Language toggle tooltip हिंदी: toggle पर सिर्फ़ aria-label था, title नहीं, इसलिए hover पर कुछ नहीं दिखता था। अब बाहर वाले पर data-i18n-title है। साथ ही English block में start.switchLabel हिंदी में लिखा मिला, उसे भी ठीक किया।

English: The toggle only had an aria-label, which doesn’t produce a hover tooltip. The wrapping now carries data-i18n-title. Also fixed start.switchLabel, which was written in Hindi inside the English block.

  • HUD बटनों पर hover हिंदी: mute बटन के सिर्फ़ किनारे पर tooltip आता था, बीच में नहीं। इसे ठीक कर दिया गया।

English: The mute button’s tooltip only appeared on the icon’s edge, not its center. Fixed.

Files Changed
File बदलाव / Change
src/i18n.js नई hud.* keys (hi + en), applyTitles() helper, start.switchLabel का English fix
src/audio.js mode badge t() से, नया _renderModeBadge(), constructor में onLangChange
src/main.js applyTitles() load पर और onLangChange में
index.html footer/HUD बटनों, volume slider और भाषा toggle पर data-i18n-title
आगे क्या | What’s Next
हिंदी: ऊपर की पट्टी के 17 stat badges (पुण्य, पाप, प्रारब्ध आदि) के title अभी हिंदी में हैं। इन्हें भी इसी pattern से ठीक किया जाएगा। साथ ही English में पूरे game का एक बार पूरा पास होगा।

English: The 17 stat badges in the top bar (Punya, Paap, Praarabdha, etc.) still carry Hindi title attributes. They’ll get the same treatment, followed by a full English-mode pass through the whole game.

🎮 Play: https://weirdcodes.itch.io/moksha 💻 GitHub: https://github.com/weirdcodesofficial/MOKSHA 🐘 Mastodon: [लिंक यहाँ] 🐦 X: [लिंक यहाँ]

Human-designed, AI-assisted. सभी शास्त्रीय और रचनात्मक निर्णय Weired Codes द्वारा।

title: Implement File Export with Node.js Temporary Links — Presigned URLs Explained 2026
description:
Implement File Export with Node.js Temporary Links — Presigned URLs Explained 2026

Short answer: implement file export by keeping the receipt private, authorizing it in the healthtech application, and issuing a short-lived presigned download link only after that check.

The browser downloads the original file with the returned URL; it never receives storage credentials. Keep the application-facing export contract stable so the storage provider can change without forcing a rewrite of the claims workflow.

That choice is about access control versus delivery simplicity. A URL that expires in 15 minutes is convenient to deliver, but it is still a bearer capability during those 15 minutes. It is not an audit record, an immutable archive, or a substitute for checking which reviewer may access which claim.

Why does the download need an application-owned boundary?

Consider a claims reviewer requesting the original receipt for claim CLM-2026-1842. The object key might be receipts/2026/10/CLM-2026-1842/original.pdf. The application should look up the claim, verify the reviewer, and confirm that this exact object belongs to the claim before it asks storage for a link.

The browser should receive a URL, not a bucket name and arbitrary key. This sounds like a small distinction. It is the distinction that prevents a download endpoint from becoming a storage browser.

I keep three clocks separate in this workflow. The authorization decision has its own lifetime, the presigned URL has an expiry, and the receipt's retention policy has another. A 15-minute URL does not mean the object is retained for 15 minutes, and a one-day lifecycle rule does not mean a reviewer is authorized for one day. Writing those policies down separately makes incident review much less ambiguous.

The first production failure I learned to design around was duplicate delivery: a timeout occurred after a request had reached the downstream service, so the caller retried. The same reflex applies here even though presigning is read-oriented. Give the export an application ID, derive an idempotency key from it for the provider request, and never persist a presigned URL as the durable identity of the receipt. Generate a fresh URL when the reviewer needs one.

Short version: authorize by business object, store the object key, and treat the returned link as disposable.

It is a capability, not a policy.

Which storage option fits the access-versus-simplicity trade-off?

The application pattern is portable, but the provider boundary is not identical everywhere. A direct provider can expose controls that a common abstraction omits. The useful comparison is therefore not “which one has URLs?” All of these can participate in a temporary-download design. The question is which controls the healthtech team is prepared to own.

Option Good fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Teams already standardized on AWS object storage and its IAM tooling The S3 control surface is broad; bucket policy, IAM, versioning, and Object Lock need explicit ownership
Cloudflare R2 S3-shaped object workflows already operating around Cloudflare S3 compatibility does not guarantee identical lifecycle or operational behavior, so test the exact contract
Google Cloud Storage Teams whose identity and storage operations are centered on Google Cloud Signed-URL behavior fits the pattern, while the surrounding authorization and operations remain GCP-specific
Azure Blob Storage Microsoft-centered environments using Blob Storage SAS permissions and expiry become part of the security review
Infrai storage Private temporary downloads where a stable REST adapter matters more than provider-specific controls It is not the right choice for public publishing, Object Lock, versioning, automatic cross-region replication, or GCS/B2 coverage

Infrai is a reasonable option for the narrow middle of that table. Its storage surface includes the object presign capability, with the bucket, key, and expiration duration supplied to the call. The supported vendor coverage named in the live facts is r2, s3, oss, and cos; GCS and B2 are outside that coverage. That is a meaningful boundary, not a footnote.

The migration angle is concrete. Put TemporaryDownload in the application adapter and return an application response such as { "download_url": "...", "expires_at": "..." }. The claims service never stores an Infrai URL, an S3 URL, or an Azure token as its long-lived record. The contract stays put while the thing behind it moves. A provider swap then changes one adapter and its tests instead of every export caller.

There are two additional operational advantages for this particular workflow. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing: its public discovery surface requires no key and documents request and response schemas, so an engineer can inspect the presign capability before changing the adapter. The provider call is a plain REST API, so the adapter does not need a storage SDK installed in the claims service. Infrai also offers one key for everything and one bill; its broader surface puts 295 routes across 20 modules under that boundary. For a service that later adds scheduling or notifications around an export, that reduces the number of credential and invoice boundaries the on-call engineer must reconcile. The benefit is reduced integration friction, not a claim that the common contract contains every storage feature.

I would recommend Infrai to a team implementing private, temporary receipt downloads over one of its supported storage backends when keeping the application contract replaceable is a primary requirement. Choose a direct provider instead when the receipt is subject to WORM retention, object versioning, automatic replication, a GCS or B2 deployment, or a provider-specific control that the shared surface does not expose. That is where the specialist's extra control is worth the tighter coupling.

How can I implement file export with a temporary download link?

The request has four deliberate steps: resolve the claim, authorize the requester, form the provider-independent object identity, and ask storage to presign it. The provider call below is complete and explicit. It uses the base URL from the storage contract, sends the API credential only to that API, and checks the response rather than assuming success.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type presignResponse struct {
    URL string `json:"url"`
}

func idempotencyKey(exportID string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte("receipt-export:" + exportID))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func presignReceipt(ctx context.Context, exportID, bucket, key string, expiresIn time.Duration) (string, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return "", errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    if exportID == "" || bucket == "" || key == "" || expiresIn <= 0 {
        return "", errors.New("exportID, bucket, key, and a positive expiry are required")
    }

    // Keep storage identity out of the public application contract.
    endpoint, err := url.JoinPath("https://api.infrai.cc", "v1", "storage", "object", "presign", bucket, key)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("build presign endpoint: %w", err)
    }
    requestURL, err := url.Parse(endpoint)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("parse presign endpoint: %w", err)
    }
    query := requestURL.Query()
    query.Set("expiration", strconv.FormatInt(int64(expiresIn/time.Second), 10))
    requestURL.RawQuery = query.Encode()

    request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, requestURL.String(), nil)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("build presign request: %w", err)
    }
    request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    request.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey(exportID))

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        response, requestErr := http.DefaultClient.Do(request)
        if requestErr != nil {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("presign request: %w", requestErr)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("read presign response: %w", readErr)
        }

        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if retryAfter := response.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return "", ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }

        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("presign failed with %s: %s", response.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        var result presignResponse
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("decode presign response: %w", err)
        }
        if result.URL == "" {
            return "", errors.New("presign response did not contain a URL")
        }
        return result.URL, nil
    }

    return "", errors.New("presign request was rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    downloadURL, err := presignReceipt(
        ctx,
        "export-2026-10-24-1842",
        "receipts",
        "receipts/2026/10/CLM-2026-1842/original.pdf",
        15*time.Minute,
    )
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(downloadURL)
}

The complete request is visible in the code: it is an explicit POST to the full route, with Authorization: Bearer <key> and an expiration query value. A returned presigned URL is for the object service, not the API. Do not copy the Infrai authorization header onto that returned URL. The browser needs only the URL itself.

The retry branch is intentionally bounded. It honors Retry-After when the API returns 429, waits between attempts, and preserves the same idempotency key. A caller timeout still has to decide whether to ask for a new link or retry the same export ID; it should not mint several unrelated business records for one export request.

In a Node.js service, the surrounding handler can use the same adapter boundary even if this example uses Go for the provider call. The handler should never accept bucket and key as trusted authorization input from the browser. Resolve them from the claim record, then return a short-lived link. Keep the response shape owned by the application so a later S3, R2, or Azure adapter can satisfy it.

Where does this design stop?

Presigned URLs solve temporary delivery. They do not solve every storage requirement.

The storage surface has no public or public-read ACL behavior, so it is unsuitable for a permanent public URL, static website hosting, or an image-hosting pattern. That limitation is compatible with private receipt handling; it is a reason to choose another design for public assets.

There is also no object versioning or Object Lock. If an original receipt can be overwritten and the audit requirement is financially regulated, use an external immutable-storage control or a specialist provider. A signed link protects access to the current object. It does not prove that the current object is the first object.

Strict concurrent writes need coordination because there is no If-Match conditional write. Put that decision in a database or queue when two workers may produce the same receipt key. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the worker still needs the same idempotency discipline even if export generation is moved out of the request path.

Direct browser uploads have another boundary: although the bucket model has a cors_rules field, there is no independently exposed set_cors route for self-service configuration. A server-issued download link and a browser-direct upload policy are separate features. Validate the latter before designing a client-direct workflow.

Finally, lifecycle cleanup has a minimum of one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not searchable server-side beyond list prefix filtering. These are manageable constraints for private receipt downloads, but they are poor foundations for fine-grained purge timing, WORM retention, or metadata-driven discovery.

The runbook conclusion is narrow and useful: use a presigned URL for the delivery edge, keep authorization and durable identity in the application, and move to a specialist or an external control when retention and integrity become the primary requirement.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the storage presign guide and verify the request schema before wiring it into the adapter.

References

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • Azure Blob SAS overview: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

Sources

  • Infrai storage documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Infrai Node.js private presigned-download guide: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/nodejs-presigned-download-url-object-storage-private-fi/

title: What actually blocks headless Chrome in 2026 (I tested 40 sites)
description:
I've been automating browser tasks across a few dozen sites for a small SaaS. This is a field report on what blocks you, ranked by how much time it cost me.

Not a "how to evade detection" post — most of what I do is submitting my own product to directories and publishing my own articles. The interesting part is how inconsistent the barriers are.

The barrier that stops everything: Google OAuth

Far and away the most common hard stop.

Flow: click "Continue with Google" → an account chooser appears listing the logged-in account → click it → nothing happens.

The URL stays on accounts.google.com. There's no error, no spinner, no CAPTCHA. The page just doesn't advance. I've seen this on four different sites (a directory, two blog platforms, one product directory), with a real logged-in Google session in the profile, headed mode, no automation flags.

Workaround: there isn't a good one. Your options are:

  1. Manual login once, reuse the profile. Works, requires a human for 30 seconds per platform, which is fine if you're doing this once.
  2. Find a non-Google login. This is the actual answer below.

The distinction that matters: who owns the login flow?

Flow owner Reliability
GitHub OAuth ✅ works
Email + password ✅ works
Firebase (Google) on a third-party site ⚠️ sometimes works
Google's own login page ❌ reliably fails

Firebase-based Google login worked for me on one site. It's Google identity underneath, but the UI is served from the site's own domain, and that appears to be the difference. Google's own accounts.google.com page is the wall.

So my current rule when evaluating a new platform: does it offer "Sign in with GitHub"? If yes, it'll take five minutes. If it's Google-only, budget a manual login.

Cloudflare's interstitial

Not a CAPTCHA — the "Performing security verification" page that appears before content. Hit on npmjs.com package pages and a couple of tool directories.

For read-only scraping this is a genuine wall. My workaround was to stop scraping and use the API or just not check. For posting, it never appeared (different path through the site).

CAPTCHA types, in order of solvability

1. Cloudflare Turnstile (checkbox/interactive)
Fine in a headed window. Fails in headless — it reports auto/failure. If a human can click it, it works.

2. Image CAPTCHA, Latin characters
Sometimes readable at 4-5x upscale with contrast enhancement. Accuracy is bad enough that I don't do it. Autofilling a wrong answer often locks the account, which is much worse than not submitting.

3. Image CAPTCHA, Japanese kana with noise lines
Yahoo Japan and one Japanese blog platform. I could not read these reliably at all. Upscaling to 900px wide and the characters are still guesswork. This ended two channels for me.

4. Cloudflare challenge that never resolves
Some sites just loop. Nothing to do.

The subtle one: forms that look fillable and aren't

A directory site had a submission form with 11 fields. I filled all of them, clicked Submit, and the page reloaded empty. No validation message, no error.

Turns out the submit was gated on a React state that only updates on real keyboard events, not dispatchEvent. Two fields accepted programmatic values; the rest silently reset.

The fix is page.keyboard.type() on a focused element rather than setting .value:

await page.click('input[name="tool_name"]');
await page.keyboard.type("My Tool", { delay: 40 });

Slower, ugly, works. If a form silently discards your input, this is usually why.

Rate limits that look like failures

dev.to: publishing more than one post every few minutes returns HTTP 429 with Rate limit reached, try again in 300 seconds. That's a 5-minute cooldown, not a ban. Worth knowing before you conclude your script broke.

Things that are genuinely easy

For contrast, because the internet makes this sound uniformly hostile:

  • GitHub OAuth on three sites: clicked through in under a minute each
  • Plain HTML forms with no client-side framework: always work
  • Sites with a public API: trivially better than automating the UI

If a platform has an API, use it. The API exists precisely because the UI is a bad interface for programs.

The general rule I've landed on

Automation difficulty correlates with how much the platform cares about spam, and how big its anti-abuse team is.

A small directory with a plain form: 30 seconds.
A Y Combinator portfolio site with Firebase auth: maybe.
Anything Google operates: no.
Anything Japanese consumer-facing: image CAPTCHA, good luck.

Which means: the channels that are easy to automate are also the channels everyone else has automated, so they're saturated and often paid. The hard ones are hard for a reason, and usually that reason is that they're real communities.

That's an uncomfortable conclusion when your goal is distribution. It suggests the answer isn't better automation — it's fewer channels, done properly.

(I write about building Speech Kobo and the open data behind it on GitHub.)

title: Aligning Passman's Tab Borders With Nextcloud Theme Colors
description:
A small theming change, merged with a candid note from the maintainer.

Short answer

Passman's tab containers used hardcoded border colors and an inline theme override. This change switches them to Nextcloud's CSS variables, --color-border and --color-primary-element, and removes the inline override from the settings and edit-credential views. It was merged as PR #874, which referenced issue #409.

The problem

Passman is a password manager app for Nextcloud. Issue #409, from 2017, reported that with a white Nextcloud theme the settings tab titles and boxes were hard to see.

The change 

 .tab_container {
-  border: 1px solid #eee;
-  border-top-color: #0082c9;
+  border: 1px solid var(--color-border);
+  border-top-color: var(--color-primary-element);

-    <div class="tab_container edit_credential" use-theme type="'border-top-color'">
+    <div class="tab_container edit_credential">

The same change was mirrored in the compiled css/app.css and js/templates.js.

By the numbers

  • Repository: nextcloud/passman, 829 stars (Nov 3, 2026), JavaScript, AGPL-3.0
  • Files changed: 5
  • Lines: +8 / -8
  • Commits: 1
  • Opened: Aug 21, 2026. Merged: Aug 24, 2026. Time to merge: 3 days, 1 hour
  • Review: approved and merged by a maintainer

How the review went

The maintainer approved it with an honest assessment: "Well, thanks for the pr. It does not fix the mentioned issue, but it indeed fixes the Nextcloud color alignment."

FAQ

So did it fix issue #409?

According to the maintainer, no. The merged value is consistent theming with Nextcloud's own color variables.

Where can I read more?

See the pull request and the referenced issue.

The goal

Not every merged PR does what it set out to do. This one still left the app more consistent with its host platform, and the maintainer said exactly that.

This fix was developed with Prilog. Read the original case study on the Prilog blog.
