title: Your .npmrc Says Ignore-Scripts. The Repo's .npmrc Says Otherwise — and the Repo Wins
description:
I added one line to my own npm config a few months ago and stopped worrying about install hooks. The line was ignore-scripts=true, sitting in my user-level .npmrc, and in my head it worked like a lock on my front door. Any package I installed could bring whatever code it wanted in its install step, and my machine would just refuse to run it. That was the deal I thought I'd made with npm.

Then cryptostrapon asked a question in the comments on the install-hooks piece that I couldn't answer from memory. If a repo ships its own .npmrc that says ignore-scripts=false, does that beat my setting? I had a guess. My guess was wrong in the direction that matters, so I ran the test instead of arguing from memory.

The test was small on purpose. I built a package with one preinstall hook and nothing else. The hook writes a small marker file with a timestamp and prints a line, and the package itself does nothing at all. Then I installed it three ways on my own machine, node v24.22.1 and npm 10.9.4, and checked for the marker file after each install. The marker file is the whole test. If it's there, the hook ran. If it's not, it didn't.

Problem 1: the repo outranks you.

npm reads its config in layers, and the project layer sits on top. A .npmrc in the project folder beats the one in your home folder, which beats the global one, which beats the built-in defaults. I knew this in the abstract. I had never watched it eat my own safety setting.

First install: only my user config in play, ignore-scripts=true, no repo config at all. I asked npm what the effective value was and it said true. The install finished, and there was no marker file. The hook stayed silent. So far, the lock worked.

Second install: same user config, untouched. The only change was a repo .npmrc with one line in it, ignore-scripts=false. I asked npm for the effective value again and it said false. My own setting, in my own home folder, had just lost a vote I didn't know was happening. The install finished, and this time the marker file was there, timestamped 2026-11-17T00:07:40Z. The hook had run. I ran that second install again later to keep a clean copy of the marker as evidence, and it wrote a fresh one at 00:08:49Z. Same result twice.

That is the shape of the problem. Your personal setting is not a lock. It's a default, and a default is exactly the kind of thing a project folder is allowed to replace. One line in a repo you just cloned can switch your protection off, and the file that does it sits in plain sight in the repo root, in a file most of us never open before installing.

And before anyone pictures a villain: most repos that set ignore-scripts=false are not trying anything. Plenty of them do it for a boring, legitimate reason. Native packages and build tools often need their install hooks to finish setup, and a repo that sets the value to false is usually just making sure a fresh clone works the first time for everyone. The setting is doing its job. The problem is that the same file, with the same one line, is also the whole attack surface, and nothing in the process distinguishes a helpful repo from a hostile one. Your user config can't tell the difference either. It just loses.

Problem 2: nothing tells you it happened.

This is the part that bothered me more than the override itself. The two installs looked identical from the outside. Both printed the same calm line, "added 1 package". The second one even swallowed the hook's own printed line. The hook ran, wrote its file, and npm showed me nothing about it. I only knew because I went looking for the marker file on purpose.

Think about what that means for a real install. You clone something, you run the install, the output looks normal, and a hook you believed you'd blocked has already run. There is no warning, no yellow text, no hint that your setting lost. The tool did exactly what its config layers told it to do. It just never told you which layer won.

I keep coming back to that silence, because it breaks the one feedback loop that would save you. If npm printed one line, something like "project config turned install hooks back on", the whole issue would be a footnote. You'd see it, shrug, and decide for yourself. Instead the decision happens in a file you didn't write, in a layer you didn't know was voting, and the output looks the same either way. A protection that fails silently is worse than no protection at all, because the silent one still lets you feel safe.

Problem 3: the command-line flag is the only setting that's actually yours.

Third install: same repo config, still saying false, but this time I added --ignore-scripts to the install command itself. The hook stayed silent. No marker file. The flag beat the repo file, the way the repo file had beaten my user config.

That ordering is the honest picture. A flag you type wins over every file. A file in the project wins over a file in your home folder. A file in your home folder only wins when nothing above it has an opinion. Your user config is the weakest voice in that room, and it's the one most of us trust the most.

The catch is obvious, and it's the reason this matters less than it should and more than it does. A flag only protects the install where you remember to type it. Nobody types a flag on every install. We set a config once, forget about it, and trust it forever. That's the whole appeal of a user-level setting, and it's exactly the trust the layering quietly breaks.

So what do I actually do with this now? I stopped treating ignore-scripts=true in my own config as a safety net and started treating it as a preference. For installs I care about, the flag goes on the command. For repos I don't know well, I look at the .npmrc before the install, the same way I'd glance at a package's install hook before running it. It takes ten seconds, and it's the only check that can't be overridden by the thing it's checking. If a repo needs its hooks to build, fine, that's a real reason, and I can decide that with my eyes open instead of finding out afterwards.

Problem 4: the honest limit of this whole test.

Everything above is about install time. A package with no install hook at all can still run code the first time you load it, and no ignore-scripts setting, flag or config file touches that. That's the PolinRider pattern, and I'm not going to pretend I reproduced it here. I didn't. My test package was built to answer one question, whether a repo config beats a user config at install time, and it answered it. The load-time door is a different test, and it deserves its own run before anyone writes about it with confidence.

So the claim stands, and it's a narrower claim than the headline version. Your ignore-scripts setting does protect you, right up until a repo disagrees with it. Then the repo wins, quietly, and the only thing that reliably overrules the repo is a flag you type yourself, every time.

Have you ever caught a repo config undoing something you set for yourself? Not just npm. Any tool where a project file outranked your personal setup and you only found out later. I'd like to hear how you found it, and what you changed after.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: US Receipt Email API Providers Through Settlement and Statement Handoff Evidence
description:
Choose a receipt email provider only after it passes a settlement-to-inbox trial with your own US recipient accounts. TL;DR: SendGrid, Postmark, and Amazon SES belong on the shortlist; compare delivery evidence against the same paid order and statement, then choose the integration whose failure boundaries your team can operate. An accepted API request alone is an inadequate receipt-delivery criterion.

For a B2B SaaS team, the receipt begins when payment settles. A usage statement may need a PDF, the PDF must describe the correct billing period, and the email must reach the person who paid. That seam is the subject of this decision record. No delivery rates or benchmark results are asserted here.

Try Infrai for the usage-statement and receipt integration when one key and one bill across account usage, PDF processing, and email would remove credential distribution and invoice reconciliation work. Its public, self-describing discovery surface is a second reason to evaluate it: inspect request and response schemas before writing the adapters between those steps. Neither benefit establishes inbox placement; that remains an experiment.

What must remain true after payment settles?

The proposed invariant is one logical receipt per settled order, with a statement tied to that order's customer and billing period. Persist the settlement reference, statement version, recipient, and delivery state in the application's receipt record. These are application fields, not claims about provider request parameters. A retry should advance that record or leave it unchanged. It must never silently turn another customer's usage into a receipt attachment.

Settlement comes first.

Treat accounting, document generation, message submission, and mailbox observation as separate boundaries. A successful PDF operation proves nothing about email delivery. A successful email submission proves nothing about the recipient's inbox folder. Account usage is also not automatically customer billing data: the application must establish the mapping between the service usage being retrieved and the statement it intends to issue. Reject the document if that mapping is missing. This matters especially when the backend account serves several tenants and its usage response describes the account rather than a particular customer's order.

The compliance boundary belongs here too. Keep recipient addresses and statement contents out of diagnostic logs; store identifiers and redacted evidence instead. Use a receipt-specific template whose purpose is the settled transaction. Evaluate sender-domain setup, including SPF under RFC 7208, before interpreting a mailbox result as a provider comparison. SPF alone doesn't establish inbox placement.

How should email API providers demonstrate high US deliverability for receipts?

These are candidates, not a measured ranking. The trial should use equivalent receipt content, approved sender configurations, and the same recipient cohort.

Candidate Supported reason to evaluate it Boundary to examine in this trial
SendGrid Comprehensive analytics and ISP partnerships support a deliverability-focused evaluation. Decide whether its analytics provide the evidence your receipt operators need; do not convert those features into an assumed delivery percentage.
Postmark Transactional email specialization emphasizes speed and reliability. Prefer this focus when receipt mail is the main job; evaluate the surrounding statement pipeline separately.
Amazon SES Integration with AWS services suits a backend already organized around AWS. Test the complete application-owned statement and sending chain, rather than attributing every failure to the mail provider.
Infrai Account usage, PDF processing, and email share one API key and bill; public discovery supplies schemas for integration. Measure the statement handoff and receipt evidence together, with an explicit polling budget for communication events.

The alternative stack of Stripe metering, Puppeteer, and SES makes the seams visible. Budget for two service account setups and credential sets, Stripe and AWS; Puppeteer adds a rendering runtime rather than a third hosted-service signup in this design. The application still owns usage-to-statement mapping, rendering deployment, document transfer, email submission, and correlation across those steps. Do not describe that arrangement as three identical API subscriptions.

The trade-off is explicit: the combined approach means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one shared outage surface. Choose it only if the integration benefit outweighs that concentration for this workload.

Make the usage-to-document handoff explicit

The following Python program exercises the narrow seam between account usage and PDF generation using the same key and base URL. It prints the complete PDF response because assuming an attachment URL field would hide another schema decision. Email submission follows only after the application validates that response and associates the resulting statement with the settled order.

Inputs are environment variables: the API key, a schema-valid PDF request serialized as JSON, and a stable statement-operation key. Obtain the current PDF request schema from public discovery, construct the request for your document, and put the literal marker __USAGE_JSON__ inside the document text field. The program replaces that marker with HTML-escaped usage JSON. It does not prescribe an undocumented request field or imply that raw account usage is already a customer-ready receipt. Use a dedicated test account whose usage is appropriate for the trial statement.

import html
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
OPERATION_KEY = os.environ["STATEMENT_OPERATION_KEY"]
TEMPLATE = os.environ["PDF_REQUEST_JSON"]
MARKER = "__USAGE_JSON__"


def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    backoff = 2 ** attempt
    if not value:
        return backoff
    try:
        seconds = float(value)
    except ValueError:
        target = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
        seconds = (target - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
    return max(backoff, seconds, 0)


def request(method, path, payload=None, operation_key=None):
    data = None if payload is None else json.dumps(payload).encode()
    headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + KEY}
    if data is not None:
        headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
    if operation_key:
        headers["Idempotency-Key"] = operation_key
    for attempt in range(4):
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            BASE + path, data=data, headers=headers, method=method
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            reason = error.read().decode(errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {reason}") from error
            time.sleep(retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt))
    raise RuntimeError("Retry budget exhausted")


def fill(value, usage_text):
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return value.replace(MARKER, usage_text)
    if isinstance(value, list):
        return [fill(item, usage_text) for item in value]
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return {key: fill(item, usage_text) for key, item in value.items()}
    return value


def main():
    template = json.loads(TEMPLATE)
    if MARKER not in json.dumps(template):
        raise ValueError("PDF_REQUEST_JSON must contain the usage marker")
    usage = request("GET", "/account/usage")
    usage_text = html.escape(json.dumps(usage, indent=2))
    payload = fill(template, usage_text)
    result = request(
        "POST", "/pdf/generate", payload, operation_key=OPERATION_KEY
    )
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Before running it, verify the selected capability's idempotency declaration and current schemas in discovery. Keep the same operation key and payload for retries of one statement version; allocate a new key for a new version. The platform specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window. Maintain the application's durable receipt record beyond that window. A timeout needs reconciliation before another submission; the program surfaces transport errors rather than guessing whether a write completed.

This is deliberately a statement probe, not a finished receipt sender. It requires a real request template as configuration. The final email adapter must use its documented schema, validate the PDF result, and preserve the receipt record's identity across submission and evidence collection.

Run the settlement replay experiment

Use 12 synthetic settled orders and 6 controlled US recipient mailboxes as a proposed test fixture. These numbers are experiment inputs, not production measurements. Assign each order an immutable customer mapping, billing period, expected statement contents, recipient, and statement version. Include a repeated settlement notification, a temporarily throttled submission in a test harness, and a timeout after a simulated acceptance. Keep these simulated cases distinct from actual provider responses in the evidence ledger.

First run the statement handoff. For each candidate, use the same expected receipt contents and record statement readiness, submission acceptance, provider delivery evidence, and independently observed mailbox placement as distinct timestamps. Keep secrets out of the ledger. For Infrai, plan communication-event collection as polling, and include the polling interval in the measured observation delay. Otherwise an aggressive poller can appear to improve delivery even though it only notices the same event sooner.

Define the gate before sending:

  • Identity passes only if every statement matches the settled order's tenant, period, and expected contents. Any cross-customer document fails the candidate integration immediately.
  • Replay passes only if repeated settlement input and retry simulation leave one logical receipt operation, with ambiguous outcomes held for reconciliation.
  • Observation passes only if the controlled mailboxes contain all expected receipts within a proposed 10-minute window, with the provider evidence and folder placement recorded separately. Record spam-folder placement as a failure for this trial.
  • Operability passes only if a teammate can distinguish document failure, submission failure, and missing mailbox evidence from the redacted receipt record.

Do not average away a wrong attachment.

A small controlled cohort cannot establish a general US deliverability rate. Repeat the exercise with representative domains and production-approved content before committing; sender configuration, content, and recipient mix must remain visible in the interpretation. The decision rule is to reject identity or replay failures first, then compare mailbox results and observation delay among the survivors. If delivery evidence is equivalent, use integration ownership as the tie-breaker. That gives the single-key approach a fair opportunity without making administrative convenience a substitute for delivery.

Rejected default and the case where it fits

Reject an automatic switch to a different sender whenever receipt evidence is late. Late polling, an unknown submission outcome, and actual rejection are different states; changing providers before resolving them can create duplicate receipts. A manually reviewed resend tied to the original order is easier to reason about than an uncorrelated second send.

Infrai is not a good fit for a receipt architecture that requires immediate pushed communication events; the polling boundary is a limitation for that requirement. Choose a specialist whose documented event contract passes your trial instead. Postmark's transactional focus is a concrete reason to test it first when transactional email operations dominate the project. SendGrid deserves attention when analytics are central to the decision, and SES fits an AWS-centered backend. Keep the consolidated candidate for teams willing to operate the polling boundary and gain a simpler statement-to-email integration.

References

  • Sender Policy Framework specification
  • SendGrid documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • Amazon SES developer guide

If the usage-statement boundary fits your receipt system, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: AWS Config announces managed conformance packs
description:
AWS Config now offers managed conformance packs. AWS builds and maintains these packs for specific compliance and governance frameworks. When you deploy one, you choose a framework, and AWS Config evaluates your resources against it. AWS keeps the pack up to date as things change. When new AWS Config managed rules map to the framework's controls, or when the framework itself is revised, AWS updates your deployed pack automatically. Because AWS maintains a consistent pack definition in every supported Region, you can deploy the same framework across Regions without building or maintaining Region-specific rule sets. With managed conformance packs you no longer have to track framework changes or update rules yourself.

Previously, to evaluate resources against a framework such as PCI DSS or SOC 2, you started from a sample conformance pack template, customized it for your environment, and then updated it yourself whenever new rules became available or the framework changed. Managed conformance packs remove that work, so your coverage stays current without manual template changes. Each pack includes the managed rules available in the Region where you deploy it and adds new rules as they become available there, so you don't need a separate template for each Region. You can set rule parameters to fit your environment. Compliance results and compliance scores appear in the AWS Config console alongside your other rules and conformance packs.

Managed conformance packs cover frameworks including PCI DSS v4, SOC 2, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and CIS Controls, along with AI governance frameworks such as the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF 1.0. For the full list, see the AWS Config documentation page.

Managed conformance packs are available in all AWS commercial Regions except Middle East (UAE) and Middle East (Bahrain). For the full list of supported Regions, see AWS Capabilities by Region. Evaluations are billed at standard conformance pack evaluation rates. To get started, open the AWS Config console and choose Conformance packs. To learn more, see the AWS Config Developer Guide and the AWS Config pricing page.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

UPM

1000

1000

Cap height

710

710

x-height

530

530

Ascender

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: Our thirty second timeout let one call to the customs portal run for forty minutes
description:
Every evening a Python worker submits our export declarations to our customs broker's API, one consignment at a time, so that the lorries leaving at six the next morning have their clearance. Years ago a hung partner call had taken down a service of ours, and since then every outbound client we own has a timeout. This one used requests with timeout=30. We read that as: no call can take longer than thirty seconds.

In October the broker's platform had a bad night. Their gateway stayed up, but responses came back a few kilobytes at a time. One submission returned a large validation report, and its call ran for forty one minutes without raising anything. The worker processes declarations in order, so the three hundred behind it waited. Ninety consignments missed the morning lorries.

The requests documentation is precise about this, and we had never read it. The timeout is not a limit on the whole response. It applies to connecting, and then to each wait for data on the socket: the exception is raised only if no bytes have arrived for thirty seconds. A server that sends something every twenty nine seconds can keep a call open for as long as it likes. A slow trickle never trips a timeout that only measures silence.

Our dashboard did not help either. We recorded the duration of calls that completed and the number that timed out. A call that never finished appeared in neither, so for forty minutes the graphs showed a quiet evening.

The worker now enforces a total deadline per call. It streams the response and checks the elapsed time on every chunk, abandoning the call at sixty seconds whatever the server is doing, and the submission goes to a retry queue instead of blocking the run. Declarations are submitted by four workers in parallel, so one stuck call delays a quarter of the run at worst. We also emit a metric for calls in flight with their age, and an alert fires when any outbound call has been open for longer than twice its deadline.

We audited the other clients and found the same assumption in eleven of them. The library's name for the setting and our idea of what it meant were the same word for two different things.

– Sergey Shinder

title: The 8.9% you publish: auditing a visibility gate that is statistically indistinguishable from random
description:
Every prediction platform grows a gate. Not the model — the filter after the model, the code deciding which predictions the public may see. Ours is one boolean, is_visible, on a table with 47,150 rows. 8.98% are visible; the other 91% are computed, stored, graded, and hidden.

A gate is a claim: the rows I publish are better than the rows I suppress. That claim is testable. Almost nobody tests it. This is the audit, run against production data — including the part where the gate fails.

The setup: six gate-related columns, three of them dead

ai_predictions holds one row per model per match. Columns that look like they participate in the publish decision:

is_visible          boolean   47,150 populated
rec_level           varchar   46,721 populated   (A/B/C/D)
bet_worthiness      smallint  21,002 populated   (1..8)
veto_reason         text      10,223 populated
gate_reason         text           0 populated
gate_want_visible   boolean        0 populated
direction_gate      varchar        0 populated

Three of six are NULL on every row. That is the first finding — gate_want_visible at 0% occupancy says the gate was refactored and the audit trail did not survive. veto_reason survives on 10,223 rows, which is a reason code we can work with.

Baseline: 47,150 rows, 46,996 settled, 46,877 graded, 26,773 hits (57.11%), 3,796 models, 16,898 matches.

Step 1 — the pooled comparison, and why it is nearly useless

Start with the obvious query — the one that will mislead you.

SELECT is_visible,
       count(*)                                              AS n,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit)                            AS hits,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit)
             / nullif(count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL), 0), 2) AS hit_pct
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE hit IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1;

is_visible | n     | hits  | hit_pct
false      | 42684 | 24360 | 57.07
true       |  4231 |  2413 | 57.53

A lift of +0.48pp. With 4,231 published rows against 42,684 suppressed, the standard error of that difference is 0.80pp, so z = 0.60. Wilson intervals: visible 56.05–59.04, hidden 56.60–57.54 — overlapping across almost their entire width.

The gate's output is not measurably different from its own reject pile. Publish a random 8.9% sample instead and you would land within noise of what the gate actually publishes.

Two caveats. The gate need not be useless to produce this number — only diffuse: 4,231 rows from 543 models, selected by a mechanism that varies per model, pool flat even if each local gate works. And the audit was possible only because 42,684 of 42,918 suppressed rows (99.45%) were graded. Stop grading what you hide and the gate becomes unfalsifiable.

Step 2 — stratify by model, and watch the sign flip

The pooled query collapsed 3,796 models into one number. Redo it per model, keeping only models that publish some and suppress some — else it degrades to "always shows" vs "never shows".

WITH per_model AS (
  SELECT model_id,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND is_visible)    AS vis_graded,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit AND is_visible)                 AS vis_hits,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND NOT is_visible) AS hid_graded,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit AND NOT is_visible)             AS hid_hits
  FROM ai_predictions
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT count(*)                                                   AS models_compared,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE hid_hits * 1.0 / hid_graded
                          > vis_hits * 1.0 / vis_graded)          AS gate_is_worse,
       round(avg((vis_hits * 1.0 / vis_graded
                - hid_hits * 1.0 / hid_graded) * 100), 2)         AS mean_lift_pp
FROM per_model
WHERE vis_graded >= 5 AND hid_graded >= 5;

models_compared | gate_is_worse | mean_lift_pp
218             | 146           | -7.92

On 146 of 218 models, the published rows are worse than the hidden ones. Mean per-model lift is −7.92pp. Across the 194 models publishing at least 5 graded rows, visible rows average 56.05% and their suppressed siblings average 63.15%.

This is Simpson's paradox, and it is why a pooled gate audit is worthless. The pooled number looks fine only because visible rows are unevenly distributed: 387 of the 675 models with ≥20 graded rows (57.3%) never publish a single row, contributing zero to the "visible" bucket. The pooled average is a weighted sum whose weights have nothing to do with the gate's competence.

Step 3 — the tier system does not rank what it claims to rank

rec_level is the human-facing grade: A strongest, D weakest. It is populated on 46,721 rows.

rec_level graded rows hit % 95% Wilson published share
A 1,052 52.95 49.93–55.95 15.97%
B 2,027 63.15 61.06–65.19 14.41%
C 15,859 57.66 56.91–58.41 9.46%
D 27,514 56.56 56.00–57.12 7.78%

A is the worst grade in the table — 3.61pp below D, z = −2.31, p ≈ 0.021. B is the best, 6.6pp over A. The ordering is B > C > D > A: rec_level does not encode "how likely this row is to be right", and 1,052 rows carry the strongest label while being the weakest cohort.

Now the gate's behaviour inside each tier:

tier published hit % suppressed hit % gate lift
A 58.33 (n=168) 51.92 (n=884) +6.41pp
B 62.33 (n=292) 63.29 (n=1,735) −0.96pp
C 57.50 (n=1,501) 57.68 (n=14,358) −0.18pp
D 56.14 (n=2,141) 56.60 (n=25,373) −0.46pp

Inside tier A the gate works. Inside B, C and D it does not. And the published mix is 168 A / 292 B / 1,501 C / 2,141 D — 86.86% of published rows come from the two lowest grades. The gate operates where it has no edge and stays quiet where it has one: an A row is barely more likely to surface than a D row (15.97% vs 7.78%), and that 2× ratio cannot rescue an inverted tier.

Step 4 — a confidence inversion visible in one table

If the gate were a confidence threshold, publication would rise with confidence. That column is an integer 1–10, not a percentage.

confidence graded published % hit %
3 8,212 4.46 53.64
4 8,978 7.03 60.16
5 11,780 12.57 56.04
6 9,534 12.48 55.07
7 4,329 8.45 60.04
8 2,041 4.26 65.51
9 549 1.09 73.77
10 58 0.00 56.90

Publication peaks at 5–6, where accuracy sits below average, and collapses to 1.09% at 9 — the most accurate bucket in the table at 73.77%. The 58 rows at 10 are never published.

So it is not a confidence filter. rec_reason says what it actually is:

"结构未知（样本不足或无此组合）"    12,932 rows
"结构B但非竞彩/北单(观察)"          7,490 rows
"低质结构 ROI-8.3% (n=222)"         3,043 rows
"低质结构 ROI-4.8% (n=31)"          2,399 rows
"低质结构 ROI-0.2% (n=493)"         2,075 rows

The gate keys off a structure bucket and labels it with a bucket-level return figure computed over n=31, n=222, n=493 prior rows. That is the failure mode in one line: a decision about a single match made by a statistic computed over a different set of matches. It also explains the negative per-model lift — bucket membership is a property of market shape, not of the evidence for that particular match.

Step 5 — two integrity failures that block any future audit

Published rows carrying a veto. veto_reason is populated on 10,223 rows; 803 of them sit where is_visible = true. 19.0% of the published set has a recorded reason for being rejected. Either the flag is written after publication, or the veto is advisory and not wired into the publish path. Both are unverifiable from outside, and both mean the gate has no single source of truth.

Partial slates. 4,232 published rows span 4,212 of 16,898 matches — 24.93% carry at least one published row, and exactly 4 matches are fully published. A reader is not seeing "this match has a published view" but "this match had one model whose row survived", with the model varying per match. Any comparison built on that surface compares different things under one label.

Step 6 — what an auditable gate looks like

None of this is fixable with a threshold. The gate has to become a decision with a recorded counterfactual and a published scorecard.

import math

def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n
    d = 1 + z * z / n
    c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / d
    h = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / d
    return c - h, c + h

def audit_gate(vis_hits, vis_n, hid_hits, hid_n, min_lift_pp=3.0, z_crit=1.96):
    """PASS only if the gate beats its own reject pile by a margin
    that this sample can actually resolve."""
    pv, ph = vis_hits / vis_n, hid_hits / hid_n
    pooled = (vis_hits + hid_hits) / (vis_n + hid_n)
    se = math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / vis_n + 1 / hid_n))
    lift_pp = (pv - ph) * 100
    lo, hi = wilson(vis_hits, vis_n)
    need_n = 2 * pooled * (1 - pooled) / (min_lift_pp / 100) ** 2
    return {
        "lift_pp": round(lift_pp, 2),
        "z": round((pv - ph) / se, 3),
        "vis_ci": (round(lo * 100, 2), round(hi * 100, 2)),
        "n_needed_per_arm": round(need_n),
        "verdict": "PASS" if (lift_pp >= min_lift_pp
                              and abs((pv - ph) / se) >= z_crit
                              and min(vis_n, hid_n) >= need_n) else "FAIL",
    }

print(audit_gate(2413, 4231, 24360, 42684))
# {'lift_pp': 0.46, 'z': 0.578, 'vis_ci': (56.05, 59.01),
#  'n_needed_per_arm': 544, 'verdict': 'FAIL'}

The n_needed_per_arm term matters: at a 57% base rate, resolving a 3pp lift takes ~544 graded rows per arm. Both arms clear that bar, so the effect is genuinely absent — which blocks the usual answer ("we need more data").

Four changes follow: publish the gate's own scorecard, not only its output; keep grading suppressed rows, since 99.45% coverage is what made this audit possible; wire up the dead columns or delete them; and make the decision and the label one event, since 803 published rows with a veto reason mean the publish and skip paths can disagree.

The uncomfortable summary

A gate publishing 8.9% of 47,150 graded rows, with a pooled lift of +0.48pp (z = 0.60), a per-model lift of −7.92pp across 218 models where it fails on 146, an A-tier 3.6pp below its own D-tier, a confidence curve that publishes most where accuracy is lowest, and 19% of its output carrying a veto reason.

That is not a tuning failure. It is what happens when a publication decision is made by a bucket statistic and never scored against its own counterfactual. The fix is not a better threshold — it is making the gate answerable to the rows it threw away, which requires having graded them.

title: Assemble Parts in Minimum Time: Greedy Min-Heap Solution in Java (Code Interview Problem)
description:
This problem looks easy, and most candidates find the right idea within minutes. Then many of them implement it in a way that passes the examples and fails on half of all other inputs. Here's the problem, the trap, and a solution you can defend in an interview. You may also know it as "connect ropes with minimum cost".

The Problem

A factory builds a product from N parts. Assembling two parts of sizes a and b takes a + b units of time and produces one new part of size a + b. Parts are assembled two at a time until only the final product is left.

Write a method that calculates the minimum total time to build the final product. The input consists of two arguments: numOfParts, the number of parts, and parts, a list of integers with the size of each part.

public class AssembleParts {

  public static long minimumTime(int numOfParts, List<Integer> parts) {
    // implement your code here
  }
}

Example: numOfParts = 4, parts = [8, 4, 6, 12]. Output: 58.

  1. Assemble the parts of sizes 4 and 6: time 10. Remaining parts: [8, 10, 12].
  2. Assemble the parts of sizes 8 and 10: time 18. Remaining parts: [18, 12].
  3. Assemble the parts of sizes 18 and 12: time 30.

The total time is 10 + 18 + 30 = 58. No other order is faster.

Ask Before You Code

In an interview, clarify the input before you write a line. Interviewers expect it, and it shows how you'll work in a team: you don't build on assumptions.

  • Why numOfParts? The list already knows its size. Ask whether the two can differ, and validate them if they can.
  • Can the list be empty, or contain a single part? Then no assembly is needed, and the time is 0.
  • How large can the values be? Sums grow quickly. With large parts, the total doesn't fit into an int, so return a long.
  • Can sizes be negative or zero? A negative size makes no sense for a physical part, so reject it.

The Trap: Sorting Only Once

The example suggests a pattern: always assemble the two smallest parts. A tempting implementation sorts the list once and then walks through it, adding each new part to the next one:

Collections.sort(list);
long total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < list.size() - 1; i++) {
  int merged = list.get(i) + list.get(i + 1);
  total += merged;
  list.set(i + 1, merged);
}

It returns 58 for the example. But try [1, 1, 1, 1]:

  • Sorting once: 1 + 1 = 2, then 2 + 1 = 3, then 3 + 1 = 4. Total: 9.
  • Always the two smallest: 1 + 1 = 2, then the other 1 + 1 = 2, then 2 + 2 = 4. Total: 8.

The mistake: after a merge, the new part is not necessarily one of the two smallest anymore. The sorted order is out of date after the first step. In a test with 10,000 random lists, the sort-once version gave a wrong answer for 6,034 of them. The two examples in the problem just happen to work.

The Greedy Idea and Why It Works

Look at what the total time really counts. Every time a part takes part in an assembly, its size is added to the total, and it stays inside the new part for every later assembly. So:

total time = the sum of (size of each original part × the number of assemblies it goes through)

To keep the total small, the largest parts should go through the fewest assemblies, and the smallest parts can go through the most. That's exactly what happens when you always assemble the two smallest parts currently available. If a larger part went through more assemblies than a smaller one, swapping their places would reduce the total, so the greedy choice can't be beaten. This is the same argument that proves Huffman coding optimal.

The Solution: A Min-Heap

We need a structure that always gives us the smallest element, and accepts new elements that may belong anywhere in the order. That's a min-heap, and in Java it's a PriorityQueue:

public class AssembleParts {

  public static long minimumTime(int numOfParts, List<Integer> parts) {
    if (parts == null || numOfParts != parts.size()) {
      throw new IllegalArgumentException("numOfParts must equal the number of parts");
    }

    PriorityQueue<Long> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();   // min-heap: smallest part on top
    for (int part : parts) {
      if (part < 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Part sizes can't be negative: " + part);
      }
      heap.add((long) part);
    }

    long totalTime = 0;
    while (heap.size() > 1) {
      long merged = heap.poll() + heap.poll();   // the two smallest parts
      totalTime += merged;
      heap.add(merged);                          // the new part competes again
    }
    return totalTime;
  }
}

Complexity: each poll and add costs O(log n), and there are n − 1 assemblies, so the time is O(n log n). The heap needs O(n) extra space. The method doesn't modify the caller's list, and it uses long so large inputs can't overflow. See Big O notation for how to analyze algorithms like this one, and choosing the right data structure for when a heap is the right tool.

Tests That Would Have Caught the Bug

Write the tests first, and include more than the examples from the problem statement:

class AssemblePartsTest {

  @Test
  void examplesFromTheProblem() {
    assertEquals(58, AssembleParts.minimumTime(4, List.of(8, 4, 6, 12)));
    assertEquals(59, AssembleParts.minimumTime(5, List.of(3, 7, 2, 10, 5)));
  }

  @Test
  void inputsWhereSortingOnceFails() {
    assertEquals(8, AssembleParts.minimumTime(4, List.of(1, 1, 1, 1)));
    assertEquals(80, AssembleParts.minimumTime(6, List.of(5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5)));
  }

  @Test
  void edgeCases() {
    assertEquals(0, AssembleParts.minimumTime(0, List.of()));
    assertEquals(0, AssembleParts.minimumTime(1, List.of(42)));
    assertEquals(7, AssembleParts.minimumTime(2, List.of(3, 4)));
  }

  @Test
  void largeValuesDoNotOverflow() {
    int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    assertEquals(5L * max, AssembleParts.minimumTime(3, List.of(max, max, max)));
  }

  @Test
  void invalidInput() {
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> AssembleParts.minimumTime(3, List.of(1, 2)));
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> AssembleParts.minimumTime(2, List.of(1, -2)));
  }
}

assertEquals shows the expected and the actual value when a test fails, which assertTrue(result == 58) can't do.

The strongest test compares the solution with a brute force that tries every possible order. It's far too slow for real inputs, but for lists of up to seven parts it finishes instantly and is obviously correct:

@Test
void matchesBruteForceOnRandomInputs() {
  Random random = new Random(42);
  for (int run = 0; run < 1000; run++) {
    List<Integer> parts = new ArrayList<>();
    int n = 1 + random.nextInt(7);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      parts.add(1 + random.nextInt(20));
    }
    assertEquals(bruteForce(parts), AssembleParts.minimumTime(n, parts), parts.toString());
  }
}

// Tries every possible pair at every step: exponential, only for small test inputs
private static long bruteForce(List<Integer> parts) {
  if (parts.size() <= 1) {
    return 0;
  }
  long best = Long.MAX_VALUE;
  for (int i = 0; i < parts.size(); i++) {
    for (int j = i + 1; j < parts.size(); j++) {
      List<Integer> rest = new ArrayList<>(parts);
      int merged = parts.get(i) + parts.get(j);
      rest.remove(j);
      rest.remove(i);
      rest.add(merged);
      best = Math.min(best, merged + bruteForce(rest));
    }
  }
  return best;
}

All six tests pass with the min-heap solution. The sort-once version fails the counterexamples and the random test.

Related Problems

The same greedy idea solves several well-known problems:

  • Connect ropes with minimum cost: the same problem with ropes instead of parts.
  • Optimal merge pattern: merge sorted files with the fewest total record moves.
  • Huffman coding: build the code tree by repeatedly combining the two least frequent symbols, which gives the shortest compressed text.

When you recognize the pattern "repeatedly combine the two smallest", reach for a min-heap.

Problems like this one, where the obvious solution has a hidden flaw, are what coding interviews are made of. My book walks through more of them, with the same approach: understand the problem, find the trap, then write the efficient solution:

title: How the work of UX is changing
description:
I recently attended the PUSH UX conference in Munich, and one slide from Kris Hedstrom, Head of UX/UI Design at On, has stuck with me ever since:

“We can build almost anything. Should we?”

It sums up a shift I see in my own daily work. Building has become cheap, and the technical process is no longer the bottleneck. So the job of designers and developers shifts from making to deciding: what belongs on a page, what gets left out, and how we shape the flood of AI output so people can still make sense of it.

Every element has to earn its place

More features don’t automatically mean a better product. An overloaded UI can achieve the opposite of what was intended: users get overwhelmed and can no longer find what they came for.

Sometimes the best design decision is to leave something out. A calm, focused page protects a product’s perceived value. Premium brands know this well: the less there is on the page, the more valuable the product feels.

Putting numbers on it

Kris showed how they measure what is actually earning its place on a page. On a product detail page, for example, they track every element: how often people click on it and how much those clicks are worth in the end. “Value” here basically means: how likely is it that someone who clicks on this element ends up buying?

They plot both on one chart and every element lands in one of three groups:

  • Engagement drivers: high click-through, lower value per click. People use them a lot to explore, like color thumbnails or the size chart.
  • Value drivers: fewer clicks, but a higher expected value per click. In the example, people who engage with “How to wear it” generate noticeably more value per click, even though few of them click it.
  • Neither: low on both. These are the candidates to simplify, merge or remove.

The chart below is a simplified version of the example from the talk.

Personally, I found this approach really exciting, and I want to try it in one of my own projects. The prerequisite, of course, is that you already have solid tracking in place. Once you track every interactive element and can link it to purchases, you can build a chart like this yourself. One caveat: it shows correlation, not cause. People who open “How to wear it” may simply be closer to buying already. Still, it’s a great tool for conversations with stakeholders. It shows which features can be removed, and it makes room to try new things without cluttering the page.

Designers are moving beyond Figma

Apart from the talks, I talked to a lot of people at the conference. One thing came up again and again: more and more designers are moving away from Figma. You read about this all the time on LinkedIn, and to be honest, I always thought it was just the LinkedIn people who work like this. But it was crazy to see how many actually do it in real projects. Designers who always worked in Figma now pull the codebase locally for the first time and build their prototypes directly with Claude.

They use these prototypes for user interviews and then hand the branch over to the developers, who finish the feature. One designer told me he now opens pull requests himself for small design changes. Just like developers no longer need to know every CSS property by heart, designers no longer need to know every trick in Figma. It’s the same shift again: building a prototype is no longer the hard part. The hard part is deciding what is worth building at all.

Too much output is a UX problem

As a developer, I run into a similar problem every day: LLMs produce more output than we can take in. Think of the pull request with 120 changed files that a local agent generated (LGTM). Reviewing these huge PRs annoys us developers all the time, but I never thought of it as a UX problem. It is one, though.

The question is the same as on the product page: what actually earns its place? We need well-established UX practices to shape that output:

  • What is relevant in this diff, and what can be collapsed?
  • Which changes affect which part of the system?
  • How should an agent’s output be structured so a person can review it?

And it’s the same with the things we build for our customers. If we build a chatbot that answers user questions, our users get just as annoyed by a giant wall of text as we do. So we have to think about how to present the answer in an attractive way. Take a shopping assistant: instead of a long text, it should show a few product cards, built from components of our existing design system. That’s what dynamic, generative UI is about. The information becomes tangible again, and the user stays in control.

Less making, more deciding

Measuring elements on a product page, designers prototyping directly in code, agents writing huge PRs: it all comes back to the same point. We can build almost anything now, and it’s getting easier every month. So the real work for UX, and honestly for us developers too, is deciding what deserves a place. And if we can back those decisions with data, even better.

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now provides full session summaries
description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now keeps a full session summary for every session. It's a single record that gives a snapshot of what happened in the conversation. Summary chunks cover the conversation in more detail, while the full session summary captures the overall picture of where the session stands. AgentCore Memory updates it as new events arrive, so it always reflects the session so far. This works well for developers who want a quick recap rather than a play-by-play.

Full session summaries come with the summary strategy and need no extra setup. Every memory that has a summary strategy gets them automatically, including existing sessions. Each summary is stored as a long-term memory record next to the session's summary chunks. You retrieve it with the Memory operations you already use, and you can filter by record type to return only full session summaries.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is available. To get started, see the Summary strategy documentation.

title: Role of Python in Backend Web Development
description:
Introduction

Due to technological changes, websites and web applications are now getting very important for the development process, especially while dealing with the clients. Be it an e-commerce site, banking application, social networking site or the booking site; all should have a good backend for functioning effectively. As while the frontend is responsible for handling the front side of the product for the user, the backend is responsible for handling data, business logic, server, etc. Some of the languages used in the backend programming are Java, PHP, JavaScript and Python. Among all, Python has gained importance as one of the most loved programming language among the programmers.Python in Backend Web Development helps developers build secure, scalable, and efficient web applications with less complicated code.

What Is Backend Web Development?

"Backend Web Development" involves the development of a website or web application on the server-side. It takes care of all operations that occur in the background every time a user uses the website.
Server: The server receives requests from the users and processes them.
Application logic: This includes rules and operations necessary to carry out different operations.
Database: A place where information such as user details, products information, order and transactions are kept.

What Is Python?

It is one of the high-level programming languages. The features of the language are simplicity in syntax and readability. It can be used in various industries, including web development, software development, automation, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data science. Some of the reasons why developers opt for Python language are its ability to produce clean code. In contrast with other programming languages, Python produces code that consists of fewer lines. Moreover, Python has a large library of tools for developing applications.

Role of Python in Backend Web Development

Python is useful for controlling the server side functionality of websites and applications. The programming language assists the developers in developing application logic, receiving requests from users, dealing with the databases, and connecting different services together.

  • Management of Server-Side Logic
    The most important task of backend development is related to management of the application logic performed at the server side.Using Python, developers can develop all the functions needed to perform different actions. These include user registration, log-in procedures, order processing, payment procedures, and form submission.For instance, if a user registers himself or herself on a website, then using Python developers can receive the input from users, validate it and store it in the database.

  • Database Management and Integration
    Each web application needs a database to store and manage data. Python helps developers easily connect backend applications to various database management systems.
    The database management systems supported by Python include:

  1. MySQL
  2. PostgreSQL
  3. SQLite
  4. MongoDB

Python provides libraries and utilities through which developers can perform database actions like adding, modifying, fetching, and deleting data.For instance, an online shopping website can utilize Python to fetch product data, modify availability of the products, and store order details.

  • API Development and Integration
    API stands for Application Programming Interface. It enables different software applications to interact and exchange data.Python is extensively employed for the development of APIs connecting websites to mobile applications, payment gateways, third-party applications, and various other software.For instance, an e-commerce site might use an API to connect with a payment gateway for facilitating payments through the internet.The Python frameworks like Flask, Django, and FastAPI are some of the popular choices when it comes to the development of APIs.

  • User Authentication and Security
    Security is an important aspect in backend web development. The websites need to ensure the security of the data of the users and prevent any unauthorized access to this data.Python can be used for several security-oriented processes, which include:

  1. User registration and login process.
  2. Hashing of passwords.
  3. Session management.
  4. Role-based access control.
  5. API authentication.

Frameworks like Django have inbuilt capabilities for the purposes of user authentication.However, developers should also adopt other security best practices.

  • Developing Scalable Web Applications The term scalability denotes the capability of an application to deal with more and more users, requests, and data without impairing its performance.There are several ways to develop scalable web applications with the help of Python, using such concepts as its frameworks, caching, database features, and background processing.A programmer can utilize such techniques as Redis, Celery, as well as cloud services together with Python in order to perform background processes and enhance application performance.For instance, an online shopping website may implement background processing to send confirmation emails regarding orders without hindering the checkout process.

Popular Python Frameworks Used in Backend Development

Python in Backend Web Development plays an important role in building modern websites and web applications. It helps developers manage server-side operations, handle databases, create APIs, and develop secure and scalable applications. With powerful frameworks such as Django, Flask, and FastAPI, Python makes backend development easier and faster. Its simple syntax and flexibility make it a popular choice for both beginners and professional developers.

  • Django Django is a high-level Python framework for developing web applications rapidly and in a highly secure and maintainable way.It uses Model Template View architecture and has many inbuilt features, which include:
  1. Authentication of users.
  2. Database management.
  3. Routing of URLs.
  4. Admin interface.
  5. Security.

Django can be used for developing content management systems, e-commerce sites, and social networking websites.

  • Flask Flask is a minimalistic Python web framework, which allows developers to have a certain degree of freedom.In contrast to Django, Flask does not have such an extensive list of features. The key features are as follows:
  • Simple application architecture.
  • Flexibility in the development process.
  • Routing for URLs.
  • Support for API development.
  • Database integration.

Flask is widely used for the development of small and medium-sized web applications, prototyping, and API development.

  • FastAPI FastAPI is a state-of-the-art Python framework primarily designed to build APIs fast and effectively.It incorporates asynchronous programming and automatic documentation, which makes it perfect for applications handling several requests at once. The following are the main characteristics of FastAPI:
  1. High-speed API development.
  2. Automated interactive documentation.
  3. Validation of data.
  4. Asynchronism.
  5. Python type hints.

FastAPI is highly suitable for the development of contemporary backend systems and API applications.

Benefits of Using Python for Backend Web Development

  • Ease of Learning
    The programming language uses simple and easy-to-understand syntax. Even beginners will easily grasp the basics without having to understand complex programming structures. Therefore, Python is a good starting point for learning backend programming.

  • Quicker Development
    Python comes with pre-built frameworks that contain libraries and components that make development much quicker and easier by allowing developers to reuse them.

  • Wide Array of Libraries
    Python possesses a wide array of libraries that cater to different software development needs. Developers can leverage these libraries for databases, APIs, authentication, testing, automation, and many other purposes.

  • Active Developer Community
    Python boasts of a huge developer community in different parts of the world. Both beginners and experienced developers will be able to find tutorials, documents, open source projects, and answers to programming issues.

  • Compatibility with Latest Technologies
    Python is compatible with technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, data analytics, cloud computing, and automation.It enables developers to create applications that combine backend features and latest technologies.

Real-World Applications of Python in Backend Development

Python is used across different industries to develop and manage web applications.
E-commerce Websites: Managing customer accounts, product information, orders, and payments.
Social Media Platforms: Handling user profiles, content management, and notifications.
Banking Applications: Supporting backend operations, transaction processing, and data management.
Healthcare Applications: Managing appointments, patient information, and online services.
**Educational Platforms: **Supporting student registration, course management, and online learning systems.
These examples demonstrate how Python supports different types of backend operations across industries.

Skills Required to Become a Python Backend Developer

Being skilled only in Python programming is not sufficient to be a professional backend developer. It is necessary to have some knowledge of the technologies and concepts employed in developing applications in real world.
Python programming: Knowledge of variables, data types, functions, loops, object-oriented programming and exceptions handling.
Python frameworks: **Acquaintance with frameworks such as Django, Flask and FastAPI for developing backend applications.
**Database management: **Practical knowledge of databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB.
**Frontend Technologies: Understanding of HTML and CSS – basic frontend technologies for building web pages.
API Development: **Familiarity with the concept of APIs and development of REST APIs.
**Version Control: Knowledge of Git and GitHub.
Testing and Debugging: Ability to find and fix errors.
Application Deployment: Understanding how to deploy applications using cloud services and web servers.
In addition, experience in projects is very important as it shows how different backend technologies work together.

Career Opportunities in Python Backend Development

With companies creating digital platforms and web applications, it is necessary to have qualified backend developers in various industries.Some career options one can pursue through learning Python and its backend frameworks include:

  1. Python Backend Developer
  2. Python Web Developer
  3. Django Developer
  4. Flask Developer
  5. API Developer
  6. Software Developer
  7. Full Stack Developer

These careers may require different skill sets according to the organizations’ needs and the project. Having hands-on experience with building projects and understanding databases, APIs, and frameworks will benefit one’s career.

Conclusion

This is a highly useful language in the field of backend web development in the contemporary world due to its ease, flexibility, and efficient development tools. This language can be applied for many different purposes in the field of backend web development including database management, API development, and more. Python in Backend Web Development can enable upcoming developers to develop a strong foundation in server-side programming. They gain those skills required for building web applications by learning how to use the frameworks of Python, which include Django, Flask, FastAPI, and database management as well as API integration. No matter if you are a beginner programmer starting your programming career or a new software developer in need of improving his/her technical skills, learning Python will be of great benefit to you.

title: Not one of our 662 headings balances its lines, and the fix is two Tailwind classes and no reflow
description:
text-wrap: balance and text-wrap: pretty are the cheapest typographic upgrade available to a web page, and the reason they do not get applied is that nobody can tell you what they would be worth on your particular site. So I measured it on Nakodo, which has 76 public pages, 662 headings and about 3,200 blocks of body text.

What the site does today

Every heading on every public page computes to the default:

text-wrap on 662 headings: wrap (662 of 662)
hyphens on 662 headings:   manual (662 of 662)
non-breaking spaces in the HTML of all 76 pages: 0
soft hyphens: 0

No balancing, no automatic hyphenation, and no manual widow control either, which is the honest state of most sites. The stylesheet does contain the utilities, because Tailwind only emits what is used:

.text-balance{text-wrap:balance}.text-pretty{text-wrap:pretty}

Four uses across 582 source files. Two of them are 13px tour notes on the home page, and two are the description slots inside alert.tsx and alert-dialog.tsx, which arrived with the component library and are only reachable behind the login. The public typography has none.

Measuring a widow

Line breaks are not in the DOM, so the only way to count rendered lines is to ask the layout where each word ended up. A Range per word, grouped by rounded top, gives lines with their word counts and widths:

const r = document.createRange();
r.setStart(node, m.index);
r.setEnd(node, m.index + m[0].length);
const rect = r.getBoundingClientRect();
items.push({ top: Math.round(rect.top), word: m[0], left: rect.left, right: rect.right });
// group items by top, within 4px, and each group is a rendered line

For the 662 headings (76 h1, 576 h2, 10 h3):

Rendered lines Headings
1 552
2 97
3 13

110 headings wrap at all, and 20 of those end on a single word. That is the classic defect, and here it is in full, with the last word and how wide that last line is as a share of the heading's widest line:

/guides/micro-influencers-on-youtube    "them"         18%
/guides/instagram-and-tiktok-...        "TikTok"       27%
/tools/engagement-rate-calculator       "calculator"   38%
/youtubers/tech                         "sponsor"      26%
/tiktokers/books                        "brand"        21%
/for/saas                               "doesn't"      15%
/alternatives/hypeauditor               "them"         18%

The four calculator pages are the clearest case, because their titles are near-identical and all four break the same way: "YouTube engagement rate calculator" puts the word "calculator" alone on line two, 229px of it under a 599px line.

What balance does, measured

Inject one declaration and measure the same headings again:

const st = document.createElement("style");
st.textContent = "h1,h2,h3{text-wrap:balance}";
document.head.appendChild(st);
Before After
Heading lines, total 785 785
Median last line as a share of the widest line 41.5% 100%
Headings whose line count changed 0

Nothing moves vertically. Not one of the 110 multi-line headings gains or loses a line, so no layout shifts, no cards get taller, no grid rows change. What changes is the distribution of words between lines that already existed, and a median last-line share of 100% means that after balancing, the last line is typically the widest one, which is what an even block looks like. The 20 widows all improve: 18% to 85%, 14% to 83%, 38% to 67%, 25% to 100%.

That is the entire cost and benefit of text-balance on this site. One class on two components, no reflow, and the twenty ugliest headings stop being ugly.

What pretty does, measured

The same test on body text, with one page excluded for a reason I will come back to. 3,163 blocks on 75 pages (1,726 p, 1,125 li, 312 dd), of which 2,838 take more than one line:

Last line as a share of the widest line Before With text-wrap: pretty
10% or less 278 150
15% or less 462 337
20% or less 616 523
25% or less 759 717

365 blocks improved, zero got worse, zero changed line count, and the total height of all 75 pages was identical to the pixel before and after. The worst offenders are the ones you would wince at in print: a 210-character paragraph on product seeding whose third line is 2% of the width of the other two, and a list item on the privacy notice doing the same thing.

pretty fixes a bit over half of the worst cases rather than all of them, which is the honest shape of this feature: it can only pull a word down from the line above when that line has a word it can spare. A 15-character word at the end of a tight measure stays where it is.

The page I had to throw out

The home page reported a 150-character paragraph as 127 rendered lines. That is not a layout bug, it is my measurement meeting the hero animation: 45 leaves on a requestAnimationFrame loop and a tour of example cards, so the client rects I was collecting word by word were taken at different moments of different frames, and every word landed on its own "line".

Two lessons. Range-rect measurement assumes a still page, so freeze or exclude anything animated before you believe a line count. And the reason it only happened once is that this site has exactly one page with animation on it, which I know from an earlier sweep where 75 of 76 pages returned an empty document.getAnimations().

What I am changing

text-balance on the content heading components and text-pretty on the body text, both measured above as free: no height change on any page, no line-count change anywhere, 20 heading widows and 365 ragged paragraph tails improved. The remaining 150 tiny last lines are a copy problem rather than a CSS one, and the places they show up are mostly list items where the sentence could simply be shorter.

If you want to see the before state, it is still live while I ship this: the four calculators all break their titles the same way, the niche pages end their headings on the word "brand", and the guides are where the paragraph tails are.
