title: A low drift score is not a completed staging job
description:
Give the score a specific job

VirtualStagingFlow’s Room 08 record has an appealing technical result. Framing passed, and architecture drift is 9.7. The note calls it the lowest drift among the tool’s tested rooms.

The same note says the kitchen was barely staged. Only accessories were added.

That makes this a useful example for anyone building a review interface around benchmark data. The automatic result and the task completion question need separate places in the interface. For this output, I would display the structure measurement beside the recorded description of what changed.

The VirtualStagingFlow benchmark record concerns real CC0 apartment photographs. The broader benchmark remains partial. Blind human scoring is planned, so I would not present these records as a completed blind comparison.

Read the kitchen record in context

Room 08 is the loft kitchen photo. Its recorded settings were Stage a photo, Contemporary, Stage for General, and Clear first. The room type was Kitchen, with no custom request.

The source image was 1600x1200. The output was 2048x1536, and its aspect ratio was preserved. Alignment succeeded. The score file reports 173 inlier matches.

Those facts help describe the technical result. They do not change the written observation that the staging amounted to accessories.

For a review application, I would show a task completion prompt beside this row: is the amount of furnishing appropriate for the intended kitchen image? The record does not establish a universal amount of staging that every kitchen needs. It gives a concrete reason to inspect this particular result.

I would also keep the settings visible during that inspection. A reviewer should see what the operator requested before deciding whether the delivered change was sufficient.

A different reason to pause

Room 09 shows why an exception queue belongs ahead of any numeric ranking. Its architecture drift is 5.7, but alignment failed. Framing is unknown.

The record explains the failure. The original’s nearly blank white walls supplied only 5 keypoints in the evaluated top 65% of the frame. The method needed 25 inlier matches. The score fell back to an unaligned measurement, with no long straight lines available to check.

The note explicitly says to read this as unmeasured rather than near perfect. I would route that row to manual inspection before allowing its drift value into a ranked view.

This is a different review decision from Room 08. The kitchen has a successful measurement and a question about the amount of staging. Room 09 lacks a reliable aligned measurement. Keeping those reasons visible helps a reviewer decide what to inspect next.

Build a small exception queue

The downloadable results data has a top level tools array. A tool’s initial room record is stored in room01. Additional records, where present, are in rooms, with a room field identifying each one.

The following snippet reads that structure. It flags explicit alignment failures and unknown values in selected review fields.

import json
from pathlib import Path

data = json.loads(Path("data/results.json").read_text())
checks = ("framing_pass", "architecture_drift", "aspect_ratio_kept")

for tool in data["tools"]:
    rooms = []
    if isinstance(tool.get("room01"), dict):
        rooms.append(("01", tool["room01"]))
    rooms.extend((r["room"], r) for r in tool.get("rooms", []))

    for room_id, result in rooms:
        reasons = []
        if result.get("alignment_ok") is False:
            reasons.append("alignment failed")
        for key in checks:
            value = result.get(key)
            if value is None or (
                isinstance(value, str) and "unknown" in value.lower()
            ):
                reasons.append(f"{key} unknown")
        if reasons:
            print(tool["id"], room_id, "; ".join(reasons))

The identity check against False is deliberate. Some room01 records omit alignment_ok. The snippet does not turn that omission into an explicit failure. For the selected review fields, missing values, null values and strings containing unknown trigger review. A known false framing result remains a known failure, rather than being relabelled unknown.

This is a selected field check, not a recursive search through every null in the file. For example, an empty custom request belongs to the recorded settings and does not trigger this queue.

Keep completion review beside technical review

Running the snippet on the supplied data flags several rooms across different tools, including VirtualStagingFlow Room 09 for failed alignment and unknown framing. Room 08 does not enter that queue.

That is the intended limit of the code. It finds measurement exceptions. It does not decide whether a kitchen has been furnished enough.

The written methodology describes drift as a proxy and says it should never be used alone. Room 08 gives that caution a practical purpose. After checking whether a score is usable, return to the recorded task and the delivered image. For this kitchen, the next review question is about the work completed.

For Room 08, I would keep a completion review open even though the exception queue is clear. The reviewer could approve the limited accessory changes if they match the intended brief, or request a more substantial result. The important implementation choice is to make that decision explicit. An empty exception list should never silently become approval of the image.

title: Engineering AI Discover
description:
The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer

By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi

We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.

Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.

This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.

Why an intelligence layer?

Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.

The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:

  1. Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.
  2. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.
  3. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.
  4. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.
  5. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.
  6. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.
  7. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.

System Architecture

When a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.

The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.

A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.

Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.

The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.

Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.

Key Decisions

Each challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.

1. Design the product and architecture around LLMs

We reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.

This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.

2. Make existing systems composable

Keeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.

Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.

In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.

3. Plan first, then execute

To contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.

Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.

This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.

4. Stay model and capability agnostic

The best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.

That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.

Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.

Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.

5. Make page generation asynchronous

Inference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.

Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.

Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.

6. Enforce safety in code

Some rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.

For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.

Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.

Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.

7. Remember what members tell us

A taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.

In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.

The member holds the remote

In this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.

  • The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.
  • Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.

What’s next

It would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.

We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:

  • How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.
  • What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.

Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.

This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.

Acknowledgements

We would like to thank Adi Suresh, Akash Katipally, Allan Johns, Becks Wood, Bhargav Mangipudi, Carrie Santiago, Chris Martin, Claire Campbell, Corey Waldin, Dana Sittler, Daneo Zhang, David Leen, Devon Bryant, Dharamendra Kumar, Dharini Chandrasekaran, Ebony Turner, Federico Roa, Gianfranco Cuoco, Guru Tahasildar, Haley Clanton, Haresh Chudgar, Ivan Provalov, James Schultz, JingXu Yang, Josie Shaw, Kamelia Aryafar, Kate Cummings, Kathleen Garrity, Kelley Robinson, Kevin Du, Kevin O’Connor, Kyla Moore, Kyle Lind, Laura Matsuura, Leah Cusella, Lingyi Liu, Lingyong Wang, Mallory Walkup, Matthew Pereira, Michael Galassi, Minsu Jang, Moumita Bhattacharya, Paran Jain, Paul Lee, Qusai Al-Rabadi, Scarlet Chen, Sergi Perez, Sriram Rao, Stephen Shaw, Sura Elamurugu, Varad Pathak, Yesu Feng, Zainab Mahar Mir, and Zhongli Cheng for their contributions to this work.

title: Property Mail DNS: Go Staging Zone Preflight Before Production MX Changes
description:
A property management company's production mail should keep reaching its provider while the platform team rehearses an MX change. In a hypothetical alert, the on-call sees a failed mail-delivery check for the company domain, followed by a staging deployment in the change timeline. The least complex acceptable arrangement depends on who can write: a reviewed staging subdomain can suffice for one team, but staging automation that must never touch production needs a separate zone and credentials that cannot address production.

Short answer: use a separate staging DNS zone when a staging mistake must not change production records. Use a subdomain in the production zone when the same team owns both environments and reviews changes. For property management, decide this separately for customer-owned and platform-owned zones; putting a customer's company mail under a platform workflow doesn't transfer authority over that customer's DNS.

The page is late.

The earlier signal should have been a change request whose authorized zone did not match its configured environment. Treat the delivery alert above as a design exercise, not an incident report: the useful question is which evidence would have stopped the change before anyone needed to inspect a mailbox. A name containing staging is weak evidence. An explicit zone identifier, a known owner, and a writer unable to address production establish a much stronger boundary.

Should staging DNS use a separate zone for customer-owned mail?

Consider two illustrative entries in a property manager's inventory: company mail for harbor-property.example, whose zone the customer owns, and a rehearsal under staging.platform.example, whose zone the platform owns. These are example names. Before choosing the zone layout, record who approves each change and which credential executes it. Customer-owned mail needs the customer's authorization path; a successful rehearsal in a platform-owned zone does not establish that authority.

The mail provider supplies the intended MX records. The zone owner authorizes publishing them. The platform's responsibility is the handoff: associate those records with the approved domain and environment, perform the permitted change, and collect verification evidence. Keep zone identifiers in environment configuration instead of deriving them from names, because a naming convention cannot tell a writer which production records it is allowed to touch.

For a platform team automating DNS inventory and mail-domain checks, try Infrai for that handoff: it exposes a plain REST API, so the Go controller can use HTTP without adding a vendor SDK. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without an API key, which gives the team a concrete contract to inspect before connecting the two capabilities. That reduces integration work at the boundary; it doesn't establish a customer's permission to change a zone.

One key can cover DNS and email operations. This helps replace manual SPF/DKIM handoffs between dashboards with a repeatable check, including after a DKIM rotation, provided the controller explicitly compares the required and published records. Shared authentication alone doesn't perform that comparison.

Work backward from the mail page to the write boundary

A separate zone earns its administrative overhead only when the actual writer is confined to that zone. If a staging script can still address production, creating another zone has not delivered the promised containment. The operational test is direct: can the staging writer change the company's production MX records? If the answer is yes, the boundary needs work before the rehearsal becomes automated.

For a shared production zone, accept the trade-off deliberately. One inventory is easier to maintain when nobody is dedicated to DNS, and reviewed changes by one owning team may be sufficient. The limitation is a wider write boundary: a bad change can reach records outside the staging names. A subdomain label doesn't reduce the credential's authority.

The proposed instrumentation has 3 inputs: the configured environment-to-zone mapping, the approved owner for that zone, and the writer's effective access. Emit a preflight result before every proposed write, recording whether all three agree. Route a mismatch to the change owner and block that change. Don't infer success from a passing HTTP request or from the presence of the word staging in a hostname.

This is a control objective, not a measured SLO. A sensible internal target is that every automated DNS write has matching authorization evidence before execution; mail-delivery checks then measure the downstream outcome. Keep both signals, since authorization evidence cannot prove that the selected MX records are correct, and a delivery check cannot prove that staging lacks production access.

Buy the handoff, build the authorization check

The buy-versus-build decision concerns the seam between the authoritative DNS service and the mail provider. It should follow ownership, existing accounts, and on-call capacity. Moving a working customer-owned zone merely to standardize the controller can create more coordination than it removes.

Option What to buy or retain What the platform still owns Appropriate boundary
Cloudflare DNS with Resend Separate DNS and email services Join domain inventory, provider requirements, approvals, and verification in the controller A customer already uses Cloudflare and the mail workflow selects Resend
Amazon Route 53 with Amazon SES DNS and email services within AWS Connect the two services and review which writer can touch each zone The operating team already manages its DNS and mail workflow in AWS
Infrai DNS and email A shared REST surface using one API key Enforce zone ownership and reconcile the DNS and mail evidence A platform wants one HTTP integration across the handoff
An internal controller over existing providers Retain the current services and build the glue Maintain contracts, credentials, reconciliation, and alert ownership Customer ownership makes provider consolidation undesirable

Cloudflare plus Resend means 2 provider signups and 2 credential sets for this comparison. Route 53 plus SES can share an AWS account signup, but still has 2 service permission surfaces; the credential arrangement depends on the access design. In either stack, the platform would write glue to match a domain's DNS inventory to its mail-provider state and preserve the environment boundary. Calling all alternatives a pile of unrelated accounts would be misleading.

Infrai is not suitable for a team whose customer requires the existing direct-provider workflow to remain the operating boundary; retain Cloudflare or Route 53 there. The combined approach also concentrates vendor trust, billing, and operational dependency in one provider. Budget the controller's maintenance and the team's on-call load alongside that concentration.

A Go preflight joins inventory to mail-domain inspection

The following program demonstrates the narrow read handoff. It retrieves DNS domain inventory, requires an exact match for an operator-approved domain, and feeds the matched value into the email-domain lookup using the same key and base URL. Configure INFRAI_API_KEY and MAIL_DOMAIN before running it.

It deliberately treats inventory as opaque JSON instead of assuming undocumented envelope fields. The recursive exact-string match is an inventory-presence check; it doesn't establish zone ownership, inspect MX records, or prove mail delivery. Inspect the published response schemas before extending it into a reconciler that selects specific fields. Keep the configured zone identifier and the authorization check outside this small read example.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func get(client *http.Client, key, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+path, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 4 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(until); remaining > 0 {
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func matchDomain(value any, target string) string {
    switch v := value.(type) {
    case string:
        if v == target {
            return v
        }
    case []any:
        for _, item := range v {
            if found := matchDomain(item, target); found != "" {
                return found
            }
        }
    case map[string]any:
        for _, item := range v {
            if found := matchDomain(item, target); found != "" {
                return found
            }
        }
    }
    return ""
}

func run() error {
    key, domain := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("MAIL_DOMAIN")
    if key == "" || domain == "" || strings.ContainsAny(domain, "/?# ") {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and MAIL_DOMAIN to an approved domain")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    inventory, err := get(client, key, "/dns/domain/list")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var decoded any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(inventory, &decoded); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    matched := matchDomain(decoded, domain)
    if matched == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("approved domain absent from inventory")
    }
    mail, err := get(client, key, "/email/domain/get/"+url.PathEscape(matched))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Println(string(mail))
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The retry budget is 5 attempts, with exponential backoff unless Retry-After supplies the delay; each HTTP attempt has a 20-second timeout. Those are example client settings, not service guarantees. Both operations read state, so this sample has no write retry to deduplicate. A write controller needs an explicit idempotency design before it retries a change.

The returned mail-domain response is evidence for the next check, not permission to publish anything. MX selection, SPF/DKIM reconciliation, and ownership approval remain distinct decisions in the workflow. DMARC adds another mail-domain policy concern; its specification is useful context, but a DMARC check should not be substituted for verifying the intended MX records.

Set the page threshold at the boundary

Capacity planning starts with the inventory the team can actually review. Count customer-owned and platform-owned zones separately, then estimate the review work created by rehearsals and record rotations before increasing automation concurrency. A separate zone reduces the possible record blast radius; it also adds administrative inventory that someone must maintain.

Page on actionable evidence.

A proposed production-targeting write from staging deserves a blocked change and an accountable responder. An inventory lookup that finds no exact domain match deserves investigation, but this small preflight alone cannot justify a production-mail incident page. Set that threshold too loosely and every onboarding mismatch consumes the same attention as a delivery failure; set it too narrowly and the first useful signal is the mailbox complaint. The false-positive cost is the on-call time diverted from actual mail impact.

Further reading

References for the provider choices and mail-policy boundary:

  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation

title: Improving HTML code blocks readability with a syntax highlighter
description:
A code block written by hand is pretty simple: use the 'pre' and 'code' HTML elements and the browser gives you a monospace font and keeps your line breaks, but it stops there. So every keyword, string, comment and variable comes out in the exact same color, which is fine for a few lines of YAML, but for a few hundred lines of TypeScript painted in a single flat tone, maybe not. Improving readability for those cases doesn't require shipping a highlighting library to the reader's browser (unless you want to) and is quite simple to do.

Highlighting code blocks with ShikiJS

ShikiJS uses the same TextMate grammars and themes that VS Code uses, which means the code on your page ends up looking like the code in your editor. And because it can run anywhere, the highlighting may happen while the page is being built, so the reader downloads plain HTML with the colors already baked in, or may happen in the browser, your choice.

The rehype plugin is the piece that wires ShikiJS into a unified pipeline. So, if you write your posts in Markdown, the plugin sits between the Markdown to HTML conversion and the stringifier.

import fs from 'node:fs/promises'
import rehypeShiki from '@shikijs/rehype'
import rehypeStringify from 'rehype-stringify'
import remarkParse from 'remark-parse'
import remarkRehype from 'remark-rehype'
import { unified } from 'unified'

const file = await unified()
  .use(remarkParse)
  .use(remarkRehype)
  .use(rehypeShiki, {
    themes: {
      light: 'vitesse-light',
      dark: 'vitesse-dark',
    },
  })
  .use(rehypeStringify)
  .process(await fs.readFile('./post.md'))

Now, if you write your posts directly in HTML, like I do, there's no Markdown step at all. The plugin works on the syntax tree, not on Markdown, so you can parse the HTML with rehype-parse and hand it the same tree.

import fs from 'node:fs/promises'
import rehypeParse from 'rehype-parse'
import rehypeShiki from '@shikijs/rehype'
import rehypeStringify from 'rehype-stringify'
import { unified } from 'unified'

const file = await unified()
  .use(rehypeParse, { fragment: true })
  .use(rehypeShiki, { theme: 'vitesse-dark' })
  .use(rehypeStringify)
  .process(await fs.readFile('./post.html'))

Either way, what the plugin looks for is a code element carrying a specific class, which is exactly what the remark-rehype plugin produces and what you should be writing when you're not using it.

<pre><code class="language-typescript">const answer = 42</code></pre>

Worth noting

  • Use theme for a single theme and themes for a light and dark pair. The pair version emits CSS variables, so switching between them is a matter of toggling a couple of custom properties instead of highlighting everything twice;
  • The default export shares one highlighter instance across processes, but if you care about bundle size, import rehypeShikiFromHighlighter from @shikijs/rehype/core and pass your own highlighter loaded with only the languages you actually use;
  • The postprocess transformer hook never runs here. The plugin operates on the syntax tree rather than on HTML strings, and that's on purpose, so if you rely on a transformer that rewrites the final HTML, you'll need a workaround to do that.

Highlighting inline code

Code blocks are the obvious win, but there's always inline code sitting in the middle of a sentence, and by default that stays gray while everything around it is colored. ShikiJS can handle those too, it just needs to be told which language each one is.

That's what the tailing curly colon syntax is for. It's off by default, so you enable it explicitly.

.use(rehypeShiki, {
  inline: 'tailing-curly-colon',
  theme: 'vitesse-dark',
})

From there, you append a marker to the end of the snippet with the language you want, right before the closing tag.

<!-- HTML -->
<p>Call <code>console.log("Hello World"){:javascript}</code> and move on.</p>

<!-- Markdown -->
This snippet `console.log("Hello World"){:javascript}` will be highlighted.

The marker itself is stripped from the output, so the reader never sees it. It's a bit of noise in the source, but it's the price to pay for highlighting code in the middle of a sentence.

Worth noting

  • The marker has to be the very last thing inside the code element;
  • The language has to be one that ShikiJS knows about and, if you went with a fine-grained bundle, it must be one you actually loaded;
  • Snippets without a marker are left completely alone, which is convenient. File names, flags and environment variables usually read better plain than syntax highlighted as something they're not.

Wrap-up

Two options in a config object and a small marker convention, and your posts go from walls of gray monospace to something people can actually scan. No client-side library, no flash of unstyled code, no extra requests (unless you want them). Your readers won't notice it, and that's kind of the point, they'll just stop bouncing off your code blocks.

This article was created with the help of AI because, while I'm good at being a software engineer (I hope so), I suck at being a writer. On the other hand, the silly jokes and wordplay are completely mine because I'm really good at those. Also, the content comes from things I've done or learned, has been verified and is edited to be straight to the point, since AI loves to stall, but I hate it.

title: Replacing Access & Excel Macro Apps With a Web App
description:
Many profitable businesses still run a critical process on a Microsoft Access database or an Excel workbook full of VBA macros. It started as a smart shortcut. Years later it holds the pricing logic, the customer history and the month-end report, it lives on one shared drive, and only one person really understands it. Replacing it is not a rewrite of screens. It is a migration of data, hidden business rules and daily habits, and that is where most projects fail.

At Loop Origin I build custom web applications on Laravel, Vue, Nuxt and PostgreSQL, and as a Principal Software Engineer I have moved several of these spreadsheet-era systems to the browser. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command and code sample myself. This is the playbook I use.

How do you replace an Access or Excel macro app with a web app?

Direct answer: Inventory every table, form, query, macro and report first. Extract the data with scripted, repeatable imports, and capture each business rule as a test before rewriting it. Build the web app in small modules, run it in parallel with the old file, reconcile outputs daily, then cut over one team at a time and freeze the legacy file as read-only.

Signs it is time to move

You do not need to migrate just because Access is old. Move when the risk is real:

  • More than a few people need to edit at once, and you see locking errors or "who has the file open?" messages.
  • The file is corrupted or restored from backup more than once a year.
  • Remote staff or branches need access, and you are passing copies by email or VPN.
  • An auditor or customer asks who changed a value, and you cannot answer.
  • The one person who knows the VBA is leaving, or already left.
  • Integrations (accounting, e-commerce, couriers) are done by copy-paste.

Your options compared

Option Best for Main strengths Main risks Ongoing cost drivers
Keep Access, move tables to SQL Server or PostgreSQL Small teams on one office network Fast, little retraining Front end still on desktops; VBA knowledge risk stays Desktop licences, one maintainer
Low-code (Power Apps, AppSheet and similar) Simple forms and approvals inside one vendor's ecosystem Quick to build, built-in hosting Per-user licensing, limits on complex logic, lock-in to the platform Licences grow with every user
Off-the-shelf SaaS The process is standard (CRM, helpdesk, basic inventory) No build, vendor maintains it Your special rules may not fit; data export limits Subscription per seat or tier
Custom web app (Laravel/PostgreSQL + Vue or Nuxt) Core processes with unique rules and integrations You own the code and data; fits the real workflow; any device Needs a disciplined migration and a maintainer Hosting, maintenance retainer

I usually recommend custom only when the logic is the business's edge or the integrations are complex. If a standard SaaS covers the process, buy it.

Step 1: Inventory the legacy app

Treat the Access file or workbook as a system with parts, not a document. For Access, the open-source mdbtools package reads .mdb and .accdb files on Linux:

# List tables, dump the schema, export each table to CSV
mdb-tables -1 legacy.accdb
mdb-schema legacy.accdb postgres > schema_from_access.sql
for t in $(mdb-tables -1 legacy.accdb); do
  mdb-export legacy.accdb "$t" > "export/${t}.csv"
done
# Saved queries (newer mdbtools versions)
mdb-queries -L legacy.accdb

Forms, reports and VBA modules do not come out cleanly this way. Open the file in Access, use the Database Documenter, and export each VBA module to text from the editor. For Excel, list every sheet, named range, formula-heavy column, pivot and macro.

Record the results in an inventory sheet:

Item Type Used by How often Business rule inside? Keep, change or drop
tblOrders Table Sales, Finance Daily No Keep
qryMonthEndCommission Query Finance Monthly Yes: commission tiers Keep, test first
frmQuickQuote Form + VBA Sales Daily Yes: discount caps Change
rptOldBranchSummary Report Nobody since 2023 Never No Drop

Expect to drop a real share of the old reports. Ask who opened each one in the last year.

Step 2: Turn hidden rules into tests

The dangerous logic hides in VBA event handlers, query expressions and cell formulas: discount caps, rounding, tax, commission tiers, status changes. Before rewriting any of it, write down known inputs and outputs from the legacy system and turn them into tests. These are characterization tests: they pin down what the old system does today, bugs included, so you can choose which behavior to keep. I wrote about the technique in Characterization Tests Before You Refactor AI-Written Code.

// tests/Unit/CommissionTest.php (Pest)
// Each row: [monthly sales, expected commission] taken from the legacy query's output
dataset('legacy_commission', [
    [0, 0.00],
    [49999, 1499.97],
    [50000, 2500.00],
    [120000, 7200.00],
]);

it('matches the legacy month-end commission', function (int $sales, float $expected) {
    expect(app(\App\Services\Commission::class)->for($sales))->toBe($expected);
})->with('legacy_commission');

Take the expected values from real runs of the legacy file, not from someone's memory of the rules.


AI-generated image.

Step 3: Design the new data model, then import repeatably

Access schemas often carry years of drift: text columns holding dates, duplicate customers, "Yes/No" stored three ways, and no foreign keys. Do not copy that into PostgreSQL. Design a clean schema, then write an import that maps and cleans the legacy data, and run it again and again until it is boring.

// app/Console/Commands/ImportLegacyOrders.php (excerpt)
public function handle(): int
{
    $rows = SimpleExcelReader::create(storage_path('legacy/tblOrders.csv'))->getRows();
    $bad = 0;

    DB::transaction(function () use ($rows, &$bad) {
        foreach ($rows as $r) {
            $date = Carbon::createFromFormat('m/d/y H:i:s', $r['OrderDate'], 'Asia/Karachi');
            $customer = Customer::firstWhere('legacy_id', $r['CustomerID']);
            if (! $date || ! $customer) { $bad++; Log::warning('skip', $r); continue; }

            Order::updateOrCreate(
                ['legacy_id' => $r['OrderID']],
                ['customer_id' => $customer->id, 'ordered_at' => $date,
                 'total' => round((float) $r['Total'], 2)]
            );
        }
    });

    $this->info("Imported with {$bad} rejected rows");
    return self::SUCCESS;
}

Two habits matter. Keep a legacy_id on every migrated row so you can trace any record back. And make the import idempotent with updateOrCreate, so you can rerun it on fresh exports during the parallel run. Check the date format against your own export, because mdb-export output depends on version and options.

Step 4: Build in modules, not one big bang

Pick the module that hurts most, often order entry or approvals, and ship that first while the rest stays in the old file. Add the things a shared file never had: proper roles and permissions per team and branch, and a record of who changed what. I covered both in Laravel RBAC for Multi-Organization Portals and Immutable Audit Trails in Postgres for SaaS.

Keep the screens familiar at first. Users who spent ten years on one Access form will accept a cleaner web form with the same field order far faster than a redesign.

Step 5: Parallel run and reconcile

For two to four weeks, both systems run. Import fresh legacy data every night, and compare the outputs that matter: order totals by day, invoice counts, commission per salesperson, stock on hand.

-- Daily reconciliation: new system vs nightly legacy import
SELECT d.day,
       l.total AS legacy_total,
       n.total AS new_total,
       n.total - l.total AS diff
FROM generate_series(current_date - 30, current_date, '1 day') AS d(day)
LEFT JOIN legacy_daily_totals l ON l.day = d.day
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT ordered_at::date AS day, SUM(total) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY 1
) n ON n.day = d.day
WHERE COALESCE(n.total, 0) <> COALESCE(l.total, 0);

Every difference is either a bug in the new app, a bug in the old one, or a data-entry mistake. Decide each one with the business owner and write the decision down.

Step 6: Cut over and freeze

Move one team or branch at a time. On cutover day, run the final import, set the legacy file to read-only, and keep it archived with its exports. Do not delete it for at least one audit cycle.

Failure modes I see most

Failure What causes it Prevention
Totals differ by small amounts Different rounding between VBA, Excel and PHP Test rounding rules explicitly; store money as integers or fixed decimals
Dates shift by a day Time zones and text dates in the legacy file Parse with an explicit format and time zone; reconcile by day
Users keep the old file "just in case" No read-only freeze, no trust in the new numbers Freeze on cutover; share reconciliation results
A forgotten monthly report breaks finance Inventory skipped rarely-used items Ask finance and management to sign off the inventory
Scope doubles mid-project Every wish list item added "while we are at it" Phase 1 replaces what exists; improvements come after cutover

Migration checklist

  1. Inventory every table, query, form, report, macro and integration, with an owner for each.
  2. Mark each item keep, change or drop, signed off by the business.
  3. Write characterization tests from real legacy outputs for every business rule.
  4. Design a clean schema; map every legacy column to it or to "dropped".
  5. Build an idempotent import with legacy_id traceability and a rejected-row log.
  6. Ship the highest-pain module first, with roles and an audit trail.
  7. Run in parallel with nightly imports and a daily reconciliation report.
  8. Cut over team by team, then freeze and archive the legacy file.
  9. Train users on the screens they use, not on the whole system.
  10. Agree on a maintenance owner before go-live.

FAQs

How long does an Access to web app migration take?

It depends on the number of forms, rules and integrations, not file size. A focused single-process app can move in weeks; a database running several departments is a phased project. The inventory in Step 1 is the only honest basis for an estimate.

Can we keep using Excel for reporting?

Yes. Many teams are happiest when the web app is the source of truth and exports clean Excel files or a read-only reporting connection. Just stop editing master data in spreadsheets.

What happens to the VBA code?

It becomes requirements and tests, not code you port line by line. Read it to find the rules, capture them as tests, then implement them cleanly in the new app.

Is moving Access tables to SQL Server enough?

Sometimes, for a small team on one network. It fixes storage and multi-user locking but not remote access, audit history or the single-maintainer risk in the forms and VBA.

Should we choose low-code instead of custom?

If the process is simple and you already pay for that vendor's ecosystem, low-code can be the right choice. Choose custom when the rules are complex, the integrations matter, or per-user licences will grow with your team.

How do we avoid losing data during cutover?

Run the import many times before cutover, keep a rejected-row log at zero or explained, reconcile daily during the parallel run, and archive the final legacy file read-only.

The short version

Treat the Access file or macro workbook as a real system. Inventory it, test its hidden rules, import its data repeatably, build in modules, prove the numbers with a parallel run, then cut over and freeze. The screens are the easy part; the rules and the data are the project.

title: Trace a rounded pillar back to the staging record
description:
A staging result can keep a window while changing another permanent feature nearby. The local REimagineHome notes make that distinction unusually concrete. For Room 07, they record the window and radiator as kept, while the top of the right pillar was rounded. An outlet and pipe were also added on the left. The input is a real living-room photograph credited as CC0, not an AI-generated interior.

These observations belong to the test-log entry dated 2026-10-21. The REimagineHome page and aggregate results do not fully represent that later round, so the local log and individual score files are the relevant evidence here. Proposed realism ratings for the round remain draft and pending review.

The technical task is to expose the measurements beside those observations without promoting an image-wide statistic into a diagnosis of a particular wall. Run this Python from the project root. It reads the selected local score files and prints the recorded fields:

import json
from pathlib import Path

fields = ("line_displaced_frac", "line_missing_frac", "edge_ssim", "aligned")
for path in sorted(Path("results/reimaginehome").glob("[0-9][0-9]-score.json")):
    if path.name[:2] not in {"06", "07"}:
        continue
    data = json.loads(path.read_text())
    block = data.get("architecture")
    source = "architecture"
    if not isinstance(block, dict):
        block = data.get("structure")
        source = "structure"
    if not isinstance(block, dict):
        block = {}
        source = None
    row = {"room": path.name[:2], "source": source}
    row.update({key: block.get(key) for key in fields})
    row["framing_pass"] = (data.get("framing") or {}).get("pass")
    print(json.dumps(row))

Actual output from the local files:

{"room": "06", "source": "architecture", "line_displaced_frac": 0.3119, "line_missing_frac": 0.2751, "edge_ssim": 0.7194, "aligned": false, "framing_pass": null}
{"room": "07", "source": "architecture", "line_displaced_frac": 0.2549, "line_missing_frac": 0.2776, "edge_ssim": 0.7116, "aligned": true, "framing_pass": true}

Room 07 passes framing and has aligned measurements. Nevertheless, the visual note records the rounded pillar. Its line fractions summarize detected structural lines across the evaluated region; they do not measure the pillar individually or count changed windows. The preserved window and altered pillar can coexist in the same result.

Room 06 helps keep that interpretation disciplined. Its log says the window and stove were kept, although the room was re-rendered and brightened. Its architecture block explicitly reports failed alignment and an unaligned fallback. The script preserves that status. It also preserves JSON null, and uses the legacy structure block only when an architecture object is unavailable, reporting the source rather than blending fields. That compatibility fallback is separate from the scorer's unaligned fallback, which already lives inside architecture here.

A reviewer following the pillar concern should keep the original and staged image paired with this row. The row explains whether the measurements describe an aligned comparison; the log identifies the feature that prompted concern. Neither supplies a measured distance for the rounding, and the files do not establish how much of the reported line displacement belongs to that feature. Publishing such a distance would add precision the evidence does not contain. The recorded observation is sufficient to flag the image for inspection.

Under the MLS guide, last checked on 2026-10-19, MLS Now prohibits modifying permanent structural features. The pillar observation deserves review under that restriction even though the window was kept and framing passed. These measurements cannot certify compliance.

The methodology remains v0.2 draft. Results are partial, current editor assessments are not blind, and blind evaluation has not started. The value of this extraction is traceability: it connects a particular output to its measurement state while leaving the feature-specific conclusion anchored in the recorded visual observation.

title: A 9-TiB OLTP Benchmark on PostgreSQL
description:
At Microsoft Ignite, HorizonDB was announced to be 8x faster than traditional PostgreSQL, based on an I/O-bound HammerDB TPROC-C workload that showed 427,770 NOPM without specific tuning, 8x the 52,167 NOPM measured with self-managed PostgreSQL on the same compute.

I observed the same throughput on HorizonDB and reproduced the PostgreSQL side with a tuned HA configuration: 128 GB of shared buffers on huge pages, two standbys, and synchronous commit to at least one. The result was 50,648 NOPM, very close to the published number. But the interesting question is not the number itself. What is PostgreSQL waiting for at that throughput, and what happens when that constraint is removed? This post identifies the first bottleneck. The following three remove the bottlenecks one by one until the limit moves inside PostgreSQL itself.

The workload

Here is the definition of the benchmark workload I've run:

Setting Tested value
HammerDB 6.1.1, direct CLI
Workload PostgreSQL TPROC-C, function-based driver
Dataset 95,000 warehouses, nonpartitioned
Reported size after loading About 8.92 TiB
Workload concurrency 512 virtual users, plus the monitor
Ramp-up / measurement 15 / 45 minutes
Warehouse selection All warehouses enabled
Keying and thinking time Disabled
Connection pooling / time profiling Disabled
Driver-requested vacuum Disabled, while server autovacuum remained enabled
Transaction counter Timestamped samples every 10 seconds

HammerDB reports new orders per minute (NOPM) and PostgreSQL transactions per minute (TPM). These are the relevant driver choices, apart from connection details:

dbset db pg
dbset bm TPC-C
diset tpcc pg_count_ware 95000
diset tpcc pg_storedprocs false
diset tpcc pg_partition false
diset tpcc pg_driver timed
diset tpcc pg_rampup 15
diset tpcc pg_duration 45
diset tpcc pg_allwarehouse true
diset tpcc pg_keyandthink false
diset tpcc pg_connect_pool false
diset tpcc pg_timeprofile false
diset tpcc pg_vacuum false
vuset vu 512

The database was loaded before the timed test (with some pain, as described in a previous blog post, because loading nine terabytes takes a long time and HammerDB can't resume a failed load).

A dataset larger than the caches

The primary had 512 GiB of RAM, including 128 GiB of shared buffers. Even the machine's total memory was a small fraction of the database size. This is how we define an I/O bound workload: the working set is larger than any cache. All warehouses were enabled, and the measured read waits and sustained physical I/O showed frequent reads beyond the caches.

The baseline machines and durability

The initial deployment used three PostgreSQL VMs across three Azure availability zones:

  • Each database VM: E64ds_v5, 64 vCPUs / 512 GiB RAM.
  • Each data disk: 20,480 GiB Premium SSD v2, provisioned at 80,000 IOPS / 1,200 MB/s.
  • Data and WAL: the same ext4 filesystem.
  • Client in the primary's zone: D64ds_v5, 64 vCPUs / 256 GiB RAM.
  • PostgreSQL 17.11, Patroni 4.1.5, Ubuntu 24.04.
  • Three separate etcd members for the distributed configuration store.

This configuration used synchronous_commit=on, fsync=on and full_page_writes=on. A commit required local WAL synchronization and durable WAL acknowledgment from at least one of the two cross-zone standbys. Azure's torn-write prevention requires a supported NVMe controller, kernel and filesystem, with the application issuing aligned atomic direct writes. This run used PostgreSQL 17's ordinary buffered writes, so full-page logging remained enabled for torn-page recovery.

The standby acknowledgment confirms a flush, not replay. Network transport, standby storage, and acknowledgment processing can all contribute to the wait.

Continuous WAL archiving was disabled for this lab.

The PostgreSQL profile

I used the following PostgreSQL profile for the baseline and the later tests. The commit-mode overrides are described in the posts where they apply:

Area Important settings
Memory shared_buffers=128GB, work_mem=16MB, effective_cache_size=352GB
Shared-memory backing Explicit 2-MiB huge pages, huge_pages=on
Connections max_connections=640
WAL wal_compression=zstd, wal_buffers=64MB, max_wal_size=64GB
Synchronization wal_sync_method=fdatasync, fsync=on, full_page_writes=on
Checkpoints checkpoint_timeout=30min, checkpoint_completion_target=0.9
Planner / I/O random_page_cost=1.5, effective_io_concurrency=64, jit=off
Query parallelism max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0
Autovacuum 8 workers, 10-second naptime, vacuum scale factor 0.01
Autovacuum cost control Limit 3000, delay 2 ms
Monitoring track_io_timing=on, track_wal_io_timing=on

effective_cache_size is a planner estimate. WAL volume can trigger checkpoints before the 30-minute timeout.

Result: 50,648 NOPM (New Orders per Minute)

The measured interval ran from November 6, 2026, 23:21:13 UTC to November 7, 00:06:15 UTC. The result message was:

TEST RESULT : System achieved 50648 NOPM from 116618 PostgreSQL TPM

To observe active backends, the collector used grouped pg_stat_activity data:

SELECT count(*) AS sessions,
       wait_event_type, wait_event
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
  AND state = 'active'
GROUP BY wait_event_type, wait_event
ORDER BY sessions DESC;

Repeated measured-window samples gave:

Wait Active-client observation share
IO:DataFileRead 79.6%
LWLock:WALWrite 10.8%
IPC:SyncRep 5.2%

DataFileRead means PostgreSQL is waiting for a relation-file read, which may be served by the operating-system cache or the device. The guest disk counters confirmed substantial physical read activity during this run:

Primary data-disk observation Value
Read / write IOPS Approximately 51,130 / 30,469
Read / write bandwidth Approximately 429 / 412 MiB/s
Mean read / write request completion 7.98 / 10.95 ms
Guest busy time Approximately 100%

Delivered IOPS were near the provisioned disk budget. Together, the read waits, I/O rate, and request latency put the device-read path first in the investigation.

Next: change the storage constraint

HorizonDB combines shared buffers and local NVMe caching with a distributed page-storage fleet. Cache misses are served by this fleet, rather than the single provisioned data disk used in this test. This explains why the workload achieves higher throughput than this PostgreSQL configuration can support.

On PostgreSQL, increasing the storage budget would let me observe how the remaining waits changed. LWLock:WALWrite already accounted for 10.8% of active-client observations and could become the next bottleneck as read waits decreased.

In part 2, Faster SSDs for PostgreSQL: From Read I/O to WAL Waits
, I move the primary to Ultra SSD and then remove standby acknowledgment waiting to examine the primary's own path. In this series, the goal is to identify what limits PostgreSQL throughput as these constraints are reduced or bypassed. The investigation starts with disk reads, checks remote commit acknowledgments, follows local synchronization into the OS, and ends with shared-page coordination inside PostgreSQL.

Schéma, licence, conventions de calcul et requêtes de contrôle pour le fichier du 17 novembre 2026.

Le catalogue du comparateur Quel salon de jardin est publié sous licence CC BY 4.0, sous deux formes : un CSV et un JSON. Le fichier daté du 17 novembre 2026 contient 364 lignes, une par modèle publié et indexé sur le site. Il ne contient ni photo ni lien vers les marchands.

Formats et mise à jour

  • CSV : UTF-8 avec BOM, séparateur virgule. Le BOM impose encoding="utf-8-sig" en Python, sinon la première colonne s'appelle ﻿slug.
  • JSON : une enveloppe de métadonnées autour des lignes.
  • Les deux fichiers sont régénérés après chaque relevé de prix. Leur date_releve est le jour du relevé le plus récent, pas la date de collecte de chaque ligne.

L'enveloppe JSON comporte les clés nom, producteur, source, licence, licence_url, date_releve, nb_lignes, colonnes (nom et description de chaque colonne) et lignes.

Schéma

Identification et classement :

  • slug, url_fiche, nom, marque, type

Caractéristiques :

  • matiere_structure, places, couleurs
  • largeur_cm, profondeur_cm, hauteur_assise_cm, poids_kg
  • longueur_table_cm, largeur_table_cm, diametre_table_cm : ensembles repas ou salons de balcon, quand la valeur est publiée
  • garantie_mois

Prix et offres :

  • prix_min_eur, prix_max_eur, prix_par_place_eur, nb_offres, marchands, date_releve

Conventions :

  • cellule vide = valeur non publiée pour ce modèle (pas zéro) ;
  • prix en euros TTC, hors livraison ;
  • prix_par_place_eur = prix_min_eur / places, arrondi au centime ;
  • date_releve au format AAAA-MM-JJ, heure de Paris ;
  • marchands : noms séparés par un point-virgule, sans URL.

Taux de remplissage

Sur les 364 lignes :

Champ Lignes renseignées
matiere_structure 356
prix_min_eur 337
places 290
hauteur_assise_cm 164
poids_kg 77
largeur_cm et profondeur_cm 44
longueur_table_cm et largeur_table_cm 37
diametre_table_cm 7

Les 44 lignes avec une emprise au sol complète comptent 29 bains de soleil, 10 salons de jardin bas, 3 salons d'angle et 2 ensembles repas. Un agrégat de dimensions calculé là-dessus décrirait surtout des bains de soleil.

Requêtes de contrôle

Compter les lignes et les types, en Python standard :

import csv
from collections import Counter

with open("salons-de-jardin.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

len(rows)  # 364
Counter(r["type"] for r in rows)
# Salon de jardin bas 212, Ensemble repas de jardin 64,
# Bain de soleil 36, Salon de jardin d'angle 26,
# Salon de jardin pour balcon 26

Vérifier la date et la taille du fichier JSON avant de l'exploiter :

jq '{date_releve, nb_lignes}' salons-de-jardin.json
# {"date_releve": "2026-11-17", "nb_lignes": 364}

Si nb_lignes ou date_releve ne correspondent plus, le fichier a été régénéré depuis : les chiffres de cet article sont alors à reprendre.

Reproduire les médianes du site

Le site agrège prix_min_eur, c'est-à-dire le prix le plus bas relevé pour chaque modèle, et ne publie une médiane que pour les groupes d'au moins trois modèles. Il s'agit d'une médiane basse : sur la liste triée, la valeur d'indice floor(0.5 * (n - 1)). Sur un groupe de taille paire, statistics.median ou pandas.Series.median(), qui moyennent les deux valeurs centrales, peuvent donner un autre résultat.

Deux périmètres coexistent :

  • médiane d'ensemble « salon de jardin » : bains de soleil exclus, soit 566,99 € sur 301 modèles ;
  • tableaux par matière et par places : tous les modèles avec un prix, bains de soleil inclus.

Quelques valeurs au 17 novembre 2026 :

Groupe Modèles avec prix Médiane
Aluminium 127 1 406 €
Résine tressée 127 499,90 €
Acier 38 234,71 €
« 2 places » 61 203,99 €
« 10 places et plus » 25 799,99 €

Les libellés de places sont des tranches et non des effectifs exacts : « 2 places » couvre 1 à 2, « 4 places » 3 à 4, « 6 places » 5 à 6, « 8 places » 7 à 9, « 10 places et plus » 10 et au-delà. Pour regrouper la colonne places comme le site, il faut appliquer ces bornes.

Ces médianes rapprochent des modèles différents à une date donnée. Elles ne mesurent pas l'effet propre d'une matière, d'une marque ou d'une taille.

Licence, citation et copies

CC BY 4.0 : réutilisation libre, y compris commerciale, avec attribution à Quel salon de jardin (Bastien Hugon EI). Forme de citation demandée :

Quel salon de jardin (Bastien Hugon EI), « Prix et dimensions des salons de jardin vendus en ligne en France », relevé du 17 novembre 2026, https://quel-salon-de-jardin.fr/donnees, licence CC BY 4.0.

Des copies existent sur data.gouv.fr, Hugging Face, Kaggle, Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24176950) et dans le dépôt salons-de-jardin-donnees sur GitHub. Ces copies peuvent dater d'un relevé antérieur ; la version à jour des fichiers et de leur description se trouve sur la page de données du site.

title: Node.js Express Storage: Store Generated Images in Per-User Folders with Lifecycle Deletes
description:
A marketplace that retains signed documents has two different clocks: the access-control clock (who may read an object now) and the deletion clock (when it must disappear). Treating a user folder as both creates a quiet compliance failure. Short answer: keep authorization in Node.js and Express, keep each object private under a tenant-scoped key, record delete_at in a database, and use lifecycle automation as a backstop that you can observe.

The field guide: which retention shape fits a marketplace?

Retention shape Pick this when The catch
Application worker Signed documents have individual legal or contractual deadlines Retries, leases, idempotency, and audit events become your responsibility
Object-storage lifecycle Every object under a prefix shares one age rule A timer cannot see a revoked tenant, a dispute hold, or a database exception
Hybrid policy Most generated images expire uniformly, with occasional holds Two clocks must agree, and their disagreement needs an alert

For per-user AI images, the hybrid shape is usually the easiest to explain in a review. The database owns tenant_id, image_id, created_at, delete_at, and the reason for retention. A short-lived prefix can have a uniform lifecycle rule, while the worker handles signed-document exceptions. The rule is a safety net, not evidence that an individual deletion happened on time.

One line is worth keeping in the design doc.

A folder is a naming convention, not an authorization boundary.

How should Node.js and Express separate user access from object retention?

Use opaque identifiers in keys; email addresses change and can leak personal data. A practical layout is tenants/{tenantId}/images/{imageId}/original.webp, with a thumbnail beside it. The request handler loads the image row by image_id, compares its tenant_id with the authenticated session, and only then creates an upload target or a download response. A client-supplied key never proves ownership.

Deletion should be idempotent. A retry after a timeout must reach the same state as the first attempt, including the case where the object is already absent. Claim a row, call the storage adapter, and write an audit event for the outcome. If two workers race, a lease or transaction prevents both from claiming the same row.

Here is the policy boundary I keep small and boring. It has no vendor-specific SDK, so the authorization and retention decisions remain portable.

type ImageRecord = {
  tenantId: string;
  imageId: string;
  objectKey: string;
  deleteAt: Date;
  state: "ready" | "deleting" | "deleted";
};

interface ObjectStore {
  remove(key: string): Promise<"removed" | "absent">;
}

function imageKey(tenantId: string, imageId: string): string {
  if (!/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$/.test(tenantId) || !/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$/.test(imageId)) {
    throw new Error("invalid identifier");
  }
  return `tenants/${tenantId}/images/${imageId}/original.webp`;
}

async function expireImage(
  row: ImageRecord,
  store: ObjectStore,
  now = new Date(),
): Promise<"not-due" | "deleted"> {
  if (row.state === "deleted" || row.deleteAt > now) return "not-due";
  row.state = "deleting";
  await store.remove(row.objectKey);
  row.state = "deleted";
  return "deleted";
}

The regular expression only keeps keys predictable. It does not authorize anything. Keep secrets out of logs and source control; the OWASP guidance is clear on that point. If a storage call returns a transient failure, leave the row claimable and record the attempt rather than marking the image deleted.

What should lifecycle, deletion workers, and observability prove about old images?

Lifecycle rules are excellent for repetitive age-based cleanup. Put abandoned generations under a distinct prefix and give them a shorter expiry. For a signed document or an image covered by a hold, calculate the deadline in application time and persist it. Do not replace a contractual date with an implicit creation-time timer; clock drift and time zones become visible only after a customer asks why a file vanished early.

The worker scans for delete_at <= now, claims a bounded batch, calls remove, and records removed or absent. A queue retry can hide a growing backlog, so expose counters for claimed, completed, already-absent, and failed operations. Alert on the age of the oldest due row, not only on a failed request.

I start with a 15-minute budget for due work, then change it when queue volume and the signed-document promise demand something else. Your mileage may vary. The important part is that the budget is written down and tested with a clock you control.

Emit one structured event per transition: image.retention.claimed, image.object.removed, image.object.absent, and image.retention.failed. Include a redacted tenant identifier, image ID, scheduled deadline, attempt number, and correlation ID. Never log a presigned URL; it is a bearer credential. A useful dashboard shows due objects by age, outcomes by reason, and rows stuck in deleting.

Test the unpleasant paths deliberately. Run a worker twice against the same row. Expire a hold, release it, and verify that the next scan claims it. Simulate a storage timeout and check that the audit event and retry counter agree. A 409-style duplicate claim should be a visible metric, not an excuse to delete without ownership checks.

Where does this design stop being a good fit?

The limitation is important: this approach is not suitable when users require permanent public URLs, cross-region archival replication, or byte-level search inside image content; choose a system that explicitly supports those requirements. It also assumes someone can operate a worker, rotate credentials, and review its alerts. When that operational budget does not exist, a single uniform lifecycle rule is simpler, but it cannot express per-document holds or prove application-level authorization.

The access-control choice is concrete. Direct browser uploads reduce delivery work when private signed URLs and CORS are acceptable. An Express proxy is the better fit when the service must inspect bytes or enforce a fixed egress boundary. Pick the boundary first, then make the storage key and deletion audit follow it.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339
