title: Designing a browser game older players can start in ten seconds: what the classics get right
description:
Short answer: the classic card, board and puzzle games are easy for older players to start because they need no tutorial, never punish slow reactions, and let you take back a mistake. Those are design choices, and any browser game can copy them.

Google's "People also ask" box shows the question "What is the best free game for seniors?" under puzzle-game searches. Going through the classic games listed on SlowDen, a free browser-game site, the ones that answer it well have the same handful of traits. None of them is about the art.

1. Can the player start without reading anything?

Solitaire, mahjong, chess and checkers need no onboarding, because the rules already live in the player's head. You cannot borrow that familiarity for a new game. What you can do is make the first action obvious: one thing on screen that clearly wants to be clicked.

2. Does anything depend on reaction speed?

Every classic on the list is turn-based. Nothing moves until the player does. If your game has a timer, ask whether the timer is the fun or just the default. Break 5, a daily word ladder, handles this well. Its rule is "take as long as you need", and finishing within five minutes only earns an optional badge.

3. Is the input "select, then target"?

Master Chess by CodeThisLab moves a piece with two clicks: click the piece, then click the square. Dragging a small piece across a board is hard with a touchpad and harder with an unsteady hand. Two separate clicks are forgiving and work the same on touch.

4. Can a mistake be undone?

Klondike from OnlineFreeSolitaire (made by Marin Kišić) lists undo and hints in its own description. Undo turns a misclick from a loss into nothing. It is usually a few lines of state history, and it removes the most common reason a new player quits.

5. Is every level actually winnable?

Mahjong Classic by Igrunka Games says its level generator only makes layouts that have a solution. That one sentence answers the question every solitaire player eventually asks: "was this deal even possible?" If your generator can make an unwinnable board, either fix it or tell the player.

6. Can the player choose how it looks?

Crossword Rally offers two styles, a white Classic Paper look and a dark Midnight Ink look. Its own instructions say to pick whichever is easier on your eyes. A light/dark choice is cheap, and for some players it decides whether they can play at all.

7. Can they play against the computer instead of strangers?

English Checkers Online Multiplayer by Smartberry offers three ways to play: the computer, players online, or someone on the same device. An offline opponent removes the social pressure of a stranger waiting for your move.

A quick checklist for your own game

Question Cheap fix
Is the first action obvious? One highlighted target on the first screen
Does speed decide the result? Make the timer optional, or a bonus
Is drag required? Accept click-then-click as well
Can a misclick be undone? Keep a small move history
Can a level be unwinnable? Validate generated levels
Is there one fixed colour scheme? Offer light and dark
Is a human opponent required? Add a simple computer opponent

Where to see these games

All of the games above are free in a browser. Each one is made by the studio named next to it, not by SlowDen. SlowDen collects them on its Puzzle and 2 Player shelves. If you have built a calm, turn-based browser game, you can submit it to SlowDen.

Written for the SlowDen blog. Listing details were read from SlowDen's catalogue on 17 November 2026.

title: I built Itzma to run vector search inside my applications
description:
How close can I bring vector search to where I actually need it?

I started building Itzma because I wanted to use it in my own projects. If an application needs to find the nearest vectors, can I make that a library call and keep the data in object storage? I wanted to see how far I could take that design and what I’d run into once I started using it myself.

Itzma is an open-source, embedded vector database written in Rust, with Python bindings. It’s still in beta.

The application runs the search

The application opens a namespace and queries it in-process. With an object storage backend, the bucket holds the durable data. There’s no separate vector database server to deploy.

That split raises a question I find more interesting than the initial setup. If two application processes write to the same namespace, what keeps them from overwriting each other’s changes? Itzma uses conditional writes from the object store to coordinate updates. The storage backend is part of how the database works, right down to what happens when writers overlap.

Try it from Python

Install Itzma from PyPI with pip install itzma. You can start in memory. This example inserts two vectors and asks for the closest one using cosine distance.

import itzma
store = itzma.Store("memory://")
schema = itzma.Schema(dim=4, metric=itzma.Metric.COSINE)
docs = itzma.Namespace.create(store, "docs", schema)
docs.upsert([
    {"id": "a", "vector": [1, 0, 0, 0]},
    {"id": "b", "vector": [0, 1, 0, 0]},
])
hits = docs.query([0.9, 0.1, 0, 0], top_k=1)
print(hits.ids)  # Expected nearest ID is "a"

To try the same flow against S3, point itzma.Store at s3://your-bucket/your-prefix with credentials configured. The namespace and query use the same API. For a first run with persistence on your machine, you can also point the store at a local directory.

There’s more to play with once you have a query running. Itzma supports dense and sparse retrieval, HNSW and SQ8 indexing, and filters on typed attributes.

What would you try it on?

If you have an application where you’d like to run vector search in-process, I’d like to hear what you’d need from Itzma to try it there.

Take a look at itzma.dev and start playing with it. If an example is hard to follow, a query gives you an unexpected result, or there’s a feature you’d need, tell me here or open an issue on GitHub. And if there’s something you’d like to build or fix yourself, open an issue and let’s talk through it.

GitHub and quickstart · Python package on PyPI · Rust crate on crates.io

title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

title: Testing MCP Servers Directly with MCP Inspector
description:
If you test an AI assistant by trying prompt injection strings for hours, you are testing the wrong boundary.

An LLM is a non-deterministic routing engine. When the model decides to run a task, it emits a structured request to a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server Anthropic's open-source release. That server executes real code on an operating system or database.

To find security vulnerabilities quickly, remove the model entirely. You can interact with the server directly over raw JSON-RPC 2.0 and test its functions like any standard API.

Why prompt injection is the wrong testing tool

Many developers assume their MCP tools will only ever receive clean arguments generated by an AI model. Because the assistant usually behaves politely, developers often forget defensive parameter validation AppSec research on agentic tools.

If you only test tools by arguing with a chatbot interface, you face two hurdles. First, the model's safety guardrails may block your test payloads before they reach the tool. Second, the model might rewrite your strings into valid values.

Real attackers do not need to persuade the model if they can interact with the protocol transport directly. Connecting an evaluation client straight to the server lets you audit the actual application boundaries without token burn or model interference.

Talking directly to JSON-RPC

Anthropic maintains an interactive testing harness called MCP Inspector (@modelcontextprotocol/inspector) that connects directly to servers over standard input and output (stdio) or HTTP transports MCP Inspector documentation.

Instead of opening a web chat interface, you can run the Inspector from your terminal to list all declared capabilities:

# Enumerate declared tools directly without invoking an LLM
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli \
  python3 server.py -- \
  --method tools/list --format json

The target server replies with a list of tools, descriptions, and JSON Schema definitions for every accepted property. The double dash (--) ensures Inspector does not confuse the server's runtime flags with its own options.

Once you have the schema, you can invoke any tool immediately with tools/call. Here is how a tester sends raw payload arguments straight into the target function:

# Send a command injection probe directly to a tool argument
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli \
  python3 server.py -- \
  --method tools/call \
  --tool-name git_log \
  --tool-args-json '{"branch": "; id"}'

Every parameter travels directly to the backend handler. You get immediate, deterministic feedback.

Spotting the dangerous sink

Consider an MCP server designed to let an agent inspect Git repositories. Below is an illustrative vulnerable implementation written in Python using FastMCP:

# Illustrative vulnerable FastMCP server (server.py)
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import subprocess

mcp = FastMCP("DevOps-Helper")

@mcp.tool()
def git_log(branch: str) -> str:
    """Returns commit logs for a git branch."""
    # Dangerous sink: shell=True with concatenated user input
    result = subprocess.run(
        f"git log --oneline {branch}",
        shell=True,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True
    )
    return result.stdout or result.stderr

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Runs the stdio JSON-RPC listening loop
    mcp.run()

The author expected the LLM to pass clean branch names such as main or feature-login. When you send ; id with MCP Inspector, subprocess.run passes the raw string to the system shell, which executes the appended command with the server process privileges.

Reviewing how data reaches sensitive operations is a fundamental skill in software auditing. To see more practical examples of input tracing in modern applications, take a look at the CodeReviewLab guide to tracing untrusted input to dangerous sinks.

Securing the tool handler

Fixing this flaw requires two defences. First, avoid running system commands through a shell interpreter. Second, enforce a strict allowlist on caller arguments before they reach any operating system API.

Here is an illustrative remediated version of the tool:

# Illustrative secure FastMCP server (server.py)
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import subprocess
import re

mcp = FastMCP("DevOps-Helper")
BRANCH_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_\-\.\/]+$")

@mcp.tool()
def git_log(branch: str) -> str:
    """Returns commit logs for a git branch."""
    # Reject unexpected characters and leading command flags
    if not BRANCH_PATTERN.match(branch) or branch.startswith("-"):
        raise ValueError("Invalid branch name format.")

    # Safe sink: direct array arguments with shell=False
    result = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "log", "--oneline", "--", branch],
        shell=False,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=10,
        check=False
    )
    return result.stdout or result.stderr

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

This pattern disables shell meta-character parsing entirely. Passing -- ensures Git does not treat a branch name starting with a dash as an option flag.

Parameter validation inside the tool protects the underlying host, but it does not prevent an LLM from misinterpreting poisoned data returned by external tools. For a deeper breakdown of system boundaries in agent environments, check out the CodeReviewLab guide to MCP security.

When the server attacks your inspector

There is an important catch when testing third-party or untrusted MCP servers. Your testing harness is also software, and it can be vulnerable.

Early releases of @modelcontextprotocol/inspector had serious flaws. Versions prior to 0.14.1 ran an unauthenticated local Node proxy binding to 0.0.0.0 on port 6277 CVE-2025-49596 security advisory. This allowed malicious websites to execute commands locally through cross-origin requests or DNS rebinding.

Later, stored cross-site scripting in the OAuth debugging interface allowed rogue servers to trigger local command execution Miggo Security's writeup on CVE-2025-58444. Even in the modern v2 series, versions before 2.12.0 could be exploited by a malicious server returning forged OAuth URLs that injected PowerShell commands on Windows systems Pillar Security advisory for CVE-2026-119025.

When assessing an untrusted server, keep these precautions in mind:

  1. Always update @modelcontextprotocol/inspector to version 2.12.0 or later before connecting to untrusted hosts.
  2. Never start the Inspector with authentication disabled using flags such as DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH=true.
  3. Run your assessment inside an isolated container or virtual machine rather than directly on your primary workstation.

Review checks for MCP servers

When auditing or building an MCP server, verify these core areas:

  • Input boundaries: Validate every argument against a strict schema. Reject undeclared properties and unexpected types.
  • Process isolation: Never pass tool arguments into shell=True or unescaped terminal strings. Pass isolated argument lists directly to executables.
  • Transport authentication: If using remote Streamable HTTP transports, ensure the server authenticates callers and checks OAuth token scopes against expected resources.
  • Description integrity: Audit tool descriptions returned by tools/list to ensure external sources have not embedded prompt injection payloads inside metadata.

Testing tools directly gives you fast, repeatable results without relying on model luck. If you want to practise tracing untrusted inputs across different languages and frameworks, visit CodeReviewLab to work through hands-on review challenges.

Have you tried automating MCP server checks in your CI pipeline yet?

title: Orchestrating LLM Agents: Self-Host Hatchet on VPS
description:
💡 Originally published on Bijak Technology Enterprise Journal with full interactive parameter benchmarks.

Execution failures in multi-step LLM chains caused by HTTP 504 Gateway Timeouts or unhandled worker crashes represent a major operational nightmare for agentic AI engineers. When an AI workflow involves long-running document analysis, recursive entity extraction, or dynamic web scraping spanning several minutes, traditional stateless HTTP architectures collapse under real-world load.

Without persistent step-level state tracking, a crash at minute five forces the entire pipeline to restart from scratch. This wastes valuable LLM API tokens and causes cloud infrastructure bills to balloon rapidly. While implementing an asynchronous AI queue architecture using Redis works well for lightweight job queues, it lacks native durable execution mechanics required to maintain complex Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) state across server crashes.

Architectural Shift: Stateless Queues vs. Durable Execution Engines

To build resilient enterprise LLM orchestration pipelines, engineering teams must transition from simple task queuing to durable stateful execution. Durable engines like Hatchet combine a lightweight, high-throughput Go engine with robust PostgreSQL state persistence.

Every individual step in an AI workflow is isolated and transactionally committed to the database. If a worker node suffers an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) event or network disruption mid-execution, Hatchet resumes execution precisely at the point of failure (step-level recovery) without re-running previously successful LLM calls.

Here is a technical breakdown comparing the primary AI orchestration choices:

Architectural Parameter BullMQ (Redis In-Memory) Hatchet Engine (Self-Hosted) Temporal Cloud (Managed SaaS)
Execution Model Stateless Job Queue Durable Stateful DAG Durable Event Sourcing
State Persistence Transient (Volatile RAM) ACID-Compliant (PostgreSQL) Distributed Log Store
Step-Level Recovery Manual Retry Logic Native / Step-level Auto Native / Step-level Auto
Orchestration Latency Sub-millisecond Low Latency (<10ms) Variable Cloud Latency
Cost Predictability High (Fixed VPS Cost) High (Fixed VPS Cost) Low (Pay-per-Event Cloud)
Operational Overhead Low Low (Docker Native) High (Vendor Lock-in)

Relying on managed SaaS vendors often results in unpredictable monthly bills as transaction volume scales up. Deploying Hatchet on self-hosted infrastructure presents an optimal path for data sovereignty, cost control, and operational stability.

Deploying Hatchet Engine on Hostinger KVM VPS Infrastructure

Self-hosting the Hatchet Engine requires hardware with guaranteed CPU allocations and rapid storage I/O to handle constant PostgreSQL state updates. Leveraging a high-performance Hostinger KVM VPS infrastructure powered by NVMe storage provides the necessary throughput to process thousands of workflow step updates per second without I/O bottlenecks.

The deployment architecture consists of three core services: PostgreSQL as the durable state store, the Hatchet Engine/Controller, and the isolated Worker Nodes executing your LLM agents. This stack seamlessly pairs with an orchestrated multi-AI agent setup via Docker Compose.

volumes:
 hatchet_pgdata:

Advanced Fault Tolerance & Token Bucket Concurrency Control

A critical advantage of the Hatchet Engine is its native implementation of rate limiting and concurrency control via the Token Bucket algorithm. When running agentic AI loops that make parallel requests to external API providers like OpenAI or Anthropic, unmanaged execution inevitably causes HTTP 429 Rate Limit Exceeded errors.

By unifying step-level retry policies with engine-level token bucket limits, engineering teams achieve three key outcomes:

  1. Execution State Recovery: In the event of a total host failure, Hatchet automatically re-assigns uncompleted DAG steps to alternate active workers within milliseconds.
  2. Token Bucket Concurrency: Prevents API throttling by enforcing strict rate limits per LLM provider directly at the execution engine layer.
  3. Optimized RAM Footprint: TypeScript and Python workers consume system memory only during active step evaluation, significantly reducing idle memory overhead on your VPS compared to continuous polling loops.

Transitioning long-running LLM workflows from fragile stateless queues to a durable execution model backed by Hatchet and PostgreSQL guarantees high availability and operational reliability. Running this stack on top of a dedicated Hostinger KVM VPS server guarantees low latency and fixed, predictable infrastructure costs.

title: Autopsy #12: Moving the Entire App Engine Off the Main Thread
description:
620 ms Stalls on Every Column Click

A client-side table PR enabled multi-column sorting and automatic snapshot persistence for a collaborative spreadsheet editor. On 200-row fixtures in CI, sorts finished in 2 ms.

When enterprise customers opened 100,000-row production workbooks, Long Task observers recorded 620 ms main-thread stalls per column click, dropping scroll input and collapsing frame rates to 4 FPS. Each sort ran Array.prototype.sort over 100,000 JS objects, then called JSON.stringify(rows) and IndexedDB put(), allocating 90 MB of transient strings and triggering 140 ms V8 major GC pauses.

  • T+00:00: Enterprise customers open 100,000-row production workbooks after the release.
  • T+03:00: Long Task observers record 620 ms main-thread stalls per column click, dropping frame rates to 4 FPS.
  • T+08:00: Each sort runs Array.prototype.sort + JSON.stringify(rows) + IndexedDB put(), allocating 90 MB of transient strings.
  • T+12:00: V8 major garbage collection pauses hit 140 ms on every sort direction toggle.

Why requestIdleCallback Time-Slicing Failed

In #perf-ui, the first patch wrapped the sort loop in requestIdleCallback and chunked rows into 5,000-item slices. Local synthetic benchmarks showed shorter individual task bars.

In production, it failed. An interactive sort cannot yield mid-comparison without blocking the user's result for seconds, JSON.stringify(rows) still froze the main thread for 190 ms in one synchronous call, and a concurrent edit mutated the row array mid-slice, corrupting sort order.

Five Layers From 620 ms Main-Thread Freeze to 60 FPS

Recovering 60 FPS required moving the entire data engine off the UI thread: isolating state in a Dedicated Web Worker, returning sorted indices via zero-copy ArrayBuffer transfers, persisting binary buffers in OPFS, batching numeric sorts inside Wasm linear memory, and coordinating UI updates through an actor mailbox.

Compare Main-Thread Sorting Against the Worker Actor Engine

Dissecting the Off-Thread Architecture

01 → 02: Moving the 90 MB Allocation Off the UI Thread

The Performance flamegraph showed 410 ms of JS sorting and 140 ms of Major GC sitting directly on CrRendererMain, starving scroll and pointer events. Relocating the 100k-row store into Dedicated Web Workers immediately freed the main thread to stay at 60 FPS during heavy sorts.

However, a naive postMessage(sortedRows) still froze the main thread for 115 ms during structured cloning of 100,000 objects. Instead, the Worker sorts an index Uint32Array and transfers ownership via postMessage({ indices }, [indices.buffer]), using Typed Arrays & Zero-Copy Transfers so the UI thread receives the sorted order in < 0.2 ms and only renders the 40 visible viewport rows.

02 → 03: Replacing JSON.stringify + IndexedDB With OPFS

The remaining 190 ms spike in the Worker trace was JSON.stringify(rows) before indexedDB.put(). Writing raw binary column buffers directly inside the Worker using FileSystemSyncAccessHandle in Origin Private File System (OPFS) eliminated JSON serialization overhead completely and persisted 100k-row snapshots in under 6 ms.

03 → 04: Batching Numeric Sorts Inside Wasm Linear Memory

When sorting numeric columns in a Wasm module, an early prototype called a Wasm comparator once per pair from JS (1.6M crossings), spending more time marshaling arguments than sorting. Passing the entire column buffer once into linear memory avoids Wasm-JS Boundary Overhead and finishes 100k-row sorts in 4.5 ms.

04 → 05: Actor Message Passing Without Shared-State Races

To prevent user edits from colliding with an in-flight sort, the UI and Worker communicate through Actor-Over-Worker Architecture: UI dispatches immutable commands ({ type: 'SORT', col, reqId }), and the Worker processes its mailbox sequentially, discarding stale reqId responses on the client.

Transferring Zero-Copy Indices From the Worker Actor 

// engine.worker.ts
self.onmessage = ({ data }: MessageEvent<{ type: 'SORT'; col: number; reqId: number }>) => {
  if (data.type !== 'SORT') return;
  const indices = sortColumnInWasm(data.col); // Uint32Array of 100k row indices
  syncAccessHandle.write(new Uint8Array(indices.buffer), { at: 0 });
  self.postMessage({ type: 'SORTED', reqId: data.reqId, indices }, [indices.buffer]);
};

Architectural Invariants:

  • Keep the main thread strictly for UI: Never sort, filter, or JSON.stringify >10k-row datasets on CrRendererMain.
  • Transfer ArrayBuffers, never clone object graphs: Pass Uint32Array index buffers via the transfer list so postMessage runs in O(1).
  • Persist binary state in OPFS: Use FileSystemSyncAccessHandle inside the Worker instead of JSON-serialized IndexedDB blobs.

Golden Rule: Don't time-slice a 600 ms data engine on the UI thread; move state, Wasm sorts, and OPFS persistence to a Worker and transfer ArrayBuffer indices.

Bir satış ekranında "Bu fırsat kaç gündür bu aşamada?" sorusu masum görünür. Ama aynı soruya CRM'in kendi ekranı, haftalık Excel raporu ve yöneticinin aklındaki sayı üç farklı cevap verebilir. Biri fırsatın açıldığı günden saymıştır, biri son güncelleme tarihinden, biri de fırsat bir aşama geri gidip tekrar ilerlediğinde sayacı sıfırlamıştır. Deal aging bu yüzden basit bir tarih farkı değil, bir tanım ve veri modeli meselesidir.

Ben Koray Yalçın; lead yönetimi, CRM ve satış operasyonu altyapıları kuruyorum, ağırlıklı olarak gayrimenkul projelerinde reklamdan satış ofisine uzanan hattın veri tarafında çalışıyorum. Bu yazıda fırsat yaşlanmasını (deal aging) bir geliştirici gözüyle ele alıyorum: yaşı hangi kaynaktan hesaplayacağız, aşama içi yaş ile toplam yaşı nasıl ayıracağız, geri dönen fırsatları nasıl ele alacağız, takvim günü ile iş günü arasında nasıl seçim yapacağız ve uyarıları gürültüye dönüştürmeden nasıl üreteceğiz. Kavramın kısa tanımı için sözlükteki deal aging nedir sayfasına bakabilirsiniz; burada "bu sayıyı nasıl güvenilir üretiriz" kısmına odaklanacağım.

Daha önceki yazılarımda CRM aşamalarını bir durum makinesi olarak tasarlamayı ve append-only bir aşama geçmişi tablosu tutmayı işlemiştim. Bu yazı da o tablonun üzerine kuruluyor. Aşama geçmişi olmayan bir sistemde yaş hesaplamak mümkündür ama sonuçlar kırılgan olur.

1. Yanlış kaynak: updated_at

En yaygın hata, yaşı fırsat tablosundaki updated_at alanından hesaplamaktır. Bu alan, bir danışman nota bir cümle eklediğinde, bir entegrasyon telefon numarasını normalize ettiğinde ya da toplu bir etiket güncellemesi yapıldığında değişir. Sonuçta hiç ilerlemeyen bir fırsat, sırf birisi dokunduğu için "taze" görünür. Ters yönde de sorun var: aşama değiştiği halde başka bir alan güncellenmediyse ve sistem updated_at alanını yalnızca belirli alanlarda tetikliyorsa, yaş olduğundan büyük görünür.

Yaşın tek güvenilir kaynağı, aşama değişikliklerinin zaman damgasıyla tutulduğu bir geçmiş tablosudur. Minimum yapı şöyle:

CREATE TABLE deal_stage_history (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  deal_id       bigint      NOT NULL REFERENCES deal(id),
  from_stage    text,                       -- ilk kayıtta NULL
  to_stage      text        NOT NULL,
  changed_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,       -- işin gerçekleştiği an
  recorded_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), -- sisteme yazıldığı an
  changed_by    text        NOT NULL,       -- kullanıcı veya entegrasyon adı
  source        text        NOT NULL        -- 'ui', 'api', 'import', 'backfill'
);

CREATE INDEX ON deal_stage_history (deal_id, changed_at);

changed_at ile recorded_at ayrımı önemli. Bir danışman sahadan dönüp akşam "dün randevu yapıldı" diye aşamayı güncellediğinde iş dün olmuştur ama kayıt bugün yazılmıştır. Yaş hesabı iş zamanını, denetim ise kayıt zamanını kullanmalıdır. Geriye dönük düzeltmelere izin verecekseniz changed_at değerinin recorded_at değerinden ne kadar geride olabileceğine bir sınır koymak, raporların geçmişe dönük sessizce değişmesini engeller.

2. Üç farklı yaş, üç farklı soru

"Fırsatın yaşı" tek bir sayı değildir. Pratikte üç ayrı ölçü işe yarar ve her biri başka bir soruya cevap verir:

  • Toplam yaş: Fırsat açıldığından bu yana geçen süre. "Bu müşteriyle ne zamandır uğraşıyoruz?" sorusunun cevabı.
  • Aşama içi yaş (mevcut ziyaret): Fırsatın şu anki aşamaya son girişinden bu yana geçen süre. "Şu an nerede takıldı?" sorusunun cevabı. Uyarıların çoğu buna dayanır.
  • Aşamada kümülatif süre: Fırsatın bu aşamada geçirdiği toplam süre, geri dönüşler dahil. "Bu fırsat bu aşamada gerçekte ne kadar zaman harcadı?" sorusunun cevabı.

Fark, geri dönüşlerde ortaya çıkar. Örnek bir senaryo düşünelim: Fırsat 1 Ekim'de "Teklif" aşamasına girdi, 20 Ekim'de müşteri yeni bir daire tipi isteyince "Sunum" aşamasına geri alındı, 25 Ekim'de tekrar "Teklif" aşamasına geçti. Bugün 5 Kasım ise aşama içi yaş 11 gündür, ama teklif aşamasında kümülatif süre 30 gündür. Yalnızca aşama içi yaşa bakan bir uyarı sistemi, bu fırsatı "yeni teklif" gibi gösterir. Bu bilinçli bir tercih olabilir, ama bilinçli olmalıdır.

3. Aşama ziyaretlerini SQL ile çıkarmak

Geçmiş tablosundan her aşama ziyaretinin başlangıç ve bitişini pencere fonksiyonlarıyla çıkarabiliriz. Bir sonraki kaydın zamanı, mevcut ziyaretin bitişidir; sonraki kayıt yoksa ziyaret hâlâ açıktır.

CREATE VIEW deal_stage_visit AS
SELECT
  h.deal_id,
  h.to_stage                                   AS stage,
  h.changed_at                                 AS entered_at,
  LEAD(h.changed_at) OVER w                    AS exited_at,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY h.deal_id, h.to_stage ORDER BY h.changed_at) AS visit_no
FROM deal_stage_history h
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY h.deal_id ORDER BY h.changed_at, h.id);

Buradan üç yaşı tek sorguda üretmek mümkün:

SELECT
  d.id AS deal_id,
  d.current_stage,
  now() - d.created_at                                   AS total_age,
  now() - v_cur.entered_at                               AS age_in_current_visit,
  SUM(COALESCE(v.exited_at, now()) - v.entered_at)       AS cumulative_in_stage,
  MAX(v.visit_no)                                        AS visits_to_stage
FROM deal d
JOIN deal_stage_visit v
  ON v.deal_id = d.id AND v.stage = d.current_stage
JOIN deal_stage_visit v_cur
  ON v_cur.deal_id = d.id AND v_cur.stage = d.current_stage AND v_cur.exited_at IS NULL
WHERE d.status = 'open'
GROUP BY d.id, d.current_stage, d.created_at, v_cur.entered_at;

visits_to_stage sütunu kendi başına değerli bir sinyaldir. Aynı aşamaya üçüncü kez giren bir fırsat, ya müşteri tarafında gerçek bir belirsizlik olduğunu ya da aşama tanımlarının ekip tarafından farklı yorumlandığını gösterir. İkisi de konuşulması gereken bir durumdur.

Bir kontrol notu: d.current_stage ile geçmiş tablosundaki son kayıt birbirini tutmalıdır. Tutmuyorsa birisi aşamayı geçmiş tablosunu atlayarak değiştirmiştir. Bunu bir veri sağlığı sorgusuyla her gün kontrol etmek, yaş raporuna güvenin ön koşuludur.

4. Takvim günü mü, iş günü mü?

Cuma akşamı teklif aşamasına giren bir fırsat pazartesi sabahı "3 günlük" görünür; oysa ekip açısından hiç zaman geçmemiştir. Bayram tatilleri olan bir haftada bu etki daha da büyür ve haftalık rapor yapay olarak kötüleşir. Bu yüzden aşama içi yaş için iş günü kullanmayı öneriyorum; toplam yaş ise müşteri açısından anlamlı olduğu için takvim günü kalabilir.

İş günü hesabını kod içinde "hafta sonlarını çıkar" mantığıyla yapmak yerine bir takvim tablosuyla yapmak daha sağlamdır. Resmi tatiller, ofisin kapalı olduğu günler ve farklı ülkelerdeki satış ofisleri bu tabloda yaşar:

CREATE TABLE business_calendar (
  calendar_code text NOT NULL,     -- örn. 'ofis_tr', 'ofis_kktc'
  day           date NOT NULL,
  is_working    boolean NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (calendar_code, day)
);

CREATE FUNCTION business_days_between(p_cal text, p_from timestamptz, p_to timestamptz, p_tz text)
RETURNS int LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
  SELECT COUNT(*)::int
  FROM business_calendar c
  WHERE c.calendar_code = p_cal
    AND c.is_working
    AND c.day >  (p_from AT TIME ZONE p_tz)::date
    AND c.day <= (p_to   AT TIME ZONE p_tz)::date;
$$;

İki ayrıntı önemli. Birincisi, gün sınırı ofisin saat diliminde hesaplanmalı; UTC ile hesaplanan bir gün sınırı, gece yarısına yakın girişlerde bir gün kaydırma üretir. İkincisi, giriş gününü saymayıp çıkış gününü saymak gibi bir kural seçip her yerde aynı kuralı uygulamak gerekir. Hangi kuralı seçtiğiniz, tutarlı uygulamanızdan daha az önemlidir.

5. Eşikler aşamaya göre, veri olarak

Tek bir "30 günü geçen fırsatlar" eşiği her aşama için anlamsızdır. İlk görüşme aşamasında beş iş günü bekleyen bir fırsat ciddi bir sorunken, kredi onayı ya da tapu süreci bekleyen bir fırsat için aynı süre tamamen normaldir. Gayrimenkulde özellikle proje lansmanlarında karar süreleri uzun olabilir ve bu uzunluk tek başına kötü bir şey değildir.

Eşikleri kodda değil, sürümlü bir tabloda tutuyorum:

CREATE TABLE stage_aging_rule (
  pipeline_code   text NOT NULL,
  stage           text NOT NULL,
  warn_bdays      int  NOT NULL,   -- dikkat eşiği (iş günü)
  critical_bdays  int  NOT NULL,   -- kritik eşik (iş günü)
  valid_from      date NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (pipeline_code, stage, valid_from),
  CHECK (critical_bdays > warn_bdays)
);

Eşik değerlerini tahminle değil, kendi geçmiş verinizden seçmek daha savunulabilirdir. Kazanılan fırsatların bu aşamada geçirdiği sürelerin dağılımına bakıp, örneğin yüksek bir yüzdelik dilimi dikkat eşiği olarak almak iyi bir başlangıçtır:

SELECT stage,
       percentile_cont(0.5)  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY bdays) AS median_bdays,
       percentile_cont(0.8)  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY bdays) AS p80_bdays,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS n
FROM (
  SELECT v.stage,
         business_days_between('ofis_tr', v.entered_at, v.exited_at, 'Europe/Istanbul') AS bdays
  FROM deal_stage_visit v
  JOIN deal d ON d.id = v.deal_id
  WHERE d.status = 'won' AND v.exited_at IS NOT NULL
) t
GROUP BY stage
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 30;

HAVING satırındaki örneklem eşiği bilinçli: az sayıda kapanışla hesaplanan bir yüzdelik, eşik olarak kullanılamayacak kadar oynaktır. Yeterli veri yoksa eşiği ekiple konuşarak başlatıp veri biriktikçe güncellemek daha dürüsttür.

6. Günlük snapshot: "Geçen hafta nasıldı?" sorusu

Yaşı her zaman now() ile hesaplarsanız, "üç hafta önce kritik durumdaki fırsat sayısı kaçtı?" sorusuna cevap veremezsiniz; çünkü o fırsatların bir kısmı o günden beri kapanmış ya da aşama değiştirmiştir. Geçmişten yeniden hesaplamak teorik olarak mümkündür ama geriye dönük düzeltmeler yüzünden sonuç her seferinde biraz farklı çıkar.

Çözüm, her gün sabit bir saatte açık fırsatların yaş durumunu bir snapshot tablosuna yazmaktır:

CREATE TABLE deal_aging_snapshot (
  snapshot_date        date   NOT NULL,
  deal_id              bigint NOT NULL,
  stage                text   NOT NULL,
  owner_id             bigint,
  age_bdays_in_visit   int    NOT NULL,
  cumulative_bdays     int    NOT NULL,
  visits_to_stage      int    NOT NULL,
  health               text   NOT NULL CHECK (health IN ('ok','warn','critical')),
  rule_version         date   NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (snapshot_date, deal_id)
);

rule_version sütunu, eşikler değiştiğinde eski snapshot'ların hangi kuralla sınıflandırıldığını korur. Eşikleri gevşettiğiniz hafta "kritik fırsatlar azaldı" diye sevinmemek için bu bilgiye ihtiyacınız olur. Snapshot işi idempotent olmalı: aynı gün iki kez çalışırsa ON CONFLICT (snapshot_date, deal_id) DO UPDATE ile aynı sonucu üretmeli.

7. Uyarıları gürültüye çevirmemek

Yaş hesabı doğru olsa bile, her sabah yüzlerce "fırsat yaşlandı" bildirimi gönderen bir sistem kısa sürede görmezden gelinir. Benim uyguladığım birkaç kural:

  • Durum geçişinde uyar, durumda değil. Bir fırsat "dikkat"ten "kritik"e geçtiğinde tek bir bildirim gider; kritik kaldığı sürece her gün tekrar gitmez. Snapshot tablosunda dünkü ve bugünkü health değerini karşılaştırmak bunu kolaylaştırır.
  • Bilinen bekleme nedenini sayaçtan ayır. Müşterinin kredi onayı beklediği, yurt dışında olduğu ya da belirli bir tarihte döneceğini söylediği durumlar için fırsata bir bekleme nedeni ve beklenen tarih alanı eklenebilir. Beklenen tarih geçmediği sürece fırsat "bekliyor" olarak işaretlenir ve kritik listede görünmez. Beklenen tarih geçtiğinde normal kurallar devreye girer.
  • Sahibine önce, yöneticiye sonra. İlk bildirim fırsatın sahibine gider. Belirli bir süre içinde aşama değişmez ya da bir aktivite girilmezse özet, ekip liderinin haftalık listesine düşer.
  • Aktivite yaşı ayrı bir sinyal. Aşama değişmemiş ama son üç gün içinde müşteriyle görüşülmüş bir fırsat, hiç dokunulmamış bir fırsattan farklıdır. Son anlamlı aktiviteden bu yana geçen süreyi ikinci bir sinyal olarak tutmak, yanlış alarmları ciddi biçimde azaltır.

Bu kuralların hepsi teknik olduğu kadar organizasyonel tercihlerdir. Kodun görevi bu tercihleri açık, sürümlü ve denetlenebilir hale getirmektir.

8. Sık karşılaşılan tuzaklar

  • Aşama atlama: Fırsat "Sunum"dan doğrudan "Rezervasyon"a geçtiyse arada kalan aşamalarda sıfır gün geçirmiş olur. Bu bir hata değildir, ama aşama bazlı ortalama sürelerde bu fırsatları ayrı tutmak gerekir.
  • Toplu göçler: Pipeline yeniden tasarlandığında yüzlerce fırsat aynı anda yeni aşamalara taşınır ve hepsinin aşama içi yaşı sıfırlanır. Bu kayıtları source = 'backfill' ile işaretleyip, yaş hesabında göç öncesi eşdeğer aşamaya giriş zamanını korumak gerekir.
  • Kapanan ve yeniden açılan fırsatlar: Kaybedildi olarak kapatılıp aylar sonra yeniden açılan bir fırsat için toplam yaşın ilk açılıştan mı yoksa yeniden açılıştan mı sayılacağı açıkça kararlaştırılmalıdır.
  • Sahip değişikliği: Fırsat başka bir danışmana devredildiğinde yaş sıfırlanmaz, ama yeni sahibin performansını değerlendirirken devralma tarihinden itibaren geçen süreye bakmak daha adildir.

Sık Sorulan Sorular (SSS)

Deal aging ile sales cycle aynı şey mi?
Hayır. Sales cycle, kapanmış fırsatların açılıştan kapanışa kadar geçen süresidir ve geriye dönük bir ölçüdür. Deal aging ise açık fırsatların şu anki durumunu anlatır ve operasyonel müdahale içindir. İkisi aynı aşama geçmişinden beslenir ama farklı sorulara cevap verir.

Geçmiş tablosu olmayan mevcut bir CRM'de nereden başlamalıyım?
Bugünden itibaren aşama değişikliklerini kaydetmeye başlayın ve mevcut açık fırsatlar için tek bir başlangıç kaydını source = 'backfill' ile yazın. Geçmiş için elinizdeki en iyi tahmini kullanın ama bu kayıtları raporlarda ayırt edilebilir tutun. Birkaç ay içinde güvenilir bir veri birikir.

Eşikleri ne sıklıkla güncellemeliyim?
Sabit bir takvim yerine, kazanılan fırsatların dağılımı belirgin biçimde değiştiğinde güncellemek daha mantıklıdır. Her değişikliği yeni bir valid_from ile kaydetmek, raporların geriye dönük karşılaştırılabilir kalmasını sağlar.

Hazır bir CRM kullanıyorsam bunları kendim mi kurmalıyım?
Birçok CRM aşama geçmişini tutar ve dışa aktarma ya da API ile erişim sağlar. Bu geçmişi kendi veritabanınıza veya veri ambarınıza alıp yaş hesabını orada yapmak, tanımlar ve iş günü takvimi üzerinde tam kontrol verir. Kullandığınız aracın güncel dokümantasyonunu kontrol edin.

Yaşlanan fırsatları otomatik olarak kayıp işaretlemeli miyim?
Ben önermiyorum. Otomatik kapatma, veriyi temiz gösterir ama gerçekte hâlâ ilgilenen müşterileri sessizce kaybetmenize yol açabilir. Daha iyi yol, kritik eşiği aşan fırsatları sahibine "devam mı, bekleme mi, kapanış mı?" sorusuyla sunmak ve kararı bir insanın vermesidir.

Deal aging, doğru kurulduğunda satış hattındaki tıkanıklıkları erken gösteren en pratik sinyallerden biridir; yanlış kurulduğunda ise kimsenin güvenmediği bir kırmızı liste üretir. Farkı tarih farkı formülü değil, aşama geçmişi disiplini, iş günü takvimi, aşamaya özgü eşikler ve akıllı uyarı kuralları yaratır. Siz fırsat yaşını aşama içi mi, kümülatif mi izliyorsunuz? Yorumlarda tartışalım.

title: Responsive trên báo giá, vỡ trên điện thoại: 4 chỗ cần soi
description:
Giả sử một phòng khám thú y ở Thủ Đức nhận bàn giao website, trong báo giá ghi "giao diện responsive, tương thích mọi thiết bị". Mở trên laptop, mọi thứ ngay ngắn. Lần đầu chủ phòng khám mở bằng điện thoại khi đang đứng ở quầy: bảng giá tiêm phòng tràn ra ngoài, cả trang trượt ngang, nút gọi nằm sát nút Zalo tới mức ngón cái chạm trúng cả hai.

Dòng "responsive" trong báo giá thường chỉ có nghĩa là theme gốc co giãn được. Những phần thêm vào sau, như bảng giá tự dựng, banner thiết kế riêng, đoạn mã nhúng từ bên thứ ba, mới là chỗ hay vỡ. 4 chỗ dưới đây đáng soi trước ngày nhận bàn giao.

Thẻ viewport là dòng đầu tiên phải có
Thiếu thẻ này, trình duyệt điện thoại giả định trang rộng như màn hình máy tính rồi thu nhỏ cả trang lại, chữ li ti dù CSS viết đúng. Mở mã nguồn trang và tìm trong phần head:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Một lỗi khác hay gặp là thêm maximum-scale=1 hoặc user-scalable=no để chặn phóng to. Người lớn tuổi cần phóng to mới đọc được, đừng tước của họ quyền đó.

Phần tử tràn ngang tìm ra được trong vài giây
Trang trượt ngang được trên điện thoại nghĩa là có một phần tử nào đó rộng hơn màn hình. Bật chế độ thiết bị trong Chrome DevTools, chọn một khổ điện thoại, rồi dán đoạn sau vào tab Console:

const w = document.documentElement.clientWidth
document.querySelectorAll('body *').forEach(el => {
  const r = el.getBoundingClientRect()
  if (r.right > w + 1) console.log(Math.round(r.right), el)
})

Đoạn mã in ra mọi phần tử có mép phải vượt quá bề ngang màn hình. Thủ phạm quen mặt là ảnh đặt cứng chiều rộng theo pixel, bảng nhiều cột, khung bản đồ hay video nhúng. Phần tử nằm trong một khung đã có cuộn ngang riêng cũng sẽ hiện ra, bỏ qua những dòng đó.

Bảng giá cần khung cuộn riêng thay vì kéo cả trang
Bảng năm sáu cột không bao giờ vừa bề ngang một chiếc điện thoại cầm dọc. Có 2 cách sửa. Bọc bảng trong một khung có overflow-x: auto để chỉ bảng cuộn ngang, phần còn lại đứng yên. Hoặc với bảng ít dòng, chuyển mỗi dòng thành một thẻ xếp dọc trên màn hình hẹp. Với ảnh, max-width: 100% đi cùng chiều cao tự động là đủ để ảnh không bao giờ rộng hơn khung chứa.

Nút bấm phải đủ chỗ cho ngón tay chứ không phải cho chuột
Trên máy tính, 2 nút cách nhau vài pixel vẫn bấm chuẩn. Ngón cái thì to hơn con trỏ rất nhiều. 2 nút liên hệ đặt sát nhau là kiểu lỗi khiến khách gọi nhầm, ngại, rồi tắt luôn trang. Cách thử nhanh nhất là cầm máy bằng một tay, đứng, bấm từng nút bằng ngón cái. Nút nào phải nhắm mới trúng là nút cần to hơn hoặc cách xa hơn.

Google đọc bản điện thoại trước bản máy tính
Khi thu thập và xếp hạng, Google lấy bản trang hiện trên điện thoại làm gốc. Nếu bản điện thoại bỏ bớt nội dung cho gọn, như bỏ bảng giá hay phần hỏi đáp, thì với Google phần đó coi như không có. Responsive làm đúng không tự đẩy trang lên cao, nó chỉ gỡ một rào cản. Những công cụ AI trả lời bằng cách đọc trang web cũng cần đúng thứ ấy: nội dung đầy đủ, đọc được, không phải đoán.

Responsive khác web mobile riêng và web động ở đâu, 4 cách tự kiểm không cần biết code và 5 lỗi hay gặp có trong bài manhdigital.com/blog/responsive-la-gi. Còn cơ chế Google đọc trang qua bản điện thoại và những gì cần kiểm nằm ở bài về mobile-first indexing.

title: Build Once, Grow Freely: Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite
description:
Enterprise workloads are getting bigger, more variable, and harder to predict, especially as agentic applications introduce spiky, unpredictable demand. Most data platforms weren't built for this reality—to cope with demand, they bolt AI services onto aging architecture, leaving customers to manage, monitor, and pay for multiple systems to get the job done. That fragmentation slows your teams down and limits how fast and how far your agentic applications can run.

In a traditional database architecture, storage is tied to the machine that runs your queries. Scaling up, adding a replica, or restoring a backup comes down to copying data from one machine to another, and the bigger the database, the longer that takes. My colleague Abhishek Chauhan calls this “storage gravity.” “Data doesn’t want to move,” he wrote for the MongoDB Engineering Blog. The bigger the data gets, the harder it pulls.

MongoDB built Atlas Infinite precisely for this reality; purpose-built to absorb spikes in demand with flexible, elastic scaling. Whether you’re launching a first prototype or running at petabyte-scale in production, Atlas Infinite enables you to build on a foundation that scales with you and never forces re-architecture. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search supported on Atlas Infinite in public preview, your database and retrieval live in one platform, with nothing to stitch together.

How Atlas Infinite works

A new deployment option within MongoDB Atlas, Atlas Infinite separates compute from storage so each scales independently and rapidly. Storage moves into a fully managed layer that handles replication, durability, and backup across availability zones, so compute no longer has to carry the data with it.

The impact is dramatic. Read replicas come online in minutes because there's no data to copy. A single shard holds up to 128 TB, so you no longer shard just to add disk space. You only pay for the data you store, not capacity provisioned in advance, so a small team never has to buy a bigger compute tier just to get more disk. And it’s all driven by the same MongoDB API, drivers, and tooling, so your application doesn’t need to change.

The separation of storage and compute matters most where agentic applications grow fastest: the retrieval layer. Every answer an assistant gives and every step an agent takes starts with a search over your data, and the data behind that search, especially vector embeddings, can grow large quickly. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search running natively on Atlas Infinite, that data lives on the same foundation as the rest of your application and can grow without re-architecture. Build your agentic workload once and keep scaling it on the same foundation as demand grows.

Figure 1. Compute and storage as independent layers in Atlas Infinite.

Retrieval, built into the database

Many retrieval stacks are cobbled together from disconnected components—a database, a search engine, and a vector database—which means running all of those separate parts, plus managing the pipelines that keep everything in sync. On Atlas Infinite, retrieval is part of the platform, so there are fewer pieces to build, secure, and maintain. Here is what that looks like:

  • One platform, nothing to stitch together: On Atlas Infinite, your database and retrieval work together seamlessly, with no separate search engine or vector database to stand up, sync, or monitor. MongoDB Atlas keeps your indexes in sync with your data automatically, so there is no pipeline for your team to build or maintain, and no extra systems to copy sensitive data into or secure. With Atlas Infinite, retrieval is built in, alongside the ability to scale to absorb unpredictable demand with zero waste.
  • Start small, never outgrow your data platform: A team can start with a 5GB prototype that includes semantic search and keep building on the same foundation. Rather than sizing and maintaining two infrastructures, storage grows automatically with your data, billed only for what you store. The operational data behind your search has room to grow to petabyte scale on Atlas Infinite, with no re-platforming when the application takes off.
  • Agent memory and context retrieval: Give agents one place to store and retrieve context, history, and state alongside your operational data. Support thousands of agents hitting your retrieval layer while also persisting agent memory and context within a single, durable system that scales when they need it.

Figure 2. Search and Vector Search run alongside the database on Atlas Infinite, with indexes kept in sync automatically and data stored once in Atlas-managed storage.

How Atlas Infinite handles your largest text and vector workloads

Separating compute from storage in the database also changes the scaling behavior and economics of large retrieval workloads. Text and vector data lives in the database first, where it drives storage requirements. Because Atlas Infinite manages that storage separately from compute, the economics come down to one property of the data: how well it compresses.

Databases shrink data on disk with compression, which works by finding repetition. Text is full of repetition: common words, repeated field names, predictable structure. Text in MongoDB typically compresses to about 40% of its original size. An embedding is an array of decimal values with almost no repetition, so it shrinks by only about 13%. In practice, a vector takes up as much space on disk as it does in your application.

How each deployment option stores that data

Atlas Core uses attached storage volumes. Each node in a replica set keeps a full copy of the data on its own disk, provisioned ahead of time with room to grow, and compute and storage come in matched tiers. That gives every node complete isolation and predictable performance, and it's the right fit for many workloads, especially ones where data and query load grow together.

Vector workloads tend to be storage-driven because high-dimension embeddings are so large. A RAG knowledge base can hold hundreds of gigabytes of embeddings, which drives up storage needs relative to query volume. On Atlas Core, storage can drive scaling decisions: once you outgrow a tier’s maximum disk size, you have to move up a tier to get more storage, even if you don’t need more compute, and very large datasets eventually call for sharding.

On Atlas Infinite, compute and storage scale independently. Storage is billed per logical (uncompressed) GB of data you store, metered hourly. Replication across availability zones happens inside the storage layer and isn't billed separately. There's no headroom to provision, and because a shard holds up to 128 TB, a growing dataset doesn't push you to a larger compute tier or to more shards. Because embeddings barely compress, their logical size and their size on disk are nearly the same, so you pay only for the data you store and nothing for the copies and headroom underneath it. As vector collections grow to hundreds of millions of documents, that billing model becomes an advantage.

Here is an example. For a collection with 100 million documents, each with a 1,024-dimension float32 embedding and about 1 KB of other fields, storage is roughly 500 GB uncompressed.  Assuming moderate query traffic, an M30 cluster tier’s compute is sufficient.

On Atlas Core, since embeddings barely compress, the data shrinks to ~435GB on disk. Each node also needs space for the oplog and room for the collection to grow. At 1.3× headroom, that comes to about 565 GB per node, more than the 512 GB an M30 supports, so the cluster has to move up to an M40 for the disk. On Atlas Infinite, the cluster stays at the compute tier its queries need, and storage is billed once on the 500 GB it holds. With storage billed once and no tier-up for disk, the total monthly cost of this deployment, Search Nodes included, comes out about 25% lower than on Core. At 1 billion vectors (about 5 TB), it is about 30% lower, and the gap keeps widening as vector data grows. These figures are modeled on list prices in US East, with Search Nodes sized to the smallest tier that fits the index, so your results will vary.

Where the difference is smaller

Text-heavy search workloads also see a TCO benefit on Atlas Infinite, around 5% to 10% cost reduction at multi-terabyte scale. Text compresses well, so Core's storage cost per GB is already low. The advantage of Atlas Infinite comes from deferring early tier-ups and delaying sharding for disk. Under 500 GB, the two deployment options are roughly even on cost, so a smaller workload gets Atlas Infinite’s room to grow without paying more for it. Choose the deployment option based on the elasticity and growth you expect.

Get started with Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite

MongoDB Search and Vector Search are available on Atlas Infinite in public preview on AWS. Choose Atlas Infinite as the deployment option for your next workload, add a search index the way you would on Atlas Core, and keep building on the same foundation as your application grows. Whether you’re prototyping an AI feature or running a large production application, you can start small and keep going. Start with the Atlas Infinite documentation.

title: Jackery and Shopify: Two Paths Through a Portable Power Catalog
description:
Cover: archived official product-page screenshot; capture date not independently confirmed.

Portable-power shoppers do not all enter a store with the same vocabulary. One person searches for a specific battery; another wants backup for a home and has not selected the equipment. On the Jackery US site, the visible navigation separates product type from scenario and offers an additional comparison route. These are observations of the US storefront on 17 November 2026, not evidence of the brand's internal data model, Shopify plan or conversion performance.

Build navigation around the customer's starting question

The product-type path is useful when a shopper knows the category: a power station, solar panel, battery pack or accessory. The scenario path begins with the job, such as home backup or outdoor use. On the reviewed site, the home-backup navigation also names different solution levels. The two paths serve different intents; neither should imply that every item in a scenario is automatically compatible with every other item.

For a Shopify implementation, use navigable collections or landing pages for both entry points, and then let a product detail page explain the specific model and its options. Maintain the relationships behind the page rather than pasting the same long list into every menu. Where a package is selected, identify its actual included products and conditions from the real catalog.

Put a boundary around scenario copy

Scenarios are a discovery aid, not an engineering guarantee. For example, a claimed transfer time alone does not establish that a particular medical device will operate uninterrupted. Do not use scenario tags as a compatibility engine or extrapolate a US product's price and service terms to the UK. Let the exact product, applicable region and current manufacturer documentation govern the content.

Translate names and service promises into decisions

The reviewed navigation contains both HomePower and Explorer names and several version suffixes. A customer may reasonably need help working out whether two names denote the same product, a newer version, or a different kit. An interface can put the full model name beside a short plain-language purpose, and provide a structured comparison of what the buyer receives. The potential confusion is a design hypothesis; the page alone does not show how many customers are confused.

Warranty and membership language also needs its own place in the information hierarchy. The site presents membership benefits and separately lists extended-warranty products. A merchant should distinguish the included warranty, optional paid coverage, eligibility and regional terms, and link to the current policy. Do not promise identical coverage across countries or assume that a membership benefit applies to every purchase.

When an existing customer adds a solar panel or cable, preserve the exact model and generation in the source record. A context-specific link to the relevant accessory can be useful, but the linked item's availability and the manufacturer's compatibility guidance still require checking.

A small Liquid display layer

The sample uses a product metafield custom.purchase_guide referencing a metaobject containing scenario_notes, model_notes and accessory_notes. Each is a merchant-verified multi-line text field. This keeps the scenario, the model and any accessory conditions separate; it does not implement navigation, a selector, purchase logic or compatibility checks.

{%- comment -%}
  Information display example; not production-ready.
  Display merchant-verified text only. This does not determine compatibility,
  electrical safety, medical suitability, inventory, delivery, or runtime.
{%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign guide = product.metafields.custom.purchase_guide.value -%}
{%- if guide != blank -%}
  {%- assign scenario_notes = guide.scenario_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign model_notes = guide.model_notes.value -%}
  {%- assign accessory_notes = guide.accessory_notes.value -%}
  {%- if scenario_notes != blank or model_notes != blank or accessory_notes != blank -%}
<section class="purchase-guide" aria-label="Product information">
  <h2>{{ product.title | escape }}</h2>
  {%- if scenario_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Use cases</h3>
    <p>{{ scenario_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if model_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Model and options</h3>
    <p>{{ model_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
  {%- if accessory_notes != blank %}
  <div class="purchase-guide__item">
    <h3>Accessories and conditions</h3>
    <p>{{ accessory_notes | escape | newline_to_br }}</p>
  </div>
  {%- endif %}
</section>
  {%- endif -%}
{%- endif -%}

Implementation boundaries and tests

The code is an information-display example, not an install-ready production component. It does not evaluate electrical compatibility, calculate runtime, verify certifications, check inventory, promise shipping or create a working configuration flow. Populate fields only after checking the specific model, market and manufacturer documentation. Shopify's admin or an app must create the definitions first; Liquid does not create metafields.

In a development theme, verify a missing reference, an empty entry, every field by itself and a fully populated entry. Empty values must not create empty headings or false defaults. Test special characters, line breaks, narrow screens, keyboard navigation and the theme's heading hierarchy. Verify actual availability, variant behavior and checkout with the real store integrations. No Shopify production-theme, checkout or physical-product test is claimed here.

The example assumes the reference is rendered in the correct template, that its metaobject has the named multi-line plain-text fields, and that the merchant has made the entry available to the storefront. escape treats content as text; newline_to_br retains its line breaks. See Shopify's metafield and metaobject documentation.

How to evaluate the design

Ask a test participant to reach an appropriate product once from a category and once from a situation. Then ask them what is included and which requirements they still need to check. Look for wrong turns and missing context; do not infer conversion gains without measured evidence. Preserve the manufacturer's terms when describing what a package includes.

Source: Jackery US HomePower product page. Its navigation and commercial details can change.

title: I Built a Motion CAPTCHA in Go That Is Harder for AI and Crawlers to Read
description:
Traditional CAPTCHAs are becoming easier for automated systems to interpret. OCR, computer-vision tools, browser automation, and vision-language models can often process static visual challenges.

So I built Gotcha: an open-source, self-hosted motion CAPTCHA library for Go.

Repository: https://github.com/ravikumariitk/gotcha

How it works

Gotcha hides a numeric challenge inside moving visual noise.

A single frame looks like noise, while the answer becomes readable when the animation plays. This makes the challenge harder for basic OCR, single-frame analysis, and simple crawler automation to interpret.

Gotcha is designed to create friction for automated visual reading. It is not marketed as AI-proof, because determined attackers may still use vision models, optical-flow analysis, browser agents, or other techniques.

Features

  • Signed and expiring challenge tokens
  • Replay protection
  • Five-attempt challenge limit
  • MP4 rendering when ffmpeg is available
  • PNG-frame fallback when MP4 encoding is unavailable
  • Configurable colors and textures
  • Self-hosted deployment
  • No external CAPTCHA service required
  • Standard Go HTTP integration
  • MIT licensed

Installation 

go get github.com/ravikumariitk/gotcha@v0.1.0

Basic usage 

package main

import gotcha "github.com/ravikumariitk/gotcha"

func main() {
    gotcha.ConfigureSecret("your-long-random-secret")

    challenge := gotcha.NewChallenge(
        5,
        "standard",
        gotcha.ParseAppearance(
            []string{"#0ea5e9", "#f8fafc"},
            "noise",
        ),
    )

    valid, latency, err := gotcha.VerifyCode(
        challenge.Token,
        "12345",
    )

    _, _, _ = valid, latency, err
}

A real application normally exposes two endpoints:

GET  /challenge
POST /verify

The browser receives the signed token and motion media from /challenge, keeps the token in memory, and submits the token with the user’s answer to /verify.

Important security note

Gotcha is a CAPTCHA and abuse-friction layer, not a complete authentication system.

For production applications, combine it with:

  • Rate limiting
  • MFA or step-up verification
  • Account lockout or throttling
  • Session security
  • Monitoring and alerting
  • Server-side authorization

Challenge state is stored in process memory, so distributed deployments should use request affinity or shared state.

Why open source?

The goal is to make the CAPTCHA mechanism transparent and controllable. Developers can inspect the token format, rendering behavior, verification rules, and fallback behavior instead of depending entirely on a third-party CAPTCHA service.

The motion-noise concept is related to the work documented in DrMikeMaik/GOTCHA, which explores motion-based human-versus-algorithm challenges and attack techniques.

Feedback is welcome—especially from Go developers and security researchers interested in testing the rendering approach and its resistance to automated visual analysis.

Try it 

GOTCHA_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" go run ./examples/login

Then open:

http://localhost:8080

GitHub: https://github.com/ravikumariitk/gotcha
