title: Recording a YouTube live stream with yt-dlp (the flags that actually matter)
description:
If you've tried to grab a YouTube live stream with yt-dlp and ended up with half a broadcast or just an error, the thing to know is that a live stream isn't a finished file - it's an ongoing feed, and a couple of flags decide what you actually get.

Here's what I've landed on.

Just record from now 

yt-dlp "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIDEO_ID"

Point it at a stream that's live and it records from the current moment until the broadcast ends (or you ctrl-c). No special flag needed for a basic capture - the live URL is the same /watch?v= one as any other video.

Catch it from the start 

yt-dlp --live-from-start "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIDEO_ID"

By default yt-dlp joins where the stream currently is, so anything broadcast before you ran the command is gone. --live-from-start rewinds to the beginning. It can pull a lot of data for a long stream and it's slower because it has to walk every fragment, but it's the only way to get the opening.

Wait for a stream that hasn't started yet 

yt-dlp --wait-for-video 30-600 --live-from-start "URL"

A plain command just errors out if the stream isn't live yet. --wait-for-video MIN-MAX keeps re-checking (those are the min/max seconds between checks) and starts the moment it goes live. Handy to leave running ahead of a scheduled premiere.

Keep a playable file if the capture drops 

yt-dlp --live-from-start --hls-use-mpegts -N 4 "URL"

A capture can run for hours, so assume it'll get interrupted. --hls-use-mpegts writes to an MPEG-TS container that stays playable even if the process dies mid-stream, so you keep what you recorded instead of a corrupt file. -N 4 grabs a few fragments at once to keep up with a high-bitrate stream. When it ends cleanly you can --remux-video mp4 if you need something more portable.

The honest caveats

  • A live stream can't be retried. For a normal video a failed fragment is just re-requested. In a live capture there's no going back in time, so if the connection drops for a stretch, that part of the broadcast is simply gone.
  • Some live formats need a PO token now. Missing it shows up as missing formats or a capture that stops after a short while.
  • Keep yt-dlp updated. Player changes break live extraction faster than they break normal downloads - run yt-dlp -U before a scheduled capture, not during one.

Why it's worse on a server

If you're running this from a VPS or a CI runner, you've got two problems stacked. YouTube throttles and blocks datacenter IPs harder than home connections, so a server capture is more likely to hit a mid-stream block. And because a live stream can't be replayed, that block turns into a permanent gap instead of a retry. The free fix is to run captures from a clean residential IP, keep yt-dlp current, and use --live-from-start --hls-use-mpegts so an interruption still leaves a usable partial file.

fwiw I run a hosted API for exactly this "works on my laptop, dies on the server" problem (I built importly.io - you POST a URL and get the file or transcript back from infra that isn't blocked), so if you're capturing from a server and don't want to babysit IPs it might save you some time. For a one-off from your own machine though, the flags above are all you need.

Full writeup with the related guides: https://ytdlp.org/guides/yt-dlp-download-youtube-live

title: A walk through the data structures (DSA) inside cheesedb.dev (a Go database engine for agentic memory)
description:
Some use cases and implementation of data structures and algorithms inside CheeseDB, an embedded database for AI agent memory, written in Go with only the standard library. For each one the page says what it does, why it is there, what would break without it, and links to the exact lines on GitHub:

→ Topological sort for free: ids only go up, so id order already is one.
→ Kahn's in-degree trick: one counter per leg instead of rechecking every parent.
→ BFS with a queue: a recall walks down the graph, no recursion.
→ DP on a DAG: one pass in id order finds everything a crash left half-erased.
→ Min-heap: top-k search in about 30 lines.
→ Swap-remove: delete from a packed array in O(1).
→ Branch and bound: skip disk reads that a rounded score proves can't win.
→ Binary search: a lower bound over a sorted table.
→ Producer–consumer: one goroutine batches many writes into one fsync.

If you are learning DSA, the best next step is reading one real file. internal/ledger/state.go is about 300 lines: just the graph, no disk, no locks.

https://cheesedb.dev/inside.html

title: Amazon API Gateway REST APIs now support JWT authorizers
description:
Amazon API Gateway now offers a native JWT authorizer for REST APIs, a new authorizer type that validates JSON Web Tokens directly in the gateway. Until now, validating tokens from an OpenID Connect or OAuth 2.0 identity provider other than Amazon Cognito required a Lambda authorizer. You now configure token validation instead of writing and operating code for it.

You can define one or more issuers, the audiences accepted for each, the signing algorithms you permit, and any additional claims a token may present. API Gateway verifies each token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and claims on every request. You can attach one authorizer to many methods and require different scopes on each. This fits machine-to-machine APIs, mobile and web backends, and multi-tenant APIs that accept tokens from several identity providers.

The JWT authorizer works on Regional, edge-optimized, and private REST APIs, and is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see Amazon API Gateway documentation and AWS blog post.

title: loadtest: an HTTP load tester in Rust that does not hide server stalls
description:
You have an HTTP service and two questions about it: how many requests per second can it take, and what does the slow end of the latency look like? The average is rarely the interesting number. Users remember the request that took a second, so the numbers that matter are p99 and p99.9.

Most quick load tests work the same way. They open a fixed number of connections, and each connection sends a request, waits for the answer, and sends the next one. This is called the closed model. It is simple, and it has a blind spot: when the server freezes, the load tester freezes with it. It sends nothing during the stall, so it records almost nothing bad. The report looks clean exactly when the server behaved worst. This effect has a name, coordinated omission.

loadtest is an HTTP load tester in the spirit of wrk, wrk2 and oha, built on Tokio and hyper. It can run the closed model, or a fixed request rate (the open model) that does not hide server stalls. Latency goes into an HDR histogram, and you get percentiles up to p99.9, a status-code breakdown, error classes, a live terminal view while it runs and a JSON report at the end.

The README says who it is for: backend developers who want a single small binary to measure a local or staging HTTP service, and people curious about why closed-loop benchmarks lie about tail latency.

What it does

Two load models. By default, -c N connections send requests back to back until -n requests are done or the -z duration ends. Adding -q R sets a target rate in requests per second and switches to the open model. There, -c becomes the maximum number of requests in flight.

A full latency picture. Min, mean, standard deviation and max, then p50, p75, p90, p95, p99 and p99.9, plus a ten-bucket histogram in the text report.

Status codes and errors. Responses are counted per status code. Failures are classed by kind, for example timeout when a request passes the -t limit, or a refused connection.

A live view. In a terminal, a ratatui screen shows progress, requests per second (last second and overall), the current percentiles, status codes, errors and a requests-per-second sparkline. q, Esc or Ctrl-C stops early and still prints the report.

A JSON report. --json prints the same numbers as JSON, with the histogram buckets and a per-second timeline, and -o file writes it to a file. That makes it easy to keep results from a CI job or compare two runs.

Real requests. You can set the method (-m), headers (-H 'K: V'), a body (-d) or a body from a file (-D file).

How to use it

Install it from GitHub with Cargo:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/loadtest --locked

The repository includes a small target server as an example, so from a clone you can try everything locally:

cargo build --release
cargo run --release --example hello_server -- 8080 &      # a local target

loadtest http://127.0.0.1:8080/ -n 50000 -c 50            # closed model, 50 connections
loadtest http://127.0.0.1:8080/ -z 30s -q 2000 -c 200     # open model, 2000 req/s
loadtest http://127.0.0.1:8080/api -m POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
         -d '{"x":1}' -n 1000 --json > report.json

The flags, in short:

  • -n N or -z 30s: stop after N requests (default 200) or after a duration.
  • -c N: connections (closed) or max requests in flight (open), default 50.
  • -q R: target rate in requests per second, which switches to the open model.
  • -t 20s: per-request timeout, counted as the error timeout.
  • --json, -o file: JSON report on stdout and/or to a file.
  • --no-tui: no live view. It is also off when stdout is not a terminal.

Why the open model matters

The README has a demonstration that is worth repeating, because it is the reason the tool exists. The bundled hello_server has a /stall route that freezes for one second every five seconds.

Six seconds with one connection, closed model:

  min 0.088  mean 0.171  stdev 5.369  max 1001.983
  p50 0.130  p75 0.159  p90 0.195  p95 0.218  p99 0.272  p99.9 1.550

Six seconds at 200 requests per second, open model:

  min 0.287  mean 105.567  stdev 228.500  max 1000.959
  p50 0.504  p75 4.053  p90 450.559  p95 702.975  p99 941.567  p99.9 996.863

Both runs saw the one-second freeze: the max is about 1000 ms in each. But the closed run sent nothing while its only connection was stuck, so the freeze is a single sample out of 34,810 and p99 looks perfect at 0.272 ms. The open run kept its schedule, so every request that was due during a freeze waited, and p90, p95 and p99 show what users would actually have felt.

These numbers come from the README's own run with client and server on the same laptop. They say nothing about your service. What they show is the difference between the two models on the same server.

How it works

  • The runner uses one hyper_util pooled client. In the closed model, c tasks loop: send, read the whole body, record. In the open model, a dispatcher sleeps until start + i/rate and spawns request i. The request waits for one of c slots, and its latency is measured from the moment the dispatcher fired. So time spent waiting for a slot, which means the server is slow, counts. The dispatcher never waits for responses, which is how it keeps the schedule during a stall.
  • The stats are a mutex-protected hdrhistogram covering 1 µs to 1 hour with 3 significant digits, plus status and error counters, bytes and per-second completions.
  • The live view is redrawn every 100 ms from a snapshot and runs on its own thread.

Things to know

  • http:// only. No TLS, no HTTP/2, no HTTP/3.
  • One URL per run. No request files and no scripting.
  • The generator has limits. The open model spawns a task per request. At very high rates on one machine, the generator itself becomes the bottleneck and latencies climb. The README notes that on the author's laptop it holds 5,000 requests per second, but not 20,000.
  • What latency includes. Reading the full body is included, and so is connection setup for new connections. There is no warm-up phase and no per-phase breakdown (DNS, connect, time to first byte).
  • Recording takes a mutex per request, which the README describes as fine up to tens of thousands of requests per second.

What is tested. cargo test runs 5 unit tests (the recorder, the text and JSON report, histogram buckets adding up, duration parsing, and the TUI rendered into ratatui's TestBackend) and 8 integration tests against a local hyper server. Those check that exactly n requests reach the server, the status-code breakdown, that duration mode stops on time, that the open model hits its target rate, timeout and connection-refused classification, and that method, headers and body are sent. One test checks the main claim directly: the open model exposes a 500 ms stall that the closed model's p99 hides.

Why I built it

Because a load test that reports a good p99 while the server was frozen is worse than no load test: it gives you a number to trust. The closed model is the default in many tools and in most hand-written scripts, and its blind spot is not obvious until you see the two outputs side by side.

I wanted a small tool where the open model is one flag away, where latency is measured from the moment the request was dispatched and not from the moment a connection became free, and where a test in the repository proves the difference. The rest, the histogram, the live view and the JSON report, is what makes it comfortable to use every day on a local or staging service.

Get the code

The source, the example server and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/loadtest. It is MIT licensed. Point it only at services you own or are allowed to test.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: MySQL to Databricks: Replicate the Binlog Into Unity Catalog in Seven Steps
description:
Databricks is where the joins, the notebooks and the models run. The orders they depend on are written in MySQL, one row at a time, all day long. How those rows get from MySQL to Databricks decides whether a status that flipped this morning is visible this afternoon, or only after tonight's reload.

The common ways to move the data:

  • Dump and load. mysqldump or SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE writes files to a cloud bucket, and COPY INTO or Auto Loader picks them up. You keep an export script, a bucket and a Databricks job. Freshness is hours to daily, and a changed or deleted row only arrives through a full reload or a merge you write.
  • Debezium and Kafka, read with Structured Streaming. Changes show up in seconds. The price is Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium and a Databricks job that stays running, plus your own merge logic for updates and deletes.
  • Lakeflow Connect. Databricks lists MySQL among its managed change data capture (CDC) connectors. It runs on Databricks serverless compute with nothing to host, and the rows land in streaming tables governed by Unity Catalog.

This post walks through a fourth option. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, reads the MySQL binary log (binlog) directly and commits the rows as Apache Iceberg tables into Unity Catalog. Databricks shows them as managed Iceberg tables, and DuckDB and Spark can query the same files through the same catalog.

I ran every step below against MySQL 8.4 and a Databricks workspace on Google Cloud, with OLake Go v1.1.0. The snapshot of 48 records took 25 seconds, and a change sync of 12 records took 22 seconds. Each figure in this post is from that run.

The MySQL to Databricks pipeline at a glance

  • Source: a MySQL database called shop with two tables, customers and orders, and the binlog on in ROW format
  • Writer: OLake UI from its Docker Compose install, with one job in Full Refresh + CDC mode
  • Catalog: Unity Catalog, which keeps the tables as managed Iceberg tables in the catalog's managed storage
  • Readers: the Databricks SQL editor on a 2X-Small serverless SQL warehouse, then DuckDB 1.5.5

You need: MySQL 5.7 or later, a Databricks workspace with Unity Catalog, an admin who can turn on external data access, Docker, and about 30 minutes.

Step 1: Prepare MySQL for CDC

OLake Go reads the same stream that MySQL replicas use. The server needs the binlog on with a server_id, the ROW format and FULL row metadata. These lines go in my.cnf, followed by a restart:

server-id = 1
log_bin = mysql-bin
binlog_format = ROW
binlog_row_metadata = FULL
binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 604800

Statement-based logging does not carry row images, which is why the format has to be ROW. The last line keeps 7 days of binlog, so a paused job can catch up. On Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), Aurora, Azure or Cloud SQL, the same settings live in a parameter group or a server setting instead of my.cnf.

To replay my data, create the two tables. Skip this block if you are pointing at tables you already have:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(200), city VARCHAR(100), tier VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT, product VARCHAR(100), amount DECIMAL(10,2), status VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id));

Insert whatever rows you like. Mine held 8 customers and 40 orders, and the statements in step 7 update two customers named Liam Carter and Zara Ali.

Next comes the user OLake Go logs in as, fresh table statistics, and a check of the result:

CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'olake'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '<password>';
GRANT SELECT, REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT ON *.* TO 'olake'@'%';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

-- Table statistics: the chunked snapshot plans its chunks from them
ANALYZE TABLE customers, orders;

SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('log_bin', 'binlog_format', 'binlog_row_metadata', 'server_id');
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'olake'@'%';

⚠️ Do not drop the ANALYZE TABLE line. The first sync splits each table into parallel chunks using table statistics, and a freshly created or freshly loaded table has none. Without them the sync stops with stats not populated for table[shop.orders]. Please run ANALYZE TABLE to update table statistics.

Step 2: Set up Unity Catalog in Databricks

OLake Go writes through Unity Catalog's Iceberg representational state transfer (REST) endpoint. Databricks allows writes through that endpoint for managed Iceberg tables only (Databricks: access tables from Iceberg clients). The workspace needs four things, set once:

What Where Why
External data access on the metastore Catalog, the gear icon, Metastore Without it the endpoint refuses every client that is not Databricks itself
A catalog with managed storage Catalog, Create catalog OLake Go creates one schema per job inside it
EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA for the writing principal On the catalog Unity Catalog checks it before it serves a table to an outside engine
A personal access token Settings, Developer, Access tokens It goes out as a bearer token on every catalog call

Then run the grants in the Databricks SQL editor, with your own principal in place of the example:

-- The catalog OLake Go writes into. Its managed storage holds the Iceberg files.
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS lakehouse MANAGED LOCATION '<external location URL>/lakehouse';

-- What the writing principal needs: browse and create schemas, then read and write tables in them
GRANT USE CATALOG, CREATE SCHEMA ON CATALOG lakehouse TO `olake@example.com`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE, SELECT, MODIFY ON CATALOG lakehouse TO `olake@example.com`;
GRANT EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA ON CATALOG lakehouse TO `olake@example.com`;

Granting on the catalog means every schema created later inherits the privileges. In my workspace the catalog was called datazip, and the token expired after seven days. The SQL in this post says lakehouse, so put your own catalog name in its place.

⚠️ ALL PRIVILEGES does not contain EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, and only the catalog owner can grant it (Databricks: Unity Catalog privileges). Even a catalog owner has to grant it explicitly.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and connect MySQL 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and log in with admin / password.

  1. Open Sources, click Create Source and pick MySQL as the connector. Name the source and keep the OLake Go version on the latest release.
  2. Under Change data capture (CDC), leave Enable CDC on. The default Initial Wait Time is fine.
  3. Under Connection details, enter the host, port, database name, username and password.
  4. Click Set up source.

My MySQL ran in another container, so the host was host.docker.internal. The database was shop, the user was olake from step 1, and SSL was disabled for the local test.

Set up source tests the connection and then runs four binlog checks before anything is saved: binlog_access, log_bin, binlog_format and binlog_row_metadata. If one fails, the dialog names the setting and shows its recommended value.

Step 4: Add the Unity Catalog destination

Open Destinations and click Create Destination. Pick Apache Iceberg as the connector, Unity as the catalog type and Personal Access Token as the authentication type.

Field Value
REST Catalog URL https://<workspace-url>/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg-rest
Unity Catalog Name lakehouse, the catalog from step 2
Token the personal access token from step 2

Click Create. OLake Go calls the endpoint with the token and saves the destination. A permission error here points back to step 2: external data access is off, the principal lacks EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, or the catalog name is wrong.

Step 5: Create the job and run the first sync

  1. Open Jobs and click Create Job. I named mine mysql_to_databricks. Give it a schedule, either Every Day at a fixed hour or a cron expression.
  2. Select the MySQL source and the Unity destination.
  3. Under Advanced Settings, set Target Query Engines to Databricks, plus DuckDB and Apache Spark if they will read the tables too.
  4. Click Next. OLake Go discovers the tables and opens the Streams page.
  5. Tick customers and orders. Set the sync mode to Full Refresh + CDC and the ingestion mode to Upsert, and leave the Upsert Type alone.
  6. Click Create Job, then open the job's menu and choose Sync Now.

The third item is the one Databricks cares about. Under Unity Catalog, Databricks reads Iceberg v3 deletion vectors and rejects commits that carry equality deletes. With Databricks in the list, the Upsert Type on both streams was already Deletion Vector, so there was no format for me to pick.

The first sync copied 8 customers and 40 orders (48 records, 2.10 KB) in 25 seconds, container start included. It notes the current binlog position first and then reads each table in parallel chunks, so a row written during the copy is not lost.

The schema name comes from the job and the source database: job mysql_to_databricks on database shop gave mysql_to_databricks_shop. To choose your own, edit the Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page before the first sync.

Step 6: Query the tables in Databricks

Nothing has to be registered. The tables are managed Iceberg tables in the catalog, and the SQL editor or a notebook reads them by three-part name:

SHOW TABLES IN lakehouse.mysql_to_databricks_shop;

SELECT id, name, city, tier
FROM lakehouse.mysql_to_databricks_shop.customers
ORDER BY id;

SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(sum(amount), 2) AS total
FROM lakehouse.mysql_to_databricks_shop.orders
GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

A 2X-Small serverless SQL warehouse was plenty for these checks. DESCRIBE EXTENDED on either table shows the Iceberg provider and the deletion vectors in its properties.

OLake Go adds four columns to every table: _olake_id (a hash of the primary key), _op_type, _olake_timestamp and _cdc_timestamp. MySQL tables get two more, _cdc_binlog_file_name and _cdc_binlog_file_pos.

Step 7: Change rows in MySQL and sync again

A full copy proves little. These are the 12 changes I made in MySQL after the first sync, 7 inserts and 5 updates:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  ('Maya Patel', 'maya@example.com', 'Pune', 'silver'),
  ('Lucas Silva', 'lucas@example.com', 'São Paulo', 'bronze');
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product, amount, status) VALUES
  (9, 'Laptop', 1299.00, 'placed'), (9, 'Mouse', 25.50, 'placed'),
  (10, 'Monitor', 349.99, 'placed'), (3, 'Keyboard', 89.00, 'placed'), (7, 'Webcam', 79.90, 'placed');
UPDATE customers SET tier = 'gold',      updated_at = NOW() WHERE name = 'Liam Carter';
UPDATE customers SET city = 'Abu Dhabi', updated_at = NOW() WHERE name = 'Zara Ali';
UPDATE orders    SET status = 'delivered', updated_at = NOW() WHERE id IN (1, 4, 7);

Choose Sync Now a second time. This sync read 12 records (563 bytes) from the binlog and finished in 22 seconds end to end.

For customers, the sync wrote one new data file holding 4 rows: the 2 inserts and the new versions of the 2 updated rows. One deletion vector, a small bitmap per data file that marks replaced positions, retires the 2 old versions. The commit report in the sync log says the same thing: addedDataFiles=1, addedRecords=4, addedDVs=1 and addedPositionalDeletes=2.

orders has the same shape, with 8 rows and 3 deleted positions, and the equality delete count stays at 0.

Now run the SELECT from step 6 again, without any refresh. Liam Carter is gold, Zara Ali has moved to Abu Dhabi, and the two new customers are in the result.

The _op_type column records how each row arrived: r for the 6 untouched snapshot rows, c for the 2 inserts and u for the 2 updates. A delete is marked d. The orders roll-up matched MySQL to the cent: 16 delivered orders for 8659.68, 18 placed for 10522.26 and 11 shipped for 6397.25.

Schema changes. A column added in MySQL is added to the Iceberg table on the next sync, and the new schema is committed to Unity Catalog. Widening changes such as int to bigint are applied. Narrowing ones fail the sync rather than corrupt the table.

Read the same tables from DuckDB

DuckDB attaches the Unity Catalog catalog as an Iceberg REST catalog with the same token. Unity Catalog hands it short-lived storage credentials per table, so DuckDB needs no cloud keys of its own.

INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;
CREATE SECRET unity (TYPE iceberg, TOKEN '<personal access token>');
ATTACH 'lakehouse' AS uc (
  TYPE iceberg,
  ENDPOINT 'https://<workspace-url>/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg-rest',
  SECRET unity,
  ACCESS_DELEGATION_MODE 'vended_credentials'
);
SELECT id, name, city, tier
FROM uc.mysql_to_databricks_shop.customers
ORDER BY id;

DuckDB 1.5.5 returned the same 10 customers and the same orders roll-up as Databricks. Spark 4.0.1 with Iceberg 1.10.0 did too, through the same endpoint. The principal behind the token needs EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA for these readers as well.

Data types worth a look

MySQL Databricks shows Note
int, mediumint, smallint, tinyint INT
bigint BIGINT
decimal(p,s) DOUBLE round at query time when you need exact decimal arithmetic
float FLOAT
datetime, timestamp TIMESTAMP Coordinated Universal Time (UTC); datetime has no zone in MySQL and is read as UTC
enum, json, time, bit(1), text types STRING time arrives as text

In my run DESCRIBE showed orders.amount as DOUBLE, and its sums still matched MySQL to the cent.

Tips and limits

  • Keep the binlog longer than your longest pause. MySQL deletes binlog files after binlog_expire_logs_seconds, and a job paused beyond that needs a fresh snapshot. Seven days of binlog on a busy server can be tens of gigabytes, so size the disk for it.
  • Tables need a primary key. Without one, inserts replicate, but updates and deletes cannot be matched to a row and are not applied. Add a primary key or a unique index first.
  • These are Iceberg tables, not Delta tables. If a pipeline needs native Delta Lake features on these rows, load them into a Delta table downstream.
  • Freshness is a schedule, down to one minute, not a continuous stream.
  • A null-path error points at the delete format. Can not create a Path from a null string [ErrorCode: 2015] is what Unity Catalog returns when a client commits equality delete files. Set Databricks as a target query engine and start that table again from a full refresh.

How the MySQL to Databricks methods compare

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where the data lands What you run
Lakeflow Connect MySQL connector CDC, run by Databricks yes, through CDC streaming tables governed by Unity Catalog nothing to host; Databricks serverless compute
Debezium, Kafka and Structured Streaming seconds yes, with your own merge logic Kafka topics, then tables written by a Databricks streaming job Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium and a running Databricks job
mysqldump or INTO OUTFILE, then COPY INTO or Auto Loader hours to daily no; full reloads or your own merge tables written by a Databricks job an export script, a bucket and a Databricks job
OLake Go into Unity Catalog (this post) CDC on a schedule down to one minute yes, as deletion vectors Iceberg tables that Databricks, DuckDB and Spark all read one Docker Compose stack, open source; your storage and your own compute

Lakeflow Connect is the simpler choice when Databricks is the only reader and you want Databricks to run the pipeline. The route in this post makes sense once a second engine needs the same rows, because the tables are written once and nobody makes a second copy.

FAQ

Does this work with MySQL on RDS, Aurora, Azure or Cloud SQL?

Yes. Hosted MySQL works the same way as a server you run yourself. The only difference is that the binlog settings go in a parameter group or a server setting, not in my.cnf.

What are the _cdc_binlog_file_name and _cdc_binlog_file_pos columns for?

They record where in the binlog each changed row came from. MySQL tables carry them on top of the four columns every OLake Go table has. Leave them out of dashboards, or use them when you want to see which binlog file a change was read from.

Should I change the Initial Wait Time on the source?

Usually not. The default is fine, and 10 seconds was enough for my two-table database. Raise it only if the binlog is large and a later sync times out while finding its saved position.

Who compacts the tables and expires old snapshots?

Unity Catalog does both on managed Iceberg tables when predictive optimization is on (Databricks: Iceberg tables). Check that it is enabled for the catalog you write to. Spark's rewrite_data_files also works through the same Unity Catalog endpoint.

Where to go from here

  • Point the source at a real database, and size the binlog volume for the retention you chose.
  • Before production, replace the personal access token with a service principal that uses OAuth machine-to-machine credentials. An expired token fails the next sync at its first catalog call.
  • The Spark connection, the command line setup and the full type mapping are in the MySQL to Databricks guide on olake.io.

If something behaves differently on your workspace, drop the exact error text in the comments and I will take a look.

title: Shipping chat mockups from your terminal: an MCP server for realistic message screenshots
description:
Most teams need a realistic chat screenshot long before they need a production chat backend. A landing page that promises "your messages, everywhere" but shows a grey rectangle of lorem ipsum reads as a half-finished product. Hand-built Figma mockups work right up until someone asks for a third platform, a dark mode variant, or a change in the copy at 6pm on a Friday.

MockupChat takes that job away from the design file: it renders conversations for 16 messaging apps (WhatsApp, iMessage, Discord, Slack, Telegram, Tinder, TikTok, and friends) with platform-accurate bubbles, ticks, tails, read receipts and status bars, then exports a PNG — or an MP4 that plays the conversation out message by message.

The interesting part for this audience: it is not locked inside a web UI. There is a public REST API and a stateless MCP server, so an agent can compose a conversation, validate it, and hand back an editor link without a human opening a browser tab.

Wiring it into an agent

The MCP endpoint is a single streamable HTTP URL. No auth, no key, no account:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mockupchat": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://mockupchat.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}

Five tools are exposed, and they are scoped deliberately small:

Tool What it gives you
list_platforms The 16 platform skins, their capabilities, and where the free/Pro export boundary sits
list_templates Public templates, filterable by platform or name, paginated
get_template One template as editable chat JSON plus a link that opens it in the editor
compose_chat Up to 8 participants and 40 messages, with validated senders and dates
validate_chat Checks a version-1 chat document without saving, fetching media or rendering

A typical agent loop looks like this:

  1. list_platforms to confirm the platform and its export rules.
  2. list_templates to find a starting point for the tone you need (a support thread, a launch announcement, a group chat).
  3. compose_chat with the script you wrote — it validates participant ids and timestamps for you.
  4. validate_chat if you assembled the JSON by hand.
  5. Open the returned editorUrl, review it, export.

The REST route, when you do not want MCP

Same data, plain HTTP, if you are wiring this into a build script rather than an agent:

curl https://mockupchat.com/api/v1/compose \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "platform": "whatsapp",
    "title": "Fictional launch demo",
    "participants": [
      {"id": "me", "name": "Alex", "isMe": true},
      {"id": "sam", "name": "Sam", "isMe": false}
    ],
    "messages": [
      {"senderId": "sam", "text": "Ready for the demo?", "at": "2026-10-15T09:41"}
    ]
  }'

The response contains the chat document and an editorUrl. The API hands you a document and a link — it does not render images server-side. Export stays in the browser, which keeps the service simple and keeps your content off a server.

There is an OpenAPI 3.1 spec at https://mockupchat.com/openapi.json if you would rather generate a client.

The rules that matter

Invented content only. The service is for fictional conversations: demos, lessons, marketing mockups, stories. Not for repackaging a real person's messages, and not for anything that looks like a genuine quote from a real customer. The API response carries a fictional provenance marker, and you are expected to keep that label when you publish.

Free means watermarked. Exporting a PNG for WhatsApp, iMessage or Instagram works without an account, with a small watermark. Other platforms, device frames, social formats (1080×1350, 1080×1920) and silent MP4 export are part of Pro.

The MCP server has no access to you. No OAuth, no scopes, no project access, no uploaded files. It only ever sees the chat you send it.

Rate limits exist. 64 KiB per request, 60 requests per minute per IP per Cloudflare location, shared across MCP and API. A 429 comes with a Retry-When header.

Editor links are readable by anyone who has them. Conversation data is encoded in the URL fragment, so treat those links as shareable artifacts, not secrets.

When it is the wrong tool

If you need a real chat backend, real users, real message history — none of this applies. This is a mockup and content generator. And if you need pixel-perfect control over every bubble, a design file is still the better tool. The sweet spot is the middle: a convincing conversation, generated in seconds, in a format you can drop into an ad, a deck, an app store page or an onboarding flow.

title: Audit-Friendly Email Verification APIs
description:
A practical design for email verification endpoints that remain explainable when retries, delayed messages, and support questions arrive together.

Email verification looks like a small authentication feature until a production incident asks a simple question: why was this account still unverified after the user clicked the link?

The answer is often spread across an API log, a message provider, a worker queue, and a database row. When each component has a slightly different idea of the current state, the endpoint may work in the happy path but become difficult to operate. My preferred approach is to make the verification workflow an explicit, auditable boundary in the backend.

Why verification APIs become hard to audit

Most implementations begin with three actions:

  1. Create a verification token.
  2. Send an email containing the token.
  3. Mark the user as verified when the token is opened.

The hidden complexity is in the transitions between those actions. A client can retry the create request. A worker can deliver the same message twice. A user can click an old link after requesting a new one. The email can arrive after the token has been revoked. If the system only records verified = true, these cases collapse into one vague outcome.

The useful design question is not “did the email send?” It is “which verification attempt owns this result, and can I prove the transition?”

For engineers maintaining an API, this distinction saves time during support work. It also makes automated tests less dependent on reading an inbox by guesswork. A clear pattern for validating approval emails in CI is useful here: treat the message as evidence for a state transition, not as the state itself.

Model the workflow as a state machine

Give each verification attempt an identifier and a small set of allowed states. For example:

created -> sent -> opened -> accepted
                    \-> expired
                    \-> revoked

The exact names are less important than the ownership rules. An attempt should not move from expired back to accepted, and a second click on an already accepted token should be safe and predictable. This is where many implementations gets vague: they validate the token, then update the user without checking the attempt's current state.

I normally keep these fields together:

  • verification_id: a public correlation identifier
  • user_id: the account being verified
  • token_digest: a hash of the secret, never the raw token
  • state: the current state of the attempt
  • expires_at: the acceptance deadline
  • created_at and updated_at: transition evidence
  • accepted_at: when the account actually became verified

Keep the raw token only long enough to put it in the message. The database needs the digest, so a leaked row does not become a ready-made login link. This small detail is easy to miss during a quick implementation.

Use PostgreSQL as the source of truth

The user record and verification attempt should be updated with a deliberate transaction boundary. A typical acceptance operation is:

  1. Hash the presented token.
  2. Lock the matching attempt row.
  3. Check its state and expiration timestamp.
  4. Transition the attempt to accepted.
  5. Mark the user as verified.
  6. Commit both changes together.

The row lock matters when two requests arrive nearly together. Without it, both requests can observe sent and both can claim success. The second request should instead receive an idempotent result or a clear conflict, depending on your product contract.

An audit table can record verification_id, prior state, next state, request identifier, and a reason code. Do not store the token in that table. The audit record is for explaining behavior, not for reconstructing secrets.

You also want a uniqueness rule for active attempts, or a documented policy for multiple attempts. Replacing the old token without marking it revoked is a common source of “which link should work?” incidents. The database should make the answer unambiguous.

Design the REST API around safe retries

The create endpoint should accept an idempotency key from the client. Store the key with the resulting verification attempt, and return the same response when a request is retried. This keeps a network timeout from creating several valid messages for one user.

The acceptance endpoint can use a response model like this:

{
  "verification_id": "ver_8f2c",
  "status": "accepted",
  "message": "Email verification completed"
}

For an already accepted attempt, returning the same successful status is often friendlier than treating a browser refresh as an error. For an expired or revoked attempt, return a stable application error code, not a detailed explanation of whether a token existed. This reduces information leakage while giving the frontend something actionable.

The logs should connect the request ID, verification ID, and state transition. They should not log the token, full verification URL, or the complete email address. Authentication email design also benefits from setting safer boundaries around authentication emails, especially when links cross browser sessions or providers.

Keep test email data inside an explicit boundary

Integration tests need a mailbox that behaves consistently, but test data should still have a lifecycle. Use a dedicated test domain or temp org mail fixture, tag every message with the test run, and delete or quarantine messages when the run ends. Do not let a shared inbox become an accidental database for tokens.

For tests, assert the important chain rather than only checking that a message exists:

  • the API returns one verification ID for a retried create request;
  • the message contains the expected verification ID;
  • the acceptance request changes exactly one attempt;
  • a second acceptance is safe;
  • an expired token cannot verify the account;
  • the audit record explains each transition.

This test shape catches races that a basic “open email and click link” script will miss. It also makes failures easier to reproduce locally.

A practical implementation checklist

Before shipping an email verification API, check that:

  • token secrets are stored as digests;
  • state transitions are validated inside a transaction;
  • concurrent acceptance requests cannot both perform the first transition;
  • create requests support safe retries;
  • expiration and revocation are explicit states;
  • logs contain correlation IDs but no secrets;
  • test messages have an owner and deletion policy;
  • metrics distinguish sent, opened, accepted, expired, and rejected attempts.

The goal is not to build a complicated workflow engine. It is to make a small authentication boundary honest about state, ownership, and time. When an email is delayed or a client retries, the REST API should still tell one consistent story, and PostgreSQL should be able to prove how that story happened.

title: Building Secure Authentication: Important Practices for Backend Developers
description:
Authentication is a fundamental part of modern web application development. Whether it is a task management platform, an e-commerce website, or a personal dashboard, applications need a reliable way to identify users and control access to their information.

While developing an Authentication System as part of my internship learning at Valentius Kryptix, I explored how backend technologies can work together to create a secure and structured authentication process.

The project focuses on understanding user registration, password security, token-based authentication, and protected API endpoints using Node.js and Express.js.

Why Authentication Matters

Authentication is more than simply checking an email address and password. It establishes whether a user is allowed to access an application. Without proper authentication, sensitive information and user-specific resources may become accessible to unauthorized people.

A good authentication design should validate user input, protect credentials, manage login sessions, and reject unauthorized requests.

The Role of Backend Technologies

Node.js provides the runtime environment for the backend, while Express.js makes it easier to create API endpoints and organize request handling.

PostgreSQL can be used to store user information in a structured relational database. For password security, bcryptjs provides password hashing functionality. Instead of storing plain-text passwords, the application stores password hashes and verifies login attempts against those hashes.

JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provide another important part of the process. After successful authentication, a backend can issue a signed token. The client can then include this token when requesting access to protected API endpoints.

Understanding the Authentication Flow

A typical authentication flow begins when a user registers with valid details. The backend validates the input, checks for an existing account, hashes the password, and stores the relevant information.

During login, the backend verifies the submitted credentials. If they are correct, it generates an authentication token with an appropriate expiration time.

For protected routes, authentication middleware checks the token before allowing a request to continue. Missing, invalid, or expired tokens should result in an unauthorized response.

Additional features such as email verification and password recovery can further improve account security. These processes should use secure, time-limited tokens and appropriate validation.

Important Security Lessons

This work helped me understand some important backend security practices:

Never store passwords in plain text.

Validate user input before processing requests.

Use secure password hashing techniques.

Set appropriate JWT expiration times.

Protect private API routes with authentication middleware.

Keep database credentials and JWT secrets in environment variables.

Test both successful and unsuccessful authentication scenarios.

Security should be considered throughout development rather than added as an afterthought.

Conclusion

Working on an Authentication System has helped me connect theoretical backend concepts with practical API development. Understanding password hashing, JWT authentication, middleware, and database integration has strengthened my knowledge of building secure backend applications.

This is an ongoing learning journey, and I look forward to applying these practices in more real-world projects.

title: Node.js Video Generation Cancellation — Durable Job IDs and Audit Control
description:
For a promo-video service, the bill is driven first by generation work that has been accepted and is still running, not by the few bytes needed to remember its state. Persist the provider's job ID at submission time, expose an idempotent cancel action, and append the actor and target to an audit record. That is the short answer: a bad prompt must remain stoppable after the browser tab, Express process, or deployment that submitted it has disappeared.

The storage decision follows from that answer. Keep a small control record for each request; do not keep every intermediate rendition merely because storage looks harmless beside generation. A useful cost model is total = generation work + retained bytes over time + delivery, and the first term dominates while an accidental job runs. Cancelling changes that term immediately. Retention policy changes the second term later.

This is also where vendor portability becomes concrete rather than aspirational. Application code should own a stable submit/status/cancel contract and an internal job ID, while an adapter owns the provider job ID and provider-specific HTTP path. Switching the implementation behind that interface then changes an adapter and migration procedure, not every controller, database query, and UI button.

Infrai is a concrete fit at that adapter boundary when the team wants one REST contract to cover video submission, status, and cancellation while retaining the option to change the vendor routed behind it. Its public discovery surface describes the current schema and vendor readiness, so the contract can be checked rather than inferred from marketing copy.

That distinction matters.

How should a Node.js service cancel a running video generation job?

At minimum, the durable record needs an application job ID, the provider name, the provider job ID, current state, creation time, and cancellation fields. The cancellation fields should include who requested it and when. Record the audit intent before making the remote call, then record the result; otherwise a process crash can leave an expensive action with no accountable trace.

Do not use an in-memory map as the source of truth. It loses the only handle required by POST /v1/video/cancel/{id} during a restart, exactly when an operator is trying to stop work. Consider the full sequence: the API accepts a request, the provider returns an ID, Express responds to the browser, a deployment replaces the process, and then an operator notices that the prompt named the wrong product. If the ID lived only in process memory, the cancellation button has nothing authoritative to send; if it was committed before the response, any healthy instance can resolve the internal record, verify the tenant, append the actor's intent, and call the adapter. A relational table is adequate because this is control-plane state, not media payload. Put the generated object in private object storage and issue a presigned URL when an authorized user needs it; never turn the control record into a public media URL.

One practical state machine is submitted -> running -> completed, with cancel_requested allowed from the first two states and cancelled recorded after the provider confirms the action. A completion racing with cancellation is ordinary distributed-systems behavior. Treat the provider's observed state as evidence, retain the cancellation request as audit history, and avoid rewriting history to pretend the race never happened.

The following client is deliberately small. It shows the remote boundary that a Node.js/Express controller would call through an adapter, while keeping the example in Python so the retry and error behavior are visible in one place. It uses the verified cancel route, sends no invented request fields, sets the HTTP method explicitly, and retries a rate limit without spinning.

import os
import time
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def retry_delay(response: requests.Response, attempt: int) -> float:
    value = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
    if value:
        try:
            return max(0.0, float(value))
        except ValueError:
            retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
            return max(0.0, (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
    return min(2 ** attempt, 30)


def cancel_video(provider_job_id: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"{BASE_URL}/video/cancel/{provider_job_id}",
            headers=headers,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            break
        time.sleep(retry_delay(response, attempt))
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("Cancellation remained rate-limited after five attempts")

    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Cancellation failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text}"
        )
    return response.json()

Cancellation is safe enough to expose as a direct UI action without a confirmation ceremony because repeating the intent should converge on the same outcome: stop this job. The application still needs to serialize its own state update, however. Use a transaction or compare-and-set so two clicks do not create contradictory audit rows, and key the operation by the application job ID. Idempotence does not mean invisibility; both the first request and repeated attempts can be attributable without pretending they represent separate cancellations.

Persist first. Respond second.

The storage bill is mostly a retention-policy question

Smart cropping one source image into several aspect ratios creates a tempting pile of derivatives: square, portrait, landscape, thumbnails, plus old revisions after a marketer edits the crop. The expensive mistake is retaining all of them indefinitely without distinguishing reproducible cache objects from source assets and published outputs.

Use three classes. Preserve the private source while the customer or compliance policy requires it. Preserve the selected published output for the campaign's lifetime. Treat alternate crops, previews, and abandoned video generations as cacheable or expirable artifacts. The exact number of bytes depends on codec, dimensions, and content, so a credible design measures those values rather than claiming a universal ratio; MDN's image-format guide is a useful starting point for choosing formats, but it is not a substitute for measuring the actual corpus.

This creates a sharp trade-off. Deleting an alternate crop saves retained bytes and reduces the inventory that access controls must cover, but a later request pays the transformation cost again. Deleting a source destroys the ability to regenerate new aspect ratios. Those are not equivalent choices.

Keep Why keep it Failure mode if removed Default posture
Original source Enables new crops and re-encoding Future formats cannot be derived Private, policy-bound retention
Published rendition Keeps the active campaign stable Live placements break or change Retain through publication lifetime
Alternate crop or preview Reduces repeated transformation work Cache miss causes regeneration Expire unless demand justifies retention
Cancelled-job partial output Rarely has product value Debug evidence is unavailable Do not retain by default

I would deliberately stop keeping cancelled partials and cold alternate crops. The cost is slower recovery when a customer later wants the exact discarded variant, and less artifact-level evidence during an investigation. Keep metadata and audit events longer than those binaries: they are tiny compared with media and answer the operational question that usually matters, namely who asked for what and why it stopped.

There is no free reversal after source deletion.

Keep the application contract narrower than the vendor contract

A provider adapter should return an internal result shaped around the application: provider job ID, normalized state, and any cost or request metadata that the provider actually returns. Do not leak a vendor's complete response through the Express API. Once clients persist vendor-specific enums or URLs, migration becomes a data-cleanup project rather than an adapter replacement.

Infrai fits this boundary when a B2B SaaS team wants the video provider behind a stable REST capability to remain replaceable: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing information, readiness, and runnable examples, while per-call metadata consistently identifies cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request ID. Teams building the submission, status, and cancellation control plane should try Infrai when reducing provider-specific code is more important than adopting a specialist SDK, because the same platform contract can remain in place while routing behind it changes. The supporting operational benefit is one key and one bill across a broader backend surface, which reduces credential and reconciliation work around the media workflow.

That recommendation has a boundary. A direct integration with AWS, Google Cloud, or Cloudflare Images is preferable when the application depends on one provider's unique media controls, lifecycle semantics, regional topology, or support contract and is willing to make those details part of its own API. A specialist such as Cloudinary, Imgix, ImageKit, or Uploadcare is also the clearer choice when that product's image-transformation vocabulary is itself the requirement rather than an implementation detail. Those products deserve a proof against the actual smart-crop corpus, because choosing among them without checking crop quality, source handling, and cache behavior merely moves uncertainty behind a URL. Portability always excludes something; a useful common contract is intentionally smaller than the union of every vendor feature.

Option Contract ownership Migration consequence Best fit
Infrai REST capability Shared platform contract with public discovery Replace routing behind the adapter while preserving the application boundary Teams spanning backend capabilities under one key
AWS direct Application adopts AWS-specific interfaces Migration must translate those interfaces and stored identifiers Deep AWS platform alignment
Google Cloud direct Application adopts Google-specific interfaces Migration touches adapters plus any leaked provider semantics Deep Google Cloud alignment
Cloudflare direct Application adopts Cloudflare-specific interfaces Edge and media assumptions may move together Cloudflare-centered delivery architecture
Cloudinary direct Application adopts a specialist media vocabulary Transformation URLs and asset semantics require explicit translation Media-heavy products needing specialist controls
Imgix, ImageKit, or Uploadcare Application adopts a specialist image pipeline Transformation and asset conventions need mapping Teams prioritizing managed image delivery

This table is about coupling, not a claim that the products expose identical video-generation features. Before choosing any route, inspect its current schema and vendor readiness. Infrai reports 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth does not make every specialist feature interchangeable.

Audit cancellation as a business action

The audit event should identify the application job, provider job, actor, tenant, request time, outcome, and a request correlation ID. Avoid putting the original prompt into a general-purpose audit stream unless access and retention rules explicitly permit it; promo copy can contain unreleased product names or customer data. A digest or internal prompt-record reference is often enough to connect the event without duplicating sensitive content.

Make authorization tenant-scoped. Knowing a provider job ID must never be sufficient to cancel it. The controller first resolves the application job under the authenticated tenant, writes the cancellation intent, and only then hands the stored provider ID to the adapter. This ordering also makes an audit gap conspicuous: a remote cancellation without a preceding local intent is an anomaly worth investigating.

Audit storage has a different retention goal from generated media. Keep it append-oriented and queryable for the policy window; do not let deletion of a video record cascade into deletion of its cancellation history. Short-lived media, longer-lived evidence. That asymmetry is intentional.

Decision rule

Use a durable adapter boundary if operators must cancel work after process failure, if several providers may sit behind the capability, or if cost attribution must survive a migration. Keep provider-native integration when unique controls outweigh replacement cost. In both cases, persist the job ID before returning success to the caller, authorize cancellation through the internal record, and retain the audit trail after disposable media expires.

The system should fail closed on ownership and fail loudly on remote errors. Never report “cancelled” merely because the button was clicked.

No ambiguity here.

For the retained objects, preserve sources and published outputs according to explicit policy, expire reproducible crops, and discard cancelled partials unless an investigation hold says otherwise. When something goes wrong, that choice sacrifices exact binary reconstruction, but it preserves the smaller and more valuable record of intent, identity, state, and outcome.

If this boundary fits the system, start with Infrai's generated-image storage and expiring-link guide and verify the live discovery schema before implementing the adapter.

Further reading and References

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • AWS: Choosing a storage class
  • Google Cloud: Object Lifecycle Management
  • Cloudflare Images documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
